Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 5, verse 1 (part 1 of 4):

Student: I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿O you who have believed, fulfill [all] contracts. Lawful to you is the meat of grazing livestock except that which is recited to you [in the Qur'an], but not while you are in the state of ihram hunting game. Indeed, Allah ordains what He wills (1). O you who have believed, do not violate the rites of Allah or the sacred month or the sacrificial animals or the garlands [marking them] or those coming to the Sacred House seeking bounty from their Lord and [His] approval. And when you have come out of ihram, then hunt. And do not let the hatred of a people for having obstructed you from al-Masjid al-Haram lead you to transgress. And cooperate in righteousness and piety, but do not cooperate in sin and aggression. And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is severe in penalty﴾ [al-Ma'idah 1-2].

Shaykh: I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah the Exalted said: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿O you who have believed, fulfill [all] contracts.﴾ First, this surah is Madani, and it is among the last of the Qur'an to be revealed. For this reason the scholars said: whatever is permitted in it, permit it; whatever is prohibited in it, prohibit it. No ruling in it is abrogated; rather, all the rulings in it are muhkam (definitive). It is Madani because it was revealed after the Hijrah, and everything revealed after the Hijrah is Madani even if it was revealed in Makkah. Otherwise, in it is the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion and completed My favor upon you and have approved for you Islam as a religion﴾ [al-Ma'idah 3]. This was revealed at 'Arafah while the Prophet ﷺ was standing there.

The basmalah: there is no need to repeat the discussion of it, since it has already been covered: that it is an independent verse of the Book of Allah, not part of the surah before or after it, and it is recited at the beginning of every surah except Surah Bara'ah (al-Tawbah).

It is connected to an implied element, and this implied element is estimated as a verb that is delayed (after the phrase) and suitable to the topic that the basmalah precedes. This is the best of what has been said about the connection of the basmalah. Accordingly, if you want to read, you say: the prepositional phrase is connected to an implied verb whose estimate is: "In the name of Allah I read." That is, the estimate is: "In the name of Allah I read." If you want to perform ablution, you estimate: "In the name of Allah I perform ablution." If you want to slaughter a slaughtered animal, you say: "In the name of Allah I slaughter." This is the estimate.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿O you who have believed﴾. Know that when speech begins with this phrase, ﴿O you who have believed﴾, then, as 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Lend it your hearing" — meaning, pay attention to it — "for it is either good that you are commanded to do, or evil that you are forbidden from, or a report in which there is benefit for you."[[Narrated by Ibn al-Mubarak in al-Zuhd (36), and Sa'id ibn Mansur in al-Sunan (50), from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud.]] Like the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, indeed the polytheists are unclean﴾ [al-Tawbah 28], and what is similar to that. The point is that it must be for good, or for evil, or for a report that includes good or evil.

Know also that when speech begins with it, it indicates that what follows is among the requirements of faith: affirmation of it if it is a report, and acting upon it if it is a command; and that opposing that is a deficiency in faith.

Know also that Allah, the Exalted, begins address with it in order to stir up the one addressed, because when it is said, ﴿O you who have believed﴾, it is as if He is saying: your faith compels you to do such and such, or to leave such and such, according to the context.

﴿O you who have believed, fulfill [all] contracts.﴾ "Fulfill them" means: bring them complete and whole, without deficiency. Allah, the Exalted, has explained the warning against those who take full measure from others but do not give full measure themselves, in His saying: ﴿Woe to the defrauders (1) who, when they take a measure from people, take in full (2), but when they give a measure or weight to them, they cause loss﴾ [al-Mutaffifin 1-3].

So ﴿awfu﴾ means what? It means: bring them complete. From this is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And fulfill the covenant﴾ [al-Isra' 34], ﴿and give full measure when you measure﴾ [al-Isra' 35], and what is similar to that.

And ('uqud) is the plural of ('aqd), which is: what a person binds himself to with another. Its opposite is ḥall (untying). You say: "I tied (ʿaqadtu) the rope," and "I untied (ḥallaltu) the rope." So the 'uqud are: what a person binds with another. They are of many kinds, among them: sale, hire, pledge, endowment, marriage, and other than these.

And His saying: ﴿fulfill [all] contracts﴾ is general: any contract must be fulfilled. But it must be restricted by what the Sharia has brought, namely that the contract is not prohibited. If the contract is prohibited, the texts indicate that it is not to be fulfilled, indeed that fulfilling it is forbidden, because of the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Any condition that is not in the Book of Allah is void, even if it were a hundred conditions."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2168), and Muslim (1504/8), from the hadith of 'A'ishah.]]

Then He said: ﴿Lawful to you is the meat of grazing livestock﴾. ﴿Uḥillat﴾ is a verb in the passive form of what? It is the passive whose agent is not named, but its agent is known and not unknown, because the agent here is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, as Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And do not say, regarding what your tongues describe falsely, "This is lawful and this is unlawful," to invent falsehood against Allah﴾ [al-Nahl 116]. So the one who makes lawful here is Allah.

And His saying: ﴿bahimat al-an'am﴾. Al-bahimah is that which does not speak; every animal that does not speak is a bahimah, because what speaks is clear and known, while what does not speak is obscure (mubham), so it is called bahimah.

And His saying: ﴿al-an'am﴾ means three kinds: camels, cattle, and sheep. The idafah of bahimah to al-an'am is from the category of attributing a thing to its genus, as you say: "a ring of iron," and "a door of wood," and what is similar to that. It is as if He said: the bahimah from among the an'am.

The bahimat al-an'am are the camels. When we say: "and they are the camels, cattle, and sheep," are we explaining the bahimah or the an'am?

Students: The an'am.

Shaykh: The an'am, meaning camels, cattle, and sheep.

﴿except that which is recited to you﴾. This is an exception from His saying: ﴿bahimat al-an'am﴾, because bahimat al-an'am is a singular noun in the construct, so it is general for everything. ﴿Bahimat al-an'am﴾, He said: ﴿except that which is recited to you﴾, and what is meant by this is what will come in the verse after it, in His saying: ﴿Prohibited to you are carrion and blood﴾, and so on to the end. This is what is recited to us.

﴿not while you are hunting game﴾. This is an exception from His saying: ﴿Lawful to you is the meat of grazing livestock﴾. It may be a circumstantial clause (hal), and this is closer, because it is attached to the active participle. That is: lawful to you while you are not hunting game, and you are in ihram.

His saying: ﴿muḥillī al-ṣayd﴾ means: those who permit it for themselves, by hunting it. ﴿Wa-antum ḥurum﴾ is a circumstantial clause. Ḥurum is the plural of ḥarām, and it refers to one who has entered into ihram for Hajj or 'Umrah, or who has entered the sacred precinct (ḥaram) even if he is not in ihram. The sacred precinct in Makkah is known by its boundaries, and likewise in Madinah, but Madinah is not like Makkah in sanctity; it is less, as will be mentioned, Allah willing.

﴿Indeed, Allah ordains what He wills﴾. This sentence serves as a reason for what precedes it. When He, the Mighty and Majestic, mentioned permission and prohibition, He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah ordains what He wills﴾. Is this a legislative ruling or a cosmic ruling?

Students: Both.

Shaykh: Yes, it includes both the cosmic ruling and the legislative ruling. Whatever Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, wills, He rules by it, because none can repel His judgment. If He wills, He makes this lawful and that unlawful; if He wills, He obligates this and grants leniency in that. Likewise, if He wills, He decrees for His servants wealth and security, and if He wills, He decrees the opposite. The cosmic and legislative rulings are all by the will of Allah, and no one objects to the judgment of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, as He said: ﴿The judgment is only for Allah﴾ [Yusuf 40], meaning: judgment belongs only to Allah, ﴿He has commanded that you not worship except Him﴾.

His saying: ﴿yurid﴾ — which of the two wills is meant? We say: it is the cosmic will, considering the ruling is cosmic, and the legislative will, considering the ruling is legislative. Accordingly, we must distinguish between the two wills: the cosmic and the legislative.

The difference between them: the cosmic will means the (divine) decree (mashi'ah), so it applies to what Allah loves and what He does not love, and what He wills always occurs in every case. As for the legislative will, it means love (mahabbah), so "yurid" means "yuhibb" (loves), and it applies only to what Allah loves; the willed thing may occur or may not occur. This is the difference between the cosmic and legislative wills.

* In this noble verse there are benefits, among them: the excellence of faith, by addressing the believers with the address of Allah, the Exalted.

* Among them: the importance of what is mentioned after this call, because in speech there is a difference between saying "do such and such," and saying "O so-and-so, do such and such." Which is stronger? The second is stronger, because you called him so that he would pay attention to you. So there is importance in what is mentioned after this call.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the obligation to fulfill contracts, because of His saying: ﴿fulfill [all] contracts﴾. The default in a command is obligation, especially when it concerns the rights of others, and a contract concerns the rights of others, since it is the binding of something between you and another. So the command to fulfill is for obligation.

* Among them: that all contracts are lawful. The reasoning: Allah commanded them, and Allah commanded fulfilling them, and Allah does not command fulfilling indecency at all. But this is not absolute in its generality, since what the Sharia has prohibited is excluded from it, such as the sale of gharar (uncertainty), the sale of the "calf of the pregnant she-camel" (habal al-habalah), usury-based sale, gambling, and what is similar to that.

* Among them: that contracts are concluded by whatever indicates them, whether by speech or action, by word or gesture or writing. From where is this benefit taken? Because Allah stated the contract without restriction, so whatever becomes a contract between people is a contract.

From this branch many issues: among them, the permissibility of sale by mu'atah (exchange by conduct). Do you know mu'atah? Mu'atah is that a person comes to the baker, and there is a sign that says: "the loaf for one riyal." He places the riyal in the place of the money and takes the loaf. This is a sale by what? By mu'atah; there is no offer and acceptance in words, no sale or purchase spoken, yet people know it is a contract.

Likewise: boarding buses. A person enters, the bus door is open, he enters and pays the fare to the one at the door, and does not conclude the hire with a formula. This too is a hire by mu'atah.

Likewise: marriage is concluded by whatever indicates it, and it does not require the word "I married you." If he says: "I have given you my daughter in ownership (mallaktuka)," and he says: "I accept," is the contract valid or not?

Students: It is valid.

Shaykh: Yes, it is valid, because this is well known. And it has come in the hadith of the woman who gave herself in marriage, in al-Bukhari, the phrase: "I have given her to you in ownership (mallaktukaha) with what you have of the Qur'an."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5030), and Muslim (1425/76), from the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd.]]

* Among the benefits of this verse: the obligation to fulfill the conditions stipulated in a contract. That is: if two men conclude a contract between them, a sale or other, and they stipulate conditions, what is the default? The obligation to fulfill the condition. This is because His saying: ﴿contracts﴾ includes fulfilling the contract itself and its attributes, which are its conditions, since conditions in a contract are in reality attributes of the contract, and the command to fulfill the contract is a command to fulfill it along with what it includes of attributes.

If the two contracting parties stipulate a condition and a dispute arises over whether this condition is valid or not, who is right? The correct position is with the one who says it is valid, until the one who prevents it establishes evidence for the prohibition. On this basis, we leave people to their transactions until we are certain that there is a violation of the Sharia in them. So the default in transactions is what?

Student: That they be upheld; the obligation to fulfill.

Shaykh: Yes, the default is that you leave them as they are, until evidence establishes that they are prohibited.

Does this include fulfilling pledges? Yes, because a pledge ('ahd) is a contract, as in another verse: ﴿And fulfill the covenant; indeed, the covenant will be questioned﴾ [al-Isra' 34].

Does this include fulfilling a promise (wa'd)? If you say to a person: "I will pass by you tomorrow at such-and-such an hour," is it obligatory for you to fulfill that?

Students: Yes.

Student: Not by this verse.

Shaykh: The correct view is yes, it is obligatory for you to fulfill it, because a promise is a pledge, and because breaking a promise is one of the characteristics of the hypocrites. When the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Indeed the hypocrite, when he promises, breaks it,"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6095), and Muslim (59/107), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] he did not intend to convey to our understanding this trait of the hypocrites; rather he wants us to avoid it and beware of it. For this reason, the preponderant view is that fulfilling a promise is obligatory, and that it is not permissible for a person to break a promise except for a legitimate excuse.

It is strange that some who are deluded by the morals of disbelieving nations say to their companion when they promise him: "It is an English promise"? Even though the disbelievers are among the furthest people from fulfilling promises. And it would have been right for him to say: "It is a promise..."

Student: "A Muslim's."

Shaykh: Yes, "a believer's," because the believer is the one who does not break a promise except for a legitimate excuse.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that all livestock quadrupeds are lawful, because of His saying: ﴿Lawful to you is the meat of grazing livestock﴾. And other than the livestock, are they lawful or not? We say: they are lawful, but not by this verse; rather by His saying: ﴿It is He who created for you all that is on the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah 29].

Accordingly, if we doubt whether a creeping or flying animal is lawful or unlawful, the default is that it is lawful. Whoever prohibits it, we say: bring the evidence; otherwise it is lawful.

If we doubt whether a lawful animal was slaughtered in the legal manner or not, what is the default? The default is its absence. The default is the absence of the legal slaughter, because slaughter is an act whose existence must be verified. So if we find, for example, a limb of a sheep and do not know whether it was slaughtered or not, we say: it is not lawful, because the default is the absence of slaughter unless there is an apparent indication that outweighs this default.

If there is an apparent indication that outweighs this default, then we act on it. So if we find the leg of a sheep near a house of the Muslims, we do not know whether it was slaughtered or not; the default is non-permissibility. But here there is an apparent indication that outweighs the default, namely that its presence among the houses of Muslims indicates that it was slaughtered, so this apparent indication takes precedence over the default. For this reason the scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, said: if a person finds a slaughtered sheep in a town most of whose people are those whose slaughter is lawful, it is lawful, even though there is a possibility that the one who slaughtered it was not one whose slaughter is lawful, but the apparent indication is stronger.

* Among the benefits of this verse: referring to what has been mentioned or what will be mentioned. From where is this taken?

Students: ﴿except that which is recited to you﴾.

Shaykh: ﴿except that which is recited to you﴾. This is a reference to what will be mentioned. The scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, have used this in their works, and the one we have seen use it most is who? Ibn Hajar. Ibn Hajar did not refer back to things very much! And yet sometimes he forgot to fulfill it, may Allah have mercy on him. So it is permissible to refer to something mentioned or that will be mentioned, as He said: ﴿except that which is recited to you﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the default regarding the bahimah of the an'am is permissibility, as we established a moment ago. The reasoning for the exception from this ruling: ﴿Uḥillat﴾ and ﴿illa﴾.

The scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, said: exception is the criterion of generality. It is a standard: if you find something with an exception, know that the ruling is general, because when He excluded this individual from its individuals, it is known that the ruling encompasses all the individuals.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that hunting is not lawful for one in ihram, because of His saying: ﴿not while you are hunting game and you are in ihram﴾; nor for one who is in the sacred precinct, because one who is in the sacred precinct has entered a sanctified atmosphere, a sanctified space in which hunting is forbidden, so hunting is forbidden to him.

**The Shaykh:** Lakin law sadahu sayudan halalan, ya'ni anhara al-dam wa samma Allah wa qatalahu, hal yahillu aw la yahillu?

* **Students:** La yahillu.
* **A student:** Yahillu.
* **The Shaykh:** Onzur al-ayah: ﴿Not hunting game while you are in the state of ihram (pilgrim consecration)﴾.
* **Students:** Ma yahillu.
* **The Shaykh:** La yahillu, li-annahu qala: ghayra muhillih al-sayd. Fa-dalla dhalika 'ala annahum idha qatalūhu fa-huwa haram, fa-la yahillu lahum an yuhillūhu li-anfusihim. Wa lihadha 'abbara Allah 'an sayd al-sayd bi-l-qatl, fa-qala ta'ala fi ayah ukhra: ﴿O you who believe, do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram﴾ [al-Ma'idah]. Wa ma'lum annahu la yuridu an yaqtula bi-ghayr al-sayd al-shar'i, li-anna al-qatl bi-ghayr al-sayd al-shar'i manhiyyun 'anhu, sawa'an kana al-insan muhriman am ghayra muhrim. Lakin lamma kana al-sayd fi hal al-ihram haraman sara hadha al-sayd bi-manzilat al-qatl, fa-yakunu al-masid haraman.
* Wa min fawa'id al-ayah al-karimah: ta'zim al-ihram, wa annahu yuharramu 'ala al-muhrim al-sayd, li-'alla yansaba wara'a al-sayd fa-yansa al-ihram. Idh min al-ma'lum al-an fi ahl al-sayd annahum shaghufuna bihi, wa annahu ya'khudhu bi-lubbihim wa 'uqulihim, hatta innaka tara al-sayyad yalhaqu al-sayd wa al-hasa yadmi qadamahu wa al-shawku yakhruquha wa ma'a dhalika la yubali. Law uhilla al-sayd lil-muhrim latalaha bihi 'an ayyish? 'An ihramihi wa ghafal.
* Wa min fawa'id al-ayah al-karimah: ithbat al-hukm lillah, li-qawlihi: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands what He wills﴾.
* Wa min fawa'id al-ayah aydan: ithbat al-iradah lillah fi qawlihi: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands what He wills﴾.
* Wa min fawa'id al-ayah al-karimah: al-ishara ila annahu la yahillu lil-insan an yu'tariḍa 'ala al-ahkam al-shar'iyyah. Lima dha? Li-anna Allah khatamaha bi-qawlihi: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands what He wills﴾. Khatama al-ayah lamma dhakara anwa'an min al-ahkam qala: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands what He wills﴾.

Then Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾. We will speak about the basmalah (the formula "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful"), although this has passed us many times, but perhaps some of the brothers were not present.

The basmalah is an ayah from the Book of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and it begins every surah except Surat Bara'ah (al-Tawbah), for it does not begin with the basmalah. The reason is that every ayah that was revealed, the Prophet ﷺ would indicate its place; but in Surat Bara'ah he did not mention the basmalah. So the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, left it without the basmalah. However, it became unclear to them whether it was independent or part of al-Anfal, so they placed a separation between them without the basmalah. As for what some common people say, that the jinn snatched it away, this has no basis whatsoever, and it is not permissible to believe it.

For this reason some common people say, and I have seen it myself in some mushafs: "I seek refuge in Allah from the Fire, and from the wrath of the Almighty, and from the plots of the wicked," in place of the basmalah. This is forbidden and not permissible.

We say: this is how the Companions wrote it, and they are our exemplars and our role models.

It is part of an ayah in Surat al-Naml, because Allah the Exalted mentioned it by way of narration.

If we consider it an ayah, is it independent or attached to what follows it?

It is independent, not attached to what follows it, so it is not counted among its ayat. But people have differed concerning the basmalah in Surat al-Fatihah: is it independent, or is it one of the ayat of al-Fatihah?

The correct view is that it is independent, because the verbal and practical Sunnah indicate this. As for the verbal: in the sacred hadith (hadith qudsi, a hadith in which Allah speaks in the first person), Allah the Blessed and Exalted said: "I have divided the prayer between Myself and My servant into two halves. When he says: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾, Allah says: 'My servant has praised Me.'"[[Recorded by Muslim (395/38) from Abu Hurayrah.]] and he mentioned the hadith, and did not mention the basmalah.

As for the practical Sunnah: the Prophet ﷺ did not pronounce the basmalah aloud.[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (743) and Muslim (339/52) from Anas.]] This is what is established from him. His leaving off pronouncing the basmalah aloud in the audibly recited prayers indicates that it is not part of al-Fatihah; otherwise he would have pronounced it aloud as he pronounces the rest of its ayat.

It remains to be said: the basmalah begins with a preposition (harf al-jarr), and it is well known that prepositions must have a governing element called the mutaʿallaq (the element to which the preposition is attached). So where is its mutaʿallaq?

The answer: its mutaʿallaq is omitted and is to be understood after it. As for its being omitted, it is because it is not present, so it must be understood (muqaddar).

As for its being understood after it, this is for two reasons:

The first reason: to seek blessing by beginning with the name of Allah.

The second reason: to indicate restriction (al-hasr), as if you were saying: I do not recite, for example, except with "In the name of Allah."

So is it understood as delayed or as preceding?

Delayed, for the two reasons we have mentioned. And how do we understand it? Do we understand it as a noun or as a verb? And do we understand it as general or as specific?

These are four possibilities: do we understand it as a verb or as a noun?

We say: we understand it as a verb, because the verb is the original element in governing, and therefore you will not find a noun acting like a verb except under conditions; and when the verb is the original, its being understood is more appropriate than understanding a noun.

And do we understand it as general or specific?

We say: we understand it as specific, because the specific indicates the intended meaning more than the general does. Now let us give examples. If we understand: "In the name of Allah, I begin," this contradicts the more appropriate option in two respects: "In the name of Allah, I begin" contradicts it in two respects:
The first: we understood it as a noun.
The second: we understood it as general.

If he says: "In the name of Allah, I begin," it contradicts it in one respect only, which is that you understood it as general.

If you say: "In the name of Allah, my recitation," it contradicts it in one respect only, which is that you understood it as a noun.

If you say: "In the name of Allah, I recite," this is the best of the understandings, because it is a verb, delayed, and specific, so it is more indicative. The evidence is that you understand the specific appropriate verb from the hadith: "Whoever has not slaughtered, let him slaughter in the name of Allah."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (985) and Muslim (1960/1) from Jundub ibn Sufyan.]] This indicates that you understand the appropriate specific verb.

When performing wudu': "In the name of Allah"; the understanding: "I perform wudu'." When reciting: "In the name of Allah"; "I recite." When writing: "In the name of Allah"; "I write."

As for "the name of Allah": it is a singular noun in construct with Allah the Mighty and Majestic, so it implies beginning with every name of Allah. Thus when you say "In the name of Allah," it is as if you said "With every name of Allah."

"Allah" is a very great word, a proper noun for Allah the Majestic and Exalted, which is not named by anyone else, neither in the Jahiliyyah nor in Islam. It is the root of all the names, and for this reason the names do not come except after it, following it, because it is the origin.

* **A student:** (...) Beginning with "In the name of Allah" in the middle of surahs?
* **The Shaykh:** Beginning with "In the name of Allah" in the middle of a surah: some scholars mentioned that it is a Sunnah, meaning recommended. The correct view is that it is not recommended, because Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan﴾ [al-Nahl 98]. So for example, if you say: "I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan, In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful, ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾" [al-Baqarah 284], then you have added to it. It is as if you were saying only: "I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan." If someone says: "Isn't this an action, and should I not begin every action with the basmalah?"
We say: if you say this, then say: "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful. I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan." But the correct view is that it is not recommended to begin with it.
* **A student:** But, Shaykh, in schools the students are taught and it is repeated to them (...).
* **The Shaykh:** Yes, they are taught so that they will not take it as a Sunnah.
* **A student:** May Allah reward you well. Some innovators say: "Allah is capable of all things." Is Allah, glorified and exalted, capable of creating Himself?
* **The Shaykh:** I seek refuge in Allah!
* **The student:** And some of them say: Is Allah capable of the non-existent? Such questions.
* **The Shaykh:** This is not contrary to the truth. We say: as for being capable of creating Himself, how could this be? Because before Himself He was non-existent, so how could it be?

As for His capability over the non-existent, yes, He is able to create what did not exist before it existed. Are the heavens and the earth eternal and without beginning?

Not at all. They are not eternal and existent; they came to exist after they were not. Everything other than Allah exists after it did not exist. But they (the innovators) say: the devil's sons said to him: "When the worshipper dies you do not care about him, but when the scholar dies you rejoice greatly?" He said: "Yes, because the scholar is more harmful to me than the worshipper." He said: "The death of the worshipper, when he dies, he dies for himself; but the scholar is the one who wages war against me, so I rejoice when he dies." They said: "Fine, we want an example." So he sent to the worshipper and said: "Can Allah place the heavens and the earth in an egg?" What did the worshipper say?
He said: "It is impossible, it cannot be." He sent to the scholar and said: "Can Allah place the heavens and the earth in an egg?"
He said: ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Yasin 82]. He (the devil) said: "Well done, this is a good man; this worshipper may have lived a hundred years, and he described Allah with incapacity." The scholar spoke a true word: if Allah the Mighty and Majestic wills to place the heavens and the earth in an egg, He says "Be," and it is. And although we do not grasp this with our minds, the important thing is that the devil casts such things upon a person.

But when a person says: "I believe in Allah, and that He is capable of all things, and that His command, when He intends a thing, is only to say to it, 'Be,' and it is," this disappears.

* **A student:** What is the difference between the possible non-existent and the impossible non-existent?
* **The Shaykh:** Not at all. All of this is among the methods of the mutakallimun (scholastic theologians), and one should not investigate them at all.

* * *

* **A student:** I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful. ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who created the heavens and the earth and made darknesses and light. Yet those who disbelieve equate others with their Lord. (1) He is the one who created you from clay and then decreed a term, and there is an appointed time with Him; then you still doubt. (2) And He is Allah in the heavens and on the earth; He knows what you conceal and what you declare, and He knows what you earn﴾ [al-An'am 1–3].
* **The Shaykh:** I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. In the previous lesson we began speaking about the basmalah, did we not?

We reached His saying, blessed and exalted: ﴿In the name of Allah﴾, and we mentioned that this great name is the origin of the names, and that no one is named by it except Allah the Mighty and Majestic.

As for His saying: ﴿the Most Merciful﴾: al-Rahman is derived from mercy, but it is in the form fa'lan, and this form indicates vastness and fullness, so its meaning is: He who has vast mercy. For this reason some of them explained it as: the one who has general mercy. But the correct view is that He is the one with vast mercy, who has mercy on whomever He wills, the Mighty and Majestic. It indicates the attribute more than the act; it is more indicative of the attribute of Allah than of an act.

As for ﴿the Especially Merciful﴾: it is also an intensive form from mercy, but it indicates the act more than the attribute. Al-Rahman came first because it is an attribute, and al-Rahim came because it is an act: He is Rahman, who shows mercy. Allah the Blessed and Exalted mentioned that He is Merciful to the believers, and the intended meaning there is the special mercy.

So al-Rahman indicates what? It indicates the attribute, and al-Rahim indicates the act; that is, He has mercy.

The scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, divided mercy into two types: general and special. As for the general, it encompasses all creation: the believer and the disbeliever, the righteous and the wicked, the young and the old, the animal and the rational; all creation is under the mercy of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and no one is excluded from this general mercy.

The special mercy is that which is specific to the believers. The difference between them is that the special mercy is connected to the mercy of the Hereafter, so Allah the Mighty and Majestic has mercy upon the believers in this world and mercy in the Hereafter.

As for the general mercy, it has no effect except in this world. For this reason we say: the disbelievers in the Hereafter are treated with justice, not with mercy. Animals and non-rational beings are also treated with justice, for Allah judges between them, between the animals; then He commands them to become dust, and they become dust, with no bliss.

So mercy is of how many kinds? Two types: general, which encompasses all creation; and special, which is specific to the believers.

The difference between them is that the general is only in this world, while the special is in this world and the Hereafter. O Allah, have mercy upon us by Your mercy.

And mentioning these two noble names at the basmalah, which precedes the servant's act and speech, is an indication that if Allah does not have mercy on you, you will not benefit from this act or this speech. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ said: "No one will enter Paradise by his deeds." They said: "Not even you, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Not even I, unless Allah covers me with His mercy."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5673) and Muslim (2816/71) from Abu Hurayrah.]]

He said: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who created the heavens and the earth﴾. The "al" here (in al-hamd) is for comprehensiveness; that is, all praise, in every respect, is established for Allah the Mighty and Majestic. The "lam" in His saying ﴿lillah﴾ is either for exclusivity (al-ikhtisas) or for entitlement (al-istihqaq).

There is no contradiction between the two meanings, and on this basis it is both for entitlement and exclusivity, because the "al" in His saying ﴿al-hamdu lillah﴾ is for generality, and no one deserves praise in the fullest generality except Allah the Mighty and Majestic. So the "lam" is for entitlement, and for exclusivity as well. But what is praise (hamd)?

Many people define hamd as "praise for a beautiful voluntary quality." But this is not correct, because praise (thana') is the repetition of praise. The evidence for this is His saying, blessed and exalted, in the sacred hadith: "When the servant says ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾, Allah says: 'My servant has praised Me.' And when he says ﴿the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾, He says: 'He has extolled Me.'"[[Recorded by Muslim (395/38) from Abu Hurayrah.]] This indicates that thana' is the repetition of the complete attribute, and the derivation indicates this, because thana' comes from thanayy, which is repeating a thing, or returning part of a thing to another part.

As for their saying "for a beautiful voluntary quality," it is not correct with regard to Allah the Mighty and Majestic, because Allah is praised for what He does, and He chooses what He wills, and He is praised for the perfection of His inherent attributes that do not extend to anyone else. He is praised for the perfection of His life, and praised for the perfection of His self-subsistence (qayyumiyyah). The first is an inherent attribute, and the second is a transitive attribute, and also inherent, as was explained earlier.

So the correct view is that praising Allah is for His actions that He chooses, and for His perfect inherent attributes. So how do we define it?

We say: hamd is describing the praised one with perfection, out of love and veneration.

Hamd is describing the praised one with inherent and transitive perfection, out of love and veneration. This is because describing someone with perfection may be done without love for him, but out of hope for what he will reward you with; and you may love him, or praise him, not out of love and veneration, but out of fear of his evil.

So hamd must be qualified as being out of love and veneration. If it is not out of love and veneration, it is madh (praise in a general sense). Look at the depth of the Arabic language, how it distinguishes between hamd and madh though they are equal in letters in kind and number!

The letters are three, that is the number; the kind is the same letters (ḥā', mīm, dāl), but the order of the letters differs. Hamd and madh differ in meaning because of the difference in this order. The relationship between them is that of particular and general: every hamd is madh, but not every madh is hamd, because hamd, as we said, must be out of love and veneration, while madh may be otherwise. A man may praise a ruler or a minister, or the like, without love for him or veneration of him, but hoping for his gift or fearing him. But hamd is not like that.

Ibn al-Qayyim (may Allah have mercy on him) explained the differences between them in his book *Badai' al-Fawa'id*, which our Shaykh urged us to study when seeking knowledge. He said it is a great book. *Sayd al-Khatir* by Ibn al-Jawzi resembles it in some respects, but in depth, meaning and benefit they are not equal and cannot be compared. Ibn al-Qayyim (may Allah have mercy on him) clarified the differences between *al-hamd* (praise, in the sense of gratitude and glorification) and *al-madh* (commendation), and he examined the topic thoroughly until he brought it to maturity. He also said that our Shaykh, meaning Ibn Taymiyyah (may Allah have mercy on him), when he investigated such matters, produced astonishing wonders, may Allah have mercy on him. But, as it is said:

"The lightning flashed from Najd, and I said to it:
Away from me, for I am preoccupied with other things."

This is because Shaykh al-Islam did not have leisure to speak at length about such matters. He spoke about things of greater importance. Our brother and colleague Farid ibn Abd al-Aziz al-Zamil collected the grammatical discussions that Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah addressed into a treatise, but it has not yet been published. This is good. A similar example occurs in *Iqtida' al-Sirat al-Mustaqim*, where, in discussing the words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿وَخُضْتُمْ كَالَّذِي خَاضُوا﴾ [At-Tawbah 69] (*"and you plunged in as those before you plunged"*), he investigated the matter in a way you will not find in any other book, may Allah have mercy on him.

To return to our topic. *Al-hamd* is describing the one who is praised with perfection, out of love and exaltation.

﴿لِلَّهِ﴾: We said that the *lam* here is *lam al-istihqaq wa'l-ikhtisas* (the lam of entitlement and exclusivity). No one deserves all praise from every aspect except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

This praise mentioned is exclusive to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. He, may He be exalted, is worthy of being praised, and perfect praise belongs to Him alone.

As for *Allah*, it is a proper name (*'alam*) for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and expressing Him by it is better than expressing Him by anything else. Some people now say: "The Truth said such and such, the Truth said such and such." It is true that Allah is the Manifest Truth, but make your expression conform to the expression of the early generations (*al-salaf*). They say: "Allah said," or they say: "Our Lord said." As for "the Truth said," a person uses it to open the minds of listeners, so that the hearer asks: "Who is this Truth?" But we say: "Allah said," which is the name upon which divinity (*al-uluhiyyah*) and worship are built, and that is better. Yet there is no harm in saying: "Our Lord said," or "Your Lord said," just as the Messenger (ﷺ) would sometimes say to his companions: "Do you know what your Lord said?"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (846) and Muslim (71/125), from the hadith of Zayd ibn Khalid.]]

﴿اللَّهِ﴾: It is derived from *al-uluhiyyah* (divinity). *Alaha* means *ta'abbada* (to worship), not *tahayyara* (to be bewildered), as some have claimed, because when a person says "Allah," he does not find bewilderment; he finds a well-known Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, in whom there is no bewilderment. They say its origin is *al-Ilah*, but the hamza was dropped due to frequent use. They also say its parallel is *al-nas* (the people), whose origin is *al-unas*, and the words *khayr* (good) and *sharr* (evil), whose origins are *akhyar* and *ashrar*.

So ﴿اللَّهِ﴾ originally was *al-Ilah*, and it comes from *alaha*, meaning *ta'abbada* (worshipped); *alaha-hu* means *ta'abbada lahu* (worshipped Him). Is it derived or is it a solid noun (*jamid*)?

The correct view is that it is derived. No name of Allah, no name of His Messenger (ﷺ), and no name of the Qur'an is ever a solid noun, because a solid noun means it has no meaning except to indicate the specific referent alone. As Ibn Malik said, a proper name is:

"A noun that specifies the named absolutely, its proper name like *Ja'far* and *Khirniq*."

So if we said that the names of Allah, or the names of the Messenger, or the names of the Glorious Book are solid nouns, that would mean they indicate only the specification of the named. Instead, we say they are derived, indicating both the specification of the named and the meaning from which they are derived. This is necessary.

So ﴿اللَّهِ﴾ is derived from *al-Ilah* or *al-uluhiyyah*, which is worship of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

﴿الَّذِي خَلَقَ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضَ﴾ (*alladhi*): This is a description of the divine name ﴿اللَّهِ﴾: ﴿who created the heavens and the earth﴾.

﴿خَلَقَ﴾ means He brought them into existence according to a firm decree, because the basic meaning of *khalq* (creation) in the language is *taqdir* (determination). As the poet said:

"Indeed you measure what you have decreed, while some people decree but do not measure."

(*yafri*) means *yaf'al* (does). (*tafri ma khalaqta*) means *ma qaddarta* (what you have determined), and no one can prevent you. Thus *khalq* is bringing into existence with a firm determination.

As for ﴿السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضَ﴾: ﴿السَّمَاوَاتِ﴾ is the object of ﴿خَلَقَ﴾. There is no objection to saying that it is an object, contrary to those who said it is not valid for it to be an object, because the object must be affected by the verb and must exist, while the creation of the heavens and earth affected them before they were created. But we say this is overly artificial. The correct view, held by most grammarians (*al-mu'rabin*), is that *al-samawat* is the direct object.

﴿خَلَقَ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضَ﴾ ﴿السَّمَاوَاتِ﴾ comes from *sama yasmu*, meaning *'ala* (rose high). Allah has explained that there are seven of them, that they are layered (*tibaq*), that they are strong (*shidad*), and that they were built *bi-aydin*, meaning with power.

﴿وَالْأَرْضَ﴾ is conjoined to ﴿السَّمَاوَاتِ﴾. It is singular in form, but this does not prevent plurality when plurality is established. Note this condition: it does not prevent plurality if it is established that it is—what? Plural. If it had not been established that they were plural, we would say they are one, because that is what the wording implies. But we say the intended meaning is the genus (*jins*), and then it does not contradict plurality. Plurality is established by the apparent meaning of the Qur'an and the explicit Sunnah. As for the Qur'an, Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Allah is the One who created seven heavens and of the earth the like thereof﴾ [At-Talaq 12], meaning in number. No one can say that ﴿the like thereof﴾ refers to their nature and attributes, because the difference between heaven and earth is clear, so it is certain that the intended meaning is number, and that is correct.

As for the Sunnah, it is explicit. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever unjustly seizes a span of land, Allah will encircle him with it on the Day of Resurrection from seven earths."[[Narrated by Muslim (1610/137), from the hadith of Sa'id ibn Zayd.]] So *al-ard* (the earth) here means the genus, and this does not contradict plurality. The plurality of the earths is established by the apparent meaning of the Qur'an and the explicit Sunnah: they are seven.

﴿وَجَعَلَ الظُّلُمَاتِ وَالنُّورَ﴾: ﴿جَعَلَ﴾ means *khalaqa* (created). But if it means created, what is the wisdom in expressing creation by *ja'ala* (made/placed)?

It has been said: the wisdom is variety in expression (*tafannun fi al-'ibarah*), meaning changing the wording while the meaning remains the same, which is sometimes part of eloquence.

It has also been said: the wisdom is that light cannot subsist except with something else. Light cannot exist except with something else. For example, the light of the sun now cannot become apparent unless there is a body that receives it. That is why between us and the sun there is darkness, where there is no light, because light's effect cannot appear unless it falls upon a body. You can see now the difference between the sun shining on a body that receives heat and a body that does not, and on a body that receives whiteness' brightness and one that does not. Light cannot exist by itself and cannot be apparent unless it is reflected upon a body. This is the wisdom of His saying ﴿وَجَعَلَ﴾.

Another wisdom: darkness and light are both sensory (*hissiyyah*) and non-sensory (*ma'nawiyyah*).

Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan: ﴿Certainly, those who say, "Allah is the third of three," have disbelieved. And there is no god except one God. And if they do not desist from what they are saying, there will surely afflict the disbelievers among them a painful punishment. Will they not repent to Allah and seek His forgiveness? And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful. The Messiah, son of Mary, was not but a messenger; messengers had passed on before him. And his mother was a supporter of truth; they both used to eat food. Look how We make clear to them the signs; then look how they are turned away. Say, "Do you worship other than Allah that which controls for you no harm or benefit? And Allah is the Hearing, the Knowing." Say, "O People of the Scripture, do not commit excess in your religion beyond the truth and do not follow the inclinations of a people who had gone astray before and led many astray and strayed from the soundest way."﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 73–77].

Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Certainly, those who say, "Allah is the third of three," have disbelieved﴾. I think we have already discussed the verse.

﴿لَقَدْ كَفَرَ الَّذِينَ قَالُوا﴾ contains emphasis: how many emphatic particles are there?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: May Allah bless you. Why does Allah emphasize His speech with emphatic devices, even though He, the Mighty and Majestic, is the most truthful of speakers?

Student: This is a report, and a report may be contradicted by the disbelievers, so He came with this emphasis to argue against the opponent.

Shaykh: Because of the possibility of contradiction and denial. Good. But if the one who denies will deny regardless of emphasis?

Student: No, there is additional emphasis.

Another student: (...).

Shaykh: Because the Qur'an is in clear Arabic language, important matters are sworn to by Allah, even though they are already established by His report, the Mighty and Majestic.

Who are these three, ﴿ثَالِثُ ثَلَاثَةٍ﴾?

Student: The Jews and Christians (...).

Shaykh: (...) ﴿لَقَدْ كَفَرَ الَّذِينَ قَالُوا إِنَّ اللَّهَ ثَالِثُ ثَلَاثَةٍ﴾ ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ ثَالِثُ ثَلَاثَةٍ﴾. Who are they?

Student: The Christians.

Shaykh: Who are the three?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: Good. They say Allah is the third of three, so they affirm a plurality of gods. By what did Allah refute their statement?

Student: Allah refuted their statement by His saying: ﴿and there is no god except one God﴾.

Shaykh: ﴿وَمَا مِنْ إِلَهٍ إِلَّا إِلَهٌ وَاحِدٌ﴾. Is this restriction (*hasr*), or a mere statement without restriction?

Student: A statement.

Shaykh: A statement without restriction.

Student: Restriction.

Shaykh: What is its method? I mean, by what is the restriction made?

Student: By *ma min ilah illa ilah* ("there is no god except God").

Shaykh: It seems you have not studied rhetoric. Have you studied it?

Student: A little.

Shaykh: A little. What is the method of restriction?

Student: Negation and affirmation.

Shaykh: Negation and affirmation, correct. Negation and affirmation: ﴿وَمَا مِنْ إِلَهٍ إِلَّا إِلَهٌ﴾. This restriction is emphasized by the superfluous *min*. Do you know in rhetoric that all superfluous particles are emphatic?

Student: Yes.

Shaykh: Yes, correct, every superfluous particle is considered emphatic.

* * *

Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And if they do not desist from what they are saying, there will surely afflict the disbelievers among them a painful punishment﴾.

First, the grammatical analysis (*i'rab*): (*wa in lam yantahu layamassanna*): *in* is a conditional particle, with no difficulty, governing a negated present-tense verb. ﴿لَيَمَسَّنَّ﴾ is the answer to what?

Student: The answer to the condition.

Shaykh: The answer to the condition is problematic. If we say it is the answer to the condition, it is problematic, because the answer to the condition does not come in this form. Rather, it is the answer to an implied oath, together with its *lam* (the *lam al-muwatta'ah*, the preparatory lam for an oath). The implied sense is: "If they do not desist from what they say, the disbelievers among them will surely be touched by a painful punishment." The word ﴿لَيَمَسَّنَّ﴾ cannot be the answer to the condition, because of the presence of the *lam* that prepares for the oath and the presence of emphasis in ﴿لَيَمَسَّنَّ﴾.

As for His saying: ﴿الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا مِنْهُمْ عَذَابٌ أَلِيمٌ﴾, does this contradict His saying ﴿لَقَدْ كَفَرَ﴾ and then say ﴿لَيَمَسَّنَّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا مِنْهُمْ﴾? No, because the meaning is: a painful punishment will touch those among them who persisted in their disbelief. As for one who repents, Allah will accept his repentance.

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿And if they do not desist from what they say﴾, meaning from multiplying gods and from saying that Allah is the third of three. ﴿Will surely touch﴾, meaning will afflict. ﴿Those among them who disbelieved﴾, meaning those who persisted in disbelief, because they are disbelievers.

In ﴿الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا مِنْهُمْ عَذَابٌ أَلِيمٌ﴾, *'adhab* (punishment) is the subject of *yamass* (touch), and ﴿أَلِيمٌ﴾ means *mu'lim* (painful). The punishment of the disbelievers is painful, both psychologically and physically. Psychologically, they are rebuked with humiliating reproach, to the point that one of them is told mockingly: ﴿Taste it, indeed you are the mighty, the noble﴾ [Ad-Dukhan 49]. There is no doubt this is the greatest humiliation, one who is punished and has boiling water poured over his head, and then is told: ﴿Taste it, indeed you are the mighty, the noble.﴾ This is humiliation and great punishment. And Allah says to them: ﴿Be silent therein and do not speak to Me﴾ [Al-Mu'minun 108]. This is a punishment that breaks hearts.

As for physical punishment, do not ask. When they cry out for help and their pleas for water intensify, they are given water like molten brass that scorches faces before it reaches the bowels, and when it reaches the bowels it cuts them to pieces. We ask Allah for well-being. So it is painful: ﴿Every time their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins that they may taste the punishment﴾ [An-Nisa' 56]. When the skin is roasted it no longer feels, but they are given other skins ﴿that they may taste the punishment. Indeed Allah is ever Mighty and Wise﴾ [An-Nisa' 56]. So it is painful, painful to the heart and painful to the body.

* There are benefits in this verse. Among them: whoever claims a plurality of gods is a disbeliever, because he denies hearing (revelation), reason and natural disposition (*fitrah*). He denies hearing: the evidences for affirming the oneness of Allah are countless, are they not?

* Students: Yes.

Shaykh: Countless. He denies reason, because if there were many gods the world would not be in order: ﴿If there were in them gods besides Allah, they would have been ruined﴾ [Al-Anbiya' 22]. ﴿Allah has not taken any son, nor is there with Him any god. Otherwise, each god would have taken away what he created, and some would have overcome others﴾ [Al-Mu'minun 91]. The situation cannot remain orderly with multiple authorities. Now consider it yourselves: if you were on a journey and the leaders of the group were many, would the matter be in order? No. Where would we go, to this one or that one or that one? Would their word be united? No. This is a rational proof: ﴿otherwise each god would have taken away what he created and some would have overcome others﴾, and it must be so. Now the whole universe is harmonious, not colliding or contradicting, which indicates that its manager is one, may He be glorified and exalted. We say this with certainty, not merely because we lived in a land of monotheism, but because we are certain that multiple gods cannot be.

Natural disposition: every person is born upon the fitrah, every person, as the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿So set your face toward the religion, inclining to truth, the natural disposition of Allah upon which He created mankind. No change is there in the creation of Allah﴾ [Ar-Rum 30]. So plurality of gods is false by hearing, reason and natural disposition.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation that there is no god except Allah, based on His saying: ﴿and there is no god except Allah﴾ [Ali 'Imran 62].

If someone says: Are there not gods other than Allah, by Allah's naming them? Allah said: ﴿So their gods, which they invoked besides Allah, did not avail them at all﴾ [Hud 101]. And Allah said to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿And do not set up with Allah another god﴾ [Al-Isra' 39], and many verses indicate the existence of gods. How can this be reconciled with this great restriction, ﴿there is no god except Allah﴾?

The answer is very simple. We say: all these gods are false and avail nothing. That is why we say: "there is no god" means "there is no god who has the attribute of being a true god" that is omitted, and the meaning is: "there is no true god except Allah." With this the problem is resolved. This is supported by the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿That is because Allah is the Truth, and what they invoke besides Him is falsehood﴾ [Al-Hajj 62].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the opening of the door of repentance for everyone who has done wrong, however great his wrongdoing is. This is because of His words: ﴿And if they do not desist﴾ to the end of the verse. Allah the Exalted related their disbelief, and yet He presented to them that they should desist from what they say. From this is derived the generosity of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, His munificence, and His kindness, and that He offers His enemies that they desist from what they have described Him with, so that the painful punishment does not befall them.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of the justice of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, namely that He does not punish anyone except one who persists in his disbelief and disobedience.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a forceful warning against persisting in disbelief and polytheism, and that whoever persists in it will have a painful punishment.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 5, verse 2 (part 1 of 4):

Then He, exalted is He, said: "O you who have believed, do not violate the rites of Allah or the sacred month or the sacrificial animals or the garlands [marking them] or those coming to the Sacred House seeking bounty from their Lord and [His] approval."

We say concerning His words "O you who have believed" what we said concerning the first verse.

"Do not violate the rites of Allah": i.e., do not violate their sanctities. The word "shaʿāʾir" (rites) is the plural of "shaʿīrah," which means the great acts of worship, such as the Hajj, the ʿUmrah, and the like. That is because the legal rulings are of two kinds, rites and non-rites: the great rulings are called rites. Allah, exalted is He, said: "Indeed, aṣ-Ṣafā and al-Marwah are among the rites of Allah" [al-Baqarah 158].

"Nor the sacred month": the word "month" here is intended as a genus, not a single month. So what are the sacred months? The sacred months are four, which Allah, exalted is He, specified in His saying: "Indeed, the number of months with Allah is twelve months in the Book of Allah the day He created the heavens and the earth, of which four are sacred" [at-Tawbah 36]. The Prophet ﷺ specified these months by name: they are Dhul-Qaʿdah, Dhul-Hijjah, and al-Muḥarram, and the fourth is Rajab, the Rajab of Muḍar, which lies between Jumada and Shaʿban [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4406) and Muslim (1679/29) from the hadith of Abu Bakrah].

These are the sacred months. That is, do not violate them by sins, and do not violate them by fighting either, because fighting in the sacred months is forbidden. Even with the disbelievers, it is not permitted for us to initiate fighting against them in the sacred months, except in self-defence, or if it is a continuation of earlier fighting. Pay attention: the ruling on this matter and the scholars' disagreement concerning it will come, God willing.

"Nor the sacrificial animals": i.e., do not violate the sacrificial animals. By "al-hady" (sacrificial animals) is meant what is brought to the Sacred Precinct of camels, cattle, or sheep. And how is it violated? Its violation is by slaughtering it before it reaches its place of sacrifice. So if a person drives the sacrificial animal from the miqat, from Dhul-Hulayfah, and then wishes to slaughter or sacrifice it before reaching Makkah, this is forbidden and not permitted. For this reason He said: "Nor the sacrificial animals."

"Nor the garlands" (al-qalāʾid) is the plural of what? 
* Student: Qalādah.
* Shaykh: The plural of "qalādah." So what is meant by the garlands? What is meant by the garlands is that with which the necks of the sacrificial animals are garlanded. It was their custom to place a garland on the neck of each one, as a sign that it was a sacrificial animal. Into this garland they would attach worn-out sandals and the ends of water-skins, meaning the ends of waterskins and the like, as a sign that these are for the poor. So when a person sees this sheep or this camel with this garland on it, he knows that it is a sacrificial animal, so he respects it and does not harm it in any way.

"Nor the garlands": it may be said that "qalāʾid" is more general than that, and that what is meant is: nor what you have bound yourselves to of covenants, promises, and others. But the context indicates the first meaning: the sacrificial animals and the garlands, that is, the garlands of the sacrificial animals.

"Nor those coming to the Sacred House seeking bounty from their Lord and approval": i.e., do not violate them either. "Those coming" means intending. "The Sacred House" is the Kaʿbah. "Seeking bounty from their Lord and approval." Allah called it a house because it is in reality a house, being a chamber with corners and a roof, and so it is a house. He described it as sacred because of the sanctity and veneration it holds. For this reason, what is around it is also sacred; even the trees within the Sacred Precinct are sacred, although trees are inanimate.

And the pebbles?
* Student: Likewise.
* Shaykh: No, they are not sacred. Pebbles and dust are not sacred; for this reason you may break up pebbles, and you may carry dust out of the Sacred Precinct, unlike trees.

As for trees that do not grow, such as those that have dried up, and broken branches: are they sacred or not? The answer: they are not sacred; dry trees that have finished are not sacred.

"Seeking bounty from their Lord and approval": the phrase "seeking" (yabtaghūn) is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from "those coming" (āmmīn). As for "the Sacred House," it is the object of "āmmīn." "Yabtaghūn" means they seek. "Bounty from their Lord": the bounty here includes both worldly bounty and otherworldly bounty. The proof is His saying, blessed and exalted, when He mentioned the rulings of the Hajj: "There is no sin upon you in seeking bounty from your Lord" [al-Baqarah 198]. This is worldly bounty, pointing to one who comes to Hajj and buys and sells, or hires out his camel or his car, or the like. Here He says "seeking bounty from their Lord," which encompasses both bounties: the bounty of this world and the bounty of the Hereafter.

As for His saying "and approval" (riḍwānan), it means approval from Allah, mighty and majestic is He. There are two readings of it: with a dammah on the rāʾ and with a kasrah: "ruḍwānan" and "riḍwānan." His saying "and approval," i.e., from their Lord, or more general than that: do they seek approval from Allah, mighty and majestic, or approval from Allah and from His prophets, His friends, and His chosen ones? It is general, but the fundamental principle is that they seek bounty from Allah, mighty and majestic.

* Student: Shaykh, may Allah bless you. As for what we said, that a promise is a covenant and that a covenant must be fulfilled: if a man makes an exception and says "in shā' Allāh" regarding a promise, for example, must he in every case say "in shā' Allāh," since a promise concerns what is to come?

* Shaykh: By context, and perhaps the promiser's gesture indicates this: he says "in shā' Allāh" like this with his hand, meaning confirmation.

* Student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you. We said that the fulfilment of conditions stipulated in a contract is obligatory. So, for example, in a marriage contract: if the wife stipulates that he should not take another wife over her...
* Shaykh: That he should not marry another woman over her.
* Student: Yes. Must he fulfil this condition, or may he say this condition...?
* Shaykh: This is a question: does the fulfilment of conditions include the conditions of marriage?
The answer is yes. Indeed, the Prophet ﷺ said: "The most deserving of conditions to be fulfilled are those by which you made lawful the private parts" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2721), the wording is his, and Muslim (1418/63), from the hadith of ʿUqbah ibn ʿĀmir].
He says: if the woman stipulates to her husband that he will not marry another over her, is the condition valid? It is valid. And if the wife stipulates that he divorce the wife he has with him? It is not valid. The difference is clear: the second involves aggression against the first wife, whereas the first involves aggression against no one. In the first, the husband refrains from what Allah has permitted him, but by his own choice; he is the one who agreed. But if he insists on marrying and does marry, what then? We say: she has the option; if she wishes she remains with him, and if she wishes she annuls the marriage.
* Student: Shaykh, may Allah bless you. Regarding the wording of marriage contracts: is a marriage valid with any wording, or only with the wordings found in the noble Qur'an?
* Shaykh: No, it is valid with any wording, not at all. If he says: "I have made you owner of my daughter," or "I have given you my daughter," and it is known that by "gift" he means not free of charge, there is no harm. Whatever the contract indicates is valid, without detail.
* Student: We said that the scholars mentioned, regarding the words of the Mighty and Majestic, "Fulfil the contracts," that the address is to the People of the Book. Does "Fulfil the contracts" include that they affirm what has come?

* Student: Should we say: it does not allow this?
* Shaykh: No, it does not allow it; because the disbeliever is told first: embrace Islam, and then he is commanded with the branches of Islam.
* Student: They cited a hadith, Shaykh.
* Shaykh: What?
* Student: What ʿAmr ibn Ḥazm wrote, interpreting this verse, that it is intended for the People of the Book?
* Shaykh: That is not correct, is it clear? Also: "not violating the game while you are in the state of iḥrām" — does the disbeliever become sacred in iḥrām?
* Student: Shaykh, what if we say the verse bears both meanings?
* Shaykh: No, it does not bear them; it is only for the believers.
* Student: Shaykh, may Allah bless you. We mentioned that if the two contracting parties dispute a condition of the contract, the word of the one who affirms is accepted?
* Shaykh: Dispute over what?
* Student: Over a condition of the contract: this one says "this condition [exists]," and that one says "no, it is not in the contract."
* Shaykh: Did we mention this? No, no, regarding the validity of the contract: if the two contracting parties dispute, one says "the contract is valid," and the other says "the contract is not valid" — that is what we mentioned, not the validity of the condition.
* Student: Regarding conditions, Shaykh?
* Shaykh: Conditions, the original state is their non-existence. That is, if they dispute the existence or non-existence of the condition, the original state is non-existence of the condition. If they dispute the validity of the condition, whether it is a valid condition or not, after they have bound themselves to it, the original state is its validity.
* Student: May Allah honour you, Shaykh. The matter of the woman who stipulated that her husband not marry over her: we said that if he marries, she has the right to annul. Must the husband pay the dowry?
* Shaykh: No, the husband has no dowry, because he is the one who violated the condition. Yet his obligation is not discharged even in this case, because in this case she only annulled under compulsion, and he in reality deceived her. But we say: he may marry, because we do not restrict him; however, he did not fulfil the condition, and she perhaps would not annul, because she wants to remain with her husband, but under compulsion.
* Student: Is he sinful, Shaykh?
* Shaykh: Yes, he is nearer to sin, unless a need arises and necessity compels him, which is another matter.

* Shaykh: It is general, it is general, although the benefits have not come.

*Shaykh:* That he slaughters it before it reaches its place of sacrifice. Good, may Allah bless you, excellent.

﴿The garlands﴾: what are the garlands?

*Student:* "Garlands" (qala'id) is the plural of "garland" (qala'idah), and it is what is hung on the necks of the offering, and in them are placed, for example, worn-out things like sandals or...

*Shaykh:* What is hung on the necks of the offering as a sign that it is an offering, so that it is respected.

*Student:* Yes.

*Shaykh:* May Allah bless you.

Where did we stop at ﴿Those making for the Sacred House﴾?

*Student:* ﴿And when you have come out of ihram, then hunt﴾.

*Shaykh:* Yes. ﴿Those making for the Sacred House﴾ means: those intending the Sacred House, while they seek bounty from Allah and good pleasure.

He said: ﴿And when you have come out of ihram, then hunt﴾. Come out of ihram from what? From the state of ihram, as in His words at the beginning: ﴿while you are in ihram﴾, ﴿not violating the game while you are in ihram﴾. Then He said: ﴿And when you have come out﴾, that is, from your ihram, ﴿then hunt﴾. The coming out meant here is the first coming out, which occurs by throwing the Jamrat al-'Aqabah on the day of Eid and shaving or trimming, and this is what is meant by His words: ﴿when you have come out﴾. It does not mean coming out of the entire ihram, as the Sunnah has come with it: "Whoever has thrown and shaved, everything becomes lawful for him except women."[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (1978) from the hadith of 'A'ishah; al-Nasa'i (3084) and Ibn Majah (3041) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn 'Abbas.]]

As for His words ﴿then hunt﴾: its original form is (fa-ishtadu), but for a morphological reason the ta' was changed to ta', and the meaning is: hunt the game. But He did not say: fa-sidu, because hunting needs work, movement and effort (iftial), and if you wish, say also: inf'iʻal. ﴿When you have come out, then hunt﴾. And it will come to us, God willing, whether the command here is for permissibility or for lifting a prohibition, and the ruling on original hunting will be considered.

﴿And let not the hatred of a people, because they barred you from the Sacred Mosque, lead you to transgress﴾. There is a reading: ﴿shana'an﴾ with a sukun on the nun, and a reading: ﴿in sadduku﴾. Ash-shana'an is hatred, and what is meant by "a people" here, although it is indefinite, its referent is known: the people of Makkah. That is: let their hatred not move you, if they bar you from the Sacred Mosque, to transgress. This is an indication that they would bar them from the Sacred Mosque, but if they bar you, do not transgress.

As for the reading ﴿an sadduku﴾, the clause is a causal clause: do not let their hatred move you, on account of their barring you, to transgress. Is it clear?

So the meaning differs with the two readings. On the reading with a kasra on the hamzah, it is a report about what is expected; on the reading with a fatha on the hamzah, it is a report about what has occurred. The first meaning is: let not the hatred of these people move you, if they bar you from the Sacred Mosque, to transgress. And on the second: let not the hatred of a people move you, because they barred you from the Sacred Mosque, to transgress.

His words ﴿barred you﴾: that is, they turned you away. This applies exactly to what Quraysh did at the Battle of Hudaybiyyah, for they barred the Prophet (ﷺ) and made lawful the rites of Allah, made lawful the sacred month, the offering and the garlands. Everything that Allah forbade in this verse, Quraysh violated, and they barred the people most entitled to the House from the House of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

His words ﴿from the Sacred Mosque﴾: that is, the one possessing sanctity and glory. There is no doubt that this mosque has sanctity and greatness. It is the first house established for people to worship Allah at, and it is the Sacred Mosque, which every Muslim is obliged to visit, an individual obligation without which his Islam is not complete, by Hajj, by consensus, or by Hajj and 'Umrah, with differences among the scholars (may Allah have mercy on them) regarding the obligation of 'Umrah. So it is the Sacred Mosque.

As for its being called "mosque," it may be said that the whole earth is a mosque, and the most fitting land to be described thus is this sacred place. Or it may be said that what is meant by the Sacred Mosque is the mosque of the Ka'bah, which was taken as a mosque because they barred them from reaching it, and what surrounds the mosque follows it, and the origin is the mosque. For this reason the scholars (may Allah have mercy on them) agreed that circumambulation is a pillar of 'Umrah and Hajj. The circumambulation of ifadah and the circumambulation of 'Umrah are agreed to be a pillar, and that Hajj is not valid without it, nor 'Umrah without it.

﴿That they transgress﴾: this is connected to His words ﴿let not... lead you﴾, that is: let it not lead you to aggression. And "that" (an) is in the sense of a verbal noun in the accusative by removal of the preposition, and its estimate is: 'alā an ta'tadu (upon that you transgress), that is: let this not lead you to aggression.

Then He said: ﴿And cooperate in righteousness and piety﴾. That is: cooperate, make it reciprocal, and this cannot be except from two sides. For when you say "help your companion," the request for help is from one side. But when He says "cooperate," the meaning becomes: let each one help his brother. ﴿In righteousness﴾, which is doing acts of obedience, ﴿and piety﴾, which is abandoning what is prohibited. So if your brother seeks your help in one of the acts of worship, help him, so that you share in the reward. If he says to you: bring me water for ablution, bring it. If he says: buy me a garment with which to cover my nakedness in prayer, buy it for him. If he says: guide me to the direction of the qiblah, guide him to it. Indeed, even if he does not ask you, help him too.

Likewise, piety: cooperate in piety, that is, in abandoning what is prohibited. If a person seeks your help in breaking a musical instrument, help him; in pouring out wine, help him; in destroying books of innovation, help him; and so on.

﴿And do not cooperate in sin and aggression﴾. "Sin" is the disobediences related to the right of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and "aggression" is the disobediences related to the rights of the servants. When one of them is mentioned separately from the other, it comes to include it. That is, if "sin" is mentioned alone, it includes aggression against people; if "aggression" is mentioned alone, it includes sin, because aggression against the right of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is sin.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 5, verse 2 (part 3 of 4):

﴿And cooperate not in sin and transgression, and fear Allah.﴾ When He mentioned these commands and prohibitions, He commanded taqwa (God-consciousness) of Him, the Mighty and Majestic. That is: fear Allah lest you oppose His command or fall into what He has forbidden. Taqwa has been explained in several ways, and the best of them is to say: taqwa is taking a shield against the punishment of Allah by carrying out His commands and avoiding His prohibitions. It decreases in proportion to what is lacking of that. So the person who has acts of disobedience and sins, but these do not take him out of Islam, we say: his taqwa is deficient. Some of the salaf (early pious generations) used to withdraw when it was said to them, "Fear Allah," and some of them would even collapse out of fear of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. We knew some people in this condition. That is, if you said to one of them, "Fear Allah," he would tremble, his face would flush, and he would become humble. By contrast, now if you say to someone, "Fear Allah," he says, "What am I doing?" even though he is violating the sanctity of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. So it is obligatory upon the servant to have taqwa of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in compliance with His command, exalted is He.

﴿Indeed, Allah is severe in punishment.﴾ The connection of this sentence with what precedes it is that it is a warning to whoever does not, what? To whoever does not fear Allah. And al-'iqab (punishment) means retribution, that is, being held accountable for a sin.

* There are benefits in this verse. First: the prohibition of making the sacred symbols (sha'a'ir) lawful; due to His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, do not violate the sacred symbols of Allah﴾.
* Among its benefits: that violating the sacred symbols of Allah and what is mentioned in the verse is a deficiency in faith; due to His saying: ﴿O you who have believed﴾.
* Among its benefits: that complying with what is mentioned in the verse is among the requirements of faith, by which faith increases.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the glorification of the sacred symbols, because Allah attributed them to Himself, and what is attributed is honored and magnified according to the one to whom it is attributed.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of violating the sacred month by fighting, and likewise by acts of disobedience other than fighting, since acts of disobedience in these sacred months are greater than acts of disobedience in other times.

The scholars have differed regarding fighting in the sacred month:
Some of them say that it has been abrogated (mansukh).
Others say that it is muhkam (firm, not abrogated). Those who say it has been abrogated argue that the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, fought in the sacred month. After the conquest of Makkah in Ramadan, he went out against Hawazin and Thaqif and fought them in Dhu al-Qa'dah. Likewise, the Battle of Tabuk took place in a sacred month: when? In Muharram. This indicates that fighting in the sacred month has had its prohibition abrogated.
But the correct view is that it remains in force, and that it is not permissible to begin fighting in the sacred month. However, if it is in defense, or if it is a continuation of an earlier military campaign, then that is permissible. The story of Hawazin and Tabuk is to be interpreted in this way, because the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him and his family, only campaigned against them because it was said to him that they had gathered against him, so defense was necessary.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the prohibition of violating the sacrificial animals (al-hady) and showing them respect; due to His saying: ﴿nor the offerings, nor the garlands﴾.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: acting upon indicators (qara'in), because these garlands are an indicator that this is a sacrificial animal. Acting upon indicators has been brought by the Sunnah, and indeed the Quran alluded to it. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And David and Solomon, when they gave judgment concerning the field when the sheep of a certain people pastured in it by night, and We were witness to their judgment. So We gave understanding of it to Solomon﴾ [al-Anbiya' 78, 79]. The field had been grazed at night, and this was known from its traces.
Likewise, Solomon, peace be upon him, when two women disputed before him over the surviving child, and the child belonged to the younger, and he asked for a knife to split it between the two women in halves: the elder agreed, but the younger refused. So he ruled in favor of whom? The younger, because her refusal to have it split indicates that she is the mother, out of compassion.
Likewise, the witness of Yusuf said: ﴿If his shirt is torn from the front, then she has told the truth, and he is of the liars. But if his shirt is torn from the back, then she has lied, and he is of the truthful﴾ [Yusuf 26, 27].
Likewise, the Sunnah has brought the acting upon indicators. When the Prophet ﷺ conquered Khaybar and demanded the wealth of Huyayy ibn Akhtab, Salam ibn Mishkam said to him: "It has been exhausted." He said: "How could it be exhausted? The covenant is recent and the wealth is great!?" Then he ordered al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam to subject him to punishment. When he felt the punishment, he said: "Hold on, I see Huyayy circling around a ruin there." They went to the ruin, and in it was a great hoard of buried gold, said to be enough to fill an ox-hide. Why did the Prophet, peace be upon him, rule that there must be wealth, that it was great? Because the covenant was recent and the wealth was great; where would it go?
Acting upon indicators is necessary, but on condition that it is not mere accusation. If it is merely an accusation with no basis, then it is not permissible, because the original state is innocence and safety.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the obligation to respect pilgrims and those who visit to build (the sanctuary); due to His saying: ﴿nor those coming to the Sacred House﴾. It indicates that aggression against them is more severe than aggression against others.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: an indication of sincerity for those who head to the Sacred Mosque. From where is this taken? From His saying: ﴿seeking bounty from their Lord and His good pleasure﴾.
