Here someone asks: what about one who heads to the House for other than this purpose, such as to visit a relative or for trade? For visiting a relative, perhaps we would say this is among what is sought for the sake of Allah's countenance. But for trade, does it fall under this or not?
It falls under it without doubt, but the mention was based on what is most common. A qualifier based on what is most common, the people of usul (principles of jurisprudence) say, has no implicit meaning (mafhum). On this basis, His saying ﴿seeking bounty from their Lord and His good pleasure﴾ is not a restriction, but is based on what is most common, like His saying, exalted is He, regarding stepdaughters: ﴿and your stepdaughters who are in your guardianship, born of your wives with whom you have consummated the marriage﴾ [al-Nisa' 23]. The daughter of the wife is forbidden to the husband once he has consummated the marriage, even if she is not in his guardianship; but the mention of "in your guardianship" is based on what is most common.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: it is permissible for a person to perform an act of worship seeking reward and pleasure from Allah, and that this is among the highest stations, in contrast to whom? In contrast to the Sufis, who say: "Worship Allah for Allah." If you worship Him for His reward, your worship is deficient. May Allah fight them! Did not Allah praise Muhammad ﷺ and his companions in His saying: ﴿You see them bowing and prostrating, seeking bounty from Allah and His good pleasure﴾ [al-Fath 29]? There is no doubt that Muhammad, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, and his companions are the highest of people in station. But these people, because of their deficiency, thought that you must worship Allah for Allah alone, we ask Allah for well-being, and this contradicts what the Prophet ﷺ and his companions were upon.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: an indication of the favor of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, upon those who headed to the Sacred House, an indication of His favor. From where do you derive it?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: May Allah be the one sought for help, may Allah guide you. This is farthest from the point, but since it came after this...
* Student: ﴿seeking bounty from their Lord and His good pleasure﴾.
* Shaykh: You have ﴿bounty﴾, ﴿from their Lord﴾, and ﴿good pleasure﴾. Which of the words is it from?
* Student: ﴿bounty﴾.
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: ﴿good pleasure﴾.
* Shaykh: No, there is nothing but ﴿their Lord﴾. The attribution of lordship (rububiyyah) to them is evidence of His care for them, blessed and exalted is He, because lordship is of two kinds: general and specific. It is indicated in His saying: ﴿They said, "We have believed in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Musa and Harun"﴾ [al-A'raf 121, 122]. Which is the general one? ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾. ﴿Lord of Musa and Harun﴾ is the specific one. So, Allah, exalted is He, attributing His lordship to them is an indication of His care for them, the Mighty and Majestic, and among that is that He enabled them to come to the Sacred Mosque.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: affirmation of good pleasure (ridwan) for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and that it is among the greatest goals of the believers. Rather, it is their greatest goal. Have you understood, O people? Good pleasure is one of the attributes of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, which the people of the Sunnah and the community (Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah) affirm in its literal sense. They say: Allah is pleased, displeased, and angry. His good pleasure is among the attributes of His perfection, the Mighty and Majestic, and it is a cause of reward: when Allah is pleased with the servant, He rewards him.
The people of ta'til (denial of attributes) interpreted ridwan as reward, and they said: it is a metaphor (majaz) for reward, expressed by it because it is its cause. So it is an expression of the cause for the effect. It is said: what prevents this? Allah affirmed good pleasure for Himself in the Quran, and the Prophet ﷺ affirmed it in the Sunnah: "Indeed Allah is pleased with three things for you" [narrated by Muslim (1715/10) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah]. The texts on this are numerous, and the salaf of the Ummah agreed upon it. They agreed upon it, and the way to know their consensus (ijma') is that nothing contrary to that was reported from them, while they were reading the Book and the Sunnah. Not one of them was reported to have interpreted ridwan as reward.
This is a path that a person should be attentive to, because someone may say: what is the evidence that the salaf agreed that good pleasure has its literal meaning?
We say: the evidence is that they recited the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger ﷺ with this wording, and not a single letter was reported from them indicating that it was not intended.
If Allah is pleased, and good pleasure is one of His attributes, is it among the essential attributes (sifat dhatiyyah) or the actional attributes (sifat fi'liyyah)?
The answer: it is among the actional attributes, because every attribute of Allah that occurs due to a cause is an actional attribute, since the fact that it occurs due to a cause indicates that it occurs by the will of Allah. So good pleasure is an actional attribute, and anger is an actional attribute, and descent is an actional attribute, and so on.
So the rule for you is: every attribute of Allah that occurs due to a cause is actional, because before the cause exists it does not exist.
This is the view that we hold to be our religion before Allah: that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is pleased and angry, and dislikes and loves, in reality and not as metaphor. And Allah knows best.
* * *
* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the outcast. ﴿Prohibited to you are carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, that which has been dedicated to other than Allah, the strangled animal, the animal beaten to death, the animal killed by a fall, the animal gored to death, that which has been eaten by a predator, unless you slaughter it, and that which is sacrificed on stone altars, and that you seek decision through divining arrows. That is a grave sin. This day those who disbelieved have despaired of your religion, so do not fear them but fear Me. This day I have perfected for you your religion, completed My favor upon you, and approved Islam as your religion. But whoever is forced by severe hunger, not inclining deliberately to sin, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Ma'idah 3].
* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the outcast. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿Prohibited to you are carrion and blood﴾. This is an explanation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Lawful to you are the grazing animals, except what is recited to you﴾.
* Student: The remaining benefits.
* Shaykh: Then let us complete the benefits of the verse before it. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And when you have come out of ihram, then hunt﴾ ﴿when you have come out of ihram﴾: that is, from the state of ihram. ﴿then hunt﴾ and this is like an exception to His saying: ﴿not violating game while you are in ihram﴾.
* What is derived from this sentence: when a person comes out of ihram, hunting becomes lawful for him. Does the intended meaning refer to full release or to part of it? The Sunnah has explained that the intended meaning is part of it, because when the first release (tahallul) occurs, hunting becomes permissible for him, and all the prohibitions of ihram become permissible except for women. So His saying ﴿when you have come out of ihram﴾ contains some generality (ijmal), which the Sunnah has clarified.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: we mentioned the lawfulness of hunting, and the Sunnah has explained that the lawfulness of hunting has known conditions in the books of the scholars.
If someone says: you mentioned that hunting after release is permissible, though it is a command; how can that be?
We say: when a command comes after a prohibition, it indicates permissibility. This is what most of the usuliyyun (scholars of the principles of jurisprudence) hold. It was also said that a command after a prohibition lifts the prohibition. The difference between the two views is that if we say it indicates permissibility, the thing commanded becomes merely permissible. If we say it lifts the prohibition, the ruling on the thing commanded returns to what it was before the prohibition. Each of the two views has a basis. As for those who say a command after a prohibition indicates permissibility, they say: when the prohibition came upon something permissible, it abrogated it entirely, even if the prohibition was against something recommended, it abrogates it entirely. Then the command after the prohibition returns, and its meaning is what? Permissibility.
As for those who say a command after a prohibition lifts the prohibition, they say: when a prohibition came against something, it became forbidden. When the prohibition is lifted, the forbidden thing must remain as it was before. So let us consider now: do we say that it is recommended for every person who has been released from ihram to take a shotgun in order to hunt game? No, no one says this, but it is permissible for him. As for His saying, exalted is He, regarding Friday: ﴿And when the prayer has been concluded, disperse through the land, seek of the bounty of Allah, and remember Allah often﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 10], this command is for recommendation, because seeking provision is a recommended matter. According to the second view, which says a command after a prohibition indicates permissibility, it would be permissible. The closer view is what we mentioned in the versified rules, which is that it lifts the prohibition, and for this reason we said: what? (Take it and you will be fulfilled).
The command after a prohibition is for permissibility, and in one opinion it is to lift the prohibition; take it and you will be fulfilled.
This is the closer view.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: a person must act justly even with his opponent and with one who has wronged him; due to His saying: ﴿And let not the hatred of a people prevent you from being just﴾ [al-Ma'idah 8].

- Among the benefits of this noble verse: it is not permitted to transgress against another person, even if one dislikes them, and even if they have barred one from obedience.
However, if one treats them with the same treatment they gave, this is not objectionable, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner as he transgressed against you﴾ [al-Baqarah 194].
- Among the benefits of this noble verse: a warning against following one's desires and against driving the self to aggression when enmity and hatred arise. For it is the habit and nature of a person, when he hates someone, to treat him with what? With aggression and harshness, because his self compels him to do so. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, warned against this.
- Among the benefits of this noble verse: an allusion to what occurred from Quraysh at the Battle of al-Hudaybiyyah (the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah). This is His saying: ﴿that they barred you from al-Masjid al-Haram (the Sacred Mosque)﴾. Whether the reading is with a kasra on the hamzah, ﴿in they barred you﴾, or with a fatha, there is no difficulty regarding what preceded if it is read with a fatha. If it is read with a kasra, there is a difficulty, because al-Ma'idah was revealed after al-Hudaybiyyah. But the meaning would be: if their barring you from the Sacred Mosque recurs, supposing and assuming it. We have said there are two readings of the verse: ﴿أَنْ صَدُّوكُمْ (an saddukum)﴾, and this presents no difficulty, because ﴿أَنْ (an)﴾ here is causal, meaning: their hatred should not lead you, because they barred you from the Sacred Mosque, to transgress. But what presents difficulty is ﴿وَلَا يَجْرِمَنَّكُمْ شَنَآنُ قَوْمٍ إِنْ صَدُّوكُمْ عَنِ الْمَسْجِدِ الْحَرَامِ أَنْ تَعْتَدُوا (And let not the hatred of a people prevent you from being just if they barred you from the Sacred Mosque, transgress...)﴾. It is said: this is a conditional, and a conditional refers to what? To the future. So the answer to this is: the meaning of the verse is, if their barring you recurs, or if it is supposed that they bar you, then do not transgress.
- Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of the sanctity of al-Masjid al-Haram; this is from His saying: ﴿from al-Masjid al-Haram﴾.
Some scholars have cited His saying ﴿from al-Masjid al-Haram﴾ to show that the statement of the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning the multiplication of reward, "Prayer in al-Masjid al-Haram is worth a hundred thousand (prayers)"[[Narrated by Ibn Majah in his Sunan (1413), and the wording is his, and Ahmad in his Musnad (15271), from the hadith of Jabir, with the wording: "And a prayer in al-Masjid al-Haram is better than a hundred thousand prayers elsewhere."]], covers all the boundaries of the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram), everything included within its boundaries. But this argument is open to question. Firstly: we do not concede that what is meant by al-Masjid al-Haram here is what lies within the boundaries of the Haram, because if we were asked: what did the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and those with him intend? Did they intend only to enter the boundaries of the Haram, or to reach the Mosque of the Kaaba?
- Students: The second.
- Shaykh: The second, without doubt. So the meaning is that He mentioned the highest thing they would bar them from, which is reaching the mosque in which the Kaaba is.
Secondly: we say, since there is a clear and explicit proof from the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) that what is meant by the multiplication is the Mosque of the Kaaba, as in Sahih Muslim: "A prayer in this mosque of mine is better than a thousand prayers in other mosques, except the Mosque of the Kaaba"[[Narrated by Muslim (1396 / 510), and al-Nasa'i in his Sunan (2898), and the wording is his, from the hadith of Maymunah.]], then, since we have something explicit on this, there is no need to interpret the texts according to what we have understood.
- Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation of cooperating in righteousness and piety; this is from His saying: ﴿And cooperate in righteousness and piety﴾. Is this dependent on another seeking your help, or is it absolute?
- Student: Absolute.
- Shaykh: The verse is general and absolute, whether you are asked for assistance or not. It is obligatory upon you to help in righteousness and piety.
- Among the benefits of this noble verse: the exhortation to righteousness and piety. From where is this derived? Because if one is commanded to cooperate in it, then commanding it is all the more so; that is, we are commanded to cooperate in righteousness, so doing righteousness is all the more so.
- Among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of cooperating in sin and transgression; this is from His saying: ﴿And do not cooperate in sin and transgression﴾. Whether or not you are asked for assistance, do not help him in sin and transgression. Is it among assisting in sin and transgression for a person to rent his house to someone who makes wine in it? Yes.
Is it among assistance to sell a television to someone who uses it for forbidden things? Yes. This is a general rule, and it has very many branches.
- Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation of fearing Allah, and that opposing what has been mentioned contradicts the fear of Allah; this is from His saying after He commanded what He commanded and forbade what He forbade: ﴿And fear Allah﴾.
- Among the benefits of this noble verse: the severity of Allah's punishment, Mighty and Majestic, and a warning against opposing Him; this is from His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is severe in punishment﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 5, verse 3 (part 1 of 3):

Then Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Forbidden to you are carrion, blood⟩ to the end. ﴿Forbidden﴾ is a verb in the passive voice, whose doer is not named, and the doer is who? Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, so the doer has been omitted because it is known.

If someone says: Here He says ﴿Forbidden﴾, while in Surat al-Baqarah and al-Nahl He says: ﴿He has only forbidden to you carrion﴾ [al-Baqarah 173], [al-Nahl 115], ﴿He has only forbidden﴾, attributing the prohibition explicitly to Allah. Why, then, does the expression differ?

The answer has two aspects.

The first aspect: the eloquence of the Qur'an cannot be grasped by all people, because it is the speech of whom? The speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and Allah, the Exalted, we cannot encompass in knowledge, neither in His essence nor in His attributes. So the eloquence of the Qur'an is greater than our minds can grasp. On this basis, or on this answer, one must refrain from such matters, and we say: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, expressed there with ﴿He has forbidden﴾ (ḥarrama), attributing the verb to Himself, and here He expressed with ḥurrimat, and this is a matter beyond our minds. By this, every believer refrains from trying to force an explanation of the difference.

As for the second aspect: it can be said that there He said ﴿He has only forbidden﴾ (innamā ḥarrama), because it is in the form of restriction (ḥaṣr) concerning four matters. It is as if He said: He has forbidden only this, unlike what you forbade yourselves in the Jahiliyyah: ﴿Allah did not appoint any bahīrah, nor sā'ibah, nor waṣīlah, nor ḥām﴾ [al-Ma'idah 103]. So He said: He has forbidden only this, to manifest His grace, and that He has forbidden to people only four categories.

﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾. Here the definite article (al) ﴿carrion (al-maytah)﴾ is for specifying the reality, meaning every carrion is forbidden. Carrion is that which has died of itself (ḥatf anfihā), or which was slaughtered in a manner not prescribed by the Law. This is carrion: that which died of itself, meaning without the act of an agent, or by the act of an agent, but not in the lawful manner. For example, if an animal fell ill and died, we say: this died of itself. And if a person broke its neck and it died, we say: this is an unlawful slaughter (dhakāh ghayr shar'iyyah). Excepted from carrion is the carrion of the sea, for it is not forbidden, due to the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Lawful to you is the game of the sea and its food﴾ [al-Ma'idah 96]. ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbbas said: "Its game is what is taken alive, and its food is what is taken dead."[[Reported by al-Daraqutni in his Sunan (4728), and al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur (3/198), from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas, with nearly this wording.]] And in the hadith of ʿAbdullah ibn ʿUmar: "Two carrions and two bloods have been made lawful for us: as for the two carrions, locusts and fish."[[Reported by Ibn Majah (3314), and Ahmad in his Musnad (5723), from the hadith of ʿAbdullah ibn ʿUmar.]]

Locusts are excepted as in the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar. Locusts are not aquatic; locusts live only on land, yet their carrion is lawful. Why? First: because requiring their slaughter is an obligation that is impossible; who can catch every locust and slaughter it? Second: because there is no blood in them that needs to be drained, therefore they were made lawful.

Does the prohibition of carrion necessarily mean that it is impure (najis)? We say: it does not necessarily follow, but there is evidence of its impurity, which is His saying: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to one who eats it, unless it be carrion, or blood poured forth, or the flesh of swine, for indeed it is impure﴾ [al-An'am 145], meaning what was mentioned. So what is excepted from the carrions? Locusts, and the carrion of the sea.

﴿And blood﴾. Blood here is unrestricted, and the definite article (al) in it is for specifying the reality, but it is restricted in Surat al-An'am to ﴿poured forth blood﴾, to exclude the blood that remains in the veins after slaughter, for that is not forbidden. What is forbidden is the poured-forth blood that flows at slaughter, or flows when a vein is cut, or the like. In the Jahiliyyah they used to eat carrion, not caring about it, and they would say: How do you forbid what Allah has killed, while you do not forbid what you have killed? meaning by slaughter. They also used to eat poured-forth blood: a person would open a vein of his she-camel and suck it, so Allah the Mighty and Majestic forbade it. Blood is restricted by what? By poured-forth blood. Accordingly, the liver is not forbidden, the spleen is not forbidden, the kidneys are not forbidden, the blood in the heart is not forbidden, the blood that remains in the veins is not forbidden, because Allah restricted blood to the poured-forth.

Second: ﴿The flesh of swine﴾ is forbidden, and the swine is well known; it is an evil animal whose nature is to eat filth, insects, and the like. It is also known for lacking jealousy (ghayrah), and whoever feeds on it takes on its nature. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ forbade every animal with fangs among beasts of prey, and every bird with talons, because creatures with fangs and talons are by nature aggressive, and they prey upon others; so they were forbidden, lest a person be affected by eating from them. Likewise, it is said—as is well known—that the flesh of swine is little in jealousy.

Fourth: ﴿That over which the name of other than Allah has been invoked﴾. Ihlāl originally means raising the voice, and what is meant here is that over which the name of other than Allah has been mentioned, such as when one says: in the name of the Messiah, in the name of ʿUzayr, in the name of such-and-such president, in the name of such-and-such saint, in the name of the Prophet, in the name of Jibril, in whatever name. If it is slaughtered in the name of other than Allah, it is forbidden.

﴿And the strangled﴾: the strangled of itself, and the strangled by the act of an agent. The strangled of itself is like when it pulls the rope or collar on its neck, then it tightens on it until it is strangled, or it puts its head—as some of the salaf said—between two branches of a tree, then it is unable to pull it out and is strangled. The correct view is that it includes both the strangled (mukhtanaqah) and the one strangled (munkhaniqah): the one strangled by the act of an agent, meaning if a person held it and squeezed its neck until it died, the correct view is that it enters under the strangled, although this is called mukhtanaqah; it covers both this and that. So the strangled is the one that dies by strangulation, whether by its own act or by the act of an agent.

﴿And the beaten to death﴾: from (al-waqdh), which is severe striking until it dies. A person, for example, strikes an animal with severe blows until it dies, whether with a stick, or with a stone, or with a rope, or otherwise. This too is not lawful, because it is beaten to death (mawqūdhah).

﴿And the fallen﴾: that which falls from a high place, whether high from above or high from below. The one that falls from a mountain has fallen from above, and the one that falls from the mouth of a well to its bottom has fallen from below. So the fallen is forbidden, because it dies without lawful slaughter.

﴿And the gored﴾: (faʿīlah) in the meaning of (mafʿūlah), that is, the mantūḥah, which is the one that gored its fellow until it killed it, because this death is not by the act of an agent from whom slaughter is valid.

﴿And what the beast of prey has eaten, except what you have slaughtered﴾. What the beast of prey has eaten, like the wolf, the dog, the lion, and the like. So what is meant by the beast of prey here is everything that attacks animals and eats them.

As for His saying: ﴿What the beast of prey has eaten﴾: if you are asked: how is it that what the beast of prey has eaten is extracted from its belly? It is said: the meaning is what it killed in order to eat it; this is the meaning of the verse, or what it began to eat.

﴿Except what you have slaughtered﴾. Let us now count how many prohibitions Allah the Mighty and Majestic has enumerated: carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, what was invoked over for other than Allah, the strangled, the beaten to death, the fallen, the gored, and what the beast of prey has eaten: nine. The tenth: and what is sacrificed on the altar stones (nuṣub). Are these nine all covered by the exception in His saying ﴿except what you have slaughtered﴾, or only some of them?

* Students: Only some of them.
* The Shaykh: Only some of them, certainly, because carrion cannot be slaughtered, since it has already died and is finished. The flesh of swine likewise cannot be made lawful by slaughter. What was invoked over for other than Allah also cannot be made lawful by slaughter—except that a person reaches it before its death, and it was not the one over which the name of Allah was mentioned, such as when one hears a person slaughtering a sheep and saying: in the name of the Messiah, then he slaughters it and departs, and we reach its slaughter before it dies; this falls under the verse. But if he has cut the two jugular veins, it is considered in the state of the dead, so slaughter cannot reach it afterward. So the exception begins from His saying: ﴿the strangled, the beaten to death, the fallen, the gored, and what the beast of prey has eaten﴾: how many? Five. The gored may be reached before it dies; the fallen likewise; what the beast of prey has eaten likewise; the beaten to death likewise, you may reach it before it dies.

If someone asks: by what is the slaughter of these things that have been struck by a cause of death accomplished?

We say: slaughter is accomplished by cutting the windpipe (ḥulqūm) and the gullet (marī'), or by cutting the two jugular veins (wadajayn), or by cutting three of the four, or by cutting all four, according to a difference among the scholars. The strongest of the views is that slaughter is accomplished by cutting the two jugular veins, this is the strongest view, and that its perfection includes cutting the windpipe and the gullet as well. So what are the two wadajān? They are the thick veins surrounding the windpipe. What do you call them in Egypt?

* A student: al-wadajayn.
* The Shaykh: Is it "al-wadajayn" with this wording? Yes. And here?
* A student: Jalamid.
* The Shaykh: Jalamid. And among you?
* A student: al-Wardan.
* The Shaykh: al-Wardan is closest to the Qur'an, and perhaps the language is broad, that it is al-wardān: ﴿And We are nearer to him than the jugular vein﴾ [Qaf 16].

In any case, if it reaches it and cuts its jugular veins before it dies, then this is slaughter. But what is the sign of death? Must it move its hand, its leg, its eye, its ear, or its tail, or is movement not a condition?

Most scholars say: it must move, because if you slaughter it and it does not move, it means it has died. Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the sign of life is that there flows out of it blood that is flowing, poured forth, hot, and red, because when an animal dies its blood turns black, and it passes from heat to coldness, and it also coagulates, as it does when slaughtered. So he, may Allah have mercy on him, says: if red, hot blood flowing from it comes out, then it is lawful, whether it moves or does not move, because it may not move due to the severity of what has befallen it; it may have fainted, for example, and it moves neither its eye, nor its leg, nor its tail. What the Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, held is the correct view: whenever red, hot, flowing blood comes out of it, it is slaughtered.

﴿And what is sacrificed on the altar stones﴾: meaning what is slaughtered upon idols, and they used to slaughter upon idols seeking nearness to them, and this is shirk. This differs from His saying ﴿what was invoked over for other than Allah﴾, because the former is that over which the name of other than Allah was mentioned, whether in front of the idol or away from the idol; whereas this is what was slaughtered upon the idol, the idol being in front of him, and he slaughters for that idol.

Then the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And that you seek decision by the arrows﴾. Meaning: it is forbidden to you to seek decision by the arrows. The connection between this matter and what precedes it is clear, because seeking decision by arrows is what the seeker intends in order to reach what is better for him; and likewise here, regarding foods, he wishes to consume what is better for him.

What is the meaning of seeking decision by arrows? Istiqsām is seeking the portion (qasm), meaning seeking what Allah apportions to you. It resembles, in the Islamic religion, istikhārah. In the Jahiliyyah, when one of them wanted a matter and the right course was not clear to him, he sought decision by the arrows (azlām, plural of zalam), which are arrow-shafts/lots; he would seek a decision by them, writing upon them: "Do," "Do not," and the third blank. Then he places them in a bag or the like, mixes them, and draws one of them. If "Do" comes out, he does; if "Do not" comes out, he does not; and if the third comes out, what? He repeats. They only made the third, which has neither "do" nor "do not," so that the seeking would be prolonged; for if there were only two, it would be decided at the first attempt. But they make the third so that the decision is delayed, perhaps they would prefer one thing over the other.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿That is defiance (fisq)﴾. ﴿That﴾ refers to what? To all that preceded, or to seeking decision by the arrows? The rule is: if the demonstrative or the pronoun can refer to everything that preceded, it is taken as referring to it.

As for His saying ﴿fisq﴾: fisq means departure from obedience, and from it their saying: "the fruit fasaqat," when it comes out of its skin. Likewise, one who departs from obedience is a fāsiq, departing from what he ought to be.

Then the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿Today those who disbelieve have despaired of your religion﴾. The definite article here is for the known (ʿahd); is it the present ʿahd? ﴿Today﴾ means the day in which this verse was revealed: ﴿those who disbelieve have despaired of your religion﴾, meaning they have despaired of changing or altering it, because the Islamic religion—praise be to Allah—has spread, become clear, and manifested.

﴿So do not fear them, but fear Me﴾, because there is no need now for fear, since your religion has become manifest, and these disbelievers have despaired of eliminating it. So do not fear them, fear Me. Fear (khashyah) is the dread that results from knowledge; the evidence for that is Allah's saying: ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾ [Fatir 28].

The people of knowledge said: the difference between khashyah and khawf is that khashyah is from knowledge, while khawf does not necessarily arise from knowledge.

Second: khashyah arises from the greatness of the one feared, even if the one fearing is strong; but the one feared is stronger than him. Khawf does not indicate the greatness of the one feared; it indicates only the weakness of the one who fears. This is a clear difference: khawf indicates the weakness of the fearer before the one he fears, even if the latter is not strong. A four-year-old child fears an eight-year-old child, though the latter is weak. But one who has khashyah of a king or a powerful ruler, it is said that he is khāshin.

﴿So do not fear them, but fear Me. Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾.

﴿Today﴾: the definite ʿahd here is also present.

﴿I have perfected for you your religion﴾, meaning I made it complete; and the meaning is not that I completed its laws, because after this verse some laws were revealed.

His saying ﴿I have perfected for you your religion﴾ means: what you worship Allah by.

﴿And I have completed My favour upon you﴾, which is the perfection of the religion, and it is the greatest of blessings; and the meaning of its completion is that there is no deficiency in it.

﴿And I have approved for you Islam as a religion﴾: I have approved for you Islam, which Muhammad ﷺ brought, as a religion by which you worship Allah, so do not take any religion other than it.

Then, after mentioning these great blessings upon us, He said, returning to what began in the verse: ﴿But whoever is compelled by severe hunger, not inclining toward sin﴾. ﴿Compelled﴾ means necessity has befallen him; the root of iḍṭurra is (iḍtarra), then the tā' was changed into ṭā' for a well-known morphological reason in the science of ṣarf.

﴿In severe hunger﴾: makhmaṣah is famine. Listen to the saying of the Messenger, may the prayers and peace of Allah be upon him: "If you were to rely upon Allah with the reliance due to Him, He would provide for you as He provides for the birds: they go out in the morning hungry (khimāṣan), and return full (biṭānan)."[[Reported by al-Tirmidhi (2344) and Ibn Majah (4164), from the hadith of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab.]] So makhmaṣah means famine.

﴿Not inclining toward sin﴾: meaning not leaning toward sin, nor desiring it, but out of necessity he eats of these forbidden things. ﴿Indeed Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾, so He forgives him. This, meaning His saying ﴿But whoever is compelled by severe hunger, not inclining toward sin﴾, explains His saying in the two preceding verses: ﴿But whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing﴾ [al-Baqarah 173]. So His saying ﴿not desiring﴾ means not wishing these prohibited things, but necessity compelled him to them.

﴿Nor transgressing﴾: meaning not aggressing, desiring sin. ﴿Indeed Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾.

The verse contains many benefits, which we will mention—Allah willing—in the next lesson.

* Student: May Allah be good to you, how do we distinguish the definite article of present ʿahd (...)?
* The Shaykh: The one for present ʿahd is the one that refers to your present time. One of its rules is that every "al" after a demonstrative for presence: "this man," "this place," "this mosque," is for the present ʿahd.
* Student: The mental ʿahd?
* The Shaykh: The mental one means what is known in the mind, such as when you say: I went with my opponent to the judge; it is known that the judge intended is the one who judges between people.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 5, verse 3 (part 2 of 3):

As for the reference-back definite article (al-'ahd al-dhikri), it is when the article (al) points to something already mentioned, such as the Almighty's saying: ﴿As We sent to Pharaoh a messenger (15), but Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger﴾ [al-Muzzammil 15-16].

* Student: May Allah reward you well. We said that His saying ﴿except what is recited to you﴾ does not fall under the exception from His saying ﴿the grazing animals﴾.
* Shaykh: It is an explanation of His saying ﴿except what is recited to you﴾.
* Student: Yes, and blood is not included in it.
* Shaykh: Yes, blood is from the grazing animals, but swine is not included in it, because swine is not from the grazing animals. Is that clear? On this basis, it is an explanation of what can be explained from His saying ﴿the grazing animals﴾.
* Student: May Allah reward you well. We learn from it that carrion is impure, due to the Almighty's saying: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to an eater who eats it, unless it is carrion﴾. Then Allah said: ﴿or blood poured forth﴾. So is blood impure?
* Shaykh: Yes, the blood that comes from other than a human.
* Student: I mean from a human.
* Shaykh: No, human blood is a different matter. Is a human eaten, so that his blood would be included in this? No. Answer!
* Student: He is not eaten.
* Shaykh: He is not eaten. And even if a person is compelled to it? If he is compelled, is it permitted or not? Answer, brother!
* Student: It is not permitted.
* Shaykh: And even if he is compelled?
* Student: Even if he is compelled.
* Shaykh: Do you agree with him on this?
* Students: No.
* Shaykh: You do not agree. So does that mean that if a person is traveling, and is compelled to eat, and he has a companion who can slaughter him, he may slaughter him and eat?!
* Student: No.
* Another student: He said: a dead person.
* Shaykh: No, we have not come to the dead person now.
* Student: If he is alive, then we agree with him.
* Shaykh: You agree with him?!
* Student: One does not eat from him.
* Shaykh: Correct. If he is alive, it is not permitted. This is by consensus: that you kill a person in order to preserve your own life. There is no difficulty in this. But if he is dead, the well-known position among us, meaning in the Hanbali school (madhhab), is that it is not permitted to eat him even if he is dead, due to the words of the Prophet ﷺ: "Breaking the bone of the dead is like breaking it while alive"[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (3207) and Ibn Majah (1616) from the hadith of 'Aisha.]]. So if he says: O people, I will die if I do not eat from him, we say: then die, this is your appointed term. Some scholars, and it is the view of al-Shafi'i, hold that it is permitted for the living to eat the dead in cases of necessity, and they reasoned that the sanctity of the living is greater than the sanctity of the dead.
* Student: Shaykh, if a predator cuts one of the two jugular veins, or both, does that count as (...) slaughter?
* Shaykh: No. For this reason the scholars said: if a predator cuts the jugular veins, or the jugular veins together with the windpipe and the gullet according to one opinion, or cuts its entrails, its entrails meaning its intestines and stomach, then it is in the ruling of the dead and slaughter does not benefit it. But this requires consideration, because the verse is general: ﴿and what the predator has eaten, except what you have slaughtered﴾.
* Student: In His saying ﴿O you who believe, do not violate the rites of Allah﴾, and then He joined to it His saying ﴿nor the offering, nor the garlands﴾. Does the conjunction here indicate that these are not among the rites of Allah?
* Shaykh: No. As the Almighty said: ﴿Guard the prayers, and the middle prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah 238], this does not indicate that the middle prayer is not among the prayers. But the specific may be joined to the general to give it special emphasis.

* * *

* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿They ask you what has been made lawful for them. Say: The good things have been made lawful for you, and what the trained hunting animals catch for you, which you train as Allah has taught you. So eat of what they catch for you, and mention the name of Allah over it, and fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning﴾ [al-Ma'idah 4].
* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Earlier, Allah the Exalted explained the unspecified in His saying ﴿except what is recited to you﴾, and that they are how many? What?
* Student: His saying ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾.
* Another student: Yes, how many? How many are they?
* Student: Nine, Shaykh.
* Shaykh: Read: ﴿Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, what has been dedicated to other than Allah, the strangled, the beaten, the fallen, the gored, and what a predator has eaten, except what you have slaughtered, and what has been sacrificed on the altars﴾. How many? Ten. What is carrion in the sharia?
* Student: It is that which died of its own accord, or by the act of someone without lawful slaughter.
* Shaykh: Even if the one who acted is Allah?
* Student: Even if the one who acted is Allah, glorified and exalted.
* Shaykh: If it died without the act of any agent, even if the agent is Allah, then it is carrion.
* Student: That which died of its own accord in an unlawful manner.
* Shaykh: That which died of its own accord, or was slaughtered?
* Student: An unlawful slaughter.
* Shaykh: An unlawful slaughter. Is anything excepted from carrion?
* Student: Locusts and fish are excepted from it.
* Shaykh: Fish and locusts are good. What is the evidence for the exception of fish?
* Student: The saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "It has been made lawful for us..."[[Already cited.]]
* Shaykh: No, from the Quran.
* Student: The saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, about the sea: its food is lawful for you.
* Shaykh: No, brother, the Quran is not transmitted by meaning. May Allah reward you well.
* Student: ﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea and its food, as a provision for you﴾.
* Shaykh: Well done. ﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea and its food, as a provision for you﴾. What is the indication of the verse?
* Student: The saying of Ibn 'Abbas that "lawful for you" means what you hunt.
* Shaykh: That the game of the sea...
* Student: Is lawful for you.
* Shaykh: What is caught.
* Student: What is caught alive.
* Shaykh: And its food?
* Student: And its food is what is caught dead.
* Shaykh: Well done. Likewise also the story of the detachment that found the ambergris, and the Prophet, peace be upon him, approved their eating it[[Narrated by Muslim (1935/17) from the hadith of Jabir.]]. What is the evidence that the carrion of locusts is lawful?
* Student: The saying of the Prophet ﷺ in the hadith of Ibn 'Umar: "Two carrions and two bloods have been made lawful for us. As for the two carrions: locusts and fish. As for the two bloods: the liver and the spleen"[[Narrated by Ibn Majah (3314) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar.]]. The evidence is his saying: locusts.
* Shaykh: Well done. As for his saying "locusts", some scholars criticized this hadith for its weakness when traced to the Prophet. But this criticism is itself flawed, because if we say it is not traced to the Prophet, then it is a companion report (mawquf) with the ruling of a traced report (marfu'), since when Ibn 'Umar says "it has been made lawful", he means the Messenger, peace be upon him. Now, the blood?
* Student: The blood is absolute, and it was restricted in Surat al-An'am to being poured forth blood.
* Shaykh: Well done. The intended meaning is poured forth blood. Which verse restricted it?
* Student: In Surat al-An'am.
* Shaykh: Yes. So the blood that remains in the veins after slaughter, is it lawful or unlawful?
* Student: Lawful, Shaykh.
* Shaykh: Lawful?
* Student: The blood that remains in the liver.
* Shaykh: No, in the veins after slaughter?
* Student: No, in the veins, Shaykh, it is unlawful.
* Shaykh: After slaughter?
* Student: Lawful, Shaykh.
* Shaykh: Is that established?
* Student: Established, Shaykh.
* Shaykh: Good. Do you agree with this?
* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: Yes indeed. Every blood after the animal has been slaughtered is lawful. That is, you may take the vein and suck it after you have slaughtered the animal. If there is a lot of blood in the heart, is it permitted to eat it?
* Student: The heart?
* Shaykh: No, what is the heart? The blood that is in the heart.
* Student: Yes, it is permitted.
* Shaykh: What is present! Is it permitted to eat it?
* Student: It is not permitted. Only the liver and the spleen.
* Shaykh: Only? What does Sulaym say?
* Student: Sulaym says: May Allah pardon you. He says: if a person's prohibition is for prohibition, then this is not unlawful, and if it is that the soul leaves it (...).
* Shaykh: The issue is not that he leaves it. Even if he leaves the whole heart, it does not matter to us. But our discussion is: is it lawful to eat it or not? It is lawful. Is it poured-forth blood?
* Students: No.
* Shaykh: It is not poured-forth blood. Blood after the animal has been slaughtered is lawful, there is no difficulty in it.

﴿the flesh of swine﴾ is clear. ﴿what has been dedicated to other than Allah﴾, what does it mean?
* Student: Ihlal originally means raising the voice, and what is meant here is what was slaughtered for other than Allah, what was intended for other than the face of Allah.
* Shaykh: What was intended for other than Allah?
* Student: What was slaughtered for other than Allah.
* Shaykh: Wrong.
* Student: What the name of other than Allah was mentioned over.
* Shaykh: What the name of other than Allah was mentioned over. Such as saying what?
* Student: "In the name of the Messiah."
* Shaykh: "In the name of Muhammad, in the name of the president, in the name of the king, in the name of the minister." It is unlawful, even if it is not for worship?
* Student: Yes, even if it is not for worship.
* Shaykh: Even if it is not for worship. Well done, may Allah bless you.

﴿the strangled, the beaten, the fallen, the gored﴾. Are these not from the carrion?
* Student: Yes, Shaykh, they are from the carrion.
* Shaykh: What is the wisdom in Allah specifying them?
* Student: For emphasis on them.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: Shaykh, they may be reached in time, but carrion cannot be reached.
* Shaykh: For the exception.
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: His saying ﴿except what you have slaughtered﴾. These descriptions are descriptions of the cause of death. What is the difference between the strangled and the beaten?
* Student: The strangled is one that strangled itself, or died by strangling. The beaten is one that died by being struck.
* Shaykh: Yes. The meaning of the strangled is one that was choked until it was strangled and did not breathe. The beaten is one that died from being struck or the like. Does the fallen include one that falls into a well?
* Student: It is included.
* Shaykh: It is included. So falling happens from high to low. Yes.
* Student: From high or from low, meaning from a mountain or from...
* Shaykh: Meaning whether it falls from above to the ground, or falls from above the ground to below, any faller. What do you say about one that was crushed, run over by a car? Is it unlawful or lawful?
* Student: If it died before it could be reached, it is unlawful.
* Shaykh: Yes. And what is closest in meaning to what Allah mentioned?
* Student: The beaten.
* Shaykh: The beaten?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Yes. The saying of Allah ﴿except what you have slaughtered﴾ is an exception from what?
* Student: From what came before, from what can be reached.
* Shaykh: From what came before, from what can be reached. And these are?
* Student: Read the verse, Shaykh: carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, what was dedicated to other than Allah, the strangled, it may be reachable, and it may not be reachable, the strangled...
* Shaykh: The point is "except what you have slaughtered."
* Student: Well done. If it was possible to reach it, though strangled, then...
* Shaykh: Meaning every one that can be reached from what came before?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: As for swine, it is forbidden for its kind, not because of a deficiency in the cause of its death.
* Student: The saying of Allah ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾. What is meant by this day?
* Another student: ﴿Today﴾, the lam in it is for the presential reference (al-'ahd al-huduri).
* Shaykh: No, I am not asking you to explain the lam. What is meant by "today" in ﴿Today I have perfected﴾?
* Student: This is the day of 'Arafah.
* Shaykh: The (al) in His saying ﴿Today﴾?
* Student: For the presential reference.
* Shaykh: His saying ﴿I have perfected for you your religion﴾.
* Student: That is: it came to them complete.
* Shaykh: That is: it came to them complete. Does it raise an objection that Allah sent down verses after this containing rulings?
* Student: It raises an objection.
* Shaykh: How is it reconciled?
* Student: It is said regarding those that were revealed in...
* Shaykh: They were revealed on the day of 'Arafah, and verses containing rulings were revealed after them. So do we say that every report of verses being revealed after this is incorrect? Well, if it is correct, how do we reconcile it with His saying ﴿Today I have perfected﴾?
* Student: There is no difficulty in it, because we said that "today" here means the perfection of the religion. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, informs that this religion is complete and perfect, and this does not entail that the religion was completed on this day on which this verse was revealed.
* Shaykh: Yes indeed, correct. That is, it is a statement that the religion is complete, and it does not mean that it is finished. For this reason He distinguished, saying: ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion and completed My favor upon you﴾.

His saying: ﴿whoever is compelled﴾?
* Student: Necessity forced him.
* Shaykh: Necessity forced him, meaning what?
* Student: Necessity forced him to eat this carrion, the nine mentioned.
* Shaykh: That is, if he does not eat?
* Student: He would die and perish.
* Shaykh: He would be harmed. We mentioned that what is forbidden is not made lawful by necessity except under two conditions?
* Student: The first: that he is not inclined toward sin, meaning he does not want to eat it, due to His saying ﴿whoever is compelled by hunger, not inclining toward sin﴾.
* Shaykh: No, I mean: when does necessity justify doing a forbidden act?
* Student: If he does not eat the forbidden, he will perish, or fear that he has...
* Another student: Two conditions: first, that the necessity is genuine for this matter, so he finds nothing else; second, that his necessity is removed by this forbidden thing.
* Shaykh: Well done. This is important: that there is nothing by which the necessity can be averted except this, because if there were something else, he would not be compelled.
And the second: that his necessity is removed by it. We required this so that someone would not say: then it is permitted to treat with the forbidden. We say: treatment with the forbidden is not permitted. Did you understand, everyone? Why?
First: because he is not compelled to it, since his illness may be cured by another medicine, or his illness may be cured without medicine. How many people have reached the lowest condition and then Allah the Mighty cures them without any cause. That is one. The second? Everyone!
* Student: His necessity is removed.
* Shaykh: That his necessity is not removed by this medicine. A person may take medicine and not be cured, unlike one who eats the forbidden out of hunger. If a person finds only carrion, for example, then his necessity cannot be removed except by eating it. And if he eats, does it get removed or not? What?
* Student: It is removed, yes.
* Shaykh: It is removed, yes. If he eats until his stomach is full, it is over. Now, the famine (makhmasah)?
* Student: The hunger.
* Shaykh: Do you have evidence that it means hunger?
* Student: The saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "If you relied upon Allah with the reliance due to Him, He would provide for you as He provides for the bird: it goes out hungry in the morning and returns full in the evening"[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (2344) and Ibn Majah (4164) from the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab.]].
* Shaykh: Well done. The saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "If you relied upon Allah with the reliance due to Him, He would provide for you as He provides for the bird: it goes out khimaasan, that is hungry, and returns bitaanan, that is full"[[Already cited.]].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of the mentioned kinds of livestock.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: the wisdom of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, regarding what He has made lawful for us and what He has forbidden us. For it has been established medically that these forbidden things are harmful, and because of their harm Allah forbade them.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of blood, except what is excepted.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of swine flesh. Does its fat fall under this too? Yes, by consensus the fat of swine is unlawful, even according to the Zahiris, who say that swine fat is unlawful, because "flesh," when used absolutely, includes all parts of the animal. But if it is said "flesh and fat," then they are distinguished. When it is said "flesh," the flesh of camels, the flesh of sheep, the flesh of cattle, the flesh of swine, it becomes inclusive of what?  Inclusive of all of them.

We move from this benefit to another benefit, which is: that the flesh of camels nullifies wudu', whether it is red meat, white meat, or any part of the body. This is the preponderant view: that the flesh of camels nullifies wudu', whether it is from the red meat, or the white meat, or the intestines, or the tripe, or other parts.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: the magnification of shirk, and that it affects even food, due to His saying ﴿and what has been dedicated to other than Allah﴾.

* Among its benefits: the prohibition of what is slaughtered in the name of anyone other than God, whether it is invoked in the name of a king, a prophet, a president, a homeland, or anything else, based on the general wording of His words: ﴿and that which has been dedicated to other than God﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of the animal strangled (al-munkhaniqah), the animal beaten to death (al-mawqudhah), the animal that falls from a height (al-mutaraddiyah), the animal gored by another (al-natihah), and that which has been partly eaten by a predator.

* Among its benefits: whatever of these is found still alive, having not died, and is then slaughtered, is lawful, based on His words: ﴿except what you slaughter﴾. We have already discussed in the tafsir when an animal is considered to have been reached alive: must it move its hand, foot, tail, or eye? We explained that the preponderant view is that if red, flowing blood comes out of it, then it is alive.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the effect of intention on action, based on His words: ﴿and what is sacrificed on the altars﴾, that is, to idols. Such an animal is forbidden even if the name of God was mentioned over it. This is due to the effect of what? Intention. Intention affects even the lawfulness and unlawfulness of things.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of seeking the decision of the divining arrows (al-istiqsam bil-azlam, the arrows used for divination). Does this include seeking decision by anything other than them? The answer is yes, because it is based on illusion and not on reality. But God has replaced His servants with what? With istikharah (seeking guidance from God through prayer). As for seeking decision by any other means, it is not permissible. If someone wished to seek a decision by saying, "If a grown man comes out to me, I will travel, and if a small child comes out to me, I will not travel," and similar ways of seeking decision, this is forbidden and impermissible.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the indication that seeking decision by the divining arrows is wickedness (fisq), and the purpose of this is to deter from it.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: whoever seeks decision by the divining arrows loses his authority (wilayah), his leadership in prayer (imamah), and his uprightness ('adalah). This is because the wicked person loses his authority, cannot lead prayer, and is not regarded as upright. Therefore, anything for which uprightness is a condition, the one who seeks decision by the arrows is not entrusted with it. However, regarding leading prayer, according to the preponderant view there is no harm in praying behind a wicked imam. But when we want to put forward someone to lead the prayer, we do not put forward a wicked person. Yet suppose he has been put forward.
The congregation gathered before you a man who shaves his beard and another man who does not shave his beard, and you also do not shave your beard. If the one who shaves comes forward, is it wise for you to say, "Step back"?
The answer: No, because in that is evil and corruption, unless you know that if you do so he will repent and give it up, in which case, yes. Otherwise, do not do it. Pray behind him, and his wickedness is upon himself.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the disbelievers have despaired of turning people away from their religion, based on His words, exalted is He: ﴿Today those who disbelieved have despaired of your religion﴾. A similar statement is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed, Satan has despaired of being worshipped in the Arabian Peninsula" [Reported by Muslim (2812) from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah]. We raised a difficulty concerning this and answered it. What is the difficulty? That shirk has occurred. It is said: this is a report about what was in the minds of these disbelievers, and it does not follow that what was in their minds must occur; rather, circumstances may change.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of fearing the disbelievers in a way that leads to compromise in God's religion, based on His words: ﴿So do not fear them, but fear Me﴾.

* Among its benefits: the declaration of God's favour upon this community, and to Him belongs all praise and grace for the perfection of the religion, based on His words: ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾.

* Among the benefits of the verse: the nobility of that day on which the religion was perfected, because if it were not so, His words ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾ would have no purpose. There is, therefore, an indication of the nobility of that day. But must we honour that day with what God has not honoured it with? No. Rather, we restrict ourselves to what has come concerning its nobility. For this reason, when a Jew said to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, "Indeed, God revealed a verse which, if it had been revealed to us, the community of the Jews, we would have taken that day as a festival," and he recited the verse: ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion, and completed My favour upon you, and approved for you Islam as a religion﴾ [al-Ma'idah 3], 'Umar said, "I know when it was revealed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ)." He mentioned that it was revealed on Friday, on the Day of 'Arafah [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (45) and Muslim (3017) from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab]. But the important matter is that we do not glorify that day more than what has come. I only said this to ward off the view of one who says that we should honour the day on which the Messenger (ﷺ) was born. When the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about fasting on Monday, he said: "That is a day on which I was born and on which I was sent," or: "on which it was revealed to me" [Reported by Muslim (1162) from Abu Qatadah al-Ansari].
It is said: that he specified it as the day of his birth indicates that it has a nobility. It is answered: nobility is received from the Shariah, and the Prophet (ﷺ) did not mention the nobility of the day of his birth by its date in the month, but mentioned its nobility by its day in the week, and there is a difference between this and that. Secondly: the nobility given to this day on which the Quran was revealed to the Messenger and on which he was born is only fasting. This is what the Sunnah has come with, and nothing beyond that. So if anyone wished to increase prayer on Monday on the basis that it is the day on which the Messenger was born and sent, we would say: this is an error.

* Among the benefits of this verse: that we, holding fast to the religion, must be proud of it, based on His words: ﴿I have perfected for you your religion﴾. God attributed it to us so that we may take pride in it, be strong through it, and defend it. Is this the case with the state of people today?
As for the state of people today, many Muslims, regrettably, are the opposite. Many Muslims are ashamed to say that they are Muslims, and this is great humiliation.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that God, mighty and majestic, has graciously bestowed upon His servants the completion of His favour, based on His words: ﴿and completed My favour upon you﴾.

* Following from this: He, mighty and majestic, praises Himself for the blessings He has bestowed, in order to endear Himself to His servants through His blessings. For this reason, a hadith says: "Love God for the blessings with which He nourishes you" [Reported by al-Tirmidhi (3789) from Ibn 'Abbas]. This is what accords with human nature: any person who does good to you, you will love him, and he is a created being like you. How much more so the Creator, mighty and majestic!

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that whatever contradicts what the Shariah has brought is not pleasing to God nor accepted, based on His words: ﴿and approved for you Islam as a religion﴾. This encompasses the whole religion, and its branches, which are considered part of the religion according to the one who does them. For example, has God approved disbelief for His servants? No. Has He approved for His servants that they innovate in His religion what is not part of it? No. So this phrase ﴿approved for you Islam as a religion﴾ means in its foundations and its branches, in its totality and in its parts.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the mercy of God, exalted, toward His servants, in that He permitted for them what is forbidden in cases of necessity. There is a verse that serves as a principle for all prohibited things, which is His words, blessed and exalted: ﴿And He has already explained to you what He has forbidden to you, except what you are compelled to﴾ [al-An'am 119]. The verse you recited just now is more general, because the verse in Surah al-Ma'idah says: ﴿But whoever is compelled﴾ to what? To what is mentioned, in order to eat from it. As for what you pointed to, ﴿And He has already explained to you what He has forbidden to you, except what you are compelled to﴾ [al-An'am 119], it is general and comprehensive. It remains to be asked: if a person is compelled to drink wine out of thirst, would he drink it?
* Students: He would not drink it.
* The Shaykh: We say: if his necessity is removed by it, then yes, because the verse contains no exception. But the scholars say that his necessity cannot be removed by drinking wine, because it only increases his burning and thirst. Therefore, if he is compelled to swallow a morsel that is choking him, and he has a cup of wine, here it is permissible for him to drink what will allow him to swallow the morsel, because here the necessity is removed by it. Have you understood?

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the application of intention and its effect on actions, based on His words: ﴿not inclining to sin﴾.

* Among its benefits: that one must be cautious in violating what is forbidden, and that one's self and desire must not overwhelm him so that he leans (yatajanaf), that is, inclines or tends toward sin. Rather, he must seek what is right.
Can it be inferred from the noble verse that it is not permissible to eat from the carrion and what is mentioned except in the amount that keeps one alive, or is he permitted to eat until he is full?
* Students: The first.
* The Shaykh: Yes, the first, unless he knows he will not find anything to eat, and he has no container in which to carry the carrion. In that case he is compelled to eat until he is full, and he carries with him in his stomach its water and its sandals. But if he knows he will reach something to eat before the necessity returns, is it permissible for him to eat more than his necessity? No. If he knows he will not reach food until the necessity returns, and he has nothing to carry this carrion in, is it permissible for him to eat until he is full? Yes, because he is compelled to do so.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: deriving rulings from the names of God, mighty and majestic. This is because the names of God, especially the transitive ones, must have an effect. This is what we pointed to earlier: a transitive name is not believed in completely except by affirming it as one of God's names, affirming the attribute it contains, and affirming its effect. From where is this derived? From His words: ﴿Indeed, God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. The scholars, may God have mercy on them, derive rulings from such expressions, like His words, exalted is He: ﴿Except for those who repent before you gain power over them. So know that God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Ma'idah 34]. That is, if highway robbers repent before they are captured, the prescribed punishment (hadd) falls from them.
It is mentioned that one of the Bedouins heard a reciter reciting the saying of God, exalted is He: "As for the thief, male or female, cut off their hands as a recompense for what they have earned, as an exemplary punishment from God. And God is Mighty and Wise," and he said, "Repeat the verse, you made a mistake." So he repeated it, and the reciter recited: "...And God is Forgiving and Merciful." The Bedouin said, "You made a mistake, repeat it." So he repeated it, and the Bedouin caught it on the third time and said: ﴿And as for the thief, male or female, cut off their hands as a recompense for what they have earned, as an exemplary punishment from God. And God is Mighty and Wise﴾ [al-Ma'idah 38]. He said, "Now you are right: Mighty and Wise, so He cuts off." If He had said "Forgiving and Merciful," He would not have cut off. See the understanding. There is no doubt about this.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of these two names of God, the Forgiving and the Merciful, and the affirmation of the attribute they contain and the effect they contain, because "the Forgiving" is transitive, and likewise "the Merciful."

Then God, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿They ask you what has been made lawful for them﴾.

* A student: The meaning I mentioned has become unclear to me in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾. We said that the intended meaning is that the religion is complete, and not that the intended meaning is..
* The Shaykh: Complete, yes.
* The student: Complete. So this would be true from the first day the Shariah was revealed, meaning this Shariah.
* The Shaykh: No, this is not true, because on the first day the Shariah was revealed the whole Shariah was not complete, and it cannot be said: ﴿Today I have perfected﴾ when only a small part of it had been revealed.
* A student: Does the meaning become that the great laws were completed?
* The Shaykh: The great laws were completed, and likewise these great laws, and among them are those that come after, all of which are complete.
* A student: Shaykh, may God be good to you: what is the connection of seeking decision by the arrows with tatayyur (augury, taking omens)?
* The Shaykh: This is not a matter of tatayyur. Tatayyur occurs without the person's will, while seeking decision by the arrows is by the person's own action. For example, tatayyur is when one sees a bird, and its flight goes in a certain direction, so he takes it as an omen and decides to act or to refrain. But seeking decision is from his own action itself.
* The student: But Shaykh, if we say: if a grown man came out to them, for example, and said..
* The Shaykh: Yes, indeed. That is, if he said that, saying: "I will seek decision by this," unlike the one who takes omens, who, as soon as something comes out to him, leaves or proceeds. As for this, he has made this thing the cause. So there is a difference between one who comes without intention and one who comes with intention.
* A student: Shaykh, what is common today is seeking decision with a metal coin, such as saying, for example, if the face comes up, two friends who disagree over whether they should go or not say: "If the face comes up, we go, and if the face does not come up, we stay"?
* The Shaykh: Yes, this is from seeking decision by the arrows.
* The student: May God pardon you, Shaykh. Someone who takes part in celebrating a birthday and says: "We celebrate the birthday just as you celebrate Monday fasting, because many people are now confused about birthday celebrations"?
* The Shaykh: We have mentioned that glorification is a legal ruling that requires proof. Was the birth of the Messenger (ﷺ) glorified in the way people do today?
* The student: No.
* The Shaykh: Very well. Furthermore, the Messenger (ﷺ) did not mention the day of his birth by its date in the month; he mentioned it by its day in the week. Do these people consider it by the month or by the week? By the month. Also, we have told you that it has not been established that the Messenger (ﷺ) was born on the twelfth day, and that some modern scholars of verification have established that his birth was on the ninth day.
* A student: Shaykh, may God be good to you: the matter the brother mentioned earlier, if it is intended as a lot-drawing, such as when two actions are equal for those who disagree, going and not going are equal, and they do not intend it for knowledge?
* The Shaykh: This is not permissible, because lot-drawing is only in matters of rights, not in decisions to proceed or return. This is undoubtedly seeking decision by the arrows.
* A student: Shaykh, the natihah (gored animal)... the one hit by a car, is it more similar to the mawquudhah or the natihah?
* The Shaykh: This one says: which is closer, what happened by being run over by a car? Is the closer one from the mawquudhah or from the natihah?
* A student: Or from the mutaraddiyah?
* The Shaykh: What do you say?
* Students: The mawquudhah.
* The Shaykh: No, the mawquudhah.
* A student: Shaykh, the natihah is... (...).
* Another student: If the car is (...).
* The Shaykh: The natihah is when two beasts gore each other, and I do not think the driver of the car wants to gore the sheep!
* A student: Shaykh, may God be good to you: what is the difference between necessity (darurah) and need (hajah), and the matters that follow from them?
* The Shaykh: The difference is that need belongs to the category of complements (kamaliyat), while necessity belongs to the category of averting harm. For example, a person wearing a garment that protects him from cold; if he took it off, the cold would harm him, but he would suffer some discomfort because it is not complete. So he puts on another garment over the first. Is that, relative to the first garment, a need or a necessity?
* Students: A necessity.
* The Shaykh: The first is a necessity, because we said that if he does not wear a garment he will be harmed by the cold, so when he wears a garment, we say: this is a necessity for him. But putting on another garment merely to avert discomfort, not to avert harm, we say: this is a need. The difference between them is clear: only necessity permits prohibited things, while need permits disliked things.
* A student: Shaykh, I would say: some legal theorists (usuliyyun) distinguish, saying: what is forbidden in itself may not be committed out of necessity, while what is forbidden for something else may be committed out of need. What is your view of this distinction, Shaykh?
* The Shaykh: It is not correct. I say it is not correct, because what is forbidden for something else is like what is forbidden in itself with respect to the obligation to avoid it.
* A student: Shaykh, may God bless you: the animal eaten by a predator, or the mutaraddiyah, which we found to have a fatal wound, the discharge of its entrails or similar, meaning something from which it cannot live afterward; then we slaughtered it and red blood came out. Is this a valid slaughter?
* The Shaykh: Yes, this is lawful, which makes it lawful. However, they said: if its innards have not been separated (ma ubinat hashwuhu), then this is not lawful. For example, if all its intestines were cut, or its stomach was taken out, outside, that is, it was cut, or its jugular veins were not severed. But we have mentioned that the apparent meaning of the noble verse is generality.

Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan.

﴿They ask you what has been made lawful for them. Say: "Lawful for you are the good things, and what the trained hunting animals have caught for you, training them as Allah has taught you. So eat of what they catch for you, and mention the name of Allah over it, and fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning." (4) Today the good things have been made lawful for you, and the food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you, and your food is lawful for them. And [lawful are] the chaste women from among the believers and the chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture before you, when you have given them their compensation, being chaste, not unlawful fornicators or those taking secret lovers. And whoever rejects faith, his deed has become worthless, and he, in the Hereafter, will be among the losers.﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 4, 5].

Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan. We have already discussed the verse that explains the forbidden things from among what Allah has made lawful. What are they?

Student: Carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, what has been dedicated to other than Allah, the strangled animal, the animal beaten to death, the animal that falls to its death, the animal gored to death, and what has been partly eaten by a beast of prey.

Shaykh: How many is this? Eight, nine, or ten?

Student: Ten, yes.

Shaykh: His saying: ﴿except what you slaughter﴾. To what does the exception refer?

Student: To all of it?

Shaykh: All of what, exactly?

Student: The strangled animal, the animal beaten to death, the animal that falls to its death, the animal gored to death, and what has been partly eaten by a beast of prey, except what you slaughter.

Shaykh: To the strangled animal, the animal beaten to death, the animal that falls to its death, the animal gored to death, and what has been partly eaten by a beast of prey, except what you slaughter. And by what does the slaughter (tadhkiyah) take place?

Student: By its blood flowing forcefully and the name of Allah being mentioned over it.

Shaykh: By its blood flowing forcefully and the name of Allah being mentioned over it. But is it required that it move after slaughter, or is it not required?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: The condition is that blood flows from it as it normally flows from a slaughtered animal, namely red, flowing, warm blood, not black, cold blood. This indicates that it is alive. Some scholars said: it must move, either with its eye, its tail, or its leg. But the verse indicates that whenever it is slaughtered, it becomes lawful.

Shaykh: What is the meaning of His saying: ﴿and what is sacrificed on the stone altars﴾?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: What is its meaning? "What is sacrificed on the stone altars": how so?

Student: They slaughter at the idols (...).

Shaykh: How? Beside the Ka'bah, at the idols, the images?

Student: Shaykh, there were idols at the Ka'bah where they slaughtered, and this is different..

Shaykh: Alright, but what if the stone altars were in (...)?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: Alright, but what is the meaning of "slaughtered on them"? That is, slaughtered to Allah upon the head of the idol?

Student: No, Shaykh, at it.

Shaykh: For it. Slaughtered at it means for it.

Student: Slaughter is not required to be for Allah; even if it is for Allah, it is through seeking intercession or (...).

Shaykh: What do you say?

Students: Slaughtered for it.

Shaykh: "Slaughtered on them" means for them. What is the difference between "what is sacrificed on the stone altars" and "what has been dedicated to other than Allah"?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: "What has been dedicated to other than Allah" even if it is not from the stone altars. So the first is an act and the second is a statement. "What is sacrificed on the stone altars" is an act, even if the name of the altar is not mentioned. As for "what has been dedicated to other than Allah," it is a statement.

He, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Today those who disbelieved have despaired of your religion﴾. How do we reconcile this verse with reality? Because until now the disbelievers have not despaired of our religion; they fight us and deceive us?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: Wrong.

Student: (...) at the revelation of this verse, but the situation changed afterward.

Shaykh: That they despair does not mean it must be the reality, correct? Just as Satan despaired of being worshipped in the Arabian Peninsula, yet he was worshipped. So we say: the despair that struck the hearts of the disbelievers when they saw the great conquest and the victory of Islam, they said: "That's it, the Arabs can no longer apostatize." This was based on their creed, and reality was otherwise.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾. The "al" here, for which kind of definiteness is it?

Student: For the definiteness of presence (al-'ahd al-hudhuri).

Shaykh: The definiteness of presence? What is "hudhuri"?

Student: The definiteness of presence is that which comes after every demonstrative noun.

Shaykh: We don't have a demonstrative noun? "Today" is a pointer to the present day; that is, the present day. Which day is it?

Student: The day of 'Arafah.

Shaykh: Which day of the week?

Student: Friday.

Shaykh: Friday, well done.

That they despair does not mean it must be the reality, correct? Just as Satan despaired of being worshipped in the Arabian Peninsula, yet he was worshipped. So we say: the despair that struck the hearts of the disbelievers when they saw the great conquest and the victory of Islam, they said: "That's it, the Arabs can no longer apostatize." And this was based on what? On their creed and their assumption, and reality was otherwise.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 3]. The "al" here, for which kind of definiteness is it?

Student: The definiteness of presence, Shaykh.

Shaykh: The definiteness of presence? What is "hudhuri"?

Student: The definiteness of presence is the one that comes after every demonstrative noun.

Shaykh: We don't have a demonstrative noun. ﴿Today⁠﴾ points to the present day, that is, the present day. Which day is it?

Student: The day of 'Arafah.

Shaykh: The day of 'Arafah. Which day of the week?

Student: Friday.

Shaykh: Friday. Well done. His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿So whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing﴾ [Al-Baqarah 173]. ﴿fa-man id-turra﴾ has two readings. We say it now: ﴿fa-mani id-turra⁠﴾ with a kasrah, ﴿fa-manu id-turra⁠﴾ with a dammah. That is, there are two readings: ﴿fa-manu id-turra⁠﴾ for harmony with the dammah on the verb ﴿id-turra⁠﴾; the second reading: ﴿fa-mani id-turra⁠﴾ according to the original rule, which is breaking the meeting of two sukūns with a kasrah. ﴿fa-mani id-turra⁠﴾ is one, ﴿fa-manu id-turra⁠﴾ is the other.

Student: The hamzah.

Shaykh: No, no, the hamzah has nothing to do with it. The vowel is on the nun: ﴿fa-manu⁠﴾ and ﴿fa-mani⁠﴾, the nun is either damm or kasr.

Student: (...) meeting of two sukūns?

Shaykh: Yes, the meeting of two sukūns. Because the hamzah of ﴿id-turra⁠﴾ is a hamzat al-wasl, and the hamzat al-wasl is sakin or mutaharrik?

Students: Sakin.

Shaykh: Sakin. The original rule is that when two sukūns meet, what precedes is kasred. That is the rule, but here it was given a dammah to harmonize with the dammah of the ṭā', because it may be easier in pronunciation. ﴿fa-manu id-turra⁠﴾ may be easier for a person than ﴿fa-mani id-turra⁠﴾.

What is meant by al-makhmasah?

Student: Hunger.

Shaykh: Yes, al-makhmasah is hunger.

In another verse: ﴿So whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing﴾ [Al-Baqarah 173]. Is there a contradiction between them?

Student: No, it is not...

Shaykh: How?

Student: Because one who is compelled by hunger is neither desiring nor transgressing.

Shaykh: So ﴿neither desiring⁠﴾ refers to carrion, and ﴿nor transgressing⁠﴾ means eating more than necessity. Do you understand? But some scholars explained "desiring" as one who goes out of the faith, and "transgressing" as one sinful in his journey. Is this explanation correct?
