* Among them: the Jews and Christians affirm that love is established for Allah, as they say ﴿We are the children of Allah and His beloved﴾.

Some from this Ummah have denied the attribute of love for Allah, saying: Allah does not love and is not loved. They interpreted the love that Allah affirmed for Himself in a way that the apparent wording does not indicate. They said: love is reward or the will for reward, and they explained it by one of two meanings, because their school holds that will is established for Allah, while reward is something separate from Allah, part of what is caused (mafulat) and not part of the attributes. These are the Ash'aris, who say: there is no love between Allah and the servant; love is only reward or the will for reward.

The Jews and Christians said this, saying ﴿We are the children of Allah and His beloved﴾, so they affirmed that Allah the Exalted loves and that they are His beloved.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the Jews claim what would imply that they are better than this Ummah. Its aspect: they said that in the context of rejecting the Prophet's ﷺ message, as if they said: we are more worthy of prophethood than you, O Arabs: ﴿We are the children of Allah and His beloved﴾.

* Among its benefits: an indication of what is well known among the Children of Israel, that they are the chosen people of Allah, and they consider themselves the best of the worlds, and better than the Arabs from whom Islam arose and through whom it appeared.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: Allah's denunciation of this claim from two aspects: the first is rejecting what they claimed; the second is establishing what makes this claim impossible.

* Among its benefits: in debate, one should first refute the argument of one's opponent, then bring what establishes one's own position. This is why you find scholars who mention the statements of scholars and their disagreements mentioning first the refutation of the view opposed to theirs, then what establishes their own views. All of this rests on the well-known principle: clearing away before adorning (at-takhliyah qabla at-tahliyah).

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: Allah's punishment of the Jews and Christians has not ceased and will not cease. This is from His saying ﴿why does He punish you﴾, not ﴿why did He punish you﴾, to indicate that Allah's punishment of them is continuous, because the present tense indicates continuity. The Jews in particular are punished and scattered, because their claim of love and sonship is greater than the Christians' claim. And they, God willing, will receive the final punishment at the hands of the Muslims, when they fight the Muslims and the Muslims kill them, to the extent that a Jew hides behind a tree and the tree calls out: "O Muslim, there is a Jew behind me, so kill him!" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2926) and Muslim (2922/82), from Abu Hurayrah.]

* Student: Can it be said regarding His, blessed and exalted, saying ﴿We are the children of Allah﴾ that the Jews meant literal sonship, and that there was a son of Allah among them, for example as al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan al-Basri said: "'Ali addressed us," meaning the people of Kufa, though he was not present, and as we say: "We were victorious over the disbelievers at Badr," though we were not present at all?

* The Shaykh: As for if they were all descendants of Isa, there would be no harm; if they were all descendants of Uzair, there would be no harm. But they are not like that.

* Student: Is there any evidence, O Shaykh?

* The Shaykh: I have not seen anyone say this. You mean the meaning: "The Jews said: among us are the children of Allah, and the Christians said: among us are the children of Allah." No.

* Student: ﴿We are the children of Allah﴾, since Uzair (...)?

* The Shaykh: No, they did not intend that.

* Student: Can one not take from this verse ﴿The Jews and the Christians said: We are the children of Allah and His beloved﴾, that since Allah, Mighty and Majestic, did not deny the attribute of this claim, it is a refutation of the Ash'aris? For Allah, Mighty and Majestic, did not deny the matter of love, but denied that it applies to them. Can this be evidence in refuting the Ash'aris?

* The Shaykh: Glory be to Allah! Did we not say this?

* The students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: We said: they know of Allah's attributes what these deniers do not know. If we say this, it is the best evidence for this.

* Student: You said: the Ash'aris said love is reward or the will for reward. Why "or" here, as a precaution against what? I did not understand.

* The Shaykh: Some of them say this and some say that: some said love is reward, and some said it is the will for reward.

* Student: Is the will for reward, or reward itself, among the acts?

* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. The reason is that they explained it both ways, because they said: they affirm the will themselves; they affirm that Allah is willing and has a will, and that Allah is a creator and has a creation. So reward would be something created, separate from Allah, one of His acts, not one of His attributes. The will is one of His attributes and they affirm it.

* Student: Shaykh, can it be taken from His, the Exalted, saying ﴿We are the children of Allah and His beloved﴾ that truth is taken from whoever brings it?

* The Shaykh: How so?

* Student: Because He did not deny their affirmation of the attribute of love.

* The Shaykh: In fact, it is not the subject of dispute so that we say they did not deny it. The subject of dispute is that they made this claim. There is no doubt that truth is taken from whoever brings it, and this has come up for us often; we have explained that the Messenger ﷺ accepted truth from the devil, Allah accepted truth from the polytheists, and the Messenger accepted it from the Jews also.

from whoever brings it, and this has come up for us often; we have explained that the Messenger ﷺ accepted truth from the devil, Allah accepted truth from the polytheists, and the Messenger accepted it from the Jews also.

* * *
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the punishment of the Jews and Christians is continuous, as we said.
* Among its benefits: the affirmation of causes, from His saying ﴿for your sins﴾.

* Among its benefits: caution against what suggests falsehood. He said ﴿why does He punish you for your sins?﴾ and did not say "why does He punish you," because if He had said it without joining ﴿for your sins﴾, it would have implied that Allah punishes without sin.

* * *
* Student: ﴿And when Musa said to his people: O my people, remember the favour of Allah upon you when He appointed prophets among you, made you kings, and gave you what He had not given anyone else among the worlds. (20) O my people, enter the Holy Land which Allah has prescribed for you, and do not turn back on your heels, lest you return as losers﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 20, 21].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿O People of the Scripture, Our Messenger has come to you, making clear to you after a lull in messengers﴾.

* Among the benefits of the previous noble verse, from His saying ﴿Rather, you are human beings from among those He has created﴾: "bal" here we explained as an annulling retraction.

* It is derived from it that these who claimed to be the children of Allah and His beloved are human beings, and human beings are equal before Allah, and the most honoured of them before Allah is the most pious.

* Among its benefits: affirmation of Allah's creation of human beings. Someone may say this is unnecessary, as it is known. But Allah said ﴿from among those He has created﴾, making clear that they are created, like the rest of mankind.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, forgives and punishes whom He wills. But is this mere will, that He forgives if He wills and punishes if He wills, or must there be a cause?

The answer: the second; there must be a cause.

It has become clear to us an important principle: every act that Allah has linked to His will follows wisdom, since Allah has no bare will, but His will is joined with His wisdom, blessed and exalted, as Allah said: ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills; indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ [Al-Insan 30].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of will for Allah, and the will here means the universal will (al-irada al-kawniyya). Know that there is no division in it; that is, it is not divided into universal will and legislative will, unlike "will" (irada), so will (mashi'a) is one thing: the universal will.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the exclusivity of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in dominion, and that there is no owner besides Him. From which words of His? Answer.

* Student: ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾.

* The Shaykh: Yes, ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens﴾. What is the reason?

* Student: The fronting of the prepositional phrase over...

* The Shaykh: The predicate, correct: the exclusivity of Allah, the Exalted, in dominion.

If someone says: Allah the Exalted affirmed dominion for His servants in His saying ﴿or what you possess of its keys﴾ [An-Nur 61], ﴿or what your right hands possess﴾ [An-Nisa 3], and the like?

We say: the two kinds of dominion are not equal. Allah's dominion is general and complete, while the human's dominion is limited and deficient. That is why a person may not destroy his property even though it is his property. If a person wanted to burn his property, we would say: that is not possible; we restrain him and prevent him, because it contradicts what Allah has commanded, indeed it is what Allah has forbidden.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that between the heavens and the earth there are great creatures that required that they be counterpart and equal to the heavens and the earth. From where is this derived? From His saying: ﴿and what is between them﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the return of all creatures is to Allah alone; from His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and to Him is the final return﴾, meaning the return.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 5, verse 19 (part 1 of 3):

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿O People of the Scripture, there has come to you Our Messenger, making clear to you [the truth] after a lapse of messengers﴾. In this single verse there are two calls to the People of the Scripture.

﴿O People of the Scripture﴾: the intended meaning is the Jews and the Christians.

﴿there has come to you Our Messenger﴾: this is Muhammad ﷺ.

﴿making clear to you﴾: ﴿making clear﴾ is a circumstantial clause (al-jumlah al-haliyyah) describing (rasul, "messenger"). The meaning is: while he makes clear to you, that is, explains and elaborates.

Allah, blessed and exalted, did not mention what is made clear, so that the meaning would be general, because omitting the object indicates generality. This is a well-known rule in the Arabic language: omission indicates generality.

So here, ﴿making clear to you﴾: what does he make clear? We say: he makes clear everything that people need to have made clear. For this reason Allah said in the Noble Qur'an: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation of all things﴾ [al-Nahl 89].

His saying ﴿after a lapse of messengers﴾ means: the making clear occurs after a lapse of messengers, that is, a period of time in which no messenger came. We do not gain much benefit from knowing the exact duration of this period, but we know that it was a long period, estimated at about six hundred years between 'Isa (Jesus) and Muhammad ﷺ, because the last of the prophets sent to the people was 'Isa, peace be upon him, and after him Muhammad ﷺ. There is no prophet between them.

For this reason, what is mentioned in some histories, that Khalid ibn Sinan and so-and-so and so-and-so were prophets sent after 'Isa, is all untrue, because the Prophet ﷺ informed us that there was no prophet between him and 'Isa. What proves this is that 'Isa said: ﴿announcing a messenger who will come after me, whose name is Ahmad﴾ [al-Saff 6]. No one came after 'Isa except Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him and his family.

﴿after a lapse of messengers﴾: the lapse is specified only to make clear that people were in the greatest need of the sending of a messenger. This is the reality, for Allah, the Exalted, looked upon the people of the earth and despised them, Arab and non-Arab, meaning He hated and abhorred them, because they were not upon any religion except remnants of the People of the Scripture, a few remnants, as Allah said: ﴿Why were there not among the generations before you those of remaining virtue who would forbid corruption on earth?﴾ What? ﴿Except a few of those We saved from them﴾ [Hud 116]. Only a few remained. And these few too needed a messenger. Therefore He specified the lapse, which was the long period of about six hundred years, to make clear how great people's need was for what? For the sending of the Messenger, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him and his family.

Then He said: ﴿lest you should say﴾, meaning: lest you say. So ﴿an-taqulu﴾ (lest you say) and what follows it here expresses purpose (ta'lil). The meaning is: We sent him to you so that you could not argue and say: ''There came to us no bringer of good news nor warner.'' That is because of what? Because of the length of the period. No messengers or prophets had come to them, so they would argue, saying: ''There came to us no bringer of good news nor warner.''

As for His saying ﴿there came to us no bringer of good news nor warner﴾: this ﴿min﴾ (from/any) is parsed by the grammarians as superfluous (za'idah) in form, but it adds emphasis in meaning. This is a well-known rule among the rhetoricians: all superfluous particles indicate emphasis. The original sentence would be: ''There came to us no bringer of good news nor warner.'' This is the original form, but when ﴿min﴾ is added, it becomes a stronger indication of negation than if it were not added. For this reason they say that negation can be explicit in generality when the negating particle is ﴿la﴾ (no), or when it is accompanied by a superfluous prepositional particle, whether ﴿min﴾ or the letter ba'.

Here He says ﴿min bashir﴾ (any bringer of good news). We said that ﴿min﴾ is superfluous in terms of i'rab (grammatical case-endings). So who can parse it?

* A student: ﴿bashir﴾ is a subject in the nominative case, and the sign of its nominative is a presumed ḍammah on its final letter, prevented from appearing by the occupation of the position by the vowel of the prepositional particle.

* The Shaykh: ﴿bashir﴾ is a subject in the nominative, with a presumed ḍammah on its final letter, prevented from appearing by what? By the occupation of the position by the vowel of the superfluous prepositional particle. For the prepositional particle is a verbal tool, so its effect on the wording must be greater than its effect on the meaning.

An extraneous question: if we conjoin to the subject that is genitive because of ﴿min﴾ a word to which ﴿min﴾ was not attached, what do we do?

* A student: It is put in the nominative with a visible vowel.

* The Shaykh: It is put in the nominative, obligatorily?

* The student: Obligatorily, yes.

* The Shaykh: Obligatorily.

* A student: There are two options.

* The Shaykh: There are two options.

* The student: Either it is put in the nominative with a ḍammah, by conjoining the conjunct to the position of the thing conjoined, or it is put in the genitive with the vowel of this prepositional particle, by conjoining it to its wording.

* The Shaykh: That is, both are permitted. So His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Ma lakum min ilahin ghayruhu﴾ (You have no god other than Him) [al-A'raf 59], and ﴿ghayruhu﴾ (other than Him), both are correct. The conjunct after a genitive introduced by a superfluous prepositional particle may be treated according to its position or according to its wording.

﴿there came to us no bringer of good news nor warner﴾. ﴿bringer of good news﴾ gives glad tidings of good. And ﴿warner﴾ warns of evil.

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Then there has come to you a bringer of good news and a warner﴾, meaning: now you have no argument.

Who is ﴿there has come to you a bringer of good news and a warner﴾? It is the Messenger of Allah, Muhammad, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him and his family.

﴿Then there has come to you a bringer of good news and a warner, and Allah is over all things competent﴾. He concluded this verse with the attribute of power, as an indication that He, blessed and exalted, is able to send messengers and able not to send messengers, and that the whole matter is in His hand, blessed and exalted is He.

* A student: We mentioned that there is no prophet after 'Isa. How about some prophets who died after 'Isa, peace be upon him, like Yahya and Zakariyya? That is, they died before 'Isa was raised, and also, Shaykh, ...?

* The Shaykh: They died before what?

* The student: They died after him.

* The Shaykh: After 'Isa?

* The student: Yes, Shaykh. And they also mention, in the books of the Christians, and the Muslims agreed with them on it, such as Ibn Kathir and others, names of prophets like Daniel and Ezekiel. Do we deny all of this, Shaykh?

* The Shaykh: It needs proof.

* The student: Shaykh, Ibn Kathir narrates in al-Bidayah wa'l-Nihayah, and affirms Daniel.

* The Shaykh: Between Ibn Kathir and 'Isa there are nations; this needs proof, because the hadith is authentic from the Prophet, peace be upon him, that there was no prophet between him and 'Isa.[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3442) and Muslim (2365 / 143) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] And there is no statement of anyone after him to rely on.

* The student: Is he not a messenger?

* The Shaykh: The original state is that this is not so.

* A student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you. It was mentioned in the verse, and what you said about it, in His saying ﴿and what is between them﴾, that what is between the heavens and the earth is a great creation. Therefore Allah, mighty and majestic, made it a counterpart to the heavens and the earth. So what is the extent of the accuracy of the statements of the astronomers about those creatures that lie between, what they call space, and those immense distances that the mind cannot count? Do they agree with this, or is it contrary to our law?

* The Shaykh: What the astronomers mention on this matter is not to be affirmed or denied, like the reports of the Children of Israel: neither affirmed nor denied, and we do not agree with them, because the distances are, as you said, immense. Even some of them say that the stars we see tonight are the stars of yesterday, and their light did not reach us until after twenty-four hours. Is this reasonable?!

In any case, we neither affirm nor deny these things, but we know that there are creatures there. We have mentioned before what we know: the winds, the clouds, the rains, the moon, the stars. All of these are between the sky and the earth.

* A student: The estimate... and our saying: this is a superfluous particle, is such a thing permitted in the Qur'an, Shaykh?

* The Shaykh: No, qualify it. If there is a superfluous prepositional particle in the verse, say: superfluous in i'rab. Some grammarians call it a particle of connection (harf silah), but there is no basis for this. Rather, it should be said that it is a superfluous prepositional particle in i'rab. Among the phrases that may be used is: ''it is superfluous, superfluous.'' What is the meaning of ''superfluous, superfluous''? It is superfluous in wording and superfluous in meaning. The first is superfluous from the intransitive verb, from zāda yazīdu (to increase), which is intransitive, and the second is from zāda (transitive). Because zāda can be intransitive and can be transitive. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And those who are guided﴾ what?

* The students: ﴿He increases them﴾ [Muhammad 17].

* The Shaykh: Is it transitive or intransitive? Transitive. And you say: zāda al-mā' (the water rose), which is intransitive.

* The student: The estimate, Shaykh. The basic principle in the estimate of the verse, you say: in other than the Qur'an?

* The Shaykh: It is not necessary.

* The student: Meaning it is permitted to say...?

* The Shaykh: Yes, because the estimate is not the actual reality. A person may estimate something that is impossible. Allah, the Exalted, estimated something impossible, He said: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would have been ruined﴾ [al-Anbiya' 22]. This is impossible, but it is by way of supposition.

* A student: Shaykh, may Allah bless you. The negation in the matter of generality, if the negating particle is ''la'' at the end of the sentence.

* The Shaykh: The ''la'' of generic negation (la al-nafiyah lil-jins).

* The student: (...) that it is the generic negation or the other one?

* The Shaykh: The ''la'' of generic negation. There is a ''la'' that they call the ''la'' of unity (al-nafiyah lil-wahdah), and this does not indicate generality.

* A student: May Allah be good to you. His saying ''what is between the heavens and the earth'': does it include what is between the first heaven and the earth, or between the seventh heaven and the earth?

* The Shaykh: What?

* The student: His saying ﴿and what is between them﴾, does it include what is between the first heaven and the earth?

* The Shaykh: This is the apparent meaning: what is between the lowest heaven and the earth.

* The student: Does this not include the angels who are in the heavens? The angels who are in the heavens are not included in this?

* The Shaykh: No. ﴿the dominion of the heavens﴾ is inside the heavens; it is not inside ﴿what is between them﴾; it is inside the heavens.

* A student: Shaykh, the grammarians say that the criterion for superfluous ''min'' is that it come after a negation or something resembling negation, and that its object be indefinite. And they say the sign of a prepositional particle is that when it is deleted the sentence remains sound.

* The Shaykh: Correct.

* The student: Sometimes there is a verse where the sentence remains sound with the particle deleted, yet it is not superfluous, such as His saying: ﴿Whatever sign We abrogate or cause to be forgotten﴾ [al-Baqarah 106], and His saying: ﴿He will forgive you of your sins﴾ [al-Ahqaf 31]?

* The Shaykh: Yes, this is not superfluous. This ''min'' is an explanation of ''ma''. Because in ﴿ma nansakh﴾ (whatever We abrogate), ''ma'' is a conditional noun, and all conditional nouns are ambiguous, so ''min'' comes here for clarification, and is not superfluous. Ibn Malik says about ''min'':

''It is added after negation or its like, to govern an indefinite noun, as in: ''No refuge is there for a rebel from [Allah's decree]''.''

It may also be added with a definite noun, but this is rare.

* A student: We mentioned before that the lands are seven. Where are the remaining six?

* The Shaykh: The remaining six are within the depths of this earth, because the Prophet ﷺ said: ''Whoever unjustly takes a span of land, Allah will collar him with it on the Day of Resurrection from seven earths.''[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3198) and Muslim (1610 / 137) from the hadith of Sa'id ibn Zayd.]] This indicates that the earths are within this earth. But how? We do not know.

* A student: May Allah bless you, Shaykh. The people of the interval (ahl al-fatrah) before the mission of the Prophet ﷺ, concerning whom many texts report that many of them enter the Fire: were they charged with the religion of 'Isa, which was the last to be revealed, or were they charged with the creed of Ibrahim, who was from the Arabs?

* The Shaykh: No, they were charged only with the creed of Ibrahim, because 'Isa was sent to his own people, like other prophets. But the apparent view, and Allah knows best, is that there is no objection to someone adhering to the religion of Ibrahim or the religion of Musa at that time, since no messenger had been sent to him.

* The student: If he, while in the land of the Arabs, received the message of 'Isa, for example, must he believe in it?

* The Shaykh: It is not obligatory.

* * *

* A student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿And when We appointed for Musa forty nights, then you took the calf [as deity] after him while you were wrongdoers (51). Then We pardoned you after that, that you might be grateful (52). And when We gave Musa the Scripture and the criterion that you might be guided (53). And [mention] when Musa said to his people: O my people, you have wronged yourselves by your taking of the calf, so return in repentance to your Creator and kill yourselves. That is best for you in the sight of your Creator. And He accepted your repentance; indeed, He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah 51-54].

* The Shaykh: Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And when We appointed for Musa forty nights﴾. Allah had previously appointed him thirty nights and completed them with ten. ﴿So the term set by his Lord was complete, forty nights﴾ [al-A'raf 142].

Allah appointed him for His private conversation this period, and Musa appointed his brother Harun over his people and said: ﴿Take my place among my people, do right, and do not follow the way of the corrupters﴾ [al-A'raf 142]. So Harun was Musa's successor among his people when he went to the appointment of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Then the Children of Israel, out of their insolence and obstinacy, made a calf of gold, and took it as a god. The originator of this idea was a man called al-Samiri. They made, from the ornaments which it is said they had taken from the people of Pharaoh, a bull, a calf, and made for it a hollow through which the wind entered from the rear and came out of the mouth. So when the wind entered they heard from it a sound like the lowing of a bull.

Al-Samiri said: ﴿This is your god and the god of Musa﴾ [Ta-Ha 88]. Musa had gone to seek his god and had gone astray; for this reason thirty nights passed and more, as he sought this god, but he forgot and strayed and wandered. And this is your god and the god of Musa. Harun kept reminding them of this and said: ﴿Your Lord is the Most Merciful, so follow me and obey my command﴾ [Ta-Ha 90]. He was a prophet, but they persisted in arrogance and said: ﴿We will not cease to be devoted to it until Musa returns to us﴾ [Ta-Ha 91], and they persisted in worshipping the calf.

Musa, peace be upon him, returned and found them in a state that was not pleasing, contrary to what he had left them upon. He became angry, threw down the tablets, which were the Torah that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, had written with His own hand, threw them out of intense anger, and seized his brother by the head and beard, dragging him toward himself violently, saying: ﴿What prevented you, when you saw them going astray (92), from following me?﴾ [Ta-Ha 91-92]. This was out of intense anger; otherwise, in a state of contentment, he would surely first have asked: how did they go astray, before saying: ﴿What prevented you, when you saw them going astray, from following me?﴾

But a human being is a human who is affected by what affects human states. He said: ﴿O son of my mother, do not seize my beard or my head. Indeed, I feared that you would say: ''You caused division among the Children of Israel and did not observe my word''﴾ [Ta-Ha 94]. Notice that he feared from Musa, peace be upon him, that he would say: ''You caused division among the Children of Israel.'' For if he had spoken, or increased their admonition, they would have divided into two groups: one group with Harun, and another group with al-Samiri. So it is as if he, peace be upon him, left that out for fear of this. And even so, they also persisted in what they were upon, taking him as a god until they worshipped him. The story is detailed in Surah Ta-Ha. They took him as a god; for this reason He said: ﴿Then you took the calf [as deity] after him﴾. ﴿the calf﴾ is the first object of ﴿you took﴾, and the second object is omitted, and the estimate is: then you took the calf as a god.

His saying: ﴿after him﴾ indicates that they did not take it at the very first moment, but there was an interval. As I told you, when the period that Musa, peace be upon him, had set was over, and Allah then added to it, they said: ''This is the god, but he has forgotten.''

His saying: ﴿while you were wrongdoers﴾: the waw here is for the circumstantial clause, describing the subject of ﴿you took﴾. The meaning is: and the situation is that you are wrongdoers, having no excuse. And how could they have an excuse when their prophet Harun was saying: ﴿O my people, you are only being tested by it, and indeed your Lord is the Most Merciful, so follow me and obey my command﴾ [Ta-Ha 90]?!

Then, after this ugly and monstrous deed, Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿Then We pardoned you after that﴾. Consider His words: ﴿while you were wrongdoers﴾. Were they wronging themselves or wronging others? They were wronging themselves, for every disobedient person wrongs himself; if the harm of his disobedience extends to others, he has wronged both himself and others.

﴿Then We pardoned you﴾ means: We overlooked this act and lifted the punishment from you.

﴿So that you might be grateful﴾ means: in order that you may give thanks. Here "la'alla" (so that) expresses purpose (ta'lil). As we have mentioned before, "la'alla" comes with several meanings: among them purpose, which is frequent in the Noble Qur'an; hope (raja'); wish (tamanni); apprehension and fear (ishfaq); and expectation (tawaqqu'). All of these are known from context.

As for His words ﴿so that you might be grateful﴾, gratitude (shukr) is good action (al-'amal al-salih), as it has come in the Qur'an. Its proof is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Allah commanded the believers with what He commanded the messengers, when He said, Exalted is He: ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds﴾, and He said regarding the believers: ﴿Eat of the good things with which We have provided you, and give thanks to Allah﴾." [Narrated by Muslim (1015/65) from Abu Hurairah.] This shows that gratitude is good action, and there is no doubt about this.

Know that gratitude is only given in return for a favour, unlike praise (hamd), which is given for the perfection of the one praised and for his bounty. Thus the cause of praise is more general than that of gratitude, but gratitude is more general than praise in terms of its scope, as it is connected with the heart, the tongue and the limbs, as the poet said:
"Three blessings from me have benefited you: my hand, my tongue, and my hidden heart."

There are several benefits in these two verses. Among them: the exposure of the faults of the Children of Israel, for they took the calf as a god when their prophet was absent.

Among its benefits: the affirmation of the speech of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, based on His words: ﴿And We appointed for Moses thirty nights﴾ [al-A'raf 142]. A promise is generally made between two parties by speech. Moreover, Allah spoke at that appointment, to the extent that Moses, peace be upon him, out of his intense longing to see Allah, said: ﴿My Lord, show me Yourself that I may look at You﴾ [al-A'raf 143].

Among them: the exposure of the foolishness of the Jewish people, the people of anger, when they took the calf as a god. What is strange is that they themselves made the calf with their own hands and then took it as a god. But do not be surprised, for whomever Allah leads astray, there is no guide for him. The pre-Islamic Arabs did something similar or worse. It is said that they would make a god from dates, and when they were hungry—

*Student: They ate it.

*Shaykh: When they were hungry, they ate it. They do not claim that it brings them provision; they know it cannot possess that. Yet they eat it. They say that when they descend upon a land, they take four stones, choose the best of them to be a god, and set the other three as supports for the cooking pot on which they place the pot.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: the Children of Israel have no excuse for taking the calf as a god, because the proof was established against them, based on the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿while you were wrongdoers﴾.

Can it be derived from this verse that if they had taken the calf as a god without wronging anyone, they would not have been blamed? Or is it said that this is only a description of their state? Both possibilities are allowed. It may be that this is a description of their condition, that they took it as a god without any excuse. It may also be evidence that when a person is excused, he is not held to account. This is supported by the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And your Lord would never destroy the cities until He sent in their mother-town a messenger reciting to them Our verses; and We would not destroy the cities except when their people were wrongdoers﴾ [al-Qasas 59].

Accordingly, the verse contains evidence that whoever commits a bad deed—shirk or less than it—while being excused, has no punishment. Then, if he claims to be Muslim, he is judged outwardly by that, since he is a Muslim. If he claims adherence to another religion and the religion of Islam has not reached him, he is treated in this world according to the religion he follows, and his affair in the Hereafter is with whom? With Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. This is the detailed explanation of the issue of excuse due to ignorance.

If someone calls himself a Muslim, testifies that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, establishes prayer, pays zakah, performs Hajj and 'Umrah, and says he is a Muslim, but has some shirk in him out of ignorance, having lived in a land where this shirk prevails and not knowing that it is shirk, then he is treated—what? As a Muslim, according to his outward condition. Likewise, in the Hereafter, Allah does not hold him to account, because he is excused.

As for one who is excused but does not claim to be Muslim, adhering to a specific religion, he is treated in this world as the disbelievers are treated, meaning the people of that religion, and in the Hereafter it is said: his affair is with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Among the benefits of the second verse: the demonstration of Allah's favour to the Children of Israel, that after they committed this shirk based on error in religion and foolishness in intellect, Allah pardoned them: ﴿Then We pardoned you﴾.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: Allah forgives all sins without exception, but after repentance, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah; indeed Allah forgives all sins. Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ [az-Zumar 53].

But if someone says: does the noble verse not indicate that they repented? It is said: other verses indicate that they turned in repentance to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and returned to Allah, and that the cloud shaded them, and they were commanded that some of them kill others. When Allah knew from them the sincerity of their return to Him, and that they complied even to the point of killing, Allah pardoned them.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: whoever has been granted a religious blessing by Allah is obliged to be grateful for it, just as for a worldly blessing, based on His words: ﴿Then We pardoned you after that, so that you might be grateful﴾.

Which is greater as a favour? Religious blessings are without doubt greater. So when Allah bestows upon you a religious blessing, consider it among the greatest blessings and be thankful for it. Gratitude for religious blessings is of their kind. For example, whoever Allah has granted knowledge, part of thanking Allah for it is to learn and spread his knowledge.

Likewise, whoever Allah has granted wealth, part of thanking Allah for this wealth is to give charity from it, benefit the poor, maintain ties of kinship, and be dutiful to his parents.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of causes (ilal) in the acts of Allah. From where is this taken? From His words: ﴿so that you might be grateful﴾. There is no doubt for us in this: all the acts and rulings of Allah are based on causes and wisdoms, though some of them are known and some are not.

As for one who says that the acts and rulings of Allah the Exalted are not based on wisdom and are not explained by a cause, he is without doubt misguided in his religion and foolish in his intellect.

Then the Mighty and Majestic said, explaining another of the greatest blessings: ﴿And when We gave Moses the Scripture and the Criterion﴾. ﴿We gave Moses﴾ means: We bestowed upon him. "Atayna" with the long vowel takes two objects, unlike "ataynā" (without the madd), which takes only one object, because "ātā" with the long vowel means "gave" and "atā" means "came."

He says: ﴿We gave Moses the Scripture﴾, meaning We bestowed it upon him. The "al" in ﴿al-Kitab﴾ is for definiteness (al-'ahd), that is, the known mental reference: the Book known to you, which is the Torah. It was called a Book because it is written, for Allah wrote the Torah with His own hand, may He be exalted.

﴿And the Criterion﴾: the waw is a conjunction, and ﴿al-Furqan﴾ is coordinated with ﴿al-Kitab﴾. Is it something other than it, or is it the same, but of the type of coordinating an attribute with the thing it describes?

The answer: the second. The Criterion is the same as the Book, for the Torah is a Criterion; Allah distinguished by it between truth and falsehood, between justice and oppression, between the friends of Allah and the enemies of Allah, and so on with whatever makes distinction and differentiation.

Accordingly, its coordination is of the type of coordinating what? An attribute with the thing it describes. Have you seen the words of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High, who created and proportioned, and who decreed and guided﴾ [al-A'la 1-3]? "The One who decreed and guided" is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, but this is of the type of coordinating one attribute with another attribute.

He, may He be exalted, says: ﴿and the Criterion, that you may be guided﴾. "La'alla" here is for purpose, as already mentioned. ﴿Tahtadun﴾ means: you take the path of guidance. The guidance meant here, which Allah mentioned, is both guidance of instruction (irshad) and guidance of success (tawfiq). This is because what Moses was given was knowledge; whoever is guided by it has knowledge, and likewise knowledge produces action for whoever is granted success. So we explain guidance here as what? As the guidance of knowledge and the guidance of success, the cognitive and the practical.

Benefits of the noble verse: First, Moses was a prophet, indeed a messenger, because Allah gave him the Book, and everyone whom Allah gave the Book is a messenger, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿We certainly sent Our messengers with clear proofs, and revealed with them the Scripture and the Balance﴾ [al-Hadid 25].

Among them: praise of the Torah, in that Allah called it a Criterion.

Among them: the wisdom in giving the Book and the Criterion to Moses, which is guidance.

Among them: knowledge is a cause of guidance, as indicated by the purpose clause in His words: ﴿that you may be guided﴾. But must the cause always produce its effect, or may an impediment exist? An impediment may exist.

Accordingly, no one should object to us by saying: do we not find among scholars those who were not guided?

We say: because of an impediment. Otherwise, the principle is that knowledge is the cause of guidance and that guidance occurs through knowledge, but there may be obstacles and distractions that prevent a person from benefiting from the knowledge Allah has given him, as is well known.

*Student: "Ataa" with the long vowel—a verse has puzzled me, Shaykh.

*Shaykh: Which is it?

*Student: In Surah al-Ahzab, in a written reading with a hamza of qat', it is read "ātaw," the verse: ﴿And if they had been entered upon from its surrounding areas, then asked to commit fitnah, they would have given it, and they would not have hesitated therein except briefly﴾ [al-Ahzab 14]. Perhaps its origin is "la-ataw-hā"?

*Shaykh: Yes, I think there are two readings: ﴿la'ataw-hā﴾ and ﴿la'ātawhā﴾.

*Student: Has the meaning changed, Shaykh?

*Shaykh: Undoubtedly it has changed, but each has its aspect, and the two readings convey two meanings. ﴿And if they had been entered upon from its surrounding areas﴾.

There are two readings: ﴿la'ataw-hā﴾ and ﴿la'ātawhā﴾. As for ﴿la'ataw-hā﴾, it is clear: ﴿then asked to commit fitnah﴾, meaning someone invited them to fitnah and they would have responded. Is it clear?

Or ﴿la'ātawhā﴾: they would have responded and given another fitnah, not the fitnah to which they were invited; and the verse would contain two benefits: first, their acceptance of fitnah; second, their increasing it.

*Student: Which reading is relied upon by people?

*Shaykh: No, ﴿la'ātawhā﴾.

*Student: ﴿la'ātawhā﴾?

*Shaykh: Yes.

*Student: The orthography differs.

*Shaykh: How?

*Student: Meaning the rasm, Shaykh, ﴿la'ataw-hā﴾ with the short vowel.

*Student: ﴿la'ātawhā﴾, because the hamza is before the alif and not directly above it.

*Shaykh: If it is before it, then it is "la-ātawā." It is before it in your copy?

*Student: All the mushafs we have are like this, with it before.

*Shaykh: Yes, and what is above the alif in yours?

*Student: Nothing.

*Shaykh: In mine there is no hamza, but it is elongated; this is elongated.

*Student: Is this how it is pronounced?

*Shaykh: Yes indeed.

*Student: Shaykh, some people derive that calling to tawhid divides the Muslims?

*Shaykh: What people?

*Student: Calling to tawhid and creed divides the unity of the Muslims. From this it is built that Harun did not object to the Children of Israel when they took the calf as a god, meaning as intercession: ﴿And to Thamud, their brother Salih﴾ [al-A'raf 73] (...). How do we respond to them?

*Shaykh: The response to them is easy. As for the first verse, Harun feared that, but who said it would happen had he called them? In fact they refused him and said: ﴿We will not cease to be devoted to it until Moses returns to us﴾, so it became known that they were arrogant.

As for ﴿then they are two factions contending﴾ [an-Naml 45], this contains no evidence that a person should not call. Rather, it is evidence that the people to whom Salih was sent split, as people split over the call of the Messenger, peace be upon him: some believed and some disbelieved.

*Student: Shaykh, may Allah reward you with good. What are some of the impediments and distractions that turn a scholar or a seeker of knowledge away from guidance?

*Shaykh: That there be in his heart an evil intention, such as seeking by his knowledge other than Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. This may deprive him of the blessing of knowledge, and this is among the gravest things. The second thing: sins. Sins drag one another along. When a person who has been given knowledge by Allah disobeys, he is deprived.

* * *

*Student: ﴿And when Moses said to his people: O my people, remember the favour of Allah upon you when He made among you prophets and made you kings and gave you what He had not given anyone among the worlds (20). O my people, enter the Holy Land which Allah has prescribed for you and do not turn back on your heels, for you would become losers (21). They said: O Moses, indeed therein is a people of tyrants, and indeed we will never enter it until they leave it. But if they leave it, then indeed we will enter (22). Two men from those who feared, upon whom Allah had bestowed favour, said: Enter upon them through the gate, for when you have entered it, indeed you will be victorious. And upon Allah rely, if you are believers﴾ [al-Ma'idah 20-23].

*Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O People of the Scripture, there has come to you Our Messenger, making clear to you after a interval of messengers﴾, and so on to the end.

* Among the benefits of this verse: it is appropriate that a person be addressed—that is, the addressee be called—by the attribute that requires him to carry out what is directed to him, based on His words: ﴿O People of the Scripture﴾. This exists in the Arabic language: when you address a believer you say, "O believer," and when you address a man you say, "O man," as if you are reminding him of what should have moved him to listen to you and comply with what you direct to him.

There are benefits in this—that is, in our addressing the speech by calling with the attribute that requires compliance:
* First: rebuking this man if he opposes, since he should not oppose while characterized by this attribute.
* Second: urging him to agree, in view of this attribute he has.
That is why we find the Messenger ﷺ always saying: "It is not lawful for a man who believes in Allah and the Last Day..." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (104), Muslim (135/44), from Abu Shurayh al-'Adawi], and "It is not lawful for a woman who believes in Allah and the Last Day..." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1088), Muslim (1339/420), from Abu Hurairah].

* Among the benefits also: the establishment of blame against them by others.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, was sent to the People of the Scripture, the Jews and the Christians, based on His words: ﴿Our Messenger has come to you﴾, meaning to you.

* Among its benefits: those among them—that is, among the Jews and Christians—who disbelieved in Muhammad, may the peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family, are disbelievers, because they disbelieved in the Messenger who was sent to them.

As for their claim that they believe in Allah and the Last Day, we say: this is not sufficient; you must believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, and the Last Day.

* One of the benefits of this noble verse is praise of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for being sent by Allah, based on His saying: ﴿Our Messenger﴾.

* Another benefit is that it establishes proof against the community (ummah). This is the Messenger of Allah, and he is a proof (hujjah) upon them, peace be upon him. The mere fact that Allah testified that he is His Messenger was itself a proof. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿But Allah bears witness to what He has sent down to you; He sent it down with His knowledge, and the angels bear witness﴾ [an-Nisa 166].

* Another benefit of this noble verse is that the Messenger, peace be upon him, has no share in anything of lordship (rububiyyah). What is the reason for this? He is a messenger, and a messenger cannot be a partner of the one who sent him in what is exclusive to Him.

* Another benefit is that the Prophet (ﷺ) makes things clear to creation, and that there is nothing in what he brought that is obscure or riddle-like, based on His saying: ﴿makes clear to you﴾.

* Another benefit is the refutation of those Mufawwidah (those who delegate the meaning of the names and attributes of Allah) who say: "We know nothing of the meanings of Allah's names and attributes. Our duty is only to recite and not to interpret." This statement is among the greatest and most corrupt of statements. Indeed, Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, said that it is one of the worst statements of the people of innovation (ahl al-bid'ah) and heresy (ilhad).

It is regrettable that many people, even some scholars, think that this is the methodology of the Salaf (the early righteous generations), and they say: "The methodology of the Salaf is delegation (tafwid)." In reality, they have not known the methodology of the Salaf. The methodology of the Salaf is delegation of the modality (kayfiyyah), because the intellect is unable to grasp it and the Sharia has not revealed it. As for the meaning, they affirm it, establish it, confirm it, and explain in detail what requires detailed explanation. This is a well-known matter from their books.

* Another benefit of this noble verse is that just as the Messenger, peace be upon him, makes things clear to the Arabs, he also makes things clear to the Children of Israel, that is, to the People of the Book.

If someone says: "How can he make things clear to them when his language differs from theirs? The language of the Jews, even those in Madinah during the Prophet's time, differs from the Arabic language."

We say: It is through translation. For this reason, Islam did not spread in non-Arabic lands except through translation.

* Another benefit of the noble verse is that if we need to learn foreign languages in order to explain the Sharia, this is one of the attributes of the Prophet (ﷺ), that he makes things clear to people by whatever means. Have you understood?

Based on this, whoever learns a language other than Arabic for the sake of calling to Allah will be rewarded for it, because it is a means to what? To conveying and spreading the Sharia.

* Another benefit of this noble verse is that the message of the Prophet (ﷺ) came after a gap (fatrah) in the messengers, with no messenger between him and Jesus, based on His saying: ﴿after a gap in the messengers﴾.

* Another benefit is that the longer the period of time since a message, the more people become in need of what? In need of the Messenger. For this reason Allah made it a great favor upon the People of the Book that a messenger came to them after a gap. You know that this also occurs in tangible reality: a person who drinks water while very thirsty longs for water and needs it more than someone who drinks it while already satisfied. Is that clear?

* Another benefit of this noble verse is the affirmation of the earlier messages for the Messenger, peace be upon him, based on His saying: ﴿after a gap in the messengers﴾. It appears to me that this indicates that the Messenger (ﷺ) is the last of the prophets, based on His saying: ﴿of the messengers﴾, meaning that there is no messenger after him.

This is what Allah has explicitly stated in His Book in His saying: ﴿But he is the Messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets﴾ [al-Ahzab 40]. Consider His saying: ﴿the Seal of the Prophets﴾, and He did not say "the Seal of the Messengers," although He said: ﴿Messenger of Allah﴾. This is because a person may be a prophet without being a messenger. Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, is the Seal of the Prophets.

* Another benefit of this noble verse is the mercy of Allah the Exalted toward creation, in that He sent the messengers so that the proof would not stand against Allah. This is derived from His saying: ﴿lest you say: there came to us no bringer of good news and no warner﴾.

In this there is evidence that whoever has not received the message is excused, and this is clear from His saying: ﴿lest you say: there came to us no bringer of good news and no warner﴾.

* Another benefit of this noble verse is that a person has no argument based on divine decree (qadar) for opposing the messengers. From where is this derived?

* Student: Allah the Exalted said: ﴿lest you say: there came to us no bringer of good news and no warner﴾, which indicates an excuse.

* Shaykh: What is the indication?

* Student: They have no right to make an excuse.

* Shaykh: Yes. If they had a right, it would not have been removed by the sending of messengers. Is that clear? And so it is.

* Another benefit of this noble verse is that messages are confined to two things with no third, namely good news (bisharah) and warning (indhar), because people, in relation to the messages, divide into two categories: the obedient, for whom there is good news, and the disobedient, for whom there is warning.

* Another benefit of this noble verse is the strength of the argument of those people if Allah had not sent them a messenger, based on His saying: ﴿no bringer of good news﴾, because the word ﴿min﴾ ("no") here is for emphasis. It is as if they are emphasizing that there came to them neither a bringer of good news nor a warner.

* Another benefit of this noble verse is emphasis of speech through meaning (at-tawkid al-ma'nawi). I do not mean the emphasis of the grammarians. The grammarians say that emphasis (tawkid) is of two kinds: emphasis of meaning (ma'nawi) and emphasis of wording (lafzi). What is done by repeating the word is lafzi, and what is done by the known particles is ma'nawi. But I do not mean this. I mean that meaning may be emphasized by a whole sentence, namely His saying: ﴿So there has come to you a bringer of good news and a warner﴾.

* Another benefit of it is that whenever emphasis is needed, there is no fault in repetition. For this reason it is among the etiquettes of the sermon (khutbah) that a person repeats at important points, and this is not considered incoherence (ayy), nor is it considered excess.

* Another benefit of this noble verse is that the message of the Prophet (ﷺ) includes these two foundations of the messages, namely good news and warning, based on His saying: ﴿So there has come to you a bringer of good news and a warner﴾, meaning Muhammad (ﷺ).

* Another benefit of it is the affirmation of the power of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, based on His saying: ﴿And Allah is Able over all things﴾.

* Another benefit is that nothing is excluded from the power of Allah the Exalted. Everything is within His power, and no thing is excepted.

As for the statement of some, such as the author of Tafsir al-Jalalayn (Jalal al-Din al-Mahalli and al-Suyuti): "The intellect is specified as not being able to act upon its own essence," this is an error. Yet it is correct according to the principle of those who deny voluntary actions (al-af'al al-ikhtiyariyyah). There are people in this ummah who say that voluntary actions do not subsist in Allah the Exalted. He is not able to do them. For example, descending to the lowest heaven is forbidden in their view, sitting upon the Throne is forbidden, laughing is forbidden, coming on the Day of Resurrection is forbidden. Every action He performs by His will and choice, they consider forbidden. Why is it forbidden? They say: "Because it is impossible, and the impossible, by its very name, is not an object of power, like the combination of two contradictories."

It is said to them: This is a mistake. Rather, there are things that Allah cannot be described by, such as sleep for example. It is impossible that Allah sleeps. Is that clear? It is impossible that He eats and drinks.

So if someone said: "Is Allah able to eat, drink or sleep?"

We say: This is a question that does not arise at all, because it is impossible.

But can He descend to the lowest heaven, come to judge between the servants, sit upon the Throne, laugh and be pleased?

It is possible, because this does not contradict His perfection, unlike sleep, eating and drinking, which contradict His perfection.

* Another benefit of this noble verse is that speech should be concluded with what fits the situation. Its reason is that the opposition of the People of the Book to the Messenger, peace be upon him, means that they are exposed to punishment, and Allah is not incapable of punishing them, because of the completeness of His power.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when Moses said to his people, "O my people, remember the favor of Allah upon you"﴾. (Idh) here is an adverbial (zarf). Among the established rules of the grammarians: every adverbial or prepositional-plus-genitive phrase must have something it depends on (muta'alliq), because it occurs only as a complement (ma'mul) or as a complement of time/place (ma'mul fihi). If it is an adverb, it is ma'mul fihi; if it is a prepositional phrase, it is in the position of a direct object (maf'ul bihi), and thus ma'mul fihi. Therefore every prepositional phrase or adverb must have a dependent element. This dependent element is in reality the governing word ('amil). For this reason the author of al-Jumal said:

"The preposition must have a dependence
on a verb or its meaning, like 'murtaqi'."

The reasoning for this is that we say: it is necessary, because the adverb is ma'mul fihi, so there must be a verb in which it occurs, and the prepositional phrase is in the position of a direct object. Here one says: ﴿And when Moses said﴾.

(Idh) here is an adverb requiring a governing word. I observe that all the grammarians of i'rab—except those whose i'rab of the Noble Qur'an we do not know—whenever (idh) occurs, generally estimate for it: "remember when Moses said."

Here, do we say that the dependent element of (idh) is (udhkur, "remember"), so that the address is directed to the Messenger ﷺ, or is the intended meaning "remember" (plural), i.e., O People of the Book?

We say: this or that is possible. If it is the second, the meaning is that Allah Himself reminds them; if it is the first, the meaning is that He commanded His Messenger to remind them. The implication of both meanings is one: "Remember when Moses said to his people"—and they are the Children of Israel.

﴿O my people, remember the favor of Allah upon you﴾.

As for his saying ﴿O my people﴾, he addressed them with the call used for one who is distant. The people of rhetoric (ahl al-balaghah) said: this indicates their aversion, their turning away, and their dullness.

There is no doubt that the Children of Israel were among the most arrogant of people, even toward their Prophet Moses, peace be upon him. Therefore he said: ﴿O my people, remember the favor of Allah upon you﴾. The favor (ni'mah) is bounty and kindness, and the meaning is: remember this favor so that you may be grateful for it.

Then he explained this favor, saying: ﴿when He made among you prophets﴾. This (idh) is connected to ﴿favor﴾, because it carries the meaning of bestowal (in'am), i.e., remember Allah's bestowal upon you when He made among you prophets.

His saying ﴿made among you﴾: (fi) here is for location (zarfiyyah), and we should keep it in its meaning and not take it to mean (min, "from"), i.e., "prophets from you." Rather we say "among you," because a prophet comes from the trusted ones of his people and from the nobles of his people. It is like His saying: ﴿He it is who raised among the unlettered a messenger from among themselves﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 2].

﴿when He made among you prophets﴾: the word ﴿prophets﴾ has two readings: ﴿anbi'a'﴾ and ﴿anbiya'﴾, and both are correct recitations, since both are among the seven canonical readings.

Here, is the meaning of "prophets" messengers, or prophets who are below the rank of messengers? This is possible either way, since among them were messengers and among them were prophets without a message.

﴿and made you kings﴾: i.e., He made you kings. Consider the difference between the prophets and the kings. For the prophets He said: ﴿among you prophets﴾; for the kings He said: ﴿made you kings﴾. Is the meaning of the second expression like the first? But He made kingship general, because any one of them could be a king, unlike prophethood, which is from Allah; therefore He said: ﴿among you prophets﴾ and did not say "made you prophets"?

Or it may be said: ﴿made you kings﴾, and kingship here is relative—i.e., because you were humble servants of the family of Pharaoh, you have now become free, owning yourselves, and no one restricts you in what you wish?

Answer: this is possible and that is possible. It is possible that the meaning is ﴿made you kings﴾, i.e., made kings to arise among you; but regarding prophethood He said ﴿among you prophets﴾, because not everyone can be a prophet, whereas kingship may be held by any one. Or the intended kingship here is relative kingship: that is, considering that you were humble and servants of the family of Pharaoh, you have now become owners of yourselves. There is no doubt that both have occurred.

﴿And He gave you what He had not given anyone among the worlds﴾. (Atakum) means "gave you." The difference between (ataka) and (ataa) is that (ataka) means "came to you," and (ataakum) means "gave you"; therefore (ataakum) takes two objects, though their origin is not subject and predicate. The first object in this verse is the kaf (you), and the second is (ma), i.e., that which He had not given anyone among the worlds.

His saying ﴿lam yu'ti﴾: its original form is "lam yu'tihi," but what was omitted? The returning pronoun that refers back to the relative noun, and the original is: "what He had not given him to anyone among the worlds." On this basis, is ﴿anyone﴾ the second object or the first? The second.

﴿anyone among the worlds﴾: i.e., among the worlds who preceded you, and even those in your time. Notice that he did not say "what He will not give" (ma lan yu'ti); rather he said ﴿ma lam yu'ti﴾, and there is a difference between them. If he had said "what He will not give," the Children of Israel or the people of Moses would have become the best of people until the Day of Resurrection, and no one would be given the like of them. But when he says ﴿ma lam yu'ti﴾, it means in the past, and this is so, because Allah has given this Ummah—praise be to Allah—what He did not give the Children of Israel or others.

﴿And He gave you what He had not given anyone among the worlds﴾.

Then He said: ﴿O my people, enter the Holy Land which Allah has prescribed for you﴾. ﴿O my people, enter the holy land﴾.

* Benefits in this noble verse: it is fitting for the caller (da'i) to remind those he addresses of Allah's blessings upon them, because reminding them of blessings produces in them love of Allah. For this reason a hadith says: "Love Allah for the blessings He nourishes you with" [Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (3789) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: whenever Allah bestows a blessing upon His servant, the servant is obligated to hear and obey more than what is obligatory on others.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: an indication that the presence of prophets among people is one of the greatest blessings, because Allah put that before kingship, saying: ﴿He made among you prophets and made you kings﴾. There is no doubt that people's need for this is greater than their need for kingship, though they need both.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the precedence of the rank of scholars over rulers. What is its basis?

* Students: ﴿when He made among you prophets﴾.

* The Shaykh: ﴿when He made among you prophets﴾, and the scholars are the heirs of the prophets.

﴿and made you kings﴾, and rulers belong to this category: either they are kings, or heirs of them, or their deputies, or the like.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: whoever Allah grants knowledge has received a great blessing that requires remembrance, and this is so, because their prophet Moses, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, reminded them of this blessing.

And you yourself now know this by yourself: if you imagined yourself ignorant, not knowing how to perform ablution or how to pray, nor what is obligatory in ablution, nor what is obligatory in prayer, nor what invalidates ablution, nor what invalidates prayer, you would be blind, without guidance. So when Allah bestows upon you the knowledge of these matters, it is a great blessing that nothing equals. Especially since this Ummah—praise be to Allah—feels that it inherits the best of the prophets, Muhammad ﷺ; the scholars of this Ummah feel this, that they are heirs of Muhammad, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: is releasing a person from restriction (hajr) a blessing of Allah? Is it possible?

* Student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: According to the second meaning, releasing a person from restriction is one of Allah's blessings upon him, because he gains some freedom. You know the concept of restriction; I think it was covered earlier in fiqh.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a person should remind someone with particular emphasis of a particular blessing Allah has bestowed upon him; this is due to His saying: ﴿And He gave you what He had not given anyone among the worlds﴾.

If someone said: this leads to the addressee becoming self-admiring and saying, "Who am I?"

We reply: if this is feared, it is prohibited; and every situation has its appropriate speech. But if mentioning this thing entails that one carry out the command of Allah, then it should be mentioned and there is no harm. Have you understood this?

For this reason, on the Day of Resurrection people will seek intercession through Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus, by what? By the virtues and honors Allah bestowed on them.

* A student: Glad tidings. Sometimes a person is compelled to them in order to win people over, and he may continue this for days—meaning repeatedly. There may be people in the gathering or the mosque to whom he reads glad tidings, saying for example: "Rejoice, you are on good; this is righteousness; you will receive reward," and for the sake of teaching. Is there in this, O Shaykh, any...?

* The Shaykh: The reality is that every situation has its speech. It may be wise not to repel people by mentioning threat and warning, and it may be the opposite. For example, if you are addressing a specific person immersed in sins, then here the aspect of warning may be better; but with warning you say: "My brother, the door of repentance is open, and remember the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another god﴾ [al-Furqan 68], where He mentioned the greatest major sins, yet still said: ﴿except one who repents﴾ [al-Furqan 70]." Every situation has its speech; you cannot mention one particular thing.

* A student: How do you imagine, O Shaykh, that the People of the Book have an excuse when the Messenger ﷺ was sent to them with the message (...)?

* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. Rejecting the truth may be arrogance, and it may be due to a doubt that occurs to a person. We know that the scholars of the Children of Israel rejected the truth out of arrogance, because Allah says: ﴿Is it not a sign for them that the scholars of the Children of Israel know it?﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 197]. But the common folk among the Children of Israel had a doubt, among which: their scholars say that Muhammad is Arab, and Allah says: ﴿He it is who raised among the unlettered a messenger from among themselves﴾, yet they do not mention to them His saying: ﴿and others from among them who have not yet joined them﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 3], so they become confused.

Student: ﴿Which God has prescribed for you. And do not turn back on your heels, for you will turn back as losers.﴾ (21) They said, "O Moses, indeed there are in it a people of tyrants, and indeed we will never enter it until they leave it. And if they leave it, then indeed we will enter." (22) Said two men from those who feared [Allah] and upon whom Allah had bestowed favor, "Enter upon them through the gate, for when you have entered it, indeed, you will be victorious. And upon Allah rely, if you should be believers." (23) They said, "O Moses, indeed we will never enter it as long as they are within it. So go, you and your Lord, and fight. Indeed, we are sitting right here." (24) [Moses] said, "My Lord, indeed I do not possess except myself and my brother, so part us from the defiantly disobedient people." (25) [Allah] said, "Indeed, it is forbidden to them for forty years, [during which] they will wander throughout the land. So do not grieve over the defiantly disobedient people." (26) [Al-Ma'idah 20-26].

* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, says: ﴿And [mention] when Moses said to his people, "O my people, remember the favor of Allah upon you when He made among you prophets and made you possessors of dominion and gave you what He had not given anyone among the worlds."﴾

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿O my people﴾, concerning Moses, peace be upon him.

﴿O my people, enter the Holy Land﴾. The address here, ﴿O my people﴾, contains two things. The first: there is in it some [attempt at] appeasing them, and that they would not pay attention or listen to the speech unless it came with the address and the term "people." The second: he said ﴿O my people﴾ to win their sympathy, because there is a difference between the addressee being from your people or not from your people.

﴿Enter the Holy Land which Allah has prescribed for you﴾. The word ﴿enter the land﴾: he did not say "fight until you enter," he said ﴿enter the land﴾.

Then his saying ﴿which Allah has prescribed for you﴾ also contains good news that they would be victorious. In these two phrases there are two glad tidings: the first is ﴿enter the land﴾; the second is ﴿which Allah has prescribed for you﴾. The prescribing here is the decreed prescription (kitabah qadariyyah), because prescription is of two kinds: legislative prescription (kitabah shar'iyyah), such as the Exalted's saying: ﴿Fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you that you may become righteous﴾ [al-Baqarah 183], and decreed prescription, such as the Exalted's saying: ﴿And We had already written in the Zabur, after the reminder, that the earth will be inherited by My righteous servants﴾ [al-Anbiya' 105].

As for His saying ﴿Allah has prescribed for you﴾, I say: the prescription here is decreed prescription, not legislative; if it were legislative it would have been construed with ʿalā: "kutiba ʿalaykum," and the meaning would not be sound.

﴿And do not turn back on your heels﴾, i.e., do not return, after you had been advancing toward fighting, on your heels, because retreating on one's heels and turning back is defeat and humiliation; for this reason, turning one's back on the day of battle was strongly forbidden.

﴿For you will turn back as losers﴾. Do not turn back and so turn back [as losers]. Turning back (inqilab) implies disappointment; therefore He said ﴿you will turn back as losers﴾, and ﴿losers﴾ is a circumstantial state (hal) from the waw in His saying ﴿you will turn back﴾.

So what was the answer? The answer, as you hear now, was: ﴿They said, "O Moses, indeed there are in it a people of tyrants."﴾

Notice the address ﴿O Moses﴾. They did not say "O Prophet of Allah" or "O Messenger of Allah"; they said ﴿O Moses﴾. This is undoubtedly rudeness in address, that they addressed their prophet by his name; for this reason Allah forbade this Ummah to address the Messenger ﷺ by his name in His saying: ﴿Do not make the call of the Messenger among yourselves like the call of some of you to others﴾ [an-Nur 63], according to one of the two interpretations of His saying ﴿Do not make the call of the Messenger among yourselves like the call of some of you to others﴾. Some scholars say the meaning is: do not call him by his name as one of you calls another, though the verse includes this meaning and also includes the second meaning, which is: when he calls you, do not make his call like the call of one of you to another; if you wish you respond, and if you wish you do not respond. Rather, it is obligatory upon you to respond. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿O you who have believed, respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you to that which gives you life﴾ [al-Anfal 24].

Here they said: ﴿O Moses, indeed there are in it a people of tyrants﴾, so they mentioned a cause that indicates their cowardice, their weakness, and the weakness of their resolve, indeed the absence of their resolve.

﴿Indeed there are in it a people of tyrants﴾. The jabbar is: the insolent, the one great of body and tall, derived from the Arabic saying: a jabbarah palm tree, and the jabbarah palm is the strong, tall palm. To this day this meaning exists; one says: so-and-so has an orchard whose palms are jabbar, meaning strong and tall, such that a person cannot reach its fruit with his hand.

So ﴿jabbarin﴾ means: tyrannical in character, strong in body. This meaning revolves around this: tyrannical in character, and second, strong in body; we cannot fight them.

﴿And indeed we will never enter it until they leave it﴾. Glory be to Allah! This is the speech of children!

﴿We will never enter it until they leave it﴾: who would they fight if there were no one in it? Nothing. This indicates the foolishness of the Children of Israel: they will not enter it until they leave it. They also emphasized this meaning by saying: ﴿And if they leave it, then indeed we will enter.﴾

Consider their saying ﴿if they leave it﴾; they did not say "when they leave it," as if they were deeming their departure unlikely; because the conditional "in" (in) is distinguished from "when" (idha) in that with "in" the condition may be realized or unrealized, and may even be impossible, whereas "idha" indicates the occurrence of the condition, but it fixes the time of the condition's occurrence. Pay attention: if you say, "If Zayd stands, I will stand," you find the difference between it and your saying, "When Zayd stands, I will stand," is it not so? "When he stands" means that he will stand, but I will not stand except when he stands; it is a condition for timing the standing. But "if Zayd stands, I will stand" is a condition for the occurrence of standing, which may occur, may not occur, or may be impossible. As in Allah's saying: ﴿Say, "If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of the worshippers"﴾ [az-Zukhruf 81]; this concerns Allah. Concerning the Messenger: ﴿If you should associate [others with Allah], your deeds would surely be nullified﴾ [az-Zumar 65]. Both matters are utterly impossible: neither that the Most Merciful have a son, nor that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, the caller to sincerity and tawhid, associate partners.

So they are saying: ﴿And if they leave it, then indeed we will enter﴾, meaning: as if they regard as utterly unlikely that they would leave it. For this reason they were afflicted with wandering (tih), which is getting lost and not being guided to this place, as will come, Allah willing.

Consider also their saying ﴿And if they leave it, then indeed we will enter﴾: they emphasize their entry if those [people] leave. And if those [people] leave, would the entry need to be emphasized? It does not need to be. But, glory be to Allah, if one reflects on the state of this angry nation, one finds that they are in utmost foolishness of mind, just as they are in utmost misguidance in religion.

Whoever seeks further clarification on this matter should refer to the book of Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, Ighathat al-Lahfan, for he spoke about the characteristics of the religious communities in a manner that cannot be surpassed.

﴿Said two men from those who feared [Allah] and upon whom Allah had bestowed favor, "Enter upon them through the gate."﴾

First: we ask about the structure of this noble verse: ﴿Said two men from those who feared [Allah] and upon whom Allah had bestowed favor﴾. Is ﴿rajulan﴾ known to be indefinite, or definite?

* Student: Indefinite.

* Shaykh: Reflect? ﴿Said two men﴾?

* Students: Indefinite.

* Shaykh: By consensus? Is there no dissenter? Yes, ﴿rajulan﴾ is indefinite.

﴿From those who fear﴾ must be a description (sifah) of ﴿rajulan﴾.

[The following repeats the earlier passage of the commentary, as in the source, with minor variation.]

Next: ﴿from those who fear﴾ must be a description of "rajulan"; for what follows an indefinite noun from a clause or its equivalent is a description of it.

And ﴿yakhafuna﴾ here is the relative clause (silat al-mawsul). ﴿From those who fear﴾ is the relative clause.

﴿Upon whom Allah had bestowed favor﴾: is ﴿anʿama﴾ here the object of ﴿yakhafuna﴾, or is it governed by an omitted verb? I am asking about ﴿anʿama﴾, not about its i'rab; I ask whether it is the object of ﴿yakhafuna﴾ or not.

* Students: A verb.

* Shaykh: Yes, ﴿anʿama﴾ is a verb, not an object. The object of ﴿yakhafuna﴾ is omitted, and we will estimate it shortly, God willing. ﴿Anʿama﴾ is a verb; ﴿from those who fear, Allah had bestowed favor upon them both﴾: ﴿anʿama﴾ is a verb, a verbal sentence, whose place in i'rab is a description of ﴿rajulan﴾, and it may be a circumstantial state (hal) from it, since it is an indefinite noun that has been specified; when an indefinite noun is specified, a circumstantial state may occur from it. Do you understand?

But someone may say: is it not more appropriate in construction to say: "Said two men upon whom Allah had bestowed favor, from those who fear"?

The answer: No; because if it is considered a circumstantial state, then the description that directly follows its head is more suitable for proximity. If "Allah had bestowed favor upon them" is taken as a state, then the description that is attached to its described noun in i'rab is more suitable for adjacency; for the state follows its described noun in meaning but is separate from it in i'rab, unlike the descriptive adjective (na't). So we say: if we make this a state, it will be placed after the directly preceding description.

Second: ﴿from those who fear﴾ is a prepositional phrase, so it is in the category of a single word, and ﴿anʿama﴾ is a clause; a description with a single word is more suitable for adjacency than a description with a clause. Since the description may be a single word, a prepositional phrase, or a clause, eloquence requires placing ﴿from those who fear﴾ first.

﴿Said two men﴾: Allah the Exalted did not specify who these two men were, and we have no necessity in knowing their identities. The important thing is what they said. As for knowing who they are: if this were among matters on which belief is based, Allah would have clarified it either in the Qur'an or through the tongue of the Messenger ﷺ.

As for His saying ﴿from those who fear﴾: fear of whom? They fear Allah; therefore we say the object of ﴿yakhafuna﴾ is omitted, its estimate being: Allah.

And His saying ﴿Upon whom Allah had bestowed favor﴾: with what did He bestow favor? Allah bestowed favor upon them in several matters:

First: the fear of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, for fear of Allah is among the greatest blessings, since fear of Allah entails avoiding Allah's prohibitions and performing His obedience.

Second: Allah bestowed upon them strength, strength of soul; for they are now confronting whom? They confront a nation; all of Moses' people said to him: ﴿We will never enter it﴾; these two men faced the whole nation, which indicates courage and sincere resolve. Undoubtedly this is a blessing when Allah grants the servant strength and courage and indifference to numbers, since numbers are nothing in the face of truth.

Allah also bestowed upon them soundness of judgment; for everyone who read the glad tidings that Moses, peace be upon him, mentioned will surely advance: ﴿Enter the Holy Land﴾ [al-Ma'idah 21], and the second: ﴿which Allah has prescribed for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah 21]. Yes. So Allah bestowed favor upon them in these three respects, and it may be more than this. He says: ﴿Enter upon them through the gate.﴾

First: ﴿Enter the Holy Land﴾. What is the meaning of "holy"?

The scholars said: its meaning is purified, purified from polytheism, because this land was the land of the prophets, (...).

Then what is this land? What is intended by it?
