The answer is that we say: since the relative noun is highly indefinite, it became like the conditional noun, and when the response of the conditional noun is a command or prohibition, it must be connected with "fa". This is clear, and similar to it is: ﴿The adulteress and the adulterer, flog each one of them﴾ [al-Nur 2].

﴿Cut off their hands﴾: "aydin" (hands) is here in the plural, although the intent is that one hand be cut from each of them. So how is it in the plural? Does the meaning mean that we cut off four hands, or what?

We say: no, we do not cut off four hands; rather, two hands are cut from the male and female thief. But the more eloquent usage in the Arabic language is that when a dual is annexed to something that indicates plurality, it is made plural, to avoid two duals coming together in what is like a single word, since the annexed and the annexed-to are like one word. For this reason Allah said: ﴿If you two turn in repentance to Allah﴾, two, ﴿your hearts have inclined﴾ [al-Tahrim 4], although one woman has one heart; ﴿Allah has not made for any man two hearts within his body﴾ [al-Ahzab 4]. But the more eloquent usage in Arabic is that the annexed noun be plural when annexed to a dual, to avoid, what? The coming together of two duals in what is like a single word. The dual is permissible outside the Qur'an; for example, "qtau yadayhuma" (cut off their two hands) is permissible, and the singular is permissible: "qtau yadahuma" (cut off their hand), unless this leads to confusion and disagreement, in which case the first part of the annexed construction must follow the reality. For example, if you say: "I bought from the two men their slave," here if it was one slave, you must say "their slave," which indicates that the slave is shared between them. If you bought from each one his slave, you say "their two slaves"; if you bought a group, meaning each one had two slaves and you bought all four, what do you say? "Their slaves," and this is required so that the meaning is not confused. But when the meaning is clear, when something indicating plurality is annexed to something indicating plurality, it becomes plural.

﴿Cut off their hands﴾: here "yad" (hand) is unrestricted with respect to its limit, meaning the limit of the hand, and with respect to direction:

With respect to the limit: meaning, do we cut at the palm, or at the elbow, or at the shoulder? Because all of this is called a hand; the hand from the shoulder to the fingers, all of this is hand. So do we cut from the shoulder, or from the elbow, or from the palm? That is one point.

Second, the direction: "aydiyahuma," which of the two directions? The right or the left? Again the verse is ambiguous.

We say: the intent is to cut the right hand, and the limit is the palm. What made us specify the right hand?

The reading of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, who used to recite it: "fa-qta'u aymanahuma" (so cut off their right hands). If this reading is established from the Prophet ﷺ in its wording, then it is Qur'an; if it is an explanation from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, then he is a great companion, knowledgeable in tafsir. The more likely view is that it is a reading, because the Prophet ﷺ urged us to recite according to the reading of Ibn Umm 'Abd [[Narrated by Ibn Majah (138) from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud.]], who is Ibn Mas'ud. So, is the direction now determined or not? The direction is determined: the right.

Is the limit the palm, the elbow, or the shoulder?

We say: when "yad" is used without qualification, what is meant is the palm, and the evidence is the statement of Allah, blessed and exalted, concerning tayammum: ﴿then perform tayammum with clean earth and wipe your faces and your hands from it﴾ [al-Ma'idah 6]. The limit of "yad" here is what? The palm, by the explicit Sunnah in this, as in the hadith of 'Ammar ibn Yasir [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (347) and Muslim (368/110) from the hadith of 'Ammar ibn Yasir.]] and others. For this reason, when Allah, glorified and exalted, wished to extend beyond the palm, He said in the verse of wudu': ﴿and your hands up to the elbows﴾ [al-Ma'idah 6]. So it is determined that the intended hand here is the right hand, and that the limit of cutting is what?

* Student: The palm.

* Shaykh: From the joint of the palm.

Then he said: ﴿recompense﴾ (jaza'an) is here in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi), meaning: for the purpose of requiting them for their deed.

﴿for what they have earned﴾ (bima kasaba), meaning: for what they earned of crime, disobedience and transgression. This meaning supports that the intended "hand" is what? The right; because it is generally the case that a person takes with his right and gives with his right, and it is also generally the case that the right is stronger than what? Stronger than the left.

﴿A recompense for what they have earned﴾ means: a requital for them for what they earned of property built on transgression and injustice.

﴿An exemplary punishment from Allah﴾: also "nakalan" (as an exemplary punishment) is an object of purpose, meaning: to deter others, and also for them, that they not return to the like. Any person, however greedy he may be for wealth, if he knows that his hand will be cut off, will be deterred from theft out of fear that his hand will be cut.

The original meaning of "nakl" (with a kasra) is the shackle with which an animal's leg is tied to prevent it from fleeing; likewise, "nakal" prevents thieves from stealing.

So Allah, the Exalted, mentioned two wisdoms:

The first wisdom: the requital of these people for their deed, that is, the thieves, by His saying: ﴿a recompense for what they have earned﴾.

The second: preventing the habit of theft among them and others, which is in His saying: ﴿an exemplary punishment from Allah﴾.

Then He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise﴾. He concluded the verse with two great names from His names:

The first: "al-'Aziz" (the Almighty), which indicates might, dominance and subjugation.

The second: "al-Hakim" (the All-Wise), which indicates the effectiveness of His judgment and that His judgment is joined with wisdom, because "Hakim" is derived from "hukm" (judgment) and "hikmah" (wisdom). He, glorified and exalted, has perfect judgment and profound wisdom.

It is mentioned that a Bedouin sat with a reciter who was reciting: "And the thief, male and female, cut off their hands as recompense for what they earned, an exemplary punishment from Allah, and Allah is Forgiving, Merciful." The Bedouin, a desert Arab, said: "Recite the verse; your recitation is not correct." So he repeated: "And the thief, male and female, cut off their hands as recompense for what they earned, an exemplary punishment from Allah, and Allah is Forgiving, Merciful." He said: "Recite." He recited it a third time as: ﴿As for the thief, male or female, cut off their hands as a recompense for what they have earned, and as an exemplary punishment from Allah. And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise﴾. He said: "Now you are correct; because He, glorified and exalted, is Almighty and judges, so He cut off; had He forgiven and shown mercy, He would not have cut off." So look at the intelligence of this Bedouin; for the endings of verses are generally in agreement. And this is not contradicted by the statement of Allah, blessed and exalted, about 'Isa: ﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, indeed You, You are the Almighty, the All-Wise﴾ [al-Ma'idah 118], and He did not say "indeed You are the Forgiving, the Merciful," because He mentioned punishment and forgiveness, so it is as if He said: You are Almighty regarding whom You punish, and All-Wise regarding whom You reward; and reward and punishment occur only in accordance with might and wisdom.

* Student: Shaykh, if a thief, may Allah bless you, was found (...) meaning he uses only his left hand, relies on his left, does the ruling remain one: we cut off his right?

* Shaykh: Yes, even if he stole with his mouth. Yes, if he found a hanging ornament and bit it until he cut its cord, so that people would not see his hands, then he is cut off.

* Student: May Allah bless you. The grammatical sign in ﴿bikharijin﴾ [al-Ma'idah 37], what is the i'rab sign of the predicate of (ma)?

* Shaykh: You mean, how is it parsed?

The grammarians say: the "ba'" is a superfluous (za'idah) preposition, and "kharijin" is a noun in the genitive by the superfluous preposition, and its sign of genitive is the present ya'.

Or they say: "kharijin" is the predicate of "ma", in the accusative, by an assumed ya' in the place of the ya' that the preposition brought. Do you understand?

As for me, as you know, I have some latitude in grammatical matters; I say: if you wish, say: its sign of genitive or its sign of accusative is the ya', and we say: it shares in the governance of the operator; meaning two operators governed it and acted upon it, so the ya' is a sign of the genitive with respect to the preposition, and a sign of the accusative with respect to the position. Clear?

* Student: (...) the Makhzumite woman who (...)?

* Shaykh: Yes, this woman, may Allah bless you, the scholars differ in deriving her hadith; some of them say: the Prophet ﷺ only cut her hand because she stole, not because she denied the goods, but she was mentioned with this description because she was known for it, not because the ruling is based on it. Do you understand? "She used to borrow goods and deny them, so the Prophet ﷺ ordered her hand to be cut off" [[Narrated by Abu Dawud (4395) and al-Nasa'i (4887) from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar.]]. They said: the meaning of the hadith is that she used to borrow goods and deny them because she was known for this, but there is an implied element whose estimate is: so she stole, and her hand was cut off.

But this is not correct; this is a distortion of words from their places. Rather, the correct view is that denying a loan is a form of theft, because any person who wants to steal, instead of going and breaking locks and doors and taking secretly, instead comes to the person and says: "May Allah reward you with good; I need this vessel to cook with for guests, and I will bring it back to you, Allah willing," and perhaps some food will remain and be brought to you as well. He softens his speech so that he is given it, then afterwards denies it. There is no difference between this and that. For this reason, the verified view is that denying a loan is a kind of theft, because he took the property secretly.

* Student: (...) a day of punishment will be lightened for them (...) that they do not know the punishment is eternal?

* Shaykh: Yes, or they hope, but it is a hope that will not be realized.

* Student: Indeed those who disbelieved (...)?

* Shaykh: No; even if they had [the earth's ransom] they would give it to ransom themselves, but it did not happen.

* Student: (...)?

* Shaykh: All the people of the Fire.

* Student: (...) one ransom.

* Shaykh: No, even if one of them were given all the world, it would not benefit him. (...)

* * *

* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan.

Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿As for the thief, male or female﴾, and I think we have discussed its explanation.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation to cut off the hand of the male and female thief, by His saying: ﴿cut off their hands﴾.

* And among its benefits: that the cutting of their hands is addressed to the whole community, by His saying: ﴿cut off﴾, and the address is to the entire community; but the community in reality is represented by its rulers, because they are the ones who safeguard its interests. So if the rulers fall short, the community is obligated to remind them of this.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that its apparent meaning is the obligation to cut off their hands for any theft, whether small or large, whether from a protected place (hirz) or not, and whether the thief has a claim of right in taking or not. The Sunnah has restricted this generality; for example, the Sunnah restricted this generality to when it is a minimum amount (nisab) for which the hand is cut off, and the nisab is a quarter of a dinar, or three dirhams, or what equals them in goods.

So these are three things: a quarter of a dinar, three dirhams, and what equals them.

Is the original standard the quarter of a dinar, or the quarter of a dinar and the three dirhams?

This is a matter on which the scholars differ, and the effect of the difference appears in the case of someone who steals goods worth three dirhams, while the goods are not worth a quarter of a dinar. If we say that both are the basis (of the nisab), then he has stolen a nisab. If we say that the basis is a quarter of a dinar, then he has not stolen a nisab. The correct view is that the nisab (the minimum value at which the hand is cut off) is a quarter of a dinar. But in the time of the Messenger ﷺ, three dirhams were worth a quarter of a dinar, as shown by the diyah (blood money), whose assessment was one thousand mithqals of gold and twelve thousand dirhams of silver, so three dirhams were worth a quarter of a dinar. "It is established from the Prophet ﷺ that he cut off the hand for a shield worth three dirhams"[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (6795) from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar.]]. But three dirhams in that era were worth a quarter of a dinar. So the correct view is that what is taken into account is a quarter of a dinar, by which the hand is cut off.

Second: the hirz (secure place or custody). The verse does not mention the hirz. The hirz means that the thief steals property from where it is customarily kept safe. Hirz means "protected," that is, kept in the manner customarily used for safekeeping. If he steals from a place that is not a hirz, there is no cutting off of the hand. For example: where are dirhams and dinars kept?

* A student: In safes.

* The Shaykh: Yes. They are kept in houses and in chests, locked and watched. So if a person places dirhams and dinars on the threshold of the door or in a sheepfold, and they are stolen, then they have been stolen from a place that is not a hirz. If we say that the hirz is a condition, then we say there is no cutting off of the hand for the one who stole the dirhams from a place that is not their hirz. This requires evidence, for if someone challenged us and said, "His hand must be cut off because he stole," what prevents the cutting?

We say: What prevents the cutting is that the definition of theft is taking property secretly. This is one point. And the one who placed the property outside its hirz is the one who was negligent, so the hand is not cut off. Therefore, theft must be from a hirz.

The hirz of property is what custom has established for its safekeeping. This is the hirz. Does it differ?

Yes, it differs. It differs according to the types of property, and it differs according to circumstances. The circumstances of fear and chaos are not like the circumstances of security and stability, is that not so?

It also differs according to the ruler: whether he is strong or weak, and whether he is just or tyrannical. If the ruler is strong, people do not take great pains over securing their property, because the strength of the ruler prevents theft. If he is weak, it is the reverse.

If he is just, and if he is tyrannical, which of these is more protective of property: that he be just, or that he be tyrannical?

* The students: Just.

* The Shaykh: That he be just. The tyrant does not mean the strong in punishment. The tyrant is the one who rules that this man's hand is cut off and that man's hand is not cut off. So the just ruler, without doubt, people feel more secure under him than under a tyrant, not from the divine perspective, that is, not from the side of the Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, and not from the side of reality.

Also, the hirz differs according to the condition of people in terms of faith and weakness of faith. If people have faith, the hirz is easy. If they have no faith, strict precaution is necessary.

Likewise, the hirz differs according to the implementation of this penalty, the cutting off of the thief's hand. If the thief's hand is cut off, a person does not overly exert himself in securing his property, because he knows that thieves will not do it. If the hand is not cut off, and he is sentenced to imprisonment for a week, a month, two months, or a year, then strictness in securing property becomes necessary. The point is that the hirz differs according to many considerations. But for the establishment of the cutting, the theft must be from a hirz.

It is also a condition that the stolen item be respected property. If a person steals a musical instrument, then a musical instrument is not respected, and it has no value in the Sharia. So if he steals a lavish musical instrument worth five thousand or ten thousand, is the hand cut off? No, because why?

* The students: Because it is not respected.

* The Shaykh: Because it is property that is not respected in its origin. If it is not respected by its description, such as stealing an ornament in the form of an animal, the form of a lion, and the like, this is not respected by its description, because the image must be effaced or broken if it is of a kind that can be broken. So is the hand cut off or not?

We say it is cut off, taking into account what?

* The students: The original state.

* The Shaykh: The original state, that it is respected property. So it must be respected property, which means property that has value in the Sharia. As for what is not respected, the hand is not cut off for it, because it is not lawful property, it has no worth, and it has neither value nor price.

It is also a condition that there be no shubha (doubt). The thief must have no doubtful claim. If he steals from the public treasury (bayt al-mal), his hand is not cut off. Why?

Because he has a shubha, since he has a right in the public treasury. Each person has a right in the public treasury. Although it is protected, for this particular person he has a right in it.

The jurists, may God have mercy on them, have extended the discussion of shubha. Among this matter: if a free person steals from the public treasury, he is not cut off, because he has a shubha in it. The correct view is that if the shubha is strong, then yes, the hadd (prescribed punishment) is averted from him. But if it is weak and remote, then the hudud should not be suspended for the sake of his having a right of one part in a million million million, for example. That would suspend the hudud.

Among the shubahat (doubts) is when people are in a year of famine, or when the person is hungry. Which of these do we say?

* The students: The first.

* The Shaykh: The first. That is, if the famine is general, the people are in a year of drought, scarcity, and hunger, then there is no cutting, because of the existence of shubha, namely the compulsion of this thief to steal. And if the owner of the property were present, we would obligate him to give it to him.

As for when the hunger is particular, this does not prevent the cutting, because there is a difference between this and that. Every thief can claim that he is hungry, but it is general famine that prevents the cutting.

Likewise, the scholars said: the cutting is not carried out in lands of disbelief, such as for raiders, for example. Raiders in lands of disbelief are not cut, why? Because if it were carried out, it would cause aversion to Islam, and perhaps this man would flee to those lands and remain there, and this is a great corruption. But is the cutting lifted from him permanently, or is it postponed?

It is postponed. The same applies to what is happening now in some lands that have been freed from disbelief and have entered Islam. If they said, "If we establish the hudud, the people will rise against us, first the population and then the states," do we have the right to postpone until the Islamic side is strengthened?

We say: Yes, based on the fact that the hudud were revealed in the Islamic Sharia to do what?

* The students: To avert corruptions.

* The Shaykh: Delayed. Yes, to avert corruption, but they are also delayed, until the people are able to accept them. Furthermore, the purpose of the hadd is the reform of creation and the expiation of the one punished. So if its implementation would produce a greater corruption, then it should be postponed.

If the hadd is due upon a pregnant woman who stole, is the hadd carried out on her?

No, it is postponed, because cutting is feared to harm the fetus, and the fetus is innocent and has committed no offense.

If a person steals from his father's property, is he cut?

* The students: No.

* The Shaykh: Why?

* The students: Because he has a shubha.

* The Shaykh: The common people say: "The thief from a thief is like the thief from his father." The meaning is that he is not cut. The one who steals from his father, they say: he is not cut. Why?

Because he has a right in his father's property, which is the obligation to support him if he is in need.

The husband with his wife?

Likewise, because there is a shubha in it, and custom has established that each of the spouses freely uses the other's property. So for the establishment of the hadd, the absence of shubha is necessary. But, as I told you, there is a remote shubha and a near shubha.

Is the establishment of the theft a condition? If someone is accused of being a thief, do we say the hadd is not carried out on him until the theft is established?

The answer is yes, because Allah said: ﴿The thief﴾, and the description of theft does not apply to him unless it is established. Without establishment, it does not apply that he is a thief.

And by what is theft established?

Theft is established by the testimony of two just men. If one man and two women testify, the hadd is not carried out, but the property is made good, because property is established by the testimony of one man and two women, while the hadd is established only by the testimony of two men. Therefore, know that women have no role in the hudud. If four hundred women testify against a man that he committed adultery, the hadd is not carried out on him. Likewise in theft, and likewise in the rest of the hudud. Women have no role in the hudud; testimony for the hudud is only from men. So the establishment of the theft is necessary. It is established by two witnesses or by the confession of the thief. If the thief confesses, the theft is established. But is repetition of the confession a condition or not?

There is a difference among the scholars.

Some say: he must repeat the confession twice, each time in place of a witness, because two witnesses are required, so he must confess twice. If he confesses once, the theft is not established.

Some of the scholars say: it is established by a single confession, because he testified against himself, and there is no excuse for one who confesses. So the theft is established by his single confession.

And if he confesses, whether we say twice or once, can he retract? That is, is his retraction accepted, so that the hadd is not carried out on him?

Most jurists say: yes, his retraction from the confession is accepted, and on this basis there is no cutting. But he is held to the right of the human being: he makes good the property. As for the cutting, no, because he retracted his confession.

Some scholars said: he may not retract if he confessed before the judge, before the qadi.

The correct view in this is a distinction: if there are indications that support the soundness of his confession, then his retraction is not accepted. If no indications exist, then his retraction is accepted, and the matter is between him and his Lord.

So if the thief says, "I stole," and we say, "How did you steal?" and he says, "I came at night, broke the door, broke the chest, and took the money, and this house is the one I stole," and he describes it completely, then he retracts, can such a retraction be accepted?

It cannot be accepted. If a retraction of this kind were accepted, the hudud would be suspended. Indeed, Shaykh al-Islam, may God have mercy on him, said: If the retraction of the confessor were accepted in a hadd, no hadd would ever be carried out in this world, because every person could confess and then retract, especially if he was coached and told, "Retract, there is nothing against you." After the judge orders the cutting of his hand, the knife is brought, the oil is brought to cauterize the hand, and the men of the ruler are present, and then he says, "Enough, I was lax, I retract my confession." This resembles trickery, so we say this is not accepted, because there are indications showing that his confession is true, and not from trickery, and not from coercion. He is the one who showed the people the place of the theft and how the theft occurred. There is no doubt that such a retraction cannot be accepted. It is not possible.

So the establishment of the theft is a condition. What is the evidence?

* A student: The verse.

* The Shaykh: The verse: ﴿And the thief, male and female﴾, since the description of thief and thieving woman does not apply to them except by establishment. Establishment by what?

* A student: By one of two things.

* The Shaykh: And they are?

* The student: By the testimony of two just men, or by confession.

* The Shaykh: Or by confession. Good.

Is repetition necessary for the confession or not? There is a difference of opinion.

* You see, among the benefits of the noble verse: the obligation to cut off the hand of the male thief and the female thief. Which of the two hands?

* The students: The right.

* The Shaykh: The right, as Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with him, explained it in his recitation: "Then cut off their right hands." So the right hand is cut off for a quarter of a dinar.

And from where is it cut?

It is cut at the point that is truly called a hand. The least that truly is called a hand is what is cut, because whatever exceeds what truly is called a hand is doubtful.

And what is truly called a hand? What?

* The students: The palm.

* The Shaykh: The palm. So it is cut from the joint of the palm, from the wrist, and from the kaw' and what?

* The students: And the karsu'.

* The Shaykh: And the karsu'. Brother, do you know your kaw' from your karsu'?

* A student: No.

* The Shaykh: You don't know!

* The Shaykh to another student: Do you know? Say it.

* A student: The kaw' is the one next to the thumb.

* The Shaykh: Yes, the kaw' is the one next to the thumb at the end of the forearm.

* The student: The karsu' is the one next to the little finger.

* The Shaykh: The karsu' is the one next to the little finger.

And the wrist?

* The student: In the middle.

* The Shaykh: The one in the middle. Excellent. It is cut from here.

If someone says: How is it cut for a quarter of a dinar, when if it were cut intentionally, five hundred dinars would be due for it, is that not so?

That is, if a person assaulted another and cut off his hand, we say: he owes five hundred dinars. And the thief steals a quarter of a dinar and his hand is cut off.

For this reason, Abu al-'Ala al-Ma'arri raised this doubt in this matter, and he said:

A hand for which five hundred gold dinars were paid as diyah,
but when it is cut for theft, it is cut for a quarter of a dinar.
A contradiction. We have nothing but silence about it,
and we seek refuge in our Lord from the Fire.

He said, "a contradiction." The aspect of contradiction in his view is how its diyah is five hundred dinars and yet it is cut, that is, "wasted," for a quarter of a dinar. This is a contradiction, because if its diyah is five hundred dinars, it should not be cut except for the theft of five hundred dinars. And if it is cut for a quarter of a dinar, then its diyah becomes a quarter of a dinar. Otherwise it is contradictory. But they answered him, saying:

Say to al-Ma'arri: shame on whatever shame is,
the ignorance of a youth, and he is bare of the garment of piety.
A hand for which five hundred gold dinars were paid as diyah,
but when it is cut for theft, it is cut for a quarter of a dinar.
The protection of the soul is what makes it precious, and what makes it cheap
is the protection of property, so understand the wisdom of the Creator.

Its meaning: he has no knowledge and no worship.

The point in the last line: its diyah was made five hundred dinars to protect souls, so that no one would dare to cut off people's hands. And it is cut for a quarter of a dinar to protect property, so that no one would dare to steal. This is a clear and reasonable answer.

There is another answer, which may be literary: they said that when it betrayed, it became cheap, and when it was trustworthy, it became precious.

"When it betrayed," with what did it betray?

* The students: With theft.

* The Shaykh: With theft. "It became cheap": its value became a quarter of a dinar.

And "when it was trustworthy, it was precious": what was its value? Five hundred dinars. In any case, these are answers, in reality, to those who raise such doubts. Otherwise, we know with certainty that Allah does not distinguish between two things except that there is a difference which necessitates the distinction in the ruling.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿So cut off their hands﴾. If it is assumed that he has no right hand, is the left hand cut off or not?

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 5, verse 38 (part 3 of 4)**

There is a difference of opinion on this, brothers. Some say the hand is not cut off, because Allah only specified the right hand. That is, the verse only mentions the right hand, and the left hand is not cut off. They also argue that if we cut off his left hand, we deprive him of the benefit of both hands, and this is not appropriate. They compare it to the principle that the eye of a one-eyed man is not gouged out in retaliation for the eye of a person with two good eyes. That is, a man who has only a right eye gouges out the right eye of a sound person. Is his eye gouged out?

* Students: No.

* Shaykh: The well-known position of the school (madhhab) is that we do not gouge it out, because if we gouge out his eye, we deprive him of all his sight. He did not deprive the victim of sight, but Allah the Exalted says: ﴿the eye for the eye﴾ [al-Ma'idah 45], and the eye of a one-eyed man provides all of sight, so there is no equality.

I say: Some scholars say that if the thief has only a left hand, it is not cut off, because that would deprive him of what? The benefit of both hands. For this reason, Allah the Mighty and Majestic ordered that the hands and feet of highway robbers be cut off on opposite sides, so that both hands would not be rendered useless. Some say the left hand is not cut off, and some say it is cut off. If we deprive him of this, he is the one who brought it upon himself, because we only cut it off because of what? Because he is the one who committed the offense against himself. The matter is one in which the evidences pull in different directions.

If he has no hands, do we cut off a foot?

No, because it is not of the same kind. We do not cut off a foot.

If his right hand is paralyzed, do we cut it off?

* Students: No.

* Shaykh: A paralyzed hand is cut off. The verse is general, so it is cut off. We do not say we will not cut it off and instead cut off the sound left hand. Rather, we cut off the paralyzed one.

Regarding His words: ﴿cut off their hands﴾, when we cut off a hand, must we take measures to stop the bleeding, or do we let him bleed until he dies?

* Students: The first.

* Shaykh: The first. We must take measures to stop the bleeding and not let him die, because the aim is the cutting off of the hand.

May we or must we anesthetize this thief when cutting off his hand?

* Students: It is permissible.

* Shaykh: It is permissible to anesthetize him, because the amputation takes place with or without anesthesia. This differs from retaliation (qisas). Note: if a man cut off a person's hand and we ruled for retaliation, and he said, "Anesthetize his hand so that I can cut off the offender's hand," we would not anesthetize him. Rather, we make him feel the pain just as he inflicted the pain of the victim. This is a clear difference.

In the past, they would stop the bleeding by bringing oil, heating it over fire, and when the hand was cut off, they would dip the end of the forearm in this oil. When it was immersed, the mouths of the veins were sealed. But in my opinion now, medicine has advanced, and it is possible to stop the bleeding without this procedure. The obligation is that we follow the easiest method for stopping bleeding, because the aim is the destruction of the hand, and that has taken place. So if we find a way to stop the bleeding other than the cauterization that the scholars mentioned and practised in the past, then we use it.

If he steals twice, do we cut off something other than the right hand?

We say: If that happens before the amputation, then only the right hand is cut off. That is, if he steals twenty times before we cut him, we cut off only one hand. If we cut off the hand the first time and then he steals again, then his left foot is cut off, not his left hand, but his left foot. This is based on Allah's words, blessed and exalted, regarding those who wage war: ﴿or their hands and their feet be cut off on opposite sides﴾ [al-Ma'idah 33]. This means the right hand and the left foot, so that no side of him is entirely deprived of benefit.

Some scholars say: If he repeats the theft after the amputation, he is not cut off, because Allah only permitted cutting off the right hand. The basic principle is the respect due to a Muslim. So even if he repeats it twenty times, only the right hand is cut off. However, if his harm is not averted except by imprisonment or killing, we do what averts his harm. But cutting off some of his limbs, when Allah only mentioned the cutting off of one hand, is not allowed. However, the well-known position in our school is that his left foot is cut off, by analogy with whom? With those who wage war.

If he steals a third time, he is not cut off. Some scholars say his left hand is cut off. How many does he have left? One foot.

If he steals a fourth time, some scholars say his right foot is cut off. What remains for him? Nothing remains.

If he steals a fifth time?

A commoner once heard a man speaking in the mosque and saying this statement. He said: The right hand is cut off, then the left foot, then the left hand, then the right foot, and then if he steals again, he is killed. The commoner immediately responded: Fine, but with what does he steal, since he has neither hands nor feet?

Yes, but he may still steal, because he still has a forearm, and he can, for example, gather money with his hand.

* Student: (...)?

* Shaykh: No, this (...) did not come. In any case, what appears is that we do not go beyond the limit set for those who wage war. That is, we cut off his right hand, and if he returns to it, then only his left foot.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: the wisdom in the obligation to cut off the thief's hand, from His words: ﴿as recompense for what they have earned﴾.

* And among its benefits: punishment is of the same kind as the act, or if you wish, the recompense is of the same kind as the deed, because when he stole (and most people give and take with which hand? With the right hand), his hand was cut off.

If someone says: According to your view that the instrument with which he committed the theft is cut off, you would have to require cutting off the penis of the adulterer. What is the answer?

* Students: (...).

* Shaykh: Yes, the answer is clear to us in any case. Allah prescribed a specific punishment for the adulterer, and a specific punishment for the thief. But also there is the rational wisdom, because this is a textual proof (sam'i). Even by rational proof, the harm resulting from cutting off the penis is not like the harm resulting from cutting off the hand, because it would entail cutting off progeny and contradicting what the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, desires for this Ummah, which is increasing its offspring. [[As in his saying: "Marry the loving and fertile woman, for I will boast of your numbers before the nations." Narrated by Abu Dawud (2052) from the hadith of Ma'qil ibn Yasar.]] And there are other wisdoms. Therefore Allah did not require cutting off the penis of the adulterer. Rather, He required flogging and exile for the unmarried, and stoning for the married.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: the refutation of the Jabriyyah (determinists). From where?

* Students: ﴿for what they have earned﴾.

* Shaykh: ﴿as recompense for what they have earned, a deterrent from Allah﴾. There is another meaningful aspect: if the male and female thieves were compelled, it would not be valid to punish them. Why? Because the compelled person has no ruling on his action. Even one who is compelled to disbelieve, if his heart is at rest with faith, does not become a disbeliever. The main point is that the verse is a refutation of the Jabriyyah, and how many refutations there are against the people of innovation, praise be to Allah.

* Student: May Allah be good to you. We said that if the thief is a son, he is not cut off. What if he is a brother?

* Shaykh: He is cut off.

* Student: Shaykh, may Allah bless you. If we do not carry out the hadd punishment on the thief because he has a right hand that is cut off, or a one-eyed man who gouged out the eye of a sound person, how do we make them liable? How is the hadd carried out against them?

* Shaykh: The hadd is not carried out on him, but the ruler may impose a discretionary punishment (ta'zir) on him, because this is a sin for which there is no hadd.

* Student: May Allah open (the way) for you, Shaykh. If the thief, after his hand is cut off, wants to restore it, is he permitted to do so?

* Shaykh: That is a good question. That is, if the thief tries to undergo a procedure to restore his hand, is he allowed to do so?

* Students: He is not allowed.

* Shaykh: He is not allowed, because the aim is that it be cut off.

If it were retaliation (qisas) and it was carried out on him, and then he wanted to undergo a procedure to restore it, would we say that the retaliation has taken place? The retaliation has certainly taken place, there is no problem with that. But would we say that if he restores it, we prevent him? Apparently we do not prevent him. This differs from theft. In theft, the legislator's intent is the destruction of this hand, whereas the aim of retaliation is that the offender's hand be cut off just as the victim's hand was cut off. For this reason, even if we assume that the victim restored his hand and it returned perfectly sound one hundred percent, the offender is not cut off.

* Student: May Allah be good to you (...)?

* Shaykh: At the time it is removed from its place of safekeeping (hirz).

* Student: May Allah bless you. We mentioned that among the conditions for carrying out the hadd on a thief is the testimony of two men or his own confession. If, for example, a security man or a man from the public morality office (hisbah), one man, catches the thief, is the hadd carried out on him?

* Shaykh: No, because two are required.

* Student: (...)?

* Shaykh: For example, in a land of disbelief, a land of war, where they are now fighting in the lands of the disbelievers, and he steals; the carrying out of the hadd is deferred for him.

* Student: (...)?

* Shaykh: A quarter dinar. By Allah, this varies. One asks the gold sellers, and the dinar is a mithqal.

* * *

* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan: ﴿But whoever repents after his wrongdoing and reforms, indeed Allah will turn to him in forgiveness. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful. Do you not know that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth? He punishes whom He wills and forgives whom He wills, and Allah is over all things competent﴾ [al-Ma'idah 39, 40].

* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿But whoever repents after his wrongdoing and reforms, indeed Allah will turn to him in forgiveness. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾.

Have we finished the benefits? (...)

The five benefits.

* Student: Shall I read them, Shaykh?

* Shaykh: Yes, read.

* The student: First: the obligation to cut off the hand of the male and female thief.

Second: that the cutting off of their hands is addressed to the entire Ummah.

Third: the obligation of amputation for every theft. Then we mentioned the conditions, Shaykh.

Fourth: the obligation to cut off the hand of the male and female thief, and the right hand is cut off, as Ibn Mas'ud's reading explains it by cutting off the right hand.

Fifth: that the recompense is of the same kind as the deed.

Sixth: the refutation of the Jabriyyah.

* Shaykh: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: the refutation of the Jabriyyah, and this is from several aspects: from the aspect of the thief, from the aspect of (...), and from the aspect of ﴿as recompense for what they have earned﴾.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: we mentioned that the recompense is of the same kind as the deed.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: the wisdom in prescribing the hudud, from the words of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿a deterrent from Allah﴾. The deterrent here applies to others, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So We made it a deterrent for what was before it and what was after it﴾ [al-Baqarah 66]. Whoever knows that his hand will be cut off for theft will recoil from it and will not steal.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration that Allah, glorified and exalted, despite His perfect mercy and compassion, legislated the hudud and made them obligatory, because that is the very essence of mercy. Were it not for the hudud, sins would spread among people. But the hudud restrain them when faith does not restrain them. For this reason, they say: when a person is devoid of the religious restraint, he is restrained by the authority's deterrent.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of these two names from the names of Allah: al-'Aziz (the Mighty) and al-Hakim (the Wise). How often these two are paired in the noble Qur'an, because through them comes the completeness and perfection of authority.

As for al-'Aziz, it means He possesses 'izzah (might). Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned three meanings for 'izzah. The first is 'izzah in the sense of dominance (ghalabah), and from it is His saying: ﴿The more honorable will surely expel from it the more humble﴾ [al-Munafiqun 8]. And from it is the poet's saying:

Where is the one who flees, and God is the pursuer?
And the cut-off one is defeated, and the one who prevails is not the one who is cut off.

The second meaning of 'izzah is that He, glorified and exalted, is immune from every deficiency. It is derived from al-ard al-'azaz, which is the hard land that cannot be reached except with strength and large picks and iron.

The third is the 'izzah that is His perfection, that is, the perfection of His attributes.

He is al-'Aziz with a might that is His attribute,
So 'izz then has three meanings.

As for al-Hakim, al-Hakim is derived from two meanings. The first meaning is al-hukm (judgment or ruling), and the second meaning is al-hikmah (wisdom), because this root (ha', kaf, mim) indicates both: judgment and wisdom, that is, precision (al-ihkam).

As for al-hukm, the judgments of Allah are of two types. The first type is the decreed judgment (al-hukm al-qadari), and the second is the legislated judgment (al-hukm al-shar'i).

An example of the first is the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted, about the brother of Yusuf: ﴿So I will not leave this land until my father permits me or Allah decides for me﴾ [Yusuf 80]. That means "decrees." This is a cosmic judgment, and a cosmic judgment must necessarily occur. When Allah decrees something cosmically, it must come to pass.

As for the legislated judgment, an example is His saying in Surah al-Mumtahanah: ﴿That is the judgment of Allah; He judges between you﴾ [al-Mumtahanah 10], meaning a legislated judgment.

As for His saying: ﴿Then do they desire the judgment of the time of ignorance? And who is better in judgment than Allah for a people who are certain?﴾ [al-Ma'idah 50], the apparent meaning is that it is general, although the context suggests that what is meant is the legislated judgment.

However, we say that the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion. So His saying: ﴿who is better in judgment than Allah﴾ [al-Ma'idah 50] includes both the cosmic judgment and the legislated judgment.

We mentioned that the cosmic judgment must necessarily come to pass.

As for the legislated judgment: if Allah rules something upon someone legislatively, does it necessarily follow that it occurs?

The answer: No, because among people there are those who do not rule by what Allah has revealed and do not comply with the command of Allah. So it does not follow from a legislated judgment that what is judged will occur, because it is a legislation, and legislation may be opposed or may be complied with.

As for al-hikmah (wisdom), it is placing things in their proper places, in line with the saying of some of the early scholars: Allah does not command something for which the intellect would say, "I wish He had not commanded it," and does not forbid something for which the intellect would say, "I wish He had not forbidden it." So wisdom is placing things in their proper places.

If you reflect on the cosmic and legislated judgments of Allah, you will find that they are in their proper places. If your intellect grasps this, that is what is sought. If it does not grasp it, then entrust the matter to the One who possesses perfect wisdom.

We find that the laws of Islam are entirely in accord with wisdom: purification, prayer, zakah, fasting, hajj, kindness to parents, maintaining family ties, and what is similar to them, all are in accord with wisdom. We also find that the cosmic judgments are in accord with wisdom: ﴿Corruption has appeared on land and sea because of what the hands of people have earned﴾. Why? ﴿That He may let them taste part of that which they have done that perhaps they will return﴾ [al-Rum 41]. So the corruption that occurs on land or sea is corruption, but it is for a great wisdom, which is that people return to their religion and refrain from what their hands have earned of sins, and so on. In other words, the cosmic and legislated judgments of Allah are all in accord with wisdom. But it does not follow that every person understands the wisdom. It may be hidden from many people, and hidden from some people more than others. What is hidden from you, entrust to its Knower. When a woman asked 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her: "Why does a menstruating woman make up fasting but not make up prayer?" 'A'ishah said: "This used to happen to us, and we were ordered to make up the fasts, but we were not ordered to make up the prayers." [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (321) and Muslim (335/69) from the hadith of Mu'adhah.]] So the mere fact that something is legislatively judged by Allah means we know it is for a wisdom. The mere fact that something occurs among Allah's cosmic judgments, even if the benefit is not apparent to us, means we know that it is for a wisdom. So we must submit, not oppose, and not say, "How?" or "Why?" because that involves objection. Except for a man who wants to ask about the wisdom so that his heart may be reassured and so that he may know of Allah's attributes what he did not know.

The wisdom (al-hikmah): they said it has two kinds: wisdom of purpose (hikmat ghayah) and wisdom of placing a thing as it is (hikmat wad' al-shay' 'ala ma huwa 'alayh). This too has wisdom. We may say: formal (suwariyyah) and purposive (ghā'iyyah). The formal is that a thing be in this form; its being in this form is wisdom. That the prayers are, for example, five and at different times is wisdom. That they end on an odd number is wisdom: the daytime prayer's odd unit is the maghrib, and the night prayer's odd unit is the well-known supererogatory witr. This is wisdom. That these legislated matters are for a purpose is also wisdom. Likewise, the created things are wisdom in the form in which they are, and the end that these created things reach is without doubt wisdom.

So al-Hakim (the All-Wise) is derived from al-hukm (judgment), and al-ihkam (perfection and soundness), which is wisdom. Judgment is of two kinds: cosmic (kawni) and legislative (shar'i), and wisdom is of two kinds: formal and purposive. The meaning of "formal" is that the existence of a thing in this specific form is wisdom, and its purpose is likewise wisdom.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the fine conclusion of the noble verses, and that it perfectly corresponds to the rulings with which they were concluded.

Al-'Izzah (might): its meaning is dominance (al-ghalabah). There is no doubt that the obligation to cut off hands indicates might, dominance and perfect authority.

Wisdom also suits the amputation, because in it there is a stern judgment, and in it also is far-reaching wisdom: ﴿a recompense for what they earned, an exemplary punishment from Allah﴾. Therefore the sentence ﴿And Allah is Mighty, Wise﴾ perfectly corresponds to what was mentioned in the noble verse of cutting off the thief's hand and explaining the wisdom behind it.

I saw in al-Suyuti's book al-Itqan that a Bedouin heard a reciter reading: "And the thief, male and female, cut off their hands as recompense for what they earned, an exemplary punishment from Allah; and Allah is Forgiving, Merciful," and the Bedouin disapproved of this and said: "Repeat the verse." He repeated it a second time with the same wording, "and Allah is Forgiving, Merciful." Then he said: "Repeat it." He repeated it two or three times, and then recited it correctly: ﴿And the thief, male and female, cut off their hands as recompense for what they earned, an exemplary punishment from Allah; and Allah is Mighty, Wise﴾. He said: "Now you are right, because He is Mighty and judged, so He cut off. Had He forgiven and shown mercy, He would not have cut off." Look at how understanding works: he was a Bedouin who had not studied, yet it is clear that if Allah, glorified and exalted, had said "Allah is Forgiving, Merciful," it would not suit the obligation of amputation. That suits repentance: ﴿But whoever repents after his wrongdoing and reforms, indeed Allah will accept his repentance. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Ma'idah 39]. As for amputation, it suits might and wisdom.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a refutation of every clamorer who says that cutting off hands is savagery and that it would result in half the nation being maimed, having only one hand. It is derived from His saying: ﴿And Allah is Mighty, Wise﴾. It is said: rather, this is the very essence of wisdom and the very essence of correctness, because if people were left alone, chaos would arise, wealth would be seized and the secure would be plundered. So cutting off the hand is without doubt the wisdom. Look at the peoples who apply these legal hudud: how crime decreases among them, and conversely among the peoples who do not apply them. This is like the saying of one who says that killing the killer means an increase in the taking of souls. This also perfectly contradicts the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And for you in retaliation there is life﴾ [al-Baqarah 179]. So retaliation is in reality life for us, because whoever intends to kill, when he remembers that he will be killed, refrains and withholds from killing. Furthermore, it should be known that the one unjustly killed must have his killer killed, by the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And whoever is killed wrongfully, We have given his heir authority﴾ [al-Isra' 33]: a legal authority, namely that he has the right of retaliation, and a decreed authority, namely that Allah the Exalted enables him to locate this killer until he is killed. This is something observed: often the killer kills and flees, and then he comes by the decree of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. This falls within His saying: ﴿We have given his heir authority﴾, i.e., decreed and legislated. It is as if the matter is established and certain, and therefore He said: ﴿But let him not commit excess in killing﴾ [al-Isra' 33], as if He said: he must kill, i.e., the heir of the one unjustly killed, but let him not exceed in killing. That is because the heir of the one unjustly killed may be seized by zeal and anger and exceed in killing, so Allah forbade that and made the matter retaliation.

He says: ﴿But whoever repents after his wrongdoing and reforms﴾. The word "whoever" (man) here is conditional, and it is general, covering the thief and others: every person who repents after his wrongdoing and reforms, Allah will accept his repentance. Does it include the thief or not? It includes him all the more, since it comes in the context of the ruling concerning the thief: if he repents after his wrongdoing and reforms, Allah will accept his repentance.

The benefit of this, after the mention of ﴿cut off their hands﴾, is that the thief's hand may be cut off, and the prescribed punishment here expiates the sin that preceded it. But in his inmost heart he may still wish to steal whenever the opportunity arises. Will Allah accept his repentance in this state?

No, because he has not repented. He must repent. It is not to be said that it is established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that "whoever commits any of these foul deeds and is punished for it in this world, it is an expiation for him" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (18) and Muslim (1709/41) from the hadith of 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, and its wording is "whoever commits any of that and is punished for it, it is an expiation for him"]; meaning the hudud are expiations, as is also indicated by ﴿a recompense for what they earned﴾.

* This is a benefit which you may add to the benefits of the verse: that the hudud are expiations, by His saying: ﴿a recompense for what they earned﴾, and Allah does not double the punishment for him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 5, verse 39:

We say: The second verse, ﴿But whoever repents after his wrongdoing and reforms﴾, refers to one who repents after what? After the prescribed punishment (hadd) has been carried out on him by amputation. Amputation expiates what has passed. But if it is in the intention of this thief that whenever the opportunity for theft arises he will steal, will God accept his repentance? No, because he has not repented to God. The same applies to one who is executed by retaliation (qisas): if it is in his heart that he has not repented of the act he committed, and that if he were able to kill someone he would kill them, then retaliation does not expiate for him, because this concerns what is between him and God, and he has not repented in what is between him and God.

So if someone says: Does the verse contradict the hadith that prescribed punishments are expiations?

The answer: No. Prescribed punishments are expiations for what has already passed and gone. As for what remains in his heart of the desire for sin, he has not repented.

﴿So whoever repents after his wrongdoing﴾: wrongdoing (zulm) is both wronging oneself and wronging others, because if the sin extends to others there are two wrongs: wronging oneself and wronging others. If it is confined to the person alone, there is one wrong, which is wronging oneself. How strange is the poor human being who commits sin while knowing that by doing so he wrongs himself! If someone wanted to wrong him, would he not defend himself and prevent the wrong? So how does he not defend himself against himself? But desire blinds and deafens. The point is that His saying ﴿after his wrongdoing﴾ includes wronging oneself and, and wronging others.

His saying ﴿and reforms﴾ means: he rectifies what was corrupted by his wrongdoing, because wrongdoing corrupts the heart, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever abandons three Friday prayers out of negligence, God seals his heart"[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (1054) and al-Nasa'i (1369) from Abu al-Ja'd al-Damari.]]. Sins corrupt, so if he reforms, God will turn to him in forgiveness, and reform is achieved by fulfilling repentance and righteous deeds.

His saying ﴿indeed, God will turn to him﴾: ﴿will turn to him﴾ means He will accept his repentance.

Know that God, blessed and exalted, has two kinds of turning toward His servant. The first turning is enabling him to repent, and the second is accepting it from the one who repents.

From the first is His saying: ﴿Then He turned to them that they might repent﴾ [At-Tawbah 118]. Did He turn to them before they repented or after? Before, as shown by His saying ﴿that they might repent﴾. This is the turning of enabling: that God grants the person the ability to repent, so he turns to his Lord, mighty and majestic.

As for accepting repentance, it is like His saying: ﴿And it is He who accepts repentance from His servants﴾ [Ash-Shura 25], and like this verse: ﴿indeed, God will turn to him﴾, meaning He will accept his repentance.

Could ﴿indeed, God will turn to him﴾ in this verse mean that He enables him to repent?

* Student: No, that is not valid.

* The Shaykh: No; because of His saying ﴿whoever repents﴾, he has now been enabled. ﴿Indeed, God will turn to him﴾ means from this wrongdoing from which he repented. ﴿Indeed, God will turn to him. Indeed, God is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

Regarding His saying ﴿repents﴾ and ﴿reforms﴾: we said that reform means rectifying what was corrupted by his wrongdoing, through making up for the obligation where possible and by ceasing the forbidden so that he does not persist in it. This is reform, and it is indispensable.

﴿Indeed, God will turn to him﴾, ﴿Indeed, God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾: the sentence here is emphasized, with what? With (inna, "indeed"); ﴿Indeed, God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, to reassure the repentant servant that his repentance will not be in vain.

His saying ﴿Forgiving and Merciful﴾: these are two noble names of God that are frequently paired in the Qur'an, because the first brings the removal of what is disliked and the second brings the attainment of what is beloved. The first, ﴿Forgiving﴾, means for sins, and the second, ﴿Merciful﴾, means that He delivers good to His servants according to the requirement of His mercy, glorified and exalted is He.

Is "Forgiving" here an active participle, an adjective of the attributive type, or an intensive form?

We say: apparently, and God knows best, it is an intensive form (sigha mubalagha), not an active participle. The active participle is as in His saying: ﴿Forgiver of sin and Acceptor of repentance﴾ [Ghafir 3]. But this is an intensive form, and it came in that form because of God's abundant forgiveness of His servants and the abundance of those whom He has forgiven. How often God forgives us our sins because of the causes of forgiveness He has legislated for us! And how many are those whose sins have been forgiven! Therefore this name came in the intensive form.

So what is forgiveness?

Forgiveness is: covering the sin and overlooking it. This is its meaning, and we say this so that the abstract description matches the concrete one, for they say it derives from al-Mighfar, and al-Mighfar is what a fighter covers his head with to protect himself from arrows. When you consider the mighfar, you find that it achieves two things: covering and protection. So "al-Ghafur" means the one who covers the sins of His servants and protects them from their punishment. And how many sins there are! If God made people aware of our sins, it would be as al-Qahtani, may God have mercy on him, said in his Nuniyya:

By God, if they knew my hidden secret,
They would refuse to greet me, even whoever met me.

That is: if God, glorified and exalted, exposed sins, a person would be shunned. But by His kindness, mighty and majestic, He covers them, and in the end does not punish for them, as in the authentic hadith: "On the Day of Resurrection God will draw near to His believing servant, alone with him, and will make him acknowledge his sins, saying: Did you do such and such? Did you do such and such? He acknowledges, unable to deny. Then God says to him: I covered them for you in the world, and today I forgive them for you."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2441) and Muslim (2768/52) from Ibn 'Umar, and the wording is: "Indeed God brings the believer near, places His screen over him and covers him, and says: Do you recognize the sin of such and such? Do you recognize the sin of such and such? He says: Yes, my Lord. Until, when He has made him acknowledge his sins and he sees in himself that he is ruined, He says: I covered them for you in this world, and today I forgive them for you."]]; I protect him from their punishment and penalty while covering them.

"Merciful" means: possessing far-reaching mercy. God says: ﴿And if they deny you, say: Your Lord is possessed of vast mercy﴾ [Al-An'am 147].

Mercy is a real attribute of God, established by the Qur'an, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the early generations (salaf). It has been denied by the people of ta'til (negation of attributes), who judged God by their intellects and abandoned the Book and the Sunnah, because among the foundations of their creed is that the attributes are received from reason: what reason requires to be negated must be negated, what reason requires to be affirmed must be affirmed, and what reason neither requires to be negated nor affirmed they suspend judgment on. Shaykh al-Islam says that they divided on it into two groups: some suspended judgment, and most of them negated it, saying that there must be a positive proof for its establishment.

You see that this corrupt principle entails denying what has come in the Qur'an and affirming what has not come in the Qur'an, because they say: if reason establishes something, we establish it, that is, whether or not it is found in the Book and the Sunnah, and if it negates something, we negate it. They deal this way with their object of worship and their god. Without doubt, when a person reflects on this corrupt rule, he finds it a great danger, and were it not that they are excused because they said this by way of interpretation (ta'wil), their matter would be extremely serious.

We believe that God has mercy. They do not deny mercy by way of denial (takdhib), but they deny it by way of interpretation (ta'wil), and for this reason they were not declared disbelievers. Had they denied it by outright denial, they would have disbelieved, because that is denial of the report. But they deny it by interpretation, saying that mercy is reward or the will to reward. Either it is reward, and you know that reward is something separate from God, a created thing distinct from God; or it is the will to reward, which is an attribute in God's essence. But they affirm the will, which is one of the seven attributes, and it is strange that they affirm the will by a hidden path while denying mercy although its path is clear. About the will they say: we deduce that God wills by specification, meaning that He specifies, for example, a human being in this form, tall of stature, with intellect, and so on, and He specified the camel with its characteristics, the sheep with its characteristics, the sun with its characteristics, the moon with its characteristics. This indicates what? It indicates will, because were it not for will, all created things would be alike.

But they say: specification indicates will, and the indication of specification upon will is a hidden indication that not everyone knows, not even students of knowledge unless they have studied. But is the indication of blessings upon mercy clear or not clear?

* Students: Clear.

* The Shaykh: The indication of blessings upon mercy?

* Students: Clear.

* The Shaykh: Clear. Everyone knows that among God's mercy is that He made the night and the day, and made the rains and the rivers and other things; the elite and the common know it. The strange thing is that they say: we do not affirm mercy because reason does not indicate it, while we affirm will because reason indicates it. It is said: Glory be to God! Which is clearer: reason's indication of mercy or of will? Of mercy, without doubt.

* In this noble verse there are benefits. First: urging a person to repent even if he has wronged, by His saying ﴿So whoever repents after his wrongdoing and reforms, indeed God will turn to him﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 39]. God, exalted, did not say this merely to inform, but to urge repentance.

* Among the benefits of this verse: whoever repents from wrongdoing, whatever it is, even from shirk, if he repents and reforms, God will turn to him. We say this because wrongdoing includes shirk, as God says of Luqman that he said to his son: ﴿O my son, do not associate anything with God; indeed, association is a great wrong﴾ [Luqman 13].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: committing sins and abandoning obligations is wrongdoing, by His saying ﴿after his wrongdoing﴾. It is clear that a person's soul is a trust, and he must strive for what is most upright and beneficial for it; if he opposes this, he is a wrongdoer and a betrayer of the trust.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: reform is necessary in repentance, by His saying ﴿and reforms﴾. But is reform a condition of repentance for all deeds, or a condition of repentance only for the deed in which the wrong occurred? The latter. For this reason we say: the correct view is that it is permissible to repent from one sin while persisting in another (...), and he does not deserve to be called a penitent without qualification, but he is described as repentant from such-and-such. So ﴿reforms﴾ means: what was corrupted by his wrongdoing, even if not all his conditions are reformed.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: confirmation of God's turning to one who repents and reforms, by His saying ﴿indeed, God will turn to him﴾. The conditions of repentance have passed with us shortly; and they are?

* Students: Five.

* The Shaykh: Five, good.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the eloquence of the noble Qur'an, in that it concludes rulings with the names of God that suit them, by His saying ﴿Indeed, God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾.

* Among its benefits: the affirmation of these two noble names of God, Forgiving and Merciful.

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Do you not know that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth? He punishes whom He wills and forgives whom He wills.﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 40]

﴿Do you not know﴾: the address is to everyone to whom address can be directed. Everyone to whom address can be directed is included in His words ﴿Do you not know﴾, because we see that the singular address in the Noble Qur'an includes everyone who can be addressed, or we say: everyone to whom address can be directed, unless evidence shows that it is specific to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, in which case it is specific to him. For example, ﴿Did We not expand your breast for you?﴾ [Al-Sharh 1]: who is meant?

* Students: It is specific.

* The Shaykh: This is specific. But when it comes without any evidence that it is specific to the Messenger, the Qur'an addresses all people, so it is to be understood as directed to whom?: to everyone to whom address can be directed.

We have already mentioned previously the difference of opinion on this: whether it is directed first to the Messenger and then to others after him, or to others first and then to others by following him, or to everyone from whom address can proceed, and this last is the preferable view.

"Do you not know, O addressee, that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth." This verse came in its proper place, because everything before it concerned the establishment of the prescribed punishments, so the soul might say: Why this severity? Why this harshness? So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Do you not know that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾. The interrogative here is for what? For affirmation. ﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾: if He has the dominion of the heavens and the earth, then He judges as He wills and does as He wills. Therefore He said: ﴿He punishes whom He wills and forgives whom He wills.﴾ In this verse, punishment is mentioned before forgiveness; in another verse, where is it?

* Students: Forgiveness.

* The Shaykh: Forgiveness is mentioned before punishment there. The reason is clear: here the subject is what? The prescribed punishments and penalties, so it was fitting to mention punishment before forgiveness.

As for the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿He punishes whom He wills﴾: do not think that when Allah says "He does what He wills, He judges as He wills, He judges as He desires," the matter is without wisdom. Rather, He punishes whom He wills when wisdom requires punishing him, and He forgives whom He wills when wisdom requires that Allah forgive him. Therefore Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿for whoever among you wills to take the straight path﴾ [At-Takwir 28], and Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ [Al-Insan 30].

As for His words ﴿And Allah is over all things Competent﴾: He concluded with this verse, and among His power, Mighty and Majestic, is that He commanded the punishment of criminals in the manner mentioned.

Power (al-qudrah) is doing a thing without inability. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, does what He wills without inability. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And Allah is not to be cause [of failure] for anything in the heavens or on the earth. Indeed, He is ever Knowing and Competent﴾ [Fatir 44]. He, glorified and exalted, is not incapacitated by anything. The opposite of strength (al-quwwah) is what?

* Students: Weakness.

* The Shaykh: Weakness, yes.

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Allah is the One who created you from weakness, then made after weakness strength, then made after strength weakness and gray hair﴾ [Ar-Rum 54]. But the opposite of power (al-qudrah) is incapacity (al-ajz). What is the difference between them? The difference is that power (qudrah) is only from one who has will (irādah), whereas strength (quwwah) is from one who has will and from other than him. A person is called "qādir" (capable) and "qawiyy" (strong); a wall is called "qawiyy" but not "qādir," because power is only from one who has will.

﴿And Allah is over all things Competent﴾. In this noble verse there are benefits:

* First: affirmation of the comprehensiveness of Allah's dominion, Mighty and Majestic, by His words ﴿Do you not know that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾.

* Among its benefits: the general dominion of the heavens and the earth belongs exclusively to Allah. Its evidence is the fronting of the predicate in His words ﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾. The scholars of rhetoric said: the fronting of what should be postponed indicates restriction and exclusivity, so what is that?

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the dominion of the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah, and no one shares it with Him. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Those whom you invoke besides Him do not possess even a speck﴾ [Fatir 13], and He, the Exalted, said: ﴿They do not possess an atom's weight in the heavens or on the earth, and they have no share in them, nor is He in need of any of them as a helper﴾ [Saba' 22].

If someone says: How do we reconcile this noble verse and the exclusivity of the dominion of the heavens and the earth to Allah with the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Or what you possess the keys of﴾ [An-Nur 61], ﴿or what your right hands possess﴾ [An-Nisa' 3], and what is similar to that of affirming ownership to the created?

The answer is easy: Allah's dominion, Mighty and Majestic, is general; He disposes as He wills and in everything. Human ownership is specific and also restricted. A person does not dispose of his property as he wills; is he not so? He is prohibited from usury, prohibited from fraud, prohibited from unknown exchange, indeed prohibited from wasting his wealth. So ownership is limited in disposal and in substance: even of substances, a person does not own everything. He owns his particular possession, but the dominion of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is general in everything, in substances and in disposal of them. Therefore we have no right to dispose of what Allah has granted us as ownership except by Allah's permission.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: affirmation of punishment and forgiveness for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, due to the completeness of His authority. But be certain that He will not punish anyone except for a sin that deserves punishment.

* Among its benefits: affirmation of Allah's will, by His words ﴿He punishes whom He wills﴾. There is no doubt that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has complete will. All Muslims say: "What Allah wills occurs, and what He does not will does not occur."

If someone says: Allah's will in His acts is clear, meaning that He sends down rain, makes plants grow, creates the heavens and the earth, gives life and causes death; this is clear. But does He have will regarding the acts of His servants? Answer me.

* Students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Yes, He has will regarding the acts of His servants. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿And if Allah had willed, those who came after them would not have fought one another after the clear proofs had come to them, but they differed, so among them were those who believed and among them those who disbelieved. And if Allah had willed, they would not have fought one another﴾ [Al-Baqarah 253]. He repeated it twice to make clear that their action occurs by the will of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: affirmation of Allah's power over all things, by His words ﴿And Allah is over all things Competent﴾. He, glorified and exalted, is not incapacitated by anything in the heavens or on the earth.

Is anything excluded from this generality? Never; nothing is excluded. He is capable of everything, without exception (...).

* A student: (...) Accordingly, if he wishes, after the hand has been cut, to restore it to what it was, he cannot be permitted to do so. If the purpose of the punishment for fornication, which is stoning, is the destruction and killing of the person, and it is reported in some narrations about Ma'iz that when he wished to repent, the Prophet ﷺ was informed of that and said: "Why did you not leave him? He repented, so Allah accepted his repentance"[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (4419) and al-Nasa'i (7167), from the hadith of Nu'aym ibn Hazzal, and the wording is theirs; its origin is in the Two Sahihs.]]. If someone says: If his hand is cut off, and then he wants to restore it, would he restore it?

* The Shaykh: He does not restore it. If he restored it, it would no longer serve its purpose; it would not be a deterrent (nakal), because He mentioned: ﴿as a recompense for what they earned, and as a deterrent from Allah﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 38]. If the hand is restored, it is not evident that this is a thief and that the thief's hand is cut, so it would not be a deterrent. As for the story of Ma'iz, he said: "Leave him, let him repent, and Allah will accept his repentance." This matter we mentioned previously regarding not cutting off the penis of the fornicator: we said that because there is a known prescribed limit in the Shari'ah, it is not to be exceeded. There is also another meaning: the hand of the thief, when cut, becomes a deterrent, since it is visible and everyone sees it; but cutting off the fornicator's penis is hidden and no one knows of it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 5, verse 41 (part 1 of 4):

Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿O Messenger, let not those hasten to disbelief grieve you, of those who say with their mouths, "We believe," but whose hearts have not believed, and of those who are Jews, listeners to falsehood, listeners to another people who have not come to you. They distort words from their places, saying, "If you are given this, take it, but if you are not given it, then beware." And whoever Allah wants to test, you will not own for him anything from Allah. Those are the ones for whom Allah does not want to purify their hearts. For them in this world is disgrace, and for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment.﴾ [al-Ma'idah 41].

* The Shaykh: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. This is the first night we begin the tafsir of the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, after a long absence. Since there are with us now brothers who did not attend from the beginning of the study, we would like to shed some light on what relates to the tafsir of the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. So we say:

First: Knowing the tafsir of the Book of Allah is an obligation, either a collective obligation (fard kifayah) or an individual obligation (fard 'ayn). Accordingly, whoever undertakes knowing the tafsir of the Noble Quran has performed one of the obligations of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. The reason tafsir is an obligation is that Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿A Book which We have sent down to you, blessed, that they may ponder its verses﴾ [Sad 29], and He said: ﴿Do they not ponder the Quran, or are there locks upon their hearts?﴾ [Muhammad 24]. It is well known that Allah did not send down the Quran to us merely so that we worship by its recitation, but so that we know its meaning and apply it in action and knowledge. Otherwise its benefit would be small if the purpose were merely to worship Allah by reciting it. The Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, did not go beyond ten verses until they had learned them and what was in them of knowledge and action.

If someone says: To what do we refer in tafsir? The books of tafsir are many and their treatment of the Quran takes various forms, so which of them do we refer to?

We say: The most important thing we observe in this is what relates to 'aqidah (creed). Accordingly, we warn against anyone who follows the path of the people of ta'til (denial) regarding the attributes and names of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. If it is known that a tafsir is from these people, then we should beware of it, even if it contains benefits from the linguistic or jurisprudential side. But we must be wary of it in the matter of what? 'Aqidah, lest we slip.

Let us give an example of this: The Kashshaf of al-Zamakhshari is undoubtedly a good tafsir in clarifying meanings and in what aims at eloquence, and all those who came after him and followed his method are dependent upon him, to the point that you see his expression, word for word and precisely, in these tafsirs. But in the matter of 'aqidah it is bad and must be guarded against.
