* And from the benefits of this noble verse: also the ugly attribute of consuming wealth falsely, by His words ﴿devourers of the unlawful gain﴾. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, mentioned this attribute only so that we would beware of it.

* And from it, that is, among the benefits of this verse: whoever acquires unlawful wealth has a resemblance to whom?

* Students: To the Jews.

* The Shaykh: To the Jews. So those who devour usury resemble the Jews, those who consume wealth by cheating resemble the Jews, those who consume wealth by false oaths resemble the Jews. Everyone who acquires wealth by a forbidden means resembles what? The bribe-taker resembles the Jews.

* And from the noble verse: the Prophet, peace be upon him, is given the choice between judging between the Jews and not judging, by His words ﴿So judge between them or turn away from them﴾, and (aw) here is for choice.

If someone says: is the choice absolute?

The answer: no, rather it is restricted by benefit. The rule with us is that if the choice is for ease for the obligated person, it is a choice of desire, he does whatever he wishes; and if it is for benefit, it is obligatory to follow the benefit (...).

* * *

* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿They are listeners to falsehood, devourers of what is unlawfully gained. So if they come to you, judge between them or turn away from them. And if you turn away from them, they will never harm you at all. And if you judge, judge between them with justice. Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly. (42) And how would they make you judge while they have the Torah, in which is the judgment of Allah? Then they turn away after that. And those are not believers﴾ [al-Ma'idah 42, 43].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful. The Exalted said: ﴿And if you turn away from them, they will never harm you at all﴾.

* From the benefits of this noble verse in this sentence: whoever turns away from something by the command of Allah, it does not harm him; by His words ﴿And if you turn away from them﴾, meaning: if you do not judge, they will never harm you at all.

But must the absence of harm be in the present, or in the future, meaning that one may be harmed at first and then the outcome is his?

The answer: the second, because a person may be harmed at first, and then the outcome is his, and then it is as if he was not harmed.

* And from the benefits of this noble verse: it is obligatory to judge between people with justice, by His words ﴿And if you judge, judge between them with justice﴾, meaning: if you wish to judge as we gave you the choice, then judge between them with justice.

* And from the benefits of this noble verse: it is not permissible for a person to favor in his judgment a relative, a friend, a rich man, or a poor man, by His words ﴿with justice﴾. This means that he looks at the case as a case, not as the case of so-and-so the son of so-and-so.

* And from the benefits of this noble verse: affirming love for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; that is, Allah loves.

* The student: ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who are constantly repentant and loves those who purify themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah 222].

* The Shaykh: ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who are constantly repentant and loves those who purify themselves﴾. Is this love a metaphor for reward, or is it real love?

* The students: The second.

* The Shaykh: The second. The second is necessarily the meaning, so it affirms that Allah, the Exalted, loves.

Among the people of ta'wil (figurative interpretation) there are those who said that Allah, the Exalted, does not love. They said that by way of ta'wil, not by denial; that is, he did not say "Allah does not love," but rather said "He loves, but the meaning of love is such-and-such." You must distinguish between the two approaches. One who says "Allah does not love" is a disbeliever, because he denies the Quran. One who says "He loves, but the meaning of love is such-and-such" is not a disbeliever. So distinguish between denying love through ta'wil and denying it through rejection and repudiation. They say, the Ash'ariyyah and those behind them among the Mu'tazilah and all the interpreters, "Allah does not love, because love exists only between two things that are similar; and also because love renews, being attached to attributes and causes, while Allah is exalted above temporal events." So what is the meaning of love?

They said: its meaning is reward. The poor ones did not realize that affirming reward necessitates affirming love, for there cannot be reward without love, ever. Though they flee from affirming it verbally, it is necessarily entailed for them.

The gist is that they say: love means recompense. It was said to them: Allah says ﴿Then Allah will bring a people whom He loves and who love Him﴾ [al-Ma'idah 54]. They said: yes, ﴿He loves them﴾ means He rewards them, and ﴿they love Him﴾ means they do what He rewards them for. But this is without doubt contrary to the apparent wording and contrary to the consensus of the Salaf. Not one of the Salaf said that love means reward.

If someone says: do you have a text from each one of the Salaf saying that love has its real meaning? We say: no. But the fact that these texts come against them, and nothing has come from any of them, not a single letter, that they interpreted them against their apparent meaning, indicates that they were agreed upon affirming it. There is no need to transmit their consensus on every individual question, but as long as the texts of the Book and the Sunnah come against them and nothing has come from any one of them that they interpreted them against their apparent meaning, this indicates that they were unanimous in affirming it.

As for their saying that this entails that temporal events subsist in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, we say: so be it. We believe that Allah, the Exalted, does what He wills, and that among His attributes some renew and some do not, in a sense: some occur through causes and some do not occur through causes. Knowledge, for example, is eternal and everlasting, but love is not like that. If Allah loves this servant, when did His love for this servant begin? After the existence of causes, the causes of love. So His love for this particular servant is temporal, and there is no obstacle. And the subsistence of voluntary actions in Him is among the perfections of His attributes, without doubt.

* And from the benefits of this noble verse: affirming that the love of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, varies in degree; affirming that the love of Allah varies. The indication is that love here is linked to an attribute. And what is it?

* Students: Justice.

* The Shaykh: No, I mean the act of being just, because "muqsitin" is from the quadriliteral form, al-iqsat. When it is so, what is linked to an attribute increases with its increase and decreases with its decrease. Have you seen that if you say: honor the diligent student, your honoring increases with the increase in diligence and decreases with its decrease?

So, affirming that Allah loves the just indicates that the love of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, varies in degree: that He loves one more than another, and loves one and does not love another. How is the indication? Yes.

* Student: Because here it is linked to an attribute, and the attribute increases with its increase...

* The Shaykh: Correct, and this rule holds in everything.

* And from the benefits of this noble verse: encouragement to act justly, that is, to be just. What is the reason for that?

* Student: That Allah, Mighty and Majestic, loves those who act justly (al-muqsitin). This affirms Allah's love for the one who is equitable (al-muqsit), i.e., the just person, and this necessarily implies obligation and urging toward it.

* Shaykh: Meaning, when Allah informs that He loves those who act justly, what does that entail? Urging toward this. This is not merely a report; rather it is a report intended to produce what? Exhortation and encouragement toward justice.

Then Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿How will they make you judge while they have the Torah, in which is Allah's ruling?﴾ Here "how" (kayfa) is interrogative, and what is meant is wonder (al-ta'jib). The meaning is: be amazed! How will they make you judge while they have the Torah, in which is Allah's ruling, and they claim to believe in it? This is a contradiction. If they have a book by which they are guided, which they claim is their book, their law and their religion, how can they turn to judgment by other than it? This indicates doubt about their seeking judgment from the Messenger (ﷺ), and that they did not intend the truth. Had they intended the truth, they would have returned to the book they have, because they believe it is, what? True. ﴿How will they make you judge while they have the Torah, in which is Allah's ruling?﴾

So the matter now is one of doubt, and that they did not truly want arbitration. This is the reality, because when two of them committed adultery, they came to the Messenger (ﷺ), wanting him to agree with what they had themselves introduced regarding the punishment for this immorality. So the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded that the two adulterers be stoned. Then they denied this and said: "This differs from what we have." He said: "What do you have?" They said: "We have that we blacken the faces of the two adulterers and parade them through the markets as disgrace and shame." Then 'Abdullah ibn Salam, or someone else, informed him that the Torah explicitly states that the two adulterers are to be stoned. He said: "Bring the Torah." They brought it, and the reader began to read, and he placed his hand on the verse of stoning. 'Abdullah ibn Salam said to him: "Lift your hand," because 'Abdullah ibn Salam was one of the rabbis of the Jews. He lifted his hand, and there was the verse of stoning, agreeing with what the Prophet (ﷺ) had ruled. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O Allah, I am the first who established... " I think it is: "Your ruling after they had caused it to die," or: "The one who revived Your ruling after they had caused it to die."

So Allah, mighty and majestic, is expressing wonder to the Messenger (ﷺ): ﴿How will they make you judge while they have the Torah, in which is Allah's ruling, then they turn away after that?﴾ That is: after they made you judge and you ruled, they turned away and refused, until the Torah was brought, and behold, it was in complete agreement with the ruling of the Prophet (ﷺ).

His saying ﴿after that﴾ refers to the judgment (al-tahkim).

﴿And those are not believers﴾ means: these are not believers. He used "ulā'ika" with the particle "kaf" indicating the distance of the one referred to, and this is because of the lowliness of their rank, not its loftiness. The meaning is: these base people, who have sunk to the lowest of the low, are not believers. They did not believe in the Torah, nor did they believe in Muhammad (ﷺ).

As for the grammatical analysis (i'rab) of this sentence, who among you has knowledge of Arabic grammar? Who?

A student: "Ma" is a negating particle that functions like "laysa" (is not).

"Ulā'ika" is a demonstrative noun, built on kasra, in the nominative position as the subject of "ma," and the "kaf" is extra?

The Shaykh: Extra!

The student: That is, for address.

The Shaykh: And is the "kaf" added? This is new knowledge! Tell me: yes, it can be added, man. ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ [al-Shura 11]. Some grammarians said the "kaf" is extra.

The student: The "ba'" is a preposition.

The Shaykh: Then complete it. The "kaf," what do you say about it? Is it extra, or a particle indicating address?

The student: It indicates address, and the "ba'" is an extra preposition. "Al-mu'minin" is the predicate of "ma."

The Shaykh: The predicate of "ma"?

The student: It is genitive.

The Shaykh: Genitive, the predicate of "ma"?! Do you not say it functions like "laysa"?!

Another student: No, it is genitive, governed by the "ba'," an extra preposition.

The Shaykh: You cannot say: the predicate of "ma" is genitive.

The student: The predicate of "ma" is genitive, and the sign of its accusative case is the "ya'," because it is a sound masculine plural.

The Shaykh: The "ya'" is governed by the extra preposition.

The student: And we assume the i'rab.

The Shaykh: What is it, an assumed "ya'"?

A student: (...)

The Shaykh: What? We do not have a vowel mark here.

A student: The i'rab vowel belongs to the extra preposition.

The Shaykh: We do not have a vowel mark. What we have is a "ya'," and it is one of the signs of case that are letters, not vowels. That is, a "ya'" assumed on the "ya'" that is... governed by the extra preposition.

Why do we not say: since it is the same "ya'" whether the noun is accusative or genitive?

They said: For the sake of perfecting the rules. Or is there no real difference? The wording has not changed, whether you say the "ba'" is an extra preposition or that it is accusative, because the sign of the accusative in the sound masculine plural and the sign of the genitive are the same, the "ya'." But they say, for the sake of mastering the rules, one must say it this way.

His saying ﴿And those are not believers﴾: here Allah, mighty and majestic, negated that these people are believers, and He used the extra preposition. The scholars of rhetoric (al-balagha) have mentioned that all extra particles convey emphasis. Accordingly, the "ba'" here, though extra in grammatical analysis, is extra in meaning, and that meaning is emphasis. When you say "ma Zaydun qa'iman" and "ma Zaydun bi-qa'im," the second is more emphatic. ﴿And those are not believers﴾.

Among the benefits of this noble verse:
- The wonder at these Jews who make the Prophet (ﷺ) their judge seeking a dispensation, while they have the Torah.
- Whoever asks a scholar for a fatwa seeking a dispensation has some resemblance to the Jews. For this reason the scholars said: it is forbidden to seek a fatwa seeking a dispensation. They said: whoever pursues dispensations has become a heretic (tazandaq). The manner of pursuing dispensations is that when a scholar has given you a fatwa and you did not want his fatwa, you go to another scholar so that he will give you what suits you. There is no doubt that such a questioner only wanted to follow his desire rather than guidance, because he asked this scholar believing that his fatwa is what? True and law. When it did not agree with his desire, he went to ask another, so his condition declares that he does not want guidance but desire. Yes, if a person asks a scholar in his locality, and he sees no better scholar than him, but his intention is that if he were able to ask one more knowledgeable, he would do so, then we say: there is no harm in acting on his word, and if he finds a more trustworthy scholar, let him ask him. This is like using dust for purification when water is unavailable, and like eating carrion when one cannot eat slaughtered meat. Accordingly, a distinction is made between two persons who asked a scholar and then asked another. One of them asked this scholar because he sees no one in his town more knowledgeable than him, and his intention is that if he finds someone more trustworthy, he will ask him. What is the ruling on this second asking?

The students: Permissible.

The Shaykh: Permissible. The second asked the scholar in his town, believing his fatwa to be the truth, but he found it burdensome, so he asked another scholar, perhaps he would find a dispensation. This is not permissible. Look: the two of them did the same action, but their rulings differ.

- Among the benefits of this noble verse: the contradiction of the Jews, in that they seek the truth while the instrument of truth is with them. They made the Messenger a judge although the Torah contains Allah's ruling, meaning it contains what they believe to be Allah's ruling.
- Among the benefits of the verse: what came in the Torah is Allah's ruling, but when? Before it was altered and changed, and some of it was concealed while some was revealed. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Say: Who revealed the Book that Moses brought, a light and guidance for mankind, which you make into scrolls, showing them while concealing much?﴾ [al-An'am 91] (...)

* * *

A student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan: ﴿They were entrusted with the Book of Allah and were witnesses to it. So do not fear the people but fear Me, and do not exchange My signs for a small price. And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, those are the disbelievers (44). And We prescribed for them therein: a life for a life, an eye for an eye, a nose for a nose, an ear for an ear, a tooth for a tooth, and for wounds is legal retribution. But whoever gives it as charity, it is expiation for him. And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, those are the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Ma'idah 44-45].

The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿How will they make you judge while they have the Torah, in which is Allah's ruling, then they turn away after that? And those are not believers﴾. Mention the benefits you have taken.

A student: The last benefit, O Shaykh...

The Shaykh: No, all of them, their main points.

The student: The first, O Shaykh: the wonder at these Jews who came to ask the Prophet (ﷺ) for a fatwa while they have the Torah in which is Allah's ruling.

The Shaykh: The wonder, or the expression of wonder?

The student: The wonder.

Students: The expression of wonder.

A student: The wonder.

The Shaykh: The expression of wonder; that is, Allah causes us to wonder, saying: marvel at these people.

The student: The second: whoever asks a scholar for a fatwa seeking a dispensation has some resemblance to the Jews. For this reason the scholars said: it is forbidden to ask a scholar for a fatwa seeking a dispensation.

The Shaykh: It is forbidden.

The student: It is forbidden to ask a scholar for a fatwa seeking a dispensation, and they said: whoever pursues dispensations becomes a heretic.

The third: the contradiction of the Jews, in that they struck [the believers]... while the instrument of truth is with them.

The fourth: what came in the Torah is Allah's ruling, but that was before it was altered or changed.

The Shaykh: Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And they have the Torah﴾ to the end.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: the rulings in the Torah are Allah's ruling, by His saying ﴿in which is Allah's ruling﴾. But this refers to the authentic Torah. As for after it was altered, changed and concealed, the ruling is altered, by Allah's saying: ﴿Say: Who revealed the Book that Moses brought, a light and guidance for mankind, which you make into scrolls, showing them while concealing much?﴾

Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obstinacy of the Jews, and that after the truth becomes clear to them they turn away. We derive this from His saying: ﴿then they turn away﴾, because "thumma" (then) indicates sequence and delay.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: whoever seeks a fatwa in pursuit of a dispensation is not a believer, by Allah's saying: ﴿And those are not believers﴾.

But does this negate the root of faith or its completeness?

The apparent view is the second: it negates the completeness of faith.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 5, verse 44 (part 1 of 2):

Then He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which is guidance and light﴾. (إنا) ("Indeed, We") is known to be a plural pronoun for the group. But when it is attributed to Allah, it definitely means glorification, because Allah, glorified and exalted is He, is one God, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And your God is one God﴾ [al-Baqarah 163], and He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no deity except Him, and so do the angels and those of knowledge﴾ [Ali 'Imran 18].

His saying: ﴿We sent down the Torah﴾ means from above, because Allah, the Exalted, sent it down upon Musa, but He, Majestic and Exalted, wrote it with His own hand on tablets that descended from the heaven upon Musa, peace be upon him, and he brought them written on the tablets.

﴿In which is guidance and light﴾. Guidance (al-huda) is knowledge, and light (al-nur) is the effect of this knowledge. This is because a person, whenever his knowledge increases, his light and insight into the religion of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, increase. So guidance is knowledge, and light is the effect of knowledge.

﴿By which the prophets judged﴾, meaning by the Torah and what it contains of guidance and light.

﴿The prophets (al-nabiyyun)﴾. In another reading: ﴿al-nabi'un﴾. According to the reading ﴿al-nabi'un﴾, its singular is nabi' (نبيء), and it is derived from al-naba' (النبأ), meaning news. According to the reading with the hamza dropped, it has been said that it is derived from al-nubuwwah (النبوة), meaning an elevated thing, because of the elevated station of the prophets. It has also been said that it is from al-naba', but the hamza was made easier and became a yaa', so it became (al-nabi) and (al-nabiyyun).

All agree that the messengers, peace be upon them, are in the highest ranks of creation, and that they brought the news and reports. So the two opinions agree in meaning. We only say that the messengers and likewise the prophets are at the highest ranks of creation because of the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger – those are with the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favor of the prophets, the steadfast in truth, the martyrs, and the righteous﴾ [al-Nisa' 69].

﴿Who submitted (alladhina aslamu) to those who were Jews (lilladhina hadu)﴾. "Those who submitted" means complete submission, which is submission of the heart, submission of the tongue, and submission of the limbs; that is, surrendering to Allah outwardly and inwardly. Do not be surprised that the prophets are described as Muslims, because the prophets, peace be upon them, are the strongest of people in surrender to Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said about Yusuf: ﴿Cause me to die as a Muslim and join me with the righteous﴾ [Yusuf 101], and Allah, the Exalted, said about Ibrahim: ﴿When his Lord said to him, "Submit," he said, "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds"﴾ [al-Baqarah 131]. So the Islam of the prophets includes faith, because it is submission of the heart, the tongue, and the limbs.

﴿Who submitted to those who were Jews﴾ is connected to ﴿judged﴾, meaning these messengers judged by it for the Jews.

﴿To those who were Jews (lilladhina hadu)﴾: (hadu) means "they returned," referring to their repentance from worshipping the calf, for this is a return to Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿And the rabbinical scholars (al-rabbaniyyun) and the rabbis (al-ahbar)﴾. It has been said that in these two, the conjunction is of the type of conjoining attributes, and that the rabbaniyyun are the rabbis. It has also been said that there is a difference between them: the difference is that the rabbani is one who has perfected servitude to Allah and trained people in it, even if he has not reached the rank of the habr (حبر) in terms of knowledge.

And (al-ahbar) are those who have reached a great level of knowledge. So al-habr (حبر) is one of extensive knowledge. They said: it is because it agrees in derivation with al-bahr (بحر), meaning sea. But it is not a complete derivation in which the derivative and its root are identical in both letters and order. This one has the derivative and its root identical in letters but not in order, because habr (حبر) and bahr (بحر) each has three letters that agree, isn't that so?

* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: On this basis, the habr is the one of extensive knowledge who has wide knowledge, while the rabbani is below him, but he trains people in the worship of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and trains them also in knowledge.

It has been said in other than this verse: the rabbani is the scholar who trains people with the minor matters of knowledge before its major matters, because this is undoubtedly from wisdom, and it is the closest means to acquiring knowledge that a student be trained with the minor matters of knowledge before the major ones.

He said: ﴿By what they were entrusted﴾. ﴿The prophets judged by it, those who submitted to those who were Jews, up to His saying: by what they were entrusted﴾ means: they judge by what they were entrusted with from the Book of Allah; that is, by what they were made guardians of. That is, who are the first to preserve the religion, stand in its preservation, and defend it? They are the scholars, the rabbis and the rabbaniyyun. Therefore He said: ﴿by what they were entrusted﴾, that is, because of what they were entrusted with from the Book of Allah.

His saying: ﴿were entrusted (istuhfizu)﴾ means they were made guardians of it.

﴿From the Book of Allah﴾, and what is meant by it is the Torah, because of His saying: ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which is guidance and light﴾, the Torah.

﴿By what they were entrusted from the Book of Allah, and they were witnesses over it﴾. The Torah was attributed to Allah because He, glorified and exalted, wrote it with His own hand. This is the well-known view of the scholars, earlier and later.

﴿And they were over it﴾, meaning over that with which they were entrusted, ﴿witnesses﴾, because the scholars bear witness that this is the law of Allah and spread it among the servants of Allah, so they were witnesses over creation through the delivery of the law to them.

He said: ﴿So do not fear the people, but fear Me﴾. ﴿Do not fear the people﴾, meaning do not be afraid of them and submit to them, but fear Allah. This is an indication that when a nobleman among them committed adultery, they would leave him alone, and when a weak person among them committed adultery, they would enforce the legal punishment upon him.

﴿And do not exchange My verses for a small price﴾, meaning do not substitute the verses of Allah for a small price. So what is this small price? This small price is either status or bribery. They judge by other than the law of Allah in order to preserve their honor, status and leadership, or for money given to them as a bribe. Therefore He said: ﴿Do not exchange My verses for a small price﴾.

So the small price is either rank, status and honor, or what? Money through bribery. Allah described it as small because everything in this world, however great, is small. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Say, "The enjoyment of this world is little, and the Hereafter is better for those who fear Allah"﴾ [al-Nisa' 77].

﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed – those are the disbelievers﴾, meaning: any person who does not judge by what Allah has sent down, whether Jews, Christians, or others, those are the disbelievers.

(Ulā'ika) is the subject, and (hum) is a pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl). The pronoun of separation came to convey restriction and emphasis, because they said that the pronoun of separation has three benefits:
The first: conveying restriction.
The second: emphasis.
The third: distinguishing between the predicate and the attribute. For this reason it is called a pronoun of separation (damir fasl). This is clear from an example: if you say, "Zayd al-fadil" and express it differently: "Zayd huwa al-fadil," which is more eloquent in establishing excellence for Zayd?

* The students: The second.
* The Shaykh: The second. It means: he and no other. So it conveys restriction, conveys emphasis as well, and distinguishes between predicate and attribute. Because when you say "Zayd al-fadil," it may be that al-fadil is an attribute of what? Of Zayd. And the listener awaits a predicate. "Zayd al-fadil," what is the matter of Zayd the excellent? What is the situation of Zayd the excellent?

* A student: The predicate.
* The Shaykh: A person anticipates a predicate. When you say "Zayd huwa al-fadil," it does not admit that al-fadil is an attribute; it is definitely a predicate.

Does it have a place in grammatical analysis (i'rab)? It has no place in i'rab. It is a particle in the form of a pronoun and has no place in i'rab. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Perhaps we will follow the magicians if they are the victors﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 40], which indicates that it has no place in i'rab, because if it had a place in i'rab, it would be a subject (mubtada'), and al-ghalibin would be the predicate, but it has no place in i'rab.

Therefore we say: ﴿in kanu hum﴾: (kanu) – the waw is the subject of kana, and ﴿al-ghalibin﴾ is its predicate.

* In this noble verse there are benefits. Among them: the affirmation that Allah, the Exalted, sent down the Torah, because of His saying: ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Torah﴾.

* Among them: the nobility of the Torah, since Allah, the Exalted, sent it down from Himself. But as I told you in the tafsir, what is meant by the Torah is the one that was not altered or changed.

* Among them: that in the Torah there is guidance and light, because of His saying: ﴿in which is guidance and light﴾. In the Noble Qur'an Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was revealed as guidance for the people﴾ [al-Baqarah 185], so the entire Qur'an is guidance and all of it is light: ﴿And We sent down to you a clear light﴾ [al-Nisa' 174]. The Torah in this verse, Allah the Exalted said: ﴿in which is guidance and light﴾. The difference between this expression and the Qur'anic expression regarding the Noble Qur'an is great, because this one placed guidance and light in it, while the Qur'an itself is the guidance and light in this verse.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the Torah is the foundation for the prophets who came after Musa, because of His saying: ﴿by which the prophets judged﴾. Accordingly, the laws that came after the Torah are considered a completion of the Torah and a realization of acting upon it.

From this we say: Is the Gospel included in that? We say: Yes, the Gospel completes the Torah, because 'Isa, peace be upon him, said: ﴿and to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you﴾ [Ali 'Imran 50].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the permissibility of describing the prophets as Muslims, because of His saying: ﴿the prophets who submitted﴾. What is meant here is outward and inward submission, because there is an outward Islam only, as in the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, in the story of Lut: ﴿So We brought out whoever was in it of the believers. But We found not in it except one house of the Muslims﴾ [al-Dhariyat 35–36]. He made those who were in it – in the house – to be among the Muslims.

It is known that the wife of Lut was not a Muslim but a disbeliever, yet she betrayed her husband by showing Islam. Therefore Allah said: ﴿Allah presents an example for those who disbelieve: the wife of Nuh and the wife of Lut. They were under two of Our righteous servants, but they betrayed them﴾ [al-Tahrim 10]. They betrayed them, not by committing immorality, but by concealing their disbelief from them.

The point is that Islam may be applied to one who shows Islam even if his heart is hidden with disbelief. But the Islam of the prophets, peace be upon them, is the opposite of that: the Islam of the prophets is submission to Allah outwardly and inwardly.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: there is no excuse for the Jews in departing from the law of Allah, because Allah, the Exalted, appointed for them many prophets who judged for them by the Torah, but they were obstinate and disbelieved.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the people of knowledge are the heirs of the prophets in manifesting the judgment of Allah and calling to His law, because of His saying: ﴿and the rabbaniyyun and the rabbis﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: praise of the people of knowledge and that they are the guardians of the law of Allah, because of His saying: ﴿by what they were entrusted from the Book of Allah﴾. There is no doubt that the scholars are the guardians of the law of Allah. They are the heirs of the prophets, and they are the ones obliged to call to Allah with insight and to spread the law of Allah.

* Among its benefits: that the books of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, are the foundation of the sciences by which those who memorize them call the servants of Allah, because of His saying: ﴿from the Book of Allah﴾. Accordingly, is the Torah one of the books of Allah or not? Yes, it is one of the books of Allah without doubt, one of the books in which we must believe.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the scholars are trustworthy witnesses over the law of Allah, entrusted. This is the principle, but they may deviate from the principle. They may deviate from this principle, which is bearing witness to the law of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, which they spread among the people.

But is every scholar like that? No. Therefore we say: scholars are of three types: the scholar of the religion (ʿālim millah), the scholar of the community (ʿālim ummah), and the scholar of the state (ʿālim dawlah). Three types. The scholar of the religion is the one who is keen to preserve the religion, spread it among the people, and call to it, and this is the scholar in truth. The scholar of the community is the one who sees what benefits the people and issues fatwas to them accordingly, even if it contradicts the truth, because he wants to walk with this community and does not care. The third, the scholar of the state, is the one who sees what the state wants, calls to it, judges by it, and tries to twist the texts toward what the state wants.

Years ago a call to socialism appeared, due to the influence of the communists in some Arab countries, and the call to socialism and the nationalization of property emerged. Some scholars began trying to find something in the Qur'an and the Sunnah to support this method. They began bringing verses and hadiths far from their intended meaning in order to prove it. We even heard someone say that the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿He presents to you an example from yourselves: Do you have among those whom your right hands possess any partners in what We have provided for you, so that you are equal therein?﴾ [al-Rum 28] means that you and the slaves you own are equal. This is undoubtedly a distortion, because the meaning of the verse is that Allah has presented to us an example from ourselves: Would a master be pleased that his slave share with him in his properties and rights?

* The students: No.
* The Shaykh: No. ﴿Do you have among those whom your right hands possess any partners in what We have provided for you, so that you are equal therein?﴾ on the basis that they are partners to you, and this you cannot accept. Likewise, would the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, be pleased that any of His creation be a partner to Him? He is not pleased, just as you are not pleased that your slaves be partners with you in provision. This is the meaning of the verse. They also cited hadiths such as: "People are partners in three things" [Abu Dawud (3477) from a man among the companions of the Prophet, and Ibn Majah (2472), and Ahmad in al-Musnad (23082) from Ibn 'Abbas, with the wording: "the Muslims"], and similar.

We call these scholars what? Scholars of the state, meaning they see what the state wants and direct people toward it. We ask Allah for well-being.

But the rabbaniyyun scholars whom Allah entrusted with His Book cannot take this path. The scholars are of three types. Mention their types?

* A student: Scholar of the religion, of the community, and of the state.

* The Shaykh: Scholar of the religion, scholar of the community, and scholar of the state. Which of them is best?

* The student: The first, the religion.

* The Shaykh: The first is the scholar of the religion. Yes, may Allah bless you.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of fearing people in obeying the law of Allah, because of His saying: ﴿So do not fear the people, but fear Me﴾. Know that Allah, the Exalted, mentioned in the Noble Qur'an a cause for a person to fear people rather than Allah, when He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿That is only Satan who frightens his allies, so do not fear them but fear Me, if you are believers﴾ [Ali 'Imran 175]. Satan comes, for example, to the weak in religion and the weak in resolve and determination, and says: Do not do this; if you do, the nations will rise against you, the nations will object to you. So he fears. But the truly faithful one does not fear. He says: As long as I am upon insight and upon religion, I fear none but Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Therefore He said: ﴿So do not fear the people, but fear Me﴾.

* Among the benefits of this verse: that the one who deviates from the religion and from spreading knowledge deviates for one of two reasons. The first reason is fear of people. The second reason is greed for worldly things. This is derived from His saying: ﴿and do not exchange My verses for a small price﴾. If you reflect on the causes of deviation – by which I mean the deviation of scholars – you will find that it revolves around two things: either fear of people, or what? Seeking worldly things, leadership, money, and similar matters.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, those are the disbelievers, because of His saying: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed – those are the disbelievers﴾.

Scholars differed, may God have mercy on them, as to whether the generality of this verse is meant to be taken as specific: that is, whether it refers only to the Jews, because they did not judge by what God revealed, or whether it is meant in its general sense?

Some said: the verse refers to the Jews, because they did not judge by what God revealed, and so they are disbelievers. Others said: it is general. The correct view is that it is general in terms of the ruling, even if we take its wording as applying to the Jews, because the context is one of censure of them. For we say: if this ruling is established for the Jews, it is established for others as well, by way of general meaning, which is qiyas (analogical reasoning). So now, ﴿Whoever does not judge by what God has revealed, they are the disbelievers﴾. If we say that this is a general statement intended in a specific sense, and that what is meant is the Jews, then we say this is the verse's indication in its wording. But if we take it as general, regardless of the context, the verse indicates in its wording that it encompasses the Jews and non-Jews. And according to the view that it is specific, we say: whoever does not judge by what God revealed from among non-Jews is included by analogy, what is it? By meaning (ma'nawiyyan).

However, know that whoever does not judge by what God has revealed does so either out of greed, or out of disbelief in what God has revealed, or out of aggression and injustice toward others.

If it is out of greed, then he is a sinner (fasiq), like a judge before whom two men dispute, and one of them gives him a bribe, so he rules contrary to what God has revealed. Why? Seeking the bribe and out of greed. We say of this one that he is a sinner.

The second: a man before whom two men dispute, and there is enmity between him and one of them; he rules against the one who is right. We say: what is this? This is a wrongdoer and transgressor, who has no aim in ruling against him except that he wants to take revenge on him, because he dislikes him or there is some ill feeling between them.

The third: that he rules by other than what God has revealed out of aversion to what God has revealed, or out of his belief that what he rules by is better than the judgment of God, the Mighty and Majestic, or that he is free to choose between ruling by what God has revealed or by other than it. This one is a disbeliever, a disbeliever who has left Islam, because he detested Islam or thought that something other than it was better than it or equal to it. God, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And who is better in judgment than God for a people who are certain?﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:50]. That is: no one is better in judgment than God. So if he rules while believing that his ruling is like the ruling of God, then he has denied what the verse indicates, which is His saying: ﴿And who is better in judgment than God?﴾ And if he believes that his ruling is better than God's, then he is more wicked and more vile than the one who said it is equal to it.

* Student: May God bless you. What is the criterion for a person to fear God, the Mighty and Majestic, and not fear people? Then, if we look at the other side, we find, for example, in some countries rulers who oppose this truth. When is it obligatory for a person to fear them and to proclaim the truth no matter what? And when is there leeway? The person..
* Shaykh: If his intention in concealing the truth is fear for himself, then this is the one who feared people. But if his intention in concealing the truth is fear for the truth, and that if he openly declared it, the ruler who has power over him would oppose him and suppress this call, and the matter might reach others, then there is no sin in delaying the call until a time when he can openly proclaim it.
* Student: Which is greater: the one who judges by other than what God has revealed out of greed, or the one who has (...)?
* Shaykh: The second is greater, because the first has a benefit to which the soul may be drawn, whereas the second has no aim except aggression, so he is worse and greater without doubt.
* Student: Isn't it the case, O Shaykh, that whoever believes that the judgment of other than God is better than the judgment of God, or dislikes the judgment of God, becomes a disbeliever even if he does not rule?
* Shaykh: Yes indeed, without doubt. If he believes that the judgment of other than God is better than the judgment of God, or that it is like the judgment of God, then he is a disbeliever, because he is denying it; and his disbelief here is disbelief of denial. We mentioned earlier that disbelief revolves around two things: denial (juhud) and arrogance (istikbar).
* Student: May God be good to you. Sometimes a person sits with a sinner and wants to advise him, but the opportunity to advise him may not be available, either because there are others present, guests and so on, or because he has not dared to advise him at that moment. Is it permissible for him to sit with him until he can advise him later?
* Shaykh: If he can only meet him in this situation, perhaps it is permitted. But if he can meet him otherwise, then he should leave the sinful gathering and advise him at another time.
* Student: Harm may arise between him and the other, especially if he is one of the relatives. He would leave the guests' gathering to which he, that is, he had been invited..
* Shaykh: He can get up. A person can get up discreetly: either he places his hand over his nose as if he had a nosebleed, or he says like this, meaning what?
* Students: A headache.
* Shaykh: A headache. Can he?

Tutor (Talib): I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. ﴿And We prescribed for them therein that the life is for the life, and the eye for the eye, and the nose for the nose, and the ear for the ear, and the tooth for the tooth, and for wounds is retaliation. But whoever gives it as charity, it is an expiation for him. And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed - then it is those who are the wrongdoers.﴾ [al-Ma'idah 45].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We prescribed for them therein﴾ to the end. I think we did not complete the benefits of the verse before it, is that not so?
* Talib: No, Shaykh, we completed them.
* The Shaykh: No, we did not complete them. If we had completed them, then what is the difference between khashyah (fear with awe) and khawf (fear)?
* Talib: Khashyah is more specific than khawf.
* The Shaykh: Yes, what is the difference?
* The student: The difference is that khashyah is with knowledge, whereas khawf is not. That is the first difference. The second difference...
* The Shaykh: The first difference: khashyah is accompanied by knowledge, and khawf?
* The student: It may be...
* The Shaykh: Yes, it may be, or it may not be. And the second?
* The student: The second difference: khashyah is due to the greatness of the one feared, whereas khawf may be due to the weakness of the one who fears...
* The Shaykh: Due to the weakness of the one who fears, even if the one feared is not strong.
The third: khashyah is more complete than khawf; for this reason its letters, the kha', the shin and the ya', all derive from the meaning of "strong thing."

His saying: ﴿And do not exchange My signs for a small price﴾. What is the meaning of (do not exchange them)?
* Talib: Synonymy.
* The Shaykh: No, no.
* Talib: Do not substitute.
* The Shaykh: And what is meant by "small price"?
* The student: The goods of this world.
* The Shaykh: The goods of this world, whether status, leadership, wealth, or other things; all of them are small, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say, the enjoyment of this world is little﴾ [an-Nisa' 77].
﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed - then those are the disbelievers﴾. Have we taken the benefits of this?
* The students: No, Shaykh.
* The Shaykh: Then this verse is among the most difficult things for the people of knowledge, in His saying: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed - then those are the disbelievers﴾. Some scholars said: this applies specifically to the Jews, because the verses are in the context of rebuking the Jews, so it is as if Allah said: these Jews are disbelievers.
Some scholars said: its origin is about the Jews, but it is general, because the word "whoever" (man) is explicit in generality: ﴿whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed - then those are the disbelievers﴾.
The correct view is that it is general, because the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the cause.
But does the meaning "those are the disbelievers" refer to disbelief in what they judged, or to disbelievers who have left the religion?
This too is a matter of disagreement. Some scholars said: "those are the disbelievers" in what they judged, like the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Two things among people are disbelief in them: slandering lineage and wailing over the dead,"[[Narrated by Muslim (67/121) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] even though this does not take one out of Islam. Accordingly, the meaning becomes: they are disbelievers in what?
* The students: What they judged.
* The Shaykh: What they judged only, not those who have left the religion.
It was said: "they are the disbelievers" means they are described with disbelief that expels one from the religion. But the evidences indicate that this is conditioned by restrictions, or that it is restricted by conditions:
The first: that the judge knows Allah's ruling.
The second: that he knows that this ruling contradicts Allah's ruling.
The third: that he makes it a substitute for Allah's ruling.
The fourth: that he does not approve of Allah's ruling.
When these conditions are fulfilled, he then becomes outside the religion.
If it is said: Can we not say that he leaves the religion by this, like the first view? We say: even if we say he leaves the religion by this, belief in part of the Book and disbelief in part of it is disbelief in all of it, just as belief in some messengers and disbelief in some of them is disbelief in all of them.
If he judges by other than what Allah revealed while not knowing Allah's ruling, he does not become a disbeliever, because one of the conditions for judging someone a disbeliever is that the person knows it. How much more so if he judges by an interpretation from those who distort words from their places, from the scholars of evil and the scholars of the state. This is a stronger excuse for him and further from declaring him a disbeliever.
If he says: he knows Allah's ruling and is content with Allah's ruling, but he sees that it is not suitable for this time, for example, we say: this is disbelief, because the Islamic law remains until the Day of Resurrection. The One who legislated it, glorified and exalted is He, knows what suits creation, and knows that Muhammad is the Seal of the Prophets, and his law must be suitable for what? For every time and place until the end of the world.
But he must first be taught, because it may be confused for some rulers, and I am speaking now about our rulers. Many of the rulers of the Islamic nation today are ignorant of the rulings of the Sharia; they know nothing of its rulings. Then bad companions and evil associates come to him and say: this admits of interpretation, it admits of this, it admits of that. Then they present the famous, weighty phrase: the Islamic law came to bring benefits and repel harms. So it appears to them that this is a good thing. Then they say to the governors: make it a sunnah, make it a system. Yet a person's vision is limited; in such a state it may appear to him to be good, but its consequences are what? Corrupt.
So when we know that Allah forbade this thing or obligated this thing, we know that the fruitful results of what is obligatory are known, though they may be unknown to us; known in the outcome. Likewise, the corruptions in what Allah forbade may not be known to us in the present, but they are known in the outcome.
This matter is extremely dangerous, because some people rush to takfir while its conditions are absent, and great evil results from that: rebellion against rulers, misleading the common people, chaos in society, blood shed without right. Ask those who came before you of the Ummah what happened from the Khawarij, who declared Mu'awiyah a disbeliever, then declared 'Ali disbeliever, may Allah be pleased with both of them, while they stood in prayer at night and recited the Qur'an. The Prophet ﷺ informed that the Companions, and they were the Companions, "one of them would consider his prayer insignificant compared to theirs, and his recitation compared to theirs,"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3610) and Muslim (1064/148) from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him, with the wording: "Leave him, for he has companions, one of you would consider his prayer insignificant compared to theirs, and his fasting compared to theirs; they recite the Qur'an but it does not pass beyond their throats."]] and yet from their evil there resulted what only Allah knows, and whoever reads about them knows it; the last of this Ummah is like its first.
Rebellion against the leaders is undoubtedly a great corruption, and the continuation of rulers under other than what Allah revealed is undoubtedly a great harm. But the obligation is that the greater of the two corruptions be repelled by what? By the lesser of them. When blood is shed, it is very difficult to stop it, but reforming rulers may happen through gentle habituation, companionship and sincere advice; it is possible. But blood is very hard to protect once it has been spilled.
Therefore I say to you: this matter is dangerous, and the obligation upon a person is to study what the people of knowledge have said on this issue, a study free of emotion. We all love for the word of Allah to be supreme, and Allah the Exalted knows that, and we all love for the Sharia to spread among the Ummah. But we know the danger of the situation if it is said: this ruler is a disbeliever, and that ruler is a disbeliever, while we have no proof from Allah regarding it.
If we find clear, manifest, open disbelief, with proof from Allah in our hands, so that we apply the proof to reality and it becomes clear that it is disbelief, would it be permissible for us to rebel against the imam? If we say it is permissible, there must be conditions, the most important of which is that we have the capability to remove him. As for rebelling against him when we have in our hands nothing but camel-sticks and kitchen knives, while he has tanks and aircraft, is this fitting? Answer, O people.
* Students: It is not fitting.
* The Shaykh: No, and it is neither wise nor part of the Sharia. Were the Muslims, while oppressed in Makkah, commanded to fight? They were not commanded to fight, because they had no power for it. So if we suppose this ruler is a disbeliever, clear disbelief, with proof from Allah in our hands like the sun, and we see him prostrating to an idol, would we rebel against him? We do not rebel while we lack the capability. It is true that we have means: we seek help from the people of good to remove him. But rebellion of this kind is not permissible except under conditions, that we have the capability to remove him.
Where is the capability now among those who go out in groups upon groups, and then great evil results, as is well known? Moreover, these groups do not even prevail over the government itself; they prevail over whom? Over the poor, defenseless people who have no strength or power, so they kill women and children and destroy cities, under the pretext of what? That they want the word of Allah to be supreme. Yet by this act they have not achieved their aim, nor have they produced any fruit; there has only been great harm.
Therefore this matter is among the most dangerous in our present time. It requires verification, patience, careful consideration with wisdom. And when Allah wills a thing, it happens.

* * *

Then He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And We prescribed for them therein that the life is for the life﴾ [al-Ma'idah 45].
﴿We prescribed﴾ means We obligated. Prescription is of two kinds: legislative prescription and decreed, cosmic prescription. What relates to command and prohibition, which the responsible person performs, is legislative prescription; what relates to creation and bringing into existence is decreed prescription. From the first is this verse: ﴿We prescribed for them therein that the life is for the life﴾, and from the second is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We decreed to the Children of Israel in the Book﴾ to the end [al-Isra' 4].
He also said regarding prescription: ﴿Allah has decreed: "I and My messengers will surely prevail"; indeed Allah is Strong and Mighty﴾ [al-Mujadila 21]; this is decreed prescription. ﴿Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy﴾ [al-An'am 54]. The examples are many.
﴿Therein upon them﴾ means in the Torah. Mention of the Torah includes a rebuke of these Jews who claim they act by the Torah but do not apply it: ﴿like the example of a donkey carrying books﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 5].
﴿That the life is for the life﴾ means that whoever kills a soul is killed for it. The word "soul" (nafs) is general in both places: the killer and the killed. Let us look: is our law on this, or does it differ? The principle is that it is on this, and the proof for this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The blood of a Muslim man is not lawful except by one of three: the married adulterer, and a life for a life,"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6878) and Muslim (1676/25) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud.]] "a life for a life." This is the wording of the hadith, and this is the wording of the verse that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, related from the Torah: ﴿that the life is for the life﴾.
So the principle is that whoever kills a soul is killed for it. Let us consider: if a young Muslim man kills a Muslim child, is he killed for it or not?
* Talib: Yes.
* The Shaykh: He is killed for it: life for life. If a man kills a woman, is he killed?
* Talib: (...).
* The Shaykh: He is killed for her. If a sane person kills an insane person, is he killed for him? He is killed for him. If a disbeliever kills a Muslim, is he killed for him?
* Talib: He is not killed for him.
* The Shaykh: He is killed for him.
* The student: He is not killed for him.
* The Shaykh: La ilaha illa Allah. The verse before us requires that he be killed for him: a disbeliever who kills a Muslim is killed for him. If a Muslim kills a disbeliever?
* Students: He is not killed for him.
* Other students: He is killed for him.
* The Shaykh: He is killed for him, brothers. Let us know the full evidences. Now before us is that ﴿the life is for the life﴾, and the hadith "a life for a life." Is he killed for him?
* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: A father who killed his child: is he killed for him? A child who killed his father: is he killed for him? A free man who killed a slave: is he killed for him? A master who killed his slave: is he killed for him? Everything in principle is that a life is killed for a life; this is the principle.
What remains is to consider whether this generality has been specified. We say: yes, it has been specified. If the specification is not established in a matter, the principle is generality.
Let us consider: a disbeliever is killed for a Muslim. A disbeliever who kills a Muslim is killed for him, without doubt. A Muslim who kills a disbeliever is not killed for him. What removed him from the generality? What removed him from the generality is what was established from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "A Muslim is not killed for a disbeliever,"[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (111) from the hadith of Ali ibn Abi Talib.]] and the reason is that the Muslim is pure, a true servant of Allah, while the disbeliever is impure, rebellious and arrogant; the Muslim is among the friends of Allah, and the disbeliever is among the enemies of Allah. Is it clear? How could this be an equal to that or a substitute for it? So we have both transmitted and rational evidence that a Muslim is not killed for a disbeliever. This is one point.
Is a man killed for a woman?
* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Yes, he is killed. The verse is general: a man who kills a woman is killed. If someone says: a man is superior to a woman, and by him jihad is performed, enjoining good and forbidding evil, governance and judgments; they are the judges, they are the rulers, "A people will never prosper who entrust their affairs to a woman,"[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (4425) from the hadith of Abu Bakrah.]] so how can a woman be a equal to a man, so that he is killed for her?
We say: there is a general text, and there is also a specific evidence, that "a slave girl of the Ansar had ornaments of gold or silver upon her; a Jew killed her, crushing her head between two stones. She was found still alive, and she was asked: who did this to you? So-and-so? So-and-so? So-and-so? Until they mentioned the Jew, and she gestured yes," meaning he was the one who killed her, "so they seized the Jew and he confessed, and the Prophet ﷺ ordered that his head be crushed between two stones, justly, and his head was crushed between two stones,"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2413) and Muslim (1672/15) from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik.]] retaliation. Here a man was killed for what?
* Students: For a woman.
* The Shaykh: For a woman; a man was killed for a woman.
If someone says: the man is deficient compared to this woman in religion, so does his deficiency make him equal to her? We say: this has no effect, because if the killer is the lower in religion, it has no effect at all; for when a Muslim is killed by a disbeliever, the disbeliever is killed. Now, if a sane person kills an insane person, is he killed for him?
* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: If a sane person kills an insane person, he has relieved people of him and his evil; is he killed? Yes, he is killed, by the generality. If a father killed his child, is he killed? He is killed, unless evidence is found. We sought evidence and did not find a sound one. The hadith "A father is not killed for his child" has no sound chain.
The reasoning that a father is not killed for a child, because the father was the cause of the child's existence, so the child should not be the cause of his execution, is a defective reasoning, indeed a dead reasoning with no movement in it; for who was the cause of the killing? The father; it is he who killed.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 5, verse 45 (part 2 of 4):

So if it were said that killing a father in retaliation for his child is more fitting than killing a stranger for a stranger, because a father killing his child is committing something specifically forbidden in the Qur'an: ﴿And do not kill your children﴾ [al-An'am 151]. Secondly, a father killing his child is one of the greatest severances of kinship (qat' al-rahim), and this is a crime. How then would this father commit this crime, and yet we say: there is no qisas? Thus, when it is clear that the specifying evidence is not valid by transmission, nor valid by reason, the ruling must be, what? General, even in the case of a father killed for his child.

Alright, what about a child who kills his father?
* Students: He is killed.
* The Shaykh: He is killed?
* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: He is killed, without any problem? Yes, he is killed, without any problem, because killing his father is among the greatest disobedience (uquq), so it should not be overlooked and he should be killed.
Alright, a slave who killed his master?
* Students: He is killed for him.
* The Shaykh: He is killed for him?
* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: A slave who killed his master, is he killed for him?
* Students: He is killed.
* The Shaykh: Are you sure?
* Students: Yes.
* A student: That is the basic principle.
* The Shaykh: Alright, a master who killed his slave?
* Students: He is killed, that is the basic principle.
* The Shaykh: He is killed for him?
* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Yes, he is killed for him. This is the principle and its branch: he is killed for him, because of the generality of "a life for a life", and because there came in a hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever kills his slave, we shall kill him" [narrated by Abu Dawud (4515), al-Tirmidhi (1414), al-Nasa'i in al-Mujtaba (4737), and Ibn Majah (2663), from the hadith of Samurah ibn Jundub].
And if a free man kills the slave of another? He is killed for him, because if he is killed for his own slave, whom he owns, then killing him for the slave of another is all the more so. So, now, what is left to specify this verse, except...? 
* A student: One.
* The Shaykh: What is it?
* A student: A Muslim is not killed for a disbeliever.
* The Shaykh: That a Muslim is not killed for a disbeliever, and the rest remains on its generality. Whoever claims that something is excluded from this generality, we say: welcome, bring the evidence that convinces, and then we say: we believe in Allah, and the Shari'ah completes one another, so whatever is generalized in one place and specified in another, we adopt it.
Small and big: is the small one killed for the big one, and the big one for the small?
* Students: Yes.
* Other students: No.
* The Shaykh: Pay attention, the child is not killed. That is, if a child who has not reached puberty kills an adult, he is not killed, because the pen is lifted from him, and because he has no valid intent. Likewise it is said of the insane person who kills a sane person: he is not killed.
He says: ﴿the life for the life, and the eye for the eye﴾. ﴿The eye for the eye﴾ means that whoever gouges out a person's eye, we gouge out his eye, eye for eye. Is it clear?
A man gouged out the eye of a person with weak sight, while the one who gouged it has strong sight. Is his eye gouged out?
* Students: His eye is gouged out.
* The Shaykh: Subhan Allah! Yes, his eye is gouged out, just as if a healthy person kills a sick person, he is killed for him.
A man with a sound eye gouged out the eye of a person who is one-eyed (al-'awra'), the blind one?
* Students: It is not gouged out.
* The Shaykh: Why?
* Students: It is not an eye.
* The Shaykh: Because it does not see; it has lost its benefit, it is dead.
A man who is one-eyed, having only a right eye, gouged out the right eye of a sound man?
* Students: It is not gouged out.
* The Shaykh: O people, "the eye for the eye": this one-eyed man gouged out the right eye of a sound man, and he (the one-eyed) has a right eye?
* A student: It is gouged out.
* The Shaykh: It is gouged out?
* Students: It is not gouged out.
* The Shaykh: Let us see. The scholars differ on this. Some said: the eye of the one-eyed man is gouged out, and they took the generality: the eye for the eye. This one-eyed man, who has only a right eye, deliberately gouged out the right eye of a man who has two sound eyes, so it is gouged out.
If someone says: if you gouge out his remaining eye, he becomes blind? We say: who made him transgress against this man and gouge out his eye? He is the one who committed the crime against himself; we did not commit it against him.
And some scholars said: it is not gouged out, its eye is not gouged out, because that leads to the loss of a benefit for which there is no equivalent in the body, which is sight.
But some of them said: he gives the full diya (blood money). Do you understand? Now, when the one-eyed man gouged out the right eye of the sound man, while he himself has a right eye, we say: the eye of the one-eyed man is not gouged out, but he is obligated to pay the full diya for the eye of whom? The one with two healthy eyes, the full diya. Although the eye is half the diya, here he is obligated to pay the full diya, because leaving his eye is a substitute for complete sight in relation to whom?
* A student: For the one-eyed man.
* The Shaykh: For the one-eyed man, and complete sight carries the full diya. Some say: no, there is only half the diya in any case. What appears to be correct is one of two things: either his eye is gouged out, and it is said: you are the one who committed the crime against yourself; or it is not gouged out, but he is obligated to pay the other the full diya, and the penalty is doubled against him. Do you understand?
"The nose for the nose": you know that the nose has a bony bridge, and a soft cartilaginous tip. Is what is meant the soft cartilage, or the whole nose?
Some scholars say: the whole nose. If the nose is cut from the root at the forehead, we cut his nose from the forehead. Others say: no, a nose can only be matched with a nose if the cut is from the soft side of the nose, because that is what can be exacted, since it has a clear dividing boundary, and this is called the marin (the soft cartilage) of the nose, which is what is soft of it.
But the preferred opinion is the first: that retaliation is taken on the nose from the point where the offender's was, especially in our present time, as medicine is now advanced, and there can be no injustice. Those who said the nose is not subject to retaliation said: it is feared there may be injustice, the bone remains broken, and the retaliation is not complete. We say: now, praise be to Allah, in our present time medicine is advanced, and retaliation can be done to the hair's breadth. Is that not so?
* Students: Indeed.
* The Shaykh: If we say this, is the consideration the area or the proportion?
* Students: The proportion.
* The Shaykh: Do you understand the matter?
* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: The proportion or the area?
* Students: The proportion.
* A student: Shaykh, one may devise a trick against this.
* The Shaykh: If we say: the area, and the victim's nose is large while the offender's nose is small, and we say by area, and he cuts half of the large nose, half of it corresponds to the entire nose of the second, and perhaps even more, so is the consideration the area or the proportion?
* Students: The proportion.
* The Shaykh: Yes, so the consideration is the proportion. Is it clear? We have finished with the nose.
We find that some people have a sense of smell, smelling pleasant and foul odours, and another does not. If a man who can smell cuts the nose of one who cannot smell, do we cut his nose or not?
* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: How do we cut? This one does not smell; even if you placed the finest or the foulest odours with him, he would not perceive it, he would not know. Is it cut?
* Students: It is cut.
* The Shaykh: It is cut, fine, because the verse is general: ﴿the nose for the nose﴾, and because smell is not in this cartilage itself, it is in what?
* A student: I do not know.
* The Shaykh: You do not know? No, we all know. Where is smell? In the brain, not here. Do you understand? That is why there are people whose noses were cut off by war or affliction or otherwise, and they still smell, and others whose noses are sound, yet they do not smell. So the nose that smells and the one that does not are equal.
﴿And the ear for the ear﴾: the ear is also cut for the ear, whether it is deaf or not deaf, because hearing is not in this cartilage itself, but from inside. So if a person cuts another's ear, he is cut for it.
If the ear of the victim does not move, while the ear of the offender moves, is it cut?
* Students: The ear cannot move.
* The Shaykh: No, it does not move; the ear of the offender moves, and the ear of the victim does not move. Is the ear of the offender that moves cut?
* Students: Yes.
* A student: The ear does not move.
* The Shaykh: I recall that al-Hajjaj's ear moved, is that not so? In any case it is cut. They have mentioned to us people who move their ears a great deal, not slightly, but most people cannot, is that not so? Because this movement is not intended and its benefit is small. Otherwise we would say: this is like the paralysed and the sound. Moreover, the jurists, may Allah have mercy on them, said: paralysis in the ear and nose does not affect it, because the form of the ear and nose remains even if there is paralysis.
We forgot to say: "the eye for the eye": it is necessary that they match, the right with the right, and the left with the left, and likewise for the ear: right for right, left for left.
﴿The tooth for the tooth﴾: the "ba" here is undoubtedly for exchange or substitution, so the extracted tooth must be equivalent to the tooth of the offender. For example, is an incisor extracted for a molar?
* Students: No.
* The Shaykh: Is this incisor extracted for a molar?
* Students: No.
* The Shaykh: Why? Because of the lack of matching, and the "ba", as I told you now, is for compensation or substitution; a molar cannot be a substitute for an incisor, or the reverse.
If part of a tooth is broken off, that is, part of the tooth is broken, is retaliation taken?
* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Yes, retaliation is taken, and it is assessed by what?
* Students: By proportion.
* The Shaykh: By proportion. If the offender filed down the victim's tooth until half of it was gone, we file down the offender's tooth until half of it is gone. If the offender says: O people, have mercy on me, cut the tooth instead of filing, do you know filing and cutting?
* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Should we obey him?
* Students: No.
* The Shaykh: We do not obey him, because just as he caused pain to the victim, we cause pain to him. That is why if he said to us, in the matter of the eye or the ear: anesthetize me, we say: we will not anesthetize you; just as you did to the victim, we do to you.
As for the ear, if part of the ear is taken? As long as retaliation is possible, my brothers, retaliation is obligatory; it is justice.
He says: ﴿and wounds, retaliation﴾. When Allah the Exalted mentioned the organs, He mentioned wounds. But some organs were not mentioned, such as the two hands, the two feet, and the fingers, but the ruling is established for these by what? By analogy to what was mentioned.
"﴿Wounds, retaliation﴾": the word "wounds" is general, encompassing every wound, but the word "retaliation" restricts this generality, since what is understood from it is that wounds are subject to retaliation where retaliation can be exacted. The jurists, may Allah have mercy on them, say: retaliation is not possible for a wound except a wound that reaches to a bone, and a wound that does not reach a bone cannot be retaliated.
For example, a wound to the head that reaches the skull bone: is it possible or not? It is possible. A wound to the shin that reaches the bone: possible? Possible. Likewise the thigh, the back, the ribs. But the stomach? Not possible. This is according to what was said earlier.
But in my view, at the present time it is possible, because doctors have such skill that they can measure a wound with complete precision. And since Allah the Mighty and Majestic did not specify the locations of wounds, but said: ﴿wounds, retaliation﴾, we say: whenever retaliation for any wound in any location is shown to be possible, it is obligatory: ﴿wounds, retaliation﴾.
Is retaliation for wounds by area or by proportion? Pay attention, my brothers!
* Students: By proportion.
* Students: By area.
* The Shaykh: By Allah, I have a difficulty with it. For example, a man whose stomach is large and another whose stomach is small: do we consider the area or not?
* A student: The proportion.
* The Shaykh: The proportion? By Allah, it is possible; this is closer to justice. For example, someone wounds the stomach of a child: the area is how many centimetres?
* A student: Half a centimetre.
* The Shaykh: Half a centimetre, and the centimetre, I think, is the numbers on the ruler; half a centimetre or a centimetre. The centimetre of the child's large stomach, but this offender's stomach, by the grace of Allah, is like a camel's stomach. If we take area, it would have no effect at all. So the apparent view, and Allah knows best, is that wounds are by proportion.
We ask for the explanation of this verse and the difficulty: ﴿Say: bring the Torah and recite it, if you are truthful﴾ [Al 'Imran 93]. The difficulty: is the Torah not abrogated after the revelation of the Qur'an?
Indeed it is abrogated, but it is so that it may be turned back against them from their own book, because they do not believe in the Qur'an; they believe in the Torah.
* A student: The people of the Torah did not believe in the Torah nor in the Qur'an, and what is the benefit...?
* The Shaykh: They claim that this is the ruling of the Torah.
* * *
(...) * A student: ﴿by what Allah has revealed, those are the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Ma'idah 45].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Shaytan. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿And We prescribed for them therein that the life [is for] the life﴾. What is the meaning of ﴿We prescribed (katabna)﴾?
* A student: We made obligatory.
* The Shaykh: We made obligatory. Can you bring evidence that writing (al-katb) means obligation?
* The student: In His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you﴾ [al-Baqarah 183].
* The Shaykh: Yes, the evidence is in His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you﴾.
His saying: ﴿the life for the life﴾: has our law come in agreement with this or not?
* A student: It has.
* The Shaykh: Our law has come in agreement with it in which evidence?
* The student: This evidence is the act of the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning the Jew who crushed the head of the slave girl.
* The Shaykh: No.
* A student: It has come only with the exception: a Muslim is not killed for a disbeliever. In the Torah, a Muslim is killed for a disbeliever.
* The Shaykh: No, it is a hadith that matches the verse exactly.
* A student: The saying of the Messenger (ﷺ): "The blood of a Muslim man is not lawful except by one of three," and he mentioned from them: (...) [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6878) and Muslim (1676/25), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud].
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed, have you forgotten this?
His saying: ﴿the life for the life﴾: is it on its generality?
* A student: No, something has come that specifies it.
* The Shaykh: Yes, so it is not on its generality? What is excepted from it?
* The student: We said: nothing is excepted from it except that a Muslim who kills a disbeliever is not subject to retaliation.
* The Shaykh: That is, the only exception is a Muslim killing a disbeliever, for which he is not subject to retaliation. Do you have evidence?
* A student: Yes, what is established in the two Sahihs from His saying (ﷺ): "A Muslim is not killed for a disbeliever" [al-Bukhari (111), from the hadith of Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him].
* The Shaykh: "A Muslim is not killed for a disbeliever," good, and the reason is clear.
* The student: That the Muslim is higher in rank.
* The Shaykh: Higher in standing with Allah than the disbeliever, and Islam is exalted and is not surpassed.
His saying: ﴿the eye for the eye﴾: is equivalence required or not?
* A student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: That is, the right eye is not gouged out with the left? Answer.
* A student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: The right eye is not gouged out with the left, and the left is gouged out with the right?
* A student: The left for the left, and the right for the right.
* The Shaykh: Can we take this from the verse?
* A student: ﴿the eye for the eye﴾.
* The Shaykh: How do we take it?
* The student: Its definiteness (...).
* The Shaykh: ﴿the eye for the eye﴾: the definiteness indicates that the second is the first, and this requires equivalence, and because it came with the "ba" that indicates substitution, and substitution must be equal to what is substituted.
Is the eye of a one-eyed man taken for the eye of a sound man? That is, if a one-eyed man gouged out the eye of a sound man, which is equivalent to the sound man's eye, the question: is it taken or not?
* A student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: It is taken. Is there retaliation in this?
* The student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Because if you take the one-eyed man's eye, he remains blind, while that one-eyed man gouged out his eye and he remained sighted.
* The student: But the one-eyed man is the one who committed the crime against himself by gouging out his companion's eye.
* The Shaykh: So we say: the one-eyed man's eye is taken for the sound man's eye, by the generality of ﴿the eye for the eye﴾; and if it is said that this leads to his becoming blind after having been sighted, we say: he is the one who committed the crime against himself. This is one of the opinions on the matter. The second opinion, which is the position of the Hanbalis...
* A student: That he pays the full diya.
* The Shaykh: That his eye is not taken, but he pays the full diya.
﴿The nose for the nose﴾: is the nose taken for the nose even if it is above the soft part (al-marin)?
* A student: According to the school, no.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿUthaymin (Tafsīr al-Qurʾān al-Karīm) on Sūrat al-Māʾidah, verse 45 (part 3 of 4)**

**Shaykh:** We have before us the position of all the Muslims.

**Student:** The apparent meaning of the verse, yes.

**Shaykh:** The apparent meaning of the verse, yes. Is that so? That the nose is taken for the nose, even if the cut is from above the *marin* (the soft, fleshy part of the nose). The *marin* is the soft part of the nose.

But if someone said: this cannot be carried out as *qiṣāṣ* (retaliation in kind)?

**Student:** That was the case before, but now it is possible.

**Shaykh:** So we say: if retaliation is possible, the apparent meaning of the verse is that it is carried out even from above the *marin*, and this is the correct view. Now, the position of the school. Bring the position of the school.

**Student:** The position of the school is that retaliation is carried out from the *marin*, because it has a limit at which it ends.
