**Shaykh:** That retaliation is not carried out except when the cut is from the *marin*, because it has a limit at which it ends, and retaliation is possible in it.

Can the *thaniyah* (incisor) be taken for the *rubāʿiyah* (the tooth beside the incisors)?

**Student:** No, it is not valid.

**Shaykh:** How?

**Student:** Because the verse says "the tooth for the tooth."

**Shaykh:** This is tooth for tooth?

**Student:** The same tooth, because the *bāʾ* (in *bi-*, "for") does not indicate exchange.

**Shaykh:** The *bāʾ* indicates substitution (*badaliyyah*). Also, the second tooth is the first tooth, because it came with the definite article.

Do you know the *thaniyah* from the *rubāʿiyah*? What is the *thaniyah*?

**Student:** It is at the front.

**Shaykh:** All of them are at the front, up to the *rubāʿiyah*.

**Student:** In the middle.

**Shaykh:** In the middle? No, the *thaniyah* is not in the middle. They are two incisors, each one on a side. Good. They are the two adjacent teeth, and these are the *thanāyā* (incisors). The two adjacent teeth are the *thanāyā*, and behind them is the *rubāʿiyah*. So an incisor is not taken for a *rubāʿiyah*, nor the reverse, due to the lack of equivalence.

*"And for wounds, retaliation"* (﴿الْجُرُوحَ قِصَاصٌ﴾). Did we take it or not? Did we not take the tooth? We did take it. In any case, the matter of the tooth is clear, and we explained how a tooth can be taken for a tooth when it is a part of a tooth. We said you can do it with a file, the *mibrad* (file).

*"And for wounds, retaliation."* We told you that there is no wound in which retaliation is possible except a wound that reaches a bone. Otherwise it is not possible. A wound in the abdomen is not possible. A wound on the head before reaching the bone is not possible. Retaliation for wounds is not possible unless the wound reaches a bone.

Remaining for us is amputation: amputation of the hand and amputation of the foot. Perhaps, God willing, we will take them up in the benefits (*fawāʾid*), because the verse contains many benefits.

* * *

Then he said: *"And for wounds, retaliation"* (﴿الْجُرُوحَ قِصَاصٌ﴾). That is, the offender is retaliated against with the same as what he inflicted on the victim. If he wounded him on the right side of the head, retaliation is taken on the right side of his head. If on the left side, retaliation is taken on the left side, and so on.

He said: *"Whoever forgoes it as an act of charity, it is an expiation for him"* (﴿فَمَنْ تَصَدَّقَ بِهِ فَهُوَ كَفَّارَةٌ لَهُ﴾). *"Whoever forgoes it"* means: forgoes the retaliation. This has two meanings. The first meaning: the victim gives up the retaliation as charity, so retaliation is not carried out against the offender, and this is an expiation for him, because charity is an expiation. The second meaning: *"forgoes it"* means: gives up the retaliation, i.e., offers himself up to be retaliated against, so that this is an expiation for him, because if retaliation is carried out against him in this world, the offender will not be held to account for it in the Hereafter. Have you understood now?

So *"whoever forgoes it"* has two meanings. The first meaning is: he forgoes the retaliation, i.e., he pardons it. The second: he offers himself up to be retaliated against.

*"It is an expiation for him."* As for it being an expiation for the one who gives charity, the victim, that is clear, because he has done good to his brother and given charity to him with the dearest thing he has, which is himself, if the retaliation concerns a life. As for it being an expiation for the offender, it is because he surrendered himself easily, so his surrender of himself to be retaliated against is an expiation for his crime and his offence, and he is not punished for it, since God does not combine two punishments for a person: the punishment of this world and the punishment of the Hereafter.

*"It is an expiation for him"*: for whom? For the one who gives charity, whether this or that.

And *kaffārah* (expiation) is derived from *kafr*, which means covering. When a thing covers the traces of another thing, it becomes like a cover for it. For this reason there is an expiation for oaths, an expiation for *ẓihār* (the pre-Islamic divorce formula), and an expiation for killing, because these cover what results from the sins and wipe them out.

*"Whoever does not judge by what God has revealed, those are the wrongdoers"* (﴿وَمَنْ لَمْ يَحْكُمْ بِمَا أَنْزَلَ اللَّهُ فَأُولَئِكَ هُمُ الظَّالِمُونَ﴾). We say about this sentence what we said about the first sentence: is the intended meaning those among the Jews who do not judge by what God has revealed, or is it general?

Among the exegetes there are two views on this. Some of them said: it refers to the Jews, because the context of the verses concerns them. According to this view, we can say that Muslims who do this are included by way of what? By way of analogy (*qiyās*).

The second view on the matter: the verse is general to everyone who does not judge by what God has revealed, so he is a wrongdoer, whether he is a Muslim, a Jew, or other than these. This is supported by the wording, while the first is supported by what? By the context, because God said: *"We prescribed for them therein"* (﴿كَتَبْنَا عَلَيْهِمْ فِيهَا﴾), so the discussion is about the Jews. But the ruling, in reality, does not differ for a Muslim who does not judge by what God has revealed, because we say: if the wording includes him, then the ruling includes him by the verbal evidence; and if it does not include him, then the ruling includes him by the evidence of meaning, which is analogy.

And His saying *"those are the wrongdoers"* (﴿فَأُولَئِكَ هُمُ الظَّالِمُونَ﴾): *"hum"* (هم) is a *ḍamīr al-faṣl* (separating pronoun). The separating pronoun is a particle that has no place in the grammatical structure (*lā maḥall lahu min al-iʿrāb*), but it is brought in to separate the attribute from the predicate, i.e., between the description (*naʿt*) and the predicate (*khabar*). If you say: *Zayd al-fāḍil* (Zayd the virtuous), intending to inform about him that he is virtuous, it is possible that *al-fāḍil* is a description of Zayd, and the predicate has not yet come. But if you say: *Zayd huwa al-fāḍil* (Zayd is the virtuous one), it becomes certain that it is the predicate. For this reason it is called a separating pronoun. Its function is what we have mentioned. Another function is emphasis, and a third is restriction (*ḥaṣr*).

Should we say: *"those are the wrongdoers"* means that no one is a wrongdoer except these, based on the premise that the separating pronoun indicates restriction?

The answer: No. This is a relative restriction. That is: those are the wrongdoers in failing to apply what was mentioned in the verse. Otherwise, the disbelievers are wrongdoers, and the one who fabricates lies against God is a wrongdoer, and he is the greatest of the wrongdoers: *"And who is more wrongful than one who fabricates a lie against God?"* (﴿وَمَنْ أَظْلَمُ مِمَّنِ افْتَرَى عَلَى اللَّهِ الْكَذِبَ﴾) [al-Ṣaff 7].

* In this noble verse there are benefits. Among them: God obligated retaliation upon the Jews, by His saying: *"And We prescribed for them therein that the life is for the life"* (﴿وَكَتَبْنَا عَلَيْهِمْ فِيهَا أَنَّ النَّفْسَ بِالنَّفْسِ﴾).

But if someone says: how can we say that, when we have explained His saying *"whoever forgoes it as an act of charity, it is an expiation for him"* as meaning that the victim pardons the offender?

We say: yes. God obligated on them retaliation or pardon free of charge. This Ummah (community), God has granted it permission to choose retaliation or pardon free of charge, or to accept blood money (*diyah*) and reconciliation. All of this, praise be to God, is from the breadth of the law of this Ummah.

Some scholars have mentioned that the Jews are obligated to retaliation, retaliation being obligatory for them, while the Christians are the opposite: pardon is obligatory for them. To the point that it has been said that among the foundations of their law is that whoever strikes you on your right cheek, turn to him your left cheek. There is no doubt that this contains a kind of humiliation. However, in any case, we do not know the soundness of this statement, and God knows best. But it is said that the Jews are obligated to retaliation, unlike the Christians. The reason is clear: the Jews are stubborn, tyrannical, and rebellious, and it is only fitting for them that the killer be killed, so that it may be a deterrent.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the ugliness of what the Banū al-Naḍīr did to the Banū Qurayẓah. The Banū al-Naḍīr consider themselves the nobles of the Jews. For this reason, if a Naḍīrī kills a Qurayẓī, he is not killed for him. But if a Qurayẓī kills a Naḍīrī, he is killed for him. Glory be to God! They are all Jews, but he says: these are more noble and superior. And if a Naḍīrī kills a Qurayẓī, the heirs have half the blood money if they do not seek retaliation, and if it is the reverse, they have the full blood money. This is what the exegetes mentioned in this place.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: retaliation applies to souls, even if people differ in age, height or shortness, knowledge, intellect, intelligence, and other things. From where is this derived?

**Students:** From the generality.

**Shaykh:** From the generality. For this reason, if a young man, a knowledgeable, noble, and well-born man, killed an infant in the cradle, he is killed for him, because there is no consideration for differences in these things, and this is due to the generality.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: retaliation applies to the eyes, by His saying *"the eye for the eye"* (﴿الْعَيْنَ بِالْعَيْنِ﴾).

* Among its benefits: retaliation applies between noses, by His saying *"the nose for the nose"* (﴿الْأَنْفَ بِالْأَنْفِ﴾).

* Among its benefits also: retaliation applies to ears, by His saying *"the ear for the ear"* (﴿الْأُذُنَ بِالْأُذُنِ﴾).

* Among its benefits: retaliation applies to teeth, between teeth. How many organs are these?

**Students:** Four.

**Shaykh:** Four. There remain organs: the two hands, the two feet, the tongue, and other organs. Is the ruling for them like the ruling for these?

The answer: Yes. The ruling for them is like the ruling for these, by a clear and evident analogy (*qiyās jalī wāḍiḥ*). God, Mighty and Majestic, mentioned these organs (the eye, the nose, the ear, and the tooth) perhaps because the Jews would differ regarding retaliation for these things, so He stated them explicitly because of the disagreement concerning them. I say "perhaps," and I do not affirm this, because God knows best what He intended in His Book. But we know that the other organs are similar to them. For example, a finger for a finger: the little finger is taken for the little finger, and the thumb for the thumb, and what lies between them likewise. The foot for the foot, the palm for the palm, the forearm for the forearm, and so on.

But is it a condition that the amputation be from a joint, or is it not a condition?

On this there is disagreement among the scholars. Some said: the amputation must be from a joint. If it is not from a joint, there is no retaliation at all. Pay attention. For example, the forearm: its joint is what?

* **Student:** The elbow.

**Shaykh:** The elbow, on the side of the upper arm, and the palm on the side of the hand. If the offender cut off the forearm at the middle, then the amputation is not from a joint. According to the view of those who stipulate that the amputation must be from a joint, he is not amputated. Even if the victim said: cut this man from the palm, and I will forgo the excess, he is not amputated, because the condition is not met. Even if he said, for example: cut from the palm and give me the compensation for the excess, I am content with this, they say: he is not amputated.

But the correct view is to say: rather, he is amputated, because retaliation is obligatory. But on the condition that retaliation is possible.

Is retaliation according to proportion or according to measurement? It is according to proportion. The victim may have a long forearm. If we took it by measurement, we would have to take the offender's entire forearm. But if the amputation is at the middle, we say: take the middle. If it is at a third, we say: take a third. This is the preponderant view.

If it is not possible, then the correct view is that the victim may demand retaliation from the part below the joint, and he may also demand the compensation for the excess. This is the preponderant view, because God, Exalted, commanded justice, and this is justice. If the victim said: cut from the palm, and give me the compensation for the excess, we say: he has the right to that. And all the more so if he said: cut him from the joint, and I give up the excess, it is all the more so.

Our evidence for what we have preferred is the saying of God, Exalted: *"Indeed, God commands justice and good conduct"* (﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ يَأْمُرُ بِالْعَدْلِ وَالْإِحْسَانِ﴾) [al-Naḥl 90]. Whenever justice is possible, it must be upheld.

Now, if someone cut off a person's *dhakar* (male organ), is his *dhakar* cut off or not? His *dhakar* is cut off.

If it is assumed that the one whose *dhakar* was cut off was sterile, and the one who cut it off was fertile, is it cut off or not?

**Students:** It is cut off.

**Shaykh:** The one cut off is sterile, and the one who cut it off is fertile. Is it cut off or not?

**Students:** It is cut off.

**Shaykh:** It is cut off. Its parallel is the ear of a deaf man. If a person cut off the ear of a deaf man, while he (the one who cut it) can hear, his ear is cut off, because the organ itself is the organ, and sterility is an additional thing. This differs from the paralysed and the healthy. The paralysed and the healthy: for example, if he cut off a paralysed hand while he has a healthy hand, it is not cut off, because the benefit is lost in the first case, and this is an important matter.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: if retaliation is possible for all wounds, then the ruling applies, which is retaliation, by the generality of His saying: what? *"And for wounds, retaliation"* (﴿الْجُرُوحَ قِصَاصٌ﴾). The earlier scholars used to say that retaliation for wounds is not possible unless the wound reaches a bone, and this was the extent of knowledge at that time. But in our present time, retaliation can be carried out for a wound smaller than a hair in any location. So if retaliation is possible, retaliation is obligatory. This is justice, and our evidence is this great verse: *"Indeed, God commands justice and good conduct."*

Now, apart from wounds, is retaliation carried out for them, such as a slap or a blow with a stick, and the like? The scholars differ on this. Some said: the one who slaps is not slapped, but the public right is taken from him, and his matter is referred to whom? To the ruler, who determines what he sees as a deterrent against transgression. They justified this by saying that retaliation for slapping is not possible. What do you say?

**Student:** (...)

**Shaykh:** Not possible? Why?

**Student:** (...)

**Shaykh:** Yes, indeed. Because relating it to strength and force, or the reverse, is very difficult. Also, perhaps the victim's hand is large and the other's hand is small. When the victim was struck, the blow hit half his cheek, while the second person's hand is large, so if he strikes, it covers the whole cheek, and the ruling differs. So it means that retaliation is not possible.

But some scholars say that retaliation is possible, because the matter of a blow, a slap, and the like is not that a person wants to be satisfied by the pain he suffers, but that he wants to be satisfied by what? By the humiliation and degradation. For this reason, if the matter was one of joking, and he struck him on his face with force, would he say: come on, retaliation? Answer me.

**Students:** No.

**Shaykh:** No. But if the matter is one of contest, then there is no doubt that a slap involves humiliation, so he says: I do not care, the slap did not affect him. At most, the blood dispersed and then returned. The blood disperses because of the force of the blow. The place of the blow may become white sometimes, and then it returns. But what concerns me is that he humiliated me, so I want to humiliate him.

In any case, in this situation it should be said: the matter is to be referred to the opinion of the judge. If the judge sees that humiliating the transgressor, even with a light blow, involves a kind of satisfaction, then let him do it.

Likewise with the stick: is retaliation taken for a blow with a stick? We say: as for the stick with which he struck him, this is possible. But the question remains regarding the severity of the blow. As for striking him with a thin whip and then bringing a piece of wood and wanting to retaliate with it, this is not possible.

The question remains regarding whether, if he strikes him with the same thing he struck him with, retaliation is possible or not. This depends on what? On what preceded: it is not important that he strikes him with something that hurts him, or the like. What is important is that he humiliates him.

We may also address the matter of clothing: if someone tears a person's garment, is retaliation taken by tearing his garment? This is also a matter of disagreement. Some scholars say: no. If he tears his garment, he must compensate for it, either by an equivalent or by its value. If he destroys it so that it cannot be benefited from, then by an equivalent, except according to the school, as you know. If he tears it in a way that it can still be benefited from while it exists, then it is valued.

Those who said retaliation applies to a blow, a slap, and tearing a garment argued from generality, the generality of the verses: *"So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner as he transgressed against you"* (﴿فَمَنِ اعْتَدَى عَلَيْكُمْ فَاعْتَدُوا عَلَيْهِ بِمِثْلِ مَا اعْتَدَى عَلَيْكُمْ﴾) [al-Baqarah 194], and *"And if you punish, then punish with the like of that with which you were punished"* (﴿وَإِنْ عَاقَبْتُمْ فَعَاقِبُوا بِمِثْلِ مَا عُوقِبْتُمْ بِهِ﴾) [al-Naḥl 126]. Those who prohibited it said: retaliation is not possible in this, because it is difficult to measure.

If we take the preponderant view, that it is permissible to tear his garment in the same way he tore the victim's garment, then here there are two questions.

The first question: if the two garments differ, one being new and the other old, or both being new but one of good quality and the other of poor quality, is it done? You refer back to what we mentioned, which is: did the one who demanded retaliation intend exchange and equivalence, or did he intend to humiliate the one who tore his garment? Usually it is the second. On this basis, we say: he has the right to tear his garment, even if the garment of the offender is superior to the victim's in value and quality.

If we say so, the second question: is it measured by the area, or by proportion?

**Students:** By proportion.

**Shaykh:** By proportion? What is the difference between proportion and area?

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 5, verse 45 (part 4 of 4):**

* Student: If we measure it by area, the wound of the one who inflicted the injury would be small, while the wound inflicted on the other would be large, so it would follow that the garment of the other is entirely cut.
* Shaykh: You mean if the one who inflicted the injury has a long garment?
* Student: If the one who inflicted the injury has a long garment and we measure by area, it would follow that the garment of the second is entirely cut.
* Shaykh: No, on the contrary.
* Student: This is relative.
* Shaykh: The one who inflicted the injury has a long garment, and the one injured has a short garment. He cuts from it the amount of one finger...
* Student: It would follow if we said: the...
* Shaykh: The one whose garment is the size of a finger takes from it an area, and that one (the other) will be small.
So we say: it must be by what? By relativity (*bi-al-nisbah*). For if we said: by area, we would not be able to achieve what? Equivalence (*al-mumathalah*).
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: encouragement for the offender to surrender himself to the injured party or his guardians, if the offence was killing, by His saying: ﴿Whoever forgoes it as charity, it is an expiation for him﴾.
* * *
* Student: ﴿That the life is for the life, and the eye for the eye, and the nose for the nose, and the ear for the ear, and the tooth for the tooth, and wounds are subject to retaliation (*qisas*). But whoever forgoes it as charity, it is an expiation for him. And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, then it is those who are the wrongdoers.﴾ [al-Ma'idah 45].
* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: encouragement to pardon the offender, by His saying: ﴿Whoever forgoes it as charity, it is an expiation for him﴾.
* Among its benefits: encouraging the offender to surrender himself, and that this is an expiation (*kaffarah*) for him.
If someone says: it becomes an expiation for him with respect to the right of the heirs of the slain. So what is the ruling regarding the right of the slain person, whose life the killer has taken?
The answer: If Allah knows that the killer's repentance is sincere, then Allah, glorified and exalted, bears on his behalf the right of the slain person and pleases him.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed is a wrongdoer (*zalim*), by His saying: ﴿then it is those who are the wrongdoers﴾.
* Among its benefits: that whoever does not know the ruling of Allah and judges in ignorance is not a wrongdoer, but it is said: it is obligatory upon him, once he knows, to return to the truth and judge by what Allah has revealed.
If someone says: is there a contradiction between this description, ﴿then it is those who are the wrongdoers﴾, and His saying in the previous verse: ﴿then it is those who are the disbelievers﴾? That is, are they two distinct descriptions, or do they have one meaning?
The answer: Some scholars said they are distinct, and others said their meaning is one. As for the one who said they are distinct, he said regarding the first: if what drives the judge to rule other than what Allah revealed is a deviation from what Allah revealed, and his belief that something other than it is better for mankind, then this is what? Disbelief (*kufr*), whether he rules or does not rule, but his not ruling is evidence of what is in his heart.
As for one who rules while believing that the ruling of Allah is the truth, and that it is more suitable for the servants than the ruling of the *taghut*, but he wishes to wrong the one judged against him because of enmity between them, then this is a wrongdoer.
As for the one who said they are concordant and there is no distinction between them, he says: the disbeliever is a wrongdoer, by the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿And the disbelievers are the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah 254]. Based on this, the two descriptions are what?
* Student: Concordant.
* Shaykh: Concordant in referring to one subject, but the first is more evident, and each description has its own specific place.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We sent, following in their footsteps, Jesus, son of Mary﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:46], to the end of the verse.

﴿Qaffayna﴾ means: We sent Jesus, son of Mary, as one who follows (qafiyan) those who came before him, that is, as one who follows those who preceded him. It is derived from ﴿al-qafa﴾ (the back of the neck/head), because the one who follows the traces of those before him walks behind them. ﴿Qaffayna 'ala athariham﴾ means: after the footprints of the earlier messengers.

﴿Bi-'Isa ibn Maryam﴾: he was the last of the prophets of the Children of Israel, and there was no messenger between him and the Prophet (ﷺ). This is why he is described as one who follows those before him. He is attributed to his mother because he had no father.

﴿Musaddiqan limа bayna yadayhi mina al-Tawrah﴾: ﴿musaddiqan﴾ is a circumstantial state (hal) of ('Isa), meaning: while he was confirming what was before him of the Torah. His confirmation of what was before him of the Torah has two meanings. The first meaning: he confirms the Torah and says that it is true. The second meaning: he confirms its report, since Jesus, son of Mary (peace be upon him), is mentioned in it.

His saying ﴿limа bayna yadayhi﴾ means: what came before him, ﴿mina al-Tawrah﴾, which is the Book that Allah revealed to Moses (peace be upon him).

﴿Wa atayna-hu al-Injil﴾: We gave him the Injil (the Gospel) in addition to confirming what was before him of the Torah. So the Sharia of Jesus consisted of the Sharia of the Torah and the Sharia of the Injil. For this reason the Injil is not regarded as an independent book; rather, it follows the Torah. It contains only a few rulings, but most of it consists of admonitions, stories and lessons.

﴿Wa atayna-hu al-Injil﴾, ﴿fihi﴾ means: in the Injil, ﴿huda﴾ means: knowledge, ﴿wa nur﴾ means: a beneficial effect by which the heart is illuminated.

﴿Wa musaddiqan limа bayna yadayhi mina al-Tawrah﴾: the word ﴿musaddiqan﴾ here refers back to the Injil, while the first ﴿musaddiqan limа bayna yadayhi﴾ refers back to ('Isa). Thus, 'Isa confirmed what was before him of the Torah, and likewise the Book that was revealed to him, which is the Injil.

﴿Wa huda wa mau'izatan lil-muttaqin﴾: meaning, Allah the Exalted made this Injil a guidance and an admonition. Most of what is in it consists of admonitions, lessons and stories, while the rulings are mostly drawn from—?

* Student: From the Torah.

* Shaykh: From the Torah.

As for His saying ﴿lil-muttaqin﴾: first, ﴿huda﴾ is knowledge. ﴿Mau'izah﴾ (admonition) is that by which hearts are admonished, and it is a report accompanied by encouragement or warning. Every report that is accompanied by encouragement or warning is an admonition, as the Companions used to say: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) admonished us with an admonition by which hearts trembled and eyes overflowed."[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (4607), al-Tirmidhi (2676) and Ibn Majah (42) from al-'Irbad ibn Sariyah.]]

His saying ﴿lil-muttaqin﴾ means: those who are God-conscious (ittaqa Allah). Taqwa of Allah the Exalted is carrying out His command and avoiding His prohibition. It is called taqwa because a person protects himself by it from the punishment of Allah the Exalted.

* In this verse there are benefits, among them: that 'Isa (peace be upon him) is the last of the prophets, as indicated by His saying ﴿wa qaffayna 'ala athariham bi-'Isa ibn Maryam﴾. After him there is no prophet who follows him except Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah al-Hashimi al-Qurashi (peace be upon him).

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: whoever has no father is attributed to his mother, because Allah the Exalted attributes 'Isa ibn Maryam to his mother, since he had no father.

If someone says: what is an example of one who has no father? We say: there are examples of this, among them: a man commits adultery with a woman, and she bears a child from him. Here the child does not belong to the adulterer, because of the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "For the adulterer is the stone."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2053) and Muslim (1457/36) from 'A'ishah.]] So he is not attributed to the adulterer, does not inherit from him, the adulterer does not inherit from him, and the adulterer does not bear his 'aql (blood-money obligation), and so on. The point is that this child has no father.

Another example: a man performs li'an (mutual oath of condemnation) against his wife, accusing her of adultery and disowning her child. He says: "The child is not mine." Then she has a mother but no father.

The scholars (may Allah have mercy on them) differed concerning the case where an adulterer claims (istilhaq) a child who was created from his semen, when there is no competing claim: is the child attributed to him or not? Some of them said: he is not attributed to him, because of the general meaning of the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "And for the adulterer is the stone."

Others said: rather, the child is attributed to him if there is no contender, because he is his child in reality (qadaran), and there is no legal contender (shar'an), so he is attributed to him legally as he is from him in reality. This is the preponderant view: when an adulterer claims a child created from his semen and there is no contender, the child is attributed to him.

This is not contradicted by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The child belongs to the bed (firash), and for the adulterer is the stone."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2053) and Muslim (1457/36) from 'A'ishah.]] Because the hadith clearly indicates that there is a dispute between the owner of the bed and the adulterer, and for this reason he said: "The child belongs to the bed, and for the adulterer is the stone." So if it is a virgin woman with whom a man committed adultery, is there a bed? Answer me.

* Students: No.

* Shaykh: No, there is no bed. If there is no bed and the adulterer claims the child, there is no objection to attributing it to him. However, the majority of scholars hold that the child of adultery is not attributed to the adulterer even if he claims him. As you know, they relied on the general meaning of what? "For the adulterer is the stone."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2053) and Muslim (1457/36) from 'A'ishah.]]

The second view is that if the adulterer claims him and there is no contender, the child is attributed to him. The answer to this hadith is that it indicates that, in case of dispute, the child belongs to the bed, and for the adulterer is the stone.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: prophets (peace be upon them) confirm one another, as indicated by His saying ﴿musaddiqan limа bayna yadayhi mina al-Tawrah﴾.

* Among its benefits: the established revelation of the Torah and that it is true, because one of the messengers of firm resolve (Ulu al-'Azm) testified that it is true.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: 'Isa (peace be upon him) was sent down a Book, which is what? The Injil. This is clearly stated in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And He revealed the Torah and the Gospel before, as guidance for mankind﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:3-4].

If someone says: Is the Injil that is now in the hands of the Christians the same Injil that was revealed to 'Isa?

The answer: No, it is both yes and no. The Christians, and likewise the Jews, who are more wicked than the Christians in their audacity against Allah, distorted the Torah and the Injil. As Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: Who revealed the Book which Moses brought as light and guidance for mankind, which you make into scrolls, showing some and concealing much?﴾ [al-An'am 6:91] ..

The Book, which is what? The Injil. This is clearly stated in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And He revealed the Torah and the Gospel before, as guidance for mankind﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:3-4].

If someone says: Is the Injil that is now in the hands of the Christians the same Injil that was revealed to 'Isa?

The answer: No, it is both yes and no. The Christians, and likewise the Jews, who are more wicked than the Christians in their audacity against Allah, have distorted the Torah and the Injil. As Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: Who revealed the Book which Moses brought as light and guidance for mankind, which you make into scrolls, showing some and concealing much?﴾ [al-An'am 6:91]. Accordingly, one must be careful in attributing the Torah that is now in the hands of the Jews and the Injil that is now in the hands of the Christians. One must be cautious and say: not everything in them is true; rather, among them is what is distorted, among them is what is deficient, and perhaps among them is what has been added.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the Injil contains guidance and light, as His saying ﴿fihi huda wa nur﴾ indicates, and this is so. Among the guidance and light in it: it contains the description of the Prophet (ﷺ), as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, whom they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel, who enjoins on them what is right and forbids them what is wrong﴾ [al-A'raf 7:157]. And the Prophet 'Isa (peace be upon him) gave good tidings of Muhammad (ﷺ). This is part of the guidance and light.

* Among the benefits of this verse: that divine Books confirm one another, as His saying ﴿musaddiqan limа bayna yadayhi mina al-Tawrah﴾ indicates.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the emphasis on the greatness, excellence and honour of the Torah, since this verse states that 'Isa confirms what was before him of the Torah, and that the Injil likewise confirms what was before it of the Torah.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the Injil contains knowledge and admonition from which the God-conscious benefit, as His saying ﴿wa huda wa mau'izatan lil-muttaqin﴾ indicates.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: encouragement to taqwa, and that it is the cause of every good and every knowledge, as His saying ﴿wa huda wa mau'izatan lil-muttaqin﴾ indicates. There is no doubt that taqwa is the foundation of action, because whoever does not fear Allah does not act, and whoever fears Allah acts in accordance with the commands of Allah to the extent of the taqwa he possesses.

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And let the people of the Gospel judge by what Allah has revealed therein﴾. Regarding His saying ﴿And let them judge﴾ there are two readings. The first reading is what is written in the text: the lam is sukun and the mim is sukun: ﴿وَلْيَحْكُمْ﴾ (wa-l-yahkum). The second reading: the lam is kasra and the mim is fatha, and the estimated form is ﴿وَلِيَحْكُمَ﴾ (wa-liyahkuma).

On the first reading, the lam is the lam of command (lam al-amr). On the second reading, the lam is the lam of causation (lam al-ta'lil), which is sometimes called (lam kay).

Let us examine the grammatical analysis (i'rab) on both readings. ﴿وَلْيَحْكُمْ﴾ is a command from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, that the people of the Gospel judge by what Allah revealed therein. But is this command the object of an omitted verb of saying, meaning "and We said: let the people of the Gospel judge by what Allah revealed therein," or is it an independent command? It has been said: both are possible, and whenever a matter is uncertain between assuming an omission and not assuming it, the preferable option is not to assume it.

As for the second reading ﴿وَلِيَحْكُمَ﴾, it is a causal clause explaining Allah's saying ﴿And We gave him the Gospel﴾, meaning: so that it would confirm what was before it of the Torah, and so that the people of the Gospel would judge by what Allah revealed therein.

Al-hukm (judgment) is the clarification of the ruling and the binding enforcement of it, i.e., in the sense of qada' (judicial decision). Qada' is the clarification of the ruling together with its enforcement, whereas fatwa is the clarification of the ruling without enforcement.

﴿أَهْلُ الْإِنْجِيلِ بِمَا أَنْزَلَ اللَّهُ فِيهِ﴾: ﴿بِمَا﴾ means "by that which Allah revealed therein of rulings."

What is the grammatical status of (ma) in ﴿بِمَا أَنْزَلَ اللَّهُ﴾? Is it conditional or negative?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: It is a relative pronoun (mawsulah), meaning "by that which Allah revealed therein."

* * *
* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿And We sent, following in their footsteps, Jesus son of Mary, confirming what was before him of the Torah. And We gave him the Gospel, in which was guidance and light, confirming what was before it of the Torah, as guidance and instruction for the God-fearing (46). And let the people of the Gospel judge by what Allah has revealed therein. Whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, they are the defiantly disobedient (47). And We revealed to you the Book in truth, confirming what was before it of the Scripture and as a guardian over it. So judge between them by what Allah has revealed, and do not follow their desires away from the truth that has come to you. For each of you We have made a law and a way. Had Allah willed, He would have made you one community, but He tests you in what He has given you, so race to good deeds. To Allah is your return, all of you, and He will inform you about that over which you used to differ﴾ [al-Ma'idah 46–48].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We sent, following in their footsteps, Jesus son of Mary﴾, and so on to the end.

What is the meaning of His saying ﴿وَقَفَّيْنَا﴾ (waqaffayna)?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: ﴿آثَارِهِمْ﴾ (their footsteps): whose footsteps?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Moses and those prophets who followed him and who submitted (to Allah).

Why did He attribute him to his mother?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Can it be derived from this that if a child is found who has no father, he may be attributed to his mother, and this is valid?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Is the Gospel considered an independent book or one that completes the Torah?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: It completes it. Is there evidence for this?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, this is not evidence, even the Qur'an... what?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, ﴿and to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you﴾ [Al 'Imran 50]. Also, the scholars said: most of what is in the Gospel consists of admonitions and narratives, not independent rulings, and this is the reality.

His saying ﴿وَمُصَدِّقًا لِمَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ مِنَ التَّوْرَاةِ﴾: what is the grammatical analysis of ﴿وَمُصَدِّقًا لِمَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ مِنَ التَّوْرَاةِ﴾?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: ﴿وَقَفَّيْنَا عَلَى آثَارِهِمْ﴾.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Meaning, "and confirming you"?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: It does not work (...), this is the first one.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: (...) the Gospel, correct.

﴿فِيهِ هُدًى وَنُورٌ﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyah), and ﴿مُصَدِّقًا﴾ is conjoined to this circumstantial clause, so it is a circumstantial state (hal) of the Gospel.

His saying ﴿وَهُدًى وَمَوْعِظَةً﴾ is in the accusative and is conjoined. How? "And We gave him the Gospel, and We gave him guidance and admonition"?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Conjoined to what?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: To (muṣaddiqan). And what is conjoined to a state is a state, as you say: "Zayd came riding quickly and laughing," and the like.

Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿And let the people of the Gospel judge by what Allah has revealed therein﴾. There are two readings: the first, ﴿وَلْيَحْكُمْ﴾, with the lam as the lam of command; the second, ﴿وَلِيَحْكُمَ﴾, with the lam as the lam of causation.

If we say it is the lam of command, then it is the object of an omitted verb of saying, meaning: "And We said to them: let the people of the Gospel judge by what Allah revealed therein."

If we say the lam is for causation, then it is conjoined to ﴿مُصَدِّقًا﴾, meaning: confirming what is before it, and in order that the people of the Gospel judge by what Allah revealed.

His saying ﴿بِمَا أَنْزَلَ اللَّهُ فِيهِ﴾ means: by that which Allah revealed therein.

﴿وَمَنْ لَمْ يَحْكُمْ بِمَا أَنْزَلَ اللَّهُ فَأُولَئِكَ هُمُ الْفَاسِقُونَ﴾: we say about it what we said about the two preceding verses, except that here He said ﴿الْفَاسِقُونَ﴾. So is the fisq here the fisq of disobedience or the fisq of disbelief, since fisq may be of either kind? This depends on the circumstances.

The detailed distinction we mentioned earlier applies to these verses:

Whoever judges by other than what Allah revealed, turning away from Allah's judgment, claiming that it equals Allah's judgment or is more beneficial, then this is kufr (disbelief).

Whoever judges by other than what Allah revealed through aggression against the one judged, this is zulm (injustice).

Whoever judges by other than what Allah revealed out of desire in his own soul, this is fisq (defiant disobedience).

* In this noble verse: it is obligatory for the people of the Gospel to judge by what Allah revealed therein.

* Among its benefits: it is obligatory for the people of the Gospel to believe in Muhammad. The reason: among what was revealed in the Gospel is the description of Muhammad (ﷺ), and Jesus gave glad tidings of him, saying: ﴿and a messenger coming after me, whose name is Ahmad﴾ [al-Saff 6].

So if the Christians today say, "We believe in the Gospel," we say to them: you do not believe, for if you believed in the Gospel you would believe in Muhammad (ﷺ), since he is written about in your Torah, and the Gospel commands you to what is good and forbids you from what is evil, and so on. Moreover, your prophet Jesus (peace be upon him) gave you glad tidings of him.

If they say, "The one he gave us glad tidings of is named Ahmad," we say: this is another name of Muhammad (peace be upon him). His name is both Ahmad and Muhammad. This is shown by Allah's saying, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿So when he came to them with clear proofs﴾ (came): who came? He came to the Children of Israel with clear proofs indicating his truthfulness and the confirmation of Jesus through his glad tidings, ﴿they said: this is evident magic﴾. And does the word (jā'a, came) in clear Arabic indicate the past or the future? The past. So the messenger whom Jesus gave glad tidings of has come.

Has anyone come before Muhammad? No. They did not claim that someone named Ahmad had come before Muhammad; they only said, "We await that Ahmad will come." We reply that what you say is not correct, for he has come and is not awaited.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the Gospel was sent down from Allah, as shown by His saying ﴿by what Allah revealed therein﴾, which is very explicit in Allah's saying, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿He revealed the Torah and the Gospel, (3) before, as guidance for the people, and He revealed the Criterion﴾ [Al 'Imran 3–4]. Accordingly, the Gospel is the speech of Allah, since it was sent down from Him and is revealed speech, and speech when attributed to the speaker is his speech.

* Among the benefits of the verse: the affirmation of Allah's elevation (al-'uluw), the exaltedness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. From where is this derived?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: From the adverbial/locative sense? From (mā) the relative pronoun? Is it derived from (mā) or from ﴿anzala﴾?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: From ﴿anzala﴾. How so?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Descent only occurs from above. The proofs for Allah's essential elevation (al-'uluw al-dhati) are more than can be counted.

Its roots are five: the Book, the Sunnah, consensus (ijma'), reason, and innate nature (fitrah).

As for the Book, which is the Qur'an, it is filled with proofs in many respects.

The Sunnah likewise: the verbal, the practical, and the approving. As for the verbal, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High" [Muslim (772/203), from Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman], and said: "Our Lord is Allah, who is in the heaven" [Abu Dawud (3892), from Abu al-Darda']. As for the approving, he said to the slave girl: "Where is Allah?" She said: "In the sky." He approved of her and said: "She is a believer" [Muslim (537/33), from Mu'awiyah ibn al-Hakam al-Sulami]. As for the practical: when he (ﷺ) supplicated to his Lord, he raised his hands towards the sky [among them the hadith of Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: on the day of Badr... the Prophet (ﷺ) faced the qiblah and then stretched out his hands; Muslim (1763/58)]. And when he asked his Lord to bear witness on his community that he had conveyed the message, on the day of 'Arafah he began saying: "O Allah, bear witness," raising his finger to the sky and pointing it at the people [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1741) and Muslim (1679/31), from Abu Bakrah].

As for consensus: not a single letter has been found, neither with a sound chain nor a weak one, from any of the Companions, the Successors, or the Imams stating that Allah, the Exalted, is not in the sky, never.

If someone says: nor has it been found from them that they said He is in the sky? We reply: this is obstinacy. They recited the Qur'an, which mentions elevation. Has any of them been reported to have contradicted that? Then they are in consensus upon it. This is a clear way of establishing consensus: none of them interpreted the verses of elevation in a way other than what their apparent meaning indicates.

As for reason: every person knows that a higher rank is better than a lower rank, and that a higher place is better than a lower place. Elevation is a attribute of perfection, so it must be established for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

As for innate nature: ask the common old women when they want to supplicate to Allah, where do they turn? To the sky. Even the simple old woman, by her innate nature, testifies that Allah is in the sky.

Accordingly, these proofs for the elevation of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, refute the view of those who say that Allah is not in any direction, or who say that Allah is in every place, and both views are misguidance.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: whoever does not judge by what Allah revealed is a fasiq.

These are the last of the three verses. The first: ﴿فَأُولَئِكَ هُمُ الْكَافِرُونَ﴾ (they are the disbelievers); the second: ﴿فَأُولَئِكَ هُمُ الظَّالِمُونَ﴾ (they are the wrongdoers); and the third, this verse: ﴿فَأُولَئِكَ هُمُ الْفَاسِقُونَ﴾ (they are the defiantly disobedient). Are these attributes descriptions of one subject? There is a difference of opinion:

Some said: it is one subject described by one attribute, because the disbeliever is also truly described as a wrongdoer, and the wrongdoer as a fasiq; so we call the disbeliever a wrongdoer, a fasiq, and a disbeliever.

Others said: their difference is according to differing circumstances. Judging by other than what Allah revealed, we say: he is a disbeliever; the second, we say: he is a wrongdoer; the third, we say: he is a fasiq. This is the more preferred view, because the basic principle in speech is to establish new information, not to emphasize.

If that is so, we should say: each description applies to a particular circumstance:

Whoever judges by other than what Allah revealed, holding that what he judges is the sunnah and the path to follow, casting Allah's judgment behind his back, he is a disbeliever. Whoever judges by other than what Allah revealed out of aggression against the one judged or against someone else, he is a wrongdoer. Whoever judges by other than what Allah revealed out of desire in his own soul, to reach an aim he sees as desirable, he is a fasiq. Thus the verses apply according to differing circumstances.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 5, verse 48 (part 1 of 2):

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming that which came before it of the Scripture﴾. This is the last of the books, the best, the most noble, the most comprehensive and the most beneficial, and it is the Noble Qur'an.

﴿We have sent down to you the Book in truth﴾. The intended meaning of "al-Kitab" (the Book) is the Qur'an. It is on the pattern of fi'āl in the sense of maf'ūl, i.e., "maktūb" (written). It is written in the Preserved Tablet, written by the hands of the noble scribe angels, and written in the copies of the Qur'an that are in our hands. It was named thus because the legal rulings, the true reports and the beneficial stories were gathered in it. The root meaning of "kutub" is gathering, and from it comes "kutaybah" (a battalion), meaning a group of the army gathered together.

His saying ﴿bil-haqq﴾ (in truth) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to "al-Kitab", i.e., while it is clothed in truth, so that what the Qur'an brings contains the truth. This is one aspect of its meaning.

The second aspect: "We sent it down with truth", i.e., it is truth from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, so the bā' in ﴿anzalnā﴾ is transitive, meaning: We sent it down as a true sending down. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And with truth We sent it down, and with truth it descended﴾ [al-Isrā' 105].

﴿confirming that which came before it of the Scripture﴾. That which lies before it of the Scripture is not only the Torah and the Gospel, but they are the closest of the books to it. Yet all the books have been confirmed by it. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿We certainly sent Our messengers with clear evidences and sent down with them the Book and the Balance that people may maintain justice﴾ [al-Ḥadīd 25]. So it confirms every book that preceded it; for this reason no book comes after it.

His saying ﴿and a guardian over it﴾ is coordinated (ma'ṭūf) upon ﴿confirming﴾, and ﴿confirming﴾ here is a circumstantial clause relating to ﴿the Book﴾. Thus ﴿the Book﴾ is the guardian (muhaymin), and ﴿and a guardian over it﴾ means: over what lies before it of the Scripture.

As for the meaning of "al-hayminah" (guardianship), it has been said that it means "witness", i.e., a witness over it. But this is open to question, since "witness" is already covered by "confirming". It has also been said that al-hayminah means dominion and rule, i.e., it rules over the books that preceded it, has authority over them, and abrogates them. This meaning is more correct, because the Qur'an is a guardian over all the previous books.

So, ﴿muhaymin 'alayhi﴾ correctly means: it has authority, rules, and abrogates what came before. For this reason, recite to him His saying: ﴿So judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾, meaning: on the basis of that, judge between them, i.e., between the People of the Book and the Muslims, ﴿by what Allah has revealed﴾, meaning the Qur'an.

So when they come to us for judgment, we judge between them by the Qur'an, because the Qur'an is a guardian and authority over what preceded it; it is opposed but is not opposed, it judges and is not judged.

﴿So judge between them by what Allah has revealed and do not follow their desires away from the truth that has come to you﴾. This statement is addressed by Allah, Mighty and Majestic, to His Messenger ﷺ, although we know with certainty that he will not do that, isn't that so? But so that people may take a lesson: if Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), is forbidden by his Lord, who sent him, from following their desires away from the truth that has come to them, then how about anyone else?

The meaning of His saying ﴿and do not follow their desires﴾ (rather than "their sects" or something similar) is that they are upon desire, not upon guidance; so their disbelief in what Muhammad ﷺ brought is a desire, not from reason nor from the Law.

His saying ﴿away from what has come to you﴾ is related to an omitted element, and the sense is: deviating from what has come to you of the truth. This is better than supposing: "turning away from what he brought", because "turning away" carries a degree of harshness, whereas "deviating" is milder. The meaning is one, but it is proper to use fitting expressions.

So ﴿away from what has come to you of the truth﴾: we say, it is related to what? To an omitted element; the sense is: deviating from what has come to you of the truth. He did not say "away from what has come to you" or "away from what was revealed", but said ﴿of the truth﴾, to make clear that what the Messenger ﷺ brought is truth, from which it is not possible to deviate to anything else.

﴿For each of you We have made a law and a way﴾. The grammarians say that the tanwīn here is a substitute (tanwīn 'iwaḍ) for an omitted element. What is the sense? "For every nation We have made of you…" or "for every one…" The point is that this is tanwīn substituting for an omitted word.

﴿We have made of you a law and a way﴾: "made" means "appointed". "Shir'ah" (law) is that which is legislated, its root being "the watering place of water"; and "minhāj" (way) is that which is trodden, its root being "a road". Every nation has a law suited to its circumstances, place and time.

﴿Minhāj﴾ is what this nation treads: either disbelief or faith. Every nation is thus. The laws of the Jews and Christians suited their circumstances, times and places, and the law of Muhammad ﷺ suits every nation in every time and every place. So His saying ﴿For each of you We have made a law and a way﴾, after the unity of the law and the way, is in the category of silencing the opponent. That is: those who say that the law of Muhammad is unacceptable because it contradicts our laws, and not valid because it contradicts our laws, we say: you have your own specific suitable laws, and we, the nation of Muhammad, have our own specific suitable laws; and you now are considered part of the nation of Muhammad in what sense? In the sense of the call (to Islam).

﴿For each of you We have made a law and a way. Had Allah willed, He would have made you one community﴾, Subḥānahu wa Ta'ālā, because the affair is in His hand. Had Allah willed, He would have made the laws one, by which whoever disbelieves would disbelieve and whoever believes would believe. But He, Subḥānahu wa Ta'ālā, has wisdom in what He legislated; for this reason He said: ﴿but to test you in what He has given you﴾. (Yabla) means "tests" (yakhtabir). ﴿In what He has given you﴾ means: of the laws, whether they are easy and facilitated or hard and burdensome.

The first is tested as to whether he is thankful or not thankful; the second is tested as to whether he is patient or not patient, because we know that the laws differ in their ease and hardship.

With the easy laws, one is tested with thankfulness: will these people, to whom ease is granted, be thankful or not? As for the burdensome ones, one is tested with patience: will they be patient with these laws and carry them out or not? For this reason He said: ﴿to test you﴾, meaning: to examine you, ﴿in what He has given you﴾, from where? From the laws.

﴿So race to all that is good﴾: that is, hasten to it and precede others to it. "Khayrāt" is the plural of "khayr" (good), and what is meant by it is everything the Islamic law brought, for it is good. For this reason: "There was no prophet whom Allah sent except that he guided his nation to good and warned them against evil."[[Narrated by Muslim (1844/46), from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr, with the wording: "No prophet before me was there but it was incumbent upon him to guide his nation to the good he knows for them, and to warn them against the evil he knows for them."]]

﴿To Allah is your return, all of you﴾. The return is to Allah, Subḥānahu wa Ta'ālā; all creatures' return is to Allah.

Is the intended return in this world or in this world and the Hereafter? In this world and the Hereafter. Our return is to Allah in this world and the Hereafter. As for this world, our return is to Allah, who judges between us, who judges over us, and who judges concerning us. As for the Hereafter, likewise He will separate us on the Day of Resurrection: a group in Paradise and a group in the Blaze.

In His saying ﴿To Allah is your return﴾ there is a rhetorical benefit, namely restriction (ḥaṣr), through the fronting of the predicate; for our rule is that when something that should be deferred is placed first, that is evidence of restriction.

He says: ﴿then He will inform you about that in which you used to differ﴾. (Yunabbi'u) means "inform" (yukhbir). Are "nabaʾ" and "khabar" synonymous in meaning, or is there a subtle difference?

Shaykh al-Islām, may Allah have mercy on him, said: there is nothing in the language that is entirely synonymous, a hundred percent; rather there must be a difference, otherwise the Arabic language would contain superfluity. There must be a difference, as with: "asad" (lion), "darghām" and "ghaḍanfar" and the like; although their referent is one, each must contain a precise meaning that distinguishes it from the other. This is "nabaʾ".

As for "ikhbār" (reporting), it has been said that reporting is whatever is not of great importance, while "nabaʾ" is only used for matters of great importance: ﴿About what are they asking one another? About the great news﴾ [al-Naba' 1–2]; ﴿Say: It is a great news﴾ [Ṣād 67]. So "nabaʾ" is used for important, great matters, while "khabar" can be used for anything. So is "khabar" in this sense more general or not? More general.

﴿Then He will inform you about that in which you used to differ﴾, meaning: about that in which you used to differ. Then the judgment will be made with the justice of the Mighty and Majestic, and it will become clear who is upon the truth and who is not.

* In this noble verse: the affirmation that the Qur'an is the speech of Allah. From where? * Student: (...). * The Shaykh: How so? * Student: (...). * The Shaykh: To whom does the pronoun refer? ﴿We sent down﴾? * Student: (...). * The Shaykh: And the thing sent down is speech, is it not? So it indicates that the Qur'an is the speech of Allah, the Exalted.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's exaltation, from His saying ﴿We sent down﴾, and sending down is only from? * Student: (...). * The Shaykh: Yes.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: praise of the Qur'an. From where? * Student: (...). * The Shaykh: (...) ﴿in truth﴾: that the Qur'an is truth and was sent down with truth.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: the great distinction of the Messenger ﷺ, ﴿We have sent down to you﴾, and this is explained by His saying: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit brought it down (193) upon your heart﴾ [al-Shu'arā' 193–194].
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that the Qur'an confirms all the books, ﴿confirming that which came before it﴾. We have mentioned that its confirmation of what lies before it has two aspects: judging the truthfulness of the earlier revealed books, and confirming what they reported of the sending down of the Qur'an.
* Student: Some countries teach in their universities a discipline called the science of religions, and a specialist in it is knowledgeable in Islamic law and in other laws such as Judaism and Christianity. If the specialist in those countries, where there may be Christians or Jews, is asked about a ruling of the laws of those questioners, let us suppose they are Jews or Christians, will he answer them, and thereby have given them a fatwa in their religion, or must he tell them this fatwa is not valid?
* The Shaykh: It will come to us, God willing, that if they refer to us we judge by what Allah has revealed, because the ruling that they follow is abrogated and not pleasing to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, even in reporting; for if you report it to him, you have judged in his favour.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: The difference between "ila" and "ʿala": "ʿalā" indicates elevation, and "ilā" indicates the end point; so it is from an elevation, and its end is the Prophet ﷺ.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: The whole Qur'an is knowledge. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿You did not know what the Book was, nor faith﴾ [al-Shūrā 52], before revelation came to him, and He said: ﴿And He taught you what you did not know﴾ [al-Nisā' 113]. So it is knowledge and truth.
* Student: (...) in establishing the Prophet's ﷺ message (...) the Gospel with that?
* The Shaykh: If we cite this against an opponent who denies the Prophet's message, and he is a Christian for example, yes, we bring it and cite it, because it is a proof against him; for this reason Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Even if you brought to those who were given the Book every sign, they would not follow your qiblah﴾ [al-Baqarah 145].
* Student: May Allah reward you well. Would it be like one who issues a fatwa other than what Allah has revealed (...)?
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed, the descriptions are one, but you should know that judgment is distinguished from giving a fatwa in that it is binding; for the judge binds and the mufti does not bind.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: The word ﴿and guidance﴾: this is for emphasis.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed, ﴿in it is guidance﴾ the first is the second, but light is what results from the effects of this knowledge.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: The difference between "shir'ah" and "minhāj": "shir'ah" is the law of Allah, and "minhāj" is the conduct and path of the one sent to them; that is, they may believe and they may disbelieve, whereas the law is fixed. For this reason it is said: "So-and-so took the path of so-and-so," i.e., followed his way.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: Yes. We say: this is a proof against... ﴿And let the People of the Gospel judge by what Allah has revealed in it﴾. The Gospel contains the obligation to follow the Messenger ﷺ, because Allah mentioned after it: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming that which came before it of the Scripture and a guardian over it﴾, and this is from the misguidance of the Christians, that they do not understand what Allah sent down to His messengers.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: According to one of the two opinions: when we attribute these qualities to one subject, then transgression (fisq) is disbelief (kufr).
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: The Christians are the Children of Israel.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: The Torah and the Gospel are each a book for a prophet of the Children of Israel, because a messenger is sent to his own people specifically, except for the Prophet ﷺ.
* * *
* Student: I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan: ﴿And judge between them by what Allah has revealed and do not follow their desires, and beware of them lest they tempt you away from some of what Allah has revealed to you. And if they turn away, then know that Allah intends only to afflict them for some of their sins. And indeed, many of the people are defiantly disobedient (49). Is it the judgment of ignorance they desire? And who is better than Allah in judgment for a people who are certain?﴾ [al-Mā'idah 49–50].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming that which came before it of the Scripture and a guardian over it. So judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾, and so on to the end.
* From the benefits of this noble verse: that everything in the Qur'an is true; if it is a report, it is truthful; if it is a narrative, it is beneficial; if it is rulings, it is just. All that is in the Qur'an.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that the Qur'an abrogates what came before it of the books; from His saying ﴿and a guardian over it﴾.
* And among the benefits of this verse: the obligation to judge by what Allah revealed in the Qur'an when the People of the Book refer their disputes to us; from His saying ﴿So judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾. This address is to the Prophet ﷺ, but it includes the Ummah.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of following the desires of the People of the Book and other disbelievers; from His saying ﴿and do not follow their desires﴾.
* And among its benefits: that the opposition of the People of the Book to what Muhammad ﷺ brought was not founded on sound evidence nor on sound reason, but was founded on vain desire; from His saying ﴿and do not follow their desires﴾.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that whoever forbids an ugly thing should make its ugliness clear and lead people to what is better than it; from His saying ﴿away from what has come to you of the truth﴾, as if He said: do not follow their desires, but follow what has come to you of the truth.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that it is obligatory for the Muslims to have a standing identity, not following people so that they become tails of the enemies of Allah, but rather to have a standing identity for the honour of Islam; from His saying ﴿away from what has come to you of the truth﴾.
* And among the benefits of the noble verse: that what the Messenger ﷺ brought is truth.
* And among its benefits: that Allah, Subḥānahu wa Ta'ālā, diversified the laws according to the nations; from His saying ﴿For each of you We have made a law﴾.

We have already mentioned in the tafsir that the interests (maṣāliḥ) differ according to the conditions of people, their eras, and their places.

Is this also the case with regard to the Islamic Sharia, that Allah has prescribed a ruling for every situation? We pointed out in the explanation (sharh or tafsir) to this and said: even within the Islamic Sharia, its rulings vary according to times, places and circumstances, and we mentioned examples of this: "Pray standing; if you cannot, then seated; if you cannot, then lying on your side." "Pay zakat if you possess zakatable wealth; otherwise there is nothing upon you." "Perform Hajj to the House if you are able; otherwise there is nothing upon you." "Fast if you are able; but if you are unable permanently, then feed (a poor person)," and so on. You find that the Islamic Sharia itself varies with the variation of circumstances.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: people differ in their approach to receiving these laws; this is due to His saying ﴿and a method﴾ (manhajan). Thus there are among them the disbelievers and there are among them the believers.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the comprehensiveness of the power of Allah, exalted is He, and that the legislative and the cosmic affairs are in His hand. This is due to His saying ﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have made you one nation﴾, meaning: upon one religion. But He, glorified and exalted is He, possesses perfect wisdom in what He decreed and legislated.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the refutation of the Qadariyah (those who deny divine decree). Who knows this?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes. Because making them one nation, meaning one religion, necessitates that their adherence to God is by His will.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the laws (shara'i') are a trial (ibtila') from Allah, glorified and exalted is He, meaning a test (ikhtibar), and not a trial in the sense of affliction (bala') but in the sense of testing. This is due to His saying ﴿but to test you in what He has given you﴾. So the laws are for the purpose of trial, and ﴿He created death and life that He may test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾ [al-Mulk 2]. It thus becomes clear that the laws of Allah and His decreed rulings are all a trial.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the exhortation to hasten to good; this is due to His saying ﴿so race to the good deeds﴾, meaning: take hold of them, whichever of you is foremost.

If someone says: Does competing in good deeds not entail envy, in the sense that a person dislikes that someone else precedes him?

The answer: No. Because disliking that someone precedes him does not necessitate that he dislikes it when Allah bestows His favor upon someone and he goes ahead. Envy is for a person to dislike what Allah has bestowed upon others.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the return is to Allah, blessed and exalted is He, both legislatively and by decree. This is due to His saying ﴿To Allah is your return﴾. The return to Allah in the legislative sense is that He judges between us; and in the decreed sense, the matter is as Allah said: ﴿Indeed, to Us is their return, then indeed, upon Us is their account﴾ [al-Ghashiyah 25, 26].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the comprehensiveness of the knowledge of Allah, blessed and exalted is He, regarding the actions of the servants. This is due to His saying ﴿and He will inform you about that over which you used to differ﴾.

If someone says: Is the judgment in favor of the disbelievers over the believers, or of the believers over the disbelievers?

The answer: The latter; in favor of the believers over the disbelievers. This is due to the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted is He: ﴿So Allah will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection, and Allah will never grant the disbelievers a way over the believers﴾ [an-Nisa' 141]. This is one of the marvels of adjudication: that it makes clear to the opponent that he is the loser before the arbitration. But this has a wisdom: that the opponent joins the second party. The disbelievers and the believers are adversaries, and who is the one who prevails? The believers. Here Allah made clear that the decision will be made and the believers will prevail, and that Allah will never grant the disbelievers a way over the believers. He made this clear as an incentive for the disbelievers to join the ranks of the believers, for when it becomes clear to them that they are losers and that the contest and battle belong to the believer, they will join.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that mankind must necessarily differ, and this is the reality. Many verses point to it, such as His saying: ﴿He it is who created you; then among you is a disbeliever and among you is a believer﴾ [at-Taghabun 2]. Difference is unavoidable, and the reference point upon difference is the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger (ﷺ); this is due to His saying: ﴿And if you disagree over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger, if you should believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾ [an-Nisa' 59].

Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾. That is: "And We have revealed the Book to you, so judge between them by what Allah has revealed." ﴿And judge﴾ is conjoined to His saying: ﴿so judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾.

﴿And judge﴾: the address is to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him. There are two readings of (an): the damma (u) and the kasra (i): ﴿wa-an uhkum﴾ and ﴿wa-an ihkum﴾. Both are seven canonical readings. "Judge between them if they come to you for judgment," ﴿by what Allah has revealed﴾, and do not judge between them by what they have.

It has already been mentioned that the Banu al-Nadir regarded themselves as superior to the Banu Qurayza, to the extent that in matters of blood-money they made the Banu Qurayza half of the Banu al-Nadir, and they said: if a man of al-Nadir kills a man of Qurayza, he is not killed; but if a man of Qurayza kills a man of al-Nadir, he is killed.

They would bring this and similar matters before the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, wanting him to rule accordingly, but Allah, the Exalted, forbade him from that, saying: ﴿And judge between them by what Allah has revealed, and do not follow their desires﴾; because what they had established from this false principle is pure desire, whereas the judgment of Allah among creation is equal.

﴿And do not follow their desires, and beware of them lest they tempt you away from some of what Allah has revealed to you﴾. Note this is the speech of Allah to the Messenger. "Beware of them" means: be on guard with them and be cautious, ﴿lest they tempt you away from some of what Allah has revealed to you﴾.

Regarding the grammatical analysis of ﴿an yaftinūka﴾ there are two possibilities. The first: it is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for the (hu) in His saying ﴿wa-ahdharhum﴾, and the sense is: "and beware of their temptation." You know that substitution divides into five kinds; the fifth is the verbal substitute (al-badal al-lafzi), so the sense on this would be: "beware of what?" — their temptation, because (an) and what follows it are in the sense of a verbal noun.

The second: (an) and what follows it, in the sense of a verbal noun, are in the accusative by removal of the preposition, and the sense is: "and beware of them lest they tempt you away from some of what Allah has revealed to you." Both grammatical analyses have the same meaning.

The meaning of ﴿an yaftinūka﴾ is: they would turn you away (yaṣuddūka) from some of what Allah has revealed to you. The meaning of fitnah as turning away (ṣadd) occurs in the Qur'an, such as the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who have tormented the believing men and believing women and then have not repented will have the punishment of Hell and they will have the punishment of the Burning﴾ [al-Buruj 10]. "Fatanū" means what? It means "they turned away (ṣaddū)." Thus ﴿an yaftinūka﴾ means "that they turn you away."

﴿From some of what Allah has revealed to you﴾. If the warning is about some of what has been revealed, then about all of it is even more so. ﴿And if they turn away﴾ from your judgment by what Allah has revealed, ﴿then know that Allah intends only to afflict them for some of their sins﴾. This intention is a universal will (irada kawniyya), meaning will in the sense of (mashi'a). ﴿To afflict them﴾: that calamity will befall them through their aversion. ﴿For some of their sins﴾, not all of them. Some of their sins are like what we mentioned a little earlier: that the Banu al-Nadir judged unjustly between themselves and the Banu Qurayza. ﴿For some of their sins.﴾ A sin (dhanb) is whatever a person opposes his Lord by; it is a sin, whether by abandoning an obligation or committing a prohibited act.

﴿And indeed, many of the people are defiantly disobedient﴾. This sentence is a consolation to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, that he should not grieve, because many of the people are defiantly disobedient. But the lam in His saying ﴿la-fasiqūn﴾ is for emphasis, and fasiqūn means those who go outside the obedience of Allah; it is derived, in terms of etymology, from the saying of the Arabs: "fasaqat al-thamara," when the fruit came out of its sheath.

* There are benefits in this noble verse; among them: the obligation to judge by what Allah has revealed when the People of the Book come to us for judgment, by His saying ﴿And judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾. Even if they have laws that contradict the legal ruling, we do not refer to them, even if they stir up the world against us; we do not concern ourselves with that so long as we are upon the straight path, for Allah says: ﴿If you support Allah, He will support you and plant firmly your feet﴾ [Muhammad 7].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of following the desires of the disbelievers, whoever they may be.

But if someone says: if what they have mentioned conforms to the Shari'ah, shall we abandon it because they do it, or adopt it because it is Shari'ah? The second, without doubt.

From this — and it is a strange example — some people, when they heard the saying of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him: "Be different from the Magians and the polytheists; grow the beards and trim the moustaches" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5892), and Muslim (259/54), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Umar], said: the rabbis and monks of the Christians and Jews now let their beards grow — so did the content of the hadith require that we be different from them by shaving the beards, since they let them grow?

The answer is: they now let their beards grow in accordance with the natural disposition (fitrah), not in imitation of us; and if they let them grow in accordance with the natural disposition, then we let them grow too, in accordance with the natural disposition and in following the Sunnah and the Shari'ah.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation of caution regarding the Jews, the Christians and others, by His saying ﴿and beware of them lest they tempt you﴾.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: an indication that among the greatest aims of the Jews and Christians is to tempt whom? The Muslims away from what Allah has revealed. If Allah, the Exalted, spoke of this in the time of the Messenger, then the matter in our time is more severe, because they now see themselves as stronger than us in material, sensory things, so their eagerness to turn us away from the path of Allah is greater.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that if this address is directed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, supported by the revelation, whom Allah the Mighty and Majestic gave strength and resolve in the religion of Allah beyond what He gave anyone else, then what about—? Complete.

* Students: Other than him.

* The Shaykh: Other than him. And what about one who lives in our time now? So caution is obligatory. Listen to the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿And indeed, they almost tempted you away from that which We revealed to you, in order that you would invent other than it against Us; and then they would have taken you as an intimate friend﴾ [al-Isra 73] — if you had done so, you would have become their intimate and friend. ﴿And if We had not strengthened you, you would have almost inclined to them a little. Then We would have made you taste double [punishment] in life and double in death; then you would not find for yourself any helper against Us﴾ [al-Isra 74–75]. The one addressed is the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him; so what about one below him? Caution against them becomes more and more severe.

Had Allah not made him firm — and we ask Allah for steadfastness for us and for you — he would have inclined to them a little. And if he had inclined to them a little? ﴿Then We would have made you taste double [punishment] in life and double in death; then you would not find for yourself any helper against Us.﴾

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that sins have evil effects, the greatest of which is turning away from the religion of Allah and from what Allah has revealed. Thus, whenever a person disobeys Allah, he moves further from accepting the revelation and the Shari'ah; for this reason He said: ﴿And if they turn away, then know that Allah intends only to afflict them for some of their sins.﴾ For this reason some of the early generation (salaf) said: whoever is deprived of the night prayer, it is only because of a sin he has committed.

So if you notice in yourself aversion from some part of the religion of Allah, know that there is a sin upon which this aversion has been built, and the verse is explicit about this: ﴿And if they turn away, then know that Allah intends only to afflict them for some of their sins.﴾ So seek Allah's forgiveness for both the result and the cause.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that many people have gone outside the religion of Allah through wickedness, by His saying ﴿And indeed, many of the people are defiantly disobedient.﴾

Is the word "people" (al-nas) here meant as the People of the Book, or as a general term?

If we say they are the People of the Book, the difficulty is lightened; if we say it is general, a difficulty arises, because most people are disobedient with a disobedience that necessitates entry into the Fire. The evidence for this is what is established from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, that Allah will say on the Day of Resurrection: "O Adam!" He will say: "Here I am, at Your service and good pleasure!" He will say: "Bring forth from your descendants the group for the Fire." He will say: "O Lord, what is the group for the Fire?" He will say: "From every thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine."
