[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3348), and Muslim (222/379), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.] They are all in the Fire and one out of a thousand is in Paradise; may Allah make us and you among them. Ibn al-Qayyim alludes to this in his Nuniyyah with his saying:

O commodity of the Most Merciful, none attains it, among a thousand, except one, not two.

What is attained of the children of Adam among a thousand is only one, not two. This hadith indicates that most people are disobedient, and that there is no proportion between the righteous and the wicked. This is among what favours that the intended meaning of "people" is the People of the Book. If we look at the wording, we say it is general; if we look at this hadith, we must restrict it to the specific.

What was the feeling of the Companions when he said: the people of the Fire are nine hundred and ninety-nine? "They said: O Messenger of Allah, which of us is that one? He said to them: Rejoice, for you are among two nations which have never been in anything except that they increased it: Gog and Magog — among you is one, and among them a thousand." Then he said to them: "I truly hope that you will be a quarter of the people of Paradise, a third of the people of Paradise, half of the people of Paradise." So they exclaimed Allahu akbar in joy. [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3348), and Muslim (222/379), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.] O Allah, to You be praise. For this reason, most of the people of Paradise are the righteous of this Ummah, to the point that it has come in the Sunan or the Musnad: "The people of Paradise are one hundred and twenty rows, of which eighty are from this Ummah." [Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (2546), Ibn Majah (4289), and Ahmad (22940), from the hadith of Buraydah.] So the proportion becomes two-thirds.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: extreme caution against agreeing with the disbelievers. Would that the Ummah of Islam today would heed this matter, so that it does not chase after material things and the people of material things. If the Islamic Ummah today united upon this method, it would rule the world; but it has weakness of character and weakness of faith, so it has declined to what you see. We ask Allah, the Exalted, to exalt His word and honour His religion; indeed He is over all things capable.

* Student: (...) even a person sometimes (...)?

* The Shaykh: Seeking forgiveness, and prayer expiates, without doubt; the most important thing is seeking forgiveness: ﴿And those who, when they commit an immorality or wrong themselves, remember Allah and seek forgiveness for their sins — and who forgives sins except Allah?﴾ [Ali 'Imran 135].

* Student: (...)?

* The Shaykh: Yes, (...) if he sees that prayer obliges his return to the truth and his cessation, then (...) prayer forbids indecency and wrong.

* Student: (...)?

* The Shaykh: Yes, "people" — yes; because when he says "many of the people," it is not the majority. Yes indeed.

* Student: May Allah reward you well. If a person is in the lands of the disbelievers, is it permissible for him to seek judgment from them (...) his right?

* The Shaykh: If he cannot reach his right except by this, then he may seek judgment from them, not with the intention that their judgment is valid, but with the intention that they act like the police, extracting his right from this oppressor. If we did not say this, his right would be lost. So there is a difference between making them a judge on the basis that their judgment is Shari'ah, and making them a judge in order to secure his right while believing that their judgment is invalid in principle; that is, they are not legitimate Shari'ah judges. Thus they are to him in the position of what? In the position of the police, extracting his right for him.

* Student: May Allah reward you well. A man stands in prayer in the last part of the night, but he has abandoned the night prayer in order to seek knowledge in the early part of the night. Does he fall under the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Do not be like so-and-so, who used to stand (...)"? [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1152), and Muslim (1159/185), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr.]

* The Shaykh: Which is better: knowledge or tahajjud?

* The Student: Knowledge.

* The Shaykh: Then he has left something less excellent for something more excellent. But it is possible that he does both: he should not exhaust himself in the early part of the night, nor exhaust himself in the last part of the night either; he takes a little from this and a little from that. The matter is easy: if he gets up half an hour before dawn, he can pray what Allah wills, together with the witr.

* * *
* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan: ﴿And judge between them by what Allah has revealed, and do not follow their desires, and beware of them lest they tempt you away from some of what Allah has revealed to you. And if they turn away, then know that Allah intends only to afflict them for some of their sins. And indeed, many of the people are defiantly disobedient (49). Do they then seek the judgement of the time of ignorance? And who is better than Allah in judgement for a people who are certain?﴾ [al-Ma'idah 49–50].
* The Shaykh: Glory be to Him and praise be to Him. Who knows the grammatical analysis of ﴿an yaftinūka ʿan baʿḍi mā anzala Allāh﴾?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: There are two possibilities. The first?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: A substitute of the pronoun. A substitute of what kind?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: A substitute of inclusion. And the second possibility?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, that it is in the accusative by removal of the preposition, and the sense is: "from their tempting you."

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Do they then seek the judgement of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance)?﴾ The interrogative here (*al-istifham*) is for rebuke and wonderment. That is, Allah rebukes them for this, and He wants us to be amazed at what they desire. The *fa'* (ف) here came after an interrogative particle. It is known that the interrogative particle has an original position in the sentence, yet here we find nothing between the *hamza* (ء) and the *fa'*. So how can the conjunction *fa'* be applied to something that does not exist? On this, the grammarians (*al-nahwiyyun*) have two opinions.

The first opinion: whenever a conjunction comes after the *hamza*, there is an implied sentence that fits the context. This is good in one respect, but difficult in another, since it is hard for a person to know what should be supplied, and sometimes it becomes very burdensome for you, or you are unable to supply anything suitable.

The second opinion: the *fa'* has been displaced (*muzahlaqah*) from its place, and its original position is before the *hamza*. On this view, the sentence to which the interrogative *hamza* was attached is conjoined to the preceding sentence, and the estimated reading is: *fa-a-ḥukma al-jāhiliyyah* ("So do they seek the judgement of the Jahiliyyah?"). Without doubt, this is easier for the student of knowledge. And because the original principle is that nothing is omitted, although this opposes the principle in that the conjunction has been displaced from its place, it is easier in that a person is absolved of responsibility when he says that this sentence is conjoined to what precedes it.

As for His saying: ﴿the judgement of the Jahiliyyah﴾, Allah attributed the judgement to the Jahiliyyah. So what is meant by it? Is it the judgements of the people of the Jahiliyyah, such as burying daughters alive and the like, and forbidding some lawful things? Or is the meaning ﴿the judgement of the Jahiliyyah﴾, that is, a judgement described as ignorance?

We say: both meanings are correct, but the second is more general, because it includes every judgement based on ignorance, whether it is from the judgements of the people of the Jahiliyyah, who were the Arabs, or from the judgements of others. On this basis the meaning is: "Do they seek the judgement of ignorance?" Ignorance (*al-jahl*) is the absence of knowledge. Everything that contradicts the truth, which is the judgement of Allah, is ignorance or folly (*jahalah*). If it is without knowledge, it is ignorance; and if it is with knowledge but opposes the truth deliberately, it is folly.

﴿Do they seek the judgement of the Jahiliyyah?﴾ That is, they desire (*yabghun*), meaning they seek. It is clear that *ḥukm* (judgement) is in the accusative, and its governing word is *yabghūn*, so it is a fronted object (*mafʿūl muqaddam*) of *yabghūn*. The meaning is: "Do they seek the judgement of the Jahiliyyah?" The object was placed before the verb to convey restriction (*al-ḥaṣr*), as if these people desire nothing but the judgement of the Jahiliyyah, which is founded on ignorance or folly. This is because our rule is that placing before its place something that should be delayed conveys restriction.

Then He said: ﴿And who is better in judgement than Allah?﴾ (*man*) is an interrogative noun, but this interrogation carries the meaning of negation, since its meaning is: "None is better in judgement than Allah." Negation comes in the form of interrogation to be more eloquent, for when negation comes in the form of interrogation, it carries an element of challenge. It is as if the speaker challenges and says: "Show me a judgement better than the judgement of Allah." Therefore we say: when negation comes in the form of interrogation, it is more emphatic than bare negation, since it includes both negation and challenge.

﴿Who is better in judgement than Allah?﴾ The answer: no one is better in judgement than Allah, because His judgement, exalted is He, is founded on knowledge of what benefits His servants, and founded on mercy in what profits His servants. It is impossible for Him, blessed and exalted, to judge His servants by something that would be harm, or whose outcome is harm; never, it is impossible, because we know that His judgement issues from knowledge, wisdom and mercy.

﴿Who is better in judgement than Allah?﴾ The answer: no one is better. But for whom? ﴿For a people who are certain﴾ — certain of Allah, His names and attributes, and what these names and attributes entail. Those do not see any judgement better than the judgement of Allah.

As for the one who is weak in certainty, he may see that the judgement of other than Allah is what? Better than the judgement of Allah. For this reason the rightly guided caliphs never transgressed the judgement of Allah at all; even one of them would address the caliph if he slipped from Allah's judgement by mistake, address him and inform him of the truth. Therefore we say: the clarity of the goodness of Allah's judgement is only apparent to whom? To the certain.

As for those weak in certainty, they do not see that Allah's judgement is the best of judgements; rather they may believe that Allah's judgement has become outdated, that the community has differed and needs a new judgement. Such people are, as it were, saying by the tongue of their state: "Muhammad is not the Seal of the Prophets, because his religion does not include the reform of the age. The reform of the age is only achieved by these laws that were established by ignorant people, or disbelievers, or followers of these." Otherwise, it is impossible that a person who is certain of Allah, mighty and majestic, and of His names, attributes, acts and judgements, would see that the judgement of other than Allah is better than the judgement of Allah, or even that the judgement of other than Allah is equal to the judgement of Allah. Therefore the verse says: ﴿who is better﴾. And *aḥsan* (better) is an elative (*ism al-tafḍīl*), meaning that no judgement can equal the judgement of Allah, let alone be better than it.

* In this noble verse: the severe rebuke of those who seek a judgement other than Allah's. From where is this derived? From His saying: ﴿Do they then seek the judgement of the Jahiliyyah?﴾

* It is also derived from it, among its benefits: that these people are in great wonder for seeking the judgement of the Jahiliyyah and abandoning the judgement of Allah, which issues from knowledge, wisdom and mercy.

* Among the benefits of this verse: every judgement that opposes the judgement of Allah is a Jahili judgement.

On the basis of this: is it valid to describe the Muslims today as the Jahiliyyah of the eighteenth century, or is it not valid? Answer, O brothers.

Yes, many of the rulers of the Muslims may be described as the Jahiliyyah of this age, meaning this eighteenth century.

* Students: The twentieth century.

* The Shaykh: We do not recognise the twentieth century; we recognise the Hijri century.

* Students: The fifteenth Hijri century.

* The Shaykh: The fifteenth? The eighteenth, may Allah guide you!

* Students: The fifteenth, 1418.

* The Shaykh: Correct, the fifteenth. We took "18" as the century. Without doubt, those who, in their judgements and laws that oppose the Shari'ah, are without doubt the ignorant ones of this fifteenth century. They are ignorant, whether they like it or not.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah's judgement is the best of judgements, because of His saying: ﴿And who is better in judgement than Allah?﴾

It follows from this that when a person believes that Allah's judgement is the best of judgements, he submits to Allah's judgement and is fully pleased with it, whether or not he knows the wisdom behind it. This is true: any person who believes that someone's judgement is the best of judgements will follow it, and will not oppose or resist it.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah's judgement, even if it appears to some people as not beneficial, or as hindering progress—

They are ignorant, whether they like it or not.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah's judgement is the best of judgements, because of His saying: ﴿And who is better﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:50] (...).

It follows from this that when a person believes that Allah's judgement is the best of judgements, he submits to Allah's judgement and is fully pleased with it, whether or not he knows the wisdom behind it. This is true: any person who believes that someone's judgement is the best of judgements will, what? Follow it, and will not oppose or resist it.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah's judgement, even if it appears to some people as not righteous, or as hindering economic or social progress, or otherwise, is in fact mistaken; because what counts is the end result. It may appear to a person that this judgement is not suitable now, but in the end it is without doubt the righteous one, and we must be patient, and the outcome will be praiseworthy.

For example: many people today see no harm in dealing in usury (*ribā*), because in their view it stimulates the economy for both the taker and the giver.

We say: even if this appears to you, it has many corruptions. Look at the countries that practise it: what has happened to them, what has become of their condition? You will find among them classes that are extremely unequal: one of them is among the poorest of people, perhaps eating dirt from hunger and drinking mud from thirst, while another is enormously wealthy. All of this is because of this great disparity between the classes, and all of it is because of the forbidden dealing. But if people followed what the Prophet (ﷺ) established for his community, the economy would be balanced. You would find, for instance, that the rich do not become excessively rich, and they give the poor from the zakat, and the situation between rich and poor is close; no one oppresses another. But if miserliness is let loose in transactions and everything is permitted, there must necessarily be distinct classes; and when a distinct class exists, society is corrupted in security and in affection. You find the rich despising the poor, belittling and scorning them, and the poor hating the rich, because he sees that the rich has seized his wealth and become arrogant towards him, especially if he does not pay zakat.

So the principle is: who is better in judgement than Allah? No one, never. Now, regarding the laws that conform to the provisions of the Shari'ah, shall we describe them as the best of judgements?

* A student: Yes.

* Another student: Meaning in terms of conformity...

* The Shaykh: No. We say: this is the judgement of Allah. We do not say: this is the judgement of the law, because the judgement of Allah precedes the law. So we describe the judgements in laws that conform to the Shari'ah as the judgement of Allah, and that none is better than it. We do not make the praise attach to the law, because if we made the praise attach to the law, people would be deceived by that and accept the laws' judgements in every case. Rather we say: this is the judgement of the Shari'ah. Lying in law is, among states, what? Abhorrent, and they do not regard it as anything. In the Shari'ah it is abhorrent, and it preceded it. Indeed the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, made lying one of the attributes of the hypocrites, and said: "Lying leads to wickedness, and a man continues to lie and seeks out lying until he is recorded with Allah as a great liar."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6094), Muslim (2607/105), and the wording is his, from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud.]]

Sincerity in dealings is urged by the Shari'ah, and the laws also urge it. Here the praise must be attached not to the law, but to the Shari'ah.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: it is not permitted for a person to oppose the provisions of the Shari'ah with his intellect. This applies to practical jurisprudential matters (*al-ʿamaliyyat al-fiqhiyyat*), and in matters of belief and knowledge (*al-ʿaqadiyyat al-ʿilmiyyat*) it is all the more so; because if it is not permitted for a person to oppose the Shari'ah in practical matters where analogy (*qiyās*) enters, then the matters of knowledge and report—what about them? All the more so, because in reports the intellect has no room at all, except in a general sense, where it is possible.

On this basis, the error of those people who negated the attributes of Allah becomes clear, such as the Ash'arites (*al-Ashāʿirah*), the Mu'tazilites (*al-Muʿtazilah*), the Jahmiyyah and others. They erred a great error; because when Allah informs about Himself something, that means it is a judgement: a judgement that He is entitled to such-and-such, and He informed His servants of it. It is obligatory upon us to accept it in its apparent sense, without tampering with it. Those people judged Allah, exalted is He, by their intellects and said: "The intellect does not accept this, so we do not accept it, even if the Shari'ah brought it." What do they say about the verses? They interpret them and distort them. And if they rejected them explicitly, they would be disbelievers. That is, if they said that Allah did not settle upon the Throne, for example, they would have disbelieved. But if they say: "He settled upon the Throne, but the meaning of settling is such-and-such," this is an interpretation (*taʾwīl*), and it is to be examined.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the goodness of Allah's judgements is only recognised by one who has certainty. The more certain a person is, the more clearly and intensely the goodness of Allah's judgements becomes manifest to him. If you wish to know this, look at the rigorous scholars, how they derive from the legal rulings what reason is content with, because they are certain that Allah's judgement is the best of judgements, so Allah opens [understanding] to them.

* Among the benefits of this verse: a refutation of those who say that in the legal rulings, especially in transactions, there is something that departs from analogy, such as the chapter on *salam* (advance sale) and the chapter on *ijarah* (hire), and the like. We say: there is nothing in the legal rulings that departs from analogy. By analogy we mean reason and reflection. Rather, all the legal rulings are in accordance with analogy; but Allah opens [understanding] to whomever He wills of His servants: some people understand the conformity, and some do not.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 5, verse 51 (part 1 of 4):

Then Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿O you who have believed, do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies; they are allies of one another.﴾ [al-Ma'idah 51].

﴿O you who have believed, do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies﴾. The address here begins with a vocative (al-nida'). Why does it begin with a vocative? To alert the listener. When you speak without calling the person, the listener may become heedless, but when you call him, this serves as an alert, so the address begins with the vocative to draw attention to it and to show that it deserves care. Then this call is directed to those who have believed, to encourage and motivate them, because the more a person is a believer, the more he accepts the truth. The address is directed to the believers as an incentive and an exhortation to them, just as you say to a man: "O generous one, a guest is at your house," meaning what? You urge him by his generosity, because he is generous; you urge him to honour this guest.

Second: its direction to the believers is an indication that it is part of the requirement of faith to act upon what the address indicates, and the address in the verse is a prohibition against taking the Jews and the Christians as allies.

Third benefit: opposing what the address requires is incompatible with faith.

Is it incompatible with faith in its essence or in its perfection? This depends on what the context requires. It may be incompatible with faith in its essence, and it may be incompatible with faith in its perfection. So now we have questions which we direct. First, why did the address begin with the vocative?

* Student: For alerting.
* The Shaykh: To alert the listener.
* The Student: So that he feels the importance of the call...
* The Shaykh: Yes, alerting the listener and explaining that this address must be given care. And why was it directed to the believers?
* Student: As an incentive to them, so that they act.
* The Shaykh: An incentive to them.
* The Student: To them, so that they act.
* The Shaykh: So that they act, because this motivates a person. If he is told, "You are a believer," for example: the believer is not a liar, the believer is not a traitor, and similar things. Another aspect?
* Student: To show that the requirement of faith is to act upon what has come.
* The Shaykh: Excellent. To show that among the requirements of faith is that one acts upon the meaning of this address.
The third?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: What?
* The Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, that opposing the requirement of the address is a deficiency in faith, either in its perfection or in its essence.

﴿Do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies﴾. The Jews are those who claim to be followers of Musa (Moses), and the Christians are those who claim to be followers of 'Isa (Jesus). Yet both are not followers of Musa or of 'Isa after the mission of the Messenger, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him. Why? Because whoever denies one messenger has denied all the messengers. I always say this to you: whoever denies one messenger has denied all the messengers, whether he wills it or not. And I have brought you proof for it, which is His statement, exalted is He: ﴿The people of Noah denied the messengers﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 105], although the people of Noah encountered only one messenger, yet He said "they denied the messengers," because whoever denies a messenger has denied the very concept of messengerhood. So those who denied Noah are deniers up to the last of the messengers, Muhammad, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him. Therefore, the Jews deny all the messengers, disbelieve in all the messengers, and deny all the messengers. And likewise the Christians.

The Jews were named so either after their forefather Yahuda (Judah), or because of His statement, exalted is He: ﴿We have turned (hudna) to You﴾ [al-A'raf 156], that is, "those who repented (hadu)," meaning they returned.

As for the Christians, it has been said that it derives from "al-nusrah" (support), because 'Isa, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Who are my helpers for Allah?' The disciples (al-Hawariyyun) said, 'We are the helpers of Allah'﴾ [Al 'Imran 52]. It is also said that it is attributed to the well-known town in Palestine called Nazareth (al-Nasira), because 'Isa was there. Allah knows best. It is permissible that it be from this and from that, with no contradiction.

﴿Allies (awliya')﴾: that is, you take them as allies. But what is the meaning of taking as an ally (tawalli)? Tawalli means support and assistance, not in what returns to us, but in what returns to them, such as fighting. Whoever fights these Jews, meaning if the Jews fight someone, the Muslims fight him; if the Christians fight someone, the Muslims fight him, and so on. So wilaya (allegiance) here means support and assistance.

Remaining is whether love (mahabba) is also called by this term. Love is undoubtedly a means to support, because whoever loves someone supports him. But natural love is not included in this. For this reason Allah permitted the Muslims to marry from the Jews and the Christians. It is known that a husband and his wife must have love between them, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And among His signs is that He created for you spouses from among yourselves that you may find tranquility in them; and He placed between you affection and mercy﴾ [al-Rum 21].

He said: ﴿some of them are allies of others﴾. How do we parse (nu'rib) ﴿some of them (ba'duhum)﴾?

* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: It is a subject (mubtada'), brothers, a subject. So the clause is resumptive (isti'nafiyyah), and although it is resumptive, it works like a reason (ta'lil) for what precedes it. That is, they are the ones who ally with one another, so it is not appropriate for you to ally with them. Make allegiance for them: ﴿some of them are allies of others﴾. This applies to them as opposed to the Muslims; that is, they are united in opposing the Muslims. But among themselves, no; some of them are not allies of others. The evidence is His statement, exalted is He: ﴿The Jews said, "The Christians are not upon anything," and the Christians said, "The Jews are not upon anything"﴾ [al-Baqarah 113]. So they declare one another disbelievers, but with respect to the Muslims they are mutual helpers, some being allies of others. And what Allah, mighty and majestic, has mentioned exists until our day. Now you find the Christian state helping the Jewish state openly, with full candour and shamelessness, and they do not care. From here we know that it is obligatory upon us Muslims to take them as enemies, just as Allah, exalted is He, forbade us to take them as allies.

* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: What?
* The Student: (...) ﴿Do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies﴾.
* The Shaykh: Yes?
* The Student: That is, if two groups of enemies fight, and one of them is better for the Muslims than the other...
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* The Student: That the Muslims defend along with this one...
* The Shaykh: It is not permissible. But if there is a treaty between them, for example, and some of the disbelievers join the Muslims while another group joins the non-Muslims, then if they break the treaty with our allies, they have broken the treaty with us.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: The meaning differs. It is better to stop, because if you say: ﴿Do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies; some of them are allies of others﴾, you make the clause circumstantial (hal), meaning do not take them in this state. Therefore, I think it is marked on it: a compulsory pause (waqf lazim).
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, this is not like that.

......................... ∗∗∗ ...Be content of soul when the decree (al-qada') is issued.

That is, the divine decree (al-qada' al-qadari). That is, if Allah decrees against you, do not meet this with distress; if Allah decrees upon you something you dislike, do not meet it with distress and anger, but be content with what Allah, mighty and majestic, has decreed.

* Student: Some later scholars distinguished between the disbelievers who oppose Allah and His Messenger and the disbelievers from among the protected people (ahl al-dhimma), and said: those of the protected people are citizens, and it is permissible, as in the verse of al-Mumtahanah, to show kindness and justice (al-birr wal-qist), and to act justly towards them, and they distinguished the matter of allegiance between these and those. We should not ally with the polytheist disbelievers who oppose Allah and His Messenger, but as for the other disbelievers who are like the protected people, or others with whom we have a treaty, and so on, then allegiance is permissible.
* The Shaykh: This is an error. Allegiance is always forbidden. As for kindness and dealing justly, this is permissible towards those who do not fight us over religion and have not expelled us from our homes. So it is permissible for us to be kind to them and to act justly towards them, meaning to deal with them with justice, that is, to treat them with goodness and justice, there is no harm. But it must not settle in our souls that we shall be their allies, defending them and protecting them. As for the dhimmis who are in our lands, under our authority, who pay us the jizya (poll tax), it is incumbent upon us to prevent aggression against them as long as they are in our lands. But if they leave, we are not responsible for them.
* Student: May Allah be good to you, O Shaykh. Some states rule by the Sharia of Allah but call this legislation a "law" and put it in the form of articles. For example, regarding divorce they say: "Article number such-and-such: if a divorce is triple, the divorce does not take effect." Is this...?
* The Shaykh: The divorce does not take effect, no, what is...?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: In any case, the codification of the Sharia is different from arranging the chapters of jurisprudence. For example, if they make the chapter on divorce into articles, there is no problem, unless they intend to oblige the judges to rule by them, whether or not this matches their own choice. Because the matter of divorce involves disagreement; the matter of (...) and many other things.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, the scholars have always differed without any law, and it is not permissible to oblige the judge to rule by a specific thing, even if a group of jurists holds it.

* * *

* Student: ﴿Among those who say with their mouths, "We believe," but their hearts have not believed, and among those who are Jews, they listen much to falsehood, listening to another people who have not come to you. They distort words from their places, saying, "If you are given this, take it, but if you are not given it, then beware." And whomever Allah wills to be tested, you cannot avail him anything from Allah. Those are the ones whose hearts Allah did not will to purify. For them in this world is disgrace, and for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment﴾ [al-Ma'idah 41].
* The Shaykh: Excellent. The statement of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿Let not those grieve you﴾. Does it have two readings or three?
* Student: Two readings.
* The Shaykh: Recite them?
* The Student: ﴿Yahzunka﴾ and ﴿Yuhzinka﴾.
* The Shaykh: Excellent. Now, who is meant by "the Messenger"?
* Student: Muhammad, ﷺ.
* The Shaykh: Muhammad, ﷺ. O Allah, send blessings and peace upon him.

His statement: ﴿among those who say with their mouths "We believe"﴾, what is its place in meaning?
* Student: Explanatory (bayaniyyah).
* The Shaykh: Why?
* Student: Because of the relative pronoun.
* The Shaykh: Because of the relative pronoun ﴿those who hasten﴾. Who fits this description: they say, "We believe" with their mouths, but their hearts have not believed?
* Student: This applies to the hypocrites.
* The Shaykh: May Allah bless you, good.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: That is, the lam is for transitivity, and it is also called the lam of reinforcement, and the meaning is that they listen to falsehood from their rabbis, saying: "Muhammad is not a messenger."
* The Student: The lam in "al-kadhib" (the falsehood) may also be for causation, that they listen to the report from the Prophet ﷺ in order to plot (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, the lam may also be for causation, and the meaning is that they listen in order to lie, so they say: "We heard Muhammad say such-and-such." Can we interpret the verse as having both meanings?
* Student: Yes, it can be read as both.
* The Shaykh: As both together, because this happens from them, and this happens from them.

His statement: ﴿li-l-suht﴾. Are there three readings or four?
* Student: Two readings.
* The Shaykh: Two? Which are they?
* Student: ﴿al-suht﴾ with a sukun on the ha', and ﴿al-suhut﴾ with a damma.
* The Shaykh: Yes. What is meant by al-suht?
* The Student: Every wealth acquired by a forbidden means.
* The Shaykh: Every wealth acquired by a forbidden means is called suht?
* The Student: For two reasons: because it is in itself deprived of blessing, or because it destroys lawful wealth.
* The Shaykh: Either it itself has no blessing and passes away quickly, or when it mixes with something, blessing is removed from it.
* The Shaykh: The Qurazi... what? He is not killed for him, and the reverse is killed. So Allah, exalted is He, made clear that they are unjust in this ruling, and that what was prescribed for them in the Torah was what? That a life is for a life. So the meaning of "prescribed" (kutiba) here is the manner of retaliation (qisas), not the obligation of retaliation. This is what is apparent from the context. It has been said that the meaning is that Allah obligated retaliation upon them, and that they may either take retaliation or pardon. Good. Here He mentioned which of your organs?
* Student: The eye for the eye.
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* The Student: And the nose for the nose.
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* The Student: And the ear for the ear.
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* The Student: And the tooth for the tooth.
* The Shaykh: Good. Four organs. But in the body there are more than four organs, so why was it not specified?
* Student: This is by way of example, and the rest of the organs are included by way of analogy (qiyas).
* The Shaykh: This is by way of illustration, and the rest is by way of analogy. Why did He specify these and not specify the other organs, leaving these to be analogized from them?
* The Student: Because most injuries occur in them, Shaykh.
* The Shaykh: Yes, that is possible; we have mentioned it to you, but...
* The Student: Some people have (...).
* The Shaykh: What?
* The Student: At these moments, the Jews and the Christians.
* The Shaykh: Most of them are what the brother said.
* The Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: That is, it seems they disagreed about these organs, so Allah, mighty and majestic, made clear that this is its ruling, and it seems the other organs are not subject to disagreement among them.

﴿And wounds, retaliation﴾. Does it include every wound?
* Student: According to the jurists, no.
* The Shaykh: No. We are interpreting the verse; the jurists are not our concern. The jurists come later, in the detailed discussion.
* The Student: Yes, every wound.
* The Shaykh: Every wound?
* The Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Do you all agree with this?
* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Yes?
* The Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: That is, it does not include every wound, but rather it means...?
* The Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: What is the evidence?
* The Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: What is the evidence that the intended meaning is the wounds in which retaliation is possible?
* The Student: That is (...), I am surprised (...).
* The Shaykh: This is a reason; I want the evidence.
* Student: His statement, exalted is He: ﴿the tooth for the tooth﴾ and ﴿the eye for the eye﴾.
* The Shaykh: No, that is wrong; these are not wounds, these are organs.
* Student: As they said, Shaykh.
* The Shaykh: What?
* The Student: They are included in retaliation here.
* The Shaykh: Yes, but what is the evidence for the ruling? Is it clear now?
* The Student: What the Sunnah has transmitted.
* The Shaykh: Yes, what is at the end?
* Student: Enough (...).
* The Shaykh: Wrong, wrong.
* The Student: The ruling of the verse.
* The Shaykh: What (...)?
* The Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: (...) retaliation ﴿and wounds, retaliation﴾? So retaliation is only taken for a wound in which retaliation is possible. Now, what is the jurists' criterion for the wounds in which retaliation is taken?
* Student: Where there is injustice.
* The Shaykh: Yes, but what is it? They have a perceptible criterion.
* Student: That it does not reach the bone.
* The Shaykh: Yes, every wound that reaches the bone, good. And the correct view, what do you have? What is the correct view? That every wound in which retaliation is possible, whether it reaches the bone or does not reach it?
* Student: Retaliation for it is obligatory.
* The Shaykh: Retaliation for it is obligatory. Yes, go ahead. Yes, and that is so: ﴿Let them judge (wal-yahkum)﴾. By the rule that the imperative lam, when preceded by a waw, is vowelled with a sukun, and it is now present in our Mushaf.

The statement of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿And We sent, following in their footsteps, 'Isa son of Maryam﴾. Can it be taken from this that 'Isa son of Maryam is the last of the prophets of the Children of Israel?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Can it be taken?
* The Student: He said: ﴿qaffayna﴾, meaning We sent after him.
* The Shaykh: Yes, but can it be taken from it that 'Isa son of Maryam is the last of the prophets of the Children of Israel?
* The Student: Yes, it can be taken.
* The Shaykh: How so?
* The Student: Because He, glorified and exalted is He, made clear that He sent after Musa the prophets of the Children of Israel; He sent after 'Isa.
* The Shaykh: He sent after 'Isa? That is not very clear.
* The Student: That the transitivity (...).
* The Shaykh: That is, if there had been anyone after 'Isa, would he be the one who was followed (al-muqaffa)?
* The Student: Yes, he is the original.
* The Shaykh: Is that what you mean?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Do you all agree with this?
* The Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Yes. This verse, ﴿We sent, following in their footsteps, 'Isa﴾, means that if there had been a prophet after him, he would have been the one who was followed.

The jurists, may Allah have mercy on them, took from this that whoever has no father in the legal sense, his mother inherits from him the inheritance of a father. Is this correct?
* Student: (...).

**Shaykh:** Allah made ʿĪsā a son of Maryam. If he is her son, she must be his mother, since he was not attributed to anyone other than her. This is the preponderant opinion. I think we explained this to you, did we not? Did we not tell you that a son who has no legal father has his mother as his father?

**Students:** We said that regarding attribution only.

**Shaykh:** Only regarding attribution?

**Students:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** No, even in inheritance, according to the preponderant opinion, even in inheritance. If he dies leaving his mother and no father, she inherits as a mother and as a father. She takes one-third as a mother, and the remainder as a father.

The phrase ﴿مُصَدِّقًا لِمَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ﴾ (confirming what is before it) occurs often in the Qur'an, sometimes describing the Qur'an and sometimes describing something other than the Qur'an. What is the meaning of ﴿مُصَدِّقًا لِمَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ﴾?

**Student:** ﴿مُصَدِّقًا لِمَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ﴾ means that it confirms what came before it.

**Shaykh:** What it "sent forward"?

**Student:** What came before it.

**Shaykh:** Yes, confirming what preceded it?

**Student:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** Then what is the meaning of "confirming it"?

**Student:** That it confirms it and shows that it is true.

**Shaykh:** How? It confirms it and shows that it is true? Is the meaning one and the same?

**Student:** It bears witness to its truthfulness.

**Shaykh:** "Confirms it" means "bears witness to its truthfulness." That is one.

**Student:** And it supports it.

**Shaykh:** And it supports it. What is the difference?

**Student:** It confirms what came in it of reports.

**Shaykh:** How?

**Student:** It confirms what came in it of reports; it confirms its origin, and it confirms what came in it of reports.

**Shaykh:** What do you mean by "what came in it of reports"?

**Student:** I mean the reports about previous nations and later nations; the Qur'an comes confirming these reports.

**Shaykh:** That is not clear.

**Student:** It is acted upon, so long as... (...)

**Shaykh:** That is, it confirms it: it bears witness that it is true. That is one. It confirms it: it bears witness to the occurrence of what the earlier Book reported. Do you understand?

**Student:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** His words: ﴿مَوْعِظَةً لِلْمُتَّقِينَ﴾ (a admonition for the God-fearing). Why did He specify the God-fearing for this admonition, when the laws are an admonition for all people?

**Student:** Because they are the ones who benefit from it.

**Shaykh:** Because they are the ones who benefit from it. Well done.

Can it be derived from this that whenever a person's taqwa (God-consciousness) increases, his receptiveness to admonition from the heavenly Books increases?

**Student:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** Yes. How is that? We want a rule from which we can benefit.

**Student:** (...)

**Shaykh:** No.

**Student:** It increases with its increase and decreases with its decrease.

**Shaykh:** Well done, exactly. Brothers, this is a rule we have mentioned to you: a ruling attached to an attribute grows in strength with the strength of that attribute, and diminishes with its diminishing. If you say, for example, "Honor the man for his generosity," then whoever is more generous deserves more honor.

**Student:** I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming what is before it of the Book and as a guardian over it. So judge between them by what Allah has revealed, and do not follow their desires away from the truth that has come to you. For each of you We have appointed a law and a path. And had Allah willed, He would have made you one nation, but [He did so] to test you in what He has given you. So race to [all that is] good. To Allah is your return, all of you, and He will inform you about that over which you used to differ.﴾ [al-Mā'idah 48]

**Shaykh:** His words: ﴿مُصَدِّقًا لِمَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ﴾. What is the grammatical position of ﴿مُصَدِّقًا﴾?

**Student:** A ḥāl (circumstantial accusative).

**Shaykh:** From where?

**Student:** A ḥāl from ﴿الْكِتَابَ﴾ (the Book).

**Shaykh:** And His words: ﴿لِمَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ مِنَ الْكِتَابِ﴾ (what is before it of the Book): what is meant by it?

**Student:** (...) the earlier Books.

**Shaykh:** That is, all the Books?

**Student:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** ﴿مُهَيْمِنًا عَلَيْهِ﴾ (a guardian over it): what does it mean?

**Student:** It means that it is a judge over it and dominant over it.

**Shaykh:** Does this attribute indicate that the Noble Book, the Qur'an, abrogates (nāsikh, i.e., supersedes by naskh, abrogation) all the Books that preceded it?

**Student:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** Do you agree with this?

**Students:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** Yes. Now, His words: ﴿وَلَا تَتَّبِعْ أَهْوَاءَهُمْ عَمَّا جَاءَكَ مِنَ الْحَقِّ﴾ (do not follow their desires away from the truth that has come to you). How do we parse ﴿عَمَّا جَاءَكَ مِنَ الْحَقِّ﴾? What is it attached to?

**Student:** ﴿وَلَا تَتَّبِعْ أَهْوَاءَهُمْ﴾ is attached to an implied element. The meaning: "Do not follow their desires, lest you turn away from what has come to you of the truth."

**Shaykh:** "Turn away" is difficult.

**Student:** "Deviate."

**Shaykh:** "Deviating from what has come to you of the truth." Good. How did He describe the rulings they believe in as "desire"?

**Student:** Because they are not based on sound law or sound reason.

**Shaykh:** That is, their adherence to them?

**Student:** Adherence by following their desires.

**Shaykh:** By following their desires. Because, after Islam came, they must submit their disputes to Islam.

What is the difference between sharīʿah and minhāj?

**Student:** Linguistically, sharʿah means...

**Shaykh:** The meaning is: sharʿah and minhāj, is it coordination by synonymy or coordination by contrast?

**Student:** The sharʿah is the established law for all; as for the minhāj, it is the path each nation takes to apply the law.

**Shaykh:** So the sharʿah is the sharīʿah, and the minhāj is adherence to the sharīʿah (...).

Is there in the verse a refutation of the Qadariyyah?

**Student:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** Where?

**Student:** In His words, exalted is He: ﴿وَلَوْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ﴾ (And had Allah willed).

**Shaykh:** Only ﴿وَلَوْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ﴾?

**Student:** ﴿وَلَوْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ لَجَعَلَكُمْ أُمَّةً وَاحِدَةً﴾ (And had Allah willed, He would have made you one nation).

**Shaykh:** ﴿وَلَوْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ لَجَعَلَكُمْ أُمَّةً وَاحِدَةً﴾, meaning upon one religion?

**Student:** That Allah, mighty and majestic, has established that their disagreement is only by the will of Allah, glorified and exalted, and that disbelief by one who disbelieves and faith by one who believes follows the will of Allah, glorified and exalted.

**Shaykh:** Excellent, yes, correct.

* * *

**Student:** I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿And that you judge between them by what Allah has revealed, and do not follow their desires, and beware of them lest they tempt you away from some of what Allah has revealed to you. And if they turn away, then know that Allah intends only to afflict them for some of their sins. And indeed, many of the people are defiantly disobedient. Is it then the judgment of [the time of] ignorance they desire? But who is better than Allah in judgment for a people who are certain?﴾ [al-Mā'idah 49–50]

**Shaykh:** His words: ﴿وَأَنِ احْكُمْ بَيْنَهُمْ بِمَا أَنْزَلَ اللَّهُ﴾. How many recitations are there for it?

**Student:** ﴿وَأَنِ احْكُمْ بَيْنَهُمْ بِمَا أَنْزَلَ اللَّهُ﴾.

**Shaykh:** Yes, say: one.

**Student:** One.

**Shaykh:** Wrong.

**Student:** Two recitations.

**Shaykh:** Two recitations. What are they?

**Student:** ﴿أَنِ احْكُمْ﴾ and the second ﴿أَنُ احْكُمْ﴾.

**Shaykh:** ﴿أَنُ احْكُمْ﴾.

**Shaykh:** The recitation ﴿أَنِ احْكُمْ﴾ with a kasra is clear, because the letter after it is a hamzat al-wasl (connecting hamza). But why is ﴿أَنُ احْكُمْ﴾ vocalized with a ḍammah, although the rule is that such a letter is vocalized with a kasra? I have not actually mentioned this to you. Whoever knows it is a champion, the champion of the race even if he did not race.

**Student:** Observing the vowel of the kāf.

**Shaykh:** Correct, observing the vowel of the kāf. That is, it follows what comes after it: ﴿وَأَنُ احْكُمْ﴾.

His words: ﴿وَلَا تَتَّبِعْ أَهْوَاءَهُمْ﴾. In the first verse also ﴿وَلَا تَتَّبِعْ أَهْوَاءَهُمْ﴾. What is the benefit of repeating the prohibition against following these people's desires?

**Student:** Because the Jews were eager that the Prophet ﷺ should follow their desires, and for this reason Allah said...

**Shaykh:** That is, the extreme caution against following the desires of the disbelievers. Is that right?

His words: ﴿أَنْ يَفْتِنُوكَ﴾ (lest they tempt you). How do we parse it?

**Student:** There are two possibilities here.

**Shaykh:** Two possibilities. The first?

**Student:** (...) as a substitute of inclusion for the pronoun.

**Shaykh:** ﴿احْذَرْهُمْ﴾ means "beware"?

**Student:** Their temptation.

**Shaykh:** Yes, indeed: beware of them, their temptation. You know that the substitute (badal) is what is intended by the ruling.

*The follower intended by the ruling without an intermediary*
*...................*

Complete the line.

**Student:** An intermediary, a substitute.

**Shaykh:**
*...................*
*Without an intermediary, it is what is named a substitute.*

So the meaning is: beware of their temptation. What is meant by "temptation" here?

**Student:** Turning away.

**Shaykh:** Turning away, good. Is there in the verse anything indicating that sins are a cause of deviation?

**Student:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** Sins are a cause of deviation?

**Student:** (...)

**Shaykh:** From where do you take it?

**Student:** From His words: ﴿فَاعْلَمْ أَنَّمَا يُرِيدُ اللَّهُ أَنْ يُصِيبَهُمْ بِبَعْضِ ذُنُوبِهِمْ﴾ (then know that Allah intends only to afflict them for some of their sins).

**Shaykh:** Yes. Do you agree with this? It is said: it is derived from His words: ﴿فَإِنْ تَوَلَّوْا فَاعْلَمْ أَنَّمَا يُرِيدُ اللَّهُ أَنْ يُصِيبَهُمْ بِبَعْضِ ذُنُوبِهِمْ﴾, and likewise what preceded: ﴿وَمَوْعِظَةً لِلْمُتَّقِينَ﴾ (an admonition for the God-fearing).

Can it be derived from the verse that if a person sees himself turning away from the Book of Allah, mighty and majestic, whether from its verbal recitation, its meaningful recitation, or its practical recitation (i.e., acting upon it), then he must treat himself?

**Student:** It can be derived.

**Shaykh:** It can be derived from it. And that this is the cause of this turning away?

**Student:** Sins.

**Shaykh:** It is sins, exactly. Yes.

* * *

**Student:** ﴿O Messenger, let not those hasten to disbelief grieve you, [such as] those who say with their mouths, "We believe," but their hearts have not believed, and among the Jews are those who listen much to falsehood, listening to another people who have not come to you. They distort words from their [proper] places...﴾ [al-Mā'idah 41]

**Shaykh:** No, my brother, wait. This connection is wrong, because it disrupts the meaning. That is one point. The second point: I see many of our reciter brothers now, when their breath runs out, they repeat the portion before the last by a word or two, although what they repeat is connected to what precedes it, with what they did not repeat. This requires either continuity, so that the person begins from the beginning of the verse and then stops his breath at that place. What we hold is that if breath is cut short for a valid reason, one begins from where one stopped. Unless it is cut off in the middle of a word, in which case there is no harm in repeating the word. Some people recite four verses, five verses, and the five become fifteen verses, because they repeat. This is not correct, and I do not think the Companions did such a thing.

That is why, when some reciters now adhere to this, as the brother did with ﴿لَمْ يَأْتُوكَ يُحَرِّفُونَ﴾, the meaning changes. But the proper pause is at ﴿لِقَوْمٍ آخَرِينَ لَمْ يَأْتُوكَ﴾ and ﴿يُحَرِّفُونَ الْكَلِمَ مِنْ بَعْدِ مَوَاضِعِهِ﴾ (they distort words from their [proper] places).

**Student:** ﴿...they distort words from their [proper] places. They say, "If you are given this, take it, but if you are not given it, beware." And whoever Allah intends to test, you will not have any power for him against Allah. Those are the ones whom Allah does not intend to purify their hearts. For them in this world is disgrace, and for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment.﴾ [al-Mā'idah 41]

**Shaykh:** The words of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿وَمِنَ الَّذِينَ هَادُوا سَمَّاعُونَ﴾ (and among the Jews are those who listen much to falsehood). Is it a resumed (new) sentence, or is it coordinated with His words: ﴿مِنَ الَّذِينَ قَالُوا آمَنَّا بِأَفْوَاهِهِمْ﴾ (among those who say with their mouths, "We believe")?

**Student:** Both (...).

**Shaykh:** That is: ﴿لَا يَحْزُنْكَ الَّذِينَ يُسَارِعُونَ فِي الْكُفْرِ مِنَ الَّذِينَ قَالُوا آمَنَّا بِأَفْوَاهِهِمْ وَلَمْ تُؤْمِنْ قُلُوبُهُمْ وَمِنَ الَّذِينَ هَادُوا﴾. Good. If we say it like this, how do we parse ﴿سَمَّاعُونَ﴾?

**Student:** A predicate (khabar).

**Shaykh:** A predicate? That is not correct, since a prepositional phrase precedes it. Who knows?

**Student:** ﴿سَمَّاعُونَ﴾ is the subject (mubtada').

**Shaykh:** Wrong.

**Student:** (...)

**Shaykh:** If we make it coordinated with ﴿مِنَ الَّذِينَ قَالُوا آمَنَّا بِأَفْوَاهِهِمْ﴾?

**Student:** A nominative ḥāl.

**Shaykh:** A nominative ḥāl (...).

**Student:** (...)

**Shaykh:** And the estimate (taqdīr)?

**Student:** A people.

**Shaykh:** No, that is when we make ﴿وَمِنَ الَّذِينَ هَادُوا﴾ a fronted predicate.

**Shaykh:** A predicate of what?

**Shaykh:** Well done: "Among those who say with their mouths 'We believe' and whose hearts have not believed, and among those who are Jews, they are those who listen much to falsehood." You pause at ﴿وَمِنَ الَّذِينَ هَادُوا﴾, because it is coordinated with what? With ﴿الَّذِينَ قَالُوا آمَنَّا بِأَفْوَاهِهِمْ﴾. Then you say ﴿سَمَّاعُونَ﴾, meaning: they are listeners. But if we make ﴿مِنَ الَّذِينَ هَادُوا﴾ a fronted predicate, then ﴿سَمَّاعُونَ﴾ becomes an adjective of an elided noun, which is the subject. The estimate: "And among those who are Jews are a people who listen much to falsehood."

﴿سَمَّاعُونَ لِلْكَذِبِ﴾: is the lām here for causation (taʿlīl) or for emphasis (taqwiyah)?

**Student:** For causation.

**Shaykh:** The lām is for causation. Meaning: if it is for causation, what does the meaning become?

**Shaykh:** No, if it means "they listen for falsehood," then it is no longer causation.

**Shaykh:** Someone asks: What is your opinion on the statement of some contemporary scholars that the clear (muḥkam) portion on which the principles and general rules of the sharīʿah are built does not exceed one percent, and that the ambiguous (mutashābih) portion is estimated at about ninety-nine percent, and that this is why we see this great disagreement among the jurists?

**Shaykh:** I say: this indicates his ignorance, and that everything is ambiguous to him because he does not know. Otherwise, the ambiguous portion does not represent one percent of the evidences of the sharīʿah. All of them, praise be to Allah, are clear and manifest. But Allah says: ﴿And whoever Allah does not give light, for him there is no light.﴾ [al-Nūr 40]

* * *

**Student:** I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿O you who have believed, do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies; they are allies of one another. And whoever is an ally to them among you is [one] of them. Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾ (51) ﴿So you see those in whose hearts is disease hastening toward them, saying, "We fear that a misfortune may strike us." But perhaps Allah will bring victory or a decision from Him, so they will become, over what they had concealed within themselves, regretful.﴾ (52) ﴿And those who believed will say, "Are these the ones who swore by Allah their strongest oaths that they were with you?" Their deeds have become worthless, and they have become losers.﴾ [al-Mā'idah 51–53]

**Shaykh:** I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿O you who have believed, do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies.﴾

Earlier we mentioned that when Allah says ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾ ("O you who have believed"), the address begins with what? Why does the address begin with a vocative?

**Student:** To alert.

**Shaykh:** To alert?

**Student:** (...)

**Shaykh:** No.

**Student:** To a serious matter.

**Shaykh:** Yes, to show the importance of what the person is being addressed with. It is a kind of alerting, but not merely alerting; rather it is evidence of the importance of what is directed to him by this address.

We also mentioned that when ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾ is attached to faith, it has benefits?

**Student:** The first benefit: encouragement and incitement.

**Shaykh:** Encouragement and incitement, as if He said: "Because of your faith, do such and such."

**Student:** The second: that the action required of this addressee is a requirement of faith.

**Shaykh:** The second: to indicate that this action is a requirement of faith. And the third?

**Student:** That opposing the requirement of the address contradicts the perfection of faith.

**Shaykh:** Well done, that opposing the requirement of the address contradicts the perfection of faith. So, praise be to Allah, it does not need to be discussed further, because it is clear.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 5, verse 51 (part 3 of 4):

﴿Do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies﴾: ﴿the Jews and the Christians﴾ is the first object, and ﴿allies﴾ is the second object. The verb ittakhadha (to take) here, in this sense, carries the meaning of "to make," i.e., do not make them allies. The Jews are the followers of Musa (Moses), as they claim, and the Christians are the followers of Isa (Jesus).

﴿Allies﴾ is the plural of waliy, and its pattern is afla'ā; for this reason it is not declined, because of the presence of the feminine extended alif (alif al-ta'nith al-mamduda), awliyā'.

So what is the meaning of awliyā'?

The word waliy is applied to several meanings in the Arabic language, but its meaning cannot be understood or determined in every context except after surveying all its occurrences. For example, "The ruler is the guardian of whoever has no guardian" [narrated by Abu Dawud (2083), al-Tirmidhi (1102), and Ibn Majah (1879) from the hadith of 'A'isha]; this is a guardianship with a particular meaning. "The master is the walī of his freed slave" is a guardianship with a meaning. "For indeed Allah is his Mawla" [al-Tahrim 4] is a guardianship with a meaning. The point is that wilaya in the Arabic language has multiple meanings.

So which guardianship is it that Allah forbade us to take the Jews and the Christians as allies? It is support (al-munasara): that we support them, whether we support them against Muslims or against disbelievers. It is not permissible for us to support them against disbelievers unless our supporting them against those disbelievers serves the interest of Islam. If there is an interest in it, such as when a war breaks out between two groups of disbelievers and the second party does more harm to the Muslims than the other, then there is no harm in supporting them here, not for their benefit but for the benefit of the Muslims, because this falls under averting the greater of two evils with the lesser.

So "awliyā'" is the plural of "waliy," and the intended meaning of wilaya here is what? Support and assistance. Its ramifications will come, God willing, in the benefits.

He says: ﴿some of them are allies of others﴾, meaning some Jews are allies of other Jews, and some Christians are allies of other Christians, because they share one creed and one path, so by the requirement of natural disposition (fitra) it is necessary that some of them support others.

Does this include that some of them, i.e., Jews, are allies of some Christians, meaning that Christians and Jews are allies of one another?

The apparent meaning is that the verse includes this; indeed, if it were said that this is what is most immediately understood, it would be more fitting, because the prohibition concerns both groups, so each of these groups is allies of the other. Although the Jews disparage the Christians and the Christians disparage the Jews ﴿The Jews say: "The Christians are not upon anything," and the Christians say: "The Jews are not upon anything"﴾ [al-Baqarah 113], they are nonetheless one against the Muslims; they support one another against the Muslims.

﴿Some of them are allies of others﴾: this sentence serves as a justification for the prohibition, meaning it is not fitting for you to take them as allies, because these people are allies of one another, so it is not fitting for you, O Muslims, to be allies to them.

﴿And whoever among you takes them as allies, then indeed he is one of them﴾: this is a severe warning and a severe threat that whoever takes them as allies is one of them. But is he one of them outwardly? Yes, he is one of them outwardly without doubt, by reason of assistance and support.

But is he one of them inwardly? We say: it is possible; this support and assistance may lead to love, and then to following their religion, because sins draw one another along. As for the outward matter, the matter is clear. That is why Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Have you not seen those who took as allies a people with whom Allah is angry? They are neither of you nor of them﴾ [al-Mujadila 14]; meaning inwardly. Yet outwardly they are with the Jews, for example, and what is meant by them are the hypocrites in the verse we cited just before.

So ﴿whoever among you takes them as allies, then he is one of them﴾ is in what respect? Outwardly; and this may lead to the inward and to sharing with them in their beliefs, their deeds, and their manners.

Here there is a grammatical difficulty: ﴿man yatawallahum﴾. It is well known that the conditional "man" jazms (apocopates) the verb, yet here we find the verb with a fatha: ﴿man yatawallahum﴾?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: The fatha on the lam is not an inflectional fatha, because the final letter of the verb has been elided.

So this is jazm, but the weak-final verb is apocopated by deleting what? The weak letter. Indeed the weak-final verb is apocopated by deleting the weak letter. The original form, were it not for "man," would be "yatawallāhum" with an alif, ﴿and whoever among you takes them as allies, then he is one of them﴾.

﴿Indeed Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾: the sentence here is undoubtedly a resumptive (isti'nafiyya) sentence, and it serves as a justification for his saying: ﴿and whoever among you takes them as allies, then he is one of them﴾, as if he said: whoever among you takes them as allies, then he is a wrongdoer.

﴿Indeed Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾. The root of ẓulm (wrongdoing) is deficiency, and from it is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Each of the two gardens brought forth its produce and did not fall short therein at all﴾ [al-Kahf 33]. Does your brother explain to us the meaning of ﴿did not fall short therein at all﴾?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, the two gardens: ﴿We made for one of them two gardens of grapevines and surrounded them with palm trees and placed between them fields of crops (32). Each of the two gardens brought forth its produce and did not fall short therein at all﴾ [al-Kahf 32, 33]. What is the meaning of ﴿did not fall short﴾?
* The student: All its good (...).
* The Shaykh: That is, it did not diminish. So the root of ẓulm is deficiency; the root of ẓulm is deficiency, and the wrongdoer is deficient, because he has not done what is obligatory upon him, so he wrongs his soul by depriving it of its due. Thus ﴿the wrongdoers﴾ are those who deprive themselves of their due, and this is by plunging themselves into sins, either by abandoning obligations or by committing prohibited acts.

As for the phrase ﴿al-ẓālimīn﴾ here, what is the function of "al"? You must know that when "al" is attached to a derived noun, it is a relative pronoun (ism mawsul), is it not so?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Ibn Malik says:
"A descriptive, explicit, the connective is 'al' ∗∗∗ ..................."
Whenever "al" is attached to a derived noun, active or passive participle, it is a relative noun, not a particle; it is a relative noun. So here "al" is a relative noun, and we have a principle, indeed a rule: that relative nouns convey generality. Accordingly ﴿al-ẓālimīn﴾ means every wrongdoer, for Allah the Exalted does not guide them.

The guidance negated here is guidance of success (hidayat al-tawfiq); as for guidance of clarification (hidayat al-bayan), it is established for everyone, even the disbelievers, for Allah the Mighty and Majestic has guided them. Read the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Has there come upon man a period of time when he was not a thing worth mentioning? (1) Indeed, We created man from a sperm-drop mixture that We may try him, and We made him hearing and seeing (2) Indeed, We guided him to the way, be he grateful or be he ungrateful﴾ [al-Insan 1–3]; meaning he is guided, Allah guided him to the path, made it clear to him, whether he is a disbeliever or grateful. And read the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿As for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance﴾ [Fussilat 17].

So ﴿Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ is guidance of success or guidance of clarification?
* The students: Success.
* The Shaykh: Guidance of success.

* In this noble verse: the importance of avoiding taking Jews and Christians as allies is made clear, and the reason for that is that Allah began the address with a call.
* Among its benefits: that avoiding taking Jews and Christians as allies is a requirement of faith.
* Among its benefits: that taking them as allies necessitates a deficiency in faith, and may possibly nullify faith and remove it entirely.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Jews and Christians are allies of one another. Does the meaning refer to one religion or to both religions? It is general: one religion and both religions. The saying of Allah the Exalted supports this: ﴿And those who disbelieve, some of them are allies of others﴾ [al-Anfal 73].
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that a Christian inherits from a Jew, and a Jew inherits from a Christian, because of His saying: ﴿allies of one another﴾, and inheritance is based on wilaya. That is why the Prophet ﷺ said: "Give the shares of inheritance to their people, and what remains goes to the closest male relative" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6732) and Muslim (1615/2) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas]. Many scholars held this view and said: disbelief is one religion, so disbelievers inherit from one another.

Perhaps someone may say: the People of the Book inherit from one another because they share the status of People of the Book, unlike the Magians with a People of the Book.

The third opinion on the matter: a Jew does not inherit from a Christian, nor a Christian from a Jew. This view is the most correct of the opinions, based on the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "People of two different religions do not inherit from one another" [narrated by Abu Dawud (2911) and Ibn Majah (2731) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr]. There is no doubt that the Jews are upon one religion and the Christians upon another.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: clarifying that Christians, Jews, and all other disbelievers are allies of one another in opposition to whom? To the Muslims. For if this is the case between Jews and Christians, and some of them misguide others, saying: "Not upon anything," meaning not upon anything of the religion, then how much more so with others.

Given this, it follows from this benefit that it is obligatory upon the Muslims to beware of their enemies, and to set aside their differences among themselves, so that they may be one hand against whom? Against their enemies who openly declare hostility.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: warning against allying with Jews and Christians, based on His saying: ﴿And whoever among you takes them as allies, then he is one of them﴾. Does this indicate that such allegiance is among the major sins? Yes, because being one of them is like disavowing oneself from the Muslims, and it is like the saying of the Messenger ﷺ: "Whoever cheats is not of us" [narrated by Muslim (102) and al-Tirmidhi (1315), the wording of the latter, from the hadith of Abu Hurayra]. So taking Jews and Christians as allies is among the major sins, and wilaya, as we said, is support.

But does it fall under this that a person seeks help from them for a specific matter, such as having a Jewish or Christian engineer whom he employs to perfect the construction, or the perfecting of a machine, or the like?

The answer: No; because although you seek his help, you feel that you are above him, and he is to you in the position of a hired worker. Moreover, whenever a person can take a Muslim worker, that is preferable without doubt, as the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And a believing slave-woman is better than an idolatress, even though she might please you. And do not marry polytheistic men until they believe. And a believing slave is better than a polytheist, even though he might please you﴾ [al-Baqarah 221]. "And because 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) disapproved of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari (may Allah be pleased with him) employing a Christian scribe. When this Christian's writing was brought to 'Umar, he was greatly impressed, because the writing was excellent and the accounts were thoroughly precise. So he said to Abu Musa: 'Bring your scribe.' He said: 'O Commander of the Faithful, he does not enter the mosque.' 'Umar became angry and said: 'Enough! Who is this?' He said: 'This is a Christian.' He said: 'How can you trust him when Allah has deemed him a traitor?' He rebuked him severely, and Abu Musa insisted, saying: 'He is a competent man.' He said to him: 'The Christian is dead, and peace be upon you'" [narrated by al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan al-Kubra (10/127) and Shu'ab al-Iman (8939)].

That is, suppose he has now died, what would your situation be now? And he will die, sooner or later.

So observe how the rightly guided Caliph was wary of entrusting the affairs of the Muslims to non-Muslims. That is, it is not permissible for us to make him, for example, a trustee over the public treasury or a trustee over matters that concern the Muslims in general; this is undoubtedly treachery, because how could one entrust with the affairs of the Muslims someone whom Allah the Mighty and Majestic has deemed a traitor? As for a specific matter, there is no harm in it, because the Companions employed servants from among non-Muslims. But for a general matter, this is not permissible under any circumstances, because however much the disbeliever feigns sincerity toward you, know that he is an enemy.

Is it part of allegiance to seek their help against our enemies?

The answer: No. If we are in need of them, we may seek their help, on condition that we are secure from their treachery; because the Prophet ﷺ had allies when he concluded the truce with the polytheists. Who were his allies? His allies were the Khuza'a; they were with the Messenger, peace be upon him. Indeed, when Quraysh attacked Khuza'a, though they were disbelievers, the Prophet ﷺ regarded that as a breach of the covenant and campaigned against Quraysh. So the point is that seeking their help, when there is need for it, is permissible, on condition that we are secure from their treachery; if we are not secure, then it is not permissible.

Is their friendship part of allegiance to them?

Yes, friendship with them is part of allegiance to them, meaning seeking their friendship, so that the affection becomes mutual; for this reason He said: ﴿You will not find a people who believe in Allah and the Last Day loving [yuwaddūn] those who oppose Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Mujadila 22]. He did not say "yawaddūn"; He said "yuwaddūn," so that the love is between the two parties, because one who loves must give what produces love, and whoever gives what produces love does not want it to go to waste; it must be in exchange for something. Therefore we say: loving them is forbidden and not permissible: ﴿You will not find a people who believe in Allah and the Last Day loving those who oppose Allah and His Messenger, even if they were their fathers or their sons or their brothers or their kindred﴾ [al-Mujadila 22].

Is it part of allegiance that we love them when they do something beneficial to people?

Is that not allegiance? Yes; in any case we love their deed without doubt. If they do what serves the benefit of humanity, we must love their deed, because it is good and beneficial. But to love them themselves is open to examination; that is, to love them for the sake of this good deed, not in a general way, is open to examination. However, what they have done of good cannot be denied, nor can we say: they did nothing. Rather we love the good they have done. Today, unfortunately, they make airplanes for us. Do we love them for making airplanes? No, we do not love them themselves; we love their act: making airplanes we love, and we wish they would make more good aircraft for us. But as for loving them themselves, no, even though we know that when they do this they intend their own benefit. Yet as long as there is good in it, we love their deed if it is good.

Is it part of their friendship that we buy and sell with them?

No, O people; they benefit.
They buy an item for ten and sell it to us for twenty. Is this considered part of allegiance to them?
* Students: No.
* The Shaykh: No, why? Because the Messenger, peace be upon him, bought from them. The Messenger, peace be upon him, the most devout of people to Allah, bought from them, even though they would profit. But this matter has nothing to do with affection or love; rather a person does it for what? For his own benefit; he does it for his benefit. Accordingly, dealing with companies, disbelieving companies, is not considered allegiance, even though they profit, because we too will not deal with them or buy from them except for our own benefit, without doubt.

Is it part of their friendship that we host them if they host us? That is, if a disbeliever comes to you and you honor him as a guest, is this part of allegiance to them?
* Students: No.
* The Shaykh: It is not; because Allah says: ﴿Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you over religion and do not expel you from your homes, from being righteous toward them﴾, and this is kindness; ﴿and act justly toward them﴾, this is justice; ﴿Indeed, Allah loves the just (8). He only forbids you from those who fight you over religion and expel you from your homes and aid in your expulsion, from allying with them [tawallawhum]﴾ [al-Mumtahina 8, 9]. This is evident, and the wisdom is that if they fight us over our religion, expel us from our homes, and support others in expelling us, it is not wise for us to make them allies under any circumstances.

Is it part of their friendship that we share in their celebrations?
* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: How quick the answer is. Does taking part in their celebrations count as support?
* Student: Support.

Shaykh: Support? If you say "yes," it is wrong; if you say "no," it is wrong. As for what relates to worship and religious rites, there is no doubt that participating with them in these festivities is a form of loyalty (muwalah) and support (munasarah), because when you take part in their festivals and religious occasions, it is as if you are saying: "You are upon the truth," and this is not permissible. But participating in other celebrations, such as when a disbeliever has a son and makes a feast and invites you, there is no harm in going, provided it does not lead to fitnah for him, such as him saying: "I invite the Muslims, I invite the notables of the Muslims, and they come to me." If fitnah results, then no. But if it does not result and the matter is ordinary, then this is not part of loyalty or support.

A neighbor whom you honor while he is a disbeliever, is that considered loyalty?

Students: No.

Shaykh: No, this is not loyalty, because the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honor his neighbor." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6019) and Muslim (48/77), from the hadith of Abu Shurayh al-Khuza'i.] Moreover, your honoring him may be a cause for his entry into Islam.

In any case, from this we learn that the word "loyalty" (al-muwalah), which Allah has forbidden, is loyalty in the sense of support and assistance to what returns to their benefit. This is prohibited. But I told you: except if you assist and support them against whom? Against one who is more harmful to the Muslims than they are. This is not objectionable.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: whoever allies with them is one of them.

From this branches out: the strong warning against what?

Student: Against allying with them.

Shaykh: Against allying with them.

Is imitating them part of allying with them?

Students: Yes.

Shaykh: The evidence?

Students: "Whoever imitates a people..."

Shaykh: "Whoever imitates a people is one of them." [Narrated by Abu Dawud (4031) from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar.] Also, imitating them gives them joy and pleasure, and they consider themselves superior to others, since others have become followers of them, adopting what they adorn themselves with in terms of manners or other things.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the warning against injustice (zulm), because Allah the Exalted does not guide the wrongdoers, by His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾.

If someone says: what is the reconciliation between this verse and those whom Allah guided from among the people of shirk, and shirk is a great injustice, yet in the time of the Prophet ﷺ there were those who prostrated to idols and worshipped idols, and Allah guided them? What is the answer?

The answer to that is to say: this verse is restricted by other verses, and what is meant by them are those upon whom the word of your Lord has been justified, by the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has been justified will not believe (96), even if every sign should come to them﴾ [Yunus 96, 97]. Thus this absolute or general verse is restricted by what? By those upon whom the word of Allah has been justified. Such a person cannot be guided by anyone: ﴿Whomever Allah leaves astray, there is no guide for him, and He leaves them in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾ [al-A'raf 186].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the refutation of the Qadariyyah, from His saying: ﴿Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾, for in this there is clear evidence that the affair of the servants is in the hand of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. We ask Allah for guidance for us and for you. The human being is never independent in himself, and he does not govern voluntary or involuntary matters. Just as a person does not have in his hand to be healthy from sickness or sick from health, so too he does not have in his hand to be guided after misguidance. The affair is in the hand of Allah, the Glorified and Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 5, verse 52:

Then the Exalted said: ﴿So you see those in whose hearts is a disease hastening toward them﴾ [al-Ma'idah 52].

To whom is the address "﴿you see﴾"? Every time you encounter such an address, it is either to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, or to him and to whoever the address is valid for and directed at. That is: "So you see, O human, or so you see, O Prophet, ﴿those in whose hearts is a disease hastening toward them﴾," meaning they hasten in their alliance, their appeasement, and their affection toward them. For this reason it does not say "in their alliance" — so as to convey what? Generality. "﴿Hastening toward them﴾" means in everything that becomes a cause of their strength and might.

So who are "those in whose hearts is a disease"?

Diseases are of various kinds. The diseases of the hearts are of kinds just as the diseases of the bodies are, exactly. The diseases of the bodies are of kinds, are they not?

* Students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Organic diseases in a particular organ, general diseases, fevers, tremors — many kinds.
