* The student: The answer is one of two things: either it is said that it is according to the dialect "they ate me the fleas" (akaluni al-baraghith), so the subject is His saying ﴿many﴾, and the waw is a sign of the plural. This is according to the less known dialect.
* The Shaykh: And is it correct to say this in the Quran?
* The student: Our view, Shaykh, is that it is not correct.
* The Shaykh: Yes, our view is that it is not correct, because the Quran is in clear Arabic.
* The student: The second answer: that the pronoun, the waw, is the subject, and ﴿many﴾ is a partial substitute (badal ba'd min kull) for it.
* The Shaykh: Excellent, and this is more correct. Then there were not two subjects for one verb.
His saying, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And Allah is Seeing of what they do.﴾ What is meant by "Seeing" here?
* A student: Here it may include...
* The Shaykh: It encompasses.

**Student:** It includes two matters.

**Shaykh:** *Al-basirah* (insight) is by knowledge, and it is an attribute of sight. *Al-idrak* (perception) means perceiving by sight, the sight of the eye and the sight of knowledge.

His saying: ﴿بِمَا يَعْمَلُونَ﴾ (*"for what they do"*). Does it include both speech and action, or action only?

**Student:** It includes both speech and action.

**Shaykh:** How can speech be an action?

**Student:** Speech is an action.

**Shaykh:** How is it an action?

**Student:** It is an action of the tongue.

**Shaykh:** Yes, you are right, it is an action of the tongue. But speech is not an *fi'l* (deed), because *fi'l* is specific to the limbs (*jawarih*).

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿لَقَدْ كَفَرَ الَّذِينَ قَالُوا إِنَّ اللَّهَ هُوَ الْمَسِيحُ ابْنُ مَرْيَمَ﴾ (*"They have certainly disbelieved who say, 'Indeed, Allah is the Messiah, the son of Mary.'"*). We have already covered this; the beginning of the verse we have taken.

﴿وَقَالَ الْمَسِيحُ يَا بَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ﴾ (*"And the Messiah said, 'O Children of Israel...'"*). We mentioned that this clause may be a circumstantial clause (*jumlah haliyyah*). On this view, the *qad* (قد) must be understood: *"and the Messiah had (already) said."* It is also permissible for the *waw* to be conjunctive (*'atifah*), with *qala* (قال) joined to His saying ﴿لَقَدْ كَفَرَ﴾, meaning: *"and the Messiah had said to them."*

﴿وَقَالَ الْمَسِيحُ يَا بَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ اعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ رَبِّي وَرَبَّكُمْ﴾. His saying ﴿يَا بَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ﴾ is a vocative, and it points to their dullness and heedlessness, and that they are addressed only by a call, and they pay attention and awaken only through it.

﴿يَا بَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ اعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ رَبِّي وَرَبَّكُمْ﴾: ﴿اعْبُدُوا﴾ is an imperative verb from *'ibadah* (worship). *'Ibadah* is applied to two things. The first: the act of the worshipper. The second: the object of the worshipper's worship. According to the first, we say: it is humbling oneself before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, by carrying out His commands and avoiding His prohibitions. According to the second, we say: it is a generic noun for everything that Allah loves and is pleased with, of statements and actions, outward and inward. For example, it is correct to say that the worshipper's act of prayer is *'ibadah*, and it is also correct to say that the prayer itself is *'ibadah*. Its origin is from their saying *tariq mu'abbad* (a paved road), meaning what? Smoothed, leveled, made easy. For example, we call a paved road *tariq mu'abbad*, while a road that has not been paved or trodden we do not call *tariq mu'abbad*.

﴿اعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ رَبِّي وَرَبَّكُمْ﴾. Now, ﴿اعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ﴾: here, is it more fitting to take *'ibadah* in the sense of the worshipper's act or in the sense of its object? *"Worship Allah"* is closer here to the act of the worshipper.

﴿اعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ رَبِّي وَرَبَّكُمْ﴾. He mentioned worship, then He mentioned lordship (*rububiyyah*), as an indication that lordship entails divinity (*uluhiyyah*). That is, the Tawhid of Lordship necessitates the Tawhid of Divinity. Whoever acknowledges Allah's lordship is obliged to acknowledge worship, because the Lord must be worshipped, since He has the command and the judgment. When that is the case, He must be worshipped as He has legislated.

His saying ﴿رَبِّي وَرَبَّكُمْ﴾ (*"my Lord and your Lord"*): He began with Himself, so that He, peace be upon him, would acknowledge that He is a servant who is under lordship, and not a lord, as they claim.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿اعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ﴾. It has come up for us many times regarding the word *Allah*, that its origin is *al-Ilah*, but the hamzah was dropped due to frequent use, just as the hamzah was dropped in *al-nas* (الناس) from *al-unas* (الأناس), and as the hamzah was dropped in *sharr* (شر) from *ashharr* (أشر), and in *khayr* (خير) from *akhyar* (أخير).

﴿اعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ رَبِّي وَرَبَّكُمْ﴾. The word *Rabb* has also come up for us many times: it is the Creator, who is what? The Owner, the Manager, the One who possesses authority.

﴿إِنَّهُ مَنْ يُشْرِكْ بِاللَّهِ﴾ (*"Indeed, whoever associates others with Allah..."*). This is a warning, and the sentence here is a resumptive sentence (*jumlah isti'nafiyyah*) for warning.

﴿إِنَّهُ مَنْ يُشْرِكْ بِاللَّهِ﴾: by worshipping other than Allah, ﴿فَقَدْ حَرَّمَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ الْجَنَّةَ﴾ (*"then Allah has forbidden him Paradise"*), meaning He prevented him from it, because *tahrim* (تحريم) means *man'* (prevention). From it comes: Makkah is *haram* (sacred), Madinah is *haram*, and from it comes *harim al-bi'r* (the protected zone around a well), meaning what is near it, to prevent people from possessing it.

So ﴿حَرَّمَ﴾ means "prevented". ﴿حَرَّمَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ الْجَنَّةَ﴾ means its entry. *Al-Jannah* (Paradise) is the abode that Allah the Exalted has prepared for His allies, may Allah make us and you among them, in which is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived.

And what happens when Allah forbids him Paradise? Where will he be?

He says: ﴿وَمَأْوَاهُ النَّارُ﴾ (*"and his refuge is the Fire"*): the one to whom he returns, as a person returns to his home, is the Fire, the abode Allah has prepared for His enemies, whose fuel is ﴿النَّاسُ وَالْحِجَارَةُ عَلَيْهَا مَلَائِكَةٌ غِلَاظٌ شِدَادٌ لَا يَعْصُونَ اللَّهَ مَا أَمَرَهُمْ وَيَفْعَلُونَ مَا يُؤْمَرُونَ﴾ (*"its fuel is men and stones; over it are angels, stern and severe, who do not disobey Allah in what He commands them, and do what they are commanded"*) [al-Tahrim 6]. They combine strength and obedience: ﴿لَا يَعْصُونَ اللَّهَ مَا أَمَرَهُمْ وَيَفْعَلُونَ مَا يُؤْمَرُونَ﴾ (*"they do not disobey Allah in what He commands them, and they do what they are commanded"*). They are not unable to do anything they are ordered; whatever they are commanded, they are capable of it. Moreover, they are not capable of it in weakness, but rather they are stern and severe. May Allah protect us and you from it.

﴿وَمَأْوَاهُ النَّارُ وَمَا لِلظَّالِمِينَ مِنْ أَنْصَارٍ﴾ (*"and his refuge is the Fire, and for the wrongdoers there are no helpers"*). He, peace be upon him, pointed with His saying ﴿وَمَا لِلظَّالِمِينَ مِنْ أَنْصَارٍ﴾ to this: if this sentence is from the speech of Jesus, then... and if it is from the speech of Allah, then it explains their deserving entry into the Fire, and that they only deserved entry into the Fire because they are wrongdoers through their association. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿إِنَّ الشِّرْكَ لَظُلْمٌ عَظِيمٌ﴾ (*"Indeed, association [with Allah] is a great wrong"*) [Luqman 13], and He the Exalted says: ﴿وَالْكَافِرُونَ هُمُ الظَّالِمُونَ﴾ (*"And the disbelievers—they are the wrongdoers"*) [al-Baqarah 254].

His saying: ﴿وَمَا لِلظَّالِمِينَ مِنْ أَنْصَارٍ﴾. Here, can we say that it is an explicit noun in place of a pronoun (*idhhar fi mawdi' al-idmar*)? That is, if it were outside the Qur'an, it would have been said: "Whoever associates others with Allah, Allah has forbidden him Paradise, his refuge is the Fire, and he has no helpers." This can be said, but the explicit form was used in place of the pronoun in order that the attribute of wrongdoing would apply to these people, meaning that they are wrongdoers, and for the sake of generalization, meaning that the Fire is not only for these people, but for every wrongdoer: ﴿وَمَا لِلظَّالِمِينَ مِنْ أَنْصَارٍ﴾.

His saying: ﴿مِنْ أَنْصَارٍ﴾ (*"of helpers"*), meaning: those who would prevent the punishment from them, because the helper (*nasir*) is the one who keeps the enemy away from you and assists you against him.

- In this noble verse there is an explicit text on the disbelief of those who say that Allah is the Messiah, son of Mary; by His saying ﴿لَقَدْ كَفَرَ﴾.
- Among its benefits: confirming a ruling in a way that removes doubt; by His saying ﴿لَقَدْ كَفَرَ﴾. The sentence is emphasized by three emphatics: the oath, the *lam*, and *qad*.
- Among the benefits of this noble verse: the rulings of the Qur'an are often stated in general terms. That is, if Allah the Exalted had wished, He could have said: "The Christians have disbelieved." But Allah said: ﴿لَقَدْ كَفَرَ الَّذِينَ قَالُوا إِنَّ اللَّهَ هُوَ الْمَسِيحُ ابْنُ مَرْيَمَ﴾, whether they were from the Children of Israel, who are the Christians, or from others.
- Among the benefits of this noble verse: there is no disbelief except after the establishment of proof, based on the view that the *waw* in His saying ﴿وَقَالَ الْمَسِيحُ﴾ is circumstantial, meaning that they disbelieved after the matter had been made clear to them: ﴿وَقَالَ الْمَسِيحُ يَا بَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ﴾.
- Among the benefits of this noble verse: a person's affirmation of something on behalf of another is not accepted, because they claimed that Allah is the Messiah, and Jesus son of Mary denied that. He said: ﴿اعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ رَبِّي وَرَبَّكُمْ﴾ (*"Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord"*). So I am not a god for you to worship; rather, I and you are equal, we are all under the lordship of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
- Among the benefits of this noble verse: the great honor and nobility of the messengers, peace be upon them. Jesus denied that he was Allah in this great sentence: ﴿وَقَالَ الْمَسِيحُ يَا بَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ اعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ رَبِّي وَرَبَّكُمْ﴾. This is the station of the messengers and their followers, who do not desire haughtiness on earth or corruption. Consider the words of the Messenger, peace be upon him, when it was said to him: "What Allah wills and you will." Did he approve of this? No. He denied it and said: «أَجَعَلْتَنِي لِلَّهِ نِدًّا؟ بَلْ مَا شَاءَ اللهُ وَحْدَهُ» (*"Have you made me a rival to Allah? Rather, what Allah alone wills."*) [Narrated by al-Bukhari in al-Adab al-Mufrad (783), and al-Tabarani in al-Kabir (13005), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.] And likewise, the followers of the messengers, peace be upon them, do not want people to raise them above the rank Allah the Mighty and Majestic has given them. Rather, the more Allah blesses the followers of the messengers with following them, the more humble they become toward creation and toward the truth.
- Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation of worship. That is, the messengers, peace be upon them, command the worship of Allah in every religious community; by His saying ﴿اعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ رَبِّي وَرَبَّكُمْ﴾.
- Among its benefits: establishing proof against the people of association, since they associated others with Allah while He is their Lord, and idols have no role whatsoever in lordship. They do not hear, they do not see, they do not benefit, and they do not harm. They are dead, not living.
- Among the benefits of this noble verse: the argument that binds the opponent. A person, when debating, should follow the clearest evidence and that which most binds the opponent. By His saying ﴿اعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ رَبِّي وَرَبَّكُمْ﴾, He did not say, for example, "Worship Allah; you have no god other than Him." He said: ﴿اعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ رَبِّي وَرَبَّكُمْ﴾, binding them to what? Binding them to His worship, because they affirm His lordship. This is like His saying: ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا النَّاسُ اعْبُدُوا رَبَّكُمُ الَّذِي خَلَقَكُمْ وَالَّذِينَ مِنْ قَبْلِكُمْ﴾ (*"O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you and those before you"*) [al-Baqarah 21]. He said: ﴿اعْبُدُوا رَبَّكُمُ﴾ (*"worship your Lord"*), binding them to worship, because Allah is the One who created them, and He is the One who judges over them and between them.
- Among the benefits of this noble verse: Jesus has no share in divinity or lordship, by His saying ﴿اعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ﴾ (this is about divinity) and ﴿رَبِّي وَرَبَّكُمْ﴾ (this is about lordship). So Jesus son of Mary has no right to divinity or lordship. And what about the other messengers?

**Students:** They have no such right either.

**Shaykh:** And other people? Likewise. By this we know the error of those people who claim that their saints are the ones who manage the universe and direct it, and that they are in manifest error. We ask Allah for well-being.
- Among the benefits of this noble verse: association with Allah necessitates eternal abiding in the Fire; by His saying: ﴿إِنَّهُ مَنْ يُشْرِكْ بِاللَّهِ فَقَدْ حَرَّمَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ الْجَنَّةَ وَمَأْوَاهُ النَّارُ وَمَا لِلظَّالِمِينَ مِنْ أَنْصَارٍ﴾.
- Among the benefits of this noble verse: there is no refuge for creation except one of two things: either Paradise, or what? Or the Fire. There is nothing in between, just as there is nothing after truth except error, and nothing after faith except disbelief: ﴿فَمِنْكُمْ كَافِرٌ وَمِنْكُمْ مُؤْمِنٌ﴾ (*"Among you is a disbeliever, and among you is a believer"*) [al-Taghabun 2]. And regarding the recompense: ﴿مِنْهُمْ شَقِيٌّ وَسَعِيدٌ﴾ (*"Among them is one who is wretched and one who is happy"*) [Hud 105], meaning: and among them is a happy one. There is no third category.

If someone says: What do you say about the companions of al-A'raf (the Heights) mentioned in the Qur'an?

The answer is easy. We say: the companions of al-A'raf are held in a place overlooking the people of the Fire and watching the people of Paradise; that is, they are held according to what Allah's wisdom requires, and their final destination is Paradise, as He the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿لَمْ يَدْخُلُوهَا وَهُمْ يَطْمَعُونَ﴾ (*"They have not entered it, while they aspire [to enter]"*) [al-A'raf 46]. So these people, I mean the companions of al-A'raf, their final destination is Paradise. Therefore there are only two abodes for creation: the Fire or Paradise. For this reason, al-Saffarini, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his creed:

*Every human and every jinn*
*is in the abode of fire or in the bliss of Paradise.*

- Among the benefits of this noble verse: prohibition may be legislative, and it may be divine decree (*qadari*).
- Indeed, we say: from this noble verse it is derived that prohibition may be divine decree. What is its proof? His saying: ﴿فَقَدْ حَرَّمَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ الْجَنَّةَ﴾, meaning a divine decree prohibition, not a legislative one, because it is not by a person's choice.

Can prohibition occur in the sense of legislative prohibition? The answer: yes. Among its examples is His saying: ﴿حُرِّمَتْ عَلَيْكُمُ الْمَيْتَةُ وَالدَّمُ وَلَحْمُ الْخِنْزِيرِ﴾ (*"Prohibited to you are carrion, blood, and the flesh of swine"*) [al-Ma'idah 3]. And among them: ﴿أَحَلَّ اللَّهُ الْبَيْعَ وَحَرَّمَ الرِّبَا﴾ (*"Allah has permitted trade and forbidden usury"*) [al-Baqarah 275].
- Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of Paradise and the affirmation of the Fire; by His saying: ﴿الْجَنَّةَ وَمَأْوَاهُ النَّارُ﴾.
- Among its benefits: the final abode of creation is either Paradise or the Fire. As for graves, they are not the final abode; rather, they are a stopping place where people remain for as long as Allah wills, until the Hour is established.
- Among the benefits of this noble verse: an indication that association is wrongdoing; by His saying: ﴿وَمَا لِلظَّالِمِينَ مِنْ أَنْصَارٍ﴾. This is stated explicitly in the Qur'an, where Allah the Exalted says: ﴿إِنَّ الشِّرْكَ لَظُلْمٌ عَظِيمٌ﴾ [Luqman 13].
- Among the benefits of this noble verse: the wrongdoers have no helper; by His saying: ﴿وَمَا لِلظَّالِمِينَ مِنْ أَنْصَارٍ﴾. And *min* (مِنْ) here, as those knowledgeable in the Arabic language know, is an extra (*za'idah*) preposition added to convey generality and emphasis.

If someone says: How does this emphatic negation fit with the fact that disbelievers are sometimes helped, and polytheists are sometimes helped?

The answer: this is a temporary help, by which Allah tests the believers, and not a permanent help. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿إِنَّا لَنَنْصُرُ رُسُلَنَا وَالَّذِينَ آمَنُوا فِي الْحَيَاةِ الدُّنْيَا وَيَوْمَ يَقُومُ الْأَشْهَادُ﴾ (*"Indeed, We will surely support Our messengers and those who believe in the worldly life and on the day when the witnesses will stand"*) [Ghafir 51]. He the Exalted also said: ﴿إِذْ تَبَرَّأَ الَّذِينَ اتُّبِعُوا مِنَ الَّذِينَ اتَّبَعُوا﴾ (*"When those who were followed disassociate themselves from those who followed"*) [al-Baqarah 166], and He said: ﴿كُلَّمَا دَخَلَتْ أُمَّةٌ لَعَنَتْ أُخْتَهَا﴾ (*"Every time a nation enters, it curses its sister"*) [al-A'raf 38]. And it is impossible for disbelievers to help one another in repelling punishment from themselves on the Day of Resurrection. At that point there is no difficulty, because the help they receive is what? Temporary help, which Allah intends to test the believers with.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 5, verse 73 (part 1 of 2):

The Shaykh: Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Certainly they have disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the third of three."﴾ These are another group of the Christians. The Christians whom the first verse speaks of, what did they say? They said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Messiah, the son of Mary.﴾ That is, they said that the Messiah and Allah, Lord of the worlds, are one. These are different from them. They said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is the third of three.﴾ "The third of three." Who are these three? Allah mentioned them in this surah: ﴿And when Allah says, "O Jesus, son of Mary, did you say to the people, 'Take me and my mother as two deities besides Allah'?"﴾ [al-Ma'idah 116]. If the two of them are deities besides Allah, then they became three. So the "third of three" are: Allah, the Messiah, and his mother. These are the three. The Quran explains this, and the Quran explains itself. As for what has been said, that they are the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, there is consideration of it. That is, we do not interpret it by the Quran, although some of them, or some of the later ones among them, may say that these are the three: ﴿the third of three﴾.

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And there is no deity except one God.﴾ Pausing at ﴿the third of three﴾ is necessary, because if one continued, the listener would understand that the words ﴿And there is no deity except one God﴾ are part of the speech of these disbelievers.

﴿And there is no deity except one God﴾ has the meaning of (there is no god but Allah), but it differs from it in i'rab (grammatical analysis). For example, we say: (ma) is a negation particle. Complete the Arabic grammatical analysis, you all.

* Student: "And there is no deity except Allah..."
* The Shaykh: (ma) is a negation particle.
* The Student: (ma) is a negation particle, and (min) is a redundant (extra) prepositional particle.
* The Shaykh: Why is it redundant?
* The Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: That is: it is grammatically superfluous but semantically meaningful.
* The Student: (ilah) is a nominative subject (mubtada'), its nominative marker is a presumed damma at its end, prevented from appearing by the word's position being occupied by the redundant preposition. (illa) is an exceptive particle, and (ilah) is the predicate.
* The Shaykh: Do we say it is an exceptive particle, or do we say it is a particle of restriction?
* The Student: It indicates restriction.
* The Shaykh: Yes, a particle of restriction.
* The Student: A particle of restriction, and (ilah) is a nominative predicate, its nominative marker is the visible damma at its end, and (wahid) is an adjective.
* The Shaykh: May Allah bless you.

Allah refuted this statement, their saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is the third of three﴾, with His words ﴿And there is no deity except one God﴾. This is a report from the most truthful of reporters, a report emphasized by what? By the redundant prepositional particle and by restriction.

﴿And there is no deity except one God﴾. It is impossible for there to be more than one deity. ﴿Had there been within them deities other than Allah, they would have been ruined﴾ [al-Anbiya' 22]. Did Allah not say this?

* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Likewise, He also explained in another verse, in His saying: ﴿Allah has not taken any son, nor has there been with Him any deity. [If there were], each deity would have taken what he created, and some would have overcome others﴾ [al-Mu'minun 91]. That is, if each deity acted independently with what he created, and each deity wanted divinity to be for himself alone, then fighting would necessarily occur between them, and if fighting occurred between them, some would overcome others: sometimes this one prevails and sometimes that one prevails. And it is known that the one who prevails is the one deserving to be God alone, and the one who is overcome does not deserve to be God. Now consider: if you went out on a journey and appointed Zayd and 'Amr, both as commander, what would happen?

* Student: Chaos.
* Another Student: And turmoil.
* The Shaykh: Chaos and turmoil. It is never possible for deities to be many. If they were many, the whole world would be ruined. For this reason He said: ﴿And there is no deity except one God﴾, emphasizing it. He emphasized the oneness by His words ﴿One﴾. Who is it? Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

﴿And if they do not desist from what they say, there will surely afflict the disbelievers among them a painful punishment﴾: ﴿And if they do not desist from what they say﴾. There is a difficulty in the i'rab of this.

* Student: Shaykh, may Allah bless you. We said regarding the people of al-A'raf that their good deeds and bad deeds are equal, so they are detained in a place between Paradise and Hellfire. Does this mean, O Shaykh, that whoever has even one more bad deed must enter the Fire?

* The Shaykh: No. People are divided into categories. One who has bad deeds without good deeds: he goes to the Fire, and there is no difficulty with this. One whose bad deeds exceed his good deeds, who has both good and bad deeds with the bad deeds in excess: this one deserves to enter the Fire. He deserves it, but we do not state it with certainty, and he may be saved from the Fire through intercession, because among the principles of Ahl al-Sunnah wa'l-Jama'ah (the People of the Sunnah and the Community) is the division of intercession: for those who deserve the Fire, that they not enter it. A third category: those whose good and bad deeds are equal. These are the people of al-A'raf (the Heights). They do not enter the Fire and do not enter Paradise. The fourth category: one whose good deeds outweigh his bad deeds. This one does not enter the Fire and is among the people of Paradise. These are four categories, and people do not go outside them.

Can we say: and a category has good deeds without bad deeds?

* The Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Who?
* Students: The prophets.
* The Shaykh: We can say: the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, Allah informed that his past and future sins were forgiven. So he will meet Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, on the Day of Resurrection with what: with good deeds or with bad deeds? Thus the categories are five.

* Student: Shaykh, may Allah bless you. We mentioned that the people of al-A'raf look at the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire, and we mentioned at the end that their final destination is Paradise. So do we say that this looking at the Fire is a kind of punishment, or how (...)?

* The Shaykh: Yes, it is known. For this reason He said: ﴿And when their eyes are turned toward the companions of the Fire﴾ [al-A'raf 47], which indicates that they do not wish to look at them. But their sight is turned away by compulsion. When it is turned away, ﴿they say, "Our Lord, do not place us with the wrongdoing people"﴾ [al-A'raf 47].

* The Student: They are without choice?

* The Shaykh: This is the apparent meaning of the Quran: ﴿when they are turned away﴾.

* Student: May Allah reward you with good. Let us explain the verse, the saying of the Majestic and Exalted: ﴿They say, "Indeed, Allah is the third of three,"﴾ by what came at the end of the surah: ﴿And when Allah says, "O Jesus, son of Mary, did you say to the people, 'Take me and my mother as two deities besides Allah'?"﴾. If someone says: the second verse mentions taking Jesus and his mother as deities besides Allah, but not with Allah?

* The Shaykh: No, "two deities besides Allah" means alongside Allah, because the Christians acknowledge Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and they say: the deities are three.

* Student: In the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Certainly they have disbelieved who say﴾, it is well known in the language that (kafara) comes with the meaning of covering. So would this be considered an interpretation that prevents us from saying that whoever says "disbelief short of disbelief" has left the religion? It seems like an interpretation, but it prevents his excommunication.

* The Shaykh: How?

* The Student: That is, some people say: ﴿Certainly they have disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the Messiah, the son of Mary"﴾ meaning that he covered the truth, not in the sense that he committed the disbelief that expels from the religion...

* The Shaykh: No, that cannot be. This is unacceptable.

I say: this speech is not accepted. Disbelief is both legal and linguistic. The root meaning of disbelief in the language is: covering.

* The Student: Would the justification for not declaring him a disbeliever, for example, be that he says: he is not a disbeliever...

* The Shaykh: The one who says: whoever says "Allah is the third of three" is not a disbeliever, he is the disbeliever. What is this? Do you have no intellect and no knowledge? Glory be to Allah!

* The Student: No, is there an interpretation here, O Shaykh?

* The Shaykh: There is no interpretation. If a person, when someone says: ﴿Do not approach fornication﴾ [al-Isra' 32], interprets it as: the intended meaning is "do not approach marriage by a valid contract," would we obey him?

* The Student: No.

* The Shaykh: Leave these possibilities.

* Student: We do not even have an issue...

* The Shaykh: How?

* The Student: There is a real problem because of this matter, because of this point.

* The Shaykh: The problem is real. Even the disbelievers said to the Messenger: ﴿"Has he made the gods one God? Indeed, this is a bizarre thing"﴾ [Sad 5].

* Student: May Allah be pleased with you, Shaykh. Is knowledge only about shirk, into major shirk and minor shirk? And the indications of the Quran show that the two types of shirk are one category. Is the category of shirk, O Shaykh, meaning (...) the minor shirk, that they will leave the Fire after punishment, or will He multiply their punishment, one upon another?

* The Shaykh: Minor shirk, may Allah bless you, does not necessitate eternal abode in the Fire. But is it included under the Will of Allah, meaning: if Allah wills, He forgives its doer, or not? There are two possibilities. The saying of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him﴾ [al-Nisa' 48] may mean that the intended meaning is that minor shirk is major shirk, and that minor shirk must have repentance. It may also mean that the intended meaning of ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him﴾ is major shirk, about which Allah said: ﴿Indeed, whoever associates others with Allah, Allah has forbidden him Paradise, and his refuge is the Fire. And for the wrongdoers there are no helpers﴾.
