* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿Certainly they have disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the third of three." And there is no deity except one God. And if they do not desist from what they say, there will surely afflict the disbelievers among them a painful punishment. Then will they not repent to Allah and seek His forgiveness? And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful. The Messiah, son of Mary, was not but a messenger; the messengers had passed on before him. And his mother was a supporter of truth; they both used to eat food. Look how We make clear to them the signs; then look how they are deluded. Say, "Do you worship other than Allah that which does not own for you any harm or benefit, while Allah is the Hearing, the Knowing?" Say, "O People of the Scripture, do not exceed limits in your religion other than in truth, and do not follow the inclinations of a people who had gone astray before and led many astray and went astray from the sound way"﴾ [al-Ma'idah 73-77].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Certainly they have disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the third of three."﴾ I think we have discussed the verse. ﴿Certainly they have disbelieved who say﴾: does it contain emphasis?

* Student: Three emphases.

* The Shaykh: Three emphases.

* The Student: The first: the implied oath, the lam, and (qad).

* The Shaykh: May Allah bless you. Why does Allah, the Exalted, emphasize His speech with emphatic devices, though He, the Mighty and Majestic, is the most truthful of speakers?

* Student: (...) that this is a report, and a report conveys...

And among the benefits of this noble verse: Allah, glorified and exalted, does not wrong people at all, and He does not punish anyone except for a sin; by His saying ﴿That is because they disobeyed﴾ [al-Baqarah 61].

* And among the benefits of the verse that follows: the reluctance of the Children of Israel to forbid wrongdoing; by His saying: ﴿They did not prohibit one another from wrongdoing which they committed﴾ [al-Ma'idah 79].

* And among its benefits: that abandoning the forbidding of wrongdoing is a cause for the curse of Allah, His expulsion and His removal, and we seek refuge in Allah. Know that enjoining good and forbidding evil (al-amr bi'l-ma'ruf wa'l-nahy 'an al-munkar) requires conditions:

The first condition: knowledge that this is a good that is enjoined, and this is an evil that is forbidden. It is not permissible to enjoin what one does not know to be commanded, nor to forbid what one does not know to be forbidden, because of the fabrication against Allah that this involves, and the obstruction of the servants of Allah from what Allah has made lawful for them, or the prevention of them from what Allah has made lawful for them.

The second condition: that one knows this evil is actually committed by the specific person, because a thing may be evil for one person and not evil for another. The traveler eats openly and secretly during the day of Ramadan, while the resident does not eat. So eating is an evil during Ramadan for the resident, and not an evil for the traveler. Therefore the one who enjoins and the one who forbids must know that this specific person has actually committed the violation. If there is a possibility, it is obligatory to inquire. Its evidence is that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, saw a man enter the mosque and sit down while he was delivering a sermon to the people, peace and blessings be upon him. He said to him: "Did you pray?" He said: No. He said: "Stand and pray two rak'ahs, and make them brief"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (930), and Muslim (875/59), and the wording is his, from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah.]]. He did not forbid him the evil of sitting before praying until he knew that he had not prayed.

Among the conditions also: that the evil does not turn into something more evil. If it turns into something more evil, one must refrain from forbidding it, because if you forbid while knowing that it will turn into something worse, that means you have called to committing something worse than the first evil, and what is worse than the first evil is also evil. This is taken from the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And do not insult those they call upon other than Allah, lest they insult Allah in enmity without knowledge﴾ [al-An'am 108]. So abandoning the insulting of the deities of the polytheists is evil, because what is obligatory is to revile the deities, to warn against them, and to make people averse to them. But if it leads to something more severely evil, one must refrain; by His saying: ﴿Do not revile those they call upon other than Allah, lest they revile Allah﴾. So if we saw a person smoking tobacco in front of us, but we knew that if we forbade him from smoking tobacco he would go and steal people's money, harm people, and annoy them, would we denounce his smoking or not? We do not denounce it.

Likewise, if we knew, or it was strongly probable to us, that if we forbade him from tobacco he would go to a group who drink alcohol, then we do not forbid him, averting the greater of two harms by the lesser of them.

How many conditions is this? Three conditions. The scholars differed over a fourth condition: whether it is required that the one who enjoins be doing what he enjoins, or that the one who forbids be abstaining from what he forbids?

The correct view is that this is not a condition, because if we said to someone who commits evil: "Do not forbid it," it would follow that we would be commanding him with two evils: abandoning denunciation, and committing the evil that he is practicing. So we say: enjoin good and forbid evil, even if you yourself do what you forbid or abandon what you enjoin. Perhaps his enjoining and forbidding will be a cause for his commitment and uprightness, since he rebukes himself and says: "Glory be to Allah, do I forbid people from evil and do it myself?" Then he becomes upright. As for the poet's saying:

Do not forbid a trait while you yourself practice its like,
It is a disgrace upon you, great, when you do it.

His meaning is that you combine the two matters: (do not forbid and yet practice its like). Even if we supposed that it is not accepted, the person who commits evil and sees evil is obligated to two things: the first, abandoning the evil; the second, forbidding it. So if the first matter is impossible, do we say the second is impossible? No. The correct view is that a person must enjoin good even if he does not do it, and forbid evil even if he does it.

However, this will be more severe in punishment on the Day of Resurrection, because his state is like that of one who mocks Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and the rulings of the Shari'ah. How can you command something you do not do? How can you forbid something while you do it? This is nothing but a kind of mockery and derision. For this reason his punishment is more severe, since the Prophet, peace be upon him, informed that: "A man will be brought on the Day of Resurrection and thrown into the Fire, until his intestines spill out, and he will go around them as a donkey goes around its millstone. The people of the Fire will gather around him and say: 'O so-and-so, what is wrong with you? Did you not used to command us to do good and forbid us from evil?' He will say: 'Yes, I used to command you to do good but I would not do it, and forbid you from evil and I would do it.'"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3267), and Muslim (2989/51), from the hadith of Usamah ibn Zayd.]] Thus he is disgraced with this disgrace, and we seek refuge in Allah.

Let it be known that enjoining good and forbidding evil (al-amr bil-ma'ruf wa'n-nahy 'an al-munkar, the duty to command what is right and prohibit what is wrong) is different from changing evil by one's own hand. For this reason the texts (nusus) state the enjoining of good and forbidding of evil in absolute terms, while changing evil is restricted by ability, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever among you sees an evil, let him change it with his hand. If he cannot, then with his tongue. If he cannot, then with his heart." [Related by Muslim (49/78) from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.] This is because changing evil by force must come from one who has authority, such as the ruler (wali al-amr) and his deputies. Likewise, a man within his household can change evil with his hand.

* * *

Student: "You see many of them befriending those who disbelieve. Evil is what their souls have sent forward for them: that Allah has become angry with them, and in the punishment they will abide forever. Had they believed in Allah, the Prophet, and what was revealed to him, they would not have taken them as allies; but many of them are defiantly disobedient. You will surely find the most intense of people in enmity toward the believers to be the Jews and those who associate others with Allah; and you will find the nearest of them in affection to the believers those who say, 'We are Christians.' That is because among them are priests and monks, and because they are not arrogant." [Al-Ma'idah 80–82.]

Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: "Those among the Children of Israel who disbelieved were cursed..." (Al-Ma'idah 78), and so on. We mentioned in this verse an important discussion concerning enjoining good and forbidding evil, and we clarified that the ma'ruf (what is good)?

Student: The ma'ruf is what the Shari'ah has commanded.

Shaykh: What the Shari'ah has commanded, either as an obligation or as a recommendation. Good. The munkar (what is evil): meaning, what the Lawgiver has forbidden, that is, what?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: He has prohibited it, either as a prohibition (tahrim) or as a disapproval (karahah). But if it is disapproved, then one who does not denounce it is not sinful; and if it is recommended to abstain, then one who does not command it is not sinful.

We stipulated conditions for the obligation of enjoining good and forbidding evil. What is the first of them?

Student: The first: that the one enjoining or forbidding must be knowledgeable about what he enjoins and forbids.

Shaykh: Knowledgeable about what he enjoins and forbids, meaning?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: Meaning that he knows that what he enjoins is good and that what he forbids is evil. This is from which perspective? 

Student: (...).

Shaykh: From the perspective of the Shari'ah or from the perspective of reality?

Student: From the perspective of the Shari'ah.

Shaykh: From the perspective of the Shari'ah. That is, he knows that this is good or that this is evil. The second?

Student: That the evil does not turn into a greater evil than it.

Shaykh: No. We wanted to finish with knowledge.

Student: Shaykh, that the one who commits the evil must be one who is being denounced for it. So if, for example, someone broke his fast in Ramadan while traveling, one should not denounce him. Rather, one must know that he is not a traveler, such that he broke the fast without any excuse.

Shaykh: That is, one must know that the evil has been committed by this specific person, because an act may be evil in general but not evil with respect to this particular individual. Correct. The third?

Student: That the evil does not turn into what is worse than it.

Shaykh: That it does not turn into what is worse than it. Example?

Student: If a person smokes and we forbid him from smoking, and he then drinks alcohol.

Shaykh: And we know that if he gives up smoking he will turn to drinking alcohol. In this case we do not forbid him. Do we have evidence for this? Yes, the evidence is the saying of Allah, the Exalted?

Student: The evidence is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: "Do not revile those they invoke besides Allah, lest they revile Allah in enmity without knowledge." (Al-An'am 108)

Shaykh: So He forbade reviling their deities...

Student: Because it leads to reviling Allah, glorified is He.

Shaykh: To reviling Allah, and this is worse than abandoning denunciation of them.

Another example of evil turning into what is worse than it, other than the example of smoking and drinking alcohol?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: That is, like seeing a group of thieves drinking alcohol. If we forbade them or prevented them from it, they would go off to steal people's wealth and violate their honor. In this case we say: we leave them to their drinking of alcohol, so that they do not turn to what is worse. What is the fourth condition?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: That is, is it a condition that the one enjoining good must himself do what he enjoins?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: It is not a condition. Give us evidence that we must know that the one being denounced has committed the evil; meaning, if there is a possibility [that he has not], we do not forbid him from doing it.

Student: That the Messenger (ﷺ) was delivering a sermon when a man entered and sat down, and he said: "Did you pray two rak'ahs?" He said: "No." He said: "Stand up and pray two rak'ahs." [Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (930) and Muslim (875/59) from Jabir.]

Shaykh: Well done, this is very clear. Must I denounce a person whom I see walking beside a woman?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: That is, I do not denounce him until I know that the woman is non-mahram to him. And how is knowledge attained?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: Yes indeed, by asking him. Every person you ask, even the most sinful of servants, will say: "This is my sister, or my mother, or my wife." But there are circumstantial indications (qara'in, contextual evidence) that show he is committing a prohibited act. Is it permissible to act on circumstantial indications? What is the evidence?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: That is, the Prophet acted on analogy (qiyas, reasoning by analogy). Here there are three stories: the story of Yusuf, the story of Sulayman, and a story of the Prophet (ﷺ), apart from the matter of standing.

Student: The saying of Allah, mighty and majestic: "If his shirt is torn from the front, then she has told the truth and he is of the liars. But if his shirt is torn from the back, then she has lied and he is of the truthful. So when he saw that his shirt was torn from the back, he said, 'Indeed, it is from your plot. Indeed, your plot is great.'" (Yusuf 26–28)

Shaykh: What is the indication? Is the indication not that if it was torn from the back, then she is the liar?

Student: Then it was she who pulled him...

Shaykh: She pulled him. Then this is correct. And if it was torn from the front?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: That she defended herself, so his shirt was torn. May Allah bless you.

Well then, Sulayman ibn Dawud?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: (...) until it is established. The minor premise or the major premise?

Student: One of them.

Shaykh: One of them, yes?

Shaykh: The minor (al-sughra, minor premise). Because Dawud, peace be upon him, ruled for the older woman, and Sulayman acted on the circumstantial indication. What is the aspect of the indication here?

Student: (...) and the aspect of that is that leaving him with the other woman is more appropriate than (...).

Student: This is from mercy (...).

Shaykh: Well done. Because the younger woman showed mercy to him; she said: "Do not split him; he is hers," while the other one's son had been eaten by the wolf. Rule for him what concerns her. Do you understand?

For the Messenger (peace be upon him)?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: Have you heard his words? "The story of Khaybar, when the Prophet (peace be upon him) asked for the wealth of Huyayy ibn Akhtab. They said: war has consumed it. He said: How? The wealth is abundant and the covenant is recent. Then he said to al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam, that is, touch him with punishment; he ordered that he be tortured until he confessed." [Related by Abu Dawud (3006), and Ibn Hibban (5199), with the wording his, from Abdullah ibn Umar.]

This is an instance of acting on circumstantial indications, and it is abundant in the Sunnah. It is also abundant in the era of the Followers (tabi'un), among intelligent judges who acted on circumstantial indications. In the book Al-Turuq al-Hukmiyyah by Ibn al-Qayyim there is much on this subject. That concludes the discussion of enjoining good and forbidding evil.

Remaining for us is how we enjoin and how we forbid. Do we enjoin with severity or with gentleness?

We say: this depends on the state of the person. The obstinate is not like the ignorant one by origin. The ignorant one by origin we treat with kindness, gentleness and persuasion until he accepts the ruling. The obstinate or the openly defiant has a different ruling. Events that occurred during the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) also show this, among them the story of the Bedouin who urinated in the mosque, when the Prophet (ﷺ) spoke to him gently and said: "These mosques are not fit for any filth or harm." [Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (219) and Muslim (285/100), wording from Anas ibn Malik.]

Among them is the story of Mu'awiyah ibn al-Hakam, who spoke during the prayer twice. The Prophet (ﷺ) called him and informed him "that this prayer must not contain any speech of people." [Related by Muslim (537/33).]

"When he saw a man with a gold ring on his hand, the Prophet (peace be upon him) took it, removed it from his hand, and threw it away, without speaking to him. When the Prophet (ﷺ) departed, it was said to him: 'Take your ring.' He said: 'By Allah, I will not take a ring that the Prophet (ﷺ) has thrown away.'" [Related by Muslim (2090/52) from Abdullah ibn Abbas.] This is because this man had no excuse. So for every situation there is a suitable manner of speech.

Is there a difference between enjoining, forbidding and changing?

Answer: Yes, there is a difference between them. Changing is only for one who has authority and jurisdiction, and it is not opened to everyone, because if it were opened to everyone, matters would descend into chaos, and every person would see something as evil and stand up to change it with his hand, even if the doer does not consider it evil. So changing is for one who holds guardianship and authority: the ruler in his land has authority, and the man in his house has authority.

But in the street, no. In the street one has only to enjoin and forbid. As for compelling someone to do what is enjoined, or changing an evil, this is not his to do, because of the resulting chaos. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) restricted the matter of changing by ability, saying: "Whoever among you sees an evil, let him change it with his hand. If he cannot..." [Related by Muslim (49/78) from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.]

But enjoining good and forbidding evil was not restricted by ability; it is stated in absolute terms, because it is incumbent upon one who has authority and upon one who has no authority.

Is calling to Allah (da'wah, inviting people to Islam) the same as enjoining good and forbidding evil, or is it something else?

It is something else. Calling to Allah is obligatory in every case, whether you see an evil or not, and whether you see a neglect of an obligation or not. For this reason Allah, the Exalted, said: "Let there be among you a nation calling to good, enjoining what is right, and forbidding what is wrong." (Al 'Imran 104) He began with calling to good, then followed it with enjoining good and forbidding evil. So the levels are now three: the first is calling to good and explaining what is good and what is evil; the second level is enjoining good and forbidding evil; the third level is changing [evil] by enforcing the enjoining of good and the forbidding of evil.

Many people do not notice this difference and think that calling, enjoining, forbidding and changing are all the same. Where did we last stop?

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Will they not repent to Allah and seek His forgiveness?﴾ The interrogative here is not one of inquiry or seeking information, because Allah knows. Rather, it is said that it is for offering (ʿarḍ), and it is said that it is for rebuke (tawbīkh). Some scholars said that the interrogative is for rebuke; that is, Allah rebukes them for not repenting and seeking forgiveness. Others said that Allah is offering it to them, so it is an offer, as you say to a person: "Will you not visit us?" The more fitting for the generosity and bounty of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is that it be for offering, meaning that Allah offers them repentance; so in that case we say the interrogative is for offering.

Now, regarding the grammar: ﴿أَفَلَا يَتُوبُونَ﴾. It is known that the hamza of interrogation has precedence (ṣadr al-kalām), and here the conjunctive fāʾ has come, so how does the sentence stand? That is, if the conjunctive fāʾ comes, this means that the clause after it is what? Coordinated with what precedes it. This presents a difficulty, since the interrogative has precedence. The grammarians differed on this. Some said: the hamza of interrogation enters upon a clause, and the fāʾ is conjunctive to that clause which is the object of the hamza, and in that case the interrogative has precedence. How do we estimate this clause? He says: according to the context. Look for what fits the context and estimate it accordingly, since every context has what suits it. For example: ﴿أَفَلَا يَتُوبُونَ إِلَى اللَّهِ﴾, how do we estimate it? "Have they been arrogant, so they do not repent to Allah?" On the view that it is for rebuke, yes. But on the view that it is for offering? Yes (...). All of these indicate rebuke, but for the offer, one estimates a verb that indicates the generosity and bounty of Allah, for example: "Have they been heedless of the generosity and bounty of Allah, so that they do not repent?"

Some of the grammarians (those who parse the Qur'an) said: there is inversion (taqdīm and taʾkhīr) in the statement, and that the original is that the fāʾ is placed before the hamza, and the estimate is: "fa-a-lā yatūbūna" (so will they not repent). The hamza here then stands at the head of their clause which is coordinated with what came before. Without doubt this is easier for a person in terms of estimation, since it can be difficult for a person to estimate a clause suitable to the context. So when we say: the hamza is for interrogation and its place is after the fāʾ, and the fāʾ has been shifted from its place, the matter becomes easy.

His words: ﴿يَتُوبُونَ﴾ means: they return, because tāba, thāba, and anāba and what is similar to them all have close meanings. So ﴿يَتُوبُونَ﴾ to Allah means: they return to Allah from His disobedience to His obedience, from shirk to tawḥīd, from ta'ṭīl (denial of the attributes) to affirmation, and so on.

﴿وَيَسْتَغْفِرُونَهُ﴾ means they ask Him for forgiveness (maghfira). So what is forgiveness? The best of what has been said about it: it is covering up the sin and overlooking it. This is forgiveness, because it is derived from al-mighfar, which is what is placed on the head to protect against arrows during battle, and the mighfar contains cover and protection. We should not say that forgiveness is only covering the sin; rather we say it is covering together with pardon and protection from punishment. This derivation is supported by it being derived from al-maghfar, and perhaps it is also supported by what is established in the authentic hadith: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will meet His believing servant in private and make him acknowledge his sins, and when he acknowledges them, Allah will say to him: 'I have covered them for you in the world, and I forgive them for you today.'"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2441) and Muslim (2768 / 52) from the hadith of ʿAbdullah ibn ʿUmar.]] ﴿Will they not repent to Allah and seek His forgiveness? And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.﴾ The sentence is coordinated with what precedes, but it conveys that He, Mighty and Majestic, is deserving of being asked for forgiveness, and that when He is asked for forgiveness He forgives, for He is Forgiving and Merciful. Allah, the Exalted, always pairs these two noble names, because through the first the feared is removed and sins are forgiven, and through the second the desired is attained, since mercy is the bringing of good and kindness.

* In this noble verse: the urging to repent to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and the rebuke of those who do not repent. Repentance, as we have said, is returning from disobedience of Allah to His obedience, and disobedience has types. The scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, mentioned that repentance has conditions, and they are five: sincerity, remorse, ceasing from the sin, resolve not to return to it, and that it be at a time when repentance is accepted. Five conditions: sincerity, meaning that what moves a person to repent is not showing off to people or obtaining status, rank, or the like, but that what moves him to repent is fear of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and hope for what is with Him.

Second: remorse over what was done of the sin.

If someone says: remorse is an emotion, and emotion is not an act, so how can it be voluntary such that we make it a condition for the penitent?

We say: what is meant by remorse is its necessary consequence, meaning that the presence of the sinful act and its absence are not equal for him, but rather you find him sad, wishing he had not done it. Otherwise, if I say to you, for example: "Feel remorse," you cannot feel it; it is an emotion, and if I say to you: "Be happy," you cannot be happy except with a cause that calls for it. For this reason some scholars objected to this condition and said: this is a condition that cannot be attained, because it is a psychological emotion like anger, joy, and sadness. It is said: No, it is possible, in the sense that the person feels that the presence of the sinful act and its absence are not equal to him.

The third: ceasing from the sin.

* Student: The third.

* Shaykh: The third: ceasing from the sin, because whoever says he is repentant while he persists in sin is like one who mocks Allah, Mighty and Majestic. How can you say, "I repent to You, O Lord," while you are openly defying Him with sin? This is not valid; he must cease. If the sin was taking property unjustly, theft, or denial, then he must return it to its owner, or else he is lying in his repentance. If the repentance is from backbiting, he must cease from it and keep away from gatherings where it is practiced, or else he is lying; he must cease.

If we assume that his ceasing requires him to use something of what he had been disobeying with? We say: there is no harm. They gave an example of a man who had usurped land, then regretted and repented, and he is now in the middle of it and wants to bring out the bulldozers, the excavators, and others. In this state he is in the middle of the land and must use them; the bulldozers and excavators must move over it. So do we say that his action now is sinful or not? No, this is not sinful; rather it is obedience, because he uses this in order to free himself from it, he uses it to free himself from it. For this reason you find one of us cleaning himself after relieving himself and touching the impurity with his hand, and we do not say: you are sinful, nor that you are doing something disliked; rather we say he is rewarded and recompensed for that, even though he is touching the impurity with his hand, but for what? To free himself from it. Likewise, if a person applied perfume while in ihram, and perfume in ihram is prohibited, then repented and regretted and wished to remove it by washing, he must touch it with his hand, so his touching it now is obedience, because it is to free himself from this disobedience.

The fourth condition: resolve not to return in the future. The meaning is not "that he will not return in the future," but rather the intention is resolve not to return. If he returns one day, his first repentance is not invalidated, as long as at the time of repentance he was resolved not to return, because a person is human, and his soul may tempt him after repentance to return to sin. If he returns, his first repentance is not invalidated, but he needs a new repentance. Alright, so the resolve not to return; we do not say "on condition that he does not return." I think the difference between them is clear.

The fifth condition: that the repentance be at a time when repentance is accepted, namely before the sun rises from its west, because the sun will necessarily return from where it set. When it returns from where it set, all people will believe, because then they will believe that it has a Lord who manages it, since it has left what is familiar and left its habit, so people believe; but their faith will not benefit them except for one who had believed before. For this reason Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿On the day when some of the signs of your Lord come, a soul will not benefit from its faith if it had not believed before or earned good through its faith﴾ [al-Anʿām 158]. Likewise, repentance is not accepted when death arrives, because of the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And repentance is not for those who commit evil deeds until, when death comes to one of them, he says, "Indeed, I have repented now," nor for those who die while they are disbelievers﴾ [al-Nisāʾ 18]. So when death arrives and a person witnesses the unseen, that is, what was hidden and what he used to deny before, when he witnesses it and believes, that does not benefit; repentance is not accepted.

If someone says: Did the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him and his family, not offer repentance to his uncle in the context of death?

We say: Yes, but the Messenger ﷺ offered it to him and said: "A word by which I may argue for you before Allah"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3884), and the wording is his, and Muslim (24 / 39) from the hadith of al-Musayyab ibn Hazn.]], meaning that he did not affirm that it would benefit him; rather he said "I may argue for you," and arguing may benefit or may not benefit.

If someone says: Is repentance from one sin valid while persisting in another?

The answer: there is disagreement among the scholars on this. Some said: repentance from one sin is not valid while persisting in another, because repentance is returning to Allah, and this one returned in a divided manner, so it does not benefit him. Others made a distinction and said: if the repentance is from a sin while persisting in its type, it is not accepted, such as if he repents from looking at women but persists in touching women; here repentance is not accepted, because he persists in the type of sin, the type being one even if the individual instances or kinds differ.

Others said: repentance from one sin is accepted while persisting in another, but he does not deserve to be described as repentant in an absolute sense; rather we say: he is repentant from such-and-such, so he deserves a restricted repentance. He is not given the absolute description nor is the absolute description stripped from him; rather it is said: he is repentant from such-and-such. This is the most just of the sayings, because in it there is justice, since we cannot negate repentance from him absolutely nor affirm it absolutely. We say: this one is repentant, but he has not been saved from punishment, because he persists in another disobedience, so he will be punished for it.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: Allah, blessed and exalted, offering these disbelievers that they seek His forgiveness, meaning that they ask for forgiveness. Asking Allah for forgiveness has two aspects. The first: that one asks Allah for forgiveness with the wording, saying: "I seek Allah's forgiveness," "O Allah, forgive me," and the like. The second: that one does what is a cause of the forgiveness of sins. Whoever does something that is a cause of the forgiveness of sins has sought forgiveness. An example of this: "Whoever says 'Subhan Allah wa bihamdihi' a hundred times, his sins will be forgiven, even if they are like the foam of the sea"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6405), and Muslim (2691 / 28) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. This man did not say "O Allah, forgive my sins," but he did what is a cause of forgiveness. Based on this, seeking forgiveness has two aspects. The first aspect: asking Allah for forgiveness with the wording of forgiveness: "O Allah, forgive me," "I seek Allah's forgiveness," and the like. The second aspect: doing the act that causes forgiveness, which has many types. For example: "When a person performs wudu' and does it perfectly, then prays two rakʿas without his mind wandering in them, his previous sins are forgiven"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (159), and Muslim (226 / 3) from the hadith of ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan.]], and "The Friday to the next Friday is an expiation for what is between them"[[Narrated by Muslim (233 / 14) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]], and many examples. Yes.

* Student: Whoever says that repentance from negligence is not less than repentance from sin, is this (...) correct?

* Shaykh: Meaning, is it not less than non-obligation, that is?

* Student: It is not less than (...).

* Shaykh: If the negligence is negligence in an obligation, then yes, one must repent from it. If it is negligence in something non-obligatory, repentance is not required, because for something non-obligatory a person is free from it.

* Student: If someone says: the Prophet ﷺ, when he entered upon the Jew who was (...), then this Jew became Muslim, the Prophet ﷺ said: "Praise be to Allah who rescued him" (...).

* Shaykh: "from the Fire through me." Our understanding of this is that this man had not reached the point of death, but he was ill and close to death, and therefore he began looking at his father as if seeking his counsel.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: (...) this, and it also supports that Allah, the Exalted, loves those who repent and loves those who seek forgiveness.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: (...) those who say: the Messiah is the son of God, and those who say: God is the third of three. What we know of them is that most of them say: God (...) is plural in name only and one in essence; He has three hypostases: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. But the rulings are of multiple sects.

* Student: In His saying, the Exalted (...).

* Shaykh: An oath is estimated.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Yes, because the verbal jussive is with the direct "lam." Some say the clause is in a jussive position, and some say there are two operators here that governed the verb.

* Student: The rule that says the legal objectives (maqāṣid sharʿiyya) are not abandoned except (...), is this correct?

* Shaykh: What are the legal objectives?

* Student: Meaning if a person (...), it is not permissible for him (...).

* Shaykh: Bring the example; one cannot judge a rule without it.

* Student: Meaning, for example, if a person wants to rebuke someone (...) corruption, and that is not achievable for him except if he commits a minor sin (...), like sitting with him in a place where there are sins, hoping (...)?

* Shaykh: I do not see that forbidden means can never be a path to guidance. Forbidden means cannot be a path to guidance. So if, for example, we said: this man will not be guided unless you bring him music and play it for him, we do not play it for him; we invite him, and if he is guided it is for himself, and otherwise the burden is on him.

* Student: No matter how small the sin is?

* Shaykh: No matter how small.

Shaykh's commentary (Ibn 'Uthaymin, Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 5, verses 75–79:

Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan. ﴿The Messiah, son of Maryam, was no more than a messenger; messengers had passed away before him. And his mother was a woman of truth. They both used to eat food. Observe how We make the signs clear to them, then observe how they are turned away.﴾ (75) ﴿Say: Do you worship, besides Allah, that which holds no power to harm or benefit you? And Allah is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾ (76) ﴿Say: O People of the Scripture, do not exceed the limits in your religion beyond the truth, and do not follow the desires of a people who had gone astray before and led many astray, and strayed from the right way.﴾ (77) ﴿Those among the Children of Israel who disbelieved were cursed upon the tongue of Dawud and 'Isa son of Maryam. That was because they disobeyed and used to transgress.﴾ (78) ﴿They did not forbid one another from wrongdoing which they committed. How wretched was what they used to do.﴾ (79)

Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿The Messiah, son of Maryam, was no more than a messenger; messengers had passed away before him﴾. On grammar: ﴿مَا الْمَسِيحُ ابْنُ مَرْيَمَ إِلَّا رَسُولٌ﴾. It is well known that the Qur'an is in the dialect of Quraysh, because the dialect of Quraysh is the most eloquent of the Arabic dialects, and that (mā) in their usage works like (laysa), as in His saying: ﴿مَا هَذَا بَشَرًا﴾ [Yusuf 31]. But here it does not work like (laysa), because the negation has been broken (by illa). When the negation is broken, it is neutralized and does not function like (laysa).

So if you say: mā Muhammadun qā'iman ("Muhammad is not standing"), this is correct. Mā Muhammadun illa qā'imun ("Muhammad is only standing") is correct. Mā Muhammadun illa qā'iman? Incorrect; because when the negation is broken, it must be neutralized.

The Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿The Messiah, son of Maryam, was no more than a messenger; messengers had passed away before him﴾. The Messiah, son of Maryam, is the son of Maryam daughter of 'Imran, and he was called Messiah because he would not pass his hand over anyone afflicted with a defect except that he was healed by Allah's permission. As for the Messiah al-Dajjal, he is called Messiah because his eye is wiped out (he is one-eyed, a'war). It is said that he is called so because he travels the earth, like a cloud driven by the wind, and so "wipes" the earth by traversing it.

﴿The Messiah, son of Maryam, was no more than a messenger; messengers had passed away before him﴾: meaning, and he is not a god, as these people claim; rather he is a messenger sent from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and Allah, blessed and exalted, is the One who sent him.

﴿Messengers had passed away before him﴾: that is, messengers had passed on before him, so he is no novelty among mankind, since messengers preceded him, and he is like them.

﴿And his mother was a woman of truth﴾: meaning, his mother was among the siddiqat, that is, truthful in speech and belief, affirming those whose truthfulness is established by evidence, since the siddiq is the one who is truthful and affirms the truth. Allah said: ﴿And he who brings the truth and affirms it, those are the righteous﴾ [al-Zumar 33]. This is the siddiq. So his mother, may Allah be pleased with her, is a siddiqa, one of the perfect women about whom the Prophet ﷺ said: "Many men have reached perfection, but among women only four have reached perfection"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3411), Muslim (2431/70), from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari.]] and he mentioned Maryam daughter of 'Imran among them.

﴿They both used to eat food﴾: the pronoun ﴿kana﴾ refers to the Messiah and his mother.

﴿They both used to eat food﴾: so they are in need of sustenance and dependent upon it, and therefore it is not valid for them to be gods, since a god is free of need of others, as Allah said describing Himself: ﴿He feeds but is not fed﴾ [al-An'am 14].

﴿Observe how We make the signs clear to them﴾: ﴿Observe﴾ is addressed to the listener, and the first to be included in this is the Prophet ﷺ.

﴿How We make the signs clear to them﴾: meaning, observe its manner. Therefore we say that ﴿kayfa﴾ here is the object of ﴿unzur﴾ and not an interrogative; rather it is the object of ﴿unzur﴾, meaning: observe the manner in which the signs are made clear to them.

﴿Observe how We make [it] clear﴾: that is, We explain. ﴿To them﴾: that is, to the Children of Israel who claimed that Isa and his mother were two gods.

﴿How We make the signs clear to them﴾: that is, the manifest indications showing that they cannot be gods, because ﴿they both used to eat food﴾, and because 'Isa is a messenger, messengers had passed away before him, so it is not valid that he be a god when he is sent from a god.

﴿Observe how We make the signs clear to them, then observe how they are turned away﴾: ﴿anna﴾ here means ﴿kayfa﴾ (how). That is: then look again, how they are ﴿turned away﴾, that is, diverted from the truth despite its clarity and magnificence. All of this establishes Tawhid, the oneness of Allah in His divinity and lordship, and refutes what these Christians hold.

* The verse contains benefits. Among them: a person may be attributed to his mother if he has no father, as in His saying: ﴿the Messiah, son of Maryam﴾, where He attributed him to his mother.

Is one who is attributed to his mother, when he has no father, inherited from as a father's heir? 

Answer: Yes, according to the preponderant opinion, he inherits from him as a father would. Example: a man committed unlawful intercourse with a woman, and Allah forbid, and the child of fornication is not attributed to the fornicator but has a mother and no father. If he dies leaving his mother and his brother, is the inheritance for his mother, or does she inherit as a mother while his agnatic relatives inherit as agnates? On this there are two opinions among the scholars, and the correct view is that she inherits from him as a father would. On this basis, in the example we mentioned, the property of that child goes to his mother, and not to his maternal brothers or his maternal paternal uncles, since he has no agnatic connection except through his mother; as for his father's side, he has no father, so he has no agnates through the father.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the Messiah, 'Isa son of Maryam, is a messenger of the messengers of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, by His saying: ﴿only a messenger﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the attribute in which 'Isa son of Maryam is confined, with no other attribute besides it, is that he is a messenger, and a messenger cannot be a god, because he is subject to servitude from the one who sent him and bound by duties from the one who sent him.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: messengers die, by His saying: ﴿messengers had passed away before him﴾, which is an indication that 'Isa will die just as others have died.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: messengers cannot be gods. The reason is that a god does not die, while messengers die.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: praise of Maryam, peace be upon her, by His saying: ﴿and his mother was a woman of truth﴾. Thus she is of the second rank of human beings. What are the ranks? Four: the prophets, the siddiqun, the martyrs, and the righteous.

* Among its benefits: a clear refutation of the Jews who claimed that Maryam was a fornicator (baghiyy), may Allah destroy them, since a fornicator cannot be a siddiqa, for fornication is among the major sins.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: reasoning from the condition of those being spoken of to show that what they are claimed to be cannot be true while that condition exists, namely His saying: ﴿they both used to eat food﴾. This is an argument from their condition that they cannot be two gods.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, who is God, does not need food, by His saying: ﴿they both used to eat food﴾.

* Among its benefits: arguing from the clearest and most evident evidence rather than the obscure. Their eating food is a matter that cannot be denied; but if other rational proofs were brought, there might be dispute. Argument from what is perceived is more forceful than argument from what is merely rationally inferred, because rational arguments admit of dispute, whereas perceived facts do not.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: encouragement to reflection and contemplation, by His saying: ﴿Observe how We make the signs clear﴾. The command to observe comes in many places in the Noble Qur'an, in both general and specific forms. His saying: ﴿Say: Observe what is in the heavens and the earth﴾ [Yunus 101] is general, while this verse and its like are specific.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a refutation of those who delegate (ahl al-tafwid) the names and attributes of Allah, for the people of tafwid say that all the Qur'anic and Prophetic texts on the names and attributes of Allah are of unknown meaning and cannot be known, to the extent that the Prophet ﷺ would recite a hadith without knowing its meaning. For this reason they are called ahl al-tajhil (the people of ignorance-attribution).

When you read some books of scholars respected by us and by others, you find them saying of the people of tafwid that they are the Ahl al-Sunnah. They say: the Ahl al-Sunnah are of two kinds: the mufawwida and the mu'awwila. The mufawwida are those who say: we know nothing of the meanings of the verses and hadiths about the attributes, and this, in their view, is the school of the Salaf. The mu'awwila are those who distort the texts of the Book and the Sunnah.

But they have erred a great error on two counts. The first: their claim that the people of ta'wil are among the Ahl al-Sunnah. How can they be among the Ahl al-Sunnah when they distort words from their places? How can they be Ahl al-Sunnah when they stand in opposition to the creed of the Ahl al-Sunnah? It is never appropriate to call them Ahl al-Sunnah, except in contrast to the Rafidah. In contrast to the Rafidah, there is Sunnah and Shi'ah; the Shi'ah are the Rafidah, and the Sunnah are those who oppose them in belief, even if they differ among themselves.

The correct position is to say: the Ahl al-Sunnah are those who hold fast to it, unite upon it, and follow the Salaf in it.

The second: their saying that the Ahl al-Sunnah, or the Salaf, delegate the meanings. This is a lie against the Salaf, a plain lie. The Salaf do not delegate the meanings; rather they affirm and establish them. They affirm them and establish them. What they delegate is the modality (kayfiyyah). The modality they do delegate, because that is what reason requires. But the meanings they do not delegate; rather they state them, establish them, and explain them. This is well known among them. If you were to ask any one of the Salaf, or any follower of the Salaf: what is the meaning of Allah's saying ﴿The Most Merciful is established upon the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha 5]? He would say its meaning is ... what?

* Students: Elevated ('alā).

* Shaykh: And does ('alā) admit of any meaning? This is an explanation of the meaning. But if you asked him: how did He establish Himself? he would say: Allah knows best, I do not know. It is well known that the people of tafwid, as Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, said, are among the worst of the people of innovation and heresy, because their statements entail extremely grave consequences: it would follow that the messengers do not know the meanings of what was revealed to them; and that no one who does not know the meaning of what he says, unless he is insane or mad. And among them: it opens the door to the people of heresy. This view opens the door to the people of heresy, because when you read ﴿He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed; He is the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾ [al-Hashr 22] to the end of the surah, and you say: "By Allah, I do not know the meanings of these names, I do not know their meanings," the people of heresy will come to you and say: "Step aside from the battlefield; we are the ones who know." Then they interpret them, or rather distort them as they wish. Therefore this (...) or this attributed to the Salaf has opened the door of heresy wide. From there one says: there is no benefit in the Qur'an or the Sunnah, since they are not known. Then, there is no power nor strength except with Allah: they have made unknown the core and essence of the message, which is knowledge of Allah through His names and attributes.

So the summary: the way of the people of tafwid is a false way, and whoever attributes it to the Salaf has erred. Tafwid among the Salaf and their followers concerns what?

* Students: The modality.

* Shaykh: The modality. This is reason itself, for we know the meaning of establishment upon the Throne, but we do not know in what modality it is; we know the meaning of descent to the lowest heaven, but we do not know in what modality, and it is not permissible for us to picture a specific modality.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: everything Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has explained in His books revealed to the messengers is signs, meaning indications and evidences of the truth, whether the Qur'an, the Torah, or the Gospel.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: wonder at those to whom the signs were made clear and who were then turned away from the truth, and Allah forbid; hence He said: ﴿then observe how they are turned away﴾.

* Among the benefits of the verse: these people were turned away from the truth after it had become clear, as shown by the word ﴿thumma﴾ (then), which indicates a lapse of time: after the signs have become clear to you, and have become clear to them as well, they are turned away from the truth and diverted from it.

Now, (anna) and (kayfa) differ in meaning: ﴿anna yu'faku'na﴾ is a look of wonder and denunciation, whereas ﴿unzur kayfa nubayyinu lahumu al-ayat﴾ is a look of contemplation and affirmation.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 5, verse 76:

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Say: Do you worship, besides Allah, that which possesses neither harm nor benefit for you? And Allah is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾ [al-Ma'idah 76] ﴿Say﴾, i.e., O Muhammad, or say, O addressee, the one who affirms the oneness of God, to whom? To everyone who worships anyone besides Allah, say to him: ﴿Do you worship, besides Allah, that which possesses neither harm nor benefit for you?﴾

His saying ﴿besides Allah﴾ means: other than Him.

﴿That which possesses neither harm nor benefit for you﴾ means: it cannot repel harm from you, nor bring benefit to you. It has also been said that the meaning is: that which does not possess for you harm if you disobey it, nor benefit if you obey it. According to the first interpretation, there is an omission in the verse. What is the omission? [It is:] that which does not possess for you the repelling of harm. The rule is that when there is a dispute as to whether the speech contains something omitted or not, what is the basic principle?

* Student: No omission.

* The Shaykh: No omission. Accordingly, ﴿that which possesses neither harm for you⦆ means, if what?

* Student: If you disobey it.

* The Shaykh: If you disobey it and oppose it. ﴿Nor benefit⦆ means if you obey it.

﴿And Allah is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing⦆ means: how can you worship that which possesses neither harm nor benefit for you and abandon the One who is All-Hearing, All-Knowing, namely Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, who hears what you say and knows what you do, of speech and action.

* This noble verse contains benefits. Among them: rebuke of the worshippers of idols, because the interrogative in His saying ﴿Do you worship⦆ is for reproach.

* Among its benefits: that idols possess neither benefit nor harm, and this is agreed upon.

* From this benefit follows the misguidance of those who worship idols. For this reason Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And who is more astray than one who calls upon other than Allah, one who will not respond to him until the Day of Resurrection, and who are unaware of their supplication﴾ [al-Ahqaf 5] — they do not hear it — ﴿And when the people are gathered, they will be enemies to them﴾ [al-Ahqaf 6]. So they do not benefit them in this world or in the Hereafter, but rather they oppose them.

If someone says: A person may call upon an idol to remove a harm and the harm is removed, or to bring a benefit and the benefit comes, while the Qur'an clearly states that all idols neither benefit nor harm?

The answer: This is a trial, and it occurs at the time of calling upon them, not by their calling. For we believe with certainty that they cannot respond until the Day of Resurrection; even if they were called upon until the Day of Resurrection, they would not respond. Rather, Allah may test His servants by the occurrence of a thing—what?

* The students: At it (at the time of it).

* The Shaykh: At the time of the supplication, not by the supplication. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has decreed the occurrence of this thing at this specific time in which the supplication took place, and not because of the supplication. We know this with certainty, because Allah says: ﴿who will not respond to him until the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Ahqaf 5].

In what we have established there is a warning, namely that a person should beware of having the means of sin made easy for him. A person may be tested, and the means of sin are made easy for him, and he falls into it, except those whom Allah protects. For this reason, whoever has the means of sin made easy for him, yet leaves it for the sake of Allah, has a greater reward than one for whom it was not made easy.

Consider the young man who was invited by a woman of rank and beauty, and he said: "Indeed I fear Allah." This one who was invited is a man whom a woman invited, and he is a young man with desire, with neither of them having anyone present and no one watching them. He mentioned no obstacle except that he fears Allah, and this shows that all matters were made easy for him. But when he left this for the sake of Allah, Allah shaded him in His shade on a day when there is no shade but His. O Allah, make us among such people.

The point is: if those people who worship other than Allah and call upon them deceive us by the attainment of the desired outcome, the answer is that this certainly did not occur by the supplication, but occurred at the time of the supplication.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that harm and benefit are from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, because He followed the negation of harm and benefit from these idols with His saying: ﴿And Allah is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing⦆, and this is so. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to Abdullah ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him): "Know that if the whole nation gathered to benefit you with anything, they would not benefit you except with what Allah has already written for you, and if they gathered to harm you with anything, they would not harm you except with what Allah has already written against you."[1]

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of these two noble names of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: All-Hearing (al-Sami') and All-Knowing (al-'Alim).

Does He hear with hearing or without hearing?

* Student: With hearing.

* The Shaykh: What is the evidence that He has hearing from this name?

* Student: Because names have meanings.

* The Shaykh: Names have meanings, derived from their meanings. Al-Sami' means... The hearing attributed to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is divided into two kinds: a kind meaning the perception of what is heard, and a kind meaning responding.

The first is divided into three categories: one intended as a threat, one intended to show comprehensiveness, and one intended as support and assistance. Three categories. This is hearing of what? The hearing of perception, the perception of what is heard. As for the first, it is like the saying of the Blessed and Exalted: ﴿Or do they think that We do not hear their secrets and their private talk? Yes, and Our messengers are with them, recording﴾ [al-Zukhruf 80]. This is a threat.

As for the second, which is intended to show Allah's comprehensive encompassing of everything, it is like the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Allah has heard the statement of the woman who argues with you concerning her husband and complains to Allah﴾, to the end of the verse [al-Mujadilah 1].

As for the one intended as support and assistance, it is like the saying of the Exalted to Musa and Harun: ﴿Fear not; indeed I am with you both, hearing and seeing﴾ [Ta-Ha 46].

As for the one meaning answering or responding, it is like the saying of the worshipper: "Allah hears whoever praises Him," meaning He responds. For this reason it is transitive with "li" (to) and not directly, because hearing in the sense of perception is transitive directly; you say: "I heard a sound." But hearing in the sense of answering is transitive with "li"; you say: "I heard for so-and-so," meaning I responded to him, and from it is "Allah hears whoever praises Him."

Now: ﴿Indeed my Lord is the Hearer of supplication﴾ [Ibrahim 39] — of which kind?

* Students: The first.

* Another student: Both.

* Another student: Responding.

* The Shaykh: Both of them together. He is the Hearer of supplication, He hears the voice, the voice of the one who calls, and He is also the Responder to supplication, so it includes both matters.

As for al-'Alim, how comprehensive a name it is! Al-'Alim, if it is not the most comprehensive of Allah's names, it is among the most comprehensive, because knowledge relates to possible matters, impossible matters, and necessary matters, to everything. The knowledge of Allah relates to everything. He, the Mighty and Majestic, knows impossible things. An example is the saying of Allah, the Blessed and Exalted: ﴿Had there been within them gods besides Allah, they would have been ruined﴾ [al-Anbiya 22]. This is an impossible matter, yet Allah, Glorified and Exalted, knows its consequence: ﴿Had there been within them gods besides Allah, they would have been ruined﴾.

He, Glorified and Exalted, knows the possible, which is what relates to the actions of servants. All the actions of servants belong to the category of the possible, and Allah, the Exalted, knows them: ﴿Allah knows that you were deceiving yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah 187], ﴿Allah knows that you will remember them﴾ [al-Baqarah 235], ﴿And Allah knows what is in your hearts﴾ [al-Ahzab 51], and other numerous verses. Every knowledge that relates to the created is knowledge of the possible, because the created is possible; for if it were impossible it would not exist, and if it were necessary it would not cease to exist.

He, may He be exalted, also knows what relates to the necessary, He knows the necessary, which is His knowledge of Himself, the Blessed and Exalted. His knowledge of Himself is knowledge of the necessary. For this reason the scholars said: knowledge is the most comprehensive of the attributes of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Does it relate to His will, or is it a necessarily inherent attribute?

* Students: Inherent.

* The Shaykh: It is a necessarily inherent attribute. For this reason, when al-Saffarini, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

"Knowledge and speech have been related, O my friend, absolutely, to every thing."

The point is that he says "to every thing." This is correct. Speech relates even to the impossible, but knowledge, in terms of being a necessarily inherent attribute, is more comprehensive than speech.
If someone says: If you say that knowledge is an essential attribute, what is the answer regarding His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We will surely test you until We know those of you who strive and those who are steadfast, and We will test your reports﴾ [Muhammad 31]? ﴿Until We know⦆ (...).

**Commentary of Ibn ʿUthaymin (Tafsīr al-Qurʾān al-Karīm) on Sūrah al-Māʾidah, verse 77:**

﴿Say, "O People of the Scripture, do not commit excess in your religion beyond the truth."﴾ That is: say, O Muhammad.

﴿O People of the Scripture﴾ That is: O possessors of the Scripture. What is meant by them are the Jews and the Christians. By "the Scripture" are meant the Torah and the Gospel. The word is in the generic sense, and the definite article "al-" here is for previous reference, meaning: the Scripture that the addressees know.

﴿Do not commit excess (lā taghlū) in your religion﴾ That is: in your worship. Ghuluww (exaggeration, excess) is going beyond the limit. This occurred when the Jews said, "ʿUzayr is the son of God," and the Christians said, "The Messiah is the son of God," and the Jews were strict regarding things that were not prescribed for them. Although the Jews were indeed subjected to hardship, as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿So for the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We made unlawful for them good things which had been lawful for them and [for] their averting from the way of Allah many times over﴾ [al-Nisāʾ 160].

The essential point is that "do not commit excess" means: do not go beyond the limit.

﴿In your religion﴾ In your worship.

As for His saying ﴿beyond the truth (ghayr al-ḥaqq)﴾, that means excess that is other than the truth. The qualifier here is not restrictive, because all excess is untrue; rather, it is a statement of the reality. Scholars call such a qualifier, which states the reality, a "revealing attribute" (ṣifah kāshifah).

His saying ﴿beyond the truth﴾: the truth is what agrees with the Sharīʿah, and falsehood is what contradicts the Sharīʿah.

﴿And do not follow the desires of a people who had gone astray before, and led many astray and strayed from the sound way﴾
﴿And do not follow the desires of a people﴾ "Ahwāʾ" (desires) is the plural of hawā (desire). What is meant by desire here is whatever contradicts the law of Allah, because actions are either desire (hawā) or guidance (hudā). What agrees with the Sharīʿah is guidance, and what contradicts it is desire.

His saying ﴿who had gone astray before﴾ refers to their scholars and monks who distorted the religion of Allah, so they went astray and led others astray. Allah, glorified and exalted, says: follow what has been revealed to you, and do not follow the desires of these people who went astray before.

﴿And led many astray﴾ That is, they were not merely astray themselves; they were leaders in error, and so they led many astray, many of whom? Many of the people. Thus they became, may Allah protect us, astray themselves and misleading others, the opposite of the righteous reformers or the guided guides.

﴿And strayed from the sound way﴾ This is an additional clause for clarification and elucidation, because He said ﴿had gone astray before﴾: from what? He explains it with His saying ﴿and strayed from the sound way﴾. That is: from the straight path. The word "sawāʾ" (sound, even) is applied to many meanings, among them uprightness. The meaning is: from the straight path, so it is an instance of an attribute being attached to what it describes.

* In this noble verse: the Prophet ﷺ was given a specific command to say this statement. We have explained in more than one place that the Prophet (ﷺ) is commanded to convey the entire Qurʾān, but sometimes a specific matter of conveyance is directed to him for what reason? For the sake of giving it special attention.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the People of the Book have excess (ghuluww) in their religion, and this is clear. The Christians say that ʿĪsā is the son of God, and the Jews say that ʿUzayr is the son of God. They also follow their rabbis and monks and take them as lords.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: if the People of the Book are forbidden from excess, and excess in itself is a corruption, then others are likewise forbidden. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ warned against excess in religion and against excess in oneself. "He, peace be upon him, used to forbid excess in religion, and he forbade those who said: 'We fast and do not break our fast, we pray at night and do not sleep, we do not marry women, and we do not eat meat'" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhārī (5063) and Muslim (1401/5), from Anas]. "He took pebbles during the Farewell Pilgrimage and began turning them in his hand and saying: 'Throw the likes of these, and beware of excess in religion'" [Narrated by al-Nasāʾī (3057) and Ibn Mājah (3029), from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās]. He called those who wished to continue fasting without breaking their fast "the over-zealous" (al-mutaʿammiqīn) as a warning against their action. "He supplicated against those who were extreme (al-mutanaṭṭiʿūn) in their religion three times, saying: 'The extremists have perished'" [Narrated by Muslim (2670/7), from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd]. Generally, the one who is extreme tends to deviate, we ask Allah for well-being, because excess contradicts the natural disposition (fiṭrah), so this excess remains merely outward and his heart is empty of the reality of faith. For this reason "the Prophet ﷺ informed that the Khawārij (Khawārij: the early sect that rebelled against ʿAlī) would belittle the prayer of the Companions compared to their own prayer and their recitation compared to theirs, but their faith does not go beyond their throats" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhārī (3610) and Muslim (1065/148), from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī], and we seek refuge in Allah.

Generally, the one who is extreme is found such that his heart roams among people and their actions, criticizing them and objecting to them, yet he is empty of knowledge of Allah as it truly should be known, and of returning to Him and turning to Him in repentance. So beware of this, beware of this. Be upright, between excess and negligence.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: excess contradicts the truth, by His saying ﴿beyond the truth﴾.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the prohibition against following the desires of those who have gone astray, by His saying ﴿do not follow the desires of a people who had gone astray﴾.

* Among its benefits: what leads a person into error is desire. Otherwise, if a person speaks with justice and judges with equity, he would not stray from the straight path. But his desire overcomes him until he goes astray. For this reason He said ﴿the desires of a people who had gone astray﴾, then He explained their going astray ﴿from the sound way﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a warning against being a leader in misguidance, by His saying ﴿who had gone astray before and led many astray and strayed from the sound way﴾.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: a refutation of the Jabriyyah (Jabriyyah: those who deny human agency and hold that humans are compelled) who said that a person's action is not ascribed to him, that he is compelled to it, and that he has no choice in it, because the verse explicitly states that they went astray and led others astray.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of causes, by His saying ﴿and led [others] astray﴾. This misguidance was not through force, compulsion, or denial, but through a cause by which they adorned falsehood until it became, through it, the stronger.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: these misguiding and misguided people combined two evils. The first: their own going astray. The second: leading others astray. Is it possible for a person to be limited to only one of these, such as going astray himself only?

* Student: No.

* Students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: It is possible. It is possible that he is astray and does not call to error. But if he is a leader among his people, his going astray becomes an actual call, an actual call, because he will be emulated and followed. Is it possible for him to be misleading while not himself astray?

* Students: It is not possible.

* The Shaykh: It is not possible, because his leading others astray is considered?

* Students: Error.

* The Shaykh: Error. He may be carrying out what Allah has commanded in his private actions, but if he leads people astray, this is error. So it is possible for a person to be astray without misleading others, but is it possible for him to be misleading without being astray?

* Students: Misleading without being astray.

* The Shaykh: Misleading without being astray is not possible, because we say: the mere fact that he leads people astray is itself error.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the correct religion is a middle path between one who exaggerates in it and one who neglects it, by His saying ﴿from the sound way﴾. That is: from the upright way. The middle of the way is justice, which contains neither excess nor negligence.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 5, verse 78–79:

Then He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the Children of Israel were cursed upon the tongue of David and Jesus, son of Mary. That was because they disobeyed and used to transgress.﴾ [al-Ma'idah 78].

﴿Lu'ina﴾ is in the passive voice, or if you wish, say: it is in the form of what has not named its doer (mabni li-ma lam yusamma fa'iluhu, the passive form of the verb). This is the more precise, and the more precise is to say: mabni li-ma lam yusamma fa'iluhu; because if you say "mabni lil-majhul" (passive voice), it would create a problem for us with the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And man was created weak﴾ [an-Nisa 28], for here the doer is not mentioned, but is it known or unknown?

* The students: Known.

* The Shaykh: Known.

So, the expression by our saying: a past-tense verb (generally) in the form of mabni li-ma lam yusamma fa'iluhu is better than mabni lil-majhul. So who cursed them?

* A student: Allah.

* The Shaykh: If there is here a verb in the form of what has not named its doer, then who cursed?

* The students: Allah.

* The Shaykh: Allah, and the angels, and all of mankind; because everyone whom Allah curses, the friends of Allah curse him. Indeed, even people other than the friends of Allah curse him, as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said about the people of the Fire: ﴿Every time a nation enters, it curses its sister﴾ [al-A'raf 38].

﴿Those who disbelieved among the Children of Israel were cursed﴾. "Those who disbelieved" are those who did not remain steadfast upon the religion they were charged with. For example, the Children of Israel before the mission of Jesus, their religion was the religion of Moses; so if they opposed it, they disbelieved. And the Christians after the mission of Jesus and before the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ), their religion is Christianity; so whoever opposes it is a disbeliever.

He said: ﴿upon the tongue of David and Jesus, son of Mary﴾, meaning: David, peace be upon him, and Jesus, son of Mary, invoked curses upon them, saying: "O Allah, curse them."

As for His saying: ﴿upon the tongue of David and Jesus, son of Mary﴾, David is undoubtedly one of the prophets of Allah, but he was given prophethood and some kingship; the complete kingship, however, was for his son Solomon.

﴿David and Jesus, son of Mary, that﴾: the referent is the curse indicated by the verb ﴿lu'ina﴾, and here the pronoun refers to what the verb was derived from, i.e., that curse, "because they disobeyed."

As for His saying: ﴿bima 'asaw﴾, the "ba'" here indicates causation and "ma" is verbal (masdariyyah), meaning: because of their disobedience. Disobedience is the opposite of obedience, and obedience is conformity with the one who commands by avoiding what he forbade and doing what he commanded.

﴿And they used to transgress﴾: His saying ﴿wa kanu ya'tadun﴾ is coordinated with ﴿'asaw﴾, i.e., upon the relative clause, meaning: because of their disobedience and their transgression. Their transgression against whom? They transgressed against the Creator, Mighty and Majestic, by saying about Him what is not fitting for Him, and they also transgressed against creation, so some of them killed others.

As for His saying ﴿wa kanu ya'tadun﴾, if someone said: Isn't transgression a form of disobedience? The answer: Yes, it is a form of disobedience, but some individual instances may be singled out for mention because of their importance and attention they deserve, or because they are more severe and more ugly. Then He explained that transgression and disobedience, saying: ﴿They did not forbid one another from wrongdoing they committed﴾. ﴿They did not forbid one another﴾ means: some of them did not forbid others; because the form of mufa'alah indicates mutuality from both sides. And nahy (forbidding) is requesting refraining in a manner of superiority; this is nahy: requesting refraining in a manner of superiority. Accordingly, if a servant commands his master with something or forbids him from something, he is not a commander or a forbidder, because it is a request to refrain in a manner of superiority; except if the servant claims he is superior to his master, which is a claim; i.e., he may imagine that he is superior to his master, so he directs command and prohibition to him.

As for His saying ﴿'an munkarin﴾: al-munkar is what the Shari'ah has disapproved of, whether neglect of an obligation or violation of a prohibition; this is al-munkar. And is the reference for it custom or the Shari'ah? The Shari'ah; because people may disapprove of what is not munkar and may approve of what is munkar, so the reference is then the Shari'ah, not the custom of people.

As for His saying ﴿'an munkarin fa'aluhu﴾: how does He say ﴿They did not forbid one another from wrongdoing they committed﴾? Because a forbidding does not apply to a thing already done and completed; rather, the verse means: refraining from continuing in a wrongdoing they had committed; because the munkar that has been done cannot be subject to a prohibition. If a person stood up, should I say: "Do not stand"? No; if I say "do not stand," the meaning is "do not continue standing." So ﴿'an munkarin fa'aluhu﴾ means: from continuing in a wrongdoing they had committed.

﴿Surely evil is what they used to do﴾: the lam here is an introductory lam for an oath; meaning: "By Allah, surely evil..." and "bi'sa" is a past-tense verb but is in reality an expression of blame, since it is a verb indicating the expression of blame, just as "ni'ma" indicates the expression of praise.

﴿Surely evil is what they used to do﴾: "ma" is the subject and is a relative pronoun, and ﴿kanu﴾ is the relative clause; where is the returning pronoun to the relative pronoun? It is elided, and the estimate is: "Surely evil is what they used to do of it."

* * *

I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿Those who disbelieved among the Children of Israel were cursed upon the tongue of David and Jesus, son of Mary. That was because they disobeyed and used to transgress (78). They did not forbid one another from wrongdoing they committed. Surely evil is what they used to do (79).﴾

Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the Children of Israel were cursed upon the tongue of David and Jesus, son of Mary. That was because they disobeyed and used to transgress (78). They did not forbid one another from wrongdoing they committed. Surely evil is what they used to do.﴾

* Among the benefits of this verse: the cursing of the disbelievers among the Children of Israel, from His saying ﴿lu'ina﴾; and cursing, known, is expulsion and distancing from the mercy of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and deprivation of success.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that among the Children of Israel there are disbelievers and there are believers; from His saying ﴿those who disbelieved among the Children of Israel﴾; and this is the reality, for among them were believers, such as the disciples of Jesus, peace be upon him, and the seventy men whom Moses chose, and other than these.

* Among its benefits: that the one who cursed the Children of Israel were two noble messengers, who were cursed upon their tongues, namely David and Jesus, son of Mary; David was one of the prophets of the Children of Israel, but not the last of them; the last of them was Jesus, son of Mary; so their curse was at the beginning of the messages and at the end of the messages.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of causes, from His saying ﴿that was because they disobeyed﴾, for the "ba'" indicates causation; and this has been established before, and the disagreement of people concerning causes was explained, and the correct view on them was clarified, and that causes are of two kinds: sensory and legislative.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that transgression against others is worse than mere disobedience, although it is itself among the acts of disobedience; from His saying ﴿that was because they disobeyed and used to transgress﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah, Glorified and Exalted, does not wrong people at all, and that He does not punish anyone with a punishment except for a sin; from His saying ﴿that was because they disobeyed﴾.

* Among the benefits of the verse that follows: the reluctance of the Children of Israel to forbid wrongdoing; from His saying ﴿They did not forbid one another from wrongdoing they committed﴾.

* Among its benefits: that abandoning the forbidding of wrongdoing is a cause of Allah's curse, His expulsion and distancing, and we seek refuge in Allah.

Know that commanding good and forbidding evil requires conditions. The first condition: knowledge that this is a good that is commanded, and this is an evil that is forbidden; so it is not permissible to command what one does not know to be commanded, nor to forbid what one does not know to be forbidden, because of what that entails of slander against Allah and turning the servants of Allah away from what Allah has made lawful for them.
