The Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin on Surah 5, verses 90–91 (part 3 of 4):

﴿O you who believe, indeed, intoxicants, gambling, idolatrous altars, and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid it that you may be successful.﴾ (90) ﴿Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred to occur among you﴾ ... to the end of the verse. We have reached His saying: ﴿and divining arrows﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse is the strong warning against these four practices, since His saying ﴿defilement from the work of Satan﴾ requires complete aversion to them, first by describing them as defilement, and then by describing this defilement as the work of Satan.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse is the obligation to avoid intoxicants, gambling, idolatrous altars, and divining arrows, based on His saying ﴿so avoid it﴾.

* Among its benefits: avoiding these four things is a cause of success (falah). Every one of us who wants success should pursue its causes. The evidence is His saying ﴿that you may be successful﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: affirmation of the causation (ta'lil) of legal rulings, meaning that the legal rulings have praiseworthy purposes, which is wisdom (hikmah). This is shown by His saying ﴿that you may be successful﴾, and also by His saying ﴿defilement from the work of Satan so avoid it﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the Qur'an's method in stating causes is sometimes to mention the cause before the ruling and sometimes after it, according to what the context requires and the indicators of the surrounding discourse. So when God mentions a ruling and gives a cause for it, He sometimes mentions the cause first and then builds the ruling upon it, and sometimes mentions the ruling and then brings the cause. Here He mentioned the cause before the ruling. What is the cause? ﴿defilement from the work of Satan so avoid it.﴾ In His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They ask you about menstruation. Say: it is a harm, so keep away from women during menstruation﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:222], did He put the cause or the ruling first? The cause. He said: ﴿Say: it is a harm, so keep away from women.﴾ The benefit of putting the cause first is that the ruling reaches the soul when it is already at ease and awaiting the ruling. It is at ease with the cause and anticipates the ruling, because it is known that a sensible person, when told the cause, will act in accordance with it. So when a person hears His saying ﴿Say: it is a harm﴾, as soon as he hears ﴿it is a harm﴾ he will arrive at the ruling ﴿so keep away﴾ while already anticipating it. This verse is similar.

﴿defilement from the work of Satan so avoid it﴾: from the moment the cause ﴿defilement from the work of Satan﴾ is stated, the person is awaiting the ruling of prohibition. Sometimes the cause comes after the ruling, as in His saying: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to one who eats it, unless it be carrion, or blood poured out, or the flesh of swine, for indeed it is defilement﴾. This is because carrion, blood, and the flesh of swine are repugnant to natural dispositions, so He put the ruling first, since sound souls anticipate this ruling, and they may shun it even without a legal ruling; then the cause comes, matching what natural disposition requires.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the works of Satan that he commands are defilement, based on His saying ﴿defilement from the work of Satan﴾. Then do we say that the verse is evidence for the impurity (najasah) of intoxicants, since "rijs" means "najs" (impure), as in His saying: ﴿except that it be carrion, or blood poured out, or the flesh of swine, for indeed it is defilement﴾ [al-An'am 6:145]?

The answer: Yes, some scholars have used this verse as evidence for the impurity of intoxicants. But upon reflection on the noble verse, you will not find evidence in it for the impurity of intoxicants, for two reasons.

The first reason: He said ﴿defilement from the work of﴾, so it is a defilement of action (ma'nawi), and the defilement of action is the moral (ma'nawi) defilement, as in His saying: ﴿so avoid the defilement of idols﴾.

The second reason: gambling, idolatrous altars, and divining arrows are not sensory (hissi) defilement. Is the report about these four one or different? One. Intoxicants is the subject (mubtada'), the other three are coordinated with it, and then the predicate came: "defilement." So where is the evidence that these four things differ in ruling, such that the three are called moral defilement and the first is called sensory defilement? Where is the evidence? It requires evidence.

If someone says: "The indication by juxtaposition (dalalat al-iqtiran) is weak and cannot be relied upon"?

The answer: The basic principle with juxtaposition is that the ruling is uniform across all items unless there is evidence otherwise. An example of this: Abu Hanifah said that horses are forbidden. Do you know horses? They are well known. Based on His saying: ﴿and horses, mules, and donkeys, for you to ride and as adornment﴾ [al-Nahl 16:8]. He juxtaposed them with mules and donkeys, so they would be forbidden. There is no doubt that the correct view is with him, because the basic principle in juxtaposition is agreement in ruling. But horses have evidence that excludes them, which is what al-Bukhari narrated from Asma' bint Abi Bakr, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "We slaughtered a horse in Medina during the time of the Prophet ﷺ and we ate it."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5511), and Muslim (1942/38) from the hadith of Asma' bint Abi Bakr.]] This excludes horses from the ruling for mules and donkeys. Here, in the noble verse ﴿intoxicants and gambling﴾, we have no evidence that excludes intoxicants from the ruling of what is juxtaposed with it, namely gambling, idolatrous altars, and divining arrows. Accordingly, there is no indication in the verse for sensory impurity of intoxicants.

If someone says: "Is there anything in the Sunnah that indicates this?"

The answer: No, there is nothing in the Sunnah that indicates this. As for the hadith of Abu Tha'labah al-Khushani, may Allah be pleased with him, that he asked the Prophet ﷺ and said: "O Messenger of Allah, we are in the land of a people of the Book. Shall we eat from their vessels?" He said: "Do not eat in them unless you cannot find others; if so, wash them and eat in them."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5478), and Muslim (1930/8) from the hadith of Abu Tha'labah al-Khushani, in a similar wording.]] What is the answer to this hadith?

We say: those who hold that intoxicants are sensorily impure use this hadith, but there is in reality no evidence in it, because the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, only forbade them from eating in their vessels unless after washing, and another condition was that we do not find others. His clear purpose is to keep distance from mixing with them and eating in their vessels. The proof: if the cause were impurity, washing would suffice to permit eating in them; he would not make it a condition that we do not find others. But the Prophet ﷺ intended that we not mix with the People of the Book, that we keep away from them, and that we not borrow from them, lest they claim favor over us in that. This is the first point.

Second: we say, what is the basis for considering this evidence for the impurity of intoxicants?

They said: because their vessels contain intoxicants, since they consider intoxicants lawful. We reply: their vessels would also contain pork, since they consider pork lawful. What made us think that the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, considered intoxicants but not pork, or considered pork but not intoxicants, or considered both together?

There is no evidence. What becomes clear to us is that the reason for this is that we should not mix with them and should not eat from their vessels. Thus there is no evidence in this hadith.

If someone says: Did the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, not get asked about intoxicants being made into vinegar, and he said: "No"?[[Narrated by Muslim (1983/11) from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him.]] That is, if a drink ferments, may we keep it so that it becomes vinegar, or add a substance to make it vinegar? He said: "No."

We say: there is no evidence here for impurity. This is evidence that it is not permissible to keep intoxicants in one's possession; rather one should pour them out, so that the soul does not urge one to consume them. This is clear, and it contains no indication of impurity in any way whatsoever.

So whoever claims that intoxicants are sensorily impure must bring evidence. Otherwise, we cannot oblige God's servants to wash vessels of intoxicants, or wash garments if they are soiled with it, or wash bodies. Nor can we invalidate the prayers of God's servants if their garments have stains of intoxicants or their bodies are affected, except with evidence. The matter is not merely verbal, whether it is impure or not; many rulings depend on it. There must be a proof from God, may He be mighty and majestic, which allows us to oblige God's servants to something required by the text. So we say: the basic position is non-impurity, and a general prohibition does not entail impurity, as proven by the fact that poison and harmful foods are forbidden but are not impure. This is evidence derived from the well-known principle that the basic state is the absence of obligation (bara'at al-dhimmah).

Then we say: we have a positive evidence other than the original evidence, which is negation or absence: positive evidence that they are pure, that is, intoxicants are pure, and their impurity is moral.

The evidence: when intoxicants were prohibited, the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, took them out to the markets and poured them out. If they were impure, they would not have poured them out in the markets, because it is not permissible to pour anything impure in the markets of Muslims, just as urine and feces may not be poured there. Those who hold impurity answered according to their own basis; otherwise the basic position is non-impurity. But they said: the jars of intoxicants, meaning the containers of intoxicants, were not numerous enough to make the streets flow with them; that is, they did not reach an amount that would cause the roads to flow. We say: Glory be to God! Were those vessels used by the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, before the prohibition, which were more numerous: they or a drop of urine?

* Student: They are the same.

* Shaykh: They are certainly more numerous, and more than a small quantity of the number. We do not say that the streets of Medina became rivers flowing with intoxicants; we do not say this. If they said: what makes you know that they poured them out in the markets? Perhaps they poured them out at the edges of the market, where people do not pass? We say: this contradicts the unrestricted wording. They poured them out in the markets, and it does not say they poured them out at the sides of the markets. Being at the side is an added condition beyond the unrestricted wording, so it requires establishing that they poured them out at the sides of the markets. Furthermore, is it reported from the Companions that after pouring them out they washed the vessels? It is not reported; it is not reported. Had they been impure, they would have washed the vessels and transmitted this to the Ummah.

Another evidence is what is established in Sahih Muslim: "A man came with a rawiyah of intoxicants." The rawiyah is a large water-skin, which he had been storing for the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and he came to the Prophet ﷺ and presented it as a gift, not knowing that it had been prohibited. The Prophet ﷺ said: "It has been prohibited." It is known that a person may not accept a forbidden gift, whether it is forbidden in itself or because of how it was acquired, if its giver knows it. One of the Companions whispered to him: "Sell it." The Prophet ﷺ said: "What did you whisper to him?" He asked about the whispering, although one should not ask two people who are whispering, "What did you say?" But the situation required the question. Perhaps the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, heard part of the conversation. He said: "What did you whisper to him?" He said: "I said: sell it." He said: "Indeed God, when He prohibits something, prohibits its price," or as he said, ﷺ. So the man opened the mouth of the rawiyah and poured out the intoxicants in the presence of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and the Prophet ﷺ did not command him to wash it.[[Narrated by Muslim (1579/68) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Abbas.]]

Do you see: if intoxicants were impure, would the Prophet ﷺ remain silent instead of telling this man: wash the rawiyah? He would never remain silent, because this man did not know that it had been prohibited, so how would he know it was impure? Thus it becomes clear that the impurity of intoxicants is moral impurity. Although only a few of the Ummah have held this, the majority of scholars are with the evidence, and the majority say it is sensorily impure. But as you have seen, the evidences now are clear that its impurity is moral.

Based on this: what about things that now contain alcohol, such as spirit, and similarly what is used to anoint wounds and the like? Are they impure or pure? Pure, because if the basis, which is intoxicants, is pure according to what has become clear to us from the Qur'an and Sunnah, then whatever contains some of it is even more fitting to be pure.

If it is said: Do you permit a person to perfume himself with these scents or to anoint himself with these ointments?

We say: when there is need, we permit it, and by God's praise there is no difficulty for us in this. For example, a wound needs to be swabbed with spirit or something else to make it easier to stitch with a needle. There is no doubt that this is permitted, because a doubtful ruling is permitted by need, even if its origin is prohibition.

If one is not in need but uses it as perfume, is this forbidden or not? We consider: His saying, may He be blessed and exalted, ﴿so avoid it﴾. Does it mean avoiding its drinking, which leads to harm, or avoiding it absolutely? We say: since God says ﴿so avoid it﴾, then ﴿Satan only wants﴾ to the end of the verse, we know that the command to avoid refers to avoiding drinking. There is no doubt about this; avoiding anything other than drinking is a matter of doubt. Caution (wara') requires that a person does not do this except out of need, that he does not anoint himself with these things except when necessary, such as sterilizing a wound and the like.

If someone says: If these scents contain a proportion of alcohol but it is small, say five percent, does it have an effect? The answer: It has no effect. Only what affects the mixture as a whole has an effect. If it does not affect, it is not forbidden, based on the case of a man who has a vessel of water into which an impurity has fallen but has not changed it. What is that water? It is pure, because it has not been affected. Accordingly, we say: if the proportion is small even in these scents, there is no doubt that they are permissible, because a small proportion has no effect.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the mercy of God, may He be blessed and exalted, toward His servants whom He created for His worship, since He warned them against everything harmful and explained the good outcomes to them, based on His saying ﴿so avoid it that you may be successful﴾.

Then God, may He be mighty and majestic, said: ﴿Satan only wants﴾ to the end.

* In this noble verse: affirmation of will (iradah) for Satan, based on His saying ﴿Satan only wants﴾. There is no doubt that he has will. Have you considered God's saying to the angels: ﴿Prostrate to Adam,﴾ so they prostrated except Iblis [al-Baqarah 2:34], and he argued with his Lord out of will or without will? Out of will. So Satan has will.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the evil will of Satan toward the children of Adam, which is to cause enmity and hatred among them, which necessitates division.

* Among its benefits: the division of the Ummah is among the things Satan wants, since enmity and hatred undoubtedly lead to division. So everything that leads to division is among what Satan wants.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the principle we have just pointed to, that everything that leads to division is among what Satan wants. Thousands of issues fall under this: selling over the sale of a Muslim brother causes hatred and division; bidding over his bid; proposing over his proposal; and the like. So everything that leads to division is among what Satan wants.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: God's dislike, may He be blessed and exalted, for enmity and hatred among Muslims, since this is a warning beyond which there is no warning: ﴿Satan only wants to cause﴾ to the end. This is clear, because God, may He be exalted, commanded unity and forbade division. He, may He be majestic and exalted, said: ﴿And hold firmly to the rope of Allah all together and do not become divided﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:103]; He said: ﴿And do not be like those who became divided and differed after clear proofs had come to them﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:105]; He said: ﴿Indeed, those who divided their religion and became sects, you have nothing to do with them﴾ [al-An'am 6:159]; He said: ﴿He has prescribed for you of religion what He enjoined upon Noah, and what We revealed to you, and what We enjoined upon Abraham, Moses, and Jesus: that you establish the religion and do not be divided therein﴾ [al-Shura 42:13]; and He said: ﴿And do not dispute, lest you lose courage and your strength depart; and be patient. Indeed, Allah is with the patient﴾ [al-Anfal 8:46]. The two foundational sources, the Book and the Sunnah, are filled with this, that is, with the call to unity and the prohibition of division.

Is this included in that too? The students of knowledge, all the more so. But, unfortunately, when students of knowledge differ over a matter of ijtihad (independent reasoning), some of them become enemies of one another, except those whom God spares, and one of them speaks against his brother's reputation without restraint. He thus wrongs himself first, wrongs his brother second, and wrongs the servants of God who benefit from his brother, because when his brother's standing and esteem in their eyes fall, they will not benefit from his knowledge. So this person wrongs himself, wrongs his brother, and wrongs everyone who benefits from his brother's knowledge.

Therefore, one must be attentive to this, and you must believe that whoever opposes you in a matter of ijtihad has in reality agreed with you, because both of you seek the truth. He sees the truth in this matter, and you see the truth in its opposite. Which of you is the messenger of the other, whose following is obligatory? Of the two of you in this situation, who? No one. So he is right in following what he thought the evidence indicates, and you are right in following what you thought the evidence indicates. Let the hearts be pure.

* Student: Shaykh, may God bless you (...) abstaining from it and using it.
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed, because His saying ﴿so avoid it﴾ is a general expression: avoid it in every respect, in use and in drinking. But we do not assert with certainty that it refers to use, because of His saying: ﴿Satan only wishes to cause enmity and hatred between you through intoxicants and gambling﴾. Therefore we have seen it as one of the matters of scrupulousness (wara') to abandon it.
* Student: May God be good to you. We said: if the proportion of alcohol in these oils is small, it does no harm. Would the same apply, O Shaykh, to some drinks in which there is something of .. is it permitted or forbidden?
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. If it is little, drink from it. But I want to advise you: when you drink, say "In the name of God," and when you finish, say "Praise be to God."
* Student: Perhaps people (...) the prohibition of donkeys, as Asma' (may God be pleased with her) mentioned, regarding the slaughter of the horse, because eating horses is not known among people today?
* The Shaykh: No, I want to add to this for you. Among people, the front of the horse is prohibited and its rear is permitted. The common folk say: the front of the horse's body is forbidden, because it is the side one faces the enemy with in jihad. As for its rear, it is permitted, because the rear is toward the enemy when turning away, so let it be eaten.
* Student: O Shaykh, I am asking about history (...). Should we ask about it or not?
* The Shaykh: No, ask about history. Donkeys were prohibited at Khaybar, and Asma' bint Abi Bakr narrated this as evidence for the permissibility of horses. Had she not known that horses were eaten after Khaybar, she would not have mentioned this as an argument.
* Student: May God be good to you, O Shaykh. As you have mentioned, perhaps some rancor exists in a man's heart, but O Shaykh (...) with the successful remedy in (...)?
* The Shaykh: His heart? By God, my brother, I have something that is not easy. Did you understand the question? He says: a person may find, I mean, rancor or envy in his heart toward his brother, so how does he treat it? He treats it by saying to himself: you want the truth, and the matter is not a text; the matter is ijtihad. But if it were a text, we would not accept excusing him. However, if it is ijtihad, then all of us are following ijtihad.
* Student: I want an answer about the hadith: "God has cursed wine, its presser, and its drinker" [[Narrated by Abu Dawud (3674) and Ibn Majah (3380), from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, may God be pleased with them both.]], and so on, from (...), although (...) and only one drank?
* The Shaykh: Because these people assist him; this is for assisting him in it, like the curse on the one who consumes riba, its agent, its two witnesses, and its scribe.
* Student: May God bless you. Some scholars cite the hadith of the Prophet (ﷺ) prohibiting treatment with wine, and say: other things are analogized to it, such as using wine for other than medicine, and perfumes and the like, a fortiori. So it is forbidden...
* The Shaykh: But treatment with it by drinking is the case here. For this reason the scholars (may God have mercy on them) said: it is not permitted to treat with it, even for thirst; it is not permitted to drink wine for thirst. They gave as the reason that when a person drinks wine out of thirst, it only increases his thirst. Some scholars hold that it is permitted for thirst, and they do not concede that it only increases thirst. But if a person chokes on a morsel and has nothing but a cup of wine, and he chokes, and either he dies by suffocation or he drinks the cup and the morsel passes, what should he do? Does he use it? Yes indeed, he uses it out of necessity, because God, glorified and exalted, said in a general verse: ﴿And He has already detailed for you what He has forbidden to you, except what you are compelled to﴾ [al-An'am 119]. This is more general than His saying, when He prohibited carrion, the flesh of swine, and what has been dedicated to other than God: ﴿But whoever is forced by severe hunger, not inclining to sin, then indeed, God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Ma'idah 3], and the verse ... ﴿And He has already detailed for you what He has forbidden to you, except what you are compelled to﴾ is more general.
Student: May God bless you. Some of them take the hadith of the Prophet (ﷺ) prohibiting treatment with wine (...) and say: other things are analogized to it for use only, other than treatment, a fortiori?
* The Shaykh: Analogized to it?
* Student: The use only, other than treatment; like perfumes and others, a fortiori, I mean.
* The Shaykh: But treatment with it by drinking is the case here. For this reason the scholars (may God have mercy on them) said: it is not permitted to treat with it, even for thirst; it is not permitted to drink wine for thirst. They gave as the reason that when a person drinks wine out of thirst, it only increases his thirst. Some scholars hold that it is permitted for thirst, and they do not concede that it only increases thirst. But if a person chokes on a morsel and has nothing but a cup of wine, and he chokes, either he dies by suffocation or he drinks the cup and the morsel passes, what should he do? Does he use it? Yes indeed, he uses it out of necessity, because God, glorified and exalted, said in a general verse: ﴿And He has already detailed for you what He has forbidden to you, except what you are compelled to﴾ [al-An'am 119]. This is more general than His saying, when He prohibited carrion, the flesh of swine, and what has been dedicated to other than God: ﴿But whoever is forced by severe hunger, not inclining to sin, then indeed, God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Ma'idah 3], and the verse ... ﴿And He has already detailed for you what He has forbidden to you, except what you are compelled to﴾ is more general.
* * *
* Student: I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan. ﴿Satan only wishes to cause enmity and hatred between you through intoxicants and gambling, and to avert you from the remembrance of God and from prayer. So will you not desist?﴾ (91) ﴿And obey God and obey the Messenger, and beware. But if you turn away, then know that upon Our Messenger is only the clear notification.﴾ (92) ﴿There is no blame upon those who believed and did righteous deeds for what they have eaten, if they fear God and believe and do righteous deeds, then fear God and believe, then fear God and do good; and God loves the doers of good.﴾ [al-Ma'idah 91–93].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan. God, blessed and exalted, said, explaining what Satan wants from the children of Adam: ﴿Satan only wishes to cause enmity and hatred between you through intoxicants and gambling.﴾ What is the opposite of enmity?
* Student: Friendship (muwalah).
* The Shaykh: Friendship. And hatred (baghda')? Love; that is, love is the opposite of hatred. So he wants to scatter hearts and bodies. And I think we have taken the benefits.
* Student: Five benefits.
* The Shaykh: From where are the five benefits?
* Student: God's dislike of enmity and hatred among Muslims; this is the last one. Shall I say them all?
* The Shaykh: Fine.
* Student:
- Affirmation of Satan's will.
- The evil of Satan's will toward the children of Adam.
- That the division of nations is among Satan's aims.
- That everything that leads to division is among Satan's aims.
- God's dislike of enmity and hatred among Muslims.
* The Shaykh: Well done.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of causes (asbab). The basis of this is that God, exalted, informed that intoxicants and gambling are a cause of enmity and hatred, and there is no doubt about this, and no one denies it except a fool. Everyone knows that whoever is plunged into the sea will drown, and whoever is thrown into fire will burn, is it not so? Some people denied causes, and others went to extremes in affirming them. As for those who denied causes, they claimed that by their denial they were exalting God above having partners, so they went to extremes in transcendence. As for those who affirmed causes as the actual agents, they associated others with God.
As for the people of truth, they said: causes have an effect, but who made them have an effect? God. So the effect of causes is not by themselves, but by the powers God has placed in them.
This is supported by the fact that there are causes that necessitate a thing by God's decree, yet this necessitation may be lifted. Among examples: fire burns, and when Abraham was thrown into it, God said to it: ﴿O fire, be coolness and safety upon Abraham﴾ [al-Anbiya' 69], so it became coolness and safety; burning and heat were removed. Had causes been effective by themselves, Abraham, peace be upon him, would have burned. Likewise the man whom the Dajjal cuts in two pieces and then says to him: stand up, and he stands. We know that the Dajjal was not the cause of his revival; rather that is up to God, mighty and majestic. For this reason, when he kills him a third time, he cannot kill him, for God does not give him power over him after that.
So we say: causes have an effect, but not by themselves; rather by the powers God has placed in them. The evidences for this, in revelation, reason, and observation, are countless.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that everything that averts from the remembrance of God is among the commands of Satan. We have previously noted that the remembrance of God, blessed and exalted, is...?
* Student: That it is preserved by God, mighty and majestic.
* The Shaykh: No (...).
* Student: It is by the heart.
* The Shaykh: It is by the heart, the tongue, and the limbs. So everything that averts you from the remembrance of God by these things is among the commands and wishes of Satan.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: the virtue of prayer, since it is singled out for mention from among the remembrance of God, mighty and majestic. This indicates its nobility and excellence over others, as in His saying, exalted: ﴿The angels and the Spirit descend therein﴾ [al-Qadr 4]. "The Spirit" is Gabriel, who is among the angels, yet God singled him out for mention because of his nobility.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: caution against Satan diverting us from prayer, either by occupying us with our wealth, our children, our entertainment, or our pursuits, or by any other means, or by making us perform it with our bodies while our hearts are absent. So beware of Satan diverting you from prayer.
* And among its benefits: whenever a reluctance toward prayer enters your heart, know that it is from Satan and is Satan's desire.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: the emphasis on the prohibition of intoxicants and gambling, as shown by His saying: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ The emphasis is that He used the form of interrogation: meaning, after this clarification, will you desist or will you persist? What was the answer of the Companions, O brothers? "We have desisted, we have desisted."

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 5, verse 90–91 (part 1 of 4):

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿O you who have believed, indeed, intoxicants, gambling, [sacrificing on] stone altars, and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid it that you may be successful.﴾ [al-Ma'idah 90]. This verse combines a statement and a command. The statement is His saying: ﴿Indeed, intoxicants, gambling, [sacrificing on] stone altars, and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan﴾, and the command is His saying: ﴿so avoid it that you may be successful﴾. In this verse, Allah begins the address with ﴿O you who have believed﴾, and this form of address has been repeated. We have explained that beginning speech with an address indicates its importance and the attention it deserves. Then, his beginning with this description, ﴿O you who have believed﴾, indicates that acting upon it, whether by affirmation or by compliance, is one of the requirements of faith. Likewise, it indicates that opposing it, doubting it, or denying it is incompatible with faith, either in its essence or in its completeness. Thirdly: in this there is an incitement (ighra') of the addressee, as if He is saying: if you are a believer, then listen and comply.

As for His saying: ﴿O you who have believed﴾, Allah, mighty and majestic, has used "faith" without mentioning what is to be believed in, because that is known. Jibril asked the Prophet, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family, about it (i.e., about faith), and he said: "That you believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and the divine decree, its good and its evil."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (4777) from the hadith of Abu Hurairah, and Muslim (8/1) from the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab.]]

﴿Indeed, intoxicants﴾: "Innama" (indeed/only) is a particle of restriction (hasr), and restriction means affirming the ruling for what is mentioned and negating it for what is other than it. This is the original meaning, though it may also be intended to confirm the ruling for what is mentioned without necessarily negating it for others, as will become clear, Allah willing, in the commentary.

﴿Indeed, intoxicants﴾: The Prophet, peace be upon him, said regarding khamr that it is that which intoxicates. Whatever intoxicates is khamr. We do not say: whatever removes the intellect is khamr, or whatever removes sensation is khamr. Rather, we say: khamr is that which covers the intellect in a manner of pleasure and elation, because those who drink khamr find comfort, euphoria and elation in it. Accordingly, bang (al-banj) is not khamr, because although it removes sensation, a person does not find in it euphoria and elation; and in any case, bang is used only out of need and necessity.

Al-maysir is: taking wealth by way of contest (al-mughalabah). It is called maysir because obtaining it is easy (tayassur al-husul 'alayhi). An example is wagering and gambling, such as one saying: "Let us do a deal on equal terms and make the stake, for example, ten thousand riyals; whoever wins takes the ten, and whoever loses has the ten taken from him." So the matter now is gharar (uncertainty) and ignorance, and this is called maysir because of the risk, uncertainty and hazard in it. This was known among the Arabs and also at the beginning of Islam, but it has been prohibited, praise be to Allah.

﴿And stone altars﴾: al-Ansab are that which is set up to be worshipped besides Allah. ﴿And divining arrows﴾ are that by which one seeks to know what has been decreed for him (yustaqsamu bihi). The Arabs used to do this in the Jahiliyyah: they would place arrows (aqdah) in which were written: "Do," and "Do not do," and a third arrow with nothing on it. Then they would shuffle them together and someone would say: "Take one of them without knowing it," placed in a bag or the like, then it would be said: "Put your hand in and take out an arrow." If "Do" came out, he would do it; if "Do not do" came out, he would not do it; if the blank one came out, he would repeat the draw. They practised this in the Jahiliyyah, and it is based on illusions with no reality, which is why Allah, mighty and majestic, prohibited it.

As for His saying: ﴿defilement from the work of Satan﴾: al-rijs means impurity (al-najas). Rijs may be physical impurity or moral impurity. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿Allah only intends to remove from you the defilement, O people of the household﴾ [al-Ahzab 33], and He said: ﴿So avoid the defilement of idols﴾ [al-Hajj 30]. Is the meaning of rijs here physical or moral? It is moral, though it may also be physical, i.e., impure in a physical sense, as in His saying: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to one who eats it unless it be carrion, or blood poured forth, or the flesh of swine, for indeed it is defilement﴾ [al-An'am 145].
* The Shaykh: Of which of the two kinds of rijs is this verse?
* Student: Moral.
* The Shaykh: The correct view is that it is of the moral kind, because it is described by His saying: ﴿from the work of Satan﴾, ﴿defilement from the work of Satan﴾ [al-Ma'idah 90]. So His saying: ﴿from the work of Satan﴾ is an adjective of rijs and not a second predicate; for if we made it a second predicate, the meaning would be that these four — khamr, maysir, ansab and azlam — are defilement and that they are from the work of Satan. But if we make it an adjective of rijs, the meaning becomes that it is practical defilement and not physical defilement, and this is the correct view.
* Student: Shaykh, here the ten needy persons — meaning feeding ten needy persons. If there are nine and among them is a nursing woman...
* The Shaykh: A nursing infant?
* Student: Yes, a nursing infant. Shall we give them, counting this child as one of the ten?
* The Shaykh: We feed her twice, yes. He asks: if there are nine poor persons, one of them a nursing woman, is it sufficient to feed her twice? The answer: No. There must be feeding of ten needy persons who eat food, not milk.
* Student: Shaykh, may Allah bless you. If we find a poor man who supports a family of nine, and he is the tenth, but they are not with him in the town, shall we give him the expiation?
* The Shaykh: Yes, if we know that he will deliver it to them. But if we do not know, then no.
* Student: He supports them; perhaps he will sell it, for example, and go and take its money?
* The Shaykh: No, that is not permitted; it must be feeding of ten.
* Student: Shaykh, may Allah bless you. There are some drinks that contain alcohol, one or more (...). Is it permissible to do it?
* The Shaykh: We have not reached it yet.
* Student: May Allah pardon you, Shaykh. Is the verse specific to believers and not to disbelievers, Shaykh, the lack of concern for them being disbelievers? Or is there no harm (...)?
* The Shaykh: That has not come yet.
* Student: May Allah be good to you. Is an oath valid if a particular situation drives him to it, anger or rage or the like?
* The Shaykh: Yes, indeed. That is, if the oath issues from anger, is it valid or not valid? This is a matter you must take as a rule: every statement made in anger in which a person does not control himself has no weight. Every statement made in intense anger in which a person does not control himself has no weight. So if he divorces in intense anger, his wife is not divorced; if he swears in intense anger, the oath is not valid; if he makes zihar against his wife in intense anger, it is not zihar. This is a established rule, yes.
* Student: Shaykh, is transfer of ownership (tamlik) a condition in clothing?
* The Shaykh: Transfer of ownership? Yes indeed — you lend the garment and take it back in the afternoon!
* Student: Alright, Shaykh, we said: then feeding does not require transfer of ownership?
* The Shaykh: Yes, because food is benefited from once and then it is finished.
* Student: (...) he hosted the needy with raw rice (...)?
* The Shaykh: Yes. The statements of the jurists say: there is no harm in giving them raw rice, but it is good to include something to accompany it.
* Student: I say: meat, Shaykh, that is?
* The Shaykh: Yes, meat.
* Student: Are milk and dairy not food?
* The Shaykh: No, it is not food.
* Student: Is expiation obligatory for the al-yamin al-ghamus (the deliberate false oath) along with repentance?
* The Shaykh: No. The deliberate false oath can only be about something past; every oath about something past has no expiation.
* Student: May Allah be good to you. ﴿or freeing a neck﴾ — "neck" here is unqualified; is it restricted by faith?
* The Shaykh: Well done. This is something we forgot to point out. The neck here is unqualified: ﴿freeing a neck﴾. Is it valid to free a disbeliever?
Some scholars hold that it is valid, because we keep the unqualified as Allah unqualified it and we restrict what Allah restricted. The neck is mentioned unqualified here in the expiation of oaths, and mentioned unqualified in the expiation of zihar, and mentioned unqualified in the expiation of intercourse during Ramadan, while it is mentioned restricted in the expiation of killing. Some scholars said: we must leave all the texts as they are, so faith is required in the expiation of killing, and is not required in the expiation of oaths, zihar and intercourse. Others said: since the ruling is one, the unqualified must be restricted by the qualification with which the qualified was restricted, even if the cause differs. These relied on the hadith of Mu'awiyah ibn al-Hakam, that he wished to free his slave-girl whom he had slapped, so the Prophet, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family, summoned her and asked her: "Where is Allah?" She said: "In the heaven." He said: "Free her, for she is a believer."[[Narrated by Muslim (537/33) from the hadith of Mu'awiyah ibn al-Hakam.]] It is inferred from this that if she were not a believer, her manumission would not have been prescribed. They also gave a sound rationale: if a disbeliever is freed, one cannot be sure he will not return to his origin and family, since he is now free, and he may go to his people and increase their numbers in fighting the Muslims. So the correct view is that faith is necessary; the sound opinion is that faith is necessary.
* Student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, regarding clothing, is it sufficient to give clothing like children's clothing?
* The Shaykh: Yes, the apparent meaning of the verse is that it suffices, but a child who eats food (must be given adult clothing).

﴿And gambling and stone altars﴾: There is a report from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, on this. What is it?
* Student: "He said: When you hear His saying: ﴿O you who have believed﴾, then lend it your hearing, for it is either good that you are commanded to, or evil that you are forbidden from."[[Narrated by Ibn al-Mubarak in al-Zuhd (36), and Sa'id ibn Mansur in al-Tafsir (50) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud.]]
* The Shaykh: Yes. When you hear Allah say: ﴿O you who have believed﴾, then lend it your hearing, for it is either good that you are commanded to, or evil that you are forbidden from. We mentioned that opening the address with a call indicates what?
* Student: Three things.
* The Shaykh: No.
* Student: Alertness.
* The Shaykh: Alertness and bringing it about. And when it is introduced with addressing the believers, what does it convey?
* Student: It indicates that complying with what follows, whether by doing or by refraining, is one of the requirements of faith.
* The Shaykh: And affirming it, if it is a statement...
* Student: Is one of the requirements of faith.
* The Shaykh: That is one.
* Student: The second: that there is incitement in it.
* The Shaykh: Yes, incitement and urging, because describing a person with something that leads him to proceed is incitement and urging.
* Student: The third: that opposing it is among the causes of diminished faith.
* The Shaykh: Yes, that opposing it is a cause of diminished faith, may Allah bless you. Does khamr have a definition?
* Student: It is that which removes the intellect in a manner of pleasure and elation.
* The Shaykh: That which covers, not "removes"; not "removes the intellect."
* Student: Covers the intellect.
* The Shaykh: In a manner of pleasure and elation. Good. Does it have a root in physical meanings?
* Student: Khamr?
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: Yes, from what (...).
* The Shaykh: And from it is the khimar, with which a woman covers her head. Good. Maysir?
* Student: Taking wealth in a manner not in exchange.
* The Shaykh: No, that is not correct. Tell me: if I come and give you a gift, does it become maysir?
* Student: No, Shaykh, the meaning is taking wealth by way of contest, without right.
* The Shaykh: It is not that there is injustice or...
* Student: Taking wealth like contest from two sides: contest like wagering.
* The Shaykh: Yes, it is taking wealth by way of contest. Good, and it is called qimar. Why was it called maysir?
* Student: For the ease of obtaining it.
* The Shaykh: And for this a person may win several hundred thousand in a single session. Good, al-ansab?
* Student: Al-ansab are the idols that a person sets up for worship.
* The Shaykh: Because they are set up to be worshipped besides Allah. Good, al-azlam?
* Student: They are that by which one seeks to know the decree (yustaqsam bihi).
* The Shaykh: How is that? It is well known.
* Student: Arrows are placed, and...
* The Shaykh: Let us suppose they are slips of paper.
* Student: On one of them is written: "Do," or "Do not do"; when one comes out...
* The Shaykh: And the third?
* Student: The third has nothing written on it.
* The Shaykh: Good, and he places them in?
* Student: He places them in a vessel, a bag, or the like...
* The Shaykh: No, a vessel is not valid; in a vessel he would see it and take what he wants.
* Student: He places them in a pocket or the like...
* The Shaykh: Or in a bag.
* Student: Or in a bag, then he puts his hand in and takes one. If "Do" comes out, he acts on it; if "Do not do" comes out, he acts on it; and if the one with nothing written comes out, he repeats the draw a second time.
* The Shaykh: Correct. What is the meaning of (yastaqsimun)? Is it that they seek the decree by means of the arrows?
* Student: They seek what has been decreed for them.
* The Shaykh: Yes, they seek what has been decreed for them, may Allah bless you.
Regarding His saying: ﴿so that you may be successful﴾, what is (la'alla) here?
* Student: For hope (tarajji), and it is, from Allah, certain.
* The Shaykh: (La'alla)?
* Student: For causation (ta'lil).
* The Shaykh: (La'alla) is for causation, i.e., in order that you may succeed.
So what is success (al-falah)? We will take it up, Allah willing.
I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿defilement from the work of Satan﴾. We mentioned that rijs is of two kinds?
* Student: Physical and moral.
* The Shaykh: Give an example of the moral kind.
* Student: The moral is worship other than Allah, like idols.
* The Shaykh: Like? By His saying?
* Student: By His saying: ﴿defilement from the work of Satan﴾.
* The Shaykh: No.
* Student: By His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so avoid the defilement of idols﴾.
* The Shaykh: Good. The physical?
* Student: The physical is like khamr.
* The Shaykh: No. Go on.
* Student: The physical is like carrion.
* The Shaykh: Give an example, a proof?
* Student: Shaykh, pork or carrion.
* The Shaykh: Yes, but we want evidence from the Qur'an or the Sunnah.
* Student: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to one who eats it unless it be carrion, or blood poured forth, or the flesh of swine, for indeed it is defilement﴾.
* The Shaykh: Is this physical defilement or moral?
* Student: Physical.
* The Shaykh: May Allah bless you. Now, ﴿from the work of Satan﴾ means that this action is from the work of Satan. He attributed it to Satan because he inspired it and commanded man to it. Satan has been said to be derived from (shatana), meaning to be distant, because of his distance from the mercy of Allah, mighty and majestic, since Allah cursed him, expelled him and removed him from His mercy. It has also been said that it is from (shaata), meaning to be angry, and anger always makes conduct rash. The first is more correct, and the evidence for this is that it is diptote-free (ghayr masrur)... no: that it is declinable (masrouf): shaytan. Had it been from (shaata), it would have the added alif and nun and would therefore be non-declinable.
﴿So avoid it﴾: i.e., keep away from it; be on one side and it on the other.
﴿That you may be successful﴾: (la'alla) is for causation, i.e., in order that you may attain success. Success (al-falah) is attaining the sought-after and being saved from what is feared. It combines two things: attaining what is sought, i.e., obtaining what a person desires, and deliverance from what is feared. It occurs frequently in the Qur'an.

Then Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred to occur among you through intoxicants and gambling﴾ [al-Ma'idah 91]. The sentence contains restriction (hasr), its particle being (innama), i.e., Satan wants nothing but this: ﴿to cause enmity to occur among you﴾, and so on.
His saying: ﴿yurid﴾ here means: loves; and when he loves, he will do it.
﴿To cause to occur among you﴾: i.e., O believers, enmity and hatred through intoxicants and gambling. Enmity is the opposite of allegiance (wilayah), and hatred is the opposite of love. In hatred, hearts become repelled; in enmity, bodies become repelled from one another, so no one allies with another. Which of the two results from the second? Enmity; because one first hates and then becomes hostile.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 5, verses 90–91 (part 2 of 4):**

﴿Through intoxicants and gambling﴾. Here "fi" (في) is causal (lil-sababiyyah). In the Arabic language, "fi" comes with the sense of causation in many places, including the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "A woman was punished because of a cat (fi hirrah) which she confined, so she entered the Fire." (Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2365) and Muslim (2242 / 151), from 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar.) That is, because of the cat. The meaning is not that she entered into the body of the cat; rather, the meaning is that she was punished on account of it.

﴿Through intoxicants and gambling﴾. The reason it causes enmity and hatred is that the one who drinks intoxicants, may Allah protect us, becomes like a madman; he may kill, steal or commit adultery, and thereby enmity and hatred arise. As for gambling, the reason it causes enmity and hatred is that gambling is taking wealth by way of contest, and wealth is beloved to souls. So if this person takes from you a great deal of money because he defeated you in something that is not worth even a quarter of the wealth he took, then resentment will remain in his heart, and enmity will be produced.

﴿And hinder you from the remembrance of Allah﴾. Yes, Satan wants to divert us from the remembrance of Allah: from the remembrance of Allah by the tongue, from the remembrance of Allah by the limbs, and from the remembrance of Allah by the heart. This is what Satan wants from us: to divert us from the remembrance of Allah by heart, tongue and limbs. You will find that when a person intends to stand and pray, Satan discourages him, whispers to him, and yawning comes upon him, and he remains seated. If he wishes to remember Allah or recite the Qur'an, it is the same; you find him energetic in something, but when he takes the Mushaf to read, laziness comes upon him. When Satan is unable to divert a person from speech and action, he comes at him from a second direction, which is diversion of the heart, so that he diverts his heart from the remembrance of Allah. This is the great calamity, because when the heart becomes heedless of the remembrance of Allah, it causes the person to lose the matters of his religion and his worldly life. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance and who follows his desire and whose affair has been [ever] in neglect﴾ [al-Kahf 28].

Therefore, a person must observe himself in this regard: When he sits to recite the Qur'an, is his heart present? When he remembers Allah, is his heart present? When he prays, is his heart present, or is he heedless?

If he is heedless of heart in the remembrance of Allah by tongue and limbs, he has truly lost the spirit of worship. That is why you find that when a person is heedless in his prayer, he leaves it with the same heart with which he entered it, meaning the same heart, not increasing in light, nor in faith, nor in aversion to indecency and wrongdoing, although Allah the Exalted has informed us that prayer forbids indecency and wrongdoing. So why does a person not find, when he leaves the prayer, aversion to indecency and wrongdoing? Why does he not find it?

Because he has only prayed a prayer of the body alone, not a prayer of the heart. This is a point that we ask Allah the Exalted to help us with. Most people today are afflicted with it and always ask how to free themselves from it. But freedom from it is easy: it is that you try to be present of heart in prayer from its beginning to its end. Train yourself to this, compel yourself to this, until you find the pleasure of worship.

﴿And from prayer﴾. He singled out prayer for mention, repeating the preposition as a sign of its nobility and greatness. That is, he repeated the preposition, whereas the speech could have been: "and hinder you from the remembrance of Allah and prayer." He said: ﴿and from prayer﴾, as an indication of its importance. Specifying it, while it is part of the remembrance of Allah, is evidence of its nobility, and repeating the governing element (al-'amil) while it is conjoined is another evidence of its nobility and that it is worthy of being a separate section in its own right.

And ﴿So will you not desist?﴾. The interrogative here carries the sense of incitement (al-igra'), incitement to what? To ceasing. It is more eloquent than saying: "So cease." That is, after this explanation and clarification, will you cease? The answer: Yes, we cease. For this reason 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), when the verse was revealed, said: "We have ceased, we have ceased." (Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (3049) and al-Nasa'i (5540), from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab.)

* In this noble verse there are benefits, among them: the importance of the ruling, which is avoiding intoxicants, gambling, idols (ansab) and divining arrows (azlam). The reason for this is the opening of the verse with the address.

* Among the benefits: avoiding these four things is one of the requirements of faith, and falling into them is among the deficiencies of faith.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of intoxicants from whatever source, whether from grapes, dates, barley, wheat, or anything else, due to the generality of the verse. The view that only grape wine is forbidden is a weak view; firstly, because the verse is unrestricted, rather it is general, since it contains the definite article (al) prefixed to a singular noun, and the Messenger (peace be upon him) explained that intoxicant (khamr) means every intoxicating thing.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that intoxicants, both small and large quantities, are forbidden, due to the generality. However, if a drink, were you to take a little of it, would not cause intoxication, but were you to take a lot, would cause intoxication, is it forbidden?

The answer: Yes, it is forbidden, due to the saying of the Prophet (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family): "What intoxicates in large quantity, its small quantity is also forbidden." (Narrated by Abu Dawud (3681) and al-Tirmidhi (1865) from Jabir ibn 'Abdullah, and al-Nasa'i (5607) from 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr.) And because consuming the small amount that does not intoxicate is a means to consuming the large amount that does intoxicate; for when a person drinks this pleasant drink and it does not intoxicate him, it leads to his increasing it until he becomes intoxicated.

And if this drink intoxicates the one who drinks it but does not intoxicate the one who has become accustomed to it, as is found now among those who are addicted to intoxicants, may Allah grant us well-being, which does not intoxicate him, is it forbidden for them or not? It is forbidden, because if the small amount that does not intoxicate is forbidden, then this is similar to it. The non-intoxication here is in terms of the specific individual, not in terms of the strength of the drink; for this drink undoubtedly has an intoxicating strength, so it is forbidden for the one it intoxicates and for the one it does not intoxicate.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the permissibility of nabidh provided it does not reach the level of intoxication. Nabidh is water in which grapes or dates are steeped for a day or two, so the water acquires the taste of what was steeped in it without intoxicating. Is it lawful or unlawful?

The answer: It is lawful, because what is forbidden is intoxicant (khamr), and this does not intoxicate. Now, what if its duration is prolonged, exceeding three days? As long as it does not intoxicate, it is lawful. But it is advisable, once three days have passed, especially in hot weather and hot regions, not to drink it, because intoxication in it may be hidden. However, the sign of an intoxicant is that it rises, that the drink rises, because foam forms on it, and the foam lifts it above its level; this is the sign of an intoxicant.

The summary is that nabidh is lawful because it does not intoxicate, but if it is at a time or place where it is strongly presumed to have reached the level of intoxication, then caution (wara') requires avoiding it, and it is given to animals or the like.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of gambling, whether small or large, due to the generality: ﴿Indeed, intoxicants and gambling﴾. Even if the contest is between one person and another, is it so? Even if it is a small amount? Even if it is a small amount; because we say: a small amount of gambling that does not harm a person's wealth and that he does not care about is like a small amount of intoxicant which, if small, does not intoxicate, and if large, intoxicates. There is no doubt that if a contest is over a small thing, it leads to contest over a large thing; there is no doubt in this. Excepted from this is what has a benefit greater than its harm, and this is in three things which the Prophet (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family) specified when he said: "There is no competition (sabq) except in arrow-shooting, camel-racing or horse-racing." (Narrated by Abu Dawud (2574), al-Tirmidhi (1700), and al-Nasa'i (3585), the wording being al-Tirmidhi's, from Abu Hurairah.) (Al-sabq), with a fatha on the ba', is the compensation taken for the race; (al-nasl) means arrows; (al-khuff) means camel; (al-hafir) means horse.

The scholars said: The Prophet (ﷺ) excepted this only because by these the jihad in the way of Allah is carried out, through which the word of Allah is exalted, and this is a great benefit. If people know that when they race in these things, they are permitted to take a reward for them, they will increase their racing, because they will obtain something for it.

If someone says: If people turned away from these three in jihad to other means, does the ruling remain for them, or does it transfer to the other means?

The answer: Here the wording and the meaning conflict. Whoever is literalist says: the ruling remains for them, even if they are not used in war. Whoever looks to the meaning says: if they are not used in war, there is no difference between them and other things. This is the closer view, except that this is challenged by the fact that the Messenger (ﷺ) informed that at the end of time the means of war will cease and people will return to arrows. That is one point.

Second: the Messenger (ﷺ) informed that "good is in the foreheads of horses until the Day of Resurrection." (Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2849) and Muslim (1871 / 96), from 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar.)

Third: the benefit of these things may be lost in one place but not another; in caves and mountains, only horses are of use.

In any case, we want to examine the matter jurisprudentially: when a ruling is established for a reason (illah), it ceases when the reason ceases. So if we assume that people no longer use these three things in war, the reason has ceased, so the ruling ceases, and contest in them becomes like contest in other things. If they have been abandoned, people must transfer to what? To another thing. So is contest for a reward permitted in that other thing which has replaced these mentioned items?

The answer: Yes, without doubt. Accordingly, modern means of war are such that contest for a reward is permitted in them, because they stand in the place of these three things.

Something similar in some respects is the zakat al-fitr, in which mention is made of dates, barley, raisins and dried curd (aqit), and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri (may Allah be pleased with him) reported that this was their food in the time of the Messenger (peace be upon him). He said: "We used to give it in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) as a sa' of food, and our food at that time was dates, barley, raisins and aqit." (Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1506) and Muslim (985 / 17), from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.) If people turned away from barley and no longer ate it, would the ruling concerning it be nullified or not? We say: whoever is literalist says: it is not nullified, because it is specified in the hadith. Whoever is attentive to meaning says: it is nullified. The correct view is that it is nullified, and that if barley ceases to be a staple, it does not suffice for the zakat al-fitr, because the Sunnah is clear on this, clear that it must be food, as in his saying in the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both): "The Prophet (ﷺ) enjoined zakat al-fitr as a purification for the fasting person from idle talk and obscenity, and as food for the needy." (Narrated by Abu Dawud (1609) and Ibn Majah (1827) from Ibn 'Abbas.) So pay attention to this.

Now we have two examples: the zakat al-fitr, and contest in the three things. Contest in knowledge: we know that the Islamic religion was established by jihad with the tongue and the spear. Is contest in sacred knowledge permitted for a reward or not?

The well-known position of the school is that it is not permitted, and they said: The Prophet (ﷺ) restricted it by saying "there is no competition except in," and this is a restriction. Those who go by meanings say: it is permitted; debate and contest in the sacred sciences are permitted. They may have cited the story of Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) with the Quraysh regarding the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. The Romans have been defeated, in the nearest land; but they, after their defeat, will overcome, within three to nine years﴾ [al-Rum 1–4]. Who defeated the Romans? The Persians, and the Persians were a polytheistic people, and the polytheists of Quraysh inclined to their side, while the Romans were People of the Book, to whom the believers inclined and rejoiced at their victory over the Persians, even though they were disbelievers, but they were closer to the believers than the Persians in that era, due to the strength of the Persians at that time. The polytheists said: It is impossible for the Romans to defeat the Persians. Abu Bakr said: Rather it is possible. Abu Bakr affirmed the Qur'an and its reports, while they did not affirm them. So they set a term of ten years: if the Persians were defeated within these ten years, the stake would be owed by whom? By Abu Bakr; and if the Romans were defeated, the stake would be owed by Quraysh. The Prophet (ﷺ) approved this contest, because it is sacred knowledge: affirmation of the Qur'an and non-affirmation.

Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah (may Allah have mercy on him) chose this view, that contest for a stake in knowledge is permissible.

But take note of one point in this matter: this applies if the contest is aimed at reaching a legal ruling. But if the contest is so that one gains wealth from his brother, it is not permitted, because those people did not intend the religion; they intended wealth, they intended the worldly life.

Some people have exploited this matter, or exploited this view in its absoluteness, and said: Fine, since it is a matter of knowledge (...). But there must be a restriction: the intention of the contest must be reaching the truth, not reaching wealth.

As for non-sacred sciences, such as the science of grammar (nahw), for example, is contest in it permitted? Apparently not; because grammar, even if we say it is sacred, is sacred only if its aim is reaching knowledge of the Book and the Sunnah. For this reason we say: the sciences of Arabic are a means, not sought for their own sake. Now, are physics, chemistry, geography and such things permitted for contest? Contest in them is not permitted.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of idols, due to His saying: ﴿so avoid it﴾. Does this encompass everything made into an idol, of whatever material? The answer: Yes, it encompasses it, because the verse is unrestricted. Allah, blessed and exalted, has replaced the worship of idols with the worship of the All-Merciful, because a human by his nature must have something to turn to in seeking what benefits him and repelling what harms him; so Allah the Exalted replaced attachment to idols with attachment to Allah, mighty and majestic.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of seeking decision by divining arrows (istiqsam bil-azlam), which is explicit. Similar to it is what they call "your luck and your portion" (hazzak wa nasibak); if it is not included in this, it is included in gambling, and it is prohibited.

Is it similar to seek decision by the stars? For example, one says: this man was born at an auspicious hour, so his life will be happy; this one was born under the star al-Dabaran, so his life will be wretched, and such like?

The answer: Yes, it is included in this, and indeed it is a kind of shirk, because establishing a cause which Allah has not made a cause, either legally or by decree, is shirk. Allah, praise be to Him, has replaced these divining arrows with the prayer of istikharah. If a matter becomes unclear to you, one of the affairs you want to do, whether it is good or bad for you, then you should perform istikharah: you pray two rak'ahs other than the obligatory prayer, then when you finish the salam you supplicate Allah the Exalted with the well-known supplication: "O Allah, I seek Your good counsel by Your knowledge, and I seek power by Your power..." (Narrated by al-Bukhari (1162) from Jabir ibn 'Abdullah) until its end.

* Student: Wagering between one side only. These matters are not legislated. For example, one says: "I bet that if so-and-so comes tonight, three hundred riyals (...)?"

* The Shaykh: This is not a wager; it is either a ju'l (reward) or an encouragement, if there is good in it, such as my saying: "If you know such-and-such, then you get such-and-such."

* Student: People (...) those who fall into this?

* The Shaykh: Who?

* The student: "If so-and-so comes, I'll treat you to dinner at night." Trivial things.

* The Shaykh: In reality people have committed what you describe, and they have also committed something else: they toy with money, because Allah has blessed them. If you want to call someone named Muhammad and you say "Abdullah" by mistake, they say: "You owe a debt." And if you give him a cup and it is not filled, they say: "You didn't fill it, brother, you owe a debt." This is a matter we have as a kind of luxury and frivolity, and in reality it is toying with money. For this reason we are asked about this matter, and we say: You are not obliged to abide by what he said; say: "No, I will not give you."

* Student: Shaykh, some scholars say it is prohibited?

* The Shaykh: Prohibition is difficult.

The Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin on Surah 5, verses 90–91 (part 3 of 4):

﴿O you who believe, indeed, intoxicants, gambling, idolatrous altars, and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid it that you may be successful.﴾ (90) ﴿Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred to occur among you﴾ ... to the end of the verse. We have reached His saying: ﴿and divining arrows﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse is the strong warning against these four practices, since His saying ﴿defilement from the work of Satan﴾ requires complete aversion to them, first by describing them as defilement, and then by describing this defilement as the work of Satan.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse is the obligation to avoid intoxicants, gambling, idolatrous altars, and divining arrows, based on His saying ﴿so avoid it﴾.

* Among its benefits: avoiding these four things is a cause of success (falah). Every one of us who wants success should pursue its causes. The evidence is His saying ﴿that you may be successful﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: affirmation of the causation (ta'lil) of legal rulings, meaning that the legal rulings have praiseworthy purposes, which is wisdom (hikmah). This is shown by His saying ﴿that you may be successful﴾, and also by His saying ﴿defilement from the work of Satan so avoid it﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the Qur'an's method in stating causes is sometimes to mention the cause before the ruling and sometimes after it, according to what the context requires and the indicators of the surrounding discourse. So when God mentions a ruling and gives a cause for it, He sometimes mentions the cause first and then builds the ruling upon it, and sometimes mentions the ruling and then brings the cause. Here He mentioned the cause before the ruling. What is the cause? ﴿defilement from the work of Satan so avoid it.﴾ In His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They ask you about menstruation. Say: it is a harm, so keep away from women during menstruation﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:222], did He put the cause or the ruling first? The cause. He said: ﴿Say: it is a harm, so keep away from women.﴾ The benefit of putting the cause first is that the ruling reaches the soul when it is already at ease and awaiting the ruling. It is at ease with the cause and anticipates the ruling, because it is known that a sensible person, when told the cause, will act in accordance with it. So when a person hears His saying ﴿Say: it is a harm﴾, as soon as he hears ﴿it is a harm﴾ he will arrive at the ruling ﴿so keep away﴾ while already anticipating it. This verse is similar.

﴿defilement from the work of Satan so avoid it﴾: from the moment the cause ﴿defilement from the work of Satan﴾ is stated, the person is awaiting the ruling of prohibition. Sometimes the cause comes after the ruling, as in His saying: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to one who eats it, unless it be carrion, or blood poured out, or the flesh of swine, for indeed it is defilement﴾. This is because carrion, blood, and the flesh of swine are repugnant to natural dispositions, so He put the ruling first, since sound souls anticipate this ruling, and they may shun it even without a legal ruling; then the cause comes, matching what natural disposition requires.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the works of Satan that he commands are defilement, based on His saying ﴿defilement from the work of Satan﴾. Then do we say that the verse is evidence for the impurity (najasah) of intoxicants, since "rijs" means "najs" (impure), as in His saying: ﴿except that it be carrion, or blood poured out, or the flesh of swine, for indeed it is defilement﴾ [al-An'am 6:145]?

The answer: Yes, some scholars have used this verse as evidence for the impurity of intoxicants. But upon reflection on the noble verse, you will not find evidence in it for the impurity of intoxicants, for two reasons.

The first reason: He said ﴿defilement from the work of﴾, so it is a defilement of action (ma'nawi), and the defilement of action is the moral (ma'nawi) defilement, as in His saying: ﴿so avoid the defilement of idols﴾.

The second reason: gambling, idolatrous altars, and divining arrows are not sensory (hissi) defilement. Is the report about these four one or different? One. Intoxicants is the subject (mubtada'), the other three are coordinated with it, and then the predicate came: "defilement." So where is the evidence that these four things differ in ruling, such that the three are called moral defilement and the first is called sensory defilement? Where is the evidence? It requires evidence.

If someone says: "The indication by juxtaposition (dalalat al-iqtiran) is weak and cannot be relied upon"?

The answer: The basic principle with juxtaposition is that the ruling is uniform across all items unless there is evidence otherwise. An example of this: Abu Hanifah said that horses are forbidden. Do you know horses? They are well known. Based on His saying: ﴿and horses, mules, and donkeys, for you to ride and as adornment﴾ [al-Nahl 16:8]. He juxtaposed them with mules and donkeys, so they would be forbidden. There is no doubt that the correct view is with him, because the basic principle in juxtaposition is agreement in ruling. But horses have evidence that excludes them, which is what al-Bukhari narrated from Asma' bint Abi Bakr, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "We slaughtered a horse in Medina during the time of the Prophet ﷺ and we ate it."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5511), and Muslim (1942/38) from the hadith of Asma' bint Abi Bakr.]] This excludes horses from the ruling for mules and donkeys. Here, in the noble verse ﴿intoxicants and gambling﴾, we have no evidence that excludes intoxicants from the ruling of what is juxtaposed with it, namely gambling, idolatrous altars, and divining arrows. Accordingly, there is no indication in the verse for sensory impurity of intoxicants.

If someone says: "Is there anything in the Sunnah that indicates this?"

The answer: No, there is nothing in the Sunnah that indicates this. As for the hadith of Abu Tha'labah al-Khushani, may Allah be pleased with him, that he asked the Prophet ﷺ and said: "O Messenger of Allah, we are in the land of a people of the Book. Shall we eat from their vessels?" He said: "Do not eat in them unless you cannot find others; if so, wash them and eat in them."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5478), and Muslim (1930/8) from the hadith of Abu Tha'labah al-Khushani, in a similar wording.]] What is the answer to this hadith?

We say: those who hold that intoxicants are sensorily impure use this hadith, but there is in reality no evidence in it, because the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, only forbade them from eating in their vessels unless after washing, and another condition was that we do not find others. His clear purpose is to keep distance from mixing with them and eating in their vessels. The proof: if the cause were impurity, washing would suffice to permit eating in them; he would not make it a condition that we do not find others. But the Prophet ﷺ intended that we not mix with the People of the Book, that we keep away from them, and that we not borrow from them, lest they claim favor over us in that. This is the first point.

Second: we say, what is the basis for considering this evidence for the impurity of intoxicants?

They said: because their vessels contain intoxicants, since they consider intoxicants lawful. We reply: their vessels would also contain pork, since they consider pork lawful. What made us think that the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, considered intoxicants but not pork, or considered pork but not intoxicants, or considered both together?

There is no evidence. What becomes clear to us is that the reason for this is that we should not mix with them and should not eat from their vessels. Thus there is no evidence in this hadith.

If someone says: Did the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, not get asked about intoxicants being made into vinegar, and he said: "No"?[[Narrated by Muslim (1983/11) from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him.]] That is, if a drink ferments, may we keep it so that it becomes vinegar, or add a substance to make it vinegar? He said: "No."

We say: there is no evidence here for impurity. This is evidence that it is not permissible to keep intoxicants in one's possession; rather one should pour them out, so that the soul does not urge one to consume them. This is clear, and it contains no indication of impurity in any way whatsoever.

So whoever claims that intoxicants are sensorily impure must bring evidence. Otherwise, we cannot oblige God's servants to wash vessels of intoxicants, or wash garments if they are soiled with it, or wash bodies. Nor can we invalidate the prayers of God's servants if their garments have stains of intoxicants or their bodies are affected, except with evidence. The matter is not merely verbal, whether it is impure or not; many rulings depend on it. There must be a proof from God, may He be mighty and majestic, which allows us to oblige God's servants to something required by the text. So we say: the basic position is non-impurity, and a general prohibition does not entail impurity, as proven by the fact that poison and harmful foods are forbidden but are not impure. This is evidence derived from the well-known principle that the basic state is the absence of obligation (bara'at al-dhimmah).

Then we say: we have a positive evidence other than the original evidence, which is negation or absence: positive evidence that they are pure, that is, intoxicants are pure, and their impurity is moral.

The evidence: when intoxicants were prohibited, the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, took them out to the markets and poured them out. If they were impure, they would not have poured them out in the markets, because it is not permissible to pour anything impure in the markets of Muslims, just as urine and feces may not be poured there. Those who hold impurity answered according to their own basis; otherwise the basic position is non-impurity. But they said: the jars of intoxicants, meaning the containers of intoxicants, were not numerous enough to make the streets flow with them; that is, they did not reach an amount that would cause the roads to flow. We say: Glory be to God! Were those vessels used by the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, before the prohibition, which were more numerous: they or a drop of urine?

* Student: They are the same.

* Shaykh: They are certainly more numerous, and more than a small quantity of the number. We do not say that the streets of Medina became rivers flowing with intoxicants; we do not say this. If they said: what makes you know that they poured them out in the markets? Perhaps they poured them out at the edges of the market, where people do not pass? We say: this contradicts the unrestricted wording. They poured them out in the markets, and it does not say they poured them out at the sides of the markets. Being at the side is an added condition beyond the unrestricted wording, so it requires establishing that they poured them out at the sides of the markets. Furthermore, is it reported from the Companions that after pouring them out they washed the vessels? It is not reported; it is not reported. Had they been impure, they would have washed the vessels and transmitted this to the Ummah.

Another evidence is what is established in Sahih Muslim: "A man came with a rawiyah of intoxicants." The rawiyah is a large water-skin, which he had been storing for the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and he came to the Prophet ﷺ and presented it as a gift, not knowing that it had been prohibited. The Prophet ﷺ said: "It has been prohibited." It is known that a person may not accept a forbidden gift, whether it is forbidden in itself or because of how it was acquired, if its giver knows it. One of the Companions whispered to him: "Sell it." The Prophet ﷺ said: "What did you whisper to him?" He asked about the whispering, although one should not ask two people who are whispering, "What did you say?" But the situation required the question. Perhaps the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, heard part of the conversation. He said: "What did you whisper to him?" He said: "I said: sell it." He said: "Indeed God, when He prohibits something, prohibits its price," or as he said, ﷺ. So the man opened the mouth of the rawiyah and poured out the intoxicants in the presence of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and the Prophet ﷺ did not command him to wash it.[[Narrated by Muslim (1579/68) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Abbas.]]

Do you see: if intoxicants were impure, would the Prophet ﷺ remain silent instead of telling this man: wash the rawiyah?
