Therefore, when a person is tested by the ease of disobedience and abandons it for Allah's sake, Allah compensates him with something better than it.

Consider Yusuf, peace be upon him. Allah made the means of disobedience easy for him in an unparalleled way, as far as we know. He was a slave of the Aziz of Egypt, and he had a wife whom we think was among the most beautiful women, since she was the wife of the Aziz. She was taken with Yusuf and loved him intensely, until his love reached the innermost heart – the depths of the heart – and she was unable to be patient. One day her soul made it seem good to her to invite him to commit immorality. She invited him and locked the doors, and doors are plural of door, the least of them being three, in a room behind a room behind a room, with the doors closed, and no one else was there. She solicited him for herself and threatened him that if he did not comply she would imprison him and humiliate him. She said: ﴿He will surely be imprisoned and will be of the humiliated﴾ [Yusuf 32]. So he called upon his Lord and said: ﴿My Lord, prison is more beloved to me than what they invite me to. And unless You turn away from me their plan, I might incline toward them and be among the ignorant﴾ [Yusuf 33].

Do not think that the plural means there was someone with the woman; rather he meant the category, for the one who tempted him might be tempted by others, so he wanted his supplication to be general. ﴿So his Lord responded to him and turned away from him their plan. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ [Yusuf 34]. Yusuf, peace be upon him, had the means of disobedience made available to him, did he not?

* Students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Yes, and more than that: he was threatened with humiliation and imprisonment if he did not comply, yet he turned to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and in that dire necessity Allah answered his supplication. Among the seven whom Allah will shade under His shade: "A man whom a woman of rank and beauty invited, and he said: 'Indeed, I fear Allah.'"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (660) and Muslim (1031/91) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] He mentioned no barrier other than the fear of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Was it in the unseen or in the presence of witnesses?

* Students: In the unseen.

* The Shaykh: In the unseen, because there was no one else. Had someone been present, he would have said: "I fear that so-and-so or so-and-so will witness." So the main point: be watchful over yourself, whether in buying or selling or in anything else. When the means of disobedience are made easy for you, know that this is a trial from Allah (...).

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that hunting is forbidden during the state of ihram; by His saying: ﴿that Allah may know who fears Him in the unseen﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that whoever transgresses after the ruling has been made clear to him, ﴿for him is a painful punishment﴾, meaning painful.

* Among its benefits: that whoever is ignorant bears no sin if he commits the disobedience; by His saying: ﴿after that﴾.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of the knowledge of Allah, Blessed and Exalted; by His saying: ﴿that Allah may know who fears Him in the unseen﴾, and the knowledge of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, encompasses everything.

If someone says: the context of this verse indicates the renewal of Allah's knowledge, for He said: ﴿Allah will surely test you with something﴾, then said: ﴿that Allah may know who fears Him in the unseen﴾, while He, Majestic and Exalted, knew that before He created this, and before the creation of the heavens and the earth by fifty thousand years. This is a real difficulty that troubles many people: ﴿that Allah may know who fears Him in the unseen﴾, has Allah not already known?

The answer: Yes, He has known. But the answer to this is from two angles. The first: Allah's knowledge of a thing before it occurs is knowledge that it will occur, and His knowledge of it after it occurs is knowledge that it has occurred. There is a difference between a thing being known before it happens and being known after it happens.

If someone says: this is accepted regarding human knowledge; when a person knows that a thing will happen tomorrow, that is knowledge, but once it happens his second knowledge becomes stronger than his first, since his first knowledge is knowledge of certainty and his second is the eye of certainty. It is known that a person's knowledge renews and strengthens at times and weakens at others, but is Allah's knowledge one?

The answer: We do not say that when Allah, Glorified and Exalted, knows a thing as occurring, His knowledge increases by it. Never. He knows it, but He knows that it has occurred, not that it will occur, because the first knowledge does not entail any reward or punishment for the servant, whereas the second knowledge does entail reward.

As for the second angle: we say that His prior knowledge of what occurred was knowledge that it would occur, but no reward or punishment follows from that knowledge. When does reward and punishment follow? When the servant acts. So His second knowledge, which comes after the thing occurs, is knowledge upon which reward and punishment are based. This answer is necessary so that the ignorant does not think that Allah's knowledge is renewed, while we know that the knowledge of our Lord, Mighty and Majestic, has always been and always remains.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: praise for those who fear Allah in the unseen; may Allah make us and you among them. For many people fear Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, and have fear of Allah within them, but their fear diminishes when no one is around them; and when people are aware, their fear increases. That is, the root of fear is in them, but when someone is present, their fear of committing disobedience increases, out of fear of Allah's punishment and fear of people's blame. Although this is praiseworthy, it reflects weak fear of Allah, and it is feared that such a person will flatter people and be concerned about them and fall into showing off. So, O brother, let your fear of Allah be one, in secret and in public.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 5, verse 95 (part 1 of 4):

Then Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿O you who have believed, do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram.﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 95].

When He mentioned that He, glorified and exalted is He, would test them, He mentioned the ruling, saying: ﴿Do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram.﴾ Here ﴿lā﴾ is a prohibitive particle (lā nāhiyah), and the sign that it is prohibitive is the deletion of the nūn (of the verb).

﴿The game while you are in the state of ihram.﴾ The ﴿al﴾ (the definite article) is for specifying the reality. So what is forbidden game? The scholars, especially the jurists (ahl al-fiqh), may Allah have mercy on them, established a rule for this, and they said: it is the land animal that is lawful to eat. What matters is that its origin is that of a land animal, wild by nature. It is the land animal, lawful to eat, wild by nature. "Animal" (al-hayawān) is the genus; "land" (al-barr) is its opposite, the sea; "lawful to eat" (al-ma'kūl) is its opposite, the unlawful; "wild by nature" (al-mutawaḥḥish ṭab'an) is its opposite, the domesticated (al-mu'ahhal), which is the domestic animal that is familiar with people in their homes. This is the game. On this basis, sea animals do not fall under the prohibition, because they are not intended by this verse, even if they are game, but they are of the sea.

Allah, blessed and exalted, has said: ﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea and its food, as a provision for you and for the travellers; but forbidden for you is the game of the land as long as you are in the state of ihram.﴾ This verse is explicit; Allah has detailed and clarified it. How many qualifiers did we mention?

We said: land is the opposite of sea, lawful to eat is the opposite of unlawful, wild is the opposite of domesticated, which is called domestic. So if the muhrim slaughters a chicken, there is no sin on him, because the chicken is domestic, not wild. And if he slaughters a sheep, there is no harm, even though it is land and lawful to eat, because it is not wild. What matters is the origin, not the attribute that arises later. An attribute that arises later is not taken into account. So if a domestic animal becomes wild, or a wild animal becomes tame, which is taken into account?

* Students: The origin.

* Shaykh: The origin. For this reason, if a person raised a rabbit, is it permissible, when he is in ihram, to slaughter it?

* Students: No.

* Shaykh: He raised it.

* Students: It is not permissible.

* Shaykh: Why?

* Students: Because what matters is the origin.

* Shaykh: Because what matters is its origin: it is wild in origin, and domestication is something that arose upon it. And if a hen escaped and became wild, and began to fly with the birds, is it lawful or not lawful for the muhrim?

* Students: Lawful.

* Shaykh: Lawful, because its origin is that it is domesticated. So what matters is the origin. The prohibition here is only so that the pursuit of forbidden game does not divert him from his rites, so that his heart is not preoccupied, for there is nothing more intense than the diversion of hunting. The person afflicted with diversion in hunting does not settle until he pursues the game. For this reason we hear about hunters that one of them exerts himself to go out into the desert to pursue game, and thirst, hunger, thorns, the heat of the ground and the cold of winter afflict him, yet he does not mind, because his heart is preoccupied. And since Allah said: ﴿There shall be no obscenity, no wickedness and no quarrelling during the Hajj﴾ [Al-Baqarah 197], so that the pilgrim is not preoccupied, then preoccupation with game is even more diverting.

﴿Do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram, and whoever of you kills it intentionally, then a penalty equal to what he killed of the livestock﴾. The conditional clause: ﴿whoever﴾ (man) is a conditional noun, and conditional nouns convey generality, meaning: whoever among you kills it intentionally, upon him is a penalty equal to what he killed of the livestock. On this basis, His saying ﴿then a penalty﴾ (fa-jazā'un) is a subject whose predicate is omitted, and the estimate is: upon him is a penalty. ﴿Equal﴾ (mithlu) is an explicative apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) to His saying "penalty" (jazā'), and we cannot make it an attributive adjective (na't), because ﴿mithlu mā qatala﴾ is definite, since it is annexed to a relative pronoun.

﴿Penalty﴾ (jazā') is indefinite, and an indefinite noun is not described by a definite one, but we make it an explicative apposition, and an explicative apposition is close to an adjective but does not have the conditions that an adjective has.

* Student: May Allah bless you, Shaykh. Are the wild or domestic animals limited or unlimited?

* Shaykh: This is a matter of custom (ʿurf), meaning it is not defined (...).

* Student: Shaykh, in some regions, the wild [animal], among us, among them there are people, like buffaloes. In some regions they are wild?

* Shaykh: They are land animals without doubt, but are they wild?

* Student: Yes, like (...) with lions, and because...

* Shaykh: No, no, the buffalo is not wild.

* Student: If it were found, O Shaykh, indeed?

* Shaykh: Wild?

* Student: Yes, wild.

* Shaykh: How?

* Student: Wild, the buffaloes.

* Another student: Among us they are domesticated.

* Shaykh: No, it is domesticated.

* Student: Among us they are wild.

* Shaykh: Glory be to Allah, so it is treated like game?!

* Students: Yes indeed.

* Shaykh: Meaning: people go out to hunt it in the desert?

* Students: Yes indeed, it cannot be overcome except by hunting.

* Shaykh: What should be said is that one returns to custom, if it has not been specified by the Sharia as game, then one returns to custom.

* Student: Regarding the fear of Allah, glorified and exalted, people now (...) among them (...) but a person who is upright, who maintains ties of kinship and is upright in obedience to his Lord, and then begins (...) something, either with wealth or in some state of affairs (...), and even cuts off his kinship (...).

* Shaykh: Correct.

* Student: This is a matter (...).

* Shaykh: Yes, there is no doubt, it is false, this is an established reality.

* Student: If people (...) would think with their minds and reflect on the world, they would believe the reports of Allah, glorified and exalted, without doubt, without experiment.

* Shaykh: This is an established reality; that is, a person being afflicted by his sin because of his turning away from obedience to Allah is more severe than the punishment. For this reason Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿And if they turn away, then know that Allah only intends to afflict them for some of their sins﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 49]. So a person being upright, then feeling that his uprightness has weakened and he begins to commit sins, this is a punishment. One of the salaf said: "Indeed a person is deprived of night prayer by a sin that afflicts him."[[Mentioned by al-Safuri in Nuzhat al-Majalis (1/120), attributing it to al-Hasan al-Basri.]] But most people in this are heedless, thinking that the calamities that come from sins are physical calamities, and it is not so; the calamity of the heart is more severe. We ask Allah for safety.

* * *

I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿O you who have believed, do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram, and whoever of you kills it intentionally, then a penalty equal to what he killed of the livestock, judged by two just men among you as an offering reaching the Ka'bah, or an expiation of feeding the needy, or its equivalent in fasting, that he may taste the consequence of his affair. Allah has pardoned what is past; but whoever returns, Allah will take retribution from him, and Allah is Exalted in Might, Owner of Retribution.﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 95].

I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, exalted, said: ﴿O you who have believed, do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram.﴾

What is said regarding His saying ﴿O you who have believed, do not kill game﴾ is as we said regarding the previous verse, ﴿O you who have believed, Allah will surely test you with something﴾.

The connection between this verse and the one before it is clear: when He, mighty and majestic, informed them that He would test them with this game, He forbade them from killing it, saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram.﴾

The phrase ﴿while you are in the state of ihram﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl). ﴿Ḥurum﴾ is the plural of ḥarām, and what is meant is being in a state of sanctity by place and by state: by place, that they are within the sanctuary of Makkah; by state, that they are in ihram for Hajj or 'Umrah. On this basis, if a person enters the state of ihram from Dhu'l-Ḥulayfah, then from the time of his ihram at Dhu'l-Ḥulayfah he falls under the verse. And if he was not in ihram and reached Makkah, to the boundaries of the Ḥaram, then when he enters these boundaries he has become a muhrim, that is, he falls under the verse.

As for His saying ﴿do not kill game﴾, we explained game as every land animal that is lawful to eat and wild by nature; this is game, and we mentioned previously the meanings of these qualifiers.

﴿And whoever of you kills it intentionally, then a penalty equal to what he killed of the livestock﴾: whoever among you, O believers, kills it intentionally, while in ihram or while being a muhrim, ﴿then a penalty equal to what he killed of the livestock﴾. ﴿Penalty﴾ (jazā') is a subject whose predicate is omitted, and the estimate is: upon him is a penalty, that is, upon him is a penalty by which he compensates for what he killed; the explanation of this will come, Allah willing.

﴿Equal to what he killed of the livestock﴾ means that it should be similar to it, and by similarity here is meant closeness in form, because complete identity between game and livestock is impossible; rather, what is meant is closeness in form.

His saying ﴿of the livestock﴾ refers to three kinds: camels, cattle and sheep, and they are called the beast of cattle (bahīmat al-an'ām).

﴿Judged by it﴾: that is, by this penalty or this equivalent. ﴿Two just men among you﴾: ﴿two﴾ is the dual, and it is annexed to ﴿just﴾ (ʿadl), meaning two men of justice among you, and justice is uprightness in religion and manliness (murū'ah). This is justice: uprightness in religion and manliness; so the meaning of ﴿two just men﴾ is two people upright in religion and manliness.

As for religion, the jurists, may Allah have mercy on them, explained it as performing the obligatory duties and not committing a major sin nor persisting in a minor sin. This is uprightness in religion.

Uprightness in manliness is not doing what disgraces one before people and doing what beautifies one before them; that is, doing the beautiful and leaving the disgraceful. This latter varies according to conditions, lands and times: an action may not impair manliness in one land while in another land it does impair it. The standard is the customs of upright people, not the customs of the rabble, concerning whom the saying of the Prophet ﷺ applies: "Among what people have gained from the words of the first prophethood is: if you have no shame, then do what you wish."[[Related by al-Bukhari (3484) from the hadith of Abu Mas'ud.]] What is meant is those of praiseworthy manliness.

﴿Two just men among you﴾: the address is to the believers, so the judge must necessarily be from among the believers. It is possible that the address is to the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, and that one returns in this to their judgment; this will be mentioned in the benefits, Allah willing.

﴿An offering reaching the Ka'bah﴾: ﴿an offering﴾ (hadyan) is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), meaning that this penalty is in the state of being an offering.

﴿Reaching the Ka'bah﴾: that is, arriving at the Sanctuary, and what is meant is not into the interior of the Ka'bah, by the consensus of the Muslims.

﴿Or an expiation of feeding the needy﴾: ﴿or﴾ here is for choice. Whenever ﴿or﴾ comes in the Book of Allah, it is for choice; and if (...) it is for sequence, Allah clarifies it, mighty and majestic. ﴿Or an expiation of feeding the needy.﴾

His saying ﴿feeding the needy﴾ is an explanation of the expiation: that it is feeding the needy. In a reading I have: ﴿expiation of food for the needy﴾ with annexation. The expiation (kaffārah) is derived from kufr, meaning covering, and it is the ransom that covers the sin so that it leaves no trace on a person, neither in his heart, nor on his face, nor among his people.

His saying ﴿needy﴾ (masākīn): the plural of miskīn, and what is meant by it is the poor (faqīr), and it is said: faqīr, and what is meant by it is the miskīn. That is because "faqīr" and "miskīn" are words that when they are combined they differ, and when they differ they combine; that is, when one of them is mentioned it includes the other, and when both are combined each is interpreted with a separate meaning. For example, here the miskīn is the faqīr, while in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The alms are only for the poor and the needy﴾ [At-Tawbah 60], the masākīn are other than the fuqarā'.

﴿Or an expiation of feeding the needy﴾: Allah, mighty and majestic, did not specify that the food (that is, the food) is equal to the game, because equality is impossible; the food is wheat, barley, dates or the like, so it cannot equal a pigeon, an ostrich, a gazelle or the like, unlike when it is from the livestock, for then it is possible for it to be equal to it.

﴿Or an expiation of feeding the needy﴾: Allah, mighty and majestic, did not specify the quantity of this food, and its explanation will come, Allah willing, in the benefits.

﴿Or its equivalent in fasting﴾: ﴿equivalent﴾ ('adl) means equal in value.

﴿That﴾ is a demonstrative, and a demonstrative refers to the nearest mentioned thing. What is the nearest mentioned thing? The food. So the meaning is: or the equivalent of the food in fasting.

﴿That he may taste the consequence of his affair﴾: ﴿that he may taste﴾: the lām here is for causation, and ﴿taste﴾ (yadhūqa) is an imperfect verb whose subject is an implicit pronoun, permissibly, estimated as ﴿he﴾, because it refers back to ﴿whoever﴾ in His saying ﴿and whoever kills it﴾.

﴿Whoever﴾ is a relative pronoun whose wording is singular and whose meaning is suitable for both singular and plural, and the pronoun to which it refers clarifies that. On this basis we say: ﴿and whoever of you kills it﴾: one or a group? One.

﴿That he may taste﴾: that is, the killer; ﴿the consequence of his affair﴾: that is, its outcome, the heavy outcome of his matter, because the original meaning of wabāl is a heavy thing, and what is meant here is the heavy consequence, since it is well known that when a person is obliged to this penalty, a equal to what he killed of the livestock, or an expiation of feeding the needy, or its equivalent in fasting, it is burdensome for him according to his condition.

His saying ﴿that he may taste the consequence of his affair﴾: that is, the consequence of his matter and his state.

﴿Allah has pardoned what is past﴾: Praise be to Allah. ﴿Allah has pardoned﴾: that is, He overlooked and effaced ﴿what is past﴾, meaning your killing of game. Why?

Because it was before the prohibition, so the servant is not held accountable for it. This is similar to Allah's saying, blessed and exalted, concerning those who died before the change of the qiblah while they were praying toward Bayt al-Maqdis, when Allah said concerning them: ﴿And Allah would not let your faith go to waste﴾ [Al-Baqarah 143].

﴿And whoever returns﴾: that is, whoever returns after the ruling has become clear to him, ﴿then Allah will take retribution from him﴾: that is, Allah will take retribution from him, and retribution is the taking of punishment.

﴿And Allah is Exalted in Might, Owner of Retribution﴾: that is, Owner of might, and might is subjugation and dominance, and retribution is seizing the wrongdoer for what he did.

The ﴿dhū﴾ in His saying ﴿Owner of Retribution﴾ is a second predicate of the Name of Majesty (Allah), and the first predicate is ʿazīz (Exalted in Might).

* There are in fact many benefits in this verse; among them: the prohibition of killing game while in ihram or in the Sanctuary, by His saying: ﴿Do not kill game﴾.

* Among them: that killing it is contrary to the perfection of faith; the reason is that Allah addressed this prohibition to the believers.

* Among them: that complying with this, that is, avoiding killing game, is one of the requirements of faith.

* Among them: that abandoning it, that is, abandoning the killing of game, increases faith; because if killing it diminishes faith, then abandoning its killing increases it. Here we say: whoever abandons a sin, is he rewarded for it and does his faith increase by it?

The answer: there must be a distinction in the following manner. First: that he abandons it for the sake of Allah, mighty and majestic, after he had intended it, or after the whispers of the devils of mankind or jinn had adorned it for him; if he abandons it for Allah, then he is rewarded for it, because he abandoned it for Allah, mighty and majestic, and his sincerity to Allah in abandoning it is an act of obedience for which he is rewarded.

The second category: that he abandons it out of disinterest in it, neither for Allah nor because of inability to do it; this is neither for him nor against him, like a person who intended a sin and prepared for it but abandoned it, relented, saying: "By Allah, my soul is content, I did not want it." This is neither for him nor against him: not for him, because he did not produce sincerity, and not against him, because he did not do it.

The third: one who wanted the sin and strove toward it, but was unable to do it; this is recorded for him as the burden of its doer. The proof of this is the saying of the Prophet, may Allah's prayers and peace be upon him and his family: "When two Muslims meet with their swords, the killer and the killed are in the Fire." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, this is the killer, so what about the killed?" He said: "Because he was eager to kill his companion."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (31) and Muslim (2888/14) from the hadith of Abu Bakrah.]] These are the categories of abandoning what is forbidden.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 5, verse 95 (part 2 of 4):**

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: whatever game is hunted by one in the state of ihram (ritual consecration for pilgrimage) is carrion (maytah), and it is not permitted for him or for anyone else to eat it, whether he killed it with an arrow or caught it and slaughtered it, for it is still carrion. The evidence is that Allah described the hunted animal as being "killed," and it is known that killing is not a lawful slaughter (dhakah). This indicates that any game killed by the one in ihram is carrion. This is the ruling on what the one in ihram kills.

Now, what about game hunted by one who is not in ihram (muhill)? Is it forbidden for the one in ihram?

The correct answer is that there is a distinction. If he hunted it for the one in ihram, it is forbidden for the one in ihram. If he hunted it for himself or for someone else who is not in ihram, it is permissible for the one in ihram. The evidence points to this. In the hadith of Abu Qatadah (may Allah be pleased with him), he was on the expedition of al-Hudaybiyyah while not in ihram. He saw a wild donkey and asked his companions to pass him the spear, but they refused. Then he hunted the donkey and brought it to them, and the Prophet (ﷺ) permitted it for them, even though they were in ihram. However, he had not hunted it for them; he hunted it for himself, and he gives gifts to whomever he wishes.[[Agreed upon (Muttafaq 'alayh); al-Bukhari (5492), and Muslim (1196/57), from the hadith of Abu Qatadah.]]

It is evident that he did not intend it for them, because when he asked them for the spear they refused. It is natural that such a case would not involve him hunting for them, since they were the ones who refused to help him.

As for the second case, where game is hunted for the one in ihram: the hadith of al-Sa'b ibn Jaththamah (may Allah be pleased with him) relates that the Prophet (ﷺ) stayed with him as a guest. He was a skilled archer and a fast rider. He took a spear and set out to hunt, and he brought back a wild donkey. The Prophet (ﷺ) returned it to him. When he saw the effect on his face, he said to him: "We only returned it to you because we are in ihram," meaning: we are in ihram.[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1825), and Muslim (1193/50), from the hadith of al-Sa'b ibn Jaththamah.]]

The first case, the hadith of Abu Qatadah, the Prophet (ﷺ) permitted for them, while in the second he refrained from it, because al-Sa'b had hunted it specifically for the Prophet (ﷺ) out of honor, since he was his guest.

This distinction is also supported by the hadith of Jabir that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The game of the land is lawful for you," meaning those in ihram, "as long as you do not hunt it yourselves, or have it hunted for you."[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (1851), and al-Tirmidhi (846), from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah.]]

Now, if game is hunted for the one in ihram and so is forbidden to him, is it forbidden to others who are in ihram or not in ihram?

No, because the one who hunted it was not in ihram, and the game hunted by a non-pilgrim is lawful. If a person hunts a gazelle, while not in ihram, intending to give it as a gift to another person who is in ihram, then it is forbidden for the one in ihram. But there are other people in ihram. Is it lawful for them or not? It is lawful for them, and it is even more lawful for those not in ihram.

Thus we conclude that hunting by the one in ihram is forbidden, meaning that whatever he hunts is forbidden. From where do we derive this? From His saying: ﴿and whoever kills it﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the penalty (jaza') applies only to the one who acts intentionally, based on His saying: ﴿intentionally﴾. So if he made a mistake, such as shooting at a tree with game above it and hitting the game, causing it to fall, is there a penalty for him or not? There is no penalty for him. Why? Because he did not act intentionally, and if he did not act intentionally, the implication of the noble verse is that there is no penalty upon him.

﴿And whoever among you kills it intentionally, then its penalty is﴾. If he was forgetful that he was in ihram, or forgetful that killing game is forbidden, and he killed the game, is there a penalty upon him? No, there is no penalty upon him, because he was forgetful. Allah has restricted this with His saying: ﴿intentionally﴾. The general evidences that the ignorant person and the forgetful person bear neither sin, nor ransom (fidyah), nor expiation (kaffarah) also support this, such as His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Our Lord, do not take us to task if we forget or make a mistake﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:286], to which Allah said: "I have done so." And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿There is no blame upon you for what you did in error, but what your hearts intended. And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:5]. This principle is that there is no accountability with ignorance and forgetfulness. Likewise, compulsion (ikrah) is a great principle in Islamic law, and nothing may be excluded from it except by evidence. What we have established is the correct view, which is supported by the general and specific evidences.

Some scholars said that the one who errs or forgets is relieved of sin, but still owes the penalty. They based this on flawed reasoning. Firstly, on the judgment of some of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) regarding the ostrich, that a camel (badanah) is due, and for the dove a sheep, and similar cases, without making any distinction. This is one argument.

Secondly, that what involves destruction (itlaf) is equal whether done knowingly, deliberately, or otherwise. The evidence is that if a person destroys the property of another person, thinking it is his own property, is he liable for compensation or not? Without doubt he is liable. Likewise, if he destroyed it forgetfully, he is liable, and there is no problem with this. But this reasoning is flawed. As for the first argument, the judgment of some Companions without distinction: the Companions were only explaining the obligation, that is, the obligation in killing game, regardless of whether the killer is accountable or not. This requires investigation, questioning, and discussion: whether he was knowing or ignorant, mindful or forgetful. In that case, there is no evidence in what the Companions stated without qualification, because they only intended to explain the obligation.

As for the second argument, that destruction is equal whether done deliberately, forgetfully, or ignorantly, this is true, but it applies to the rights of human beings, which are based on contention (mushahhah), and so that people do not play with one another's rights.

If we said that whoever destroys another person's property while ignorant has no liability, people would play with one another's property. One would destroy this person's property and burn that person's property, claiming: "I did not know, I did not realize." Great harm would result. Therefore, the one who destroys a person's property while ignorant or forgetful must be held liable, because the rights of human beings are based on contention. Also, if we did not hold him liable, it would open the door to consuming people's wealth unjustly and to plundering one another's property.

As for the right of Allah, may He be exalted, it is based on what? On leniency and ease, and religion is ease. Thus the two cases differ. So the correct view is that whoever kills game while ignorant, forgetful, or mistaken has no penalty upon him. As for the game itself, it is carrion that may not be eaten, but the discussion here concerns the penalty.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the glorification of ihram and the glorification of the Sacred Precinct (haram). As for the glorification of ihram, the prohibition on the one in ihram from hunting means honoring the rite (nusuk), and avoiding frivolity and luxury, for if the one in ihram were permitted to hunt, he would be distracted from the rite. This is why Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿So whoever has made obligatory upon himself the Hajj [during these months], there shall be no sexual relations, no wrongdoing, and no disputing during Hajj﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:197]. All of this is so that a person may devote himself, both heart and body, to the rite he is engaged in.

As for the Sacred Precinct of Makkah, it is also evident that the verse indicates its honor and sanctity, because the Sacred Precinct is secure, as Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Have they not seen that We made a secure sanctuary while people are being snatched away around them?﴾ [al-'Ankabut 29:67]. And He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿and this secure city﴾ [al-Tin 95:3]. This city is secure for human beings, animals, and trees. For this reason, hunting in it is forbidden, cutting its trees is forbidden except for what is dead, and fighting in it is forbidden, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And do not fight them at al-Masjid al-Haram until they fight you therein. But if they fight you, then kill them. Such is the recompense of the disbelievers﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:191].

Also, on the year of the conquest of Makkah, the Prophet (ﷺ) declared that it is not permissible for anyone who believes in Allah and the Last Day to shed blood therein. When he was asked about his fighting there, he (ﷺ) answered that it had been made lawful for him only for an hour of the day, because its lawfulness involved a greater benefit than violating its sanctity for that hour. It also leads to its being respected, since there is a difference between being a land of disbelief and a land of Islam, and there was no way for it to become a land of Islam at that time except through fighting. Thus fighting was permitted out of necessity. This is why he (ﷺ) said: "Its sanctity has returned today as it was yesterday." And he said: "If anyone takes the concession to fight in it, based on the fighting of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), say: Allah permitted His Messenger, but He did not permit you."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4295), and Muslim (1354/446), from the hadith of Abu Shurayh al-'Adawi.]] This is a sound answer, and Allah, blessed and exalted, may permit whomever He wills of His creation.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation for killing game, meaning the penalty, is one of three matters: either an equivalent (mithl), or feeding the poor (ita'am masakin), or fasting equal to that. Is this an option (takhyir) or a sequence (tartib)? It is an option. Whenever "or" (aw) appears in the Qur'an, it indicates an option, as in His saying: ﴿then a ransom of fasting or charity or sacrifice﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:196], and as in His saying about the expiation for an oath: ﴿then its expiation is feeding ten needy persons with the average of what you feed your families, or clothing them, or freeing a slave﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:89].

In this verse: ﴿a penalty equivalent to what he killed﴾ and ﴿or an expiation: feeding of the poor, or the equivalent of that in fasting﴾. The word is for option, so the person who killed the game is given the choice between sending its equivalent as an offering (hady) to the Sacred Precinct, which we will explain later how the equivalent is determined, this is one option;

or feeding the poor, ﴿an expiation: feeding the poor﴾, and Allah, blessed and exalted, did not mention the amount of this food. Shall we say, ﴿an expiation: feeding the poor﴾, that the least of the plural is three, and that if he feeds three poor persons it suffices? Or shall we say that since the matter is one of equivalence, this food must be equivalent either to the game itself or to its equivalent?

The first possibility, that feeding three poor persons is sufficient, is not correct. What remains is that it must be equated with the game or with its equivalent. Scholars differed on this. Some said that the game is valued in terms of food equal to its worth, and that food is then given to the poor. Others said that the equivalent is valued, and with its value food is bought to feed the poor. Which is more beneficial for the poor?

It varies. Sometimes the equivalent is more valuable, and sometimes the game is more valuable. For example, how much is an ostrich worth? Sometimes its price rises to ten times the value of a camel, and sometimes it is cheap and the camel is worth more.

Some scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, inclined to the view that the game is valued, and others said that the equivalent is valued. If someone said that one should consider what is more beneficial for the poor, so that if valuing the equivalent is more beneficial we value the equivalent, and if valuing the game is more beneficial we value the game, this would be a good view. There is a parallel: in zakat, are trade goods valued in dirhams or in dinars? It is by what is more beneficial to the poor. If valuing in dinars is more beneficial, we value in dinars; if valuing in dirhams is more beneficial, we value in dirhams.

So if it is said in this matter that one should consider what is more beneficial for the poor, because the food is theirs, then whatever is more beneficial is applied, this would have a basis. But this view is countered by another view, namely that the default is the absence of obligation (bara'at al-dhimmah), so we do not burden the killer with more than what is required of him. According to this reasoning, what should one consider? One considers the lesser. If valuing the game is less, it is applied; if valuing the equivalent is less, it is applied.

* * *

**Student:** "It is lawful for you to hunt the game of the sea and its food, as a provision for you and for the travelers, but the game of the land is forbidden to you as long as you are in ihram. And fear Allah, to whom you will be gathered﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:96]. ﴿Allah has made the Ka'bah, the Sacred House, a means of stability for the people, and [has made] the Sacred Month and the offerings and the garlands [likewise]. That is so you may know that Allah knows what is in the heavens and what is on the earth, and that Allah is Knowing of all things. Know that Allah is severe in punishment and that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful. The Messenger has only [the duty of] conveyance, and Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:96–99]."

**Shaykh:** I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. I think we have not finished the benefits of the previous verse.

**Students:** The principles...

**Shaykh:** Yes, the principles of tafsir. We take a principle, and it concerns where we derive the explanation of the noble verses from.

**Student:** We have covered it.

**Shaykh:** We have covered it. Second: abrogation (naskh). We have covered it.

Third: the Meccan and the Medinan (al-makki wa al-madani). The terms are attributed to Makkah and Madinah. It comes to mind that the Meccan is what was revealed in Makkah and the Medinan is what was revealed in Madinah. But the well-known view among scholars is that the Meccan is what was revealed before the Hijrah, and the Medinan is what was revealed after the Hijrah, even if it was revealed in Makkah. This is the view of the majority, and it is more precise than saying that the Meccan is what was revealed in Makkah and the Medinan is what was revealed in Madinah, because there is a third category: some verses were revealed during travel, neither in Makkah nor in Madinah. Also, it is difficult to determine with precision that this verse was revealed in Makkah and that verse in Madinah, because the arrangement of the Noble Qur'an is not according to the order of revelation, and when it is not according to the order of revelation, distinguishing becomes difficult. Therefore, what the majority hold is correct: the Meccan is what was revealed before the Hijrah, even if it was revealed in Madinah or in any other place.

His saying "even if" means hypothetically, since it is well known that the Messenger (ﷺ) did not go to Madinah except after the Hijrah, and that the Medinan is what was revealed after the Hijrah, even if it was revealed in Makkah or anywhere else.

Second, we sometimes see that some scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, say: "This surah is Meccan except such-and-such a verse," or "This surah is Medinan except such-and-such a verse." This requires evidence. This exception requires evidence. Mere popularity of such a claim is not accepted, why? Because it is a mursal report, since there must be a chain of transmission from the narrator to the Messenger (ﷺ), otherwise it is not accepted. The basic rule is that all verses of Meccan surahs are Meccan, and all verses of Medinan surahs are Medinan, unless there is clear evidence, in which case we accept it.

Moreover, the predominant theme of Meccan verses is discussion of tawhid (monotheism) and resurrection (al-ba'th), because the context requires it. It was revealed among a people who denied tawhid and denied resurrection. For this reason you find in the Meccan verses that this is what predominates. In the Medinan verses, what predominates is the branches of religion, transactions, and similar matters, because tawhid and belief in resurrection had become established and firmly rooted in people's hearts, and the remaining laws of Islam were left. So you find the Medinan surahs speaking about these.

There is also another matter: we find that the story of Musa (peace be upon him) is repeated often in the Qur'an, more than other stories, sometimes briefly and sometimes in detail. This is because Allah, may He be exalted, knew that the Messenger (peace be upon him) would migrate to Madinah, and in Madinah there were Jews, and the Jews were people of arrogance and haughtiness. So it was wise for the Prophet (ﷺ) to know about the story of Musa in summary and in detail, expansively and concisely, so that he would be fully prepared for what he would face from these Jews, and so that what is mentioned in the Noble Qur'an would exactly match what came in the authentic Torah, so that the scholars of the Children of Israel would bear witness that the Qur'an is true, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Is it not a sign for them that the scholars of the Children of Israel know it?﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:197].

Also, all the prophets mentioned in the Noble Qur'an came from the Arabian Peninsula and its surroundings, because this is what the Arabs knew and transmitted among themselves. As for what is in America, the far reaches of Asia, and similar places, no detailed mention of them has come. But we know that Allah sent a messenger to them, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And there was no nation but that a warner had passed among them﴾ [Fatir 35:24]. However, Allah did not relate it to us, because He related to us what the people knew and transmitted, so that the authentic might be distinguished from the non-authentic, and so that the reports in circulation would confirm what is in the Qur'an, and the Qur'an would confirm them.

Also, as far as what concerns us regarding knowledge of the Meccan and Medinan (revelations) is that we should know that eloquence requires addressing people in accordance with their circumstances. In the Meccan (surahs) we find the verses are severe and strong, because they confront people who are fierce, powerful, eloquent and articulate; and we find that the Medinan verses, for the most part, are gentle and soft, because they address people in whose hearts faith has become firmly established and who do not need severity. This is evident. Read Surah al-Qamar and you will find how its verses are tremendous, shaking the heart in reality for whoever contemplates them well, because it speaks among a people who are stubborn and arrogant, so the verses were perfectly suited to the situation, and this is the utmost of eloquence.

As for whether the Meccan verses can be abrogated by the Medinan verses, yes, they may be abrogated. Because being Medinan, and we have established that the Medinan is what was revealed after the Hijrah, if it contains a ruling that contradicts what is in the Meccan verses and reconciliation is not possible, we say that the Medinan surahs abrogate the Meccan surahs. And Allah knows best.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the obligation of equivalence in the penalty for hunting. But in what does the equivalence consist? Is it in size, in resemblance, or in what? Equivalence is by resemblance, but exact identity is not required. Indeed the scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, said, and even the Companions said: a dove has a sheep (as its equivalent). In what does a sheep resemble a dove? How can it be an example for it? The dove flies and the sheep does not fly; the sheep differs from the dove in that it has four legs and this has two legs. The point of resemblance is that it resembles the dove in drinking water: the dove drinks water by sucking it in continuously (ya'ubbu), and the sheep drinks by sucking it in continuously. That is, it does not drink little by little. Now, we find that the hen, for example, does it drink water by sucking it in continuously? Imagine it, what does it do?
* Students: (...).
* The Shaykh: That is, sip by sip; it does not suck water in continuously. So equivalence is sometimes found in something minor.
If someone says: the statement ﴿He shall be judged by two just men among you﴾, does this differ according to time, meaning that we should appoint judges each year who judge by equivalence, or what?
We say: the scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, said: what the Companions judged is not to be changed, and all the more so what the Messenger ﷺ judged is not to be changed; because the Companions are closer to understanding the noble Qur'an than others, and because they lived in the Arabian Peninsula and know the resemblances, so their opinion is more deserving of being followed than others'. On this basis, what the Companions decided is not to be changed, even if some pedant comes and says: this penalty is not like the game, so we do not accept it, however much he advances in medicine and however much he advances in expertise. And what the Messenger ﷺ judged, all the more so, is not to be changed: he ﷺ «made a sheep (the penalty) for the hyena»[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (3801), and Ibn Majah (3085), from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abdullah with the wording: it is game, and a ram is given for it if it is hunted by one in ihram.]], so a sheep was made for the hyena, and therefore the sheep is the equivalent of the hyena. This hadith is cited as evidence that the hyena is lawful and is game, and by this Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, derived that the hyena is lawful.
As for what the Companions did not judge, is it referred back to the closest thing the Companions judged? We say, for example: if this game that the Companions did not judge is equivalent to, or close to, the game they judged, do we apply to it what the Companions judged, or do we establish a new ruling?
The correct view is the first, because what resembles what the Companions decided is analogized to it, and analogy is preferable to a newly renewed ruling, since a new ruling may arise that completely contradicts what the Companions decided. As for what does not resemble what the Companions decided, it is referred to the testimony of two just judges ﴿He shall be judged by two just men among you﴾.
What does judging require? It requires expertise, that these two judges be people with expertise in knowing game and what is close to it or similar to it among the livestock.
The second is trustworthiness: that they have trustworthiness, such that they do not judge in favor of one person with this equivalence and in favor of another person with the opposite. They must be trustworthy experts. This is based on the well-known principle indicated by the saying of Allah the Exalted ﴿Indeed, the best one you can hire is the strong, the trustworthy﴾ [al-Qasas 26]. "Strong" means the one with expertise, or strong in the work, and the strength of each thing is according to its kind. And the jinn said to Solomon, an 'Ifrit of the jinn said to him: ﴿I will bring it to you﴾, that is, the throne of the Queen of Sheba, ﴿before you rise from your place; and indeed I am strong and trustworthy for it﴾ [an-Naml 39]. So these two pillars in every work are strength and trustworthiness.
* And among the benefits of the noble verse: there must be justice in the two judges, by His saying ﴿just men among you﴾, and the trustworthiness we mentioned is part of justice.
If someone says: Is it valid for the killer to be one of the two judges, for example if this killer has expertise and knowledge, and he says: I see that this game is equivalent to this type of livestock; would his statement be accepted together with another?
There is a difference of opinion, and his repentance is necessary. As for if he has not repented, it is known that he is not among those of justice, so it is not accepted. But if we know that the man has regretted, felt remorse and repented to Allah, and says: I have knowledge, some scholars said: his statement is accepted; and others said: his statement is not accepted, because he is suspected. He in reality judges for whom? He judges for himself, so it is not accepted.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: the penalty for hunting must reach the Sacred Precinct; by His saying ﴿as an offering to reach the Ka'bah﴾ [al-Ma'idah 95]. So if it were supposed that a person entered ihram at Dhu al-Hulayfah and killed game at Badr, he must give the penalty for that game in any place?! In Makkah, without exception. This differs from other prohibitions, for other prohibitions, other than the penalty for hunting, are performed in the place where the prohibited act occurred; as evidence, the Prophet ﷺ ordered Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah «to offer ransom for the shaving of his head in its place, not in Makkah»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1814), and Muslim (1201/80), from the hadith of Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah.]]. On this basis it is said: all prohibitions of ihram may be redeemed in their place, except game, which must be in Makkah, even if it was killed outside the Sacred Precinct.
If someone says: Is it permissible to transfer the ransom for other than the penalty for hunting to Makkah?
The scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, said: it is permissible to transfer it to Makkah, because this ransom was only obligated for something related to ihram, and the end of ihram is Makkah; so it is permissible to delay the ransom until reaching Makkah. And unlike zakat, which is distributed in its place. Moreover, generally, bringing it to Makkah is harder for a person than redeeming it in his place. This is correct; meaning, whoever is obligated a ransom for a prohibited act may redeem it in his place, and he may transfer it to Makkah.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: a person may turn from the penalty for hunting, from livestock or equivalent, to expiation by feeding the poor; by His saying ﴿or an expiation: feeding the poor﴾. Is it optional or in sequence?
* Students: It is optional.
* The Shaykh: Optional; because "or" whenever it comes in the Qur'an in legal rulings, it indicates optionality.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that the ransom is an expiation for the sin and a covering for it in this world and the Hereafter; by His saying ﴿or an expiation: feeding the poor﴾.
* And among the benefits of the noble verse: these poor are not restricted to a specific number; rather he may feed them in groups, each three, or ten, or twenty, or thirty; because Allah the Exalted and Glorified stated the expiation as "the poor" without specifying, and the least of them is three.
* And among the benefits of the noble verse: a person may move in the penalty for hunting from equivalence and feeding to fasting; by His saying ﴿or its equivalent in fasting﴾. But how is the equivalence calculated?
It is said: the equivalence is that he fasts one day for each half sa'. These scholars derived this from the fact that the Prophet ﷺ made half a sa' equivalent to how much? We mention the ransom for harm; he said to Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah: «Fast three days»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1814), Muslim (1201/80).]], three days as a substitute, how many (...)?
* Students: (...).
* The Shaykh: Feeding six poor persons, half a sa' for each poor person.
And some scholars said: rather, the food is estimated and then distributed to each poor person at a mudd; if the food is large it follows that the days of fasting would be many; if we estimate, for example, that the food was estimated at fifty sa's, and we say the poor person is fed a mudd, how many? Two hundred days.
But some scholars said: he should not exceed sixty days in fasting, because the highest that has been reported for expiation by fasting is how many? Two months, which is sixty days. As for obligating him to fast six months or the like, this requires evidence. So we say: we estimate the fasting, but we do not exceed the greater expiations, which are sixty days. And this matter has not fully matured in my view.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: permissibility of discretionary punishment (ta'zir) by wealth; because this killer was obligated to this ransom so that he would taste the consequence of his act, so it is a type of ta'zir.
The scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, differed on this matter. Some said: there is no ta'zir in wealth except what the Sharia has brought, and it does not go beyond that. For example, the one who embezzles from the spoils has his entire baggage burned except the weapons (the embezzler is one who takes from the booty), and one who conceals lost property has the penalty doubled upon him.
So what the text has established we adopt, and what the text has not established we do not apply discretionary punishment by wealth, because if we punish by wealth we have taken people's property without right, and people's property is sacred. But the correct view, which is certain without doubt, is that discretionary punishment by wealth is permissible.
We say: Do you not permit that one be disciplined by beating? The answer: yes. Is beating prohibited or not prohibited in principle? It is prohibited. So discretionary punishment by wealth is not more severe than discretionary punishment by beating; humiliating a person by beating him in front of people may be more painful to him than thousands of riyals.
So the correct view is that discretionary punishment by wealth is permissible, discretionary punishment by beating is permissible, by imprisonment is permissible, by removing him from his post is permissible, and (...) among people is permissible; because the aim is to discipline him. But discretionary punishment by amputating a limb is not permissible; this is forbidden, because this, amputation of a limb, cannot be replaced, and it is a clear offense against the self.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: the vastness of the pardon of Allah the Mighty and Majestic; by His saying ﴿Allah has pardoned what is past﴾.
* And among its benefits: that whoever commits a prohibited act before knowing the Sharia, there is no sin upon him, nor expiation, nor penalty. Can we derive this benefit from the verse? It is possible or not possible?
Let us consider ﴿Allah has pardoned what is past﴾: what is past refers to what the Companions did before the revelation of its ruling, for it was not yet prohibited. As for if a person is ignorant, he did it after the revelation of its ruling, and this preventing factor of knowledge is specific to him; so there is a difference between them.
And among the benefits of the noble verse: the vastness of Allah's pardon, by His saying ﴿Allah has pardoned what is past﴾ [al-Ma'idah 95]. And among its benefits: that whoever commits a prohibited act before knowing the Sharia, there is no sin upon him, nor expiation, nor penalty. Pay attention. Can we derive this benefit from the verse?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Is it possible or not? Let us consider: ﴿Allah has pardoned what is past﴾, what is past refers to what the Companions did before the revelation of its ruling, for it was not yet prohibited at all. As for if the person is ignorant, he did it after the revelation of its ruling, and this preventing factor of knowledge is specific to him; so there is a clear difference between a person who committed a prohibited act that was not yet prohibited, and another person who committed a prohibited act that had been prohibited but he was ignorant; the two cases are undoubtedly distinct.
But it is said: why did Allah pardon him? Due to ignorance, undoubtedly, since no ruling had been revealed. So the correct view is that all the laws do not bind one who is ignorant. But perhaps the person has been negligent and remiss in seeking knowledge; meaning that he was told: this is obligatory, or this is forbidden, and he was remiss in seeking the truth, and became like the common folk who cite the Qur'an when it agrees with their desires: ﴿Do not ask about things which, if made apparent to you, would distress you﴾ [al-Ma'idah 101]. This is applying the Qur'an out of its proper context. So the sound view in every case is that the ignorant person is excused, is not sinful, and is not bound by expiation or anything else.
If someone says: this is refuted against you by the story of the man who had intercourse with his wife during Ramadan and came asking the Prophet ﷺ, for he did not know what was incumbent upon him?[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1936), Muslim (1111/81), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]
The answer: the man was not ignorant. The man knew the ruling but was ignorant of its consequences, and ignorance of what follows from a ruling is not an excuse, because the doer violated the prohibition knowingly, so he has no excuse. Accordingly, one distinguishes between ignorance of the ruling and ignorance of what follows from the ruling.
Similarly: if a man knows that fornication is forbidden and commits it while he is married, what is his punishment, what is his penalty? Stoning. If he says: hold on, had he known that its penalty is stoning he would not have committed it. We say: no, we will not hold back, because ignorance of what follows is not an excuse; you have now committed fornication believing it to be forbidden and knowing it is forbidden, so you have no excuse.
So if someone asked you: what do you say about one who commits fornication while ignorant, should the penalty be applied to him or not? If you say: no, you are wrong; if you say: yes, you are wrong. I would say: if he is ignorant of the ruling, then the penalty is not applied to him; and if he is ignorant of the punishment, the penalty is applied to him.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of pardon for Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and among His names is al-'Afuw (the Pardoner). In the transmitted supplication that the Prophet ﷺ taught Mother of the Believers 'A'ishah when she asked him: «Tell me, O Messenger of Allah, if I happen upon the Night of Decree, what should I say in it? He said: Say: O Allah, You are Pardoning and You love pardon, so pardon me»[[Narrated by at-Tirmidhi (3513), and Ibn Majah (3850), from the hadith of 'A'ishah.]]: You love pardon from You toward Your servants, and pardon from Your servants toward their brothers, so pardon me.
What is pardon? Pardon is non-accountability for a sin. Most often, pardon refers to abandoning an obligation, while forgiveness refers to doing a forbidden act.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: a warning to whoever returns to killing game after knowing; by His saying: ﴿and whoever returns, Allah will take retribution from him﴾ [al-Ma'idah 95].
* And among its benefits also: the affirmation of the noble name (al-'Aziz) for Allah the Mighty and Majestic; al-'Aziz means the Dominant whom none can overpower, and al-'Aziz means the One from whom any deficiency is impossible in any respect, and al-'Aziz is the One of might, which bestows upon whoever possesses it power, authority and other things.
* And among the benefits of the verse: that Allah the Exalted is Possessor of retribution, but against whom? Against the criminals, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, We will take retribution from the criminals﴾ [as-Sajdah 22]. For this reason Allah the Exalted is not described with retribution absolutely, nor is He named al-Muntaqim; because Allah the Exalted restricted retribution to whom?
* Student: To the criminals.
* The Shaykh: To the criminals; so we restrict what Allah the Mighty and Majestic restricted.
And here the phrase ﴿Possessor of retribution﴾ does not indicate that it is an absolute attribute of Allah; rather ﴿Possessor of retribution﴾ means only one who has retribution, but against whom? Against the criminals.
* Student: Shaykh, may Allah bless you: there is a problem with ignorance as an excuse in the hadith of Usamah when the man was killed (...) may Allah be pleased with him, (...) was he ignorant of the ruling, or was he a mujtahid who erred?
* The Shaykh: Yes, he was interpreting (mutawwil).
* The student: And the Prophet ﷺ became very angry with him?[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4269), Muslim (96/159), from the hadith of Usamah ibn Zayd.]]
* The Shaykh: Yes, there is no doubt; because the matter is grave, the matter of killing. Is not the one who errs obligated to expiation? Killing has a special status.
* The student: So the Prophet's anger was a rebuke to Usamah or a warning from him?
* The Shaykh: No, a warning; otherwise he would have killed him, because he killed a protected soul. This man, when he said "there is no god but Allah," was protected.
* Student: May Allah be good to you. We were told that scholars differed on whether the penalty is measured by the game or by its equivalent. What is the preferred view on this matter?
* The Shaykh: We have mentioned this.
* The student: No, we have not...
* The Shaykh: We did not mention this?
* The student: No.

Sheikh: No, we have mentioned it. We said: the verse is open to interpretation. And if someone said that one should consider what is most beneficial for the poor: if the value of the game is greater, we assess the game; if the value of the compensation is greater, we assess the compensation. If this were said, it would have a basis, by analogy with the value of trade goods in zakat when their value reaches the threshold in gold but does not reach it in silver, or the reverse. By what do we assess them?

Student: By what is most beneficial.

Sheikh: By what is most beneficial. Then we also said: if someone said the opposite, namely that the original state is the freedom of the person's liability, so we do not oblige him with the greater amount, that too would have a basis. The verse, in my view, is open to both of these, and we hope that a person who takes either of these will not sin. Did you note this?

Student: The certainty (al-jazm).

Sheikh: The certainty. God knows best.

Student: The Meccan verses included the foundations of religion, such as establishing monotheism and prophethood, and abrogation does not occur in these matters. So how can we say that the verse is abrogated?

Sheikh: We do not say (...). Where are you? Did we say that all Meccan verses are abrogated?

Student: Not all of them.

Sheikh: Not all of them.

Student: But they did not come with the establishment of a law, meaning a ruling of the rulings of religion, like the Medinan verses?

Sheikh: How, when they did not come with establishment? They came with the most established of establishments.

Student: (...).

Sheikh: On what?

Student: I mean, for example, a ruling of the rulings of fasting or the drinking of wine, rulings...

Sheikh: No, fasting has a ruling. Fasting was abrogated twice, indeed three times.

Student: Some scholars say: abrogation never occurs in the Meccan verses at all?

Sheikh: No, that is not correct, never, it is not correct. All of them are open to possibility, but it is known that the foundations of religion cannot be abrogated.

Student: Do you not say that abrogation occurs in the Meccan verses themselves?

Sheikh: No, we do not say it that way. But we say: the verses which are foundations of religion cannot be abrogated.

Student: The hadith of Usama, may Allah be pleased with him, contains "he testified with his tongue." And does one who seeks protection with what that man sought protection with, the one who said "there is no god but Allah," have his blood protected?

Sheikh: Yes, his blood is protected until it becomes clear that the opposite of what he said is the case.

Student: If polytheists and combatants said this, perhaps...?

Sheikh: It does not contradict. That is why, indeed, in the Afghan war against the Russians some of them would say: "I testify there is no god but Allah, and I testify that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah," when the fighters came upon them.

Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. "Lawful for you is the game of the sea and its food, as a provision for you and for the travelers; but forbidden for you is the game of the land as long as you are in the state of ihram. And fear Allah, to whom you will be gathered" (96). "Allah made the Ka'bah, the Sacred House, a means of support for the people, and the sacred month, and the offerings and the garlands. That is so that you may know that Allah knows what is in the heavens and what is in the earth, and that Allah is Knowing of all things" (97). "Know that Allah is severe in punishment, and that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful" [al-Ma'idah 96-98].

Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: "Lawful for you is the game of the sea and its food, as a provision for you and for the travelers." When Allah, glorified and exalted, explained in the previous verses the ruling on game of the land for the one in ihram, He mentioned the ruling on game of the sea, saying: "Lawful for you is the game of the sea." The one who makes lawful (al-muhill) is Allah, mighty and majestic, because the power of making lawful, forbidding and obligating is in His hand.

His saying "for you" addresses those residing in the lands, as evidenced by His saying "and for the travelers" (al-sayyarah), i.e., those who journey, the travelers who take provision from it with their goods.

His saying, exalted be He, "the game of the sea and its food": "game" (sayd) here means "what is caught" (maṣīd), namely what is taken alive. "Its food" means what is eaten without hunting, namely what the sea casts up of fish and whale. Accordingly, everything in the sea is lawful, as will come, Allah willing, in the benefits (al-fawa'id).

His saying "as a provision for you and for the travelers": "provision" (matā'an) is an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi), i.e., so that you may enjoy it. Allah, exalted, has explained in other verses that He subjected the sea so that we might eat from it fresh flesh, and as is observed now, the flesh of the sea is among the finest of meats.

His saying "and the game of the land is forbidden for you as long as you are in the state of ihram": the one who forbids is Allah, mighty and majestic. As for "the game of the land as long as you are in ihram," is the intended meaning "the game of the land" in the sense of what is hunted (maṣīd), or is the intended meaning that you hunt it?

Student: The second.

Shaykh: The second is the intended meaning, because "what is hunted" involves a distinction as previously mentioned. That is, it is forbidden for you to hunt the game of the land. This meaning requires an implied element, and the implication is: your hunting of the game of the land, because the land is not hunted, so an implication is necessary.

But if we say that "game" means "what is hunted," then there is no need for the implication, and the meaning of "the game of the land" is: what is hunted therein. It has already passed for us that the forbidden game is what, [what kind of animal]? A lawful wild land animal.

His saying "as long as you are in ihram" means: while you are in the state of ihram until you exit it.

"And fear Allah": fear Allah by performing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions. This is the most comprehensive of what has been said in explaining taqwa (God-consciousness), that it is taking a shield against the punishment of Allah by performing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions.

"To whom you will be gathered": "alladhi" is an adjective of the noble name (Allah), and "to Him you will be gathered" is the relative clause. The prepositional phrase has been placed before its governing verb to convey restriction (hasr) and to match the endings of the verses. Thus there is a semantic benefit and a verbal benefit: the semantic benefit is restriction, and the verbal benefit is the harmony of the verse endings.

The meaning of "you will be gathered" is: you will be assembled to Him, and that is on the Day of Resurrection, as people are gathered to Allah, blessed and exalted, as is explained in the Sunnah.

* In this verse there are benefits, among them: the permissibility of the game of the sea for both those in the state of non-ihram and those in ihram, which is derived from His saying "and the game of the land is forbidden for you as long as you are in ihram."

* Among its benefits: if there is water containing fish within the boundaries of the Haram, it is lawful, by the generality of His saying "Lawful for you is the game of the sea and its food." Then He said "and the game of the land is forbidden for you as long as you are in ihram." This is the preponderant view.

Some scholars said: rather it is forbidden and there is compensation for it, because it is in a safe place.

Others said: it is forbidden but there is no compensation for it. However, the apparent meaning of the noble verse is that it is lawful.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that all animals of the sea are lawful, derived from the annexation "game of the sea," and annexation implies generality, so it includes everything in the sea, of fish and whales, small and large, resembling humans, resembling wolves, resembling pigs, whatever it may be, because "game of the sea" is general.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that everything in the sea that is eaten, of fish, plants and others, is lawful, by the generality of His saying "and its food."

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of Allah's wisdom in making the game of the sea lawful while the game of the land is forbidden in ihram, because the first is easy to take and a person does not amuse himself with it as he does with game of the land, and furthermore it is a hidden game in the depths of the waters, so it is not like the visible game on the surface of the earth.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: an indication of the permissibility of storing the flesh of the sea, derived from His saying "and for the travelers," i.e., those journeying on travel.

Is the flesh of land game similar to this, i.e., outside of ihram?

The answer: yes, but it is conditioned that it not reach the point of harm. If it reaches the point of harm, such as becoming foul-smelling, its odor becoming repugnant, and it being feared for the person, then it becomes either disliked or forbidden, by the saying of Allah, exalted: "And do not kill yourselves" [al-Nisa' 29], and His saying: "And do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction" [al-Baqarah 195].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of hunting the land game for those in ihram, by His saying "and the game of the land is forbidden for you as long as you are in ihram."

You have known whether the intended meaning is what is hunted or the hunting. If the intended meaning is hunting, the matter is clear and there is no difficulty that a person in ihram is ordered not to hunt land game. But if we say the intended meaning is what is hunted, do we take the generality of the verse and say that what is hunted on land is forbidden for the one in ihram, whether he hunted it himself, or it was hunted for his sake, or someone not in ihram hunted it for him? You have known the disagreement on this: some scholars say that the one in ihram may not eat from land game whether it was hunted for him, or hunted by another, or hunted by himself. We have explained previously that the preponderant view among the scholars' opinions is: if the one in ihram hunted it, it is forbidden; if it was hunted for him, it is forbidden; if someone not in ihram hunted it for his own sake, it is lawful for the one in ihram. This is the preponderant view, in which the evidences converge.

* Among the benefits of this verse: that hunting is not lawful, the hunting of land game, for the one who has exited the first stage of release (al-tahallul al-awwal). The reason: one who has exited the first release has not ceased to be in ihram, and what remains forbidden to him of the prohibitions of ihram is women. Have you understood? This is the view of some scholars, who said: hunting is not lawful after the first release, just as women are not lawful. But the Sunnah has shown that when one exits the first release, everything becomes lawful for him except women [Abu Dawud (1978) narrated from the hadith of 'A'ishah: "When any one of you throws the pebble at Jamrat al-'Aqabah, everything becomes lawful for him except women."].

It remains to be said: the one who exits the first release will be in Mina, and Mina is part of the Haram. Do you permit the one in ihram in this place to hunt?

The answer: No, we do not permit him that, because it is in the Haram, and the game of the Haram is forbidden to the one who has exited release and to the one in ihram. But suppose this one in ihram went out to 'Arafah, and 'Arafah is outside the Haram; is it permissible for him to hunt or not? This depends on the disagreement: whoever says hunting is not lawful after the first release says he may not hunt; whoever says everything is lawful to him except women — and this is the preponderant view — says he may hunt.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation of fearing Allah, mighty and majestic, and beware of disobeying Him regarding these rulings He has prescribed; by His saying "And fear Allah."

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the warning against the punishment of the Last Day; by His saying "To whom you will be gathered."

* Among the benefits of the verse: the affirmation of the Last Day in which the gathering to Allah will occur; by His saying "To whom you will be gathered."

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the gathering is to Allah and not to other than Him; He is the one who takes charge of punishing His servants or rewarding them. This is like the saying of Allah, exalted: "Indeed, to Us is their return, then indeed upon Us is their reckoning" [al-Ghashiyah 25-26].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 5, verse 97 (part 1 of 2):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Allah has made the Ka'bah, the Sacred House, a means of stability for the people, and the Sacred Month, and the hady (sacrificial animals), and the qala'id (garlands)﴾. These are four things that Allah the Exalted made a means of stability for the people. First: ﴿Allah has made the Ka'bah, the Sacred House, a means of stability for the people.﴾ Is this "making" a legislative (shar'i) making, or a pre-destined (kawni) making, or both? The apparent view is the third: that Allah made it so both in the pre-destined order and in the legislative order.

His saying: ﴿the Ka'bah, the Sacred House﴾. Ka'bah originally means the square building. But His saying ﴿the Sacred House﴾ excludes every square structure other than the honoured Ka'bah. On this basis, His saying ﴿the Sacred House﴾ is a qualifying description that excludes others. It is not an explanation (bayan) or an apposition (badal). Rather, it is a descriptive qualifier that excludes other "Ka'bahs." His saying ﴿the Sacred House﴾ means: that which possesses sanctity (hurmah), and the sanctity of Makkah is a well-known matter.

His saying: ﴿a means of stability for the people﴾. In another recitation (qira'ah) it is read ﴿qiyaman lil-nas﴾ (qiyamam). ﴿A means of stability for the people﴾ means: by it the interests of their religion and the interests of their worldly life are established. This is like His saying: ﴿And do not give the foolish your wealth, which Allah has made a means of stability for you﴾ [An-Nisa 5], meaning: by which the interests of religion and worldly life are established. So the Ka'bah is something Allah made a means of stability for the people, by which the interests of their religion and their worldly life are established. As for the interests of religion, it is evident: the hajj and the 'umrah with the rites contained in them. As for the interests of worldly life, Allah the Exalted indicated them when He said: ﴿That they may witness benefits for themselves and mention the name of Allah﴾ [Al-Hajj 28]. Furthermore, the fruits of everything are brought to this Ka'bah as a provision from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

His saying: ﴿and the Sacred Month﴾ means: and He made the Sacred Month a means of stability for the people. Does it refer to the category (jins) or to one month? It refers to the category, so it includes the four months, which are: Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, Muharram, and Rajab. Allah made the Sacred Months a means of stability for the people because they are secure in them, since fighting in them is forbidden. Even in the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic period) it was not possible for fighting to take place in these four months: Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, Muharram, and Rajab. As for the first three, they are the months of hajj, meaning the months in which people travel to Makkah and return from it. They travel in Dhu al-Qa'dah and return in Muharram. It is known that Muharram is not one of the months of hajj, but instead of it, what? Shawwal. Yet it is among the sanctities of hajj, since people travel in the month of Dhu al-Qa'dah for hajj and return in the month of Muharram. For this reason, in the Jahiliyyah no one could attack anyone in these months at all. Even if one found the killer of his father, he would not kill him.

Rajab too was a month of honour in the Jahiliyyah, like the three months. Fighting was not possible in it, so people were secure in these months and their interests were established. They traveled and returned to their homelands, and no one harmed them.

Is this the third or the fourth? The third: Allah made the hady a means of stability for the people in their religion and their worldly life. As for their religion, through the reward they gain from Allah the Mighty and Majestic. As for their worldly life, through buying and selling, eating, benefiting from the hides, and similar things. So the hady is indeed a means of stability for the people.
