* Among the benefits of this noble verse: it is a condition for calling witnesses that the two witnesses be people of justice, because of His saying: ﴿two just men﴾. We have already defined justice. But if no just person is found, and an untrustworthy but reliable person is found, can he take the place of a just person?

Some scholars have chosen that this does take the place of justice, and that the condition of justice applies only at the time of bearing witness. That is, when you want to call witnesses, you call only two just persons. But at the time of giving testimony, necessities have their own rulings. If we find no one to testify except these two who are unjust, but who are trustworthy in honesty, then we accept their testimony. This last view is the correct one: justice is a condition where it is possible. If it is not possible, then the testimony of an unjust person is accepted, on condition of what? That he is trustworthy. How many people are unjust in their worship but honest in their testimony? We know that if we followed the condition of justice in giving testimony, taking into account the conditions the jurists mentioned for justice, many rights would be lost, because many people are not upright in the way the jurists described, may Allah have mercy on them.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the permissibility of a disbeliever's testimony when a Muslim cannot be found, because of His saying: ﴿or two others from outside your own people﴾.

Does this apply only to People of the Book, or to every disbeliever?

The apparent meaning is every disbeliever, because of His saying ﴿or two others from outside your own people﴾, whether he is a Jew, a Christian, a Buddhist, or a communist, whoever he may be, because of His saying ﴿from outside your own people﴾. Scholars have differed on this matter in three positions.

The first position: the testimony of a disbeliever is not accepted at all. They answered this verse by saying it has been abrogated, because Allah stipulated justice in witnesses, and the disbeliever is not just.

The second position: the testimony of a disbeliever is permitted on two conditions: that he be a People of the Book, and that it be in cases of necessity. So they stipulated two conditions. The first: necessity, that no Muslim is available. The second: that the two witnesses be People of the Book. These scholars argued for the condition of necessity from His saying: ﴿if you are travelling through the land﴾ and so on. They restricted it to People of the Book, because the case in which the verse was revealed involved witnesses who were People of the Book. And in establishing their argument they said: the non-requirement of Islam in this case departs from the basic rule, and whatever departs from the basic rule must be restricted to what is specifically mentioned.

There is no doubt that the answer to these scholars is easy. We say: the noble verse is general, and what counts is the generality of the wording. For this reason, when Allah wishes to restrict a ruling to People of the Book, He qualifies it, as in His saying: ﴿and the chaste women from among those who were given the Book before you﴾, and He said: ﴿and the food of those who were given the Book is lawful for you﴾ [al-Ma'ida 5]. As for qualifying what Allah has left unqualified, this is not correct. This is a principle that the student of knowledge must follow: whatever Allah and His Messenger have stated in unrestricted form, in the Qur'an and the Sunnah, it is not permissible to add a qualifier to it, ever. Because if he does so, he narrows what Allah has made broad, and takes himself as a lawgiver and as one who corrects the legal ruling. This is dangerous. So the principle is that whatever Allah and His Messenger stated without restriction must be left unrestricted, and it is not lawful to add a qualification unless there is evidence which must be followed. In that case, we say: the correct view is that two persons may testify to a bequest in the absence of a Muslim, whether they are People of the Book or not.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the superiority of the Muslim over the disbeliever. This is not problematic. The reasoning: a disbeliever's testimony is not accepted except when no Muslim is found, and this shows that the Muslim is higher in rank and standing than the non-Muslim.

If someone says: we understand that a disbeliever's testimony in matters concerning Muslims is permitted only in cases of necessity. Do you accept the testimony of disbelievers against one another?

The answer: yes. Whether it is for necessity or not, the testimony of disbelievers against one another is accepted, but on condition that the witness is just according to his own religion, just as we stipulated for the testimony of a Muslim that he be just.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: travel is called ḍarb fi al-arḍ (striking through the land). The noble Qur'an sometimes mentions travel by its name and sometimes mentions it as striking through the land. His saying ﴿and if you are sick or on a journey﴾ [al-Ma'ida 6] mentions travel and does not say "or you have struck through the land." And He said concerning fasting: ﴿So whoever among you is sick or on a journey﴾ [al-Baqara 184].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the term "striking through the land" is unrestricted, and He did not qualify it by a distance of shortening the prayer, or more, or less.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: if the two witnesses who are non-Muslims wish to give testimony, they are detained after the prayer, meaning they are made to stand after the prayer. This is because of the absence of suspicion, since the prayer is honoured, and a person fears to testify falsely after this prayer which Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, mentioned.

But is this conditional on doubt about their testimony, or do we say they are detained in every case, so that the difference between a Muslim's testimony and a non-Muslim's testimony becomes apparent?

The verse allows for two readings. His saying ﴿they shall swear by Allah if you doubt them﴾ may be read such that ﴿if you doubt them﴾ qualifies His saying ﴿you shall detain them after the prayer﴾ and His saying ﴿they shall swear by Allah﴾. It may also be read as qualifying only His saying ﴿they shall swear by Allah﴾, with ﴿if you doubt them﴾ attached to it. On the second reading, their detention is obligatory. On the first reading, their detention is not obligatory except if we have doubt about them.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: an oath may not be sworn by other than Allah, because of His saying ﴿they shall swear by Allah﴾. So if someone swears by other than Allah, even by one whom they revere, such as the Messiah for example, his oath is not accepted and is not counted, because of Allah's saying ﴿they shall swear by Allah﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: their oath is required only when there is doubt about their testimony, as is taken from His saying: ﴿if you doubt them﴾.

Does it follow from this that a judge may make the two witnesses swear when he has doubt about their testimony?

We say: yes, he may do so. No one may say that this applies only to our doubt about disbelievers. No. If someone says this applies only to our doubt about the testimony of disbelievers, the answer is: the ruling revolves around its cause. We only make them swear by Allah when there is doubt, not because they are disbelievers. So the judge may make the witnesses swear if he has doubt about their testimony.

May he also separate the witnesses when there is doubt, by meeting each of them alone and asking him detailed questions, so that if they disagree he knows their testimony is not valid?

The answer: yes, he may do so.

May he also use indirection, showing them the opposite of what he intends, in order to bring out the truth?

The answer: yes. The story of Solomon with the two women supports this. The two women set out on some business, and then a wolf ate the son of one of them. They brought their dispute before David, who ruled in favour of the older one. Then they brought it before Solomon, who asked for a knife. He said he wanted to split the child in two and give half to the older and half to the younger. The older agreed to this, why? Because she had no mercy for him, and her son had died; the wolf had eaten him, so let this be his fate too. The younger said: "O Prophet of Allah, he is hers, he is hers." She gave up her claim, why? Out of compassion and mercy. She gave it up. The meaning of her saying "he is hers" was not that he was her slave, no; it meant she had relinquished the claim. So Solomon, peace be upon him, ruled in favour of whom? The younger.[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3426) and Muslim (1720/20), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]

So if the judge doubts the testimony of the witnesses, there is no harm in his using indirection in the ruling, in order to bring out the truth.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the manner of the oath is as follows: ﴿We will not sell it for any price, even if it concerns a relative, and we will not conceal the testimony of Allah﴾ [al-Ma'ida 106]. Is it enough to convey the meaning, or must this exact wording be used?

The correct view is that the meaning suffices, because this wording is not a matter of worship that cannot be changed. Rather, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, expressed the meaning in this wording. So the reference, my brothers, is to what? The reference is to the meaning.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: an indication that kinship has an effect on inclination and emotion, because of their saying ﴿even if it concerns a relative﴾. This is a known natural matter. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, pointed to this in His saying: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they were kinsmen﴾ [al-Tawba 113], and He said: ﴿O you who believe, be upholders of justice, witnesses for Allah, even against yourselves or your parents and close relatives﴾ [al-Nisa' 135].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 5, verses 106–108 (part 4 of 5):

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: concealing testimony is a sin, as shown by His words: ﴿Then indeed we would be among the sinners﴾. Allah Almighty established this in His words: ﴿And do not conceal testimony; whoever conceals it, his heart is sinful﴾ [al-Baqarah 283]. There is no doubt that when a person conceals testimony, it entails hiding an obligatory right belonging to one person and attributing falsehood to another. For example, if someone asks you to testify that so-and-so owes him such-and-such, and you conceal it, what happens? The right is hidden, and falsehood is attributed to the one against whom testimony was not given.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the oath is returned to the claimant (al-mudda'i). This is shown by His words: ﴿If it is discovered that the two had become liable to sin, then two others shall take their place﴾, to the end of the verse. How is the oath returned to the claimant?
Zayd sued 'Amr for a hundred riyals. We asked Zayd for evidence, and he said: "I have no evidence, but I request the oath of the defendant (al-mudda'a 'alayh)." Do you understand? If the defendant swears, the dispute ends. Not that he is declared innocent; the dispute ends. This means that if the claimant later learns of evidence he did not know of before, he still holds his claim, but the dispute has ended.
If the claimant says, when the defendant refuses to swear: "Rule against him, because the dispute has ended and he cannot demand anything from me." Then if the judge decides to return the oath to the claimant, there is no harm in that. Why? Because the denier may be truthful, yet the claimant needs to establish something additional, so the judge returns the oath to him. This view is the correct one: it is permissible to return the oath to the claimant, as in this verse.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: it is permissible for the one who bears the right to investigate the case closely and scrutinize it until he discovers a right in it. This is shown by His words: ﴿If it is discovered that they...﴾, and discovery (al-'ithar) can only come after diligent inquiry (al-taharri).
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: if the two witnesses alter their testimony by adding, omitting, or substituting, then they are both sinful. This is shown by His words: ﴿If it is discovered that the two had become liable to sin﴾, and that occurs when the testimony is not valid, because this is a sin.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: when it is discovered that the two witnesses are lying, two men are brought forward from among those who have a claim against them. As you know, the case concerned a bequest (wasiyyah). So two men from among those who have a claim are brought forward, and the two must be the nearest, meaning the ones most entitled to the inheritance of the deceased. The discussion in the two verses concerns the bequest.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: an indication that inheritance goes to the nearest in kinship, in order of priority. This is taken from His words: ﴿the nearest﴾ (al-awliyan). The hadith also establishes this, the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Give the prescribed shares to their rightful owners; whatever remains belongs to the nearest male relative." [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (6732) and Muslim (1615/2) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.] Is that not so? Read the hadith.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, he said: the Prophet (ﷺ) said... Yes, it must be phrased like this.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse, as we mentioned at the beginning: the oath is returned to the claimant, as shown by His words: ﴿so they both swear by Allah﴾.
* And among its benefits, among the benefits of the noble verse: the defendant does not definitively declare void the testimony of a witness which has been shown to contain some defect. This is shown by His words: ﴿Our testimony is more worthy than their testimony﴾, using this wording and not saying "void". But His words ﴿more worthy than their testimony﴾ imply that their testimony is rejected and that the statement of the defendant is the accepted one.
* And among the benefits of this verse: if testimony or oath requires affirmation and negation, then both affirmation and negation must be mentioned. Their words, meaning the two nearest, ﴿Our testimony is more worthy than their testimony﴾: what is this? An affirmation. ﴿And we have not transgressed﴾: this is a negation. So when this is needed, both negation and affirmation must be mentioned, so that the testimony is pure.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the rejection by the two nearest of the testimony of the two witnesses is a greater transgression than the alteration of the testimony by the two witnesses. The reason is that when the witnesses alter their testimony, He said: ﴿then indeed we would be among the sinners﴾, but here He said: ﴿then indeed we would be among the wrongdoers﴾. The difference between them was explained earlier in the tafsir (interpretation).
* Among the benefits of the third verse: whenever a matter is closer to deducing what is correct and true through testimony, it is more fitting to follow it. This is shown by His words: ﴿That is more likely that they will give testimony in its proper form﴾. For when a person understands that people will stand behind him to reject his testimony and swear to its falsity, he must necessarily seek to be truthful in what he testifies.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation to fear Allah and to hear and obey Him. This is shown by His words: ﴿And fear Allah and listen﴾. The meaning of "listen" here is: respond, as was also explained earlier in the commentary.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: Allah, glorified is He, informed that He does not guide the defiant people, meaning those who depart from His obedience, and the report of Allah is true.
But this raises a difficulty: in reality, Allah does guide some defiant people and some disbelievers. How do we reconcile the reality with this true report?
The reconciliation is that we say: Allah does not guide the defiant people, meaning those for whom Allah has decreed defiance. As for one whom He has decreed to believe, he will believe without fail. The benefit of the unrestricted wording ﴿He does not guide the defiant people﴾ is an indication that Allah does not guide the defiant because they chose defiance, as He said: ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate, and Allah does not guide the defiant people﴾ [al-Saff 5]. We ask Allah to guide us and you, and to protect us from ourselves and from Satan.
* Student: May Allah reward you well. We said that the testimony of disbelievers may be accepted for one another, even without necessity. Is there no distinction between the People of the Book and others?
* Shaykh: Yes, there is no distinction. Yes indeed. But they must be upright (adl) in their own religion, just as a Muslim must be upright.
* Student: Shaykh, did we not mention that testimony after the 'Asr prayer applies to the People of the Book, who do not regard this prayer as sacred, as in the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas and as Abu Musa al-Ash'ari said?
* Shaykh: No. The correct view is that the intended prayer is the 'Asr prayer, even if they do not hold it in reverence, because it is great in the sight of Allah, and because punishment is swifter for one who gives false testimony or swears falsely after the 'Asr prayer.
* Student: And Ibn 'Abbas, Shaykh?
* Shaykh: Yes?
* Student: I mean, Ibn 'Abbas's ijtihad (independent reasoning) contradicts this.
* Shaykh: What did he say?
* Student: The hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, when we read it in the tafsir: when he said to him: "Make it after their prayer in their religion."
* Shaykh: Yes, that was his own choice.
* Student: Shaykh, may Allah bless you. If two men participate in a crime, and during the investigation many indications show that they are in fact the perpetrators, and then the investigators want to extract confessions from them, is it permissible for the investigator, for example, to meet one of them alone and say that his companion has confessed to this crime?
* Shaykh: And he had denied it before?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: No, it is not permissible. That is a lie.

So the first interpretation is the stronger.

* Shaykh: What is the reconciliation?
* Student: We say the bequest is for someone other than the nearest relatives and other than the heirs.
* Shaykh: Correct, this is the right view. The verse is not abrogated, because Allah said: ﴿to parents and relatives﴾. He excluded whoever is an heir, so what remains is whoever is not an heir, and it does not conflict with the verses of inheritance.
* Student: (...).

**Shaykh:** No. Sometimes the father is not an heir. For example, if the father is a slave, he does not inherit from his son. But there is nothing wrong with the son bequeathing to him, or being instructed to bequeath to him, especially if we say that a slave can own property by transfer (*tamlik*). The scholars differ on whether a slave can own by transfer, or whether, if something is transferred to him, the ownership goes to his master. Some distinguish: if the one who transfers is the master, the slave owns; if it is someone else, he does not.

The correct view is that the verse is not abrogated (*mansukha*). What is reported from the early scholars (*salaf*) that it is abrogated, they use the term *naskh* (abrogation) for *takhsis* (specification), because specification is in reality an abrogation of generality (*'umum*), so they call it *naskh*.

Recently, in Surat al-Ma'idah, we passed the story of calling a disbeliever to witness a bequest. That verse has a specific cause (*sabab*), but its wording is general. So do we say that this general ruling is specified by its cause, or not?

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** He says: the cause does not specify the generality. What matters is the generality of the wording, not the specific cause. What was the cause for which the verse was revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, when death approaches one of you, the testimony [shall be] between you: two just men from among you﴾, and so on to the end [al-Ma'idah 5:106]?

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** A man called two people of the People of the Book (*Ahl al-Kitab*) as witnesses to his bequest, so Allah revealed this verse. But suppose he did not find two men from the People of the Book or from the Muslims, and he called two communists as witnesses. Do we act on this, or do we say it applies only to the People of the Book?

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** How is that?

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** What?

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** (...). Now we want the general wording. The verse: ﴿two just men from among you, or two others from other than you﴾. So His words ﴿from other than you﴾ include both People of the Book and others.

Is this ruling about their testimony restricted to bequests, or even to something other than a bequest, if he testifies that the deceased acknowledged a debt owed to someone?

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** Is (...) a bequest? But in reality it is a bequest.

**Student:** We take the generality.

**Shaykh:** We take the generality. Where is the generality?

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** Where is the generality? Show us it.

**Student:** (...).

﴿from other than you﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:106] includes People of the Book and others. Is this ruling about their testimony restricted to bequests, or even to something other than a bequest, if he testifies that the deceased acknowledged a debt owed to someone?

**Student:** Even other than bequests.

**Shaykh:** Even other than bequests? But in reality it is a bequest?

**Student:** We take the generality.

**Shaykh:** We take the generality. Where is the generality? Show us it.

**Student:** Nothing has been excluded from it by a restriction, and the case of the bequest is the basis; meaning, non-bequests are included as well.

**Shaykh:** Yes, but your opponent will come and say: "We do not accept that. Give us a generality from the verse."

**Student:** Yes, indeed. He said: ﴿or two others from other than you, if you are travelling in the land and the calamity of death strikes you﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:106]. This does not limit it to bequests alone, although (...) calamity.

**Shaykh:** So His words ﴿and the calamity of death strikes you﴾ include the case of testifying to a bequest, or testifying to the deceased's acknowledgment of a debt, or other things. Do you agree with this?

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** How?

**Student:** The evidence is in His words ﴿the testimony between you﴾: "testimony" is an idafa construction (...).

**Shaykh:** But we restrict ﴿the testimony between you﴾ by ﴿two just men from among you, or two others from other than you, if you are travelling in the land﴾, and the generality is taken from His words ﴿and the calamity of death strikes you﴾, meaning: and you call them to witness this at the time of death.

Someone might ask: shall we extend every emergency to this situation?

**Student:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** Yes! Every emergency?!

**Student:** Every emergency.

**Shaykh:** For example, a person in a town whose death approaches, and who has only disbelievers with him. This may happen now with workers, since we have disbelieving workers.

**Student:** Yes, we say it, Shaykh.

**Shaykh:** We say it in an emergency?

**Student:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** How do we account for this, or how do we say this, when the verse says ﴿if you are travelling in the land﴾?

**Student:** Then it is not a restriction.

**Shaykh:** But (*in*) is a conditional particle.

**Student:** It is for explanation of this.

**Shaykh:** Explanation of what?

**Student:** Explanation of (...).

**Shaykh:** Meaning the verse was revealed to explain the actual incident, so every emergency is analogous to it in meaning. Do you agree with this?

**Students:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** Yes, and this is the correct view. You know that there are three opinions on this issue. Do you remember them?

The first opinion: this verse is abrogated, and the testimony of disbelievers is never accepted in matters concerning the rights of Muslims.

The second opinion: it is specific to bequests during travel when no Muslim is available. They gave a reason: accepting the testimony of a disbeliever is an exception to the principle. The principle is that a disbeliever's testimony is not accepted. So if something is an exception to the principle, it must be limited to what the text states in that particular case. These scholars restrict it by three specifications: travel, bequests, and People of the Book.

The third opinion: the testimony of a disbeliever is accepted in every emergency. This is closer to the principles of the Shari'ah. However, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, mentioned that in cases of doubt they should be detained after the prayer, as in the verse.

We have two verses in which there is partial generality and specificity (*'umum wa khusus min wajh*). Which one do we give priority to?

**Student:** The specific one... as for the two specific ones that conflict, either it returns to (...).

**Shaykh:** This presents no problem.

**Student:** And as for the specific (...), it is applied to both.

**Shaykh:** The conflict (*ta'arud*) arises when there is partial generality and specificity.

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** Meaning a preponderant factor (*murajjih*) must be sought. If none is found, then what? Give an example.

**Student:** No example is needed.

**Shaykh:** Give an example of a case where there is a preponderance.

**Student:** For instance, His words in Surat an-Nisa': ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that﴾ [an-Nisa' 4:24], which conflicts with His words...

**Another student:** His words, blessed and exalted: ﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind, they shall wait by themselves for four months and ten [days]﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:234]. And His words, blessed and exalted: ﴿And for pregnant women, their term is until they deliver their burden﴾ [at-Talaq 65:4]. These two verses have partial generality and specificity.

**Shaykh:** Explain, clarify this.

**Student:** The woman observes the longer of the two terms.

**Shaykh:** How?! I do not want the ruling now, but how is the conflict?

**Student:** In the first verse, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, states that she observes four months and ten days.

**Shaykh:** Whether she is pregnant or not.

**Student:** Or not pregnant.

**Shaykh:** Good.

**Student:** And in the second verse, when she is pregnant, she observes by delivering the child.

**Shaykh:** Whether her husband died or not. How do we combine them? If we find a pregnant woman whose husband died, what must she observe?

**Student:** The longer of the two terms.

**Shaykh:** The longer of the two terms, yes.

**Another student:** The pregnant woman observes by the hadith...

**Shaykh:** By delivery of the child. Based on the principle now, does she observe the longer of the two terms?

Yes, based on the principle, she observes the longer of the two terms. For example, if she delivers after two months, we say: complete four months and ten days. If she delivers after six months, we say: wait until you deliver.

By this we act on both verses. But the Sunnah shows that the pregnant woman's term is delivery of the child, even if it is less than four months and ten days. What is the Sunnah reported on this?

**Student:** The hadith about Subay'a al-Aslamiyya, that (...) entered upon her.

**Shaykh:** Abu as-Sanabil.

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** He said to her: "You are not to marry until..."

**Student:** "Until four months and ten days have passed for you." She said: "When he said that to me, I gathered my clothes around me and went to the Prophet (ﷺ) and asked him."

**Shaykh:** She informed him of what Abu as-Sanabil had said to her. Yes. What did he say to her?

**Student:** That she was free to marry.

**Shaykh:** He informed her that she was free to marry upon delivery. This shows that the generality of ﴿and for pregnant women, their term is until they deliver their burden﴾ takes precedence over the generality of ﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind, they shall wait by themselves for four months and ten [days]﴾.

From the principles: when a general term is given, and then a ruling follows that implies specification, do we act on the generality or on the specification?

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** An example: ﴿And divorced women shall wait by themselves for three periods. And it is not lawful for them to conceal what Allah has created in their wombs, if they believe in Allah and the Last Day. And their husbands have more right to take them back during that [period]﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:228]. The word ﴿divorced women﴾: if we look at its generality, what does it include? Revocable and irrevocable divorcees, that is, whether her divorce was irrevocable or revocable. And His words ﴿and their husbands have more right to take them back﴾ imply what?

It implies that this applies to revocable divorcees. So do we say that when a general term is followed by a ruling that applies only to some of its instances, it is restricted to those instances, or not?

Yes, this is also one of the matters on which the scholars differ. Some say that a divorcee who has been irrevocably divorced, whom her husband cannot take back, observes one menstrual cycle, because there is no benefit in prolonging the period for her. For a revocable divorcee there is a benefit in prolonging it, namely that the husband may take her back. But here there is no benefit, and if there is no benefit, she should be given room. It is said: her term has ended with one menstrual cycle, and she may marry.

Others say: we act on the generality. Following with a ruling on some of its instances is like mentioning some instances of a general term with a ruling that matches the generality; it does not imply specification. This is the view of the majority. The first view is the opinion chosen by Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him: that the divorcee who must observe three periods is only the revocable divorcee.

A parallel in the Sunnah is: "The Prophet (ﷺ) decided on pre-emption (*shufah*) in everything not yet divided. When the boundaries are set and the roads are marked, there is no pre-emption." [Reported by al-Bukhari (2257) from the hadith of Jabir ibn Abdullah.] If we look at the generality of the beginning of the hadith, we say: pre-emption applies to everything, even movable property. If we look at what follows, we say: there is no pre-emption except in lands where boundaries are set and roads are marked. This too is a matter on which scholars differ. Some say pre-emption is established only in lands, so if a car is shared by two people and one sells his share to a third party, his partner has no right of pre-emption, because the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When the boundaries are set and the roads are marked," and a car has no boundaries or roads.

Others say: we act on the generality, and pre-emption is established in everything not yet divided, whether land, movable property, or other things. They say: "When the boundaries are set" is a qualification of some instances of the general term, and it does not contradict the generality, so it does not imply specification. This too is disputed. However, there are hadiths indicating the generality and that pre-emption is required even in things other than land. That is, even if two men own a car and one sells his share to another, his partner has no pre-emption, because the reason for which pre-emption was established for the partner exists in land and in other things. Indeed, it may be even more contentious in other things, since the new partner may cause disputes and quarrels with the first partner that make his life miserable.

When reports from the early scholars give different interpretations of a verse, and the interpretations are possible, do we say that this difference is a genuine difference, or is it a difference of diversity (*tanawwu'*)?

**Shaykh:** It depends. Some of it is a difference of diversity, and some is a difference of contradiction (*tadad*). If it is a difference of contradiction, we must find a preponderant factor between the two views. If it is a difference of diversity, there is no real disagreement. An example is His words: ﴿Then We gave the Book to those We chose from Our servants; then among them is one who wrongs himself, and among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who is foremost in good deeds﴾ [Fatir 35:32]. Some said: the one who wrongs himself is the one who delays the prayer beyond its time. Others said: the one who wrongs himself is the one who does not pay zakat. That is one.

"And among them is one who is moderate": they said the moderate one is the one who pays zakat but does not give voluntary charity, and who prays on time but does not strive to perform it in the best manner.

The foremost in good deeds is the one who pays zakat and voluntary charity and strives to perform the prayer as it should be. Is this difference a genuine difference, such that we say there are two views on the interpretation of the verse?

No. This is a difference of diversity: each of them mentioned one kind of what is included in the verse. Some people consider this a disagreement, but it is not. They call this a difference of diversity, not a difference of contradiction. Accordingly, it is not permissible to say that the early scholars disagreed about the meaning of this verse, because all of them agreed that the one who wrongs himself is the one who neglects an obligation, the moderate one is the one who fulfils the obligation, and the foremost in good deeds is the one who goes beyond the obligation. They agreed on this, but each of them gave an example.

We want a verse containing specification that is connected to something other than an exception. Exceptions are many: ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss, except those who have believed﴾ and so on to the end [al-'Asr 103:2–3]. There are many.

**Student:** His words: ﴿So from what your right hands possess of your believing young women﴾ [an-Nisa' 4:25].

**Shaykh:** Yes, ﴿your believing young women﴾: this is specified by a description.

Similarly, His words: ﴿And pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to Allah by mankind, for whoever is able to make his way there﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:97]. When He first mentioned the generality, He then qualified it with ﴿for whoever is able to make his way there﴾. Do we take the generality or the qualification?

We take the qualification without doubt, because the qualification specifies the qualified term. Accordingly, pilgrimage is obligatory only for whom? For whoever is able.

If someone says: all acts of worship are qualified by ability, because of His words: ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ [at-Taghabun 64:16]. Then what is the wisdom in mentioning this condition for pilgrimage, and not mentioning it for prayer, for example? He did not say: "Establish prayer if you are able."

The answer is simple: the hardship in pilgrimage is more evident and clear than in other acts. Therefore this condition is stated explicitly. Fasting, since it involves some hardship, was described by Him, the Mighty and Majestic, as: ﴿Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:185]. As for what involves no hardship, commands are mentioned in absolute terms, but they are interpreted according to the general principle that there is no obligation with incapacity, because of His words: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:286], and His words: ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾.

Regarding His words: ﴿The companions of al-Aykah denied the messengers (176) when Shu'ayb said to them﴾ [ash-Shu'ara' 26:176–177], and in another verse: ﴿And to Madyan [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb﴾ [al-A'raf 7:85]: why is brotherhood mentioned in the second verse but not in the first?

**Student:** Because he attributed them to the tree they worshipped. When he attributed them to the tree, he did not grant them the brotherhood of faith, and when he attributed them to the land, he established for them the brotherhood of lineage.

**Shaykh:** That is one reason. Another reason is that when He said: ﴿The companions of al-Aykah denied the messengers (176) when Shu'ayb said to them﴾, He did not say "their brother," because they worshipped trees.

Some said: these people were not from his own people. They were not from his people, so he was not their brother by lineage. As for the first verse, he was their brother by lineage. Both views are correct.

What is your opinion on this method of tafsir: that we parse (*i'rab*) the verses, both the difficult and the non-difficult, as an exercise for the students? It reminds us of grammar. In reality we have not managed to allot time to studying grammar, whether in the Alfiyya or other works. I say: perhaps parsing will make up for it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 5, verse 106–108 (part 1 of 5):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O you who have believed, when death approaches one of you, let there be testimony between you at the making of a bequest: two just men from among you or two others from outside your own people﴾ to the end of the verse. This verse concerns an incident in which two disbelievers traveled with a Muslim man. Then death approached him, and there was no Muslim with them, so he called them both to witness his bequest. Is the testimony of these two men accepted or not? The ruling is known from this verse, and the matter is one of necessity, because there is no Muslim present. When no Muslim is found, we are compelled to accept the testimony of a disbeliever. The hadith has a stated occasion (sabab), so let us explain the verse and read the occasion, God willing.

﴿Testimony between you when death approaches one of you﴾ means: when you fall ill with the illness of death. The intended meaning is not the actual arrival of the appointed time, because if the appointed time has actually arrived, a person's statement may no longer be considered.

﴿When death approaches one of you at the making of a bequest, two﴾: the phrase ﴿at the making of a bequest﴾ is connected to ﴿testimony﴾, because (shahadah, testimony) is a verbal noun (masdar) that operates like a verb, so the adverbial phrase and the prepositional phrase may be connected to it. That is, your testimony at the time of the bequest, when death approaches one of you, is two.

﴿Two just men from among you﴾: i.e., two possessors of justice ﴿from among you﴾, O believers. So the address here, "from among you," is to the believers in general. Is there any difficulty in a person calling upon how many to witness his bequest?
* Students: Two.
* The Shaykh: That two just men should witness, there is no difficulty in it.

﴿Or two others from outside your own people﴾: Then Allah the Exalted mentioned the situation in which necessity calls for the testimony of one who is not a Muslim: ﴿or two others from outside your own people﴾. The phrase ﴿from outside your own people﴾ includes all religions of disbelief, and although the case was reported concerning two from the People of the Book, the consideration is the generality of the wording.

﴿From outside your own people﴾ means: whether they are from the People of the Book or from others.

﴿If you are travelling in the land﴾: i.e., you journey, ﴿and the calamity of death befalls you﴾. Yes, before we move on:
The question: the phrase ﴿or two others from outside your own people﴾, is it for choice (takhyir) or for classification (tanwi')?
Two from the People of the Book, but the consideration is the generality of the wording; ﴿from outside your own people﴾ [al-Ma'idah 106] means whether they are from the People of the Book or from others.
The question: the phrase ﴿or two others from outside your own people﴾, is it for choice or for classification?
The second; it is for classification. That is: or two others from outside your people, if no just man from among you is found.

﴿If you are travelling in the land﴾: i.e., you journey.
﴿And the calamity of death befalls you﴾: it is like His saying ﴿when death approaches one of you﴾ [al-Ma'idah 106]; i.e., you become certain that you are about to die, because the illness is one that is feared and whose recovery is not hoped for.

﴿You detain them both﴾: this is like an elaboration of His saying ﴿or two others from outside your own people﴾; i.e., at the performance of the testimony you detain them both, meaning the two others from outside us, and detention means stopping them; you hold them back.

﴿After the prayer﴾: i.e., after the afternoon prayer (salat al-'asr), because the afternoon prayer is the best of the prayers and it is the middle prayer (al-salat al-wusta), and the end of the day is closer to the answering of supplication than the beginning of the day, especially if that is on Friday.

﴿You detain them both after the prayer﴾: i.e., the afternoon prayer. If someone says: Why have you made the definite article (al) refer to a known (dhihni) reference, and not made it generic, so that you would say: ﴿after the prayer﴾ meaning: any prayer?
We say: "Because the Prophet (ﷺ) detained the two witnesses after the afternoon prayer" [[Narrated by al-Tabari in his Tafsir (9/89) from 'Ikrimah.]], so the Sunnah is what specified this prayer.

﴿Then they both swear by Allah﴾: i.e., they both take an oath by Him.
﴿If you doubt﴾: i.e., you have doubts about their testimony.
﴿We will not sell it for any price﴾: i.e., we will not sell this oath for any price, even if the one in whose favor the testimony is given ﴿were a near relative﴾: i.e., a person of kinship.
The summary of this oath is that they swear: we are upon the truth, our testimony is true, and it is not possible that we would bear false witness for the sake of any worldly thing, ﴿even if he were a near relative﴾.

﴿Nor will we conceal the testimony of Allah﴾: this is conjoined to ﴿they both swear﴾; i.e., and we do not conceal the testimony of Allah, meaning the testimony with which Allah has charged us, by which the bequest was established.
﴿Indeed, then we would be among the sinners﴾: i.e., if we concealed the testimony of Allah, we would indeed be among the sinners. The sentence here is emphasized with two things: (inna, indeed) and the lam (la). The meaning of ﴿among the sinners﴾ is: among those who commit sin. They say this only as added emphasis that they testified to the truth.

﴿If it becomes known that they both deserved sin﴾ [al-Ma'idah 107]: ﴿if it becomes known﴾ means: it is made clear that they both deserved sin, and that is by false testimony; i.e., it is made clear that their testimony was falsehood and lying.

﴿Then two others will stand in their place from among those who have a claim upon them, the two nearest in kinship﴾: ﴿two others will stand in their place﴾ means in the testimony, to reject their testimony. From where are these two others? He says: ﴿from among those who have a claim upon them﴾, because testimony concerning the bequest requires that something be taken from the portion of the heirs for whom? For the one to whom the bequest was made. So what the first two testified to becomes a claim upon these heirs.
As for His saying ﴿the two nearest﴾: it means they are the nearest, i.e., the people most entitled to the inheritance of the one whose bequest was witnessed.

﴿They both swear by Allah﴾: who are they? The two witnesses who are from among the heirs of the testator.

﴿By Allah, our testimony is more deserving than their testimony﴾: the lam here in His saying ﴿our testimony﴾ falls in the answer to the oath. What is their testimony? Their testimony is the negation of this bequest, while the testimony of the first two is the affirmation of the bequest. ﴿By Allah, our testimony is more deserving than their testimony﴾. If the truth is that, it follows that the testimony of the first two witnesses must be voided, and they, as we established at the beginning, are not Muslims but are from among non-Muslims.

﴿And we have not transgressed﴾: i.e., we have not transgressed by objecting and voiding the testimony.
﴿Indeed, then we would be among the wrongdoers﴾: i.e., if we transgressed ﴿we would be among the wrongdoers﴾; because their testimony entails two things: the first thing is discrediting the testimony of the first two witnesses, and the second is wrongdoing. Whose wrongdoing? The wrongdoing against the beneficiary of the bequest. Therefore He said: ﴿Indeed, then we would be among the wrongdoers﴾.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿That is more suitable that they bring the testimony in its proper form﴾ [al-Ma'idah 108]: i.e., that which has been mentioned is closer to their bringing the testimony in its proper form; meaning in the correct manner.

﴿Or they fear that oaths will be returned after their oaths﴾: i.e., those who testified first, if they know that there will inevitably follow them some of the heirs who will challenge them, they will strive to the utmost to bring the testimony in its proper form. Or, if they do not bring the testimony in its proper form, they will fear that ﴿oaths will be returned after their oaths﴾. ﴿Oaths﴾: whose oaths? The heirs'. ﴿After their oaths﴾: i.e., the oaths of the witnesses.

﴿And fear Allah and listen﴾: Allah the Exalted commanded us to fear Him by adhering to His rulings, and He confirmed this with His saying ﴿and listen﴾; i.e., listen to what I say to you and what I command you, which is the fear of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿And Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people﴾: He does not guide the defiantly disobedient people who go outside His obedience. This will come, God willing, in the lessons (fawa'id), that it is a severe warning that the sinner is liable not to be guided by Allah, Mighty and Majestic. This is the meaning of the noble verse.

It is good that we read the story so that it becomes clearer. Whoever has the tafsir of Ibn Kathir...

* Student: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and may Allah send blessings and peace upon our Prophet Muhammad and upon his family and companions all. Ibn Kathir said: (This noble verse contains a rare ruling. It was said: it is abrogated (mansukh), narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas. Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman said from Ibrahim: it is abrogated. And others said...).
* The Shaykh: Do you know what it is? That is, the testimony of a disbeliever. We will mention this, God willing, in the lessons: some scholars said it is abrogated. But this is not correct; they say: there is nothing abrogated in (al-Ma'idah), because it is among the last of what was revealed.
* The Student: (And others said -and they are the majority according to what Ibn Jarir said-: rather, it is muhkam (established, not abrogated), and whoever claims abrogation must provide proof. So His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, when death approaches one of you, let there be testimony between you at the making of a bequest: two...﴾ is the predicate of His saying ﴿testimony between you﴾. It was said: its estimated form is: the testimony of two; the genitive was removed and the genitive-complement was put in its place. And it was said: the speech indicates the estimate: that two should testify.
And His saying ﴿just men﴾ describes the two as being just.
And His saying ﴿from among you﴾ means: from among the Muslims, said by the majority. 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿just men from among you﴾: he said: from among the Muslims. Narrated by Ibn Abi Hatim [[Tafsir Ibn Abi Hatim (4/1229) (6933).]]. Then he said: it was narrated from 'Ubaydah, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Yahya ibn Ya'mar, al-Suddi, Qatadah, Muqatil ibn Hayyan, and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam something similar. And Ibn Jarir said...).
