* The Shaykh: Let us read.
* The Student: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and may Allah send blessings and peace upon our Prophet Muhammad and upon his family and companions all.
* The Shaykh: Listen to the hadith, for it helps in understanding the verse.
* The Student: Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, said: (This noble verse contains a rare ruling; it was said: it is abrogated. Narrated by al-'Awfi..).
* The Shaykh: ("Rare," meaning: of few kinds.)
* The Student: (Narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas. Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman said from Ibrahim: it is abrogated. And others, and they are the majority according to what Ibn Jarir said [[Tafsir al-Tabari (3/385).]], said: rather, it is muhkam, and whoever claims abrogation must provide proof).
* The Shaykh: Rather, the verse is muhkam, and this is the correct view. We have already told you that there is no abrogation in Surah al-Ma'idah; all of it is muhkam. Moreover, whoever claims that any text of the Qur'an or the Sunnah is abrogated must provide the evidence.
* The Student: (So His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, when death approaches one of you, let there be testimony between you at the making of a bequest: two...﴾ is the predicate of His saying ﴿testimony between you﴾. It was said: its estimated form is: the testimony of two; the genitive was removed and the genitive-complement put in its place. And it was said: the speech indicates the estimate: that two should testify.
And His saying ﴿just men﴾ describes the two as being just).
* The Shaykh: It means that those who said "there must be an estimate" argued that a body cannot be the predicate for a meaning, since "testimony" is a meaning and "two" are persons. So they said it is by an omitted genitive: the testimony of two, or: that two should testify. The correct view is that there is no need for this, and that once the meaning is understood, that is what is intended. For this reason they say: "Tonight is the crescent," where they predicate a time adverb of a substance, because the meaning is understood, and there is no need to estimate: "Tonight is the appearance of the crescent." So the correct view is that there is no estimate in the verse, and the meaning of the verse is clear.
* The Student: (And His saying ﴿from among you﴾: i.e., from among the Muslims, said by the majority. 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿just men from among you﴾: he said: from among the Muslims. Narrated by Ibn Abi Hatim [[Tafsir Ibn Abi Hatim (4/1229) (6934).]]. Then he said: it was narrated from 'Ubaydah, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Yahya ibn Ya'mar, al-Suddi, Qatadah, Muqatil ibn Hayyan, and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam something similar.
And Ibn Jarir said: others said: ﴿just men from among you﴾ means: from the tribe of the testator, and this is a view narrated from 'Ikrimah, 'Ubaydah and others.
And His saying ﴿or two others from outside your own people﴾..).
* The Shaykh: There is no doubt that the first view is the established one, because He addresses the believers: ﴿O you who have believed, when death approaches one of you, let there be testimony between you at the making of a bequest: two just men from among you﴾. Who is addressed? The believers, not the tribe in which the case occurred.
* The Student: (And His saying ﴿or two others from outside your own people﴾: Ibn Abi Hatim said: my father narrated to us, he said: Sa'id ibn 'Awn narrated to us, he said: 'Abd al-Wahid ibn Ziyad narrated to us, he said: Habib ibn Abi 'Amrah narrated to us, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: Ibn 'Abbas said concerning His saying ﴿or two others from outside your own people﴾: he said: from outside the Muslims, i.e., the People of the Book.
Then he said: it was narrated from 'Ubaydah, Shurayh..).
* The Shaykh: His saying "i.e., the People of the Book" is open to question. The correct view is that it includes the People of the Book and others, because everyone who is not a Muslim is from outside us.
* The Student: (Then he said: it was narrated from 'Ubaydah, Shurayh, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Muhammad ibn Sirin, Yahya ibn Ya'mar, 'Ikrimah, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Sha'bi, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, Qatadah, Abu Mijlaz, al-Suddi, Muqatil ibn Hayyan, and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, something similar.
According to what Ibn Jarir reported from 'Ikrimah and 'Ubaydah concerning His saying ﴿from among you﴾, that is, the meaning is the tribe of the testator, then the meaning here of ﴿or two others from outside your own people﴾ is: from outside the tribe of the testator. Something similar has been narrated by Ibn Abi Hatim from al-Hasan al-Basri and al-Zuhri, may Allah have mercy on them.
And His saying ﴿If you are travelling in the land﴾: i.e., you journey, ﴿and the calamity of death befalls you﴾. These are two conditions for the permissibility of the testimony of dhimmis when believers are absent: that it be during a journey, and that it be concerning a bequest; as Shurayh the judge explicitly stated.
Ibn Jarir said [[Tafsir Ibn Jarir (9/64).]]: Amr ibn 'Ali narrated to us, he said: Abu Mu'awiyah and Waki' narrated to us, both saying: al-A'mash narrated to us, from Ibrahim, from Shurayh, who said: The testimony of a Jew or a Christian is not permissible except on a journey, and it is not permissible on a journey except for a bequest.
Then he narrated it from Abu Kurayb, from Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash, from Abu Ishaq al-Sabi'i, who said: Shurayh said, and he mentioned something similar.
Something similar has been narrated from Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him, and this question is among those in which he stood alone. The three others disagreed with him and said: the testimony of dhimmis is not permissible against Muslims. Abu Hanifah permitted it among themselves, one against another.
Ibn Jarir said [[Tafsir Ibn Jarir (9/68).]]: Amr ibn 'Ali narrated to us, he said: Abu Dawud narrated to us..).
* The Shaykh: It does no harm for Imam Ahmad to stand alone in a ruling when he has the evidence, because whoever has the evidence is a community even if he is one person. Most of what Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, stood alone in after investigation is the correct view. This is after investigation; not everything he stood alone in, but most of what he stood alone in is correct.
* The Student: (And Ibn Jarir said [[Tafsir Ibn Jarir (9/68).]]: Amr ibn 'Ali narrated to us, he said: Abu Dawud narrated to us, he said: Salih ibn Abi al-Akhdar narrated to us, from al-Zuhri, who said: The Sunnah has passed that the testimony of a disbeliever is not permissible, either in residence or on a journey; it is only among Muslims.
Qatadah said: This verse was revealed concerning a man who died with no Muslim present, and that was at the beginning of Islam, when the land was at war and the people were disbelievers, and people inherited by bequest. Then the bequest was abrogated, the fixed shares were prescribed, and people acted accordingly. Narrated by Ibn Jarir. In this there is room for consideration, and Allah knows best.
And Ibn Jarir said: There has been disagreement concerning His saying ﴿testimony between you when death approaches one of you at the making of a bequest: two just men from among you or two others from outside your own people﴾: is the intent that he makes them his executors, or that he calls them as witnesses? Two views.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 5, verses 106–108 (part 2 of 5):**

The first view: that the two are appointed as executors (wasiyy, "guardian of the bequest") to him. As Muhammad ibn Ishaq related from Yazid ibn Abd Allah ibn Qusayt, who said: Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) was asked about this verse, and he said: "This is a man who travelled and had wealth with him, and his decree (qadar, death) overtook him. If he finds two men from among the Muslims, he hands over his estate to them and calls two just Muslims as witnesses over them." Narrated by Ibn Abi Hatim, but there is a break in its chain (inqita').

The second view: that the two are witnesses. This is the apparent meaning of the context of the noble verse. If there is no third executor with them, both qualities, executorship and testimony, are combined in them, as in the story of Tamim al-Dari and Adi ibn Badda', which will be mentioned shortly, if Allah wills. And success is from Allah.

Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) raised an objection to their being witnesses. He said: "For we do not know of any ruling in which a witness takes an oath." But this does not preclude the ruling contained in this noble verse, which is a ruling standing on its own. It is not necessary that it follow the analogy of all rulings. Moreover, this is a ruling specific to a particular testimony in a particular place, and in it there is leniency that is not granted in other cases. So if signs of suspicion arise, this witness takes an oath in accordance with what this noble verse indicates.

As for His saying ﴿you shall detain them both after the prayer﴾: al-'Awfi related from Ibn Abbas that it means the Asr prayer. Likewise said Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, Qatadah, Ikrimah and Muhammad ibn Sirin. Al-Zuhri said it means the prayer of the Muslims. Al-Suddi related from Ibn Abbas that it means the prayer of the people of their religion. The intended meaning is that these two witnesses are made to stand after a prayer at which people have gathered in their presence.

﴿then they both swear by Allah﴾, i.e., they swear by Allah ﴿if you doubt﴾, i.e., if suspicion appears to you regarding them that they have betrayed or embezzled. Then they swear by Allah ﴿we will not sell it﴾, i.e., by our oaths, as Muqatil ibn Hayyan said, ﴿for any price﴾, i.e., we will not exchange it for any small consideration of the perishable worldly life.

*The Shaykh:* His commentary "(by our oaths)" is open to question, because He said ﴿we will not sell it﴾, which is singular. How can it be explained by a plural? But if we take the pronoun as referring to the oath, the meaning is ﴿we will not sell it﴾, i.e., by the oath that we swear, so it refers back to the oath.

*The student:* (﴿for any price﴾, i.e., we will not exchange it for any small consideration of the perishable, transient worldly life.

﴿even if he were a relative﴾, i.e., even if the one against whom testimony is given were close to us, we will not show him favouritism.

﴿and we will not conceal the testimony of Allah﴾. He attributed it to Allah to honour it and to magnify its matter. Some of them recited: (﴿and we will not conceal the testimony of ālláhi﴾) in the genitive, as an oath, related by Ibn Jarir from Amir al-Sha'bi. It is also reported from some that he recited: (﴿and we will not conceal the testimony of Allah﴾ in the accusative). The first recitation is the well-known one.

﴿Indeed, we would then be among the sinners﴾, i.e., if we did any of that, whether by distorting the testimony, substituting it, altering it, or concealing it entirely.

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿And if it is discovered that the two had deserved sin﴾, i.e., if it becomes known, manifest and established against the two executor-witnesses that they betrayed or embezzled some of the property entrusted to them and it became evident against them, ﴿then two others shall take their place from among those who have a claim against them, the two nearest﴾. This is the recitation of the majority: ﴿ist̲uḥiqqa ʿalayhimu al-awwalān﴾ (the verb in the passive). It is reported from Ali, Ubayy and al-Hasan al-Basri that they recited it: ﴿istaḥaqqa ʿalayhimu al-awwalān﴾ (in the active). Al-Hakim related...

*The Shaykh:* ﴿min alladhīna istaḥaqqa ʿalayhim﴾ — this is the well-known recitation.

*The student:* The majority read ﴿ist̲uḥiqqa﴾.

*The Shaykh:* ﴿istaḥaqqa﴾. You have it with a damma?

*The student:* With a damma.

*The Shaykh:* It is a recitation, but I do not know whether it is a recitation other than that of the majority or not...
He mentions a recitation: ﴿ist̲uḥiqqa﴾, and in another recitation: ﴿ist̲uḥiqqa ʿalayhimu al-awwalīn﴾.

*The student:* He made the first the recitation of the majority.

*The Shaykh:* Yes, by Allah, it is strange.

*The student:* (Al-Hakim related in al-Mustadrak (2/259) through Ishaq ibn Muhammad al-Farwi, from Sulayman ibn Bilal, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Ubayd Allah ibn Abi Rafi', from Ali ibn Abi Talib that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited: ﴿min alladhīna istaḥaqqa ʿalayhimu al-awwalān﴾. Then he said: "Authentic according to the condition of Muslim, though they did not record it."

Some of them, including Ibn Abbas, recited: ﴿min alladhīna ist̲uḥiqqa ʿalayhimu al-awwalīn﴾. Al-Hasan recited: (﴿min alladhīna istaḥaqqa ʿalayhimu al-awwalān﴾), related by Ibn Jarir. So according to the recitation of the majority, the meaning is: when that is established by a sound report of their betrayal, then two of the heirs who are entitled to the estate shall stand, and they shall be the closest of those who inherit that property. ﴿and they shall swear by Allah: "Our testimony is more worthy than their testimony"﴾, i.e., our statement that they betrayed is more worthy, more correct and more firmly established than their earlier testimony. ﴿And we have not transgressed﴾, i.e., in what we have said of betrayal. ﴿Indeed, we would then be among the wrongdoers﴾, i.e., if we had lied about them.

This administering of the oath to the heirs, and the reliance on their statement in such a situation, is like the oath of the victim's guardians when a lawth (circumstantial evidence) appears against the killer. The entitled ones swear against the killer, and he is handed over to them in its entirety, as is established in the chapter on the qasama (oath procedure in homicide) in the rulings.

The Sunnah has come with the same as what this noble verse indicates. Ibn Abi Hatim said: Ibn Abi Hatim said: My father related to us, he said: al-Husayn ibn Ziyad related to us, he said: Muhammad ibn Salamah related to us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Abu al-Nadr, from Badhan (i.e., Abu Salih, mawla of Umm Hani bint Abi Talib), from Ibn Abbas, from Tamim al-Dari concerning this verse: ﴿O you who have believed, the testimony among you when death approaches one of you﴾. He said: "The people disowned it except me and Adi ibn Badda'. The two were Christians who used to travel to Syria before Islam. They came to Syria with their trade, and there came to them a mawla of Banu Sahm called Budayl ibn Abi Maryam, with merchandise and with a cup (jam) of silver which he intended for the king, and it was the greatest of his merchandise (ʿuẓm tijāratih). He fell ill, so he made them his executors and ordered them to deliver what he had left to his family."

*The Shaykh:* What is that?

*The student:* (ʿuẓm tijāratih).

*The Shaykh:* ʿUẓm means that it is the greatest of the merchandise he had with him. The jam is the vessel.

*The student:* (He fell ill, so he made them his executors and ordered them to deliver what he had left to his family. Tamim said: When he died, we took that cup and sold it for a thousand dirhams, then Adi ibn Badda' and I divided it between us. When we came to his family, we handed over to them what we had with us, and they missed the cup. They asked us about it, and we said: "He left nothing but this, and he gave us nothing else." Tamim said: When I became Muslim after the Prophet (ﷺ) came to Madinah, I felt sinful about that. So I went to his family, informed them of the matter, and handed them five hundred dirhams, and told them that my companion has a similar amount. They rushed to him to make him swear by what is greatest among the people of his religion. He swore, so Allah revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, the testimony among you﴾, to His saying: ﴿then they both swear by Allah: "Our testimony is more worthy than their testimony"﴾. Then Amr ibn al-As and another man from among them stood and swore, and the five hundred were taken from Adi ibn Badda'.

This was also related by Abu Isa al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Jarir, both from al-Hasan ibn Ahmad ibn Abi Shu'ayb al-Harrani, from Muhammad ibn Salamah, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, with the same chain and text, and in it: "They brought him to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he asked them for evidence, but they did not find any. So he ordered them to make him swear by what is greatest among the people of his religion. He swore, so Allah revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, the testimony among you when death approaches one of you﴾, to His saying: ﴿or they fear that oaths will be returned after their oaths﴾. Then Amr ibn al-As and another man stood and swore, and the five hundred were taken from Adi ibn Badda'."

Then he said: "This is a strange report, and its chain is not sound. And Abu al-Nadr, from whom Muhammad ibn Ishaq related this report, is in my view Muhammad ibn al-Sa'ib al-Kalbi, who is kunyah'd Abu al-Nadr, and the people of hadith have abandoned him, and he is the author of the tafsir. I heard Muhammad ibn Isma'il say: 'Muhammad ibn al-Sa'ib al-Kalbi is kunyah'd Abu al-Nadr.'"

Then he said: "We do not know of a narration by Salim, Abu al-Nadr, from Abu Salih, mawla of Umm Hani. Something of this has been related from Ibn Abbas in summary form, by another route:

Sufyan ibn Wakee' related to us, he said: Yahya ibn Adam related to us, from Ibn Abi Za'idah, from Muhammad ibn Abi al-Qasim, from Abd al-Malik ibn Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, who said: A man from Banu Sahm went out with Tamim al-Dari and Adi ibn Badda'. The Sahmi died in a land where there was no Muslim. When they came with his estate, they missed a silver cup decorated with gold. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made the two swear, and they found the cup in Makkah. It was said: 'We bought it from Tamim and Adi.' Then two men from the Sahmi's guardians stood and swore by Allah: 'Our testimony is more worthy than their testimony, and the cup belongs to our companion.' And concerning them was revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, the testimony among you﴾."

*The Shaykh:* (decorated with gold, makhawwaṣan bil-dhahab) means: inlaid upon it with something like the palm-fronds of gold, i.e., embroidered; and it is of silver.

*The student:* (The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made the two swear, and they found the cup in Makkah. It was said: "We bought it from Tamim and Adi." Then two men from the Sahmi's guardians stood and swore by Allah: "Our testimony is more worthy than their testimony, and the cup belongs to our companion." And concerning them was revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, the testimony among you﴾. Likewise Abu Dawud related it from al-Hasan ibn Ali, from Yahya ibn Adam, with the same.)

Then al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a good, strange hadith, and it is the hadith of Ibn Abi Za'idah."

Muhammad ibn Abi al-Qasim is Kufan; it was said that he is acceptable in hadith. Many of the Successors (tabi'un) related this story without a companion in its chain, among them Ikrimah, Muhammad ibn Sirin and Qatadah, and they mentioned that the swearing was after the Asr prayer; related by Ibn Jarir. Likewise Mujahid, al-Hasan and al-Dahhak also related it without a companion in its chain. This indicates that it was well known among the early generations and that it is sound.

Among the supporting evidence for the soundness of this story is also what Abu Ja'far ibn Jarir related, saying: Ya'qub related to me, he said: Hushaym related to us, he said: Zakariyya informed us, from al-Sha'bi, that a man from the Muslims was overtaken by death at Daquqa'. He said: Death overtook him, and he did not find any Muslim to call as a witness to his bequest, so he called two men from the People of the Book as witnesses. He said: They came to Kufa and went to al-Ash'ari (i.e., Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, may Allah be pleased with him) and informed him. They brought his estate and his bequest. Al-Ash'ari said: "This is a matter that did not occur after what happened in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ)." He said: He made the two swear after the Asr prayer, by Allah: "They did not betray, nor lie, nor alter, nor conceal, nor change, and this is the bequest of the man and his estate." He said: So he upheld their testimony.

Then he related it from Amr ibn Ali al-Fallas, from Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi, from Shu'bah, from Mughirah al-Azraq, from al-Sha'bi, that Abu Musa judged at Daquqa'.

These are two sound chains to al-Sha'bi from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari.

As for his saying: "This is a matter that did not occur after what happened in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)," the apparent meaning, and Allah knows best, is that he meant by it the story of Tamim and Adi ibn Badda'. It has been mentioned that the conversion of Tamim ibn Aws al-Dari (may Allah be pleased with him) was in the ninth year after the Hijrah. On this basis, this ruling is later, and whoever claims its abrogation (naskh, the cancellation of a ruling by a later one) needs a decisive proof in this matter, and Allah knows best.

Asbat related from al-Suddi: ﴿O you who have believed, the testimony among you when death approaches one of you, at the time of bequest, two just men from among you﴾. He said: "This is about the bequest at death: he makes a bequest and calls two men from the Muslims as witnesses over what he owns and what is owed to him. He said: This is in the case of residence (al-hadar), ﴿or two others from other than you﴾ in the case of travel, ﴿if you are travelling in the land and the calamity of death strikes you﴾. This man is overtaken by death while travelling, and there is no Muslim present with him, so he calls two men from the Jews, Christians and Magians, and makes them his executors and hands over his inheritance to them. They accept it. If the family of the deceased accept the bequest and know the property of their companion, they leave the two men alone. If they doubt, they bring the two before the authority. This is His, exalted, saying: ﴿you shall detain them both after the prayer, and they both swear by Allah if you doubt﴾."

Abd Allah ibn Abbas said: "It is as if I am looking at the two non-Arab men (ʿilj) when they were brought to Abu Musa al-Ash'ari in his house. He opened the document, and the family of the deceased denied it and accused them of betrayal. Abu Musa wanted to make them swear after the Asr prayer. I said to him: 'They do not care about the Asr prayer, but make them swear after their prayer in their religion.' So the two are held after their prayer in their religion, and they swear by Allah: 'We will not sell it for any price, even if he were a relative, and we will not conceal the testimony of Allah; indeed, we would then be among the sinners. Indeed our companion made this bequest, and this is his estate.' The judge says to them before they swear: 'If you conceal or betray, I will expose you among your people, your testimony will not be accepted, and I will punish you.' When he says that to them, that is closer to their bringing the testimony in its proper form." Related by Ibn Jarir.

Ibn Jarir said: Al-Husayn related to us, he said: Hushaym related to us, he said: Mughirah informed us, from Ibrahim and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that both said concerning this verse: ﴿O you who have believed, the testimony among you﴾, the verse. They said: "If death overtakes a man while travelling, let him call two men from the Muslims. If he does not find two men from the Muslims, then two men from the People of the Book. When they come with his estate, if the heirs confirm them, their word is accepted. If they accuse them, the two are made to swear after the Asr prayer, by Allah: 'We did not conceal, nor lie, nor betray, nor change.'"

Ali ibn Abi Talhah related from Ibn Abbas concerning the interpretation of this verse: "If doubt arises about their testimony, they are made to swear after the prayer by Allah: 'We did not buy with our testimony any small price.' If the guardians become aware that the two unbelievers lied in their testimony, two of the guardians stand and swear by Allah: 'The testimony of the two unbelievers is void, and we did not transgress.' That is His saying: ﴿then if it is discovered that the two had deserved sin﴾, meaning: if it is discovered that the two unbelievers lied, ﴿then two others shall take their place﴾, meaning: from the guardians, and they swear by Allah: 'The testimony of the two unbelievers is void, and we did not transgress.' So the testimony of the two unbelievers is rejected, and the testimony of the guardians is accepted."

Al-'Awfi related this likewise from Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Jarir related both.

In this way, this ruling in accordance with the requirement of this verse was established by more than one of the leading Successors and the early generations (may Allah be pleased with them), and it is the position of Imam Ahmad (may Allah have mercy on him).

As for His saying: ﴿that is more suitable that they bring the testimony in its proper form﴾, i.e., the legislating of this ruling in this acceptable manner, by making the two dhimmi witnesses swear when suspicion has arisen about them, is closer to their establishing the testimony in an acceptable form.

And His saying: ﴿or they fear that oaths will be returned after their oaths﴾, i.e., what drives them to bring the testimony in its proper form is the glorifying of the oath by Allah, observing its sanctity and reverence for it, and the fear of disgrace among people if the oath is returned to the heirs, so they swear and claim what they assert. For this reason He said: ﴿or they fear that oaths will be returned after their oaths﴾.

Ibn 'Uthaymin's commentary on Surah al-Ma'ida, verses 106–108 (part 3 of 5):

Then he said: ﴿And fear Allah﴾, meaning in all your affairs. ﴿And listen﴾, meaning obey. ﴿And Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people﴾, meaning those who depart from His obedience and from following His law.)

* The Shaykh: Well said. May Allah have mercy on him, he dwelt at length on this verse, because it contains difficulties. Yet he resolved all of these difficulties. There is a difficulty from the standpoint of i'rab (grammatical analysis) and a difficulty from the standpoint of the context. But Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, speaks as He wills and in the manner He wills, so that people may know that this noble Qur'an is suited to the circumstances. The matter is complex in its rulings, its i'rab and other respects. But, praise be to Allah, with an explanation like the one you have heard, the difficulty is removed.

Summary of the meaning: If a person travels and has no Muslim around him, only disbelievers, and he wishes to make a bequest, then he should call two witnesses to the bequest. When they reach Muslim lands, they testify, and the testimony is accepted without any further matter, unless doubt arises. If doubt arises, then at that point we require an oath. The two are detained after the prayer and made to swear by Allah that they are truthful and that they have not exchanged their testimony for any worldly gain. They are warned that oaths may be turned back after their oaths, because if the heirs of the slain swear, the testimony of the two witnesses is rejected. It is known that if a ruling is made to reject their testimony, this becomes a disgrace and humiliation for them. Perhaps, if they do not fear Allah, they will fear disgrace and humiliation. For this reason He said: ﴿That is more likely to make them give testimony in its proper form, or fear that oaths will be turned back after their oaths. And fear Allah and listen. And Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people.﴾ This is the general meaning of the noble verse.

However, it contains many benefits. We will mention some of them, asking Allah to make them easy for us and to guide us to what is correct.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the permissibility of a disbeliever's testimony in cases of necessity. But is the necessity restricted to this particular situation, or does it apply to every necessity?

First, regarding the basic question, the testimony of a disbeliever, scholars have two positions:

The first position: the testimony of a disbeliever is not accepted. This is based on the claim that this ruling is what? Abrogated (mansukh). Therefore it is not accepted. This view is rejected, because abrogation requires evidence. Moreover, many scholars have said that Surah al-Ma'ida contains no abrogation, since it is among the last parts of the Qur'an to be revealed. So this view should be set aside.

What is strange is that the one who holds this view is the majority of scholars. The view that a disbeliever's testimony is accepted is the view of Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him. How often he stands alone in a matter, and yet his view is the correct one. For example, his view on the disbelief of one who abandons the prayer: he stood alone in this view, but in reality he did not stand alone, because he has the Book, the Sunnah and the Companions with him.

On the view that a disbeliever's testimony is accepted, does this apply only to this particular case? That is, is it a condition that the two witnesses be People of the Book, since the two witnesses in this story were Christians? Is it required that they be People of the Book or not?

The well-known position in the school is that they must be People of the Book. But it will come that the apparent meaning of the verse contradicts this, and that the verse is general, covering every disbeliever.

Does this apply only to bequests, or to everything? This too is a matter of disagreement. The reason for restricting it to bequests is that this case is an exception to the rules of testimony, and the rule for exceptions is that they are limited to what? To what was reported only. That is, to what is established by the text alone. It will come, God willing, that the preferred view is that the testimony of non-People of the Book is permissible, and that testimony is permissible in bequests and in other matters, during travel and otherwise. This may occur at times. Nowadays, many hospitals are staffed by Christians. If one of these patients is at the point of death and calls upon the doctors who are with him to witness, then his case is the same.

* * *

* Student: ﴿O you who believe, when death approaches one of you, let the testimony be between you two, when a bequest is made: two just men from among you, or two others from outside your own people, if you are travelling through the land and the calamity of death befalls you. You shall detain them after the prayer, and they shall swear by Allah, if you doubt them: "We will not sell our testimony for any price, even if it concerns a relative, and we will not conceal the testimony of Allah; indeed, then we would be among the sinners."﴾ (106) ﴿But if it is discovered that they have deserved sin, then two others from among those against whom the claim was made, who are nearest to them, shall stand in their place and swear by Allah: "Our testimony is more worthy than their testimony, and we have not transgressed; otherwise, we would be among the wrongdoers."﴾ (107) ﴿That is more likely to make them give testimony in its proper form, or fear that oaths will be turned back after their oaths. And fear Allah and listen. And Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people.﴾ [al-Ma'ida 106–108].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. We have already recited and explained this verse and the one after it. What remains is the benefits.

* Among the benefits of this verse: it is recommended to call witnesses for a bequest. This is shown by His saying: ﴿The testimony between you, when death approaches one of you at the time of bequest, let there be two.﴾ The apparent meaning of the noble verse is that two men are necessary, because of His saying ﴿two﴾, and "two" is the number for the masculine. Is this verse to be taken at its apparent meaning?

The answer is that this verse is qualified by the verse of al-Baqara, which is His saying: ﴿And call upon two witnesses from among your men. And if there are not two men, then a man and two women, from among those whom you accept as witnesses﴾ [al-Baqara 282]. This is because for property, and what is aimed at for property, if the defendant does not admit the claim, proof is established by one of three things: the testimony of two men, the testimony of a man and two women, or the testimony of a man plus the oath of the claimant. These are the evidences for property and what is connected to property. On this basis, His saying ﴿two﴾ is to be understood as referring to the most complete form. That is, the most complete way of calling witnesses for a bequest is for the two witnesses to be men.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the permissibility of making a bequest when death approaches, because of His saying: ﴿when death approaches one of you﴾. This is restricted to the case where the testator's discernment has not changed. If the testator's discernment has changed, then his words carry no weight. That is, if at the time of his death he became confused and his speech became disordered, then this speech has no weight. This is well known from the principles of the Shari'a.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: it is a condition for calling witnesses that the two witnesses be people of justice, because of His saying: ﴿two just men﴾. We have already defined justice. But if no just person is found, and an untrustworthy but reliable person is found, can he take the place of a just person?

Some scholars have chosen that this does take the place of justice, and that the condition of justice applies only at the time of bearing witness. That is, when you want to call witnesses, you call only two just persons. But at the time of giving testimony, necessities have their own rulings. If we find no one to testify except these two who are unjust, but who are trustworthy in honesty, then we accept their testimony. This last view is the correct one: justice is a condition where it is possible. If it is not possible, then the testimony of an unjust person is accepted, on condition of what? That he is trustworthy. How many people are unjust in their worship but honest in their testimony? We know that if we followed the condition of justice in giving testimony, taking into account the conditions the jurists mentioned for justice, many rights would be lost, because many people are not upright in the way the jurists described, may Allah have mercy on them.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the permissibility of a disbeliever's testimony when a Muslim cannot be found, because of His saying: ﴿or two others from outside your own people﴾.

Does this apply only to People of the Book, or to every disbeliever?

The apparent meaning is every disbeliever, because of His saying ﴿or two others from outside your own people﴾, whether he is a Jew, a Christian, a Buddhist, or a communist, whoever he may be, because of His saying ﴿from outside your own people﴾. Scholars have differed on this matter in three positions.

The first position: the testimony of a disbeliever is not accepted at all. They answered this verse by saying it has been abrogated, because Allah stipulated justice in witnesses, and the disbeliever is not just.

The second position: the testimony of a disbeliever is permitted on two conditions: that he be a People of the Book, and that it be in cases of necessity. So they stipulated two conditions. The first: necessity, that no Muslim is available. The second: that the two witnesses be People of the Book. These scholars argued for the condition of necessity from His saying: ﴿if you are travelling through the land﴾ and so on. They restricted it to People of the Book, because the case in which the verse was revealed involved witnesses who were People of the Book. And in establishing their argument they said: the non-requirement of Islam in this case departs from the basic rule, and whatever departs from the basic rule must be restricted to what is specifically mentioned.

There is no doubt that the answer to these scholars is easy. We say: the noble verse is general, and what counts is the generality of the wording. For this reason, when Allah wishes to restrict a ruling to People of the Book, He qualifies it, as in His saying: ﴿and the chaste women from among those who were given the Book before you﴾, and He said: ﴿and the food of those who were given the Book is lawful for you﴾ [al-Ma'ida 5]. As for qualifying what Allah has left unqualified, this is not correct. This is a principle that the student of knowledge must follow: whatever Allah and His Messenger have stated in unrestricted form, in the Qur'an and the Sunnah, it is not permissible to add a qualifier to it, ever. Because if he does so, he narrows what Allah has made broad, and takes himself as a lawgiver and as one who corrects the legal ruling. This is dangerous. So the principle is that whatever Allah and His Messenger stated without restriction must be left unrestricted, and it is not lawful to add a qualification unless there is evidence which must be followed. In that case, we say: the correct view is that two persons may testify to a bequest in the absence of a Muslim, whether they are People of the Book or not.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the superiority of the Muslim over the disbeliever. This is not problematic. The reasoning: a disbeliever's testimony is not accepted except when no Muslim is found, and this shows that the Muslim is higher in rank and standing than the non-Muslim.

If someone says: we understand that a disbeliever's testimony in matters concerning Muslims is permitted only in cases of necessity. Do you accept the testimony of disbelievers against one another?

The answer: yes. Whether it is for necessity or not, the testimony of disbelievers against one another is accepted, but on condition that the witness is just according to his own religion, just as we stipulated for the testimony of a Muslim that he be just.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: travel is called ḍarb fi al-arḍ (striking through the land). The noble Qur'an sometimes mentions travel by its name and sometimes mentions it as striking through the land. His saying ﴿and if you are sick or on a journey﴾ [al-Ma'ida 6] mentions travel and does not say "or you have struck through the land." And He said concerning fasting: ﴿So whoever among you is sick or on a journey﴾ [al-Baqara 184].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the term "striking through the land" is unrestricted, and He did not qualify it by a distance of shortening the prayer, or more, or less.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: if the two witnesses who are non-Muslims wish to give testimony, they are detained after the prayer, meaning they are made to stand after the prayer. This is because of the absence of suspicion, since the prayer is honoured, and a person fears to testify falsely after this prayer which Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, mentioned.

But is this conditional on doubt about their testimony, or do we say they are detained in every case, so that the difference between a Muslim's testimony and a non-Muslim's testimony becomes apparent?

The verse allows for two readings. His saying ﴿they shall swear by Allah if you doubt them﴾ may be read such that ﴿if you doubt them﴾ qualifies His saying ﴿you shall detain them after the prayer﴾ and His saying ﴿they shall swear by Allah﴾. It may also be read as qualifying only His saying ﴿they shall swear by Allah﴾, with ﴿if you doubt them﴾ attached to it. On the second reading, their detention is obligatory. On the first reading, their detention is not obligatory except if we have doubt about them.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: an oath may not be sworn by other than Allah, because of His saying ﴿they shall swear by Allah﴾. So if someone swears by other than Allah, even by one whom they revere, such as the Messiah for example, his oath is not accepted and is not counted, because of Allah's saying ﴿they shall swear by Allah﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: their oath is required only when there is doubt about their testimony, as is taken from His saying: ﴿if you doubt them﴾.

Does it follow from this that a judge may make the two witnesses swear when he has doubt about their testimony?

We say: yes, he may do so. No one may say that this applies only to our doubt about disbelievers. No. If someone says this applies only to our doubt about the testimony of disbelievers, the answer is: the ruling revolves around its cause. We only make them swear by Allah when there is doubt, not because they are disbelievers. So the judge may make the witnesses swear if he has doubt about their testimony.

May he also separate the witnesses when there is doubt, by meeting each of them alone and asking him detailed questions, so that if they disagree he knows their testimony is not valid?

The answer: yes, he may do so.

May he also use indirection, showing them the opposite of what he intends, in order to bring out the truth?

The answer: yes. The story of Solomon with the two women supports this. The two women set out on some business, and then a wolf ate the son of one of them. They brought their dispute before David, who ruled in favour of the older one. Then they brought it before Solomon, who asked for a knife. He said he wanted to split the child in two and give half to the older and half to the younger. The older agreed to this, why? Because she had no mercy for him, and her son had died; the wolf had eaten him, so let this be his fate too. The younger said: "O Prophet of Allah, he is hers, he is hers." She gave up her claim, why? Out of compassion and mercy. She gave it up. The meaning of her saying "he is hers" was not that he was her slave, no; it meant she had relinquished the claim. So Solomon, peace be upon him, ruled in favour of whom? The younger.[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3426) and Muslim (1720/20), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]

So if the judge doubts the testimony of the witnesses, there is no harm in his using indirection in the ruling, in order to bring out the truth.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the manner of the oath is as follows: ﴿We will not sell it for any price, even if it concerns a relative, and we will not conceal the testimony of Allah﴾ [al-Ma'ida 106]. Is it enough to convey the meaning, or must this exact wording be used?

The correct view is that the meaning suffices, because this wording is not a matter of worship that cannot be changed. Rather, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, expressed the meaning in this wording. So the reference, my brothers, is to what? The reference is to the meaning.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: an indication that kinship has an effect on inclination and emotion, because of their saying ﴿even if it concerns a relative﴾. This is a known natural matter. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, pointed to this in His saying: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they were kinsmen﴾ [al-Tawba 113], and He said: ﴿O you who believe, be upholders of justice, witnesses for Allah, even against yourselves or your parents and close relatives﴾ [al-Nisa' 135].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 5, verses 106–108 (part 4 of 5):

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: concealing testimony is a sin, as shown by His words: ﴿Then indeed we would be among the sinners﴾. Allah Almighty established this in His words: ﴿And do not conceal testimony; whoever conceals it, his heart is sinful﴾ [al-Baqarah 283]. There is no doubt that when a person conceals testimony, it entails hiding an obligatory right belonging to one person and attributing falsehood to another. For example, if someone asks you to testify that so-and-so owes him such-and-such, and you conceal it, what happens? The right is hidden, and falsehood is attributed to the one against whom testimony was not given.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the oath is returned to the claimant (al-mudda'i). This is shown by His words: ﴿If it is discovered that the two had become liable to sin, then two others shall take their place﴾, to the end of the verse. How is the oath returned to the claimant?
Zayd sued 'Amr for a hundred riyals. We asked Zayd for evidence, and he said: "I have no evidence, but I request the oath of the defendant (al-mudda'a 'alayh)." Do you understand? If the defendant swears, the dispute ends. Not that he is declared innocent; the dispute ends. This means that if the claimant later learns of evidence he did not know of before, he still holds his claim, but the dispute has ended.
If the claimant says, when the defendant refuses to swear: "Rule against him, because the dispute has ended and he cannot demand anything from me." Then if the judge decides to return the oath to the claimant, there is no harm in that. Why? Because the denier may be truthful, yet the claimant needs to establish something additional, so the judge returns the oath to him. This view is the correct one: it is permissible to return the oath to the claimant, as in this verse.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: it is permissible for the one who bears the right to investigate the case closely and scrutinize it until he discovers a right in it. This is shown by His words: ﴿If it is discovered that they...﴾, and discovery (al-'ithar) can only come after diligent inquiry (al-taharri).
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: if the two witnesses alter their testimony by adding, omitting, or substituting, then they are both sinful. This is shown by His words: ﴿If it is discovered that the two had become liable to sin﴾, and that occurs when the testimony is not valid, because this is a sin.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: when it is discovered that the two witnesses are lying, two men are brought forward from among those who have a claim against them. As you know, the case concerned a bequest (wasiyyah). So two men from among those who have a claim are brought forward, and the two must be the nearest, meaning the ones most entitled to the inheritance of the deceased. The discussion in the two verses concerns the bequest.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: an indication that inheritance goes to the nearest in kinship, in order of priority. This is taken from His words: ﴿the nearest﴾ (al-awliyan). The hadith also establishes this, the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Give the prescribed shares to their rightful owners; whatever remains belongs to the nearest male relative." [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (6732) and Muslim (1615/2) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.] Is that not so? Read the hadith.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, he said: the Prophet (ﷺ) said... Yes, it must be phrased like this.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse, as we mentioned at the beginning: the oath is returned to the claimant, as shown by His words: ﴿so they both swear by Allah﴾.
* And among its benefits, among the benefits of the noble verse: the defendant does not definitively declare void the testimony of a witness which has been shown to contain some defect. This is shown by His words: ﴿Our testimony is more worthy than their testimony﴾, using this wording and not saying "void". But His words ﴿more worthy than their testimony﴾ imply that their testimony is rejected and that the statement of the defendant is the accepted one.
* And among the benefits of this verse: if testimony or oath requires affirmation and negation, then both affirmation and negation must be mentioned. Their words, meaning the two nearest, ﴿Our testimony is more worthy than their testimony﴾: what is this? An affirmation. ﴿And we have not transgressed﴾: this is a negation. So when this is needed, both negation and affirmation must be mentioned, so that the testimony is pure.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the rejection by the two nearest of the testimony of the two witnesses is a greater transgression than the alteration of the testimony by the two witnesses. The reason is that when the witnesses alter their testimony, He said: ﴿then indeed we would be among the sinners﴾, but here He said: ﴿then indeed we would be among the wrongdoers﴾. The difference between them was explained earlier in the tafsir (interpretation).
* Among the benefits of the third verse: whenever a matter is closer to deducing what is correct and true through testimony, it is more fitting to follow it. This is shown by His words: ﴿That is more likely that they will give testimony in its proper form﴾. For when a person understands that people will stand behind him to reject his testimony and swear to its falsity, he must necessarily seek to be truthful in what he testifies.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation to fear Allah and to hear and obey Him. This is shown by His words: ﴿And fear Allah and listen﴾. The meaning of "listen" here is: respond, as was also explained earlier in the commentary.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: Allah, glorified is He, informed that He does not guide the defiant people, meaning those who depart from His obedience, and the report of Allah is true.
But this raises a difficulty: in reality, Allah does guide some defiant people and some disbelievers. How do we reconcile the reality with this true report?
The reconciliation is that we say: Allah does not guide the defiant people, meaning those for whom Allah has decreed defiance. As for one whom He has decreed to believe, he will believe without fail. The benefit of the unrestricted wording ﴿He does not guide the defiant people﴾ is an indication that Allah does not guide the defiant because they chose defiance, as He said: ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate, and Allah does not guide the defiant people﴾ [al-Saff 5]. We ask Allah to guide us and you, and to protect us from ourselves and from Satan.
* Student: May Allah reward you well. We said that the testimony of disbelievers may be accepted for one another, even without necessity. Is there no distinction between the People of the Book and others?
* Shaykh: Yes, there is no distinction. Yes indeed. But they must be upright (adl) in their own religion, just as a Muslim must be upright.
* Student: Shaykh, did we not mention that testimony after the 'Asr prayer applies to the People of the Book, who do not regard this prayer as sacred, as in the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas and as Abu Musa al-Ash'ari said?
* Shaykh: No. The correct view is that the intended prayer is the 'Asr prayer, even if they do not hold it in reverence, because it is great in the sight of Allah, and because punishment is swifter for one who gives false testimony or swears falsely after the 'Asr prayer.
* Student: And Ibn 'Abbas, Shaykh?
* Shaykh: Yes?
* Student: I mean, Ibn 'Abbas's ijtihad (independent reasoning) contradicts this.
* Shaykh: What did he say?
* Student: The hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, when we read it in the tafsir: when he said to him: "Make it after their prayer in their religion."
* Shaykh: Yes, that was his own choice.
* Student: Shaykh, may Allah bless you. If two men participate in a crime, and during the investigation many indications show that they are in fact the perpetrators, and then the investigators want to extract confessions from them, is it permissible for the investigator, for example, to meet one of them alone and say that his companion has confessed to this crime?
* Shaykh: And he had denied it before?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: No, it is not permissible. That is a lie.

And can a person have confidence that he has hit what Allah intended?
* Student: (...).

And does he return to the books of tafsir for transmitted reports (bi-l-athar) or for reasoned judgment (bi-l-nazar)?

For this, if he wants to interpret the Qur'an after reflecting on it himself, he must return to...?

If a verse can bear two meanings, do we apply it to both, or what?
* Student: (...) there is no contradiction between them (...).
* Shaykh: There is no contradiction between them. On equal footing, or? On equal footing: if it bears two meanings equally, and there is no contradiction between them, it must be applied to both meanings together, because if it bears them, then both meanings are among its meanings. Give an example?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Well, this is one opinion. The second opinion?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: One word would make it clearer than this.
* Student: (...).

Also there is: ﴿And by the night when it departs﴾ [al-Takwir 17]. Some interpreted it to mean: when it approaches; others: when it withdraws. But this example may be objected to; it has objections: interpreting it as "withdraws" is made unnecessary by His words: ﴿And by the dawn when it breathes﴾ [al-Takwir 18], because when the dawn breathes, the night withdraws. So the first interpretation is the stronger.
If a general verse and a specific verse occur, is there a contradiction between them, or must both be acted upon?
* Student: (...) the general is applied to the specific.
* Shaykh: That means both must be acted upon. For example?

* Shaykh: What is the other verse?

* Shaykh: No.
* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: We apply it by the condition that the slave be a believer, because this unrestricted wording is restricted by the word ﴿believing﴾ in this verse.
If someone said: the application is not valid, because this is the expiation (kaffarah) for zihar (a pre-Islamic form of repudiation), which has three types, and the expiation for killing has two types.
* Student: But the discussion is not about the number of expiations; the discussion is about the slave, and the slave is shared among the expiations in (...).
* Shaykh: This is supported by the hadith of Mu'awiyah ibn al-Hakam, that the Messenger (ﷺ) said: "Free her, for she is a believer." This supports it.
Is the words of Allah the Most High part of this: ﴿It is prescribed for you, when death approaches one of you, if he leaves wealth, that he make a bequest to parents and relatives in kindness, a duty upon the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqarah 180]?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Abrogated (mansukhah).
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Al-Ma'idah? Al-Nisa'.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes. Do you agree that the verse of al-Baqarah is abrogated by the verse of al-Nisa'?
* Students: (...).
* Shaykh: No. This hadith does not abrogate; the hadith clarifies the abrogating text. Allah abrogated it by the verse of inheritance. But is this abrogated by the verse of inheritance?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, explain.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: What is the reconciliation?
* Student: We say the bequest is for someone other than the nearest relatives and other than the heirs.
* Shaykh: Correct, this is the right view. The verse is not abrogated, because Allah said: ﴿to parents and relatives﴾. He excluded whoever is an heir, so what remains is whoever is not an heir, and it does not conflict with the verses of inheritance.
* Student: (...).

**Shaykh:** No. Sometimes the father is not an heir. For example, if the father is a slave, he does not inherit from his son. But there is nothing wrong with the son bequeathing to him, or being instructed to bequeath to him, especially if we say that a slave can own property by transfer (*tamlik*). The scholars differ on whether a slave can own by transfer, or whether, if something is transferred to him, the ownership goes to his master. Some distinguish: if the one who transfers is the master, the slave owns; if it is someone else, he does not.

The correct view is that the verse is not abrogated (*mansukha*). What is reported from the early scholars (*salaf*) that it is abrogated, they use the term *naskh* (abrogation) for *takhsis* (specification), because specification is in reality an abrogation of generality (*'umum*), so they call it *naskh*.

Recently, in Surat al-Ma'idah, we passed the story of calling a disbeliever to witness a bequest. That verse has a specific cause (*sabab*), but its wording is general. So do we say that this general ruling is specified by its cause, or not?

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** He says: the cause does not specify the generality. What matters is the generality of the wording, not the specific cause. What was the cause for which the verse was revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, when death approaches one of you, the testimony [shall be] between you: two just men from among you﴾, and so on to the end [al-Ma'idah 5:106]?

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** A man called two people of the People of the Book (*Ahl al-Kitab*) as witnesses to his bequest, so Allah revealed this verse. But suppose he did not find two men from the People of the Book or from the Muslims, and he called two communists as witnesses. Do we act on this, or do we say it applies only to the People of the Book?

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** How is that?

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** What?

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** (...). Now we want the general wording. The verse: ﴿two just men from among you, or two others from other than you﴾. So His words ﴿from other than you﴾ include both People of the Book and others.

Is this ruling about their testimony restricted to bequests, or even to something other than a bequest, if he testifies that the deceased acknowledged a debt owed to someone?

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** Is (...) a bequest? But in reality it is a bequest.

**Student:** We take the generality.

**Shaykh:** We take the generality. Where is the generality?

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** Where is the generality? Show us it.

**Student:** (...).

﴿from other than you﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:106] includes People of the Book and others. Is this ruling about their testimony restricted to bequests, or even to something other than a bequest, if he testifies that the deceased acknowledged a debt owed to someone?

**Student:** Even other than bequests.

**Shaykh:** Even other than bequests? But in reality it is a bequest?

**Student:** We take the generality.

**Shaykh:** We take the generality. Where is the generality? Show us it.

**Student:** Nothing has been excluded from it by a restriction, and the case of the bequest is the basis; meaning, non-bequests are included as well.

**Shaykh:** Yes, but your opponent will come and say: "We do not accept that. Give us a generality from the verse."

**Student:** Yes, indeed. He said: ﴿or two others from other than you, if you are travelling in the land and the calamity of death strikes you﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:106]. This does not limit it to bequests alone, although (...) calamity.

**Shaykh:** So His words ﴿and the calamity of death strikes you﴾ include the case of testifying to a bequest, or testifying to the deceased's acknowledgment of a debt, or other things. Do you agree with this?

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** How?

**Student:** The evidence is in His words ﴿the testimony between you﴾: "testimony" is an idafa construction (...).

**Shaykh:** But we restrict ﴿the testimony between you﴾ by ﴿two just men from among you, or two others from other than you, if you are travelling in the land﴾, and the generality is taken from His words ﴿and the calamity of death strikes you﴾, meaning: and you call them to witness this at the time of death.

Someone might ask: shall we extend every emergency to this situation?

**Student:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** Yes! Every emergency?!

**Student:** Every emergency.

**Shaykh:** For example, a person in a town whose death approaches, and who has only disbelievers with him. This may happen now with workers, since we have disbelieving workers.

**Student:** Yes, we say it, Shaykh.

**Shaykh:** We say it in an emergency?

**Student:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** How do we account for this, or how do we say this, when the verse says ﴿if you are travelling in the land﴾?

**Student:** Then it is not a restriction.

**Shaykh:** But (*in*) is a conditional particle.

**Student:** It is for explanation of this.

**Shaykh:** Explanation of what?

**Student:** Explanation of (...).

**Shaykh:** Meaning the verse was revealed to explain the actual incident, so every emergency is analogous to it in meaning. Do you agree with this?

**Students:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** Yes, and this is the correct view. You know that there are three opinions on this issue. Do you remember them?

The first opinion: this verse is abrogated, and the testimony of disbelievers is never accepted in matters concerning the rights of Muslims.

The second opinion: it is specific to bequests during travel when no Muslim is available. They gave a reason: accepting the testimony of a disbeliever is an exception to the principle. The principle is that a disbeliever's testimony is not accepted. So if something is an exception to the principle, it must be limited to what the text states in that particular case. These scholars restrict it by three specifications: travel, bequests, and People of the Book.

The third opinion: the testimony of a disbeliever is accepted in every emergency. This is closer to the principles of the Shari'ah. However, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, mentioned that in cases of doubt they should be detained after the prayer, as in the verse.

We have two verses in which there is partial generality and specificity (*'umum wa khusus min wajh*). Which one do we give priority to?

**Student:** The specific one... as for the two specific ones that conflict, either it returns to (...).

**Shaykh:** This presents no problem.

**Student:** And as for the specific (...), it is applied to both.

**Shaykh:** The conflict (*ta'arud*) arises when there is partial generality and specificity.

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** Meaning a preponderant factor (*murajjih*) must be sought. If none is found, then what? Give an example.

**Student:** No example is needed.

**Shaykh:** Give an example of a case where there is a preponderance.

**Student:** For instance, His words in Surat an-Nisa': ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that﴾ [an-Nisa' 4:24], which conflicts with His words...

**Another student:** His words, blessed and exalted: ﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind, they shall wait by themselves for four months and ten [days]﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:234]. And His words, blessed and exalted: ﴿And for pregnant women, their term is until they deliver their burden﴾ [at-Talaq 65:4]. These two verses have partial generality and specificity.

**Shaykh:** Explain, clarify this.

**Student:** The woman observes the longer of the two terms.

**Shaykh:** How?! I do not want the ruling now, but how is the conflict?

**Student:** In the first verse, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, states that she observes four months and ten days.

**Shaykh:** Whether she is pregnant or not.

**Student:** Or not pregnant.

**Shaykh:** Good.

**Student:** And in the second verse, when she is pregnant, she observes by delivering the child.

**Shaykh:** Whether her husband died or not. How do we combine them? If we find a pregnant woman whose husband died, what must she observe?

**Student:** The longer of the two terms.

**Shaykh:** The longer of the two terms, yes.

**Another student:** The pregnant woman observes by the hadith...

**Shaykh:** By delivery of the child. Based on the principle now, does she observe the longer of the two terms?

Yes, based on the principle, she observes the longer of the two terms. For example, if she delivers after two months, we say: complete four months and ten days. If she delivers after six months, we say: wait until you deliver.

By this we act on both verses. But the Sunnah shows that the pregnant woman's term is delivery of the child, even if it is less than four months and ten days. What is the Sunnah reported on this?

**Student:** The hadith about Subay'a al-Aslamiyya, that (...) entered upon her.

**Shaykh:** Abu as-Sanabil.

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** He said to her: "You are not to marry until..."

**Student:** "Until four months and ten days have passed for you." She said: "When he said that to me, I gathered my clothes around me and went to the Prophet (ﷺ) and asked him."

**Shaykh:** She informed him of what Abu as-Sanabil had said to her. Yes. What did he say to her?

**Student:** That she was free to marry.

**Shaykh:** He informed her that she was free to marry upon delivery. This shows that the generality of ﴿and for pregnant women, their term is until they deliver their burden﴾ takes precedence over the generality of ﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind, they shall wait by themselves for four months and ten [days]﴾.

From the principles: when a general term is given, and then a ruling follows that implies specification, do we act on the generality or on the specification?

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** An example: ﴿And divorced women shall wait by themselves for three periods. And it is not lawful for them to conceal what Allah has created in their wombs, if they believe in Allah and the Last Day. And their husbands have more right to take them back during that [period]﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:228]. The word ﴿divorced women﴾: if we look at its generality, what does it include? Revocable and irrevocable divorcees, that is, whether her divorce was irrevocable or revocable. And His words ﴿and their husbands have more right to take them back﴾ imply what?

It implies that this applies to revocable divorcees. So do we say that when a general term is followed by a ruling that applies only to some of its instances, it is restricted to those instances, or not?

Yes, this is also one of the matters on which the scholars differ. Some say that a divorcee who has been irrevocably divorced, whom her husband cannot take back, observes one menstrual cycle, because there is no benefit in prolonging the period for her. For a revocable divorcee there is a benefit in prolonging it, namely that the husband may take her back. But here there is no benefit, and if there is no benefit, she should be given room. It is said: her term has ended with one menstrual cycle, and she may marry.

Others say: we act on the generality. Following with a ruling on some of its instances is like mentioning some instances of a general term with a ruling that matches the generality; it does not imply specification. This is the view of the majority. The first view is the opinion chosen by Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him: that the divorcee who must observe three periods is only the revocable divorcee.

A parallel in the Sunnah is: "The Prophet (ﷺ) decided on pre-emption (*shufah*) in everything not yet divided. When the boundaries are set and the roads are marked, there is no pre-emption." [Reported by al-Bukhari (2257) from the hadith of Jabir ibn Abdullah.] If we look at the generality of the beginning of the hadith, we say: pre-emption applies to everything, even movable property. If we look at what follows, we say: there is no pre-emption except in lands where boundaries are set and roads are marked. This too is a matter on which scholars differ. Some say pre-emption is established only in lands, so if a car is shared by two people and one sells his share to a third party, his partner has no right of pre-emption, because the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When the boundaries are set and the roads are marked," and a car has no boundaries or roads.

Others say: we act on the generality, and pre-emption is established in everything not yet divided, whether land, movable property, or other things. They say: "When the boundaries are set" is a qualification of some instances of the general term, and it does not contradict the generality, so it does not imply specification. This too is disputed. However, there are hadiths indicating the generality and that pre-emption is required even in things other than land. That is, even if two men own a car and one sells his share to another, his partner has no pre-emption, because the reason for which pre-emption was established for the partner exists in land and in other things. Indeed, it may be even more contentious in other things, since the new partner may cause disputes and quarrels with the first partner that make his life miserable.

When reports from the early scholars give different interpretations of a verse, and the interpretations are possible, do we say that this difference is a genuine difference, or is it a difference of diversity (*tanawwu'*)?

**Shaykh:** It depends. Some of it is a difference of diversity, and some is a difference of contradiction (*tadad*). If it is a difference of contradiction, we must find a preponderant factor between the two views. If it is a difference of diversity, there is no real disagreement. An example is His words: ﴿Then We gave the Book to those We chose from Our servants; then among them is one who wrongs himself, and among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who is foremost in good deeds﴾ [Fatir 35:32]. Some said: the one who wrongs himself is the one who delays the prayer beyond its time. Others said: the one who wrongs himself is the one who does not pay zakat. That is one.

"And among them is one who is moderate": they said the moderate one is the one who pays zakat but does not give voluntary charity, and who prays on time but does not strive to perform it in the best manner.

The foremost in good deeds is the one who pays zakat and voluntary charity and strives to perform the prayer as it should be. Is this difference a genuine difference, such that we say there are two views on the interpretation of the verse?

No. This is a difference of diversity: each of them mentioned one kind of what is included in the verse. Some people consider this a disagreement, but it is not. They call this a difference of diversity, not a difference of contradiction. Accordingly, it is not permissible to say that the early scholars disagreed about the meaning of this verse, because all of them agreed that the one who wrongs himself is the one who neglects an obligation, the moderate one is the one who fulfils the obligation, and the foremost in good deeds is the one who goes beyond the obligation. They agreed on this, but each of them gave an example.

We want a verse containing specification that is connected to something other than an exception. Exceptions are many: ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss, except those who have believed﴾ and so on to the end [al-'Asr 103:2–3]. There are many.

**Student:** His words: ﴿So from what your right hands possess of your believing young women﴾ [an-Nisa' 4:25].

**Shaykh:** Yes, ﴿your believing young women﴾: this is specified by a description.

Similarly, His words: ﴿And pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to Allah by mankind, for whoever is able to make his way there﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:97]. When He first mentioned the generality, He then qualified it with ﴿for whoever is able to make his way there﴾. Do we take the generality or the qualification?

We take the qualification without doubt, because the qualification specifies the qualified term. Accordingly, pilgrimage is obligatory only for whom? For whoever is able.

If someone says: all acts of worship are qualified by ability, because of His words: ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ [at-Taghabun 64:16]. Then what is the wisdom in mentioning this condition for pilgrimage, and not mentioning it for prayer, for example? He did not say: "Establish prayer if you are able."

The answer is simple: the hardship in pilgrimage is more evident and clear than in other acts. Therefore this condition is stated explicitly. Fasting, since it involves some hardship, was described by Him, the Mighty and Majestic, as: ﴿Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:185]. As for what involves no hardship, commands are mentioned in absolute terms, but they are interpreted according to the general principle that there is no obligation with incapacity, because of His words: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:286], and His words: ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾.

Regarding His words: ﴿The companions of al-Aykah denied the messengers (176) when Shu'ayb said to them﴾ [ash-Shu'ara' 26:176–177], and in another verse: ﴿And to Madyan [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb﴾ [al-A'raf 7:85]: why is brotherhood mentioned in the second verse but not in the first?

**Student:** Because he attributed them to the tree they worshipped. When he attributed them to the tree, he did not grant them the brotherhood of faith, and when he attributed them to the land, he established for them the brotherhood of lineage.

**Shaykh:** That is one reason. Another reason is that when He said: ﴿The companions of al-Aykah denied the messengers (176) when Shu'ayb said to them﴾, He did not say "their brother," because they worshipped trees.

Some said: these people were not from his own people. They were not from his people, so he was not their brother by lineage. As for the first verse, he was their brother by lineage. Both views are correct.

What is your opinion on this method of tafsir: that we parse (*i'rab*) the verses, both the difficult and the non-difficult, as an exercise for the students? It reminds us of grammar. In reality we have not managed to allot time to studying grammar, whether in the Alfiyya or other works. I say: perhaps parsing will make up for it.

**Student:** I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. "On the Day when Allah will gather the messengers and say, 'What response did you receive?' They will say, 'We have no knowledge. Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen.'" (5:109)

**Shaykh:** I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿On the Day when Allah will gather the messengers and say, "What response did you receive?" They will say, "We have no knowledge. Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen."﴾

The word ﴿يَوْمَ﴾ (yawma, "on the day of") is an adverb of time (ẓarf). An adverb of time, or a prepositional phrase, must have a governing element (ʿāmil). This governing element is called the mutaʿallaq (the element to which it is attached). For this reason the author of the grammatical versified work said:

"A preposition must be attached to a verb, or to something having its meaning, such as the active participle (ism al-fāʿil) (as in) 'ascending' (murtaqī)."

That is, the active participle, the passive participle (ism al-mafʿūl), and what resembles them. Based on this, ﴿يَوْمَ﴾ is in the accusative case, and its governing element is omitted, because there is no element before us to which we can attribute the governing role, so we say: the governing element is omitted, and the implied meaning is: "Remember a day."

As for His saying ﴿يَوْمَ يَجْمَعُ اللَّهُ الرُّسُلَ﴾ (on the day when Allah gathers the messengers): ﴿يَوْمَ﴾ here is in construct with a verbal clause in the present tense. It is therefore in the accusative and not indeclinable (mabnī), because it is attached to a declinable verb (fiʿl muʿrab). It is only indeclinable when attached to an indeclinable verb (fiʿl mabnī).

﴿اللَّهُ﴾ (Allah) is the subject (fāʿil). Some say "the Glorious Name" is the subject, some say "the word Allah" is the subject, and some say "(Allah)" is the subject. But the better way to say it is "the Glorious Name" or "the word Allah," so that the act does not fall on the very essence of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, but on the Name. It is the subject, and ﴿الرُّسُلَ﴾ (the messengers) is the direct object. ﴿فَيَقُولُ﴾ (then He says) is conjoined to ﴿يَجْمَعُ﴾ (gathers), and for this reason it is in the nominative (marfūʿ).

﴿مَاذَا أُجِبْتُمْ﴾ (what response were you given?) may be a single word as an interrogative, or ﴿مَا﴾ may be an interrogative noun and ﴿ذَا﴾ may mean "that which" (alladhī), as Ibn Mālik, may Allah have mercy on him, said in the Alfiyya:

"Like (mā) (dhā) after an interrogative (mā), or (man), when it is not made void in speech."

So if we say that ﴿مَاذَا أُجِبْتُمْ﴾ as a whole, ﴿مَاذَا﴾ entirely, is an interrogative noun, then. And if we say ﴿مَا﴾ is an interrogative noun and ﴿ذَا﴾ means "that which," then ﴿مَا﴾ is an interrogative noun serving as the subject (mubtadaʾ), and ﴿ذَا﴾ is a relative pronoun serving as the predicate of the subject (khabar). ﴿أُجِبْتُمْ﴾ (you were answered) is in the passive form, which is called "the form of what has no named subject" (mabnī li-mā lam yusamma fāʿiluh). It is also called "the passive form" and "the form of the unknown," but the last is the better designation, because this form may be used when its subject is known yet unnamed, such as the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿وَخُلِقَ الْإِنْسَانُ ضَعِيفًا﴾ (and man was created weak) [an-Nisāʾ 28]. You cannot say that ﴿خُلِقَ﴾ is a past verb in the passive form of the unknown, why? Because the Creator is known. For this reason Ibn Mālik expressed it in the Alfiyya with the phrase "what has no named subject," and this is better.

As for His saying ﴿قَالُوا لَا عِلْمَ لَنَا﴾ (they will say: we have no knowledge), this is the answer to His saying ﴿مَاذَا أُجِبْتُمْ﴾.

As for His saying ﴿لَا عِلْمَ لَنَا﴾ (we have no knowledge): ﴿لَا﴾ here is the negation of the genus (lā al-nāfiya lil-jins), and it operates like ﴿إِنَّ﴾ (indeed), but its subject is indeclinable (mabnī) with it when it is singular. In the case of the negation of the genus, "singular" means what is not construct and not resembling a construct. Based on this, ﴿العِلْمَ﴾ (knowledge) is indeclinable on the vowel fatḥa in the position of the accusative, and ﴿لَنَا﴾ (for us) is a prepositional phrase serving as its predicate.

﴿إِنَّكَ أَنْتَ عَلَّامُ الْغُيُوبِ﴾ (indeed You, You are the Knower of the unseen) is a resumptive clause (jumla istiʾnāfiyya) that shows that they entrusted knowledge to the All-Knowing, the Mighty and Majestic, who is Allah, blessed and exalted. ﴿عَلَّامُ الْغُيُوبِ﴾: ﴿الْغُيُوبِ﴾ is the plural of (ghayb), and ﴿إِنَّ﴾ makes the noun accusative and the predicate nominative, and the ﴿كَ﴾ is its subject, ﴿عَلَّامُ﴾ is its predicate, and it is in construct with ﴿الْغُيُوبِ﴾.

As for the meaning of the verse: before we begin with its meaning, is this suitable or not suitable?

**Students:** Suitable.

**Shaykh:** Yes, it is suitable for adults and children. Is that so? Children do not need it, but its field is adults. I think, God willing, it is suitable, as long as we do not ask questions, which would waste our time. Rather, we parse, and God willing the meaning will be good.

Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿On the day when Allah gathers the messengers﴾, meaning: remember this great day, ﴿On the day when Allah gathers the messengers﴾. That is on the Day of Resurrection. He gathers them in what manner? And at what time? Is it at the beginning of the Day of Resurrection, or at its end, or what?

In such unseen matters we must stop where the text stops, because the intellect has no access to them. We do not know whether the people will be raised first, or during the day, or at the end of the day. We must mention this gathering.

His saying ﴿الرُّسُلَ﴾ is the plural of (rasūl, messenger), so it includes the messengers from the first of them to the last of them. The first of them is Noah, and the last of them is Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿فَيَقُولُ مَاذَا أُجِبْتُمْ﴾ means: what response did those to whom We sent you give you? With what did they respond? This is like His saying regarding those to whom they were sent: ﴿And on the day He calls to them and says, "What response did you give to the messengers?"﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ 65].

Based on this, Allah the Mighty and Majestic asks the messengers, and asks those to whom they were sent.
