[Reported by Ahmad (2447) from Ibn 'Abbas.] There are examples of this, including the saying of Ibrahim (peace be upon him): ﴿رَبِّ أَرِنِي كَيْفَ تُحْيِ الْمَوْتَى قَالَ أَوَلَمْ تُؤْمِنْ قَالَ بَلَى وَلَكِنْ لِيَطْمَئِنَّ قَلْبِي﴾ [al-Baqarah 260]. We take this from His saying: ﴿وَتَطْمَئِنَّ قُلُوبُنَا﴾.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: that the signs of the prophets increase their truthfulness in the hearts of people, from His saying: ﴿وَنَعْلَمَ أَنْ قَدْ صَدَقْتَنَا﴾, meaning you informed us of the truth.

* And from it: the establishment of a report by mass transmission (tawatur) and the multitude of reporters, from their saying: ﴿وَنَكُونَ عَلَيْهَا مِنَ الشَّاهِدِينَ﴾. This verse may also be used as evidence that the words of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) are true and binding, because they witnessed the Prophet (ﷺ) and witnessed his signs, and they were more certain of them than others and understood them better than others.

Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan. ﴿And when I inspired the disciples, saying: "Believe in Me and in My Messenger." They said: "We believe, and bear witness that we are Muslims." (111) When the disciples said: "O Isa, son of Maryam, can your Lord send down to us a table spread from the heaven?" He said: "Fear Allah, if you are believers." (112) They said: "We wish to eat from it, and that our hearts may be at rest, and that we may know that you have indeed spoken truth to us, and that we may be among its witnesses." (113) Isa, son of Maryam, said: "O Allah, our Lord, send down to us a table spread from the heaven, to be a festival for the first of us and the last of us, and a sign from You. And provide for us, and You are the best of providers." (114) Allah said: "Indeed I will send it down upon you. But whoever disbelieves after that among you, I will punish him with a punishment with which I will not punish anyone among the worlds."﴾ [al-Ma'idah 111–115].

Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And when I inspired the disciples to believe in Me and My Messenger﴾. The (idh) here, as we have already gone over, is an object of a verb omitted, the estimate being: "Remember when I inspired." And His saying: ﴿to believe in Me﴾, the (an) here is explanatory (tafsiriyyah), because when it occurs after a verb that contains the meaning of speech without its letters, it is called explanatory; and inspiration (wahy) is a verb that contains the meaning of speech without its letters. Among examples of this is His saying: ﴿We inspired to him: "Construct the ship"﴾ [al-Mu'minun 27]. So (an) here, the grammarians parse it as explanatory. ﴿to believe in Me and in My Messenger﴾: he repeated the preposition in His saying ﴿and in My Messenger﴾, and it is coordinated with His saying ﴿in Me﴾, because when it is coordinated upon an attached pronoun, the preposition that was in the first element is repeated; this is the most well-known usage in the Arabic language, though speech sometimes departs from the original, such as His saying: ﴿and fear Allah, through whom you ask one another, and the wombs﴾ according to one reading, while the well-known reading is ﴿and the wombs﴾ [an-Nisa 1], and such as His saying: ﴿and disbelief in Him and the Sacred Masjid﴾ [al-Baqarah 217], and He did not say "and in the Sacred Masjid." Otherwise, the rule is that when it is coordinated upon an attached pronoun, the preposition is repeated.

﴿They said: "We believe"﴾ — this is the answer to ﴿to believe in Me﴾. ﴿and bear witness that we are Muslims﴾. In such a case — i.e., ﴿that we are Muslims﴾ — it is permissible that the nun be doubled (shaddah) and that it not be doubled. If it is doubled, the pronoun ﴿bi-annana﴾ must be brought; and if it is not doubled, the nun is assimilated into the nun of the pronoun, becoming: "bi-anna muslimun." This has come in the Qur'an.

﴿When the disciples said﴾: this is also a resumptive sentence (jumlah isti'nafiyyah); the operator of (idh) is omitted, the estimate being: "Remember when the disciples said: O Isa, son of Maryam." Isa is a vocative (munada), and in such a case it is built on the damma in a position of nasb; but (ibn) came in the accusative, being an adjective or an appositive (ʿatf bayan), and it did not follow its described noun. Why? Because it is in an idafah construction. Therefore you say: "Ya Zaydu bna Abdillah," and do not say "Ya Zaydu bnu Abdillah," because if the operator — namely the governing element — were applied to it directly, it would put it in the accusative. So if the operator, when applied directly, would put it in the accusative, how much more so when the operator reaches it only through an intermediary. What intermediary?

Student: The substitution (badaliyyah).

Shaykh: The first noun is an appositive or a substitute.

﴿can your Lord﴾ has two readings: the reading ﴿hal yastatiʿu rabbuka﴾ and the reading ﴿hal tastatiʿu rabbaka﴾, and both are among the seven canonical readings. As for ﴿hal yastatiʿu rabbuka﴾, it is verb and subject; as for ﴿hal tastatiʿu rabbaka﴾, it is verb, attached subject, and object. The attached subject in (hal tastatiʿu) refers back to whom? To Isa.

﴿that He send down upon us a table spread from the heaven﴾: His saying ﴿from the heaven﴾ is a prepositional phrase functioning as an adjective of (ma'idah), because when a prepositional phrase or verb comes after an indefinite noun, it is an adjective, and if it comes after a definite noun, it is a circumstantial (hal).

He said: ﴿Fear Allah, if you are believers﴾. His saying ﴿if you are believers﴾ is connected to His saying ﴿Fear Allah﴾, because faith implies God-consciousness, and it is the condition in His saying ﴿Fear Allah﴾.

The Exalted's saying: ﴿And when I inspired the disciples﴾: is ﴿inspired﴾ here the legislative revelation (wahy shar'i) or the cosmic inspirational revelation (wahy kawni ilhami)? On this there are two opinions among the scholars. Some said it is legislative revelation, meaning: I inspired them through Isa; for it is known that legislative revelation is only for prophets and messengers, but I inspired them legislatively through their prophet Isa, peace be upon him. As for if it is cosmic revelation, then what is meant is inspiration (ilham), as in His saying: ﴿And We inspired the mother of Musa: "Suckle him"﴾ [al-Qasas 7] — We inspired, inspiration of ilham or legislative revelation? Ilham. And as in His saying: ﴿And your Lord inspired to the bee: "Take for yourself houses in the mountains"﴾ [an-Nahl 68] — this is inspiration of ilham, and it is cosmic revelation, since it concerns creation.

If someone says: Is it not possible to take the verse as meaning both meanings together, so that Allah inspired their prophet Isa to convey that to them, and inspired them to accept it? The answer: yes, or no? Yes, it is possible to take the revelation as both meanings together.

And His saying ﴿the disciples﴾: the disciples (al-hawariyyun) are the pure, select companions. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Every prophet has a disciple (hawari), and my disciple is az-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7261) and Muslim (2415/48) from the hadith of Jabir ibn Abdullah] — may Allah be pleased with him. So the disciples are the select companions. Consider how these were the select companions of his, and what they did afterwards while being select. Compare these select ones with the select of this Ummah, and you will find a great difference, just as if you compared the select of the people of Musa you would find a great difference between them and the select of this Ummah — which shows you the virtue of this Ummah, which Allah chose to follow this noble Messenger, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him.

﴿to believe in Me and in My Messenger﴾: ﴿to believe in Me﴾: faith in Allah the Mighty and Majestic includes belief in His existence, belief in His lordship, belief in His divinity, and belief in His names and attributes — meaning it includes four things. Belief in His existence is against those communists who say: there is no lord; there are only natures interacting and producing one another, and otherwise there is no lord — and Allah forbid — for He has sealed their hearts; we ask Allah for well-being. Belief in His lordship is a refutation of those who say that Allah the Exalted has a helper in creation or has a partner. For this reason Allah negated that in His saying: ﴿Say: "Call upon those you claim besides Allah; they do not possess an atom's weight in the heavens or on the earth, and they have no share in them, and He has no supporter among them." And intercession with Him does not benefit except for one whom He has permitted﴾ [Saba 22–23].

Belief in His divinity, meaning His being singled out in divinity, is a refutation of whom? Of those who set up with Allah another god to worship as they worship Allah, like the polytheists of Quraysh. Belief in His names and attributes is a refutation of two groups: the Mu'attilah and the Mumaththilah. The Mumaththilah associated partners with Allah, saying for example: "Allah has a face like our faces, and a hand like our hands, and an eye like our eyes," and such things; these are polytheists, are they not?

The second: the Mu'attilah, who negate the face, hand, eye, foot, descent, and istiwa' and such things; these are negators, and they have a share in the saying of Pharaoh: ﴿I know of no god for you other than me﴾ [al-Qasas 38], even though they do not negate divinity but negate the names and attributes. Whoever believes in a lord who is not described with hearing or sight, nor wisdom or might, nor power, nor coming or istiwa' — has he believed in a true Lord? No.

So belief in Allah the Mighty and Majestic includes four matters: belief in His existence, belief in His lordship, belief in His divinity, and belief in His names and attributes, and what is meant is singling Him out in these things.

﴿and in My Messenger﴾: that is Isa, peace be upon him. Belief in one messenger includes the command to believe in all the messengers; the command to believe in one messenger includes belief in all the messengers, because denying one messenger is denying all the messengers. Have you not read the saying of Allah the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿The people of Nuh denied the messengers﴾ [ash-Shu'ara 105], and was there any messenger before Nuh? No, there was no messenger before Nuh; yet He said ﴿denied the messengers﴾, because whoever denies one of a kind has denied the whole kind. If they believe in Isa, they have believed in all the messengers, including Muhammad, peace be upon him, for Isa gave glad tidings of him.

﴿They said: "We believe"﴾: they said with their tongues, "We believe." ﴿and bear witness that we are Muslims﴾: to whom did they say this? To Allah or to Isa? If Isa was the one who commanded them, they would be saying it to Isa: "We believe," and "bear witness that we are Muslims." They confessed and called upon witnesses. When a person confesses and calls witnesses, the witnessing of others prevents him from denying later; for a person may confess by himself, but if there is no one to testify against him, he may deny. But they confessed with their tongues and called upon witnesses — whom did they call upon? They called upon Isa, if the meaning of "they said" is to Isa. But if the meaning is that they said it to Allah the Mighty and Majestic, then the one called as witness here is Allah, blessed and exalted.

﴿that we are Muslims﴾: i.e., submissive to Allah the Mighty and Majestic. There is no submission except with faith that Allah the Exalted is the One who commands and forbids. Know that when Islam is mentioned alone it includes faith, and when faith is mentioned alone it includes Islam; and when both are combined, Islam becomes the outward and faith the inward: Islam is the outward deeds, the utterances of the tongue and actions of the limbs; faith is the inward deeds, beliefs of the hearts, their love, hope, and other things.

﴿When the disciples said﴾: i.e., remember, O Muhammad, when the disciples — the chosen ones from the people of Isa — said:

﴿O Isa, son of Maryam﴾: look at this dry address — they did not say "O Messenger of Allah" or "O Prophet of Allah." They said: ﴿O Isa, son of Maryam, can your Lord send down to us a table spread from the heaven?﴾ "Can He send down": this poses a great difficulty with this reading, because their doubt about the power of Allah implies disbelief. So scholars were troubled: how could they say this, being the disciples?

We answer in response to this: either "istita'ah" (ability) is interpreted as "irada" (will), and this is permissible in the speech of the Arabs. You say to your companion: "O so-and-so, can you walk with me to so-and-so? I will visit him," while you know he is able; but what is meant? Do you want to walk with me? So ﴿can your Lord﴾ means "does your Lord will," and there is no doubt in their minds about His being capable, the Mighty and Majestic.

Or another answer is given: they believe in His general power, but a person may have doubt about a specific power, like the man who said to his family, while he was extravagant against himself: "When I die, burn me, then scatter me in the sea — that is, in the sea — for by Allah, if Allah has power over me He will punish me with a punishment with which He will not punish anyone among the worlds" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3481) and Muslim (2756/25) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah]. Was that man fearful or not? He was fearful of Allah, and had no doubt that He is capable, but in general; as for this specific act, he said: perhaps if he is burned and scattered in the sea, Allah will not be able over him.

So the answer becomes twofold: the first aspect: that "istita'ah" means "qudrah" (power); the second aspect: that they had faith in Allah's power over everything, but in the details a person may hesitate about their occurrence and need added reassurance. Look at Zakariyya and look at Maryam: when Allah gave him the good news that He would grant him a son, what did he say? He said: ﴿"How can I have a son, when my wife is barren and I have reached extreme old age?"﴾ [Maryam 8]. How could this be? Allah said to him: ﴿"So said your Lord: it is easy for Me, and I created you before, when you were nothing"﴾ [Maryam 9] — meaning, look at your origin: ﴿I created you before, when you were nothing﴾. So He is capable of creating a child; yet he asked for a sign of the realization of what he was given good news of.

There is a third opinion which says: ﴿hal yastatiʿu﴾ is not from "istita'ah" in the sense of inability, but from "ita'ah" (obedience): i.e., will your Lord obey you if you ask Him to send down a table to us, or will He not obey? This opinion returns to the first meaning, which is "irada" (will), because "ita'ah" means submission: so the meaning is: if you ask your Lord, will He obey you? So "istita'ah" here is not from the category of capacity and power, but from the category of obedience, which is submission when asked.

﴿He said: "Fear Allah, if you are believers"﴾: "Fear Allah" means: refrain from this request, or from this question which contains a request. ﴿if you are believers﴾: i.e., believers in His decree, content with His judgment: if He enriches you, He enriches you; if He deprives you, He deprives you; for the one who is truly a believer and truly God-fearing is content with Allah's decree and destiny, and does not ask for things outside the bounds of custom.

This is on the reading ﴿hal yastatiʿu﴾. As for the reading ﴿hal tastatiʿu rabbaka﴾, the meaning is: can you ask your Lord to send down to us a table from the heaven? Here "istita'ah" refers back to whom? To Isa: i.e., can you ask Allah, or are you too shy and do not ask? On this reading there is no difficulty, praise be to Allah. On the first reading you have learned the aspects by which the difficulty is answered.

﴿that He send down upon us a table spread from the heaven﴾: "ma'idah" is sometimes applied to food, and its original usage is to the platform upon which the food is placed; this is the original, but it may also be applied to the food. Here the meaning — and Allah knows best — is both together: a food platform, which is a tray (khiwan or khuwwan — I do not vouch for the vocalization), and upon it the food.

﴿from the heaven﴾: i.e., from above.

﴿They said: "We wish"﴾: i.e., they informed him of the reason, that they asked this strange question. ﴿"We wish to eat from it"﴾: so they were hungry. And this resembles, in some respects, though what is better than it is what the people of Musa said to him: ﴿"Call upon your Lord to bring forth for us of what the earth grows: its herbs, cucumbers, garlic, lentils, and onions"﴾ [al-Baqarah 61]. But these asked for something to descend from heaven: ﴿"We wish to eat from it."﴾ Second: ﴿"and that our hearts may be at rest"﴾: "tatma'inn" means to settle, with no unease or doubt. This is a second purpose. Third: ﴿"and that we may know that you have indeed spoken truth to us"﴾. How can they know that he spoke truly? Yes: he told them he was the Messenger of Allah; if he brought a clear sign, then he spoke truly, and if not, then he did not. But how can they say ﴿"and that we may know that you have indeed spoken truth to us"﴾ when they had already affirmed his truthfulness? This is a difficulty. The answer: either the meaning is "and that we may increase in knowledge that you have spoken truth to us" — and there is no doubt that whenever signs indicating the truthfulness of the speaker are found, knowledge of the speaker's truthfulness increases; or some of them had hesitation, and knowledge removes doubt and hesitation. But which is preferable: to think well of them and say "we know," meaning "we increase in knowledge," or to say that perhaps some of them had hesitation?

The first meaning is better: ﴿وَنَعْلَمَ أَنْ قَدْ صَدَقْتَنَا﴾ means "you have informed us of the truth." It is said: sadaqahu (he told him the truth), meaning he informed him of the truth. It is also said: sadaqahu, meaning he fulfilled what he promised him, as in the saying of Allah, ﴿وَلَقَدْ صَدَقَكُمُ اللَّهُ وَعْدَهُ إِذْ تَحُسُّونَهُمْ بِإِذْنِهِ﴾ [Al 'Imran 152], meaning: "when you were killing them by His permission," so it means He fulfilled what He had promised. It is also said: sadaqahu, when he informs him of the truth even if what he informed of did not come to pass, as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) about the Devil: "He spoke the truth to you, though he is a liar." [Reported by al-Bukhari (3275) from Abu Hurayrah.]

﴿وَنَكُونَ عَلَيْهَا مِنَ الشَّاهِدِينَ﴾ This is a fourth matter: that we witness it with our own eyes without being told about it, for reports are not like direct witnessing.

* From the benefits of the two verses: the affirmation of the revelation of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; from His saying ﴿إِذْ أَوْحَيْتُ﴾. The revelation of Allah is divided into two kinds: revelation of legislation (wahy shar') and revelation of inspiration (wahy ilham). The first relates to the Shari'ah, and the second relates to the cosmos, and you have heard examples of this in the tafsir.

* From the benefits of this verse: that 'Isa (peace be upon him) had disciples (hawariyyun), meaning: companions who were pure in their affection. Mention the end of Surah al-Saff: ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا كُونُوا أَنْصَارَ اللَّهِ كَمَا قَالَ عِيسَى ابْنُ مَرْيَمَ لِلْحَوَارِيِّينَ مَنْ أَنْصَارِي إِلَى اللَّهِ قَالَ الْحَوَارِيُّونَ نَحْنُ أَنْصَارُ اللَّهِ﴾ [al-Saff 14]. And as you have heard in the hadith: "Every prophet has a hawari, and my hawari is al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7261) and Muslim (2415/48) from Jabir ibn 'Abdullah.] This is without doubt a virtue of al-Zubayr. But Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "If I were to take a close friend (khalil) from my Ummah, I would have taken Abu Bakr." [Reported by al-Bukhari (3656) from Ibn 'Abbas.]

* From the benefits of this noble verse: faith in Allah is not complete except with faith in His messengers; from His saying ﴿أَنْ آمِنُوا بِي وَبِرَسُولِي﴾. The Prophet (ﷺ) explained that faith is "to believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and to believe in divine decree, both its good and its bad." [Reported by Muslim (8/1) from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab.] These pillars are necessary in faith, so whoever lacks one of them is not a believer.

* From the benefits of this verse: the response of the disciples to what was revealed to them, when they said: "We believe."

* From the benefits of the verse: the permissibility of omitting what is known. From where? ﴿قَالُوا آمَنَّا﴾ without saying "in You and in Your messenger," because this is understood. The absolute is interpreted in light of the restricted when it is known. So if a person concludes a contract and mentions conditions at the offer, and the other says "I accept," or "I accept the sale," for example, and he says: "I sell you this house on condition that I live in it for a year," and the other says: "I accept the sale," does the condition hold? Yes, it holds, because the wording of the sale implies this condition even if it is not stated, since it is known from the context.

* From the benefits of this verse: the permissibility of establishing a matter by calling witnesses to it; from His saying ﴿اشْهَدْ بِأَنَّنَا مُسْلِمُونَ﴾. In the transmitted supplication: "O Allah, I have entered the evening calling You to witness, and calling to witness the bearers of Your Throne, Your angels, Your prophets, and all of Your creation, that You are Allah, there is no god but You, and that Muhammad is Your servant and Your messenger." [Reported by Abu Dawud (5069) and al-Tirmidhi (3501) from Anas ibn Malik, without the phrase "and Your prophets." In al-Mu'jam al-Awsat of al-Tabarani (9356): "and I call to witness Your angels, Your prophets and Your messengers, and all of Your creation, to my testimony against myself that I testify that You are Allah, there is no god but You."] This is among the morning and evening remembrances, though there is disagreement over the authenticity of the hadith.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: that faith is Islam. From His saying ﴿آمَنَّا وَاشْهَدْ بِأَنَّنَا مُسْلِمُونَ﴾ [al-Ma'idah 111]. They did not say "believers"; they said "Muslims," which indicates that faith is Islam. A group of scholars held this view and said there is no difference between Islam and faith, citing verses like this one, and also citing the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿فَأَخْرَجْنَا مَنْ كَانَ فِيهَا مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ (٣٥) فَمَا وَجَدْنَا فِيهَا غَيْرَ بَيْتٍ مِنَ الْمُسْلِمِينَ﴾ [al-Dhariyat 35, 36]. However, this view stated absolutely is open to question. The correct position is that when Islam is mentioned alone, it includes faith, and when it is mentioned together with faith, it has a different meaning. This distinction is shown by the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿قَالَتِ الْأَعْرَابُ آمَنَّا قُلْ لَمْ تُؤْمِنُوا وَلَكِنْ قُولُوا أَسْلَمْنَا وَلَمَّا يَدْخُلِ الْإِيمَانُ فِي قُلُوبِكُمْ﴾ [al-Hujurat 14], meaning it has not entered yet but it is close to entering, since "lamma" indicates negation with the nearness of what is negated. ﴿وَلَمَّا يَدْخُلِ الْإِيمَانُ فِي قُلُوبِكُمْ﴾. So how do we explain this verse? We explain it by saying that they combined faith and Islam, so faith is in the hearts and Islam is in the limbs, meaning they believed and submitted completely to the commands of Allah and His messenger.

Then He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿إِذْ قَالَ الْحَوَارِيُّونَ﴾ to the end [al-Ma'idah 112].

* From the benefits of this verse: that the disciples, despite being sincere, had some discourtesy; from their saying: ﴿يَا عِيسَى ابْنَ مَرْيَمَ﴾.

If someone says: perhaps their law permitted them to call their prophet by his name, unlike this law, since Allah says: ﴿لَا تَجْعَلُوا دُعَاءَ الرَّسُولِ بَيْنَكُمْ كَدُعَاءِ بَعْضِكُمْ بَعْضًا﴾ [al-Nur 63]? We say: let that be so, but is it good manners for them to address 'Isa ibn Maryam (peace be upon him) by his name, while they want him to ask Allah to send this table, or is it more fitting, since they want him to ask Allah, to call him by the description of prophethood and messengerhood, since that is more appropriate and closer to the answering of their request? The answer: the second, without doubt. In any case, this address certainly contains some discourtesy.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: that these disciples wanted from the signs what would fill their bellies. The evidence: the first thing they began with was eating: ﴿نُرِيدُ أَنْ نَأْكُلَ مِنْهَا﴾, as soon as they began. This resembles the saying of the Jews when they were told: ﴿ادْخُلُوا الْبَابَ سُجَّدًا﴾ [al-Nisa 154]. What did they do? They entered upon their posteriors, on their buttocks, saying "hintah" (wheat), when they were commanded to say "hittah" (meaning: remove our sins from us). But they said: no, we want something else, which is filling the belly: wheat. These resemble that, and the origin is one, O brothers, the origin is one; they are all from the Children of Israel, so it is no wonder that their requests are similar. And Allah knows best.

* * *

* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan: ﴿وَإِذْ أَوْحَيْتُ إِلَى الْحَوَارِيِّينَ أَنْ آمِنُوا بِي وَبِرَسُولِي قَالُوا آمَنَّا وَاشْهَدْ بِأَنَّنَا مُسْلِمُونَ (١١١) إِذْ قَالَ الْحَوَارِيُّونَ يَا عِيسَى ابْنَ مَرْيَمَ هَلْ يَسْتَطِيعُ رَبُّكَ أَنْ يُنَزِّلَ عَلَيْنَا مَائِدَةً مِنَ السَّمَاءِ قَالَ اتَّقُوا اللَّهَ إِنْ كُنْتُمْ مُؤْمِنِينَ (١١٢) قَالُوا نُرِيدُ أَنْ نَأْكُلَ مِنْهَا وَتَطْمَئِنَّ قُلُوبُنَا وَنَعْلَمَ أَنْ قَدْ صَدَقْتَنَا وَنَكُونَ عَلَيْهَا مِنَ الشَّاهِدِينَ (١١٣) قَالَ عِيسَى ابْنُ مَرْيَمَ اللَّهُمَّ رَبَّنَا أَنْزِلْ عَلَيْنَا مَائِدَةً مِنَ السَّمَاءِ تَكُونُ لَنَا عِيدًا لِأَوَّلِنَا وَآخِرِنَا وَآيَةً مِنْكَ وَارْزُقْنَا وَأَنْتَ خَيْرُ الرَّازِقِينَ (١١٤) قَالَ اللَّهُ إِنِّي مُنَزِّلُهَا عَلَيْكُمْ فَمَنْ يَكْفُرْ بَعْدُ مِنْكُمْ فَإِنِّي أُعَذِّبُهُ عَذَابًا لَا أُعَذِّبُهُ أَحَدًا مِنَ الْعَالَمِينَ﴾ [al-Ma'idah 111-115].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿وَإِذْ أَوْحَيْتُ إِلَى الْحَوَارِيِّينَ﴾, and its tafsir has already been covered. Is this revelation to the disciples, or what?

* The student: There are two opinions: one is revelation through their prophet 'Isa; the second is inspiration.

* The Shaykh: That is, He revealed it to them through 'Isa.

* The student: Yes, and the second opinion is that it is inspiration.

* The Shaykh: That His revealing to them means inspiration.
Which of them is stronger?

* The student: We say the meaning includes both: legislative revelation and cosmic revelation.

* The Shaykh: Allah revealed to 'Isa a legislative revelation, and He revealed to them a decreed (qadari) revelation.
What is the meaning of al-hawariyyun?

* Student: The pure ones among his companions.

* The Shaykh: The pure ones among his companions.
The saying of Allah: ﴿هَلْ يَسْتَطِيعُ رَبُّكَ﴾ has two readings. Recite them.

* Student: ﴿هَلْ يَسْتَطِيعُ رَبُّكَ﴾ and ﴿هَلْ تَسْتَطِيعُ رَبَّكَ﴾.

* The Shaykh: ﴿هَلْ يَسْتَطِيعُ رَبُّكَ﴾ and ﴿هَلْ تَسْتَطِيعُ رَبَّكَ﴾.
On the first reading, is there a problem? This suggests they doubted Allah's power. What is the answer to that?

* Student: (...)

* The Shaykh: No, this example is not correct. It is like a man saying to his brother: "Can you walk with me? Can you go or come?" The point is that istita'ah means qudrah (ability). Another aspect?

* Student: That they believed in Allah's general power, but in the particular (...)

* The Shaykh: That is, they had faith in general power, but the power over a specific thing... this is one aspect of the answer. Second?

* Student: The meaning of ﴿هَلْ يَسْتَطِيعُ رَبُّكَ﴾ is: would your Lord obey you if you asked Him.

* Another student: They say it does not mean ability, but obedience: istita'ah means ita'ah.

* The Shaykh: Meaning?

* Student: Meaning, if you ask Him, i.e., can you ask Him.

* The Shaykh: That is, ﴿هَلْ يَسْتَطِيعُ رَبُّكَ﴾ means: would your Lord respond. This is the summary: would your Lord respond, from obedience in the sense of submission.

On the reading ﴿هَلْ تَسْتَطِيعُ رَبَّكَ﴾?

* Student: No problem.

* The Shaykh: No problem. What is the meaning?

* Student: That is, can you ask your Lord.

* The Shaykh: Can you ask your Lord? On this, there is no problem.

* Student: (...)

* The Shaykh: This resembles the saying of the Jews: "hintah," when they were told: "say hittah."

* From the benefits of this verse: that the occurrence of a thing gives more certainty than being informed about it. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The report is not like witnessing directly." [Reported by Ahmad (2447) from Ibn 'Abbas.] There are examples of this, including the saying of Ibrahim (peace be upon him): ﴿رَبِّ أَرِنِي كَيْفَ تُحْيِ الْمَوْتَى قَالَ أَوَلَمْ تُؤْمِنْ قَالَ بَلَى وَلَكِنْ لِيَطْمَئِنَّ قَلْبِي﴾ [al-Baqarah 260]. We take this from His saying: ﴿وَتَطْمَئِنَّ قُلُوبُنَا﴾.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: that the signs of the prophets increase their truthfulness in the hearts of people, from His saying: ﴿وَنَعْلَمَ أَنْ قَدْ صَدَقْتَنَا﴾, meaning you informed us of the truth.

* And from it: the establishment of a report by mass transmission (tawatur) and the multitude of reporters, from their saying: ﴿وَنَكُونَ عَلَيْهَا مِنَ الشَّاهِدِينَ﴾. This verse may also be used as evidence that the words of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) are true and binding, because they witnessed the Prophet (ﷺ) and witnessed his signs, and they were more certain of them than others and understood them better than others.

Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan. ﴿And when I inspired the disciples, saying: "Believe in Me and in My Messenger." They said: "We believe, and bear witness that we are Muslims." (111) When the disciples said: "O Isa, son of Maryam, can your Lord send down to us a table spread from the heaven?" He said: "Fear Allah, if you are believers." (112) They said: "We wish to eat from it, and that our hearts may be at rest, and that we may know that you have indeed spoken truth to us, and that we may be among its witnesses." (113) Isa, son of Maryam, said: "O Allah, our Lord, send down to us a table spread from the heaven, to be a festival for the first of us and the last of us, and a sign from You. And provide for us, and You are the best of providers." (114) Allah said: "Indeed I will send it down upon you. But whoever disbelieves after that among you, I will punish him with a punishment with which I will not punish anyone among the worlds."﴾ [al-Ma'idah 111–115].

Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And when I inspired the disciples to believe in Me and My Messenger﴾. The (idh) here, as we have already gone over, is an object of a verb omitted, the estimate being: "Remember when I inspired." And His saying: ﴿to believe in Me﴾, the (an) here is explanatory (tafsiriyyah), because when it occurs after a verb that contains the meaning of speech without its letters, it is called explanatory; and inspiration (wahy) is a verb that contains the meaning of speech without its letters. Among examples of this is His saying: ﴿We inspired to him: "Construct the ship"﴾ [al-Mu'minun 27]. So (an) here, the grammarians parse it as explanatory. ﴿to believe in Me and in My Messenger﴾: he repeated the preposition in His saying ﴿and in My Messenger﴾, and it is coordinated with His saying ﴿in Me﴾, because when it is coordinated upon an attached pronoun, the preposition that was in the first element is repeated; this is the most well-known usage in the Arabic language, though speech sometimes departs from the original, such as His saying: ﴿and fear Allah, through whom you ask one another, and the wombs﴾ according to one reading, while the well-known reading is ﴿and the wombs﴾ [an-Nisa 1], and such as His saying: ﴿and disbelief in Him and the Sacred Masjid﴾ [al-Baqarah 217], and He did not say "and in the Sacred Masjid." Otherwise, the rule is that when it is coordinated upon an attached pronoun, the preposition is repeated.

﴿They said: "We believe"﴾ — this is the answer to ﴿to believe in Me﴾. ﴿and bear witness that we are Muslims﴾. In such a case — i.e., ﴿that we are Muslims﴾ — it is permissible that the nun be doubled (shaddah) and that it not be doubled. If it is doubled, the pronoun ﴿bi-annana﴾ must be brought; and if it is not doubled, the nun is assimilated into the nun of the pronoun, becoming: "bi-anna muslimun." This has come in the Qur'an.

﴿When the disciples said﴾: this is also a resumptive sentence (jumlah isti'nafiyyah); the operator of (idh) is omitted, the estimate being: "Remember when the disciples said: O Isa, son of Maryam." Isa is a vocative (munada), and in such a case it is built on the damma in a position of nasb; but (ibn) came in the accusative, being an adjective or an appositive (ʿatf bayan), and it did not follow its described noun. Why? Because it is in an idafah construction. Therefore you say: "Ya Zaydu bna Abdillah," and do not say "Ya Zaydu bnu Abdillah," because if the operator — namely the governing element — were applied to it directly, it would put it in the accusative. So if the operator, when applied directly, would put it in the accusative, how much more so when the operator reaches it only through an intermediary. What intermediary?

Student: The substitution (badaliyyah).

Shaykh: The first noun is an appositive or a substitute.

﴿can your Lord﴾ has two readings: the reading ﴿hal yastatiʿu rabbuka﴾ and the reading ﴿hal tastatiʿu rabbaka﴾, and both are among the seven canonical readings. As for ﴿hal yastatiʿu rabbuka﴾, it is verb and subject; as for ﴿hal tastatiʿu rabbaka﴾, it is verb, attached subject, and object. The attached subject in (hal tastatiʿu) refers back to whom? To Isa.

﴿that He send down upon us a table spread from the heaven﴾: His saying ﴿from the heaven﴾ is a prepositional phrase functioning as an adjective of (ma'idah), because when a prepositional phrase or verb comes after an indefinite noun, it is an adjective, and if it comes after a definite noun, it is a circumstantial (hal).

He said: ﴿Fear Allah, if you are believers﴾. His saying ﴿if you are believers﴾ is connected to His saying ﴿Fear Allah﴾, because faith implies God-consciousness, and it is the condition in His saying ﴿Fear Allah﴾.

The Exalted's saying: ﴿And when I inspired the disciples﴾: is ﴿inspired﴾ here the legislative revelation (wahy shar'i) or the cosmic inspirational revelation (wahy kawni ilhami)? On this there are two opinions among the scholars. Some said it is legislative revelation, meaning: I inspired them through Isa; for it is known that legislative revelation is only for prophets and messengers, but I inspired them legislatively through their prophet Isa, peace be upon him. As for if it is cosmic revelation, then what is meant is inspiration (ilham), as in His saying: ﴿And We inspired the mother of Musa: "Suckle him"﴾ [al-Qasas 7] — We inspired, inspiration of ilham or legislative revelation? Ilham. And as in His saying: ﴿And your Lord inspired to the bee: "Take for yourself houses in the mountains"﴾ [an-Nahl 68] — this is inspiration of ilham, and it is cosmic revelation, since it concerns creation.

If someone says: Is it not possible to take the verse as meaning both meanings together, so that Allah inspired their prophet Isa to convey that to them, and inspired them to accept it? The answer: yes, or no? Yes, it is possible to take the revelation as both meanings together.

And His saying ﴿the disciples﴾: the disciples (al-hawariyyun) are the pure, select companions. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Every prophet has a disciple (hawari), and my disciple is az-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7261) and Muslim (2415/48) from the hadith of Jabir ibn Abdullah] — may Allah be pleased with him. So the disciples are the select companions. Consider how these were the select companions of his, and what they did afterwards while being select. Compare these select ones with the select of this Ummah, and you will find a great difference, just as if you compared the select of the people of Musa you would find a great difference between them and the select of this Ummah — which shows you the virtue of this Ummah, which Allah chose to follow this noble Messenger, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him.

﴿to believe in Me and in My Messenger﴾: ﴿to believe in Me﴾: faith in Allah the Mighty and Majestic includes belief in His existence, belief in His lordship, belief in His divinity, and belief in His names and attributes — meaning it includes four things. Belief in His existence is against those communists who say: there is no lord; there are only natures interacting and producing one another, and otherwise there is no lord — and Allah forbid — for He has sealed their hearts; we ask Allah for well-being. Belief in His lordship is a refutation of those who say that Allah the Exalted has a helper in creation or has a partner. For this reason Allah negated that in His saying: ﴿Say: "Call upon those you claim besides Allah; they do not possess an atom's weight in the heavens or on the earth, and they have no share in them, and He has no supporter among them." And intercession with Him does not benefit except for one whom He has permitted﴾ [Saba 22–23].

Belief in His divinity, meaning His being singled out in divinity, is a refutation of whom? Of those who set up with Allah another god to worship as they worship Allah, like the polytheists of Quraysh. Belief in His names and attributes is a refutation of two groups: the Mu'attilah and the Mumaththilah. The Mumaththilah associated partners with Allah, saying for example: "Allah has a face like our faces, and a hand like our hands, and an eye like our eyes," and such things; these are polytheists, are they not?

The second: the Mu'attilah, who negate the face, hand, eye, foot, descent, and istiwa' and such things; these are negators, and they have a share in the saying of Pharaoh: ﴿I know of no god for you other than me﴾ [al-Qasas 38], even though they do not negate divinity but negate the names and attributes. Whoever believes in a lord who is not described with hearing or sight, nor wisdom or might, nor power, nor coming or istiwa' — has he believed in a true Lord? No.

So belief in Allah the Mighty and Majestic includes four matters: belief in His existence, belief in His lordship, belief in His divinity, and belief in His names and attributes, and what is meant is singling Him out in these things.

﴿and in My Messenger﴾: that is Isa, peace be upon him. Belief in one messenger includes the command to believe in all the messengers; the command to believe in one messenger includes belief in all the messengers, because denying one messenger is denying all the messengers. Have you not read the saying of Allah the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿The people of Nuh denied the messengers﴾ [ash-Shu'ara 105], and was there any messenger before Nuh? No, there was no messenger before Nuh; yet He said ﴿denied the messengers﴾, because whoever denies one of a kind has denied the whole kind. If they believe in Isa, they have believed in all the messengers, including Muhammad, peace be upon him, for Isa gave glad tidings of him.

﴿They said: "We believe"﴾: they said with their tongues, "We believe." ﴿and bear witness that we are Muslims﴾: to whom did they say this? To Allah or to Isa? If Isa was the one who commanded them, they would be saying it to Isa: "We believe," and "bear witness that we are Muslims." They confessed and called upon witnesses. When a person confesses and calls witnesses, the witnessing of others prevents him from denying later; for a person may confess by himself, but if there is no one to testify against him, he may deny. But they confessed with their tongues and called upon witnesses — whom did they call upon? They called upon Isa, if the meaning of "they said" is to Isa. But if the meaning is that they said it to Allah the Mighty and Majestic, then the one called as witness here is Allah, blessed and exalted.

﴿that we are Muslims﴾: i.e., submissive to Allah the Mighty and Majestic. There is no submission except with faith that Allah the Exalted is the One who commands and forbids. Know that when Islam is mentioned alone it includes faith, and when faith is mentioned alone it includes Islam; and when both are combined, Islam becomes the outward and faith the inward: Islam is the outward deeds, the utterances of the tongue and actions of the limbs; faith is the inward deeds, beliefs of the hearts, their love, hope, and other things.

﴿When the disciples said﴾: i.e., remember, O Muhammad, when the disciples — the chosen ones from the people of Isa — said:

﴿O Isa, son of Maryam﴾: look at this dry address — they did not say "O Messenger of Allah" or "O Prophet of Allah." They said: ﴿O Isa, son of Maryam, can your Lord send down to us a table spread from the heaven?﴾ "Can He send down": this poses a great difficulty with this reading, because their doubt about the power of Allah implies disbelief. So scholars were troubled: how could they say this, being the disciples?

We answer in response to this: either "istita'ah" (ability) is interpreted as "irada" (will), and this is permissible in the speech of the Arabs. You say to your companion: "O so-and-so, can you walk with me to so-and-so? I will visit him," while you know he is able; but what is meant? Do you want to walk with me? So ﴿can your Lord﴾ means "does your Lord will," and there is no doubt in their minds about His being capable, the Mighty and Majestic.

Or another answer is given: they believe in His general power, but a person may have doubt about a specific power, like the man who said to his family, while he was extravagant against himself: "When I die, burn me, then scatter me in the sea — that is, in the sea — for by Allah, if Allah has power over me He will punish me with a punishment with which He will not punish anyone among the worlds" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3481) and Muslim (2756/25) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah]. Was that man fearful or not? He was fearful of Allah, and had no doubt that He is capable, but in general; as for this specific act, he said: perhaps if he is burned and scattered in the sea, Allah will not be able over him.

So the answer becomes twofold: the first aspect: that "istita'ah" means "qudrah" (power); the second aspect: that they had faith in Allah's power over everything, but in the details a person may hesitate about their occurrence and need added reassurance. Look at Zakariyya and look at Maryam: when Allah gave him the good news that He would grant him a son, what did he say? He said: ﴿"How can I have a son, when my wife is barren and I have reached extreme old age?"﴾ [Maryam 8]. How could this be? Allah said to him: ﴿"So said your Lord: it is easy for Me, and I created you before, when you were nothing"﴾ [Maryam 9] — meaning, look at your origin: ﴿I created you before, when you were nothing﴾. So He is capable of creating a child; yet he asked for a sign of the realization of what he was given good news of.

There is a third opinion which says: ﴿hal yastatiʿu﴾ is not from "istita'ah" in the sense of inability, but from "ita'ah" (obedience): i.e., will your Lord obey you if you ask Him to send down a table to us, or will He not obey? This opinion returns to the first meaning, which is "irada" (will), because "ita'ah" means submission: so the meaning is: if you ask your Lord, will He obey you? So "istita'ah" here is not from the category of capacity and power, but from the category of obedience, which is submission when asked.

﴿He said: "Fear Allah, if you are believers"﴾: "Fear Allah" means: refrain from this request, or from this question which contains a request. ﴿if you are believers﴾: i.e., believers in His decree, content with His judgment: if He enriches you, He enriches you; if He deprives you, He deprives you; for the one who is truly a believer and truly God-fearing is content with Allah's decree and destiny, and does not ask for things outside the bounds of custom.

This is on the reading ﴿hal yastatiʿu﴾. As for the reading ﴿hal tastatiʿu rabbaka﴾, the meaning is: can you ask your Lord to send down to us a table from the heaven? Here "istita'ah" refers back to whom? To Isa: i.e., can you ask Allah, or are you too shy and do not ask? On this reading there is no difficulty, praise be to Allah. On the first reading you have learned the aspects by which the difficulty is answered.

﴿that He send down upon us a table spread from the heaven﴾: "ma'idah" is sometimes applied to food, and its original usage is to the platform upon which the food is placed; this is the original, but it may also be applied to the food. Here the meaning — and Allah knows best — is both together: a food platform, which is a tray (khiwan or khuwwan — I do not vouch for the vocalization), and upon it the food.

﴿from the heaven﴾: i.e., from above.

﴿They said: "We wish"﴾: i.e., they informed him of the reason, that they asked this strange question. ﴿"We wish to eat from it"﴾: so they were hungry. And this resembles, in some respects, though what is better than it is what the people of Musa said to him: ﴿"Call upon your Lord to bring forth for us of what the earth grows: its herbs, cucumbers, garlic, lentils, and onions"﴾ [al-Baqarah 61]. But these asked for something to descend from heaven: ﴿"We wish to eat from it."﴾ Second: ﴿"and that our hearts may be at rest"﴾: "tatma'inn" means to settle, with no unease or doubt. This is a second purpose. Third: ﴿"and that we may know that you have indeed spoken truth to us"﴾. How can they know that he spoke truly? Yes: he told them he was the Messenger of Allah; if he brought a clear sign, then he spoke truly, and if not, then he did not. But how can they say ﴿"and that we may know that you have indeed spoken truth to us"﴾ when they had already affirmed his truthfulness? This is a difficulty. The answer: either the meaning is "and that we may increase in knowledge that you have spoken truth to us" — and there is no doubt that whenever signs indicating the truthfulness of the speaker are found, knowledge of the speaker's truthfulness increases; or some of them had hesitation, and knowledge removes doubt and hesitation. But which is preferable: to think well of them and say "we know," meaning "we increase in knowledge," or to say that perhaps some of them had hesitation?

The first meaning is better: ﴿وَنَعْلَمَ أَنْ قَدْ صَدَقْتَنَا﴾ means "you have informed us of the truth." It is said: sadaqahu (he told him the truth), meaning he informed him of the truth. It is also said: sadaqahu, meaning he fulfilled what he promised him, as in the saying of Allah, ﴿وَلَقَدْ صَدَقَكُمُ اللَّهُ وَعْدَهُ إِذْ تَحُسُّونَهُمْ بِإِذْنِهِ﴾ [Al 'Imran 152], meaning: "when you were killing them by His permission," so it means He fulfilled what He had promised. It is also said: sadaqahu, when he informs him of the truth even if what he informed of did not come to pass, as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) about the Devil: "He spoke the truth to you, though he is a liar." [Reported by al-Bukhari (3275) from Abu Hurayrah.]

﴿وَنَكُونَ عَلَيْهَا مِنَ الشَّاهِدِينَ﴾ This is a fourth matter: that we witness it with our own eyes without being told about it, for reports are not like direct witnessing.

* From the benefits of the two verses: the affirmation of the revelation of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; from His saying ﴿إِذْ أَوْحَيْتُ﴾. The revelation of Allah is divided into two kinds: revelation of legislation (wahy shar') and revelation of inspiration (wahy ilham). The first relates to the Shari'ah, and the second relates to the cosmos, and you have heard examples of this in the tafsir.

* From the benefits of this verse: that 'Isa (peace be upon him) had disciples (hawariyyun), meaning: companions who were pure in their affection. Mention the end of Surah al-Saff: ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا كُونُوا أَنْصَارَ اللَّهِ كَمَا قَالَ عِيسَى ابْنُ مَرْيَمَ لِلْحَوَارِيِّينَ مَنْ أَنْصَارِي إِلَى اللَّهِ قَالَ الْحَوَارِيُّونَ نَحْنُ أَنْصَارُ اللَّهِ﴾ [al-Saff 14]. And as you have heard in the hadith: "Every prophet has a hawari, and my hawari is al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7261) and Muslim (2415/48) from Jabir ibn 'Abdullah.] This is without doubt a virtue of al-Zubayr. But Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "If I were to take a close friend (khalil) from my Ummah, I would have taken Abu Bakr." [Reported by al-Bukhari (3656) from Ibn 'Abbas.]

* From the benefits of this noble verse: faith in Allah is not complete except with faith in His messengers; from His saying ﴿أَنْ آمِنُوا بِي وَبِرَسُولِي﴾. The Prophet (ﷺ) explained that faith is "to believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and to believe in divine decree, both its good and its bad." [Reported by Muslim (8/1) from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab.] These pillars are necessary in faith, so whoever lacks one of them is not a believer.

* From the benefits of this verse: the response of the disciples to what was revealed to them, when they said: "We believe."

* From the benefits of the verse: the permissibility of omitting what is known. From where? ﴿قَالُوا آمَنَّا﴾ without saying "in You and in Your messenger," because this is understood. The absolute is interpreted in light of the restricted when it is known. So if a person concludes a contract and mentions conditions at the offer, and the other says "I accept," or "I accept the sale," for example, and he says: "I sell you this house on condition that I live in it for a year," and the other says: "I accept the sale," does the condition hold? Yes, it holds, because the wording of the sale implies this condition even if it is not stated, since it is known from the context.

* From the benefits of this verse: the permissibility of establishing a matter by calling witnesses to it; from His saying ﴿اشْهَدْ بِأَنَّنَا مُسْلِمُونَ﴾. In the transmitted supplication: "O Allah, I have entered the evening calling You to witness, and calling to witness the bearers of Your Throne, Your angels, Your prophets, and all of Your creation, that You are Allah, there is no god but You, and that Muhammad is Your servant and Your messenger." [Reported by Abu Dawud (5069) and al-Tirmidhi (3501) from Anas ibn Malik, without the phrase "and Your prophets." In al-Mu'jam al-Awsat of al-Tabarani (9356): "and I call to witness Your angels, Your prophets and Your messengers, and all of Your creation, to my testimony against myself that I testify that You are Allah, there is no god but You."] This is among the morning and evening remembrances, though there is disagreement over the authenticity of the hadith.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: that faith is Islam. From His saying ﴿آمَنَّا وَاشْهَدْ بِأَنَّنَا مُسْلِمُونَ﴾ [al-Ma'idah 111]. They did not say "believers"; they said "Muslims," which indicates that faith is Islam. A group of scholars held this view and said there is no difference between Islam and faith, citing verses like this one, and also citing the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿فَأَخْرَجْنَا مَنْ كَانَ فِيهَا مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ (٣٥) فَمَا وَجَدْنَا فِيهَا غَيْرَ بَيْتٍ مِنَ الْمُسْلِمِينَ﴾ [al-Dhariyat 35, 36]. However, this view stated absolutely is open to question. The correct position is that when Islam is mentioned alone, it includes faith, and when it is mentioned together with faith, it has a different meaning. This distinction is shown by the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿قَالَتِ الْأَعْرَابُ آمَنَّا قُلْ لَمْ تُؤْمِنُوا وَلَكِنْ قُولُوا أَسْلَمْنَا وَلَمَّا يَدْخُلِ الْإِيمَانُ فِي قُلُوبِكُمْ﴾ [al-Hujurat 14], meaning it has not entered yet but it is close to entering, since "lamma" indicates negation with the nearness of what is negated. ﴿وَلَمَّا يَدْخُلِ الْإِيمَانُ فِي قُلُوبِكُمْ﴾. So how do we explain this verse? We explain it by saying that they combined faith and Islam, so faith is in the hearts and Islam is in the limbs, meaning they believed and submitted completely to the commands of Allah and His messenger.

Then He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿إِذْ قَالَ الْحَوَارِيُّونَ﴾ to the end [al-Ma'idah 112].

* From the benefits of this verse: that the disciples, despite being sincere, had some discourtesy; from their saying: ﴿يَا عِيسَى ابْنَ مَرْيَمَ﴾.

If someone says: perhaps their law permitted them to call their prophet by his name, unlike this law, since Allah says: ﴿لَا تَجْعَلُوا دُعَاءَ الرَّسُولِ بَيْنَكُمْ كَدُعَاءِ بَعْضِكُمْ بَعْضًا﴾ [al-Nur 63]? We say: let that be so, but is it good manners for them to address 'Isa ibn Maryam (peace be upon him) by his name, while they want him to ask Allah to send this table, or is it more fitting, since they want him to ask Allah, to call him by the description of prophethood and messengerhood, since that is more appropriate and closer to the answering of their request? The answer: the second, without doubt. In any case, this address certainly contains some discourtesy.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: that these disciples wanted from the signs what would fill their bellies. The evidence: the first thing they began with was eating: ﴿نُرِيدُ أَنْ نَأْكُلَ مِنْهَا﴾, as soon as they began. This resembles the saying of the Jews when they were told: ﴿ادْخُلُوا الْبَابَ سُجَّدًا﴾ [al-Nisa 154]. What did they do? They entered upon their posteriors, on their buttocks, saying "hintah" (wheat), when they were commanded to say "hittah" (meaning: remove our sins from us). But they said: no, we want something else, which is filling the belly: wheat. These resemble that, and the origin is one, O brothers, the origin is one; they are all from the Children of Israel, so it is no wonder that their requests are similar. And Allah knows best.
