* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan: ﴿وَإِذْ أَوْحَيْتُ إِلَى الْحَوَارِيِّينَ أَنْ آمِنُوا بِي وَبِرَسُولِي قَالُوا آمَنَّا وَاشْهَدْ بِأَنَّنَا مُسْلِمُونَ (١١١) إِذْ قَالَ الْحَوَارِيُّونَ يَا عِيسَى ابْنَ مَرْيَمَ هَلْ يَسْتَطِيعُ رَبُّكَ أَنْ يُنَزِّلَ عَلَيْنَا مَائِدَةً مِنَ السَّمَاءِ قَالَ اتَّقُوا اللَّهَ إِنْ كُنْتُمْ مُؤْمِنِينَ (١١٢) قَالُوا نُرِيدُ أَنْ نَأْكُلَ مِنْهَا وَتَطْمَئِنَّ قُلُوبُنَا وَنَعْلَمَ أَنْ قَدْ صَدَقْتَنَا وَنَكُونَ عَلَيْهَا مِنَ الشَّاهِدِينَ (١١٣) قَالَ عِيسَى ابْنُ مَرْيَمَ اللَّهُمَّ رَبَّنَا أَنْزِلْ عَلَيْنَا مَائِدَةً مِنَ السَّمَاءِ تَكُونُ لَنَا عِيدًا لِأَوَّلِنَا وَآخِرِنَا وَآيَةً مِنْكَ وَارْزُقْنَا وَأَنْتَ خَيْرُ الرَّازِقِينَ (١١٤) قَالَ اللَّهُ إِنِّي مُنَزِّلُهَا عَلَيْكُمْ فَمَنْ يَكْفُرْ بَعْدُ مِنْكُمْ فَإِنِّي أُعَذِّبُهُ عَذَابًا لَا أُعَذِّبُهُ أَحَدًا مِنَ الْعَالَمِينَ﴾ [al-Ma'idah 111-115].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿وَإِذْ أَوْحَيْتُ إِلَى الْحَوَارِيِّينَ﴾, and its tafsir has already been covered. Is this revelation to the disciples, or what?

* The student: There are two opinions: one is revelation through their prophet 'Isa; the second is inspiration.

* The Shaykh: That is, He revealed it to them through 'Isa.

* The student: Yes, and the second opinion is that it is inspiration.

* The Shaykh: That His revealing to them means inspiration.
Which of them is stronger?

* The student: We say the meaning includes both: legislative revelation and cosmic revelation.

* The Shaykh: Allah revealed to 'Isa a legislative revelation, and He revealed to them a decreed (qadari) revelation.
What is the meaning of al-hawariyyun?

* Student: The pure ones among his companions.

* The Shaykh: The pure ones among his companions.
The saying of Allah: ﴿هَلْ يَسْتَطِيعُ رَبُّكَ﴾ has two readings. Recite them.

* Student: ﴿هَلْ يَسْتَطِيعُ رَبُّكَ﴾ and ﴿هَلْ تَسْتَطِيعُ رَبَّكَ﴾.

* The Shaykh: ﴿هَلْ يَسْتَطِيعُ رَبُّكَ﴾ and ﴿هَلْ تَسْتَطِيعُ رَبَّكَ﴾.
On the first reading, is there a problem? This suggests they doubted Allah's power. What is the answer to that?

* Student: (...)

* The Shaykh: No, this example is not correct. It is like a man saying to his brother: "Can you walk with me? Can you go or come?" The point is that istita'ah means qudrah (ability). Another aspect?

* Student: That they believed in Allah's general power, but in the particular (...)

* The Shaykh: That is, they had faith in general power, but the power over a specific thing... this is one aspect of the answer. Second?

* Student: The meaning of ﴿هَلْ يَسْتَطِيعُ رَبُّكَ﴾ is: would your Lord obey you if you asked Him.

* Another student: They say it does not mean ability, but obedience: istita'ah means ita'ah.

* The Shaykh: Meaning?

* Student: Meaning, if you ask Him, i.e., can you ask Him.

* The Shaykh: That is, ﴿هَلْ يَسْتَطِيعُ رَبُّكَ﴾ means: would your Lord respond. This is the summary: would your Lord respond, from obedience in the sense of submission.

On the reading ﴿هَلْ تَسْتَطِيعُ رَبَّكَ﴾?

* Student: No problem.

* The Shaykh: No problem. What is the meaning?

* Student: That is, can you ask your Lord.

* The Shaykh: Can you ask your Lord? On this, there is no problem.

* Student: (...)

* The Shaykh: This resembles the saying of the Jews: "hintah," when they were told: "say hittah."

* From the benefits of this verse: that the occurrence of a thing gives more certainty than being informed about it. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The report is not like witnessing directly." [Reported by Ahmad (2447) from Ibn 'Abbas.] There are examples of this, including the saying of Ibrahim (peace be upon him): ﴿رَبِّ أَرِنِي كَيْفَ تُحْيِ الْمَوْتَى قَالَ أَوَلَمْ تُؤْمِنْ قَالَ بَلَى وَلَكِنْ لِيَطْمَئِنَّ قَلْبِي﴾ [al-Baqarah 260]. We take this from His saying: ﴿وَتَطْمَئِنَّ قُلُوبُنَا﴾.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: that the signs of the prophets increase their truthfulness in the hearts of people, from His saying: ﴿وَنَعْلَمَ أَنْ قَدْ صَدَقْتَنَا﴾, meaning you informed us of the truth.

* And from it: the establishment of a report by mass transmission (tawatur) and the multitude of reporters, from their saying: ﴿وَنَكُونَ عَلَيْهَا مِنَ الشَّاهِدِينَ﴾. This verse may also be used as evidence that the words of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) are true and binding, because they witnessed the Prophet (ﷺ) and witnessed his signs, and they were more certain of them than others and understood them better than others.

**Ibn ʿUthaymin's Tafsir al-Qurʾan al-Karim, on Surah 5, verse 114:**

﴿Jesus, son of Mary, said: "O Allah, our Lord, send down to us a table spread with food from the heaven.">﴾

**Grammatical analysis (iʿrab):** In His words ﴿O Allah, our Lord﴾, the word Allah (الله) is a vocative (munada, a noun being addressed) built on a final ḍamma, in a position of naṣb (accusative). The word Lord (رب) is either a substitute (badal) or an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayan). If you wish, you may treat it as a descriptive adjective (naʿt), but it has become mansub (accusative) because it is in a construct phrase (muḍaf). In His words ﴿that it may be a festival for us﴾, the clause is a descriptive clause modifying ﴿a table spread with food﴾, and ﴿a festival﴾ is the predicate of ﴿may be﴾, whose subject is a pronoun concealed within it. In His words ﴿for the first of us and the last of us﴾, the phrase is a substitute for the word ﴿for us﴾, but it is a substitute with the preposition repeated, which is a substitute of the governing element repeated, because the words ﴿for us﴾ include the first and the last. However, it came with detail in the phrase ﴿for the first of us and the last of us﴾. In His words ﴿and a sign from You﴾, the phrase is conjoined to ﴿a festival﴾. In His words ﴿and You are the best of providers﴾, the clause indicates that Allah, blessed and exalted, is described by this attribute. ﴿Provide for us﴾ (ارزقنا) is an imperative verb. But is an imperative directed to Allah called an imperative verb? It is not called that, out of courtesy toward Allah, but it is called a verb of request, a verb of asking, or something similar.

﴿Jesus, son of Mary, said: "O Allah, our Lord, send down to us a table spread with food from the heaven"﴾: that is, Jesus son of Mary said, responding to the request of these disciples (ḥawāriyyūn), asking Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to send down to them a table spread with food from the heaven. The word heaven (al-samāʾ) may mean the height, or it may mean the heaven itself, which is the protected ceiling, as has been mentioned previously.

﴿that it may be a festival for us﴾: that is, we will commemorate it whenever its time comes, because a festival (ʿīd) is a name for what returns and recurs. From this come the legislated festivals: the Festival of Fast-Breaking (ʿĪd al-Fiṭr), the Festival of Sacrifice (ʿĪd al-Aḍḥā), and the weekly festival (ʿĪd al-Usbūʿ).

His words ﴿for the first of us and the last of us﴾: the first of them are those who were in the time of Jesus, and the last of them are those who came after him.

﴿and a sign from You﴾: that is, a sign of Your power, Your hearing and Your knowledge, and a sign of the truthfulness of Jesus, peace be upon him, because these people requested the sign so that they might know that Jesus had told them the truth.

﴿And provide for us﴾: that is, give us, because provision (rizq) means giving. From this is the words of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿then provide for them from it﴾ [al-Nisāʾ 4:8], meaning: give them from it.

﴿and You are the best of providers﴾: that is, You are the best of those who give in terms of quantity and quality. No one is more generous than Allah, and no one is more bountiful than Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

* There are benefits in this verse, among them: that the prophets, peace be upon them, cannot bring everything that is asked of them, and that they, like others, are in need of Allah, asking Him and turning to Him.

* Another benefit of this verse: it is appropriate for a person, when supplicating, to mention these two meanings, divinity (ulūhiyyah) and lordship (rubūbiyyah), as shown by His words ﴿O Allah, our Lord﴾, because this is a kind of tawassul (seeking nearness through a means), in which a person seeks nearness through the divinity and lordship of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

* Another benefit of this noble verse: Jesus, peace be upon him, answered the disciples with complete trustworthiness, because he said ﴿Our Lord, send down to us a table spread with food from the heaven﴾, just as they had said: ﴿Can your Lord send down to us a table spread with food from the heaven?﴾.

* Another benefit of this noble verse: this table would be a festival for the Christians; whenever its time comes, it is a festival for them. If someone says: does this mean that we should say, whenever the times of occasions pass, we make them festivals? The answer is no, because these matters have no basis for analogy (qiyās). And it was a festival at the request of whom? At the request of their prophet, at the request of their prophet, peace be upon him.

* Another benefit of this noble verse: whatever comes contrary to what is customary and is beyond the normal course of events is a sign, as shown by His words ﴿and a sign from You﴾. The reasoning is that it was not known for a table to descend from the heaven visibly before people who could see it. Therefore its descent, especially since it was in response to a request after a proposal, is a sign and an evidence of the truthfulness of the one who speaks of the message.

* Another benefit of this noble verse: Jesus son of Mary is in need of Allah, the Exalted, of His giving. From this benefit follows the invalidity of the Christians' claim that he is a god.

* Another benefit of this noble verse: Allah, blessed and exalted, is the best of providers. This is one instance of a general rule, namely the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And to Allah belongs the highest description﴾ [al-Naḥl 16:60]. So every attribute of perfection belongs to Allah in its highest form.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: the application of the word provision (rizq) to other than Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. That is, it is correct to describe other than Allah as a provider, because provision means giving. But the most complete and perfect provision is the provision of Allah, blessed and exalted.

Allah the Exalted said: "Indeed, I will send it down to you," (in one reading: "Munziluhā ʿalaykum" [the active participle with tanwīn]). "Then whoever disbelieves afterwards" (baʿdu), meaning after its sending down. Baʿdu is built on ḍamm (indeclinable on the ḍamma) because the genitive complement (muḍāf ilayhi) has been omitted while its meaning is intended. Qabl and baʿd, when the muḍāf ilayhi is omitted and its meaning is intended, are built on ḍamm; when it is omitted and its wording is intended, they are inflected without tanwīn; when it is omitted and neither its wording nor its meaning is intended, they are inflected with tanwīn. For example, if you say: "Lillāhi al-amru min qablu wa min baʿdu" [Ar-Rum 4], here the muḍāf ilayhi is omitted and its meaning is intended. In the poet's verse:

fasāgha lī al-sharābu wa kuntu qablan ∗∗∗ akādu aghuṣṣu bi-al-māʾi al-furātī
here neither its wording nor its meaning is intended. And if you say: "Sa-azūruka min qabli wa min baʿdi majīʾi fulān," the first (qabli) has its muḍāf ilayhi omitted with its wording intended, and the second (baʿdi) has the muḍāf ilayhi present.

So either the muḍāf ilayhi is omitted or it is present with qabl, baʿd and their counterparts. If the muḍāf ilayhi is present, they are inflected without tanwīn; if it is omitted and its wording is intended, they are also inflected without tanwīn; if it is omitted and its meaning is intended, they are built on ḍamm; and if it is omitted and neither its wording nor its meaning is intended, they are inflected with tanwīn. The cases are therefore four.

Allah the Exalted says: "Then whoever disbelieves afterwards" — from which of the cases is this? What is it? It is: the muḍāf ilayhi is omitted and its meaning is intended.

"Then I will punish him" (fa-innī uʿadhdhibuhu): the fa is the connective of the response, the response to the conditional in "fa-man yakfur" (whoever disbelieves). It is connected by the fa because the clause is nominal, and whenever the conditional clause is nominal it must be linked with fa or with the sudden idhā. "Fa-innī" has two readings: "fa-innī" and "fa-innīya." As for the sukūn reading, the yāʾ is built on sukūn; as for the fatḥa reading, it is built on fatḥa because it is a first-person pronoun.

"I will punish him with a punishment (ʿadhāban) with which I will not punish anyone of the worlds" (lā uʿadhdhibuhu aḥadan min al-ʿālamīn): the pronoun in "lā uʿadhdhibuhu" — I mean the hāʾ — refers to what? To the punishment: that is, I will not punish anyone with such a punishment. "Aḥadan min al-ʿālamīn" — (uʿadhdhibu) here takes two objects. Are their origins a subject and predicate or not? No; for if you delete the governing verb and make the object pronoun in "lā uʿadhdhibuhu" a nominative pronoun, it would not be correct: if you said "huwa aḥad" it would not be valid, because the pronoun refers to the punishment.

We begin the explanation of the verse: Allah the Exalted says: "Allah said: Indeed I will send it down to you," and in a reading "munziluhā." Is this for the present or the future? That is, did Allah the Exalted promise to send it down and send it down? Or was it a promise that was not fulfilled, because Allah made a condition that the Children of Israel did not fulfil?

On this there are two opinions among the scholars. Some said: Allah sent it down, because His promise is true and He does not fail in His promise; Allah said: "Indeed I will send it down to you," or "munziluhā," then He threatened whoever disbelieved after the sending down of this sign. Others said: He did not send it down, because Allah made a condition, saying: "Whoever disbelieves afterwards among you, then I will punish him." When they saw this heavy condition, which is difficult to meet, they turned away from their request, so the table was not sent down. These supported their view by saying that the Christians know nothing of this table in their books, and they said: if it had been sent down, it would have been a festival for its first and last, as ʿIsā peace be upon him requested. Since they had no knowledge of this table, we know that they did not accept the condition Allah stipulated, so Allah the Exalted did not send it down. In reality the verse is open to interpretation; a person cannot be certain of either.

If someone says: Why do we not conclude that it was not sent down, since it is not found in their books?

The answer to this is simple: perhaps it is among what was forgotten and abandoned of the religion of the Christians, so they had no knowledge of it. Allah knows whether it was sent down or not. Whenever a verse may carry two meanings equally with no preference, then if they are not contradictory, both are taken; if they are contradictory, one suspends judgment. Here, in my view, the verse is open to whether it was sent down or not.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation that Allah the Exalted speaks; based on His saying: "Allah said: Indeed I will send it down to you."

* Among them: that the speech of Allah, blessed and exalted, is with letters and sound, because He, exalted, spoke a word that reached them, and it cannot reach them except by sound.

* Among them: that the speech of Allah is with letters, indeed with successive letters; because Allah said: "Indeed I will send it down to you, so whoever disbelieves," and these are successive letters with no difficulty.

* Among them: the affirmation of Allah's voluntary actions, meaning that He, exalted, does what He wills by choice without compulsion; for this speech arranged in letters — is it an action or not? It is both action and speech: from the perspective of its origination it is an action, and from the perspective that it is speech, it is utterance.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the danger of nations asking for signs, and that if the requested signs come, they have exposed themselves to destruction. The people of knowledge, may Allah have mercy on them, have mentioned that whenever a nation asks for a specific sign and it comes to them, the punishment becomes due upon them.

If someone says: This rule is broken by what is widely reported about the splitting of the moon: that the Quraysh asked the Prophet ﷺ for a sign, and he showed them the splitting of the moon?

The answer to this: the Quraysh did not ask for a specific sign; they asked for a sign only, and the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, is the one who specified it: he showed them the splitting of the moon.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation that punishment has a higher and a lower degree; based on His saying: "I will punish him with a punishment with which I will not punish anyone of the worlds." This is evidence that punishment varies from one person to another, and the causes of the variation in punishment are many. Among them: the paucity of the motive to sin, for the paucity of the motive to sin requires a more severe punishment for it. Consider the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Three whom Allah will not speak to on the Day of Resurrection, nor look at, nor purify, and for them is a painful punishment": they are "an aged adulterer, a proud poor man, and a man who made Allah his merchandise: he sells only with his right hand and buys only with his right hand."[[Narrated by al-Ṭabarānī in al-Muʿjam al-Kabīr (6111) and al-Awsaṭ (5577), from the hadith of Salman al-Farisi.]]

The first and second evidences:

"Ushaymiṭ" and "zān," meaning a man whom grey hair has overtaken, and this indicates the weakness of his strength in seeking marriage. He diminished him by saying "Ushaymiṭ," to belittle him. Thus the adultery of an old man is a greater punishment than the adultery of a young man, because the motive in the old man is less.

"ʿĀʾil mustakbir": ʿāʾil means poor; mustakbir means arrogant. The poor man should know himself and his station, so how can he be arrogant? Arrogance from the rich is undoubtedly easier and expected, as the Exalted said: "Nay, indeed man transgresses, when he sees himself self-sufficient" [Al-ʿAlaq 6, 7], meaning self-sufficient from others. This man is poor yet arrogant! Therefore his punishment is intensified. Whenever the cause of seeking disobedience is strong, the punishment for it becomes lighter, and whenever the seeking is weak, the punishment for it becomes more severe. Here Allah the Exalted explains that He will not punish him with anyone of the worlds.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the disbelief of those who saw the signs is not like the disbelief of those who did not see them. Which is greater? The former: he who saw the signs, for whoever has seen the signs has seen them with certainty of knowledge, indeed with the certainty of sight; and whoever has had them conveyed to him has known them with certainty of knowledge, that is, through an intermediary.

In the verse there is a reading: "Innī munzilu-hā ʿalaykum," and in it: "Fa-innīya uʿadhdhibuhu."

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 5, verse 116 (part 1 of 2):

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And when Allah says, "O Jesus, son of Mary, did you say to the people, 'Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah'?"﴾ The object of the verb "qala" (said) is His words: ﴿Did you say﴾, so the clause is in the accusative position. Know that the object of a verb of saying is only ever a clause, unless the verb is treated as a verb of thinking (ujri majra al-zann), in which case it may govern a single noun. Otherwise it is only a clause. So where is the clause here?

﴿Did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah"?﴾ In ﴿أَأَنْتَ﴾ there are two readings: ﴿آانْتَ﴾ with the second hamza lengthened (madd), and with shortening (qasr). In ﴿أَأَنْتَ قُلْتَ لِلنَّاسِ اتَّخِذُونِي وَأُمِّيَ﴾ there are two readings: ﴿أُمِّي﴾ and ﴿أُمِّيَ﴾. The verb (ittakhadha, "to take") takes two objects. The first object in this verse is the ya' in His words ﴿اتَّخِذُونِي﴾ ("take me"), and the second is His words ﴿إِلَهَيْنِ مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ﴾ ("two gods besides Allah").

﴿He said: "Glory be to You"﴾ meaning: exalted are You, far above what is unfitting. It is in the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) of a verb that must be omitted, which is why you never find a verb together with (subhan). We say it is an absolute object because the verbal noun is (tasbih), and every word that carries the meaning of the verbal noun without containing its letters is called an absolute object, and is called an ism masdar (noun of verbal noun).

﴿Glory be to You; it is not for me to say what I have no right to say.﴾ The ba' in His words ﴿بِحَقٍّ﴾ ("with truth") is a superfluous (za'ida) preposition. By "superfluous" I mean in terms of grammatical analysis (i'rab), since nothing in the Qur'an is superfluous in meaning at all; it is superfluous only grammatically, while in meaning it carries a great significance, which is emphasis (tawkid). How do we parse ﴿بِحَقٍّ﴾?

* The student: ﴿بِحَقٍّ﴾ is a predicate of (laysa) in the accusative, and the sign of its accusative is a presumed fatha on its final letter, prevented from appearing by the occupation of the position by the movement of the superfluous preposition.
* The Shaykh: A presumed fatha on its final letter, prevented from appearing by the occupation of the position by the movement of the superfluous preposition. Where is the subject of (laysa)?
* A student: Concealed (mustatir).
* The Shaykh: Concealed. It refers to what?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Well done. ﴿If I had said it, You would surely have known it﴾: this is a conditional sentence. The protasis (fi'l al-shart) is ﴿kuntu﴾, the ta' is the subject of kana, and ﴿faqad 'alimtahu﴾ is the apodosis (jawab al-shart). It is joined with the fa' because the response is introduced by (qad).

Then He says: ﴿You know what is in my soul, and I do not know what is in Your soul﴾. The grammar is clear.

﴿Indeed, You, You are the Knower of the unseen﴾. The clause is resumptive (isti'nafiyya), affirming the all-encompassing knowledge of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And when Allah says, "O Jesus, son of Mary"﴾ mean: mention, O Muhammad, to these people what was spoken by Allah to Jesus, ﴿O Jesus, son of Mary﴾. This saying will take place on the Day of Resurrection. ﴿Did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah"?﴾ There is no doubt that the interrogation here is not meant to seek information, since Allah the Exalted knows. Rather it is meant as rebuke (tawbikh). Rebuke of whom? Rebuke of those who said that Jesus and his mother are two gods. It is similar to the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿When the buried infant girl is asked, for what sin was she killed?﴾ [al-Takwir 8-9]. She had done nothing, but she is asked as a rebuke to those who did it. Likewise here, ﴿Did you say to the people﴾ is a rebuke of those who made Jesus and his mother two gods besides Allah.

As for ﴿أَأَنْتَ قُلْتَ لِلنَّاسِ﴾, the scholars of rhetoric (balagha) say there is a difference between saying "a-anta qulta" and "a-qulta". They say: when the thing questioned about comes after the interrogative hamza in the form of a noun, the aim is specification (ta'yin), specifying the doer. When the verb comes after the hamza, the aim is specifying the event that occurred. If you say, "a-qama Zayd?" you are asking about what? About the event that occurred, i.e., whether he stood or is sitting. If you say, "a-Zayd al-qa'im?" that is specifying the doer. Here, ﴿Did you say to the people﴾ specifies what? The doer. ﴿Did you say to the people, "Take me"﴾, i.e., make me ﴿and my mother two gods besides Allah﴾, i.e., objects of worship.

His words ﴿besides Allah﴾ mean: other than Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Jesus, peace be upon him, answered: ﴿Glory be to You﴾, meaning: exalted are You; I declare You free of what is not fitting for You, and it is not fitting for Allah to have a partner in worship, just as He has no partner in dominion.

Know that the glorification of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, concerns two things: first, deficiency; second, resemblance to created beings. Resemblance to created beings, although it is a deficiency, should nonetheless be explicitly stated.

﴿It is not for me to say what I have no right to say﴾: ﴿مَا يَكُونُ لِي﴾ means "it is not possible for me," and negating "to be" in this way means it is impossible. ﴿أَنْ أَقُولَ﴾ means to say to the people ﴿what I have no right to say﴾, because it is not Jesus' right to tell the people: take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah. Rather, his mission was precisely to forbid polytheism and to devote worship to Allah alone. ﴿If I had said it, You would surely have known it﴾: this sentence shows that Jesus, peace be upon him, knew that if he had said such a thing, Allah would have known it, and that is true. It will come, Allah willing, in the benefits (fawa'id) that this is a denunciation of those who worship Jesus: that had he told the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah," Allah would have known it and would not have allowed him to make this claim.

His words ﴿You know what is in my soul, and I do not know what is in Your soul﴾: the word "soul" (nafs) here means the essence (dhat). It means that what is in my soul You know, and what is in Your soul I do not know. The difference is evident, because Allah is the Creator and Jesus is a created being; the Creator knows His creation, and the created being knows about its Creator only what He has informed it of. To this points the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Should not He who created know? And He is the Subtle, the All-Aware﴾ [al-Mulk 14].

﴿Indeed, You, You are the Knower of the unseen﴾: this clause is resumptive, a confirmation of what preceded it.

* Student: In the words of the Exalted: ﴿I will punish him with a punishment that I will not inflict upon anyone among the worlds﴾, is it not permissible to say that this refers to the worlds of their time (alamin zamanihim)?
* The Shaykh: If there is evidence for this, there is no harm, as in His words: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My blessing which I bestowed upon you and that I preferred you over the worlds﴾ [al-Baqarah 47]. But if no evidence indicates it, the default is generality.
* The student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: Do you have any doubt about the message of Muhammad?
* The student: No.
* The Shaykh: You have no doubt, but when you come, say: "O Allah, grant me a table that is sufficient for you, the table of the earth."
* Student: May Allah be good to you. If a caller (da'iyah) asks Allah, glorified is He, to show people a miracle (karamah) of his, that people see the truthfulness of his call?
* The Shaykh: This is not appropriate except in a context of challenge (tahaddi). In a context of challenge there is no harm, as is reported of Khalid ibn al-Walid, may Allah be pleased with him, that he ate poison.[[Narrated by al-Tabarani in al-Kabir (3809).]] But without a challenge, no. Be patient and do not hasten the signs until your call is complete. Perhaps Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has delayed from you the signs that testify to your truthfulness, which are the miracles, since signs for the friends of Allah are miracles. It may be for the elevation of your rank and for your patience. But in a context of challenge, yes.
* Student: Glorifying Allah above deficiencies and defects, and glorifying Allah above resemblance to His creation. We said that resemblance to His creation should be explicitly stated. How is this?
* The Shaykh: Lest someone think that the perfection in the Creator is like the perfection in the created being, and however deficient the created being may be, we must say of the created being (...).
* Student: The context of the verse, O Shaykh, in the words of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿Indeed I will send it down﴾. Is it not, O Shaykh, for emphasis, and the punishment is a threat for their disobedience?
* The Shaykh: Yes, this is among what favours that it was sent down. But the fact that it is not mentioned in the books of the Christians and they do not know it, and that Jesus asked Allah that it be a feast for the first and last of them, poses a difficulty for this. This is not a distant difficulty, since it may be said that Allah the Exalted did not grant Jesus everything he asked, namely that it be a feast for the first and last of them.
* Student: The reports that Ibn Kathir mentioned, that it was sent down with a great fish upon it, from Ka'b al-Ahbar...
* The Shaykh: No, these are Isra'iliyyat. These are among the Isra'iliyyat which it would have been better for Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, to leave out.
* Student: Would these not be from their books, which indicate these things?
* The Shaykh: I do not know; the Gospels that are in their hands do not contain mention of the table.
* Student: Transgression in supplication is asking for something that is impossible in terms of existence (kawnan). What is an example of what is impossible in existence?
* The Shaykh: What is impossible in existence is to ask Allah, the Exalted, to make one a changer of creation, because this is impossible, since none possesses the power to change except Allah, Mighty and Majestic.
* Student: And if it were possible for him to breathe spirit into things, and so on.
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed, this too, if we look at the capacity of a human being. But if it is in the hand of Allah, then Allah is capable of all things.
* Student: So it is not permissible to ask Allah to empower him to do this thing.
* The Shaykh: No, it is not permissible, or rather it is impermissible by the Law, such as saying: "O Allah, make me a prophet." This is not permissible.
* Student: When "nafs" occurs in the Qur'an, is it to be understood as the essence (dhat)?
* The Shaykh: "Nafs," yes, this is the case; as in His words: ﴿Because of that, We prescribed for the Children of Israel that whoever kills a soul without a soul...﴾ [al-Ma'idah 32], and He said: ﴿the soul for the soul﴾ [al-Ma'idah 45]. So "nafs" here means the essence (dhat).
* Student: Regarding Jesus, peace be upon him, he had signs such as raising the dead and healing the blind and leper, but the Christians say that the mother of Jesus, Mary, was a harlot (baghiyya), a fornicator. How did they take her as a god alongside Jesus?
* The Shaykh: What?
* The student: These Christians, some of them say that Mary, the mother of Jesus, was a harlot, meaning she used to commit fornication. How did they take her as a god alongside Jesus?
* The Shaykh: Because they are among the most misguided of people in religion and the most foolish of people in intellect, the Christians.
* Student: Now, O Shaykh, some Christians hold that Mary committed fornication with...
* The Shaykh: What?
* The student: Among the Christians there are sects.
* The Shaykh: Sects, without doubt.
* The student: And some of them say that Mary was a harlot, because Mary means the fornicator; some Christians say this.
* The Shaykh: No, this is the Jews. No, the Christians do not say this; those who said that were the Jews.
* Student: May Allah bless you, O our Shaykh. Is it the Jews who distorted the religion of the Christians?
* The Shaykh: No, even the rabbis among the Christians; even the Christians distorted it. Now, I have not read the Gospels, but the Gospels, they say, contain much disagreement; each claims that this Gospel is the one that was revealed to Jesus.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: It is not far-fetched. I say: this is not far-fetched.

* * *

* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate: ﴿And when Allah says, "O Jesus, son of Mary, did you say to the people, 'Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah'?" He will say, "Glory be to You; it is not for me to say what I have no right to say. If I had said it, You would surely have known it. You know what is in my soul, and I do not know what is in Your soul. Indeed, You, You are the Knower of the unseen." (116) "I said to them only what You commanded me: 'Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord.' And I was a witness over them as long as I was among them; but when You took me up, You were the Watcher over them, and You are Witness over all things. (117) If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, indeed You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise."﴾ [al-Ma'idah 116-118].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And when Allah says, "O Jesus, son of Mary, did you say to the people, 'Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah'?"﴾ Let us take the benefits:

* In this noble verse: affirmation of speech for Allah (﴿إِذْ قَالَ اللَّهُ﴾). In the Qur'an there is affirmation of speech, of word, of calling, and of intimate address, and all of this indicates that Allah speaks with genuine speech, with letters and sound. This is the doctrine of the People of the Sunnah and the Community, which we believe and by which we hold ourselves accountable to Allah, and which is obligatory for every believer.

* Among the benefits of this verse: that the speech of Allah is with letters and sound. As for its being with letters, it is because the words that come after "said" are letters. As for its being with sound, it is because Allah the Exalted addresses Jesus with it, and Jesus responds to Him, which shows that it is audible speech, so it is with sound. These are two great benefits.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the rebuke of those who took Jesus and his mother as gods, from His words: ﴿Did you say to the people?﴾, since it has already been established that the purpose of this interrogation is rebuke of those who took Jesus and his mother as two gods.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the distance of the messengers, peace be upon them, from polytheism, from His words: ﴿Glory be to You; it is not for me to say what I have no right to say﴾, and this is an accepted matter, since the origin of sending the messengers is the realization of monotheism.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the glorification of Allah, blessed and exalted, from having any partner, from His words: ﴿Glory be to You﴾; since we said "(subhanaka)" means: I declare You exalted above everything unfitting for You, and the context now is the taking of a partner, so its meaning is the glorification of Allah above every partner.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: Jesus, peace be upon him, acknowledges what he does not deserve, from His words: ﴿It is not for me to say what I have no right to say﴾. Likewise his brethren among the messengers; for the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him and his family, when a man said to him: "What Allah wills and you will," said to him: "Have you made me an equal to Allah? Rather, what Allah alone wills,"[[Narrated by Ahmad (1839) from Ibn 'Abbas, with the wording: "Have you made me and Allah a rival?"]] so all the messengers know their own worth and cannot affirm what they do not deserve.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that divinity is a right specific to Allah, from His words: ﴿what I have no right to say﴾. If the messengers, indeed the best of the messengers, have no share in divinity, then others are even less entitled to it. No one deserves to be a god, and no one deserves to be worshipped besides Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah, glorified and exalted, knows what proceeds from a person of speech, from His words: ﴿If I had said it, You would surely have known it﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the good manners of the messengers, peace be upon them, with their Lord, Majestic is He, from His words: ﴿If I had said it, You would surely have known it﴾; and if You knew it, then it proceeds from Your knowledge, O Lord, and from Your decree and destiny, and nothing is hidden from You.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the application of the word "nafs" to the essence. Indeed some scholars say that applying "dhat" to "nafs" is an error, and that the original sense of "dhat" is "possessor," so it is only used in a construct form, as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿By the sky with its constellations (dhat al-buruj)﴾ [al-Buruj 1], i.e., possessing constellations; and that the application of "dhat" to "nafs" is among the newly coined expressions. Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, stated this explicitly and said that it is not from the speech of the pure Arabs; rather the essence is expressed by "nafs," meaning that the essence of a man is himself. But terminology is one thing, and classical Arabic is another.

So the meaning of His words ﴿You know what is in my soul, and I do not know what is in Your soul﴾ is: what is in my essence, and I do not know what is in Your essence. The soul is not something additional to the essence, unlike knowledge, power, hearing, sight and the like. As for the saying of some scholars that Allah affirmed for Himself a soul when He said ﴿You know what is in my soul, and I do not know what is in Your soul﴾, it is by way of leniency and figurative usage; otherwise, the soul of Allah is the very essence of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Benefits of this noble verse:

* Among its benefits: the affirmation of Allah's knowledge of what is in a person's soul, based on His words: ﴿You know what is in my soul﴾. This is like His saying: ﴿And We have certainly created man and know what his soul whispers to him﴾ [Qaf 16]. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, knows what is in your heart. Beware lest there be in your heart what opposes the command of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

* From here we derive a second benefit: the obligation of khushu' (humble attentiveness) in prayer, because if you become heedless and think about things unrelated to the prayer, you have turned away from Allah, Mighty and Majestic. This is what some scholars have affirmed. However, regarding the question of the obligation of khushu' in prayer, there is room for examination, because the Prophet ﷺ informed that: "When the prayer is called, Shaytan turns away and has a loud noise (passing wind). When the call to prayer ends, he comes back to the worshipper and begins to whisper to him, until he says: 'Remember such-and-such, on such-and-such a day,' so that he does not know how many (units) he has prayed, three or four." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3285) and Muslim (389/83), from the hadith of Abu Hurairah.]

It may be said: the Prophet ﷺ was reporting an actual occurrence, and reporting that something occurs does not imply that it is permissible, just as he informed us that we would follow the ways of those before us, the Jews and Christians [al-Tirmidhi (2180), and Ahmad in al-Musnad (21897), with its wording, from the hadith of Abu Waqid al-Laythi], yet this is not lawful for us; and just as he informed that a woman traveling (the Zaʿina) goes alone from such-and-such place to such-and-such place [al-Bukhari (3595), from the hadith of 'Adi ibn Hatim], yet it is not lawful for a woman to travel without a mahram. But what appears to me is that making khushu' in prayer obligatory involves hardship; that is, for a person not to have any passing thought or whisper is an extreme hardship.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: we do not know what is with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, so we do not know what is in His essence of what He decrees and wills, and we know of Allah's will only through the occurrence of what is willed. That is, we do not know that Allah willed rain to fall until the rain falls, and we do not know that Allah, Exalted, has decreed wars to occur among people until these wars occur. So when they occur, we know that Allah willed them, since nothing exists in His dominion that He does not will.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of the knowledge of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, of the unseen (al-ghayb), based on His words: ﴿Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen﴾. The meaning of ﴿'Allam al-ghuyub﴾ (the Knower of the unseen realities) is that You are described with this, and the intent is not multiplicity but emphasis in this attribute, regardless of its individual instances, since they cannot be counted. Some scholars have mentioned that whatever comes in the intensive form (sigha al-mubalagha) regarding Allah does not mean multiplicity but perfection; yet whoever reflects will find that it comes for this and that.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: whoever claims knowledge of the unseen has claimed to be a partner with Allah. The evidence is that He used the separating pronoun (damir al-fasl) in ﴿Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen﴾, and the separating pronoun indicates what? It indicates restriction (al-hasr); that is, You alone, and no other, are the Knower of the unseen. Let it be known that the unseen is of two kinds: relative unseen (ghayb nisbi) and absolute unseen (ghayb mutlaq). So what is the unseen that Allah has exclusively? It is the absolute unseen. As for the relative unseen, which one person knows and another does not, this is shared in its knowledge by the one who decreed it, who is Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and by the one to whom it occurred.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 5, verse 117:**

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿I did not say to them except what You commanded me: "Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord."﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:117] ﴿I did not say to them﴾, i.e., to the people, ﴿except what You commanded me, [to say]: "Worship Allah"﴾. The ﴿أَنِ﴾ (an) here is explanatory (tafsiriyyah), because it comes after a phrase that contains the meaning of speech but not its letters, namely ﴿أَمَرْتَنِي﴾ ("You commanded me").

﴿"Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord"﴾. ﴿رَبِّي﴾ (rabbi, "my Lord") is either a substitute (badal) or a qualifier (sifah) of the word ﴿اللَّهَ﴾ (Allah).

﴿And I was a witness over them as long as I remained among them﴾. Its i'rab (grammatical analysis) is clear, and there is no difficulty in it except the phrase ﴿مَا دُمْتُ فِيهِمْ﴾ (ma dumtu fihim). Indeed, (ma dama) functions like (kana) when it is preceded by the temporal ﴿مَا﴾ (ma masdariyyah, the "ma" that forms a verbal noun with a time sense). But if it is preceded by the negative ﴿مَا﴾ (ma nafiyah), then it is not one of the sisters of (kana). So if you say: ما دمت قائمًا (ma dumtu qa'imen), meaning "I did not stand in a continuous standing," then this ﴿مَا﴾ is negative.

And if you say: لا أجلس ما دمت قائمًا (la ajlisu ma dumtu qa'imen, "I will not sit as long as I am standing"), then this ﴿مَا﴾ is temporal masdariyyah. The last clause is affirmative and the first clause is negative.

Here, is it temporal masdariyyah? Yes. Accordingly, the ﴿تَ﴾ (ta') is its subject (ism), and the prepositional phrase ﴿عَلَيْهِمْ/فِيهِمْ﴾ is its predicate (khabar).

﴿So when You caused me to die, You were the Watcher over them, and You are Witness over all things﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:117]. There is no difficulty in its i'rab.

Isa, peace be upon him, says: ﴿I did not say to them except what You commanded me﴾, meaning: except that which You commanded me. And what is it? ﴿"Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord"﴾. He placed the phrase ﴿إِلَّا مَا أَمَرْتَنِي بِهِ﴾ before saying ﴿أَنِ اعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ﴾ in order to show that he, peace be upon him, was a messenger who conveys what he was commanded. So he began with what indicates the messengerhood and that he was commanded, before mentioning what he was sent with.

And his saying ﴿أَمَرْتَنِي بِهِ﴾ means: You assigned me to convey it as a command from You.

﴿"Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord"﴾. ﴿اعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ﴾ (u'budu Allah, "worship Allah"). The word ʿibadah (worship) is used in two senses. The first sense is the act of worshipping (ta'abbud). The second sense is that by which one worships (al-mutaʿabbad bihi, the act of worship itself). So if you say: "Prayer is worship," the intended meaning is the second sense. And if you say: "This man prayed to worship Allah, the Mighty and Majestic," the intended meaning is his own act of worship.

His saying ﴿أَنِ اعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ رَبِّي وَرَبَّكُمْ﴾, and his saying ﴿رَبِّي وَرَبَّكُمْ﴾ ("my Lord and your Lord"), serves to prove to them that he is not a lord.

﴿And I was a witness over them as long as I remained among them﴾, meaning: I was testifying over them concerning what they held of tawhid (monotheism) and sincerity.

﴿As long as I remained among them﴾, meaning: the duration of my remaining among them. ﴿So when You caused me to die﴾, i.e., You took me. It is said: تَوَفَّى الرجل حقَّه (tawaffa al-rajul haqqahu), meaning he took his due in full.

﴿You were the Watcher over them﴾, i.e., You are the Observer who preserves their deeds, witnesses them, and knows them.

﴿And You are Witness over all things﴾. This is generalization after specification: meaning, You are a witness over everything, including their actions and other things.

* In the verse there are benefits. Among them: the messengers, peace be upon them, are charged with conveying the message as a command from Allah, as shown by His saying ﴿مَا أَمَرْتَنِي بِهِ﴾ ("what You commanded me"). There are many evidences for this in the Qur'an, such as the saying of Allah the Exalted to His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord. And if you do not, then you have not conveyed His message﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:67].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the good manners of the messengers toward Allah, the Exalted, in that he said ﴿إِلَّا مَا أَمَرْتَنِي بِهِ﴾ ("except what You commanded me"). The reason is that it indicates that Isa is a messenger who was commanded and charged with a mission.

* Among its benefits: Isa, peace be upon him, was commanded to convey to the people that he is a servant and that Allah the Exalted is the Lord, as shown by His saying ﴿أَنِ اعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ رَبِّي وَرَبَّكُمْ﴾ ("Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord"). The lord is contrasted with the servant.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: Isa has no right to divinity (uluhiyyah) or lordship (rububiyyah), as shown by His saying ﴿رَبِّي﴾ ("my Lord"). Whoever does not possess lordship does not possess divinity.

If someone says: Did he not give life to the dead and heal the blind and the leper? The answer: Yes, but by the permission of Allah.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the messengers, peace be upon them, are witnesses over their nations as long as they remain among them, as shown by His saying ﴿And I was a witness over them as long as I remained among them﴾. And yet they are witnesses concerning what they see or hear, and not witnesses concerning a distant unseen matter that they neither see nor hear, because the messengers do not know the unseen.

* Among the benefits of this verse: that Isa, peace be upon him, was caused to die by Allah, as shown by His saying ﴿So when You caused me to die﴾. There are verses about this, among them the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿When Allah said: "O Isa, I will take you and raise you to Me and purify you from those who disbelieve"﴾ [Ali 'Imran 3:55], and so on to its end. Thus He affirmed that He would cause him to die.

The scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, have differed concerning this death (wafat). It was said that it means taking (qabd), and that it does not necessarily entail sleep or death. The use of tawaffi in the sense of taking is attested in the Arabic language, since it is said: تَوَفَّى الرجل حقَّه, meaning he took his due. On this meaning there is no difficulty in the verse at all.

Others said that it is a real death. These people denied the descent of Isa at the end of time, and they said: He died as the prophets died. This is a false view, refuted by the apparent meaning of the Qur'an and the explicit Sunnah.

The third view: the intended meaning of wafat is sleep, that Allah the Exalted cast sleep upon him and then raised him to the heaven. This view has some basis, but it is not very apparent. If this interpretation is correct, it shows that Muhammad (ﷺ) was stronger in heart than Isa, because Muhammad was taken up to the heavens while awake, and he witnessed of the signs of Allah what he witnessed, whereas Isa was cast into sleep by Allah and then raised, because he was going to witness wondrous and great creations, and the distance was great.

So we have three views. The first view: that it is death, and this is weak. The second: that it is sleep, and this has some basis. The third: that it means taking, because sleep is an additional matter beyond taking, so establishing it requires clear evidence. The third view, that it means taking, has no difficulty in it.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the all-encompassing knowledge of Allah, the Blessed and Exalted, and His watchfulness, as shown by His saying ﴿You were the Watcher over them﴾.

If someone says: Allah said: ﴿Not a word does he utter but that with him is an observer, ready﴾ [Qaf 50:18], and the intended one is the angel. How then do we reconcile the two verses?

The answer: Allah is a watcher over them through His angels, as in His saying: ﴿And We are closer to him than his jugular vein. When the two receivers receive, seated on the right and on the left﴾ [Qaf 50:16–17]. Many scholars say that ﴿نَحْنُ أَقْرَبُ إِلَيْهِ مِنْ حَبْلِ الْوَرِيدِ﴾ ("We are closer to him than his jugular vein") means: by Our angels. And ﴿عَنِ الْيَمِينِ وَعَنِ الشِّمَالِ قَعِيدٌ﴾ ("on the right and on the left, seated") does not mean the nearness of Allah Himself, the Blessed and Exalted, in contrast with the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed, the One you call upon is nearer to one of you than the neck of his mount," or he said: "than the neck of his riding-beast."[[Recorded by Muslim (2704/46) from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari.]] The difference between the two meanings is that His saying ﴿نَحْنُ أَقْرَبُ إِلَيْهِ مِنْ حَبْلِ الْوَرِيدِ﴾ means nearness to the human being in general.

It is well known that the nearness of Allah to the servant is specific to the one who worships Him or calls upon Him, i.e., to the one who worships Him or invokes Him. Nearness is not like companionship (ma'iyyah), which is divided into two kinds; rather, nearness is specific to the one who worships Him or calls upon Him. As for the one who worships Him, it is like the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The servant is nearest to his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, when he is prostrating,"[[Recorded by Muslim (482/215) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] and as for the one who calls upon Him, it is the saying of the Messenger, peace be upon him: "O people, be gentle with yourselves, for you are not calling upon one who is deaf or absent, but you are calling upon One who hears and is near,"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2992) and Muslim (2704/44) from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari.]] and "Indeed, the One you call upon is nearer to one of you than the neck of his mount."[[Recorded by Muslim (2704/46) from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari.]]

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation that Allah, the Exalted, is a witness over all things, as shown by His saying ﴿and You are Witness over all things﴾.

* This implies another benefit: that it is obligatory for the servant to be perfectly mindful (muraqabah) of Allah, the Blessed and Exalted, such that He does not find him absent when He commands, and does not find him present when He forbids, because Allah is watching over you. So you must guard against this watchfulness, and that Allah not find you absent where He commanded you, nor find you in what He forbade you.

* Student: Shaykh, may Allah reward you well. The Christians say that Isa and his mother are two gods along with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. And the verse: ﴿Did you say to the people: "Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah"?﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:116] (...)?

* The Shaykh: No, but (siwa) comes with the meaning of "less," and it comes with the meaning of "other than." Here it means "other than." Other than Allah; that is, other than singling out Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

* Student: May Allah honor you. The application of "dhat" (essence) to "nafs" (self), or "nafs" to "dhat": how did Shaykh al-Islam negate it, when...?

* The Shaykh: How did he negate it?

* The Student: He negated it, saying: it is not from the language of the eloquent Arabs?

* The Shaykh: The word "dhat": he negated the use of the word "dhat" for "nafs," the use of "dhat" for "nafs."

* The Student: Yes, indeed, Shaykh. How does he negate it when it is established for Allah, glorified and exalted?

* The Shaykh: Where?

* The Student: Now, did we not say that "nafs" is applied to "dhat"?

* The Shaykh: No, we said: "nafs" means "dhat." This is an explanation of it. Otherwise, there is no affirmation of "dhat" for Allah in the Qur'an or in the Sunnah. As for the saying of Khubayb:

"And that is for the sake of the God of ... ∗∗∗ ......................"[[Recorded by al-Bukhari (3045) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]

its meaning is: on the side of God.

* The Student: How so? We said that "nafs" means "dhat," and Shaykh al-Islam...

* The Shaykh: Shaykh al-Islam says: the use of "dhat" to mean "nafs" is an innovation (dakhil) in the Arabic language. We explained "dhat" on the basis of terminology (istilah). Now, for example, Abdullah, this figure in front of us, we call him a "dhat" and we call him a "nafs." Which of the two is the eloquent usage? "Nafs."

* Student: So does Shaykh al-Islam approve this, or does he not approve it?

* The Shaykh: No, he expresses it with it, but he says: it is not from the speech of the Arabs (...). He approves it because people went along with it, so they said: "dhat" and "sifat" (attributes).

* Student: May Allah reward you well, Shaykh. Some scholars distinguish between a prophet (nabi) and a messenger (rasul): that the prophet was not commanded to convey, while the messenger was commanded to convey his law. Is this correct?

* The Shaykh: Correct. This is what the majority (jumhur) hold, and it is what is not free from criticism. Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, holds that the prophet is like a scholar in this nation, meaning he completes the law of those who came before. But it is objected that Adam was a prophet and no law preceded him. According to the majority's view there is no difficulty, because Adam worshipped Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, by what Allah revealed to him, and his progeny at that time were few, following his example. Then when people multiplied and spread out, they disagreed, and at that point the necessity arose for messengers.

* Student: (...) They claim knowledge of the unseen. They say that such-and-such will happen in the future, and they collect money on this basis, claiming the unseen, and people believe them and give them money. What is the ruling on one of them when he dies: is funeral prayer offered for him?

* The Shaykh: The funeral prayer is not offered for him. Everyone who claims knowledge of the unseen is a disbeliever. Why? Because Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Say: No one in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah﴾ [al-Naml 27:65]. This is a negation, meaning a restriction: no one in the heavens or the earth knows the unseen except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Yes. If he has indicators (qara'in), then his claim is conjecture and guesswork (kharsh wa takhmin). Do you understand? For example, one who perceives in a person that he will become a wrongdoer; perhaps he knows this from the features of his face. It has happened with a man who saw in someone who had very beneficial writings on the religion of Islam that he would apostatize, and indeed he did apostatize and died in his apostasy. This is like the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, in that are signs for those who perceive by insight﴾ [al-Hijr 15:75]. But mere knowledge of the unseen, this is without doubt disbelief, because it is a denial of the Qur'an.

* Student: (...) Someone said to a person (...): "You are among the people of the Fire." This man said: "Since I am among the people of the Fire, then I am done; I will not pray."

* The Shaykh: Fine. "Among the people of the Fire" must be based on indicators, meaning that he does acts that make it necessary for him to be among the people of the Fire, so this is not knowledge of the unseen, because he said it only based on something. It is said: the error in this is that you testified for him that he is among the people of the Fire, and he is a specific person, and this is not permissible.

* Student: Very often, a person can hardly mention a blessing he has been given without being deprived of it. Is this considered pessimism (tashaum) or not?

* The Shaykh: This is a mistake. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And as for the blessing of your Lord, proclaim it﴾ [al-Duha 93:11]. But perhaps his mentioning it is out of boasting and self-admiration, and then he is deprived of it.

* Student: Sometimes things that do not warrant boasting or self-admiration happen, such as health, or wealth, or departure or return. Whatever it is?

* The Shaykh: This is not possible. A person is commanded to speak of Allah's blessing without boasting and without self-admiration.

* Student: We said: in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So when You caused me to die, You were the Watcher over them﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:117], the meaning, between it and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Not a word does he utter but that with him is an observer, ready﴾ [Qaf 50:18], i.e., through His angels, what is the difficulty in the verse of al-Ma'idah?

* The Shaykh: What difficulty?

* The Student: I did not understand the difficulty.

* The Shaykh: The difficulty is that Allah attributed the watching to Himself in the verse of al-Ma'idah, and in Surah Qaf He attributed it to the two angels. The reconciliation: the watching of the two angels is by the command of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, so He is the Watcher, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So when We have recited it, then follow its recitation﴾ [al-Qiyamah 75:18]. And it is known that the one who recites to the Messenger is who? Jibril. So He attributed the recitation of the Messenger to Himself because it was by His command.

* Student: Shaykh, may Allah reward you well. According to Shaykh al-Islam's view, how do we justify that Adam, peace be upon him, was a prophet?

* The Shaykh: I do not know, unless he regards him as an exception. Otherwise, there is no way to justify it. For this reason, the opinion of the majority is the correct one.
