* Student: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿I did not say to them except what You commanded me: "Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord." And I was a witness over them as long as I remained among them. So when You caused me to die, You were the Watcher over them, and You are Witness over all things. If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, indeed You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:117–118].

* The Shaykh: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Before we begin the lesson (...): when Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, asks him on the Day of Resurrection: ﴿Did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah"?﴾, he will disavow that, and say that it is not right for him, and he will glorify Allah, the Exalted, above having any partner.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 5, verse 118 (part 1 of 2):

Allah, Exalted and Majestic, says: ﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants; but if You forgive them, indeed You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise.﴾

﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants﴾ means: if You decree for them what they deserve to be punished for, then indeed they are Your servants. It does not mean that He punishes them without any sin, for He, Glorified and Exalted, is utterly far above that, due to the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿And your Lord does not wrong anyone﴾ [al-Kahf 49], and His saying: ﴿And your Lord is not ever unjust to the servants﴾ [Fussilat 46]. Rather, the meaning of ﴿If You punish them﴾ is: if You decree upon them a sin that becomes the cause of punishment, then indeed they are Your servants.

Yet, we also say: Allah, Exalted, will not decree for them sins for which they deserve punishment except when He knows what is in their hearts of turning away and of not accepting the truth. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, says: ﴿But if they turn away, then know that Allah intends to afflict them for some of their sins﴾ [al-Ma'idah 49]. So sins are a cause of turning away, we seek refuge in Allah, and He, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate﴾ [as-Saff 5].

Therefore, the word ﴿If You punish them﴾ necessarily has preliminaries: the first: that they commit what makes them deserve punishment; the second: that there is decreed for them what brings about the punishment, because they are fit for it. For Allah has promised: ﴿As for he who gives and fears Allah, and believes in the best [reward], We will ease him toward ease﴾ [al-Layl 5-7]. But the sin is the sin of the servant: ﴿And if Allah had known any good in them, He would have made them hear﴾ [al-Anfal 23].

And His saying: ﴿indeed they are Your servants﴾, by this is meant the universal servitude (al-'ubudiyyah al-kawniyyah), not the legislative servitude (al-'ubudiyyah ash-shar'iyyah), because a servant in legislative servitude does not deserve to be punished. Rather, the intended meaning is universal servitude, because Allah does whatever He wills. Allah, Exalted, says: ﴿It is He who created you, and among you is a disbeliever and among you is a believer﴾ [at-Taghabun 2].

And His saying: ﴿indeed they are Your servants﴾ — the clause, there is no hidden matter that it is the answer of what? It is the answer of the conditional (jawab ash-shart), and it is joined with the fa' (al-fa') because it is a nominal clause (jumlah ismiyyah), and a nominal clause when it occurs as the answer of a conditional, whether the conditional is jazim or not, is joined with the fa'. Some scholars versified the clauses that are linked with the fa' when they occur as the answer of the conditional, in his saying:

Nominal, imperative,
and with jamid, and with ma, and with qad, and with lan, and with the tanfis (sa/sawfa),
seven places. Here, which of the places? The nominal clause, but it is a nominal clause emphasized by (inna), so it is joined with the fa'.

He said: ﴿indeed they are Your servants, and if You forgive them, indeed You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾, meaning: if You decree for them the causes of forgiveness and You forgive them, ﴿then indeed You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾, the Exalted, the Victorious.

They said: Might (al-'izzah) is of three types: might of compulsion and dominance (‘izzat al-qahr wa al-ghalabah), might of inaccessibility (‘izzat al-imtina'), and might of nobility, which some call might of station (‘izzat al-qadr). As for the might of dominance, it is clear, such as the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿They say, "If we return to Madinah, the more honorable will surely expel therefrom the more humble." But to Allah belongs honor, and to His Messenger and to the believers﴾ [al-Munafiqun 8], and such as His saying, Exalted: ﴿Whoever desires honor — then to Allah belongs all honor﴾ [Fatir 10]. It is clear that the meaning here is dominance.

As for the might of inaccessibility, they said its meaning is: that Allah, Exalted, is greater than to be touched by anything that would be a defect or deficiency; that is, that every deficiency is impossible for Him. They returned in this to the derivation (al-ishtiqaq); they said: because it is said: "a land 'izaz," meaning hard and solid, which tools do not affect because of its firmness and hardness.

The third: the might of nobility, meaning that He, Mighty and Majestic, possesses great station and great nobility, just as you say to your friend: "You are dear (‘aziz) to me." What does it mean? It means: you have a great standing with me.

﴿al-'Aziz al-Hakim﴾. ﴿al-Hakim﴾ is derived from (hakama) and (ahkama). If it is from (hakama), then fa'il is in the sense of fa'il (active participle); if it is from (ahkama), then fa'il is in the sense of muhkim (causing to be perfected). The use of fa'il in the sense of fa'il is common, like sami' in the sense of sami' (hearing), and basir in the sense of ba'ir (seeing), and so on. But fa'il in the sense of muf'il is rare in the Arabic language, yet it is established, and from it is the saying of the poet:

Is it from Raihanah that the summoner, the one who hears (al-sami'), keeps me awake, and my companions are hungry?

The meaning of al-sami' here is al-musmi' (the one who causes to hear). So al-Hakim is derived from: al-hukm and al-ihkam. If it is from al-hukm, it means: the judge (hakim); and if it is from al-ihkam, it means: the one who perfects (muhkim). And the muhkim is the one from whom wisdom (al-hikmah) comes.

* * *

* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Allah will say, "This is a day in which the truthful will benefit from their truthfulness. For them are gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him. That is the great attainment." (119) To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is in them, and He is over all things competent.﴾ [al-Ma'idah 119, 120].

* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, Exalted, says: ﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, indeed You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾. This is the speech of ‘Isa to the Lord, Exalted, on the Day of Resurrection. It has already passed that the meaning of ﴿If You punish them﴾ is: that You decree for them a deed for which they are punished, so they are Your servants; and ﴿and if You forgive them﴾, so You prepare for them the causes of forgiveness, ﴿then indeed You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾. And it has already passed that ﴿al-'Aziz﴾ has three meanings?

* Student: Might of compulsion and dominance.

* Shaykh: Might of compulsion and dominance. And the second?

* Student: Might of nobility.

* Shaykh: Might of nobility and station. And the third?

* Student: And the third is might of inaccessibility.

* Shaykh: Inaccessibility, excellent; that is, every deficiency and defect is impossible for Him. And this last is derived from their saying: "a land 'izaz," that is, strong and solid. ﴿al-Hakim﴾?

* Student: From (hakama) in the sense of hakim (...).

* Shaykh: From (hakama) and (ahkama); (hakama) in the sense of hakim: He is the Judge in all things. (ahkama): that is, He perfected everything, as Allah, Exalted, says: ﴿The One who perfected everything﴾ [an-Naml 88].

Let us remain with the explanation of this great word. First: we must know that this is an attribute of Allah, Exalted: that He has judgment, so He is the Judge, in decree and in law, in this world and the Hereafter. And we must know that He has wisdom in everything He does and everything He judges, among matters of universal decree and matters of legislation. When we know this, we fully submit to the legislative rulings and the universal decrees. We do not say, for example, when Allah decrees a plague or decrees earthquakes and the like: this is pointless; rather we say: this is for a wisdom.

Wisdom exists in the essence of a thing, and exists in the ends of a thing, and exists in the law, and exists in the decree. So the categories are four. Wisdom in the essence of a thing: meaning that this thing, if it is created, is decreed in a manner perfectly suited. Look at the creatures and you will find their existence in this form that they were created upon perfectly consistent with wisdom.

Ask the experts in anatomy of human and non-human bodies, ask them how Allah, Exalted, composed these bodies in the most wondrous and most precise manner. How many laboratories are in the human body! Great laboratories. Look at food entering in varied forms and leaving as one type. Look at food entering in difficulty or softness, and leaving at one level. All of this is because of the laboratories. Then these laboratories, glory be to Allah, begin work without delay: the stomach, from the moment food reaches it, begins to work, with secretions from the gall bladder or others. A marvelous thing.

That the human being was created in this form, Allah made him proportionate and made him upright, not like cattle; it is perfectly suited to what the servant was created for, being created for obedience and worship, so that he can stand, sit, bow and prostrate and other things Allah obligates him with. And by this, measure.

Likewise, wisdom in legislative matters: in the very essence of the legislative commands there is great wisdom. Prayer is a connection between the human being and Allah, Exalted; he converses with his Lord standing in his recitation, he supplicates to Him in his prostration, and he humbles himself to Him with his heart. So its being in this form is wisdom.

As for ends, the ends are also wisdom. The ends of what Allah decrees by decree are praiseworthy ends. Look at the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿Corruption has appeared on land and sea because of what the hands of people have earned﴾ [ar-Rum 41]. What is the end of this? ﴿That He may let them taste part of what they have done﴾ [ar-Rum 41], and the end of this punishment: ﴿that perhaps they will return﴾ [ar-Rum 41]. So this is an end after an end, although a person, if he imagined the matter at first glance, would say: corruption is corruption, how can we say it has a praiseworthy end?

Interests also have praiseworthy ends. They are in themselves praiseworthy, and they have praiseworthy ends too. Among them: thanks for blessings. For Allah tests with evil and good. If a person is patient with evil, that is a praiseworthy end; and if he gives thanks for good, that is a praiseworthy end. Likewise these creatures — I am speaking about the law.

Also, creatures have an end. If you see the sun rise each day from a rising point other than the one of yesterday, and between its rising today and its rising yesterday there are great distances that none knows but Allah, Exalted — for with this great distance, which looks like a hair, how large is its extent? Years! We think the distance is small, no more than a hair the sun has deviated from, and it is not so; enormously great distances, each day, and it returns on the same line. Why? For great interests. People's interests differ in winter from summer, in autumn from spring: great interests. The sun also in the ripening of trees and warming the atmosphere has — glory be to Allah — something beyond imagination.

Look, for example, at the air, the horizon: you find that — even in the height of summer — it is very cold, because the lights, the rays of the sun, have nothing to reflect them; they are reflected on the earth, then generate heat, but in the atmosphere there is nothing that reflects them, so they pierce through and pass to the earth. So every creature has an end, and every legislated matter has a praiseworthy end.

So wisdom, O brothers, exists in the decreed: that is, in the very essence of the decreed, its being in this form is wisdom; second, in its end; third, in the legislated; fourth, in its end.

Reflect on the laws and you will find they are the betterment of the body and the heart: fasting, prayer, zakat, pilgrimage, monotheism and sincerity — a benefit to the body. A person is most content, most energetic, and most joyful when his heart is purified by sincerity to Allah, Exalted. Therefore, sometimes a person passes, while in worship, through a state in which he says: if the people of Paradise are in such bliss, it is sufficient. Then heedlessness comes and takes hold heavily, and perhaps what was light for him yesterday becomes heavy. And hearts are in the hand of Allah, Exalted.

So the point is that wisdom exists in these four aspects: wisdom in the creature, wisdom in the legislated matter itself; third, wisdom in the end of the creature, wisdom in the end of the legislated matter. Is it clear?

Strangely, the Ash'arites and the Jahmites denied this great wisdom, and said: Allah acts not for wisdom, because wisdom is a purpose, and Allah is exalted above purposes, accidents and parts. Rhyming nonsense — exalted above purposes (...) He has no wisdom, He does not act for wisdom, just like that, merely will; above accidents, He has no attributes: He does not laugh or become angry; and above parts, He has no face, no hand, no eye, and similar things.

But we say: this is false, and Allah is exalted above deficiency. As for wisdom, it is not a purpose by which the Wise benefits; it is the creatures who benefit from it, so that the signs of His mercy and His wisdom appear in His creation until they worship Him. Otherwise Allah is independent of us. If all the people of the earth were upon the most wicked heart of one man, would Allah diminish anything? He would not diminish it.

﴿And whoever disbelieves — then indeed Allah is Free of need⁠⁠ from whom?﴾ ﴿from the worlds﴾ [Ali 'Imran 97], all of them. He does not benefit from obedience, nor is He harmed by disobedience. But so that the signs of His mercy, His wisdom, His authority and His power appear, He made these laws. Wisdom is not a purpose by which the wise one benefits in relation to Allah, Exalted, nor a harm he repels from Himself.

As for their saying "exalted above accidents," meaning: He does not descend, does not rise above the heaven, does not laugh, does not rejoice, does not love, does not dislike — we say: this means nullifying what Allah described Himself with, and this nullification is tantamount to denial, because they nullify matters clear in meaning. It is like the one who bought a horse and said: "I bought bread." Would that be believed? It would not be believed. Their distortions of the texts are like the distortion of one who says: "I bought bread," meaning: "I bought a horse." But they do not explicitly deny; they say: Allah does not become angry; he says: He becomes angry, but what is meant by His anger is retribution or the will to retribute.

The third: parts. They say: it is impossible for Allah to have a face, an eye, a hand, a foot, or a shin. We say: Glory be to Allah. ﴿Are you more knowing, or is Allah?﴾ [al-Baqarah 140].

If they say: Allah knows best, we say: Does Allah speak falsehood? If they say: He cannot lie, He is the most truthful of speakers, we say: then how do you say He has no real hand, no real face?

The summary is that we say: denying wisdom means that all of Allah's acts are foolishness, because if wisdom is negated, then pointlessness takes its place; its opposite is necessary, since it is not conceivable that an agent does what has no wisdom without having its opposite. Praise be to Allah who guided us; we ask Allah to keep us firm, and you.

So this verse indicates wisdom in the four aspects. Let us return to its benefits:

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that ‘Isa, peace be upon him — and he is one of the Messengers of firm resolve (ulu al-'azm) — entrusts the matter to Allah, when he said: ﴿If You punish them﴾, ﴿and if You forgive them﴾. Likewise, it is incumbent upon us to entrust the matter to Allah, Exalted, regarding what He does, and not to object to Him. Allah says: ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned﴾ [al-Anbiya' 23] — ﴿He is not questioned about what He does﴾ because of His perfect wisdom, ﴿but they will be questioned﴾ because they are servants of Allah, Exalted.

* * *

* Student: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Allah will say, "This is a day in which the truthful will benefit from their truthfulness. For them are gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him. That is the great attainment." (119) To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is in them, and He is over all things competent.﴾ [al-Ma'idah 119, 120].

* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, says: ﴿Allah will say, "This is a day in which the truthful will benefit from their truthfulness."﴾

Allah, Exalted, says: ﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants.﴾ I will mention what Allah opens for us of its benefits:

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the submission of the prophets, peace and blessings be upon them, and their entrusting the matter to Allah, Exalted; because this is from ‘Isa, peace be upon him, who is one of the prophets of firm resolve.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: the term "servant" (ʿabd) may be applied to one who deserves punishment. Servitude (ʿubūdiyyah) is of two kinds, specific and general. The specific kind has two levels, the more specific and the more general. The general kind is the servitude of decree (ʿubūdiyyat al-qadr), meaning servitude of creation (ʿubūdiyyat al-takwīn). It applies to everyone. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant.﴾ No one is exempt from this servitude, and no one can oppose it. All creatures are subject to it. The most disbelieving of Allah's servants cannot prevent the decree of Allah concerning him. This general servitude applies to both the Muslim and the disbeliever, the righteous and the wicked.

The second kind is specific: the servitude to the Sharia (ʿubūdiyyat al-sharʿ), which is the humbling of a person before the law of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. To whom does this apply? To the one who has submitted his face to Allah. Thus the disbeliever is excluded, for he is not a servant of Allah in this sense.

This specific servitude is divided into the more general and the more specific. The most specific form of this servitude is the servitude of the messengers, may the prayers and peace of Allah be upon them, as in the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant, then produce a surah like it,﴾ and His saying: ﴿Then He revealed to His servant what He revealed,﴾ and His saying: ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant,﴾ and His saying: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who revealed the Book to His servant.﴾ The examples are many. He also said about Noah: ﴿Indeed, he was a grateful servant.﴾ This is the most specific type of servitude, the servitude of messengership, because the messengers, may the prayers and peace of Allah be upon them, are charged with a duty beyond what those to whom they were sent are charged with: conveying the message, patience in conveying it, calling to Allah, and other things.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: Allah, Blessed and Exalted, has the right to punish and to show mercy, or, if you prefer, to punish and to forgive. This matches the verse. But is this to be taken literally, or should we say that He punishes those who deserve punishment? This is because Allah, the Exalted, does not punish anyone who does not deserve punishment, as He, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And whoever does righteous deeds while being a believer will not fear injustice or diminution.﴾

Among the benefits of this noble verse: the wisdom of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in making creation divide into two groups: those who are punished and those who are forgiven. As He, the Exalted, said: ﴿It is He who created you, and among you is a disbeliever and among you is a believer.﴾ Were it not for this division, the virtue of faith would not be manifest, nor would jihad be prescribed, nor would enjoining good and forbidding evil, nor would the messengers have been sent. But the wisdom of Allah required that people be of two kinds.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of forgiveness, that is, the forgiveness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for whomever He wills of His servants. This is based on His saying: ﴿and if You forgive them.﴾ The meaning of forgiveness has already been explained to you: it is the concealing of a sin and overlooking it. We derive this from the etymology of the word, for it is derived from al-mighfar (a piece of armour worn on the head to protect against arrows). It is placed on the head, so it both covers and protects.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of these two noble names, al-ʿAzīz (the Exalted in Might) and al-Ḥakīm (the Wise), and the affirmation of the attributes they contain: might (ʿizzah), sovereignty (ḥukm), and wisdom (ḥikmah).

Know that the noble names may imply other meanings that the derived word itself does not indicate, but which are necessary implications. For example, al-Khāliq (the Creator) is one of Allah's names, and al-Khallāq (the Supreme Creator) is one of Allah's names. Each indicates the attribute of creation, and also implies other attributes necessary to it, namely knowledge and power, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿It is Allah who created seven heavens and of the earth the like of them. The command descends among them that you may know that Allah is over all things competent and that Allah has encompassed all things in knowledge.﴾ From this we know that the attributes are more numerous than the names. The reason is that every name must include one or more attributes, but not every attribute gives rise to a name. Therefore we say: the attributes of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, that have reached us are more numerous than His names.

If someone says: When a person reads this verse, he expects it to end with (then indeed You are the Forgiving, the Merciful), because ﴿indeed You, You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾ is the answer to ﴿and if You forgive them,﴾ and the fitting conclusion would be "then indeed You are the Forgiving, the Merciful." So what is the answer?

It is said: Although the verse is composed of two conditional clauses, they carry one meaning. Now, the verse contains two conditional clauses: ﴿If You punish them﴾ with its answer ﴿then indeed they are Your servants,﴾ and ﴿and if You forgive them﴾ with its answer ﴿then indeed You, You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise.﴾ But in reality they function as a single condition. So the punishment of the wrongdoers for their wrongdoing, and the forgiveness of those who deserve forgiveness, are both grounded in the might by which He punishes the disbelievers, and in the wisdom by which He forgives those who deserve forgiveness. This is one way of understanding it.

In another way: the division of people into these groups is what might and wisdom required, so this conclusion is the most fitting. This is the closest explanation, and Allah knows best what He intends.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 5, verse 119:

﴿Allah said: "This is a day on which the truthful will benefit from their truthfulness."﴾ In all these verses there is an affirmation that speech belongs to Allah, azza wa jall, that it is heard, and that it is with letters; for what is spoken (maqul al-qawl) consists of letters, and Allah, exalted is He, addresses whoever He addresses with it, so it is heard. Thus this is a refutation of those who say that the speech of Allah is the meaning subsisting in His essence, as is the doctrine of the Ash'aris. By "Ash'aris" I mean those who ascribe themselves to Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari, not Abu al-Hasan himself.

﴿Allah said: "This is a day on which the truthful will benefit from their truthfulness."﴾ ﴿This﴾ refers to: the Day of Resurrection. ﴿A day﴾ is the predicate of the subject; hence it is in the nominative (marfu'), and it is not a time-adverb (zarf), for if it were an adverb it would be in the accusative (mansub). However, there is a canonical reading (qira'ah sab'iyyah) in the accusative: ﴿This is a day on which...﴾ (hadha yawma yanfa'u). According to this reading, this occurrence takes place on the day on which the truthful benefit from their truthfulness.

As for His saying ﴿the truthful will benefit from their truthfulness﴾: truthfulness is by speech and by action; that is, by deed and by belief. Truthfulness in speech is the correspondence of a statement to reality; the correspondence of a statement to reality is truthfulness, truthfulness in speech. As for truthfulness in belief, it is that one's belief corresponds to one's words. An example of this: the statement of the speaker, "There is no god but Allah." This is a statement; is it truthful or false? It is truthful. But does the heart confirm it; that is, does the heart believe that there is no god but Allah or not?

If he believes it, then in his case there is truthfulness of speech and truthfulness of belief together.

Truthfulness of action is that the action follows the Shari'ah and corresponds to what is in the heart. On this basis, the innovator (mubtadi') is not truthful, and the hypocrite (munafiq) is not truthful, because his action does not correspond to what is in his heart. And the innovator is not truthful, for if he were truthful in faith he would not have departed from the Shari'ah of the Most Merciful.

﴿a day on which the truthful will benefit from their truthfulness﴾. Siddiqiyyah (the rank of being a siddiq) is a station that is the highest of the ranks after prophethood, and its discussion will come, God willing, in the benefits (fawa'id).

﴿a day on which the truthful will benefit from their truthfulness. For them are gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. ﴿For them﴾ is a fronted predicate (khabar muqaddam), and this implies restriction (ikhtisas), i.e., for them and not for others.

﴿Gardens﴾: jannat is the plural of jannah, which is the abode that Allah, azza wa jall, has prepared for the God-fearing (muttaqun), in which is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived. It occurs in the Qur'an in the singular, the plural, and the dual. The singular is by consideration of the genus, so it includes every garden. The plural is by consideration of the types, since they are many levels; Allah has prepared a hundred levels for those who strive in His cause. The dual is by consideration of the genus, as in His saying: ﴿And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾ [al-Rahman 46], then He said: ﴿And beneath them are two gardens﴾ [al-Rahman 62].

﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾: flowing is well known, and ﴿rivers﴾ is the plural of nahr, which is water. This is what we know in this world, but in Paradise there are rivers of four kinds, which Allah, exalted is He, mentioned in Surat Muhammad, saying: ﴿A description of Paradise which the God-fearing are promised: in it are rivers of water unchanging, and rivers of milk whose taste does not change, and rivers of wine delicious to the drinkers, and rivers of purified honey﴾ [Muhammad 15]. This is regarding drink. Regarding food: ﴿and for them therein is every fruit﴾ [Muhammad 15]; regarding freedom from blame for what they eat or leave: ﴿and forgiveness from their Lord﴾ [Muhammad 15].

His saying ﴿beneath them﴾ means not above them. But does it mean beneath a ceiling? No. ﴿Beneath them﴾ means beneath these trees, palaces, and tents. The flowing of these rivers, as came in the Sunnah, is without a trench[[Narrated by Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf (34954), and 'Abd al-Razzaq in al-Tafsir (3109), from Masruq as a mawquf report.]] and without digging; they flow on the surface, and there is no need for a standing trench or dug pits. Rather, they flow according to the desire of the inhabitants; a person directs them however he wishes.

﴿abiding therein forever﴾ [al-Nisa' 57]. Khulud (abiding) is a long stay; if it is emphasized with "forever" (abadiyyah), it becomes eternal. It has been said: khulud is a lasting stay unless there is evidence that it is temporary. In any case, if it is emphasized with "forever," the claim that it is a long abiding is cut off, because it has been emphasized with "forever."

﴿Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him﴾. ﴿Allah is pleased with them﴾ because of what they did in obeying Him. The fullness of His pleasure occurs when they enter Paradise; Allah, exalted is He, asks them what they want, and they enumerate to Him His blessings upon them, and He says: "Indeed, for you is that I shall let My good pleasure descend upon you, so I shall never be angry with you after it, forever." [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6549) and Muslim (2829/9), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.]] This is the complete and lasting good pleasure.

﴿And they are pleased with Him﴾: with what? With what He enabled them to do of righteous deeds in this world, and with what He rewarded them for in the Hereafter. Indeed the believer, without doubt, is delighted by the obedience of Allah, content with it, and joyful in it.

﴿That is the great triumph﴾. ﴿That﴾ refers to what Allah, azza wa jall, has mentioned: the gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein, and the good pleasure. It is pointed to with the demonstrative of distance, and that is because of the loftiness and elevation of its rank; otherwise the mention is near, but He pointed to it because of the loftiness of its rank, for it is a triumph without equal. ﴿The great triumph﴾: it is said, "The man triumphed" when he prevails with an approved victory, and this is only achieved by escaping what is feared and attaining what is sought. ﴿The Great﴾ means: possessed of supreme greatness, for which there is no equal.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the affirmation that speech belongs to Allah, azza wa jall, by His saying: ﴿Allah said: "This is a day..."﴾.

* And among its benefits: that the speech of Allah is with letters, and not the meaning subsisting in the self, because what is spoken consists of letters.

* And among them: that the speech of Allah is with an audible voice, because all of this is in the context of the dialogue with 'Isa, upon him be peace.

Know further that the word "qawl" (speech), when used without qualification, is never intended except to mean audible utterance; it is impossible that "qawl" when used without qualification be intended as the meaning subsisting in the self. Rather, when it is intended to mean the meaning subsisting in the self, it is qualified, as in His saying: ﴿They say within themselves, "Why does Allah not punish us?"﴾ [al-Mujadilah 8].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the great benefit of truthfulness, for a person on the Day of Resurrection is most in need of what benefits him, and truthfulness benefits on the Day of Resurrection.

* And among its benefits: encouragement to truthfulness and inducement to it, for mentioning that it is beneficial at that distressing time indicates the inducement to it and urging upon it. The Prophet (ﷺ) urged it in his saying: "Hold fast to truthfulness, for truthfulness leads to righteousness, and righteousness leads to Paradise. A man continues to speak the truth and seek the truth until he is recorded with Allah as a siddiq."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6094) and Muslim (2607/105), the wording being his, from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud.]]

The siddiqiyyah is the highest of the ranks of mankind after prophethood. It suffices you as persuasion of its benefit and fruit what happened to the three who were left behind; that is, whose matter was deferred and no judgment was made concerning it until revelation came. They were: Ka'b ibn Malik, Hilal ibn Umayyah, and Murarah ibn al-Rabi'. These three stayed behind from the expedition of Tabuk. When the Prophet (ﷺ) returned from it, those who made excuses came to apologize to the Messenger (ﷺ). Allah had informed about them before the Prophet (ﷺ) arrived at Medina, saying: ﴿They will make excuses to you when you return to them﴾ [al-Tawbah 94] ﴿So that you may turn away from them; so turn away from them. Indeed, they are impure, and their refuge is Hell as recompense for what they used to earn. They swear to you that you may be satisfied with them; but if you should be satisfied with them, indeed Allah is not satisfied with the defiant people﴾ [al-Tawbah 95-96].

As for the three, they were truthful and reported the truth. Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, revealed verses concerning them that are recited in prayer and outside of prayer, and one is rewarded for reciting them. He urged that we be like them, saying after mentioning the verses: ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and be with the truthful﴾ [al-Tawbah 119].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of the reward of Paradise, by His saying: ﴿For them are gardens﴾, and this is a matter believed by all Muslim groups.

* And among the benefits of the verse: that this reward is specific to the truthful. Who knows the reason for this?

* Student: The fronting of the predicate over the subject.

* The Shaykh: The fronting of the predicate over the subject indicates restriction.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: the description of the gardens, that flowing rivers run beneath the trees and palaces; how beautiful a sight and how delicious an experience. O Allah, make us among them.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that the people of Paradise abide therein forever; by His saying: ﴿abiding therein forever﴾. Does it exist now? Yes, it exists now in the heavens. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿It has been prepared for the God-fearing﴾ [Al 'Imran 133], and preparation means it is ready for its people. The Prophet (ﷺ) entered it when he was taken up on the Night Journey and saw in it what he saw[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (349) and Muslim (163/263), from the hadith of Abu Dharr.]], and it and the Fire were displayed to him when he stood to pray the prayer of eclipse.[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (540) and Muslim (2359/136), from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik.]]

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's good pleasure, by His saying: ﴿Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him﴾. Is good pleasure an attribute of action (fi'liyyah) or an essential attribute (dhatiyyah)?

* Student: Of action.

* The Shaykh: Of action, because it is connected to His will, and every attribute connected to His will is an attribute of action. Is it literal, or is it a metaphor for the intention of reward, or is it the reward itself? There are two opinions. The first: that it is literal, and this is the view that must be followed, because it is the apparent meaning of the Book, and it is obligatory to keep the Book on its apparent meaning without distortion.

If someone says: good pleasure is a meaning subsisting in the self, which strengthens, weakens, departs, and remains?

We say: what prevents us from affirming this for Allah, when He has affirmed it for Himself? What is the prevention? But we know that Allah's good pleasure is not like the good pleasure of the created being, which disappears with the slightest cause or arises from the slightest cause. Rather, it has its own causes that bring it about, and it has what removes it in a manner specific to Allah, azza wa jall; for we have a general principle, which is His saying: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾ [al-Shura 11]. The people of distortion said: Allah cannot be pleased; good pleasure is an accidental attribute, and Allah is exalted above accidental attributes, for accidental attributes are originated, and the originated subsists only in something originated. All these justifications are imaginary rather than rational, refuted by the evidence of the Book and the Sunnah affirming it. Therefore, because they do not believe in true good pleasure, they said: the meaning of good pleasure is the intention of reward, but they did not say that it is the reward; rather they said "intention," because they affirm the attribute of will.

You know that the Ash'aris affirm seven attributes: life, knowledge, power, will, hearing, sight, and speech. They said: good pleasure is the will of reward. Among them are those who do not affirm will, and they say that good pleasure is the reward itself, and the reward, as we know, is something separate from Allah, created, which comes into being by the word, the word of Allah azza wa jall. There is no doubt that this is distortion. And as you know from what we mentioned in the hadith, the good pleasure that Allah gives to the people of Paradise is the greatest of their hopes and more perfect than everything they find in Paradise of bliss. So how can we explain it by something lower, and say: it is the reward, or the intention of reward?

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the good pleasure of the people of truthfulness with Allah, azza wa jall. There is some difficulty here: is it for a person to be pleased with Allah, or not? Or is it obligatory to be pleased with Allah's decree absolutely?

The second: it is obligatory for a person to be pleased with his Lord absolutely; he must say: "I am pleased with Allah as Lord, with Islam as religion, and with Muhammad as Messenger." Do we say that this is by way of matching the wording? When He said ﴿Allah is pleased with them﴾ He said ﴿and they are pleased with Him﴾; or do we say that good pleasure here does not mean the opposite of anger, for if good pleasure is established, good pleasure is established; if it is not established, its opposite is aversion, wrath, and anger, or non-good pleasure without aversion, wrath, or anger?

It does not follow from this that a person has the choice between being pleased with Allah's decree and destiny or not being pleased. Rather, we say: it is obligatory for a person to be pleased with Allah's decree and destiny, for this is part of the completeness of being pleased with Allah as Lord. But their being pleased with Him is either by way of answering the wording with its like, or what is meant by their good pleasure is that they rejoiced in it and welcomed it, and did not seek any alternative to it, as Allah azza wa jall said: ﴿Indeed, those who believed and did righteous deeds, for them are the Gardens of Paradise as a lodging, abiding therein, not desiring any change from them﴾ [al-Kahf 107-108].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that triumph in reality is not by profit, not by the profit of dinars and dirhams, nor status and leadership. The great profit or the great triumph is a person's triumph with the Gardens of Bliss — may Allah make me and you among those who triumph therein — and for this reason He said: ﴿That is the great triumph﴾.

Then He, mighty and exalted, said: ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾. [It belongs] to Allah alone; and we derive "alone" (waḥdahu) from the fronting of the predicate, meaning: to Allah alone, not to other than Him.

﴿The dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾: He disposes of it as He wills, and no one shares with Him in His dominion. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: Call upon those you claim besides Allah. They do not possess an atom's weight in the heavens or on the earth, and they have no share in them, and He has no supporter among them﴾ [Saba' 22]. ﴿No intercession benefits with Him except for one whom He permits﴾ [Saba' 23].

His words ﴿the heavens and the earth﴾: "heavens" is plural because their number is seven, while "earth" is singular by considering it as a genus; otherwise the earths are also seven.

﴿And whatever is in them﴾: ﴿mā﴾ here is a relative pronoun, and it is expressed by ﴿mā﴾, the particle used for non-rational beings. The scholars said: this is because most of what is in the heavens and the earth is non-rational, and the greatest part of what is in the heavens and the earth is non-rational; therefore He said ﴿whatever is in them﴾. It was also said: rather, ﴿mā﴾ is used because it includes both entities and states, as if He said: ﴿whatever is in them﴾ of entities and states. And ﴿man﴾ is used for the rational only when specifying the individual himself. This is a point you will hardly find with many grammarians, but Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, in Badā'i' al-Fawā'id, pointed to it: that ﴿man﴾ is for the rational when specification is intended, i.e., identifying him; but when the generality of entities and states is intended, ﴿mā﴾ is used.

The clearest example of this is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So marry what seems good to you of women﴾ [al-Nisa' 3], and He did not say ﴿man﴾. But if someone says to a person: "Marry whomever you wish of my daughters," then ﴿man﴾ comes here for the sake of specification. This is a subtle meaning: when ﴿mā﴾ is intended to include entities and states, it is more eloquent than using ﴿man﴾.

His words ﴿whatever is in them﴾ refer to great creations. Listen to the saying of the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family: "The heaven has creaked, and it has a right to creak"[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (2312) and Ibn Majah (4190) from the hadith of Abu Dharr.]]. "Atta" means it has produced a sound like the creaking of a saddle when a load is heavy; when you load a camel, its saddle makes a sound called "atit."

﴿And He is over all things Competent﴾: that is, along with the generality of His dominion, His power is also general over everything. There is nothing existing except that He is able to annihilate it, and nothing non-existent except that He is able to bring it into being, blessed and exalted is He. Nothing is excepted from this; He is competent over everything. The author of al-Jalalayn erred in the interpretation when he said regarding this verse: "He excluded His essence, so He is not competent over it," for this is a reprehensible statement. Rather, it is the requirement of his school, since he negates that voluntary acts subsist in Allah; that is, in his view Allah does not descend, does not rise over the Throne, does not laugh, and does not rejoice. It is well known that voluntary acts occur by His will, so He is able to bring them into being and to annihilate them. Therefore this statement is reprehensible, founded on a corrupt belief.

We say: Allah is competent over everything without exception, doing what He wills, mighty and exalted.

* Student: In His saying ﴿For them are gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾, we said that fronting the predicate indicates restriction. Second: how is it restricted to ﴿the truthful﴾ when the gardens...?

* Shaykh: No, in principle there is no believer who is not truthful, so there is no problem.

* Student: His saying ﴿abiding therein forever﴾: if immortality is emphasized by "forever," does abiding in a place necessarily follow from it?

* Shaykh: Yes, that is known. If the place ceased to exist, where would the one who abides be? It is necessary.

* Student: (...) His saying ﴿If You punish them﴾ (...) causes of forgiveness (...) that Allah may forgive His servants by the requirement of His mercy, as a bounty from Him?

* Shaykh: Forgiveness has no problem; the problem is ﴿If You punish them﴾, for He will not punish them except for a sin.

* Student: My difficulty is (...) I have determined for him the causes of forgiveness.

* Shaykh: Against that, you have determined for him the causes of punishment.

* Student: (...) when he believes that Allah, glorified and exalted, may forgive, and the servant ends (...).

* Shaykh: Yes, Allah forgives what is below shirk by His bounty and grace, but his not committing shirk is among the causes of forgiveness, which lie under Allah's will.

* Student: Shaykh, may Allah reward you well, some preachers mention the description of Paradise and so on; they mentioned that a man who smoked tobacco, if Allah grants him entry into Paradise, then desires tobacco in Paradise, tobacco will be brought to him, though there is no fire in Paradise, so he goes to light a cigarette from the fire, and they take him into the Fire.

* Shaykh: It revolves (...). Who said this?

* Student: Some preachers speak this way.

* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah. This is a grave error. Know that the people of Paradise can never desire anything forbidden at all.

* Student: (...) We mentioned in the matter of servitude, O Shaykh, that general servitude is servitude to the decree (qadar).

* Shaykh: Qadar means decree.

* Student: Does this mean that animals are servants of Allah?

* Shaykh: Yes, besides humans and jinn, they are servants of Allah by decree and by law.

* Student: Now, O Shaykh, in the verse: ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾ [Maryam 93] (...).

* Shaykh: No, rather ﴿Have you not seen that to Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, and the sun and the moon and the stars and the mountains and the trees and the moving creatures and many of mankind﴾ [al-Hajj 18].

* Student: Meaning this "man" (...) being a particle for the rational (...).

* Shaykh: How?

* Student: That "man" is for the rational.

* Shaykh: "Man" is for the rational when specification is intended.

* Student: Sometimes a person, when he wants to be truthful, truthfulness puts him in an embarrassing position, like when he has something and another man asks him for it (...), and he says: "I don't have it."

* Shaykh: "I don't have it."

* Student: Yes, though he has it, but with the intent of procrastinating.

* Shaykh: This is easy: he interprets (ta'wil). In interpretation there is an alternative to lying. He says: "I have nothing to lend you," intending this, and intention specifies the general. Do you understand? Keep this as a matter of ta'wil and benefit from it: indeed, in ta'wil there is an alternative to lying.

* Student: Shaykh, may Allah bless you, (...) the saying of Allah the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Among them is one who walks on his belly, and among them is one who walks on two legs, and among them is one who walks on four﴾ [al-Nur 45].

* Shaykh: They said: it is by way of prevalence (taghlib), for the sake of the conjunction.

* Student: May Allah be pleased with you, Shaykh. If we consider the way of the messengers with their Lord, glorified and exalted, they addressed Him as though they were before Him, believing they were before Him. And the people of kalam, O Shaykh (...), spoke words, distorted, and denied the Messenger, and denied the apparent texts of the Qur'an, like the people of kalam. O Shaykh, is their sin the greatest, or the sin of one who does not acknowledge lordship?

* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed: ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is in them, and He is over all things competent﴾ [al-Ma'idah 120]. In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who created the heavens and the earth and made darknesses and light. Then those who disbelieve equate [others] with their Lord. He is the one who created you from clay; then He decreed a term, and a specified term is with Him; then you [still] doubt. And He is Allah in the heavens and on the earth; He knows your secret and your open, and He knows what you earn﴾ [al-An'am 1-3].

* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is in them, and He is over all things competent﴾.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: when Allah, glorified and exalted, mentioned what took place between Him and 'Isa, peace be upon him, and that 'Isa disavowed what the Christians claim about him, He made clear that ﴿to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾, and that 'Isa is not fit to be a god, neither he nor anyone else, because they possess nothing of what is in the heavens and the earth. From this is derived: the exclusivity of the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is in them to Allah, glorified and exalted. The aspect of exclusivity? The fronting of the predicate. The rule is that fronting what should be delayed indicates restriction, whether what should be delayed is a predicate, an object, or something else that should be delayed.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: the generality of Allah's dominion over the heavens and the earth, derived from the construct ﴿the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾, and the definite noun in construct indicates generality. Listen to the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And if you count the favor of Allah, you will not enumerate it﴾ [al-Nahl 18]. Here ﴿favor﴾ is singular and does not need a number; if we took it literally, we would say: "the favor is one." But since the definite noun in construct indicates generality, it is correct that He says ﴿you will not enumerate it﴾.

Thus, if a person says: "My slave is free," and he has slaves, which of them is freed? All of them, unless he intended a specific slave. And if he says: "My wife is divorced," and he has four? All the wives are divorced unless he intended one, because the definite noun in construct is general.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: when Allah, glorified and exalted, mentioned what took place between Him and 'Isa, peace be upon him, and that 'Isa disavowed what the Christians claim about him, He made clear that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and that 'Isa is not fit to be a god, neither he nor anyone else, because they possess nothing of what is in the heavens and the earth.

* Thus it is derived: the exclusivity of the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is in them to Allah, glorified and exalted; the aspect of exclusivity is the fronting of the predicate.

The rule: fronting what should be delayed indicates restriction, whether what should be delayed is a predicate, an object, or otherwise.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: the generality of Allah's dominion over the heavens and the earth, derived from the construct ﴿the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾, and the definite noun in construct indicates generality. Listen to the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And if you count the favor of Allah, you will not enumerate it﴾. Here ﴿favor﴾ is singular and needs no number; if we took it literally, we would say the favor is one. But since the definite noun in construct indicates generality, it is correct that He says ﴿you will not enumerate it﴾.

So if a person says: "My slave is free," and he has slaves, which of them is freed? All of them, unless he intended a particular slave.

And if he says: "My wife is divorced," and he has four? All the wives are divorced unless he intended one, because the definite noun in construct is general.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: that the heavens are a plural of number, and Allah the Exalted has clarified in His Book that they are seven heavens. He said: ﴿Say: Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the Mighty Throne?﴾ [al-Mu'minun 86]. So the heavens are seven, and they are layered, as Allah the Exalted said concerning Nuh: ﴿Have you not seen how Allah created seven heavens in layers?﴾ [Nuh 15], meaning one above another in agreement, with distances between them, as the hadith of the Mi'raj indicates, where Jibril, peace be upon him, would ascend with the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, heaven after heaven. Whenever he reached a heaven, he asked for entry and its inhabitants asked: "Who is this? Who is with you? Is he a messenger?"

We must believe in this, and deny the claim of those philosophers who say there is nothing—no heavens—rather there are galaxies, stars, and the like, and an endless space. This is a lie, because it contradicts what came in the Book and the Sunnah, and they are not more knowledgeable of Allah than the Creator, the Mighty and Exalted.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: explaining the wisdom behind singling out the earth and pluralizing the heavens. Allah, the Mighty and Exalted, mentions the earth in the singular in every place He mentions it, though the Qur'an alludes that it is seven in His saying: ﴿Allah is He who created seven heavens and of the earth the like of them﴾ [al-Talaq 12]. Perhaps one of the benefits and wisdom of this is that when a person owns the surface of the earth, he owns down to (...) all the lands beneath it. This is supported by the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever unjustly seizes a span of land, Allah will collar him with it on the Day of Resurrection from seven earths"[[Narrated by Muslim (1610/137) from the hadith of Sa'id ibn Zayd.]]. Because he owns the depth down to the seventh earth. The scholars derived from this that just as he owns the depth, he owns the air up to the sky. If someone wanted to build a shelf on the courtyard of his house—what do they call it?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No, I mean a shelf one sits on! La ilaha illa Allah! A veranda or balcony? Now, if he wanted to build a balcony over his neighbor's courtyard, he would be prevented even if it were high. If their trees extended their branches into his neighbor's air, he would demand that they be cut, or pruned if possible. So the air extends to where? To the sky; the depth extends to the seventh earth, because they are all one earth, which Allah referred to in the singular.

* And from the benefits of this noble verse: that the heavens and the earth contain something—﴿and whatever is in them﴾—and this is a known matter. The heavens contain the angels; the earth contains humans, jinn, and devils. Likewise there are things without life: mountains, clouds, stars, all established as Allah's, the Lord's dominion.

* And from the benefits of this noble verse: the generality of Allah's power over everything, by His saying ﴿and He is over all things competent﴾. This expression—I mean this attribute—is absolute: ﴿over all things competent﴾. Is He competent over what He does not will?

Yes, He is competent over what He does not will; when He wills it, it occurs. By this we know the error of people who say: "He is competent over what He wills." This is not permissible, because if you say "over what He wills" and front the object, you have restricted His power to what He wills, excluding what He does not will, and this is wrong. He is competent over what He wills and what He does not will, but what Allah wills occurs, and what He does not will does not occur.

Some later scholars said: if you say "He is competent over what He wills," you have agreed with the Qadariyyah, because they say Allah does not will the acts of the servant, and if He does not will them, He has no power over them.

So this phrasing also tends toward the statement of a innovator, the saying of the Qadariyyah. So when you hear someone say "He is competent over what He wills," tell him: "Competent, and competent over what He does not will." You have no right to restrict what Allah the Exalted has left absolute in attribution. Allah the Exalted made it absolute: ﴿and He is over all things competent﴾; do not restrict it.

If someone says: "Given what you have established, how do you answer His saying: ﴿and He is, when He wills, over their gathering competent﴾ [al-Shura 29]?"

We say: the willing here relates to the gathering; that is, when He wills to gather them, He is competent over it and does not fail at it, contrary to those who say He is not able to gather them and denied resurrection. So the restriction by will here applies to the gathering, not to the power.

If someone says: "What do you say about the man who will be the last to enter Paradise, and when Allah says to him: 'This is yours,' Allah says: 'Indeed, over what I will I am competent'" [narrated by Muslim (187/310) from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud]?

We say: yes, here the willing is restricted to a particular act; that is, as if Allah says to him: "When I willed it, I was competent over it," like His saying: ﴿and He is, when He wills, over their gathering competent﴾. The point is that we have no right to restrict what Allah the Mighty and Majestic has left absolute; rather we say: Allah is competent over everything.
